nodes.label: Biographical & literary traditions
nodes.date_label: Ancient roots · Carlyle’s On Heroes 1841 · Strachey 1918
nodes.description: A selective range of life-writing practices: ancient character portraits, private particulars and conversation, heroic interpretation, concentrated literary portraits and debates about evidence and invention. Literary experiments and editorial selection also supply resources for later historical methods.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Thomas Carlyle, On Heroes (1841); Lytton Strachey, Eminent Victorians (1918). Biography does not originate with either writer.

representative_people.context: The opening Heroes lecture gives creative individuals and practical belief a large explanatory role. This is one nineteenth-century strand, not biography’s origin or all Carlyle’s historical writing.
representative_people.works: On Heroes (1841), Lecture I opening (5 May 1840)

representative_people.context: Selects compact portraits using French eloges models and existing biographies. Woolf later praises one royal biography while criticizing another; neither authorial impartiality nor a uniform critical verdict is assumed.
representative_people.works: Eminent Victorians (1918), preface; Queen Victoria and Elizabeth and Essex, evaluated by Woolf (1939)

representative_people.context: Uses minor acts and a portrait analogy to explain a life’s selective treatment of character. One ancient practice, not the origin or entirety of biography.
representative_people.works: Alexander, opening paragraph; archive translation credited to Dryden

representative_people.context: Argues that private particulars can make many lives instructive, while proximity and friendship can both supply and distort information. His moral premise remains situated.
representative_people.works: The Rambler 60 (1750)

representative_people.context: Interweaves letters, recollected conversations and narrative, explicitly adapting Mason’s example. Claims candid portrayal rather than pure praise; actual completeness is not established by that claim.
representative_people.works: Life of Johnson (1791), opening selection in Osgood abridgment (1917)

representative_people.context: Examines verifiable evidence, invention and changing biographical conventions. Differentiates Strachey’s books and asks why failures and humble lives should be excluded; her restricted English canon is not universalized.
representative_people.works: “The Art of Biography” (1939)

representative_people.context: Boswell explicitly names his arrangement of Gray’s life as a model to adapt and enlarge. This records Boswell’s stated debt, not independent reading of Mason.
representative_people.works: Memoirs of Gray, named in Boswell’s opening

representative_people.context: Strachey explicitly values the French eloge tradition as a model for biographical writing. The original eloges were not read in this review.
representative_people.works: Biographical eloges, acknowledged in Eminent Victorians (1918), preface

representative_people.context: Strachey explicitly values the French eloge tradition as a model for biographical writing. The original eloges were not read in this review.
representative_people.works: Biographical eloges, acknowledged in Eminent Victorians (1918), preface

representative_people.context: Strachey acknowledges indispensable information from Cook’s Nightingale biography while using a different scale and angle.
representative_people.works: Life of Florence Nightingale, acknowledged in Strachey’s 1918 postscript

representative_people.context: His abridgment deliberately removes much correspondence, commentary and conversation. Editorial selection changes which Boswell later readers encounter.
representative_people.works: Abridged Life of Johnson, preface dated 28 June 1917

representative_people.context: Bourdieu explicitly uses his challenge to conventionally coherent lives without adopting all his philosophy. The cited literary text remains mediated.
representative_people.works: Le Miroir qui revient (1984), p. 208, cited by Bourdieu (1986)

representative_people.context: Levi uses dialogic and discontinuous literary narration to question a uniformly coherent historical subject. This is a named resource in his 1989 methodological argument, not proof that the novel founded microhistory.
representative_people.works: Tristram Shandy, discussed by Levi (1989)

representative_people.context: Levi uses dialogic and discontinuous literary narration to question a uniformly coherent historical subject. This is a named resource in his 1989 methodological argument, not proof that the novel founded microhistory.
representative_people.works: Jacques le fataliste, discussed by Levi (1989)

nodes.scope_note: Earlier roots and literary practices overlap with modern historical biography without forming one origin story. Plutarch is one ancient example; Johnson’s private lives precede Carlyle’s Heroes. Strachey names particular models and sources, and Woolf distinguishes his achievements and failures. Her English canon is not a universal history of biography. Translations and abridgments mediate the texts encountered here; named literary resources do not by themselves establish a school’s founding.

strands.title: Character and selective lives
strands.focus: Plutarch’s portrait analogy privileges revealing particulars over a full campaign narrative. This is a specific ancient practice, not a timeless division of genres.
strands.works: Alexander, opening

strands.title: Private particulars, conversation and narrative
strands.focus: Johnson defends instructional private detail; Boswell arranges documents and conversation, explicitly adapting Mason. Neither proximity nor a claim to candor guarantees accuracy.
strands.works: Rambler 60 (1750); Life of Johnson (1791), selected opening

strands.title: Creative individuals and historical belief
strands.focus: Carlyle’s lecture opening connects great individuals with historical creation and religious conviction. It does not define all nineteenth-century life writing, or all his own writing.
strands.works: On Heroes (1841), Lecture I opening

strands.title: Compact portraits and acknowledged models
strands.focus: Strachey chooses concentrated portraits, invokes French eloges and uses Cook’s research. Selection is a stated artistic procedure, not representative sampling of the whole age.
strands.works: Eminent Victorians (1918), preface and postscript

strands.title: Checkable evidence and invention
strands.focus: Woolf’s contrasting judgments of Strachey’s royal biographies test how documentary limits constrain imaginative form. Her conclusions remain criticism, not a settled law of biography.
strands.works: The Art of Biography (1939)

strands.title: Discontinuous narration and the coherent self
strands.focus: Levi and Bourdieu use named literary experiments to question retrospective coherence. The novels are resources for later arguments, not automatic origins of historical schools.
strands.works: Levi (1989); Bourdieu (1986), cited literary examples

strands.title: Abridgment and later readers
strands.focus: Osgood explains what his Boswell selection removes. A widely accessible edition is a particular editorial construction of the work.
strands.works: Osgood preface (1917)

nodes.label: Strategic & military scholarship
nodes.date_label: Earlier roots · Clausewitz’s On War 1832 · Delbrück’s volumes 1900–20
nodes.description: Brings strategic reasoning, critical campaign scholarship and the editing of military texts into view. Clausewitz, Jomini, Delbrück, Mahan, Corbett, interwar theorist-historians such as Fuller and Liddell Hart, and the translated Sun Tzu tradition pose different questions about judgment, evidence and the purposes of war. Vegetius’ Latin epitome of earlier military authorities, which he distinguished from histories that recorded only the deeds and outcomes of wars, is an ancient instance of compiling military texts. Professional education and academic inquiry overlap without being identical.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Carl von Clausewitz, On War (1832); Hans Delbrück joins source criticism to analysis of warfare.

representative_people.context: Examines political purpose, passion, chance and friction in an unfinished, posthumously edited work. Strategic reasoning differs from empirical verification of particular campaigns.
representative_people.works: On War (1832); selected passages in Graham translation with later editorial apparatus

representative_people.context: Joins philological criticism to checks of practical possibility, using population evidence and documentary research. Explicitly acknowledges Ranke and Beloch; possible reconstructions are not automatically established events.
representative_people.works: Geschichte der Kriegskunst im Rahmen der politischen Geschichte, four volumes (1900–1920); first preface (1900)

representative_people.context: Proposes explaining sea power within general history and its social, political and economic surroundings. His naval-professional perspective and selected Europe/America scope are explicit.
representative_people.works: The Influence of Sea Power upon History, 1660–1783 (1890), preface

representative_people.context: Treats naval operations within wider maritime coordination of armies, fleets and political purposes. Theory aids education and deliberation; this is a situated British imperial perspective.
representative_people.works: Some Principles of Maritime Strategy (1911), introduction

representative_people.context: Organizes posthumous publication and describes intellectual companionship and assistance from others. Her modest prefatory disclaimer does not make editorial work intellectually empty.
representative_people.works: Preface to On War, 30 June 1832

representative_people.context: Defends strategic principles while insisting that war also turns on morale, judgment and contingencies. His conclusion qualifies a wholly mechanical characterization.
representative_people.works: The Art of War, Mendell/Craighill translation (1862), conclusion

representative_people.context: Traditional attribution of a Chinese strategic text that prioritizes overcoming resistance and preserving forces over repeated destructive combat. Neither a fixed composition date nor a uniform Chinese tradition is asserted.
representative_people.works: The Art of War, Giles translation (1910), chapter III §§1–8

representative_people.context: Makes translation, paragraph arrangement and selective Chinese commentary part of the English text’s reception; his criticism of predecessors remains a contested editorial judgment.
representative_people.works: The Art of War (1910), translator’s preface and commentary

representative_people.context: Proposes and collaborates with Howard on a new Clausewitz translation. Strachan later assesses its modernization; translating does not simply transmit an unchanged meaning.
representative_people.works: With Michael Howard, On War (1976), translation; collaboration documented by Strachan

representative_people.context: Challenges Keegan’s culture/politics opposition while valuing The Face of Battle. Later web corrections are distinguished from the original polemic.
representative_people.works: “John Keegan and the Grand Tradition of Trashing Clausewitz” (1994)

representative_people.context: Collaborates with Paret on translating Clausewitz; readable modern vocabulary is also an object of later interpretive criticism.
representative_people.works: With Peter Paret, On War (1976), translation

representative_people.context: Questions Clausewitz through a cultural account of warfare, as represented in Bassford’s opposing reception. This is distinct from the combat-reconstruction method of his earlier book.
representative_people.works: A History of Warfare (1993), mediated by Bassford (1994)

representative_people.context: Delbrück explicitly credits demographic groundwork while correcting individual estimates. A named methodological resource, not acceptance of every army figure.
representative_people.works: Die Bevölkerung der griechisch-römischen Welt (1886), acknowledged in Delbrück’s 1900 preface

representative_people.context: Compiles earlier authorities (Cato, Celsus, Frontinus, Paternus and imperial constitutions) into what he calls an epitome, and distinguishes such teaching from histories that ‘wrote only the deeds and outcomes of wars’ (the research compiler’s translation of 1.8). Date and published translations not collated.
representative_people.works: Epitoma rei militaris, prologue and 1.8 (Latin text)

representative_people.context: Disputes Delbrück’s criticism of Polybius at Sellasia: textual Sachkritik should not run ahead of topographic survey. He reports that Delbrück changed his view after the plain was shown to be narrower than Delbrück had assumed (1903, Beilage I). Delbrück’s replies are unread.
representative_people.works: Antike Schlachtfelder in Griechenland, vol. I (1903), Beilage I

representative_people.context: Wanted a ‘science of war’ on which a true history of war would rest (‘We do not want drama; we want truth’) and dismissed Clausewitz’s work as ‘a cloud of flame and smoke’ (1926): history used as a base for theory.
representative_people.works: The Foundations of the Science of War (1926), ch. I §1

representative_people.context: A theorist-historian who used history to argue present policy. Howard (1974, as quoted by Strachan) judged The British Way in Warfare ‘brilliant political pamphleteering’; Strachan credits the idea to Corbett and holds Liddell Hart responsible for ‘disseminating’ English-language ‘darkness’ about Clausewitz.
representative_people.works: The Real War (1930); Why Don’t We Learn from History? (1944); The British Way in Warfare, as judged by Howard (1974)

nodes.scope_note: A selective teaching umbrella, weighted toward European and Anglophone scholarship, with a Chinese text and its mediated reception distinguished. Delbrück explicitly uses Ranke, Beloch and biographical research; these roots are not independent of every other historical tradition. Theory does not guarantee successful action. Marie’s editing and later translations are substantive mediation. Corbett writes for an imperial setting; neither that perspective nor Mahan’s national judgments is universalized. Bassford’s later online corrections are not assigned to his 1994 argument. Vegetius distinguishes histories, which wrote only ‘the deeds and outcomes of wars’ (a translation of 1.8), from teaching on military discipline; that ancient distinction is kept rather than merged. Kromayer (1928) observed that officers’ readings of the ancients from Folard onward projected the military theories of their own time.

strands.title: Strategic principles, uncertainty and judgment
strands.focus: Clausewitz’s friction and variable tendencies and Jomini’s qualified rules frame different questions. Neither makes war wholly mechanical.
strands.works: On War (1832), selections; The Art of War (1862 translation), conclusion

strands.title: Editing and translating strategic texts
strands.focus: Marie’s posthumous work and Howard/Paret’s translation expose mediation and interpretive choices, rather than a single transparent text.
strands.works: On War: 1832 preface; 1976 translation

strands.title: Chinese strategic writing and its translation
strands.focus: Giles’s selection and commentary mediate the attributed Sun Tzu text. Overcoming resistance is not synonymous with winning repeated battles; wider Chinese traditions and textual dating need separate inquiry.
strands.works: The Art of War, Giles translation (1910), preface and III §§1–8

strands.title: Documents and practical possibility
strands.focus: Delbrück combines textual criticism with population and physical constraints, explicitly using Beloch and acknowledging Ranke. Possible alternatives remain distinct from proven events.
strands.works: Geschichte der Kriegskunst (1900–1920), first preface

strands.title: Sea power and maritime coordination
strands.focus: Mahan proposes integrating sea power with general history; Corbett distinguishes naval operations from wider maritime strategy. This juxtaposition does not itself establish direct transmission.
strands.works: The Influence of Sea Power (1890), preface; Some Principles (1911), introduction

strands.title: Culture, politics and disputed reception
strands.focus: Keegan’s 1993 challenge and Bassford’s response are an exchange about interpreting Clausewitz. Bassford also values Keegan’s earlier work and acknowledges limits to strategic theory.
strands.works: A History of Warfare (1993), mediated; Bassford polemic (1994)

strands.title: Battlefield survey, numbers and the Delbrück–Kromayer dispute
strands.focus: Grundy’s surveys of Thermopylae, Plataea and Pylos (1892–99) and Kromayer’s expedition to Greek battlefields with General Staff officers (1900) test ancient narratives against terrain; Delbrück’s London lectures (1913) test numbers by comparison across eras, with Moltke’s 1870 deployment as a measure. At Sellasia Delbrück and Kromayer disagreed over Polybius’ reliability and over whether criticism may run ahead of survey; the claim that Delbrück changed his view after Kromayer’s survey is Kromayer’s (1903), and Delbrück’s replies are unread. Kromayer framed the work against Clausewitz’s judgment that ancient military history was the least useful.
strands.works: Grundy, The Great Persian War (1901), preface; Kromayer, Antike Schlachtfelder in Griechenland I (1903), Einleitung and Beilage I; Delbrück, Numbers in History (1913); Clausewitz, On War, II.6

strands.title: Interwar theorist-historians and the uses of history
strands.focus: Fuller wanted a ‘science of war’, called the history of war ‘a great romance’ without one, and dismissed Clausewitz’s work as ‘a cloud of flame and smoke’ (1926). Liddell Hart used history to argue present policy and attacked official history (1930, 1944); Strachan (2002) writes that for him military history was ‘a tool, a tool to communicate ideas about war that had present application’. Howard (1974, as quoted by Strachan) judged The British Way in Warfare ‘brilliant political pamphleteering’, and Strachan credits the idea to Corbett.
strands.works: Fuller, The Foundations of the Science of War (1926), ch. I; Liddell Hart, The Real War (1930) and Why Don’t We Learn from History? (1944); Howard, 1974 Neale Lecture, as quoted by Strachan (2002)

nodes.label: Anthropology & ethnography
nodes.date_label: 1800s roots · Tylor 1871 · Boas 1896 · later revisions
nodes.description: Ethnographic observation, comparison, historical reconstruction and interpretation generate different accounts of social life. Exchanges with historians involve particular works and methods; colonial knowledge, research authority and the representation of cultures are contested within and beyond the discipline.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Distinct stages include Tylor and Frazer, Boasian historical particularism, and later interpretive anthropology associated with Geertz. These do not form one continuous theory.

representative_people.context: Studies acquired culture through comparative stages and survivals; the hierarchy is his proposition, not the atlas’s classification of peoples.
representative_people.works: Primitive Culture (1871; consulted 1920 edition)

representative_people.context: Reconstructs the Nemi priesthood by comparisons of rituals and beliefs, while acknowledging that inference is not demonstration.
representative_people.works: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (1890; consulted 1894 printing)

representative_people.context: Challenges the inference of identical causes from similar customs; retains comparison after historical investigation establishes comparability.
representative_people.works: “The Limitations of the Comparative Method of Anthropology” (1896)

representative_people.context: Interprets situated public meanings; thick description requires context and argument, not mere descriptive abundance.
representative_people.works: The Interpretation of Cultures (1973), especially “Thick Description”; “Deep Play” (1972); Negara (1980)

representative_people.context: Scott explicitly takes up her emphasis on the meanings of women’s activities within social interaction.
representative_people.works: “The Uses and Abuses of Anthropology: Reflections on Feminism and Cross-Cultural Understanding” (1980)

representative_people.context: Māori scholarship joins historical interpretation and material-culture research; an earlier trajectory distinct from later methodological manifestos.
representative_people.works: The Coming of the Maori (1949)

representative_people.context: Anthropologist and collaborator in a southern Yukon life-history project; the elders are knowledge producers, not anonymous source material.
representative_people.works: Life Lived Like a Story, with Angela Sidney, Kitty Smith and Annie Ned (1990)

representative_people.context: Connects close observation, social organization and recorded statements to an account of participants’ perspectives.
representative_people.works: Argonauts of the Western Pacific (1922), introduction

representative_people.context: Asks how recurrent activities sustain social relations; functional unity is offered as a working hypothesis.
representative_people.works: “On the Concept of Function in Social Science” (1935); Structure and Function in Primitive Society (1952)

representative_people.context: Connects historical understanding and anthropological translation; this position had critics within anthropology.
representative_people.works: The Sanusi of Cyrenaica (1949); Essays in Social Anthropology (1962)

representative_people.context: Gift obligations connect social relations, law and economy; the reading should retain the essay’s publication context.
representative_people.works: “Essai sur le don” / The Gift (1925)

representative_people.context: A major contextual reading in comparative cultural inquiry; later feminist reassessments examine her place in the canon.
representative_people.works: Patterns of Culture (1934)

representative_people.context: Investigates adolescent life and cultural upbringing in Samoa; the listed evidence does not settle later disputes about her findings.
representative_people.works: Coming of Age in Samoa (1928)

representative_people.context: Develops questions about ritual, liminality and communitas through Ndembu research.
representative_people.works: The Ritual Process (1969)

representative_people.context: Relates structures and events through Pacific histories; particular interpretations remain debated.
representative_people.works: Islands of History (1985)

representative_people.context: Studies colonial knowledge practices; his earlier exchange with social historians is documented separately from the 1996 collection.
representative_people.works: Colonialism and Its Forms of Knowledge (1996); Cohn’s earlier intervention discussed by Medick (1987)

representative_people.context: Historicizes religion and the conditions that authorize symbolic practices; his specific Geertz engagement is not a dismissal of the entire corpus.
representative_people.works: Genealogies of Religion (1993), chapter 1

representative_people.works: With George E. Marcus, ed., Writing Culture (1986)

representative_people.context: Coedits the ethnographic writing debate; joint editorship does not make every chapter a shared argument.
representative_people.works: With James Clifford, ed., Writing Culture (1986)

representative_people.context: Questions how research discourse places interlocutors in another time despite the shared time of communication.

nodes.scope_note: A selective teaching map of sociocultural anthropology and ethnography, not all anthropology. Evolutionary, historical, functional, structural, interpretive, feminist and critical inquiries overlap without forming a single succession. Chinese research, Māori scholarship and collaborative histories have distinct trajectories. These approaches and rosters neither establish exclusive membership nor turn anthropology into one transferable theory.

nodes.label: National & imperial narratives
nodes.date_label: 1800s–1900s · nation-building, empire and counter-histories
nodes.description: National and imperial histories join source work to competing accounts of peoples, states, liberty and civilization. Michelet, Macaulay and Bancroft differ in method and purpose; colonial hierarchies, liberation histories and critiques of nationalist exclusions remain in tension.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: A broad context of historical production, not one school: nation-building, colonial institutions, and resistance generate different and often conflicting projects.

representative_people.context: Interweaves archives, geography, cultural life and a self-forming French people. The 1869 preface admires and disputes Thierry, credits Vico and reflects on the historian’s participation. His revolutionary history later becomes Barthes’s narrative example.
representative_people.works: Histoire de France (1833–1867), preface of 1869; Histoire de la Révolution française (1847–1853); later analysis in Barthes (1968)

representative_people.context: Connects constitutional settlement, commerce, empire and everyday manners while acknowledging crimes and failures. His education minute argues for a hierarchy of knowledge and English-trained imperial intermediaries. Distinct from Catharine Macaulay.
representative_people.works: The History of England from the Accession of James II, volume I, chapter I; “Minute on Indian Education” (2 February 1835)

representative_people.context: Combines comparative documentary criticism with a story of liberty developing from colonial institutions. His professed impartiality does not establish equal representation of all inhabitants.
representative_people.works: History of the United States / History of the Colonization of the United States, volume I (first-edition preface 1834; consulted 17th edition 1859)

representative_people.context: Uses Michelet and Thierry to question narrative transparency and examine how writing signifies historical reality. These readings do not dismiss all national histories or independently refute their factual claims.
representative_people.works: “The Discourse of History” (1967); “The Reality Effect” (1968)

representative_people.context: Michelet admires his national narrative while criticizing an explanatory commitment to the permanence of races; this is an attributed reception, not a reading of Thierry’s original work.
representative_people.works: Histoire de la Conquête de l’Angleterre par les Normands (1825), as discussed by Michelet and Kaplan

representative_people.context: Michelet names his account of humanity making itself as a central resource; this does not derive all national history from Vico.
representative_people.works: Scienza nuova, translated by Michelet in 1827 and recalled in his 1869 preface

representative_people.context: Michelet quotes him against explanations resting on fixed innate differences, in favor of investigating social and moral circumstances. Original Mill passage uncollated.

representative_people.context: Questions both colonialist and bourgeois-nationalist elitism, while recognizing overlap between popular and elite politics.
representative_people.works: “On Some Aspects of the Historiography of Colonial India” (1982)

representative_people.context: Questions modular accounts of nationalism and distinguishes colonial material and spiritual domains through a particular Bengal argument.
representative_people.works: Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World (1986); The Nation and Its Fragments (1993), “Whose Imagined Community?”

representative_people.context: Attacks colonial claims to civilization and examines damage to the colonizer; distinct from an economic explanation of abolition.
representative_people.works: Discourse on Colonialism (1950; revised 1955)

representative_people.context: Recasts the Haitian Revolution through enslaved people, leadership and revolutionary conflict; national emancipation is not a uniform explanatory model.
representative_people.works: The Black Jacobins (1938)

representative_people.context: Reinterprets slavery and abolition through capitalism and empire; his specific economic propositions remain disputed.
representative_people.works: Capitalism and Slavery (1944)

representative_people.context: Regional reconstruction and a collaborative continental history provide alternatives to one national master narrative; African historical production does not begin with postwar institutions.
representative_people.works: History of the Southern Luo I (1967); “Description of the Project,” General History of Africa I (1981)

representative_people.context: Examines national consciousness, statehood and power. Paddock’s specific criticism questions organic unity and the centrality of the state; the original books remain uncollated here.
representative_people.works: Weltbürgertum und Nationalstaat (1907); Die Ideen der Staatsräson (1924); Die Entstehung des Historismus (1936), through Paddock

representative_people.context: Argues that the national “island story” taught in schools and universities must be rethought through the frame of empire; Macaulay and Son (2012) reads Macaulay as a liberal imperialist.
representative_people.works: Civilising Subjects (2002); “A Response to the Commentators” (2003); Macaulay and Son (2012)

representative_people.context: Treats national and ethnic pasts as raw material for ideology and asks historians to resist myths, anachronism and invented continuities as they form (1993).
representative_people.works: With Terence Ranger, The Invention of Tradition (1983); “The New Threat to History” (1993)

representative_people.context: Studies Jadunath Sarkar’s “imperial liberalism” and the public quarrels through which historians in colonial India shaped the discipline, as the publisher and Joshi report (2015).
representative_people.works: The Calling of History: Sir Jadunath Sarkar and His Empire of Truth (2015)

nodes.scope_note: A teaching umbrella, not a single national or imperial doctrine. Cultural and documentary inquiry coexist with narratives of progress. Colonial policy, anticolonial histories, subaltern criticism and collective African projects have different aims; no universal nationalist origin or automatic emancipation is implied.

strands.title: Constitutional settlement, commerce and empire
strands.focus: Macaulay’s prospectus links liberties and prosperity to imperial power but also names crimes, Irish oppression and failures. Manners and material life form part of his project.

strands.title: Documentary criticism and republican beginnings

nodes.label: Economic history
nodes.date_label: 1800s roots · Economic History Society founded 1926 · multiple paradigms
nodes.description: Competing explanations investigate institutions, prices and incomes, class relations, growth, households, slavery and empire. Serial history and cliometrics use different questions and models. North’s incentives differ from Polanyi’s historically specific market society; Gerschenkron questions repeated industrial paths; de Vries connects household labor and demand; Pomeranz combines regional comparison with global resource relations.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Nineteenth-century roots include classical political economy and the German historical school (e.g. Schmoller); twentieth-century examples include R. H. Tawney, Eileen Power, and Douglass North. Further approaches include Polanyi, The Great Transformation (1944); Gerschenkron, Economic Backwardness in Historical Perspective (1962 collection); de Vries’s industrious-revolution article (1994); Pomeranz, The Great Divergence (2000). E. A. Wrigley: People, Cities and Wealth (1987); Continuity, Chance and Change (1988).

representative_people.context: Treats institutions, law and custom as part of economic explanation; his dispute with Menger concerns how abstraction should proceed.
representative_people.works: “Zur Methodologie der Staats- und Sozialwissenschaften” (1883; English translation 2021)

representative_people.context: Agrarian reconstruction tests legal and economic explanations against regional and documentary differences; religion/capitalism adds ethical and causal questions.
representative_people.works: The Agrarian Problem in the Sixteenth Century (1912); Religion and the Rise of Capitalism (1926)

representative_people.context: Combines medieval institutional research with personal reconstruction; distinguishes kinds of evidence and acknowledges editorial and documentary collaboration.

representative_people.context: Develops institutional explanations involving rules, incentives, learning and historical paths; revises assumptions of earlier neoclassical economic history.
representative_people.works: “Economic Performance through Time” (1993 Nobel lecture)

representative_people.context: Counts paid and unpaid production while distinguishing household forms, class and marital position. Her account of capitalist change retains maternalist assumptions and contested medieval comparisons.

representative_people.context: Explains changes in women’s work and wages through training, household organization and industrial/agrarian change. Her qualified optimistic interpretation differs from Clark’s longer decline account.
representative_people.works: Women Workers and the Industrial Revolution, 1750–1850 (1930); reprint preface (1969, signed 1968)

representative_people.context: Production relations and class conflict shape the effects of trade. The reply to Sweezy preserves interaction, contested historical stages and a concession about insufficient evidence.
representative_people.works: Studies in the Development of Capitalism (1946); reply to Sweezy in “The Transition from Feudalism to Capitalism” (1950), pp. 157–167

representative_people.context: Differential movements of prices, production and income support conjunctural inquiry. His 1956 introduction stresses uneven crises; later debate tests the model’s conditions and distinguishes his experiments from serial routines.
representative_people.works: Esquisse du mouvement des prix et des revenus en France au XVIIIe siècle (1933); La crise de l’économie française à la fin de l’Ancien Régime et au début de la Révolution (1944); “Panoramas de la crise” (1956)

representative_people.context: Sociologist and economist whose methodological polemic challenged conventional historical explanation.
representative_people.works: “Méthode historique et science sociale” (1903)

representative_people.context: Comparative and economic historian in dialogue with the founders.
representative_people.works: “De la méthode comparative en histoire” (1923)

representative_people.context: Quantitative economic historian whose later research connects population, nutrition, physiology and growth. The cited lecture does not verify his earlier slavery estimates.
representative_people.works: “Economic Growth, Population Theory, and Physiology: The Bearing of Long-Term Processes on the Making of Economic Policy” (1993 Nobel lecture)

representative_people.context: Treats the market-regulated economy as historically specific; uses anthropology to examine reciprocity and redistribution and challenges Smith’s barter narrative.

representative_people.context: Argues that later industrialization can differ in technology, scale, banks and state action; England’s path is not an automatic template.

representative_people.context: Relates expanding demand to household labor and resource reallocation before industrialization; considers negotiation and unequal interests within households. With Ad van der Woude, presented the Dutch Republic as 'the first modern economy' (1997).

representative_people.context: Distinguishes arguments about industrial finance and abolition; both remain contested.
representative_people.works: Capitalism and Slavery (1944)

representative_people.context: Challenges the decline thesis in abolition debates; his position is not a consensus of the field.

representative_people.context: With his co-author, critically rereads Labrousse’s experimental construction of evidence and its narrowed serial reception. This is neither rejection of every model nor unqualified defense.

representative_people.context: Comparative peasant movements join production, conflict, political organization and belief; outcomes and evidence differ across periods. Acknowledges Bloch while criticizing particular Power and Duby emphases.

strands.focus: Pomeranz challenges Huang’s involution thesis and compares household labor with industrious change. Huang’s 2002 review argues that output growth can conceal diminishing returns to work; Pomeranz’s reply opening rejects one necessary path to development.

strands.focus: Pomeranz links accessible energy and colonial resources to relief of land constraints. Huang questions whether coal availability explains divergence or industrial demand explains coal development. The exchange leaves causal weights open to examination.

nodes.scope_note: Distinguish the relevant historians, evidence, and mechanisms before claiming an influence. A subject shared with Annales or Marxism is not itself an explanation. Institutional approaches are not interchangeable, and consumption does not replace production. Household interests can conflict. Gerschenkron’s European comparison and Pomeranz’s Eurasian argument have distinct scales; neither is a universal development law. Furtado’s demand analysis and Novais’s structural criticism offer a Brazilian exchange, with primary-edition and numerical verification limits retained.

nodes.label: Military history
nodes.date_label: Earlier roots · Howard 1961 · Keegan 1976 · multiple paradigms
nodes.description: Studies campaigns and combat alongside institutions, societies, maritime power, gender and remembrance. Ancient historians such as Thucydides and Polybius already wrote about testing reports of battle, terrain and military experience; they are precursors of the genre, not its founders. From about 1900 the field was practised in archive-based campaign and army histories, university lectureships and chairs (Oxford 1905 and 1909), official histories of the world wars and an American society (1933) and journal (1937; renamed Military Affairs in 1941); much of this work was written by or for officers. Howard’s contextual reconstruction, Keegan’s critical study of battle and debates over military revolutions supply different methods and explanations. Source access, narrative framing and geographic scope shape their claims.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Ancient precursors include Thucydides and Polybius on testing reports, terrain and experience; modern roots include Clausewitz, On War (1832), and Hans Delbrück; from c. 1900, Charles Oman and J. W. Fortescue wrote archive-based campaign and army history, Grundy and Kromayer surveyed ancient battlefields, and general-staff and cabinet historical sections wrote official histories of the world wars (Edmonds from 1922; the US Army’s World War II series, such as Matloff and Snell, 1953); later examples: Michael Howard, John Keegan, and Joanna Bourke.

nodes.scope_note: A research field with overlapping objects, not one school or a progression that supersedes campaign history. Delbrück, campaign and army historians, official historians and strategic writers supply distinct resources; military historians also reinterpret and criticize them. Keegan’s restricted battle definition leaves much colonial and guerrilla experience outside its frame. European military-revolution debates extend to overseas encounters without representing the whole world’s military historiography. Bourke, Winter and Nell retain distinct questions about bodies, mourning and recognition. Scholarly collaboration, library work, editing and archival limits are part of the field’s production. Ancient writers who narrated and judged wars (Thucydides, Polybius, Arrian) are selected precursors. The selected ancient passages document statements about testimony, terrain and experience. Separately checked modern passages discuss these authors; Kromayer explicitly engages Polybius’ criticism of Ephorus. These examples do not establish continuous transmission. Clausewitz ranked ancient military history the least useful while allowing instructive exceptions. Official and semi-official histories were written from privileged records, read in proof by participants or framed by sponsoring institutions; Liddell Hart criticised them in the period. Karsten (1984), describing the ‘new’ military history, concedes that ‘some scholars explored such questions in the past’. The selection before 1960 concentrates on British, American and German scholarship; other historiographies of war are not surveyed here.

strands.title: Campaign reconstruction and documentary limits
strands.focus: Howard, Tuchman and Wedgwood connect decisions and circumstances through different narrative practices. Source access and explanatory selection remain objects of criticism.
strands.works: The Franco-Prussian War (1961); The Guns of August (1962); The Thirty Years War (1938)

strands.title: Combat experience and critical testimony
strands.focus: Keegan joins questions about bodies and behavior to criticism of memoirs, rhetoric and physical possibility. His selected battle frame does not represent all forms of war.
strands.works: The Face of Battle (1976), available excerpt

strands.title: War studies, research and teaching
strands.focus: Howard became lecturer in military studies at King’s in 1953; a new War Studies programme was approved in 1955. His King’s work combines historical study with wider social, ethical and political inquiry. Earlier work and institutional support included Laughton’s naval history, Maurice’s chair of military studies (1927; the department closed in 1948), and C. K. Webster and Hancock, whose official-history work had drawn them to war as a field. Morgan-Owen and Finch (2022) call the story of Howard rescuing the subject from an academic wilderness one he ‘consciously cultivated’. Library access, publishing and translation collaboration form part of the research setting.
strands.works: The Franco-Prussian War (1961); War in European History (1976)

strands.title: Naval history within wider explanation
strands.focus: Sea power and military/naval coordination widen a land-centered account. Mahan and Corbett state different purposes from a simple naval chronicle.
strands.works: Mahan (1890), preface; Corbett (1911), introduction

strands.title: Military revolutions: causes and chronology
strands.focus: Roberts, Parker, Rogers, Black and Lynn debate timing, mechanisms and evidence. Their accounts do not form one settled technological explanation.
strands.works: The Military Revolution Debate (1995), introduction

strands.title: Finance, bargaining and geographic scope
strands.focus: Fiscal bargaining and overseas comparisons complicate a universal route from weapons to centralized power. The selected debate remains weighted toward European questions.
strands.works: The Military Revolution Debate (1995), introduction

strands.title: Bodies, injury and masculinity
strands.focus: Bourke examines men’s bodies and wartime masculinity. This question differs from strategic success or adding women to a roster.
strands.works: Dismembering the Male (1996)

strands.title: Remembrance, mourning and recognition
strands.focus: Winter examines forms of mourning; Nell recovers Black military service from patriotic exclusion. These different projects broaden whose war is remembered.
strands.works: Sites of Memory, Sites of Mourning (1995); The Colored Patriots (1855)

strands.title: Cultural explanations and their critics
strands.focus: Keegan’s later account and Bassford’s opposition distinguish cultural interpretation from the earlier reconstruction of combat. Political purpose and culture need not be mutually exclusive.
strands.works: A History of Warfare (1993), mediated; Bassford (1994)

strands.title: Recruitment as labor and household strategy
strands.focus: Lucassen and Zürcher compare state recruitment options with recruits’ and households’ responses. Pay and freedom vary independently; different systems coexist. Their explicit use of Tilly connects fiscal capacity to recruitment and resistance.
strands.works: “Conscription as Military Labour” (1998), 405–419

strands.title: Official and semi-official history and its critics
strands.focus: General-staff and cabinet historical sections wrote large histories of the world wars from privileged records. Edmonds’s British volumes (from 1922) were ‘based on the British official records’, written partly for ‘students at military schools’ and read in proof by officers who took part. Morison’s naval history was commissioned with full records access yet declared ‘in no sense an official history’ (1947). In the US Army’s series, Matloff and Snell, formerly instructors in history and English respectively and both wartime servicemen, joined the project in 1946; their volume’s foreword, by the Chief of Military History, asked readers to see its controversies as differences ‘among comrades in arms’ (1953), and its preface credits Helen McShane Bailey’s knowledge of the War Department’s records and Evelyn Cooper’s statistics. Liddell Hart attacked documentary and ‘camouflaged’ history (1930, 1944). During and after the Second World War official commissions drew academic historians to war (Hancock and Gowing from 1941, Webster and Frankland from 1950, Howard from 1959), under closure rules and secrecy. Later studies of the genre are unread here, and the German and French official histories are known only from period mentions.
strands.works: Edmonds, Military Operations, France and Belgium, 1914, vol. I (1922), preface; Liddell Hart, The Real War (1930), preface, and Why Don’t We Learn from History? (1944); Morison, Operations in North African Waters (1947), foreword and introduction; Matloff and Snell, Strategic Planning for Coalition Warfare, 1941–1942 (1953), foreword and preface; Hancock and Gowing, British War Economy (1949); Howard, Grand Strategy, vol. IV (1972)

strands.title: Campaign and army history as scholarship, c. 1898–1950
strands.focus: Oman’s art-of-war volume (1898) and Peninsular War (1902) worked from chronicles, Record Office papers and passages omitted from printed dispatches, treated veterans’ memoirs with caution and walked battlefields. Fortescue, a civilian, wrote the army’s history as political as well as military history (1899) and distrusted regimental histories; his 1914 definition held that ‘below a certain stage of civilisation, there can be no military history’, a boundary that bears on the field’s geographic scope. Parker’s preface (1928) proposes an institutional history of the Roman legions’ organisation, recruitment and service; the abbreviation list shows extensive inscription corpora, and the body is unread. Kromayer and Veith’s preface (1928) adds strategy and tactics to the antiquarian study of ancient armies and excludes the Orient, Carthage, Gauls and Germans. Howard (1961, as reported by Kitchen and Mitchell and by Strachan) later named regimental ‘nursery history’ and the historian’s duty to examine its ‘myth’.
strands.works: Oman, A History of the Art of War: The Middle Ages (1898) and A History of the Peninsular War, vol. I (1902), prefaces; Fortescue, A History of the British Army, vols. I–II (1899), preface, and Military History (1914); Parker, The Roman Legions (1928); Kromayer and Veith, Heerwesen und Kriegführung der Griechen und Römer (1928); Howard, ‘The Use and Abuse of Military History’ (1961 lecture; 1962)

strands.title: Chairs, journals and the soldier-scholar before 1960
strands.focus: In the British institutions examined here, university teaching developed alongside officer education. Oxford made military history a special subject after the South African War, created a lectureship in 1905 and a chair in 1909, whose first holder, Spenser Wilkinson, called military history ‘the effort to understand war’; the chair, vacant from 1939, went to Cyril Falls in 1946 rather than Liddell Hart. Trinity College, Cambridge, appointed Fortescue its first lecturer in military history in 1913. At King’s College London Frederick Maurice held a chair of military studies from 1927; the department closed in 1948. In the United States the American Military History Foundation was incorporated in 1933 after discussions among ‘military and civilian archival personnel’; its journal (1937) became Military Affairs in 1941 and nearly collapsed in 1957. Strachan (2002) calls Liddell Hart and Falls ‘in many ways more a journalist than an academic’ and writes that before Howard’s appointment almost nobody who studied the history of war had not experienced it.
strands.works: Wilkinson, The University and the Study of War (1909); Fortescue, Military History (1914), lecture I; Maurice, ‘On the Uses of the Study of War’ (1927), as quoted by Morgan-Owen and Finch; Society for Military History chronology (1933–69 entries)

strands.title: War, state and society before the ‘new military history’
strands.focus: Wilkinson’s inaugural lecture (1909) held that ‘as the State is, so will its army be’ and that in war ‘the architectonic art is policy or politics, not strategy or generalship’. Maurice (1927, as quoted by Morgan-Owen and Finch) counted statecraft, economics, raw materials, science, industry and civilian morale as of ‘prime importance’ to the study of war. Hancock, editing the civil official histories, treated the armed forces as ‘no more than the cutting edge of the nation at war’ (as quoted by the same authors). Roberts (1955) proposed tactical change with wider institutional effects. Quincy Wright’s foreword (1942) describes a study of war begun at the University of Chicago in 1926 that involved ‘over fifty studies by research assistants and members of the faculty’; only the foreword is read. Karsten (1984) calls such questions the ‘new’ military history while conceding that ‘some scholars explored such questions in the past’. Hintze, Vagts, Ritter and Ropp are not yet read for this entry.
strands.works: Wilkinson (1909); Maurice, inaugural lecture (1927); Wright, A Study of War (1942), foreword; Hancock and Gowing, British War Economy (1949); Roberts, ‘The Military Revolution, 1560–1660’ (1955 lecture); Karsten (1984), opening

strands.title: Ancient historians on testimony, terrain and experience
strands.focus: Thucydides tests eyewitness accounts against one another and says Spartan secrecy and bragging prevent accurate numbers at Mantinea. Polybius requires the study of documents, the survey of places and political experience, holds that no one without experience of war can write well about it, and judges Ephorus’ land battles by the ground; his polemic is also self-promotion. Arrian prefers Ptolemy and Aristobulus because they served on the campaign. Grundy (1911) calls Thucydides’ narrative ‘in the main a military history’ subordinated to political teaching, and Kromayer (1903) adopts and qualifies Polybius’ criticism of Ephorus. Delbrück (1913, p. 16) asks: ‘Ought we to believe what Caesar informs us of concerning the gigantic armies of the Gauls, whose conquest is his glory, since we have now seen that neither Napoleon nor Frederick in this respect is to be trusted?’; Caesar’s text itself was not read. Herodotus and Xenophon appear only through modern critics: Delbrück (1913) notes that Herodotus wrote ‘forty or fifty years after the events’, Grundy (1901) that in military matters he ‘seems to have possessed little, if any, special knowledge’, and Kromayer (1903, p. 93) finds Xenophon’s account of Mantinea one-sided. These writers are precursors of a genre, not a single origin of the field.
strands.works: Thucydides, History 1.22, 5.68; Polybius, Histories 12.25e–28a, 3.33, 3.48; Arrian, Anabasis, preface; Grundy (1901), preface, and (1911), pp. 7–9; Kromayer (1903), pp. 93–96; Delbrück, Numbers in History (1913), pp. 8–10, 16

coverage.basis: Reviewed through 2000 in the original 1920–2000 experiment. Later work is not yet surveyed for this entry; selected later interventions, where present, are dated individually.

chronology.label: Ancient precursors; selected military-history scholarship from c. 1900; later interventions distinguished
chronology.selection_note: Selected contributions and witnesses, not a field origin, lifespan or complete history. Ancient precursors are context, dated only to the century; modern scholarship from c. 1900 is a selected cluster, not a foundation date.

events.label: Polybius, Histories (12.25e–28a; 3.33, 3.48)

continuation.basis: The field is older and broader than these selected works; ancient precursors are not its beginning, and no researched universal interval is proposed.

chronology.interpretation: Use dated works with an explicit selective scope. Thucydides, Polybius and Arrian are context: precursors of the genre, placed only by century, not a lineage or the field’s first years. Oman, Fortescue, Delbrück, Grundy and Kromayer (1898–1903) are a selected cluster of modern scholarly work, not a foundation date; Kromayer’s 1900 expedition is context for his 1903 volume. Official and semi-official histories (Edmonds 1922, Morison 1947, Matloff and Snell 1953) and the American society and journal (1933, 1937) are selected later events, not the beginnings of official or American military history. Howard 1961 and Keegan 1976 are contributions to an older field, not its first and last years. Later memoir dates are evidence dates, not new personal interventions by Howard.
retain: Multiple paradigms, colonial/guerrilla limits of Keegan's frame, and collaboration/editorial labour.
Ancient precursors are not a continuous lineage; the modern selection concentrates on British, American and German scholarship.
unresolved: If phase bars are useful, define their subject and geography; do not construct a universal beginning from the oldest source in this selection.
Composition dates of the ancient works were not checked; they are placed by century only. Caesar, Herodotus and Xenophon are discussed only through modern critics and are not dated here.

nodes.label: Political history
nodes.date_label: 1800s roots · Namier 1929 · Hunt 1984 · multiple paradigms
nodes.description: Examines institutions, diplomacy and struggles over power through different methods. Namier reconstructs parliamentary connections; Benson studies voters; Tilly investigates collective claims; Hunt joins political symbols and social identities. Hill, Dorothy Thompson and Flexner examine radical and rights politics, while Guha and Cooper investigate insurgency and labor under colonial rule. These approaches overlap without replacing all earlier political history.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Ranke is one major nineteenth-century root. Later examples: Lewis Namier, Charles Tilly, and Lynn Hunt’s Politics, Culture, and Class (1984). Further contexts: Namier (1929), Flexner (1959), William Appleman Williams (1959), Hill (1972), Guha (1983), Tilly (1986) and Cooper (1996).

representative_people.works: Visions of the People (1991); 'The Constitution and the Narrative Structure of Victorian Politics' (1996); The State of Freedom (2013)

representative_people.context: Politics and the People (1993): the public political sphere narrowed between 1832 and 1867 as 'the official political subject was redefined in the image of print' (p. 107, as quoted by Tilly); Re-reading the Constitution (1996) gathered the new political history.
representative_people.works: Politics and the People (1993); ed., Re-reading the Constitution (1996)

representative_people.context: Speaking for the People (1998) against 'the rise of class politics' and 'the triumph of party', for place and gender; with Taylor, the critique of 'electoral sociology' (1997); the hustings and the platform (2006; 2009); a 'conservative' rather than 'liberal' modernity (2011).
representative_people.works: Party, State and Society (ed. with Taylor, 1997); Speaking for the People (1998); Electing Our Masters (2009); 'Paternalism, Class, and the British Path to Modernity' (2011)

nodes.scope_note: Diplomatic, institutional, social, and cultural political histories persist and interact; the field did not disappear with the rise of social history. Distinguish institutional elites, electoral categories, popular organization and colonial subjects. Cultural political history can retain social and quantitative evidence; attention to popular action does not make all movements democratic. Regional examples are selective, not a globally complete political canon.

strands.title: Archives, government and religious authority
strands.focus: Ranke’s church/state inquiry and Cam’s medieval local institutions use historical records for different political problems; neither alone founded all source criticism.
strands.works: History of the Popes (1834–1836); Liberties and Communities in Medieval England (1944)

strands.title: Parliamentary connections and collective biography
strands.focus: Reconstruct actors’ social and political connections; the institutional focus raises questions about ideology and people excluded from parliamentary participation.
strands.works: The Structure of Politics at the Accession of George III (1929)

strands.title: Voters and competing group explanations
strands.focus: Benson tests class-centered interpretations against ethnic and religious voting patterns in New York; this is a local historical argument, not a universal electoral rule.
strands.works: The Concept of Jacksonian Democracy (1961)

strands.title: Radical ideas and popular political action
strands.focus: Compare religious radicalism, Chartist participation and colonial peasant insurgency without making one a derivative instance of another.
strands.works: The World Turned Upside Down (1972); The Chartists (1984); Elementary Aspects (1983)

strands.title: Rights movements and political inclusion
strands.focus: Sustained organization for women’s rights is part of political history; it is not merely an appendix to histories of officeholders. Scott’s studies of French feminists and the parity movement, known through her reviewers, examine claims to inclusion caught between the abstract individual and sexual difference.
strands.works: Century of Struggle (1959)

strands.title: Collective claims and governing work
strands.focus: Tilly connects performances and repertoires with state/economic change; Cooper asks how colonial labor categories govern social relations. Their regional units and explanations differ.
strands.works: The Contentious French (1986); Decolonization and African Society (1996)

strands.title: Political rhetoric, symbols and social identities
strands.focus: Hunt uses Geertz in an analysis of revolutionary authority and joins symbolic practices with the sociology of political actors.
strands.works: Politics, Culture, and Class in the French Revolution (1984)

strands.title: Diplomacy, conflict and expansion
strands.focus: Narrative accounts of political choices differ from Williams’s interpretation of ideology, political economy and American expansion; diplomatic history contains disagreement.
strands.works: The Guns of August (1962); The King’s Peace and The King’s War; The Tragedy of American Diplomacy (1959)

strands.title: Radical milieus, hostile sources and disputed labels
strands.focus: Davis questions inherited Ranter accounts; Thompson defends a historical milieu; Scott stresses anachronism and Smith disputes both sides’ handling of evidence and theology. These are different positions, not an adjudicated consensus.
strands.works: The World Turned Upside Down (1972); “On the Rant” and correspondence (1987)

strands.title: Local government, record production and representation
strands.focus: Cam’s inquiry connects the making of records, local courts and parliamentary representation. Documentary criticism and inferences about ordinary lives remain distinct tasks.
strands.works: Cam, Studies in the Hundred Rolls (1921), Liberties and Communities (1944), “Stubbs Seventy Years after” (1948)

strands.title: Narrative, motives and contemporary uncertainty
strands.focus: Wedgwood reconstructs decisions without giving actors knowledge of their outcome. Woolrych also asks what this approach leaves unexplained about allegiance and regional differences.
strands.works: The King’s Peace (1955); The King’s War (1958), prefaces discussed by Woolrych (1998)

strands.title: Narrative synthesis and specialist collaboration
strands.focus: Tuchman’s account of producing A Distant Mirror identifies research, medieval advice and editing. These contributions support a synthesis whose event selection and explanatory claims remain open to criticism.
strands.works: A Distant Mirror (1978), acknowledgments and foreword

strands.title: Political ideas in different social situations
strands.focus: Wood questions applying Namier’s skepticism about ideas to revolutionary America. His reading of Bailyn connects changing beliefs with social circumstances and unintended outcomes; it does not make all political action a deliberate pursuit of abstract principles.
strands.works: Namier, “Human Nature in Politics” (1955/2000); Wood, “Rhetoric and Reality” (1966/1968), 69–78

strands.title: Press freedom and institutional dependence
strands.focus: Goldman traces how municipal protection, financing and censorship shaped political printing. Public controversy emerged through conflicts among editors and authorities, rather than automatically following a declaration of press freedom.
strands.works: “Libertad de imprenta” (2000), 10–15

strands.title: Public spaces and competing explanations
strands.focus: Goldman uses a plural account of public spaces. Sábato asks whether the collection’s cultural emphasis loses explanatory specificity and overlooks republican currents or differences among cases, while recognizing its comparative value.
strands.works: Los espacios públicos en Iberoamérica (1998); Goldman and Sábato (2000)

strands.title: The new political history of Britain, 1993–2011
strands.focus: After the Social History round on Stedman Jones (1992–93), British political history took the linguistic turn and argued with it. Vernon's Politics and the People (1993) held that between the Reform Acts 'the official political subject was redefined in the image of print' and the public sphere narrowed (p. 107, as quoted by Tilly); his Re-reading the Constitution (1996) gathered Epstein, Wahrman, Joyce, Antony Taylor and Anna Clark under 'new narratives'. Vernon credited Epstein's late-1980s articles, subsequently collected in Radical Expression (1994), as inspirational 'for those like myself who followed into the field' of 'the new cultural history of British politics' (2004). Lawrence and Taylor's Party, State and Society (1997) set out to 'examine critically "electoral sociology"' (as quoted by LoPatin), and Lawrence's Speaking for the People (1998) questioned 'the rise of class politics' and 'the triumph of party' for the politics of place and gender; Vernon found it 'ambitious, but ultimately flawed' (1999) and Lawrence answered, in a response posted in 2010, that 'realist' and 'constructivist' approaches must be combined. Electing Our Masters (2009) followed the hustings and the platform; in 2011 Lawrence argued for a 'conservative' rather than 'liberal' modernity. Positions within one field, not a school; the debate entry languages_of_class holds the exchanges.
strands.works: Vernon, Politics and the People (1993), ed., Re-reading the Constitution (1996); Epstein, Radical Expression (1994); Lawrence and Taylor, eds, Party, State and Society (1997); Lawrence, Speaking for the People (1998), Electing Our Masters (2009), 'Paternalism, Class, and the British Path to Modernity' (2011); Vernon's review and Lawrence's response (Reviews in History, 1999/2010)
