nodes.label: Psychohistory / psychoanalytic history
nodes.date_label: Earlier roots; postwar growth · 1950s–80s
nodes.description: A contested range of historical uses of psychological interpretation: psychosocial life studies, psychoanalytically informed contextual history and theories of childrearing and collective fantasy. Disagreements concern sources, explanatory scale, historical variability and retrospective inference.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Erik H. Erikson, Young Man Luther: A Study in Psychoanalysis and History (1958); Peter Gay, Freud for Historians (1985). These projects should not be treated as straightforward applications of Lacan.

representative_people.context: Connects individual development with historical social orders, and asks that the identity-crisis concept itself face historical scrutiny. His later Luther formulation remains his interpretation.
representative_people.works: Young Man Luther (1958), existing metadata; “Autobiographic Notes on the Identity Crisis” (1970), selected primary passages

representative_people.context: Argues for psychoanalytic interpretation alongside external historical circumstances and distances his work from reductionist versions of psychohistory.
representative_people.works: Freud for Historians (1985); The Bourgeois Experience; methodological interview (1997)

representative_people.context: Challenges Freud’s Leonardo interpretation through translation, source context and alternative explanations. Faulty application is distinguished from disproof of all psychoanalysis.
representative_people.works: “Leonardo and Freud: An Art-Historical Study” (1956), selected passages

representative_people.context: Proposes an autonomous science linking childrearing with group fantasies. His causal theory and progressive narrative are contested, including by Pollock.
representative_people.works: Foundations of Psychohistory (1982), preface; “On Writing Childhood History” (1988), selected passages

representative_people.context: Questions deMause’s source selection and broad narrative of improvement. His later criticism of her 1983 book concerns inferences from diary silence; the exchange remains unresolved here.
representative_people.works: The Forgotten Children (1981 thesis), pp. 93–94; Forgotten Children (1983), discussed by deMause (1988)

representative_people.context: Gay values the integration of psychological and contextual explanation in his witchcraft study while disputing their relative weight. This is reception evidence.
representative_people.works: Entertaining Satan, discussed in Gay’s 1997 interview

representative_people.context: Gay recalls the 1950/1951 Freud reading circle as an impetus to his interests. Neumann’s wife also participated; the account does not name her.
representative_people.works: Freud reading circle recalled by Gay (1997)

representative_people.context: Gay recalls the 1950/1951 Freud reading circle as an impetus to his interests. Neumann’s wife also participated; the account does not name her.

representative_people.context: Criticises 1970s psychohistory shaped by American ego-psychology for assuming that psychoanalysis and history are compatible, and argues for their productive incommensurability (2012, author’s abstract).
representative_people.works: “The Incommensurability of Psychoanalysis and History” (2012)

nodes.scope_note: Erikson, Gay and deMause have different explanatory ambitions; they are not interchangeable applications of Lacan. Schapiro’s art-historical criticism supplies a methodological interlocutor, not blanket rejection of psychoanalysis. Pollock’s thesis and deMause’s later response address distinct texts and disputed evidential procedures. Original case books and wider political, religious and regional applications remain selective research limits; theoretical or clinical assertions are not established diagnoses of past people.

strands.title: Psychosocial lives and historical orders
strands.focus: Erikson places identity within somatic, ego and social orders; his later discussion relates Luther’s personal crisis to transformation. This is an attributed interpretation.
strands.works: Young Man Luther (1958); retrospective account (1970), p. 750

strands.title: Psychoanalytic resources within contextual history
strands.focus: Gay insists on external circumstances and inner life together; his qualified judgment of Demos shows disagreement about explanatory weight.
strands.works: Gay interview (1997)

strands.title: Childrearing, group fantasy and causal ambition
strands.focus: deMause proposes an independent explanatory science. His progressive model and reductionist commitment differ from other approaches represented in this umbrella.
strands.works: Foundations of Psychohistory (1982), preface

strands.title: Childhood sources, selection and silence
strands.focus: Pollock questions selected evidence and sweeping change; deMause disputes inferences from unrecorded punishment. The thesis, later book and reply are distinct texts, without independent diary collation here.
strands.works: Pollock thesis (1981), pp. 93–94; deMause (1988), selected reply

strands.title: Psychobiography and historical knowledge
strands.focus: Schapiro examines translation and contextual evidence in Freud’s Leonardo interpretation. His particular criticism neither dismisses every psychobiography nor directly rebuts Erikson.
strands.works: Schapiro (1956), selected passages

strands.title: Historicizing psychological concepts
strands.focus: Erikson asks for historical scrutiny of identity crises and the categories used to describe them. Retrospective self-interpretation itself becomes evidence requiring criticism.
strands.works: Autobiographic Notes (1970), selected passages

nodes.label: Frantz Fanon
nodes.date_label: Colonial subjectivity and liberation · 1952–61
nodes.description: Analyzes colonial domination through racialized experience, psychic injury, and struggles for liberation. A psychiatrist and political theorist whose work supplies historians with questions about subject formation, violence, and the limits of national liberation; his arguments are not confined to individual psychology.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Black Skin, White Masks (French original 1952); The Wretched of the Earth (French original 1961). Later English editions have different publication dates.
nodes.scope_note: Black Skin, White Masks (1952) treats racialized experience through psychological and social explanation; its introduction names Freud while insisting on sociogeny. The Wretched of the Earth (1961) combines liberation strategy, criticism of elite nationalism and psychiatric cases. These are connected inquiries, not one invariant doctrine or membership in psychohistory. Gendered and regional generalizations require critical reading.

nodes.label: Walter Rodney
nodes.date_label: African history and political education · 1960s–80
nodes.description: Explains underdevelopment through historically unequal relations of slavery, colonial extraction and capitalism. Regional African research, Guyanese labor history and popular education give his work distinct scales and audiences. His account of systemic constraints also investigates changing societies; dependency analysis captures only part of his scholarship and politics.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The Groundings with My Brothers (1969); How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (1972).
nodes.scope_note: A History of the Upper Guinea Coast, 1545–1800 (1970, from a 1966 thesis) reconstructs regional change; The Groundings with My Brothers (1969) concerns political education; How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (1972) offers a didactic synthesis. A History of the Guyanese Working People, 1881–1905 (posthumous, 1981) examines labor and racial divisions. His 1975 Marxism lecture distinguishes method from fixed European conclusions. James’s later strategic criticism coexists with formative intellectual exchange.

nodes.label: C. L. R. James
nodes.date_label: Revolution, popular agency, and culture · 1930s–80s
nodes.description: Places enslaved people’s revolutionary action at the center of the Haitian Revolution and reworks Marxist historical explanation through the Caribbean. His writing also investigates colonial society, race, and cultural life through cricket and autobiography.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The Black Jacobins (1938; revised 1963); Beyond a Boundary (1963). The two editions of The Black Jacobins should not be treated as an unchanged argument.
nodes.scope_note: The Black Jacobins (1938; revised 1963) and the 1971 lectures distinguish successive historical perspectives. James later sought closer study of rank-and-file leaders and praised Du Bois’s attention to political imagination. His recollections identify Trotsky, Lenin and Marx among resources, alongside Caribbean projects. Beyond a Boundary (1963) examines social divisions through clubs and treats cricket as an art. These connections do not make him a disciple of postwar British social history.

nodes.label: Eric Williams
nodes.date_label: Slavery, capitalism, and abolition · 1944 onward
nodes.description: Argues that slavery and slave-trade wealth contributed to British capitalist development, and that changing economic interests helped explain abolition. These are related but distinguishable theses whose mechanisms, timing, and weight remain debated. His work challenges accounts centered on European benevolence.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Capitalism and Slavery (1944). Distinguish the original book from later editions and from subsequent arguments about capitalism and slavery.
nodes.scope_note: The 1944 preface separates slavery’s contribution to industrial finance from industrial capitalism’s role in abolition; the conclusion gives economic forces explanatory priority. Williams names Ragatz, Pitman, Herskovits, Burch and Harlow among scholarly helpers. Drescher’s 1977 challenge concerns decline and the 1807 slave-trade abolition, not a refutation of every slavery/capitalism claim. From Columbus to Castro (1970) is a later Caribbean synthesis, here checked only bibliographically.

nodes.label: Antonio Gramsci
nodes.date_label: Prison Notebooks · 1929–35; expanding postwar reception
nodes.description: Hegemony, common sense, subaltern groups, and intellectuals help explain domination through consent as well as coercion. Later historians and cultural theorists adapt these concepts differently. Anglophone reception predates the widely used 1971 Selections and does not follow a single timetable.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Antonio Gramsci (1891–1937); Selections from the Prison Notebooks (1971). Guha’s Subaltern Studies and Hall’s cultural studies are distinct adaptations.
nodes.scope_note: Unfinished and revised prison writings reach readers through editorial selections and translations. Intellectuals are defined by social functions, common sense is historically layered, and subaltern inquiry includes organization and autonomous activity. Gramsci’s broad geographical and linguistic hierarchies are open to criticism; later adaptations are distinct projects.

nodes.label: Historicism & idealist philosophies of history
nodes.date_label: 1800s roots · Dilthey 1883 · Croce 1917 · Meinecke 1936 · Collingwood 1946
nodes.description: Groups related arguments for historical specificity and interpretive understanding. German Historismus and British and Italian idealism are not one doctrine: Collingwood’s re-enactment is a particular account of historical thought, not a method shared by everyone here. This usage differs from Popper’s criticism of predictive laws of historical development. Approaches separate documentary interpretation, the human sciences, living historical questions, developmental individuality and rethinking past arguments; their disagreements concern evidence, values, political power and historical context.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Wilhelm Dilthey; Benedetto Croce, Theory and History of Historiography (1917); Friedrich Meinecke, Die Entstehung des Historismus (1936); R. G. Collingwood, The Idea of History (1946, posthumous).

representative_people.context: Develops a foundation for human sciences encompassing history, theory and practical judgments. Later attention to expression and shared historical worlds qualifies an account based only on individual psychology; the later primary text remains separately scoped.
representative_people.works: Introduction to the Human Sciences (1883), chapters 1, 2, 6; The Formation of the Historical World in the Human Sciences (1910), through editors’ introduction and SEP

representative_people.context: Historical thought responds to present questions while drawing on preserved documents. His distinction between living history and chronicle is idealist, not a distinction between important and trivial subjects or an instruction to disregard evidence.
representative_people.works: Theory and History of Historiography (Italian 1917; consulted 1921 Ainslie translation from 1919 edition), I.1

representative_people.context: Studies individuality and development in a selected genealogy of historicism. His account of national statehood and power receives a specific, attributed criticism from Paddock; neither the definition nor the criticism represents every historicism.
representative_people.works: Weltbürgertum und Nationalstaat (1907); Die Ideen der Staatsräson (1924); Die Entstehung des Historismus (1936), through publisher and scholarly selections

representative_people.context: Re-enactment reconstructs an intelligible act of thought through evidence, not its original sensations or total immediacy. Skinner later credits changing questions and question/answer logic while emphasizing other philosophical resources.
representative_people.works: An Autobiography (1939), reception through Skinner; The Idea of History (1946, posthumous), Epilegomena §4, selected paragraphs

representative_people.context: Combines interpretive understanding with a critical method and a conception of the moral historical world. His approach bridges documentary scholarship and philosophical reflection without becoming identical to Dilthey or Croce.
representative_people.works: Grundriss der Historik (public edition 1867; consulted 1893 English translation)

representative_people.context: Provides an earlier comparison for historical individuality and the value of epochs. His theology and documentary practice differ from later philosophies; no backward influence is implied.
representative_people.works: 1824 preface; lectures on epochs (1854); selected World History reflections

representative_people.context: Dilthey expands the critical project toward historical reason and embodied human experience. This identifies a named philosophical resource, not agreement with every Kantian premise.
representative_people.works: Critique of Pure Reason; Dilthey’s Introduction to the Human Sciences (1883) as a documented reworking

representative_people.context: Dilthey contests speculative system-building while adapting objective spirit to shared historical forms. A productive appropriation with disagreement; the original Hegel corpus is not independently collated here.
representative_people.works: Objective spirit; Dilthey’s Die Jugendgeschichte Hegels (1906) and later Formation project as documented reception

representative_people.context: Hermeneutics and religious life become objects of Dilthey’s editorial, biographical and philosophical work; the intellectual setting extends beyond a private psychological portrait.
representative_people.works: Hermeneutical writings and letters; Dilthey’s 1860 hermeneutical study and Leben Schleiermachers, volume I (1870) as reception

representative_people.context: A resource in Dilthey’s expanded critical perspective and an author central to Meinecke’s selective genealogy. These distinct receptions do not establish one unbroken school.
representative_people.works: Historical philosophy; Meinecke’s Die Entstehung des Historismus (1936), through Paddock’s account

representative_people.context: An explicitly documented recipient of Collingwood’s question/answer logic, with substantial analytical-philosophical commitments. Placement records selective reception and does not label the Cambridge approach idealist.
representative_people.works: “Meaning and Understanding in the History of Ideas” (1969), reception discussed in the 2002 interview

representative_people.context: Holds that climate change collapses the distinction between human and natural history defended “from Hegel and Marx to Croce and Collingwood” (2009–22).
representative_people.works: “The Climate of History: Four Theses” (2009); The Climate of History in a Planetary Age (2021)

nodes.scope_note: German historicism, Italian idealism, and Collingwood’s re-enactment are not one doctrine; neither is this Popper’s usage of historicism.

strands.title: Understanding through historical investigation
strands.focus: Droysen makes interpretable traces, interdependent critical operations and wider conditions central; neither bare testimony nor complete psychological access suffices.
strands.works: Outline of the Principles of History (1893), selected sections

strands.title: Human sciences, theory and practical judgment
strands.focus: The 1883 program distinguishes historical assertions, theoretical uniformities and evaluations/rules. Its broad remit includes humanities and social sciences, rather than forbidding every explanatory generalization.
strands.works: Introduction to the Human Sciences (1883), chapters 1, 2 and 6

strands.title: Expressions and shared historical worlds
strands.focus: Later Dilthey situates understanding in meaningful expressions, institutions and common historical life. Hegel’s objective spirit is appropriated with different commitments; individual introspection is insufficient.
strands.works: Formation of the Historical World (1910) and related drafts, through editors and SEP

strands.title: Present questions and preserved records
strands.focus: Croce distinguishes historical thinking from preserved chronicle without rejecting preservation. His explicit engagement with Droysen joins appreciation to criticism of abstract source categories.
strands.works: Theory & History of Historiography, I.1

strands.title: Individuality, development and state power
strands.focus: Meinecke’s genealogy privileges historical development and particularity. Paddock challenges its treatment of national statehood and supposed breaks in the author’s outlook; that is an attributed interpretation based on selected passages.
strands.works: Weltbürgertum und Nationalstaat (1907); Die Entstehung des Historismus (1936), mediated readings

strands.title: Re-enactment, context and changing questions
strands.focus: Rethinking an argument differs from reliving its sensations. Skinner’s particular reception stresses questions and answers while drawing heavily on analytical philosophy; this is not the shared method of everyone in the umbrella.
strands.works: The Idea of History, Epilegomena §4; An Autobiography through Skinner’s interview

nodes.label: Explanation & objectivity debates
nodes.date_label: Earlier roots · Becker address 1931 · Hempel 1942 · Carr 1961 · Elton 1967
nodes.description: Disputes concern general laws, understanding actions, historical facts, and the possibility of objectivity. Analytic philosophy’s covering-law debate overlaps with historians’ arguments about evidence and interpretation without being identical to them. Narrative theory enters a discussion already under way.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Becker’s 1931 address (published 1932); Hempel, “The Function of General Laws in History” (1942); Dray, Laws and Explanation in History (1957); Carr, What Is History? (1961); Elton, The Practice of History (1967).

representative_people.context: Connects everyday inquiry, social memory and changing interpretation while retaining critical checks.
representative_people.works: Everyman His Own Historian (address 1931; publication 1932)

representative_people.context: Proposes testable laws and initial conditions, allowing probability and incomplete explanation sketches.
representative_people.works: The Function of General Laws in History (1942)

representative_people.context: Challenges reducing all historical explanations to a covering-law model; rational action and pragmatic questions are distinct concerns.
representative_people.works: Laws and Explanation in History (1957)

representative_people.context: Treats selection, interpretation and research as reciprocal while rejecting equal validity for every account.
representative_people.works: What Is History? (1961)

representative_people.context: Addresses research, imagination, writing and teaching; Mink cites his insistence on immersion in a period.
representative_people.works: The Practice of History (1967)

representative_people.context: Historian of evidence who distinguishes origins from explanation and treats traces as answers to questions under evidential constraints.
representative_people.works: Apologie pour l’histoire ou Métier d’historien (1949)

representative_people.context: Earlier philosophical questions about history’s uses, the explanation of moral values and the conditions of objectivity. This is not membership in the later covering-law debate.

representative_people.context: Combines rhetorical analysis of historiography with attention to source-based construction; adopts Barthes while questioning a uniform disappearance of concern with reality.
representative_people.works: “Analysing the discourse of history” (1983); The Inventions of History (1990)

representative_people.context: Examines how historical discourse constructs signification and claims reference. Historians’ engagement includes productive use and criticism, not one settled verdict on evidence.
representative_people.works: “The Discourse of History” (1967); “The Reality Effect” (1968)

representative_people.context: Asks how source survival and artistic forms shape historical perception.
representative_people.works: The Waning of the Middle Ages (1924), preface and chapter XIX opening

representative_people.context: Combines close documentary work with relations among events, peoples and epochs. Historical individuality and religious commitments coexist; his selected European scope and civilizational judgments are contestable, and he is not the sole origin of criticism.
representative_people.works: History of the Popes (1834–1836; Austin translation 1840); 1824 historical preface; lectures on epochs (1854); selected World History reflections

representative_people.context: Source search, criticism and interpretation cooperate. Material remains, accounts and monuments are not interchangeable; neither authentic documents nor individual intentions alone yield a complete historical explanation.
representative_people.works: Grundriss der Historik (public edition 1867; consulted Andrews English 1893), §§1–11, 20–24, 28–41

representative_people.context: Develops a foundation for human sciences encompassing history, theory and practical judgments. Later attention to expression and shared historical worlds qualifies an account based only on individual psychology; the later primary text remains separately scoped.
representative_people.works: Introduction to the Human Sciences (1883), chapters 1, 2, 6; The Formation of the Historical World in the Human Sciences (1910), through editors’ introduction and SEP

representative_people.context: Historical thought responds to present questions while drawing on preserved documents. His distinction between living history and chronicle is idealist, not a distinction between important and trivial subjects or an instruction to disregard evidence.
representative_people.works: Theory and History of Historiography (Italian 1917; consulted 1921 Ainslie translation from 1919 edition), I.1

representative_people.context: Re-enactment reconstructs an intelligible act of thought through evidence, not its original sensations or total immediacy. Skinner later credits changing questions and question/answer logic while emphasizing other philosophical resources.
representative_people.works: An Autobiography (1939), reception through Skinner; The Idea of History (1946, posthumous), Epilegomena §4, selected paragraphs

representative_people.context: Dilthey expands the critical project toward historical reason and embodied human experience. This identifies a named philosophical resource, not agreement with every Kantian premise.
representative_people.works: Critique of Pure Reason; Dilthey’s Introduction to the Human Sciences (1883) as a documented reworking

representative_people.context: Dilthey contests speculative system-building while adapting objective spirit to shared historical forms. A productive appropriation with disagreement; the original Hegel corpus is not independently collated here.

representative_people.context: Hermeneutics and religious life become objects of Dilthey’s editorial, biographical and philosophical work; the intellectual setting extends beyond a private psychological portrait.

strands.title: Genealogy, values and historical explanation
strands.focus: Nietzsche’s critique asks both how moral judgments arise and what they are worth; Rée and Schopenhauer are distinct interlocutors. Origin and later function must not be conflated.
strands.works: Genealogy (1887), preface and II.12–13

strands.title: Rhetoric, reference and historical achievement
strands.focus: Barthes analyzes the presentation of reality; Bann uses that analysis while questioning its scope and preserving source-based scrutiny. Formal analysis alone does not decide a historical claim’s truth.
strands.works: History/reality essays (1967–1968); Bann (1983/1990)

strands.title: The historian, surviving sources and the historical picture
strands.focus: Michelet’s account of reciprocal formation and Huizinga’s warning about surviving art raise different questions about historical knowledge; they do not deny the need for evidence.
strands.works: Michelet (1869); Huizinga (1924)

strands.title: Evidence, understanding and the historical question
strands.focus: Droysen, Dilthey, Croce and Collingwood offer different accounts of what inquiry does with traces, thought, context and practical concerns. These are explicit conceptual resources, not a common doctrine or a proved genealogy of later debate.
strands.works: Selected methodological texts (1867–1946)

strands.title: Language use and following rules
strands.focus: Wittgenstein examines varied activities and similarities rather than one essence of language. Following a rule involves a practice; an interpretation cannot supply its own application without limit.
strands.works: Philosophical Investigations, selected §§19–242

strands.title: Knowing how, action and accomplishment
strands.focus: Ryle distinguishes competent action from both an automatic movement and a performance governed by an endless series of prior theoretical decisions. A richer action description identifies purpose and circumstances.
strands.works: The Concept of Mind, II.1–3; The Thinking of Thoughts

strands.title: Narrative and historical understanding
strands.focus: White identifies particular philosophical interlocutors rather than responding to one undifferentiated philosophy of history.
strands.works: Metahistory (1973),2–3 notes

strands.title: Laws, probability and explanation sketches
strands.focus: Hempel’s demand for testable relations permits incomplete research proposals and probabilistic accounts.
strands.works: General Laws (1942)

strands.title: Action and the limits of one explanatory model
strands.focus: Dray’s challenge includes reasons, uniqueness and pragmatic questions; it is not a ban on all generalization.
strands.works: Laws and Explanation (1957); Nature of Historical Explanation (1952)

strands.title: Selection, relevance and revisable interpretation
strands.focus: Becker and Carr preserve evidence while disputing self-interpreting facts; they do not offer identical positions.
strands.works: Everyman (1931/1932); What Is History? (1961),chapter1

strands.title: Historical craft, imagination and instruction
strands.focus: Elton’s research/writing/teaching agenda and Skinner’s apprenticeship reading identify practices of training.
strands.works: Practice of History (1967); Skinner1997opening extract

strands.title: Narrative comprehension and truth
strands.focus: Mink separates grasping relations from truth tests and disputes both Gallie’s following and Hardy’s lived-narrative account.
strands.works: History and Fiction (1970)

strands.title: Knowledge of the past and speculative historical systems
strands.focus: Walsh’s scope distinguishes questions about inquiry from philosophies of the whole historical process.
strands.works: Introduction (1951)

nodes.label: Frankfurt School / critical theory
nodes.date_label: 1920s roots · Benjamin · Adorno · Habermas
nodes.description: Critical theorists draw differently on Marx, Weber, and Freud to examine domination, culture, and rationality. Benjamin’s reflections on historical time and Habermas’s public sphere offer distinct resources for historians. Benjamin’s association with the Institute and Habermas’s later work should not imply a single institutional position or doctrine.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Benjamin, “On the Concept of History” (1940); Horkheimer and Adorno, Dialectic of Enlightenment (1944/47); Habermas, The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere (1962; English 1989). Georg Lukács: History and Class Consciousness (1923), as precursor; Siegfried Kracauer.

Bourdieu’s habitus and strategies, de Certeau’s tactics, and Sewell’s account of structure offer different ways to connect agency, constraint, and meaning. These are several resources for reassessing cultural history, not a single replacement paradigm.

nodes.description: Links changes in manners and affect to interdependence and state formation. Historians adapt and contest his account of the relations between social constraint and self-restraint. nodes.label: British cultural studies
nodes.date_label: Hoggart · Williams · Hall · CCCS 1964
nodes.description: Examines culture as lived and contested, including popular forms, class, media, race, and gender. Debates among culturalist, structuralist, feminist, and antiracist projects reshape the field. It exchanges ideas with historical scholarship while retaining distinct institutional and disciplinary histories.

nodes.scope_note: Hoggart, Williams, Thompson and Hall have distinct trajectories. Birmingham is one institutional center; feminist, antiracist, ethnographic and media projects revise its questions. Culturalist/structuralist distinctions are debated, not successive closed schools. Contributors listed as theoretical resources are not thereby CCCS members. Exchanges with history do not make the fields identical.

nodes.label: Progressive & consensus historiography (US)
nodes.date_label: Contrasting frameworks prominent in the 1890s–1950s
nodes.description: A paired comparison of influential US approaches, not one school or the whole profession. Progressive interpretations emphasize economic interest and conflict; postwar consensus interpretations emphasize shared commitments across political divisions. The labels are contested and do not capture every argument of the writers grouped under them.

nodes.label: New Left & radical history (US)
nodes.date_label: 1950s–70s expansion
nodes.description: Challenges consensus interpretations through studies of class, race, capitalism, and empire. Radical diplomatic, labour, and slavery histories overlap with new social history but differ in politics and method. Their engagements with Black history do not supply that field’s independent origins. Gutman’s cultural labor history also criticizes some New Left institutional accounts. Alice and Staughton Lynd make organizer testimony and participant review part of research practice; Zinn’s selective Marxian commitments differ from Genovese’s paternalism interpretation.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: William Appleman Williams, The Tragedy of American Diplomacy (1959)—a different writer from Eric Williams; Staughton Lynd; Eugene Genovese, Roll, Jordan, Roll (1974); Herbert Gutman, Work, Culture, and Society (1976); Radical History Review (1973).

nodes.label: Historical demography & history of the family
nodes.date_label: Henry · Cambridge Group · 1950s–70s expansion
nodes.description: Combines related inquiries into population, households, childhood and intimate relations. Henry’s family reconstitution and Cambridge’s aggregate and household studies differ from Ariès’s historical concepts and Stone’s family interpretation. Pollock’s criticism questions evidence and sweeping changes in parental care. Lee and Wang’s Chinese population study challenges received Malthusian comparisons without making the field’s regional patterns uniform.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Louis Henry; Cambridge Group for the History of Population and Social Structure (1964); Peter Laslett, The World We Have Lost (1965); Wrigley and Schofield, The Population History of England (1981); Philippe Ariès (1960); Lawrence Stone (1977). Additional selections: Hajnal (1965); Laslett and Wall (1972); Pollock (1981/1983); Wrigley, Davies, Oeppen and Schofield (1997); Lee and Wang (1999).

representative_people.context: Develops historical family reconstitution at INED; his Geneva study explains why mobile urban and elite families require documents beyond one locality’s parish registers.

representative_people.context: Cambridge Group co-founder; household composition studies question a simple industrial origin of nuclear households. Household form does not measure affection.

representative_people.context: Collaborative reconstruction of fertility, mortality and marriage; distinguish the 1981 aggregate reconstruction from the 1997 family-reconstitution volume.

nodes.scope_note: Family reconstitution and aggregate reconstruction differ from histories of childhood or family meanings; Henry, Annales, and Cambridge are not interchangeable. Household composition, marriage behavior, concepts of childhood and parental conduct are different objects of study. England and France are prominent in this selection; Chinese comparative research broadens the questions without representing all non-European family histories. Later institutional webpages are retrospective sources, not an extension beyond 2000.

strands.title: Reconstituting families from historical records
strands.focus: Link records of family events while examining who disappears from observation; Henry flags mobility and social differences, and Cambridge’s 1997 study is explicitly collaborative.
strands.works: Anciennes familles genevoises (1956); English Population History from Family Reconstitution (1997)

strands.title: Reconstructing aggregate population
strands.focus: Use historical demographic observations to estimate population and vital rates; a national reconstruction is distinct from following the observed life of one family.
strands.works: The Population History of England 1541–1871: A Reconstruction (1981)

strands.title: Households and comparative marriage patterns
strands.focus: Compare household composition and marriage patterns without inferring feelings from household size or treating one region as universal.
strands.works: Household and Family in Past Time (1972); “European Marriage Patterns in Perspective” (1965)

strands.title: Childhood concepts, conduct and evidence
strands.focus: Ariès examines childhood as a historical concept; Pollock questions broad change narratives through personal documents. Affection and recognition of a separate life stage are not identical claims.
strands.works: Centuries of Childhood (1962); The Forgotten Children (1981); Forgotten Children (1983)

strands.title: Marriage, intimacy and disputed change
strands.focus: Stone’s affective-individualism interpretation meets criticism of its explanation and evidential selection. Neither prescriptive literature nor diary writers transparently represent everyone.
strands.works: The Family, Sex and Marriage in England (1977); Pollock’s thesis, pp. 96–98 and 143–144 (1981)

strands.title: Chinese population and Malthusian comparisons
strands.focus: Lee and Wang argue for forms of population regulation missed by received China/West contrasts. Their fertility and marriage claims remain arguments to test against evidence and regional variation.
strands.works: One Quarter of Humanity (1999)

strands.title: Patterns, exceptions and explanation
strands.focus: Hajnal distinguishes late marriage from remaining unmarried, acknowledges regional variation and separates identifying a pattern from explaining it. Goody questions its uniqueness and the scale of comparison.

strands.title: Local monographs and collective sampling
strands.focus: Fleury and Henry credit Goubert and other researchers, but argue that chosen parish monographs cannot simply be added into a national sample. Biraben joins their subsequent register inventory.
strands.works: Fleury/Henry (1958),665; Biraben/Fleury/Henry (1960), metadata

strands.title: Population totals and family subsets
strands.focus: Henry’s survey account distinguishes aggregate reconstruction from the smaller rural sample used for family reconstitution. Changes in sampling and uneven record quality constrain what each can establish.
strands.works: INED survey account (1978),230–232

strands.title: Observed fertility and deliberate control
strands.focus: Lee and Wang interpret delayed first births, longer intervals and earlier stopping as marital restraint. Harrell’s later review questions source completeness, regional reach and whether these patterns establish intentional control.
strands.works: One Quarter of Humanity (1999),86–90; Harrell review (2003),543

strands.title: Local evidence and collaborative reconstruction
strands.focus: Harrell’s collection brings local demographic studies together; Lee and Wang acknowledge Campbell’s contributions. A broad comparative argument still requires attention to differences among local sources.
strands.works: Chinese Historical Microdemography (1995); One Quarter of Humanity (1999), opening acknowledgment

strands.title: Family change, social differences and source selection
strands.focus: Stone qualifies affective individualism with reversals and overlapping patterns across social groups, while making a debatable assumption about surviving documents. Pollock separates childhood concepts, affection and discipline and questions how family histories generalize from their sources.
strands.works: Stone, abridged edition (1979), 21–29; Pollock, Forgotten Children (1983), 1–10

strands.title: Italian residence and marriage patterns
strands.focus: Kertzer and Hogan report patrilocal residence without the expected combination of early female marriage, large spousal age differences and low nonmarriage. Similar marriage ages among wage workers and sharecroppers complicate a simple account of proletarianization.
strands.works: “Reflections on the European Marriage Pattern” (1991), Casalecchio, 1861–1921

nodes.label: Revival of narrative / debate over quantification
nodes.date_label: Stone 1979 · Hobsbawm 1980
nodes.description: Stone diagnoses renewed interest in narrative, individuals, and culture amid dissatisfaction with some structural and quantitative explanations. Hobsbawm contests the diagnosis. This contemporary debate concerns historians’ practices; it differs from White’s earlier analysis of narrative form and does not establish that quantitative history ended.

representative_people.context: The 1979 revival diagnosis and the earlier 1978 Tuchman review are distinct interventions. In the review he praises communication while questioning the selection of events and explanatory depth. The 1979 essay restricts its diagnosis to a prominent minority and acknowledges continuing quantitative work.

representative_people.context: Questions whether changed subjects and presentation establish a retreat from explanation; small-scale inquiry can serve larger analytical questions.

representative_people.context: An earlier narrative-theory intervention, not an effect of Stone’s 1979 essay. Stone explicitly cites the book through Starn’s recommendation; citation does not erase the distinction between their projects.

nodes.label: Comparative historical sociology
nodes.date_label: Comparative programmes · 1960s–90s · earlier resources
nodes.description: Compares how states, rights, class relations and collective struggles change. Moore studies agrarian routes; Skocpol combines state breakdown with class and international relations; Tilly follows contention; Mann maps intersecting power networks. Bendix, Goldstone, Somers and Block supply different questions about authority, demography, citizenship and economic institutions. Sewell’s exchange with Skocpol makes ideology an explicit debate.

nodes.scope_note: A field of competing comparisons, not one state-centered theory. Cases range beyond Europe, but this selection is uneven and does not exhaust regional traditions. Cultural and institutional explanations can be combined; political outcomes are not inevitable stages.

strands.title: Population, institutions and state crises
strands.focus: Demographic pressures acquire political effects through institutions and elite relations, not population alone.
strands.works: Goldstone, Revolution and Rebellion (1991)

strands.title: Ideology within structural explanation
strands.focus: Sewell criticizes a restricted account of ideology; Skocpol acknowledges a problem and responds. Her reply’s opening also questions Sewell’s anonymous conception of culture; the exchange contains disagreement in both directions.

strands.title: Comparing crises and their different outcomes
strands.focus: Goldstone compares England and the Fronde, then distinguishes Castile from the Spanish monarchy’s rebellious peripheries. Similar pressures need not produce identical outcomes. Perry values the comparison but questions how far its claims travel across different societies and periods.

strands.title: Empire formation and conflicting political aims
strands.focus: Eisenstadt’s prefaces distinguish social conditions from the emergence of leaders able to organize an imperial polity. Rulers seek resources less bound to traditional groups while trying to control those resources themselves. strands.title: Questioning the units of comparison
strands.focus: Eisenstadt takes up Rokkan’s attention to cultural and territorial settings and questions exporting European state categories. Subrahmanyam separately uses Eurasian circulation to challenge autonomous-state and ideological partitions. These are distinct arguments, not a demonstrated intellectual lineage between the authors.
strands.works: Eisenstadt, Stein Rokkan Lecture (1985); Subrahmanyam, Connected Histories (1997)

nodes.label: West German historical social science / Sonderweg
nodes.date_label: Wehler · Kocka · 1960s–90s debates and extensions
nodes.description: Historical social science investigates German politics through social and economic structures. Wehler’s Empire interpretation, Kocka’s industrial and bourgeois research, and Frevert’s gender history address different questions. Blackbourn/Eley contest Sonderweg assumptions; Kocka revises parts while defending comparison. Lüdtke questions structural priorities through everyday practices. Fischer’s war-aims controversy is a related precursor.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Hans-Ulrich Wehler, Das deutsche Kaiserreich (1973); Jürgen Kocka; Geschichte und Gesellschaft (1975); David Blackbourn and Geoff Eley, The Peculiarities of German History (1984). Fritz Fischer’s 1961 intervention is a related precursor.

strands.title: Historical social science
strands.focus: Wehler’s structural political explanation and Kocka’s organizational/social comparisons differ within a broader programme.
strands.works: Wehler, Das deutsche Kaiserreich (1973); Kocka, Industrial Culture (1999)

strands.title: Sonderweg criticism
strands.focus: Critics contest the western yardstick and bourgeois-failure thesis; Kocka accepts revisions while defending qualified comparison.
strands.works: Blackbourn/Eley (1984); Kocka’s response (1988)

strands.title: War aims and a related controversy
strands.focus: An archival intervention about First World War aims supplies context for later revisionist questions.
strands.works: Fischer, Griff nach der Weltmacht (1961)

strands.title: Gender, rights and bourgeois society
strands.focus: Women’s opportunities and restrictions enter the history of German society and its political arrangements.
strands.works: Frevert, Women in German History (1989)

strands.title: Everyday practices and structural priorities
strands.focus: A specific critical exchange about workplace relations keeps actors’ practices visible alongside structures. The separately checked Lüdtke–Wehler exchange contests explanatory priorities while acknowledging some benefits and weaknesses on both sides.
strands.works: Lüdtke, “Polymorphous Synchrony” (1993), note 27 on Kocka

strands.title: A journal as a research and discussion venue
strands.focus: The four authors of the 1975 foreword proposed combining historical interpretation with social-scientific analysis. Thematic issues, research reports and a discussion forum would connect specialists and wider readers. This is an announced programme, not proof that all editorial practice fulfilled it.
strands.works: Geschichte und Gesellschaft, founding foreword (1975)

strands.title: Structural questions within inherited historical methods
strands.focus: Schieder reads Ranke, Droysen and other earlier historians as already addressing relations between individuals and larger forces. His call to revise inherited methods complicates an absolute divide between traditional history and structural inquiry; his portraits of rival traditions remain contestable.
strands.works: Strukturen und Persönlichkeiten, section I (1968 edition)

strands.title: Mentorship and political accountability
strands.focus: Wehler’s retrospective account combines intellectual gratitude to Schieder with discussion of Nazi-era writings and silence. The 1999 scholarly debate examines postwar continuities and the limits of earlier scrutiny. Methodological innovation and a liberal teaching style do not by themselves settle political responsibility.
strands.works: Wehler interview; Schulze, Helm and Ott on the historians’ debate (1999)

strands.title: Class membership and gendered self-description
strands.focus: Frevert reads the Pringsheim/Mann family’s descriptions of education, occupation and beauty against definitions of bourgeois membership. Her argument differentiates women’s and men’s positions within a class.
strands.works: Classe et genre dans la bourgeoisie allemande du XIXe siècle (1991)

nodes.scope_note: A teaching umbrella spanning a research programme, a contested German-path argument and critics. Historical social science is broader than Sonderweg; neither is synonymous with the later Historikerstreit. Long-term conditions are not inevitable causes of Nazism, and gender history broadens the programme without making all contributors doctrinal adherents. Innovation also coexisted with inherited teaching relationships and politically contested continuities across 1945; the 1998–1999 debate over historians’ Nazi pasts is a distinct episode.

nodes.label: Holocaust historiography
nodes.date_label: Earlier documentation; 1960s–90s debates
nodes.description: Investigates the persecution and murder of European Jews through policies, institutions, ideology, perpetrators, victims, and testimony. Intentionalist and functionalist debates intersect with disputes about representation and remembrance. Survivor scholarship and documentation have earlier roots; these concerns coexist rather than replacing one another in a fixed sequence.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Raul Hilberg, The Destruction of the European Jews (1961); Martin Broszat; Hans Mommsen; Christopher Browning, Ordinary Men (1992); Saul Friedländer, ed., Probing the Limits of Representation (1992); the Goldhagen controversy (1996).

nodes.scope_note: Persecution, perpetrators, victims, representation, and memory coexist. Intentionalist/functionalist disputes do not exhaust the field or precede all survivor scholarship. Wartime documentation, daily-life inquiry and rescue research complicate a perpetrator-centered canon. Explanation of radicalization is not exculpation, and disagreement over representation is not equivalent to Holocaust denial. The selection does not cover every occupied country or persecuted population.

nodes.label: Nationalism studies
nodes.date_label: Modernist debates · 1983 landmark works
nodes.description: Makes the formation of nations and traditions an object of historical explanation. Anderson, Gellner, and Hobsbawm offer different modernist accounts; ethno-symbolist and postcolonial critics question their premises. Treating national identity as historical does not require assuming that every tradition is a recent invention.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Benedict Anderson, Imagined Communities (1983); Ernest Gellner, Nations and Nationalism (1983); Hobsbawm and Ranger, The Invention of Tradition (1983); Anthony D. Smith; Partha Chatterjee, Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World (1986).

representative_people.context: Connects national imagining to print markets and language; imagined communities are not thereby unreal.

Nations, states and nationalist movements are not interchangeable; European typologies require testing beyond their original cases.

nodes.label: African history: postwar institutional expansion
nodes.date_label: Older traditions · Ibadan · Dar es Salaam · expansion from the 1950s
nodes.description: Postwar institutions challenge colonial denials of African historical agency while building on older African historical knowledge and writing. Oral traditions, documentary criticism, archaeology, and linguistics support diverse inquiries. Nationalist, Marxist, social, and cultural projects overlap and contend; their institutional expansion is not the beginning of African historical thought.

nodes.scope_note: The node concerns postwar institutions, not the beginning of African historical knowledge. Nationalist, Marxist, oral, and other methods require distinct contexts. Ibadan, Dar es Salaam and UNESCO are distinct institutional settings. Earlier Yoruba writing, West African spoken knowledge, East African reconstruction, women’s histories and labor inquiry are not one nationalist programme. Northern Africa and further African intellectual traditions still require expansion.

nodes.label: History of technology
nodes.date_label: Enduring field · SHOT 1958
nodes.description: Studies technological systems, invention, maintenance, use, and social change. Develops distinct institutions while exchanging questions with histories of science, economy, environment, and gender. Systems approaches and feminist studies of household technology show the range of its explanations. Wajcman’s feminist social-shaping questions and Bray’s Chinese domestic technologies broaden the field’s material and geographical examples.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Society for the History of Technology (1958); Technology and Culture (1959); Thomas P. Hughes, Networks of Power (1983); Ruth Schwartz Cowan, More Work for Mother (1983). Pinch and Bijker (1984) investigate technological choices; their 1987 volume with Hughes makes the exchange with STS concrete.

nodes.label: Consumption & material culture
nodes.date_label: Earlier roots; 1980s–90s expansion
nodes.description: Examines commercial promotion, household demand, goods’ changing value, taste, gender and provisioning. McKendrick, Brewer and Plumb distinguish commercial and social changes; de Vries connects consumption with household labor; Mintz links diets to colonial production. Anthropological and feminist approaches ask how objects acquire meanings and how consumer roles depend on unequal social relations.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: McKendrick, Brewer, and Plumb, The Birth of a Consumer Society (1982); Appadurai, ed., The Social Life of Things (1986); Brewer and Porter, eds., Consumption and the World of Goods (1993); Mintz, Sweetness and Power (1985). Additional readings: Douglas and Isherwood, The World of Goods (1979); Kopytoff on cultural biography (1986); de Vries on industrious change (1994); de Grazia and Furlough, The Sex of Things (1996). Maxine Berg and Helen Clifford, eds.: Consumers and Luxury (1999).

nodes.scope_note: Demand, taste, provisioning, commodities, and material objects are not one theory; gender and empire connect consumption to production. Commodity circulation, cultural biography and goods as communication are distinct questions. De Vries acknowledges conflicting household interests; feminist research does not reduce women to consumers. Much of this selection concerns Europe and the United States; Mintz’s colonial production connects regions but does not make the coverage global in every respect.

strands.title: Commercialization and the consumer-revolution thesis
strands.focus: Fashion and pottery promotion, politics, leisure and childhood are different parts of the 1982 collaboration. Its consumer-revolution framing and gender assumptions invite criticism.
strands.works: The Birth of a Consumer Society (1982)

strands.title: Households, labor and demand
strands.focus: The industrious-revolution argument connects demand with household labor, including unequal interests and negotiation among members.
strands.works: “The Industrial Revolution and the Industrious Revolution” (1994)

strands.title: Commodity histories, labor and empire
strands.focus: Trace sugar from colonial slave production to changing diets and industrial work; consumption and production belong in the same historical question.
strands.works: Sweetness and Power (1985)

strands.title: Circulation and the politics of value
strands.focus: Following exchanged things connects valuation to social and political relations; Appadurai explicitly develops a resource from Simmel.
strands.works: The Social Life of Things (1986), introduction

strands.title: Cultural biographies and changing commodity status
strands.focus: A thing’s commodity status can change over time or differ between people; material production alone does not settle its social classification.
strands.works: “The Cultural Biography of Things” (1986)

strands.title: Goods as social communication
strands.focus: Douglas and Isherwood examine goods as an information system through which people conduct social relations.
strands.works: The World of Goods (1979)

strands.title: Taste and social position
strands.focus: Read tastes and cultural practices in relation to social position, alongside approaches centered on circulation or household provisioning.
strands.works: Distinction (1979; English 1984)

strands.title: Gendered consumption, work and identity
strands.focus: Investigate the division of family labor, male and female consumer identities, class differences and state definitions; avoid one universal consumer.
strands.works: The Sex of Things (1996)

strands.title: Inventory evidence and its boundaries
strands.focus: Weatherill records selected goods across probate inventories. Missing laborers, debts, real estate and reliable clothing values constrain what household ownership can establish about society.
strands.works: Consumer Behaviour (1996), introduction1–3

strands.title: Purchasing as household work
strands.focus: Vickery’s selected households distribute purchasing tasks and authority unevenly. Expenditure diaries show practical expertise, but incomplete income records limit reconstruction of financial power.
strands.works: The Gentleman’s Daughter (1998), “Elegance” opening and notes15–18

strands.title: Material meanings and unequal possibilities
strands.focus: Vickery finds social ambition alongside attachment and remembrance. Age, resources and inheritance matter; her chapter does not establish one feminine attitude to possessions.
strands.works: The Gentleman’s Daughter (1998), “Elegance” closing discussion

strands.title: Competing chronologies and questions
strands.focus: Compare McKendrick’s eighteenth-century acceleration, Weatherill’s earlier middling ownership and de Vries’s household labor argument. Vickery questions universal motives. Different evidence and outcomes do not yield one automatic date for a consumer society.
strands.works: McKendrick (1982), introduction; Weatherill (1996), preface; de Vries (1994); Vickery (1998)

strands.title: Ming consumers and social distinctions
strands.focus: Clunas reads Wen Zhenheng’s judgments about appropriate objects as elite distinctions, then compares them with Yan Song’s confiscation inventory. These are different sources, not interchangeable records of actual purchasing.
strands.works: Superfluous Things (1991), 40–53

strands.title: Whose consumption becomes visible?
strands.focus: Clunas’s selected texts privilege elite men. Rules assigning objects to women do not directly recover women’s own meanings; subsistence consumers also remain poorly represented. Pagani highlights this limit while praising the method.
strands.works: Clunas (1991), 53–56; Pagani (1993), paragraphs 14–16

strands.title: Relics and changing value
strands.focus: Geary follows transfers and renewed authentication of relics. Their careers may change how communities value them; price equivalences and the relative frequency of different transfers remain uncertain.
strands.works: “Sacred Commodities” (1986),186–190

strands.title: Specific historical uses of theory
strands.focus: Vickery explicitly uses Bourdieu and Douglas/Isherwood; Geary cites Kopytoff. These establish particular uses with different evidence and questions, without proving uniform reception across consumption history.
strands.works: Vickery (1998), “Elegance,” note9; Geary (1986),169,188

strands.title: Luxury and European consumer culture
strands.focus: Berg and Clifford coedit a volume on luxury and consumer culture in Europe, 1650–1850. This records their editorial contribution; detailed chapter arguments remain unchecked.
strands.works: Consumers and Luxury (1999), coedited volume

nodes.label: Historians’ responses to postmodernism
nodes.date_label: Plural reassessments · 1990s
nodes.description: Brings together disputes about evidence, narrative, realism, and social explanation. Defences of historical knowledge, postmodern arguments, and revisions of cultural history are competing positions rather than a consensus or final resolution. Hunt participates in several of these reassessments, making them useful companions to her later global-era argument.

nodes.label: Ivy Pinchbeck
nodes.date_label: Women’s work and industrialization · 1930
nodes.description: Reconstructs women’s work before and during industrialization through household production, wages, training and agricultural change. She emphasizes unequal disruption while arguing for eventual benefits, a position distinct from Clark’s account of capitalist development.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Women Workers and the Industrial Revolution, 1750–1850 (1930; new preface in the 1969 reprint). The original preface acknowledges Eileen Power’s direction of the research and Lilian Knowles’s earlier guidance.
nodes.scope_note: The complete 1930 introduction distinguishes paid visibility from productive work itself and separates married women, single women and workers supporting families. Power directs the acknowledged research; Knowles gives early guidance and Dorothy George supplies specific evidence. The 1969 preface, signed 1968, calls for later occupational research without supplying it. The broad optimistic conclusion remains an attributed argument; most occupational chapters and the original conclusion are unread.

nodes.label: Alice Clark
nodes.date_label: Women, household production, and capitalism · 1919
nodes.description: Studies women’s paid and unpaid production through overlapping household and capitalist arrangements. Differences of class and marital position shape her account of changing work, training and authority; her chronology and assumptions about earlier households remain contested.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Working Life of Women in the Seventeenth Century (1919). Compare with Pinchbeck’s later-period study to examine how historians explain the relationship between economic change and women’s autonomy.
nodes.scope_note: The 1919 preface credits Schreiner, Knowles and Power’s unpublished research. Introduction and conclusion distinguish production for use, family enterprise and individual wages, while admitting conjectural medieval comparisons and incomplete causal evidence. Maternal and racial assumptions belong to Clark’s historical position. Erickson’s 1992 introduction values unpaid-work analysis while disputing chronology and household equality. Main occupational cases are not newly read; neither timeless equality nor a uniform decline for all women is established.

nodes.label: Mary Ritter Beard
nodes.date_label: Women’s agency and documentary recovery · 1930s–40s
nodes.description: Argues that women helped make historical institutions and events, and that histories must investigate their activity rather than assume universal passivity. Her work combines historical argument, collaborative synthesis and efforts to preserve and teach women’s records.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Woman as Force in History: A Study in Traditions and Realities (1946); work supporting women’s documentary collections, including the Sophia Smith Collection. Her account of agency remains open to criticism about differences among women and structures of power.
nodes.scope_note: Woman as Force in History (1946) challenges the subject-sex tradition through legal and other historical inquiry; its preface does not establish that agency cancels subordination. WCWA (1935–1940) and Smith collecting depended on Schwimmer, Grierson, donors and other collaborators. Voss-Hubbard documents Black women’s limited authority and funding within WCWA. Cott’s 1991 editorial recovery uses letters preserved by correspondents. Mary’s distinct work coexists with collaboration with Charles; legal cases and specific later theoretical criticism remain to be checked.

nodes.label: Julia Cherry Spruill
nodes.date_label: Women’s social history in colonial America · 1938
nodes.description: Investigates women’s everyday life, institutions, work and public activity in the colonial South through varied documentary evidence. Later reissues and public interpretation renew use of her work while exposing limits in whose lives become sustained research questions.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Women’s Life and Work in the Southern Colonies (1938); later reissues associated with Anne Firor Scott show that the field’s expansion also involved renewed attention to earlier scholarship.
nodes.scope_note: Richter’s complete 1999 review mediates Spruill’s shift from attitudes to empirical groundwork and her distinction between prescribed reading and actual behavior. The book examines status and regional differences, but mentions Black and Native women without sustained questions about their life and work, in Richter’s assessment. Scott’s 1972 and 1998 introductions are editorial reception; Colonial Williamsburg use is documented, while Richter’s own proposed slavery research remains an intention. Earlier methods are not membership in postwar social history, and friendship with Beard does not prove transmission.

nodes.label: Lucy Maynard Salmon
nodes.date_label: Social inquiry, evidence, and teaching · 1890s–1920s
nodes.description: Brings domestic employment, everyday evidence and critical teaching into historical inquiry. Domestic Service combines questionnaires, statistical comparison and historical explanation, treating household work as connected to wider economic change. Her practice depends on respondents, students, librarians and statistical collaborators.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Domestic Service (1897); teaching and research at Vassar, including work with cookbooks and household material evidence. Connects histories of women’s work to a wider reconsideration of what counts as a historical source.
nodes.scope_note: The 1897 preface and opening chapters explain response limits and distinguish facts from proposed remedies; the 1901 edition adds European inquiry. Distribution through college and association networks is not established probability sampling, despite Salmon’s claim to representativeness. The 1906 Apologia recalls Tyler’s teaching and describes disciplinary boundaries from her own perspective. Underhill’s manuscript and index work is acknowledged. Vassar documents later source criticism and pedagogy; original newspaper studies and contemporary reviews remain unchecked. Her earlier inquiry is not postwar social-history membership.

nodes.label: Eleanor Flexner
nodes.date_label: Women’s rights, labour, and political struggle · 1959
nodes.description: Reconstructs women’s rights organizing alongside labor, education, abolition and Black women’s activity before the 1960s. Her account makes the boundaries of a movement a historical question: contemporary and later readers disagree about its suffrage emphasis, structural explanation and exclusions.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Century of Struggle: The Woman’s Rights Movement in the United States (1959; later revised and enlarged editions). Publication, reception, and subsequent revision belong to different moments.
nodes.scope_note: The 1959 publication, 1975 revision and later editions are separate moments. James praises expanded coverage but calls for a private-property explanation; Ostrander questions integration of other reforms while recognizing the book’s narrower declared purpose. Rupp values archival reach and race/class breadth but questions absent other women of color and private relationships. Her 1992 account mediates Flexner’s use of Schomburg, Howard, Terrell and Women’s Trade Union League records. Original prefatory and archival passages remain to be collated; this is neither an exhaustive history of women nor proof that later feminist history begins with a single book.

nodes.label: Barbara W. Tuchman
nodes.date_label: Narrative, diplomacy, and war · 1960s onward
nodes.description: Builds historical narratives around decisions, personalities and political circumstances, combining readable prose with documentary reconstruction. Her accounts of research identify specialist help, conflicting evidence and uncertain inference. Critical reception asks how narrative selection relates to wider social and institutional explanation.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The Guns of August (1962). A useful case for asking how narrative pace, characterization, and the selection of events support or constrain an explanation.
nodes.scope_note: The Guns of August (1962) precedes the 1979 revival diagnosis. In “In Search of History” Tuchman explicitly invokes Ranke’s historical truth and Bowen’s reader principle while rejecting invented detail. A Distant Mirror (1978) uses Coucy as a narrative vehicle and acknowledges an unanswered initial causal question, selection bias and debts to editors, chroniclers and sociological medievalists. Stone’s 1978 criticism and Fox-Genovese’s defense are distinct interpretations, not a simple narrative-versus-analysis divide. Specialist assistance does not mean agreement with every conclusion; Tuchman is not placed in women’s history solely because she is a woman, or in Marxism because a Marxist defended her.

nodes.label: Eileen Power
nodes.date_label: Medieval economic and social history · 1920s–30s
nodes.description: Combines medieval institutional inquiry with reconstruction of individual lives for wider audiences. Her work examines women, households and economic relations through varied sources, while teaching, shared research and editorial collaboration connect projects and generations.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Medieval English Nunneries, c. 1275 to 1535 (1922); Medieval People (1924); economic history at LSE and educational work with Rhoda Power. Pinchbeck’s 1930 preface acknowledges Power’s research direction.
nodes.scope_note: Medieval English Nunneries (1922) separates rules from visitation evidence and warns that recorded faults are incomplete accounts. Medieval People (1924) uses personal reconstruction and explicit source notes. Power shares unpublished material with Clark and directs Pinchbeck’s research. Postan’s 1963 preface identifies reconstructed wording in a posthumous addition. These projects, later editing and Hilton’s particular periodization criticism should remain distinct; original cases and the criticized Cambridge chapter are not fully audited.

nodes.label: C. V. Wedgwood
nodes.date_label: Seventeenth-century political and narrative history · 1930s–60s
nodes.description: Combines narrative craft with political, military, biographical and cultural history for broad audiences. She reconstructs participants’ motives and uncertainty, while revising judgments when documents and scholarship change. Her sustained practice gives historical narrative a place during the expansion of social-scientific approaches.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Cicely Veronica Wedgwood; The Thirty Years War (1938); The King’s Peace and The King’s War; biographical work on William the Silent. These are contributions to political, military, and biographical history.
nodes.scope_note: The King’s Peace (1955) and The King’s War (1958) defend attention to sequence and contemporary experience without answering every causal question. Woolrych documents the 1961 revaluation of Strafford and criticizes occasional eulogy and weak explanation of social/regional allegiance; Parker’s war criticism is mediated through that memoir. Her cultural work includes verse and political imagination. Narrative continuity precedes the 1979 debate; original prefaces and cases are not fully collated here.

nodes.label: Frances A. Yates
nodes.date_label: Renaissance culture and arts of memory · 1960s–70s
nodes.description: Investigates mnemonic techniques, images and Renaissance intellectual culture through textual and visual reconstruction. The Art of Memory distinguishes traditions of remembering and argues that their transformations matter to the history of knowledge. Named collaborators and critics help expose both the resources and risks of this inquiry.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The Art of Memory (1966), including its treatment of Renaissance memory systems and questions about scientific method. Her historical interpretations are arguments for assessment, not a single uncontested model of Renaissance thought.
nodes.scope_note: The complete preface and concluding chapter distinguish classical rhetoric, medieval prudence, Lullism and Renaissance occult memory. Yates uses Rossi without claiming identical approaches; Bing mediates Warburg’s image questions, and Walker and R. W. Yates contribute specific work. Leibniz and secret-transmission arguments retain their hypothetical or contested status. Mnemonic arts differ from collective commemoration; Yates is not assigned a Skinner-derived method or Cambridge School membership.

nodes.label: Helen Maud Cam
nodes.date_label: Liberties and Communities 1944 · Law-finders and Law-makers 1962
nodes.description: Reconstructs medieval government through local institutions, legal records and parliamentary representation. Her research examines the making and editing of evidence as well as the relations between communities and central authority. Her contribution also includes teaching, scholarly editing and histories of historians.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Liberties and Communities in Medieval England (1944); studies of legal and constitutional history. IHR identifies local sources and medieval political history as central to her work.
nodes.scope_note: Studies in the Hundred Rolls (1921) and later collections distinguish documents from the institutions they disclose. Cam’s 1948 Stubbs opening combines appreciation with revision; Cheney identifies Maitland, Vinogradoff and documentary training, while questioning some juristic deductions and larger claims of legal progress. His memoir is a situated assessment, not a substitute for her full cases. Women’s place in scholarship is not confined to women’s-history subjects; the Ranke comparison remains undirected.

nodes.label: Dorothy Thompson
nodes.date_label: Class, women, and popular politics · postwar–1990s
nodes.description: Reconstructs women’s participation in popular radical politics while examining class, family, and community. A critical participant in a Marxist intellectual tradition, she questions both histories that overlook women and approaches that isolate them from shared political relations. Her career connects postwar labour history with debates reshaped by the women’s movement.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: “Women and Nineteenth-Century Radical Politics: A Lost Dimension,” in Juliet Mitchell and Ann Oakley, eds., The Rights and Wrongs of Women (1976); The Chartists: Popular Politics in the Industrial Revolution (1984); Outsiders: Class, Gender and Nation (1993). Her interview reflects critically on class and women’s history.
nodes.scope_note: Chartist documentary and monographic research, the 1976 women’s-politics essay, Queen Victoria (1990) and Outsiders (1993) address related but distinct questions. Her interview describes Torr’s tutoring, adult education, reciprocal work with Edward, and objections to class reduction and inflated claims for a new attention to language. Biography’s gender/power argument receives a specific contemporary criticism. The full interview is checked; monograph claims remain scoped to descriptions and scholarly accounts.

nodes.label: E. P. Thompson
nodes.date_label: Culture, class, and experience · 1960s–1990s
nodes.description: Makes culture, experience, and agency central to the historical formation of class, contributing to an early cultural reorientation within Marxist social history. He retained materialist explanation while disputing other uses of culture and theory. Feminist historians developed resources from his work while criticizing its handling of gender; he resisted some of their extensions and criticisms. This is an intertwined history of inheritance and disagreement, not a simple replacement of class by culture.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The Making of the English Working Class (1963); The Poverty of Theory, or an Orrery of Errors (1978). Edward Palmer Thompson has an individual entry here alongside Dorothy Thompson, whose research and arguments remain distinct.
nodes.scope_note: Making (1963) examines English class formation, explicitly limiting Scottish, Welsh and Irish coverage. Essays on time discipline (1967) and moral economy (1971) add distinct problems and named Annales/anthropological resources. Whigs and Hunters (1975) examines law and property; its current support is a selected review. Dorothy’s intellectual contribution is acknowledged in the Making preface; their separate authorship and reciprocal collaboration remain distinct. Primary preface and selected essay passages are checked, not all monographs or every later reception.

nodes.label: Fernand Braudel

nodes.description: Historian of multiple durations, material life, markets and capitalism. His models require historical testing and have finite lifespans. He borrows from Lévi-Strauss, engages Wallerstein and criticizes Weber’s explanation of capitalist origins.

Selected methodological and economic passages are checked; the Mediterranean monograph is not newly read in full.

nodes.label: Eric Hobsbawm
nodes.date_label: Primitive Rebels 1959 · The Age of… 1962–1994 · The Invention of Tradition 1983 · Budapest lecture 1993 · Interesting Times 2002 · How to Change the World 2011 · Fractured Times 2013
nodes.description: A historian of labour, popular protest, capitalist transformation and nations, who studies cultural evidence and explanatory synthesis across different scales; his responses to criticism revise some claims while retaining others. After Primitive Rebels (1959) and Labouring Men (1964), his four Age of… volumes (1962–1994) became, for reviewers, a synthesis of the capitalist world from 1789 to 1991; Tony Judt called The Age of Capital his greatest work and criticised The Age of Extremes for keeping the political categories of the 1930s (1995). With Terence Ranger he edited The Invention of Tradition (1983); in a 1993 lecture in Budapest he told historians to resist national myths as they formed and to hold to the difference between fact and fiction. Later books include On History (1997); the memoir Interesting Times (2002), which Perry Anderson read as a fifth volume of the same project: he finds in its explanation of remaining Communist after 1956 what most readers would see as integrity, while faulting its limited engagement with the political history of European Communism and its treatment of other Marxists; How to Change the World (2011), a history of Marxism, which Terry Eagleton credits with judiciousness while criticising its handling of ideas, including Althusser, feminism and Trotskyism; and the posthumous Fractured Times (2013).
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Primitive Rebels (1959); The Age of Revolution (1962); Labouring Men (1964); Industry and Empire (1968); Bandits (1969; revised 2000); The Age of Capital (1975); response to Stone on narrative (1980); with Terence Ranger, The Invention of Tradition (1983); The Age of Empire (1987); Nations and Nationalism since 1780 (1990); “The New Threat to History” (1993); The Age of Extremes (1994); On History (1997); Interesting Times (2002); Globalisation, Democracy and Terrorism (2007); How to Change the World (2011); Fractured Times (2013). Readings: Judt (1995); Anderson (2002); Black (2003–4); Eagleton (2011); Morgan (2013); Mayer on Evans’s biography (2020).
nodes.scope_note: The 1980 narrative reply, Bandits in its revised 2000 form, and Nations and Nationalism (1990/1992) distinguish debate, self-revision and historical synthesis. Later concessions about myth and political power are not projected into 1969. Colombian interlocutors and European comparative models supply named resources. Labouring Men and the main nationalism cases remain unread; selected primary support does not audit his entire career or generalizations. The 1993 Budapest lecture is read in full. The Age of… volumes, Primitive Rebels, Industry and Empire, On History, Interesting Times, How to Change the World and Fractured Times are unread here; they are dated and characterised through named readers (Judt, Anderson, Black, Eagleton, Morgan, the Guardian obituarists, and Mayer on Evans’s 2019 biography). No reception of The Invention of Tradition or of Nations and Nationalism is read here: the 1983 volume rests on its publisher record and the 1990 book on its preview, and Judt’s review and the 1993 lecture do not supply that reception. Criticism of individual contributors to the 1983 volume is not criticism of Hobsbawm’s conceptual programme.
