nodes.label: Roger Chartier
nodes.date_label: Lectures et lecteurs 1987 · Le monde comme représentation 1989 · Les origines culturelles 1990 · questions to White 1993 · “La nouvelle histoire culturelle existe-t-elle ?” 2003 · Collège de France 2007–2016 · Cardenio 2011 · Éditer et traduire 2021
nodes.description: A historian of reading, the book and written culture in early modern Europe who explains how textual forms, reading practices and collective representations shape social differences. His programme, set out in “Le monde comme représentation” (1989), joins material bibliography to differentiated appropriation, critically reworks Annales and uses conceptual resources without accepting every formulation. In 1993 he put four questions to Hayden White, on language, tropology, the procedures of research and relativism before the Shoah; they are known here through White’s 1995 rejoinder. In 2003 he argued that practices cannot be reduced to discourse, doubted that the new cultural history was as coherent as Lynn Hunt had claimed, and described it as a space of debate that had moved away from “the illusions of the linguistic turn”. He held the Collège de France chair “Écrit et cultures dans l’Europe moderne” from 2007 to 2016; his inaugural lecture called the tide of digital textuality a major rupture in the history of written culture, as his reviewer Christian Jouhaud quotes it. Later books, known here through their reviewers, follow the mobility of texts: the lost play Cardenio between Cervantes and Shakespeare (2011) and Éditer et traduire (2021).
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Lectures et lecteurs dans la France d’Ancien Régime (1987); “Le monde comme représentation” (1989); Les origines culturelles de la Révolution française (1990; English 1991); L’ordre des livres (1992; English 1994); “Quatre questions à Hayden White” (1993); On the Edge of the Cliff (1996); « La nouvelle histoire culturelle existe-t-elle ? » (2003); Inscrire et effacer (2005); Écouter les morts avec les yeux (Collège de France inaugural lecture, 2007); Cardenio entre Cervantès et Shakespeare (2011); The Author’s Hand and the Printer’s Mind (2013); Éditer et traduire (2021). Readings: White (1995); Jouhaud (2008, 2022); Boucheron (2014).
nodes.scope_note: The 1989 article explicitly engages McKenzie, Ricœur, Fish, Marin, Durkheim/Mauss, Elias, Ginzburg, Certeau and Foucault. Productive Foucault use coexists with a different account of appropriation; criticism of Braudel concerns an explanatory hierarchy. Social divisions include gender, generation, religion and education as well as class. The primary article is checked, but its cited works and historical examples do not thereby receive independent verification. Later work: the 2003 article is read in full; the 1993 questions to White are known only through White’s 1995 rejoinder, read in its authorised Portuguese translation; the 2007 dialogue with Darnton is read in part in Portuguese translation. The books listed here are unread unless an excerpt is separately identified: dates come from the Prismas bibliography (2022) and publisher pages, and their arguments from named reviewers (Jouhaud, Boucheron); Inscrire et effacer is listed bibliographically only. Boucheron’s expectation that medievalists will dispute his dating of the author function is an anticipated objection, not a controversy investigated here. The 1998 French Historical Studies forum is dated from metadata only, and the 1985–88 exchange with Robert Darnton is unread; neither is covered substantively.

nodes.label: Medical & health history
nodes.date_label: Earlier medical scholarship · social-medicine interventions 1930s · later social histories
nodes.description: Studies medicine, illness, healing and health in their historical settings. nodes.label: Urban history
nodes.date_label: Earlier city histories · postwar expansion · Urban History Yearbook 1974
nodes.description: Studies cities and urbanization through institutions, populations, built environments and connections beyond city boundaries. David Harvey: Social Justice and the City (1973); Walter Benjamin: Das Passagen-Werk (1982); Michel de Certeau: “Walking in the City” (1980).

Journal milestones mark consolidation, not the first historical study of cities.

nodes.scope_note: Historical geography has roots well before digital mapping. Spatial history is an overlapping set of approaches, not a synonym for GIS or one unified school. This selection foregrounds British reconstruction, Australian colonial space and a British HGIS project; wider regional traditions and Indigenous spatial knowledge require fuller treatment. Later digital projects are not backdated into the period reviewed through 2000.

nodes.label: Intellectual history
nodes.date_label: Earlier histories of thought · Lovejoy 1936 · Skinner 1969 · plural programmes through the 1990s
nodes.description: Studies thought, concepts, arguments and their production, circulation and interpretation in historical settings. History of ideas, contextual political thought, conceptual history, textual criticism and the material history of publishing supply overlapping but disputed methods. Intellectual history extends beyond the Cambridge School and beyond a canon of European philosophers.

nodes.scope_note: An enduring field with internal disagreements, not a single lineage from Lovejoy to contextualism. The existing Cambridge School and Conceptual history entries retain their specificity. Maruyama supplies one Japanese inquiry with explicit translation credit, not global representation or evidence of Cambridge influence. Social and cultural settings matter without reducing texts to reflections of social position. Women’s intellectual histories and African, Islamic, South Asian and Latin American traditions still need much fuller coverage.

nodes.label: Labour history
nodes.date_label: Webbs 1894/1920 · Thompson 1963 · expanding comparative and feminist inquiries in the 1970s–1990s
nodes.description: Studies work, workers, labour relations and collective organisation across paid, unpaid, coerced, agricultural and industrial settings. Labour history includes unions and politics, workplace authority, household economies, culture, race, gender and colonial categories. Labour and labor are spelling variants; neither social history nor British Marxism exhausts the field.

nodes.scope_note: Institutional histories, Marxist cultural analysis, feminist inquiry and colonial labour studies coexist and disagree. Thompson’s work already contains a cultural reorientation; later gender analysis involves productive inheritance as well as criticism. This selection includes Britain, the United States, France, South Asia and Africa but does not constitute global coverage. Labour institutions and historical scholarship about them have different chronologies. Fuller Latin American, Caribbean, East Asian and Indigenous labour historiographies remain priorities.

nodes.label: Ethnohistory
nodes.date_label: Earlier interdisciplinary work · Great Lakes–Ohio Valley project 1953 · Lurie 1961 · continuing regional programmes
nodes.description: Combines historical and anthropological inquiry through archives, material evidence, language, oral traditions and situated cultural interpretation. North American claims research, Wendat/Huron historical reconstruction, Nahua documentary studies and Andean historical anthropology form distinct programmes. Ethnohistory studies historical change rather than assigning some peoples to an unchanging ethnographic past.

nodes.scope_note: The field overlaps with Indigenous history but does not automatically confer Indigenous authority, community consent or decolonizing method. Claims research could serve governments as well as claimants. Indigenous authors appear here as qualified interlocutors and critics, not as members of an externally assigned school. Lurie herself disputes restricting the approach to particular peoples. The Americas dominate this initial selection; Vansina provides a comparison with African oral-tradition methodology, not proof that African history descends from US ethnohistory.

nodes.label: Joan Wallach Scott
nodes.date_label: Women’s work 1975 · Gender 1986 · Experience 1991 · Only Paradoxes 1996 · Parité! 2005 · The Politics of the Veil 2007 · “Unanswered Questions” 2008 · Sex and Secularism 2017 · On the Judgment of History 2020
nodes.description: A historian of modern France who, after studies of women’s work and the family with Louise Tilly (1975, 1978), proposed gender as a historical analysis of social relationships and power (1986), connecting symbols, normative claims, institutions and subjectivity while insisting on historical variation, and questioned experience as self-evident evidence (1991). Gender and the Politics of History (1988) made her, in Laura Lee Downs’s words, “the spokesperson for gender history”; Palmer, Valverde and Downs contested her poststructuralism. Later books, presented here through their reviewers, trace French feminists’ paradoxes between the abstract individual and sexual difference (Only Paradoxes to Offer, 1996, as Landes reads it), the parity movement (Parité!, 2005, as Dean reads it), the headscarf ban (The Politics of the Veil, 2007, as Laborde reads it) and gender in the discourse of secularism (Sex and Secularism, 2017, as Whitney and O’Grady read it); Laborde finds the veil book’s normative premises unclear, and O’Grady objects that the later book holds nineteenth-century Europeans to present moral standards. In a 2018 interview Scott asked how to write a critique of secularism without rejecting it. Answering an AHR forum on her 1986 essay (2008), she insisted that gender is useful only as a question and explained her use of psychoanalysis and fantasy to keep it critical; her reply presents the forum’s reception as geographically and politically situated, quoting Heidi Tinsman, and disputes Joanne Meyerowitz’s reading of a change of direction, asserting continuity in her concern with sexual difference. With Ethan Kleinberg and Gary Wilder she called for a theorized “critical history” (2018); Knowledge, Power, and Academic Freedom (2019), in Robin Whitaker’s account, treats academic freedom as an ethical practice and holds that disciplinary practice is no power-free zone; she has also written on the claim that history will judge (2020).
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: “Women’s Work and the Family in Nineteenth-Century Europe” (with Louise Tilly, 1975); Gender: A Useful Category of Historical Analysis (1986); “On Language, Gender, and Working-Class History” (1987); Gender and the Politics of History (1988; revised 1999; 2018); “The Evidence of Experience” (1991); Only Paradoxes to Offer (1996); “The ‘Class’ We Have Lost” (2000); Parité! (2005); The Politics of the Veil (2007); “Unanswered Questions” (2008); The Fantasy of Feminist History (2011); “The Incommensurability of Psychoanalysis and History” (2012); Sex and Secularism (2017); Theses on Theory and History (with Kleinberg and Wilder, 2018); Knowledge, Power, and Academic Freedom (2019); On the Judgment of History (2020). Readings: Valverde (1990); Downs (1993); Landes (1997); Dean (2006); Laborde (2008); the AHR forum (2008); Whitney and O’Grady (2018); Whitaker (2019); McLemee (2020).
nodes.scope_note: Existing cross-field presence warrants a visible argument, not just another name in a roster. The 1986 and 1991 interventions and the 1987 forum reply are read in her own words; “Unanswered Questions” (2008) is read in full in an authorised Spanish translation, so its wording is not given as her English. The books from Only Paradoxes to Offer (1996) to On the Judgment of History (2020) are unread here and are characterised through named reviewers (Landes, Dean, Laborde, Whitney, O’Grady, Whitaker, McLemee) and publisher descriptions; the 2000 and 2012 articles through their abstracts. The AHR forum contributions (2008) are unread: Tinsman and Meyerowitz appear only as Scott’s reply quotes or reports them. Secularism and academic freedom have no entries of their own, so those arguments appear in the description and timeline; the veil and secularism books are drawn as a contribution to postcolonial critique.

nodes.label: Natalie Zemon Davis
nodes.date_label: “The Reasons of Misrule” 1971 · “The Rites of Violence” 1973 · Society and Culture in Early Modern France 1975 · “Women’s History in Transition” 1976 · The Return of Martin Guerre 1982–83 · Fiction in the Archives 1987 · Women on the Margins 1995 · Slaves on Screen and The Gift 2000 · Trickster Travels 2006
nodes.description: A historian of sixteenth-century France whose work moved from the social history of Lyon’s printing workers to ritual, gender, storytelling and lives that crossed religious and colonial borders. By her own account (1997) she ‘combined archival work with the study of printed texts of multiple genres’, and Laurie Nussdorfer’s memorial calls her ‘the rare social historian who valued printed sources’. In ‘The Rites of Violence’ (1973) she argued that religious riot drew on ‘a store of punitive or purificatory traditions’ and had ‘a connection in time, place and form with the life of worship’, so that such violence was ‘related here less to the pathological than to the normal’; she explicitly distinguished explaining the ritual structure of violence from granting a right to commit it: ‘the rites of violence are not the rights of violence in any absolute sense’. She acknowledged the crowd histories of Rudé, Hobsbawm, Thompson and Tilly and applied Thompson’s account of the food riot’s legitimation to the religious crowd. By her own account she came to ritual through Van Gennep’s folklore and read Evans-Pritchard, Turner, Geertz and Mintz ‘eclectically … not looking for solutions, but for questions’ (1997); Thompson, for his part, called her charivari essay ‘une étude importante’ (1972). Joan Scott (1986) quoted her call to study ‘the history of both women and men’ as an early relational use of gender, and with Jill Conway she taught in 1971 what she called ‘the first course in women’s history in Canada’. In 1997 she said she came to microhistory, ‘or what I called ethnography’, through the film of Martin Guerre, on whose script she worked; her book followed in French (1982) and English (1983). Robert Finlay (1988) charged that she had ‘permitted an excess of invention’ against ‘the sovereignty of the sources’; she answered that where reconstruction stops and invention begins was ‘precisely the question I hoped readers would ask’. In her 1997 retrospect she described the ‘fiction’ of Fiction in the Archives (1987) as ‘the crafting element’, not falsification, and Women on the Margins (1995) as ‘a decentered comparison’ of three lives, whose conclusion keeps religious difference and colonial domination in view. The Holberg committee (2010) described The Gift (2000) as illuminating ‘the intricate forms of pre-market exchange and reciprocity’, Slaves on Screen (2000) as dealing with ‘the alteration of historical material in contemporary film’ and Trickster Travels (2006), with Women on the Margins, as exploring ‘the translation and transmission of cultures’; it saw her uniqueness in ‘connecting early modern Europe with new areas of comparative history’.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Natalie Zemon Davis (1928–2023); dissertation on Lyon’s Protestants and printing workers (1959); “A Trade Union in Sixteenth-Century France” (Economic History Review, 1966); “The Reasons of Misrule: Youth Groups and Charivaris in Sixteenth-Century France” (Past and Present, 1971); “The Rites of Violence: Religious Riot in Sixteenth-Century France” (Past and Present, 1973; reprinted in Society and Culture in Early Modern France, 1975); “‘Women’s History’ in Transition: The European Case” (Feminist Studies, 1976; quoted by Scott, 1986); Le Retour de Martin Guerre (Paris: Robert Laffont, 1982; the catalogue record also credits Jean-Claude Carrière and Daniel Vigne, scenarist and director of the 1982 film on whose script she worked) and The Return of Martin Guerre (Harvard, 1983); “History’s Two Bodies” (AHA presidential address, 1987; AHR 1988); Fiction in the Archives: Pardon Tales and Their Tellers in Sixteenth-Century France (1987); “On the Lame” (AHR Forum, 1988, reply to Finlay); Women on the Margins: Three Seventeenth-Century Lives (1995); A Life of Learning (Haskins Lecture, 1997); Slaves on Screen: Film and Historical Vision (2000); The Gift in Sixteenth-Century France (2000); Trickster Travels: A Sixteenth-Century Muslim between Worlds (2006); “Decentering History” (Holberg Symposium, 2010); later titles named in Nussdorfer’s memorial (unread): Leo Africanus Discovers Comedy: Theatre and Poetry Across the Mediterranean (2021) and Listening to the Languages of the People: Lazare Sainéan on Romanian, Yiddish and French (2022). Readers and critics: E. P. Thompson (1972); Lawrence Stone (1979); Joan Scott (1986); Robert Finlay (1988); Lynn Hunt, ed., with Suzanne Desan’s chapter (1989); Judith Jackson Fossett (2001); Holberg Prize committee (2010); Alexandra Walsham (2017); Laurie Nussdorfer (2023); Carla Hesse (2024).
nodes.scope_note: Read for revision 1.143: ‘The Rites of Violence’ (1973), pp. 52–53, 57, 60–61 and 90–91; her Haskins Lecture, A Life of Learning (1997), in full, cited as her later account of her course, not as evidence of what the earlier works say; ‘On the Lame’ (1988), pp. 572, 574–576, 584, 587, 600 and 602–603; Finlay’s critique (1988) in full; Stone (1979), pp. 3 and 18; Scott (1986), p. 1054; and, earlier, the prologue, conclusion and acknowledgments of Women on the Margins. Thompson’s ‘Rough Music’ (1972, by paragraph in a 2020 reprint), her AHA address (1987) and the AHA memorial (2024) are read only in short excerpts. The Return of Martin Guerre, Fiction in the Archives, The Gift, Slaves on Screen, Trickster Travels and the 2021–22 books are unread: they supply bibliographic dates and mediated interpretations only, given in her own retrospect or in named readers’ words (the Holberg committee, Fossett, Finlay, Nussdorfer). Also unread: ‘Women’s History in Transition’ (1976; her words as Scott quotes them), Estèbe’s 1975 comment on ‘Rites’ and her rejoinder, Ginzburg’s 1984 postface to the Italian Martin Guerre, Desan’s 1989 chapter and the Davis–Thompson letters (Walsham 2017; opening only). She is not presented as the founder of microhistory, cultural history or gender history: by her own account Le Roy Ladurie and Ginzburg reached microhistory by other routes, Scott quotes her as one relational voice among others, and anthropology supplied questions tested on ‘only historical evidence’. Finlay’s charge of invention and her reply are both kept, as is Fossett’s criticism (2001) that Slaves on Screen ‘raises more questions than it answers’. Not to be confused with J. C. Davis (the Ranter debate) or Donald F. Davis (Canadian urban history).

nodes.label: Lynn Hunt
nodes.date_label: Politics, Culture, and Class 1984 · The New Cultural History 1989 · Telling the Truth about History 1994 · AHA address 2003 · Inventing Human Rights 2007 · Writing History in the Global Era 2014
nodes.description: A historian of the French Revolution whose Politics, Culture, and Class in the French Revolution (1984) joined revolutionary symbols and rhetoric to the sociology of political actors, using Geertz’s interpretive frame, and whose introduction to The New Cultural History (1989) reassessed the explanatory models of social history, recognising turns toward culture within Marxist and Annales histories while questioning the priority assigned to social experience. With Joyce Appleby and Margaret Jacob she defended a “practical realism” (1994), and with Victoria Bonnell she edited Beyond the Cultural Turn (1999). In her AHA presidential address (2003) she asked how the Revolution could “produce such contradictory consequences” as terror, democracy and human rights. Inventing Human Rights (2007), which reviewers summarise as tracing rights to imagined empathy, novels and the rejection of torture, was contested by Samuel Moyn and David A. Bell. Writing History in the Global Era (2014), the book around which this atlas was first developed, argued, in her reviewer’s summary, that globalization had become a new paradigm that could wash away the gains of cultural history.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Politics, Culture, and Class in the French Revolution (1984); Introduction: History, Culture, and Text, in The New Cultural History (1989), editor; The Family Romance of the French Revolution (1992); with Joyce Appleby and Margaret Jacob, Telling the Truth about History (1994); with Victoria Bonnell, Beyond the Cultural Turn (1999); “The World We Have Gained: The Future of the French Revolution” (AHA presidential address, 2003); Inventing Human Rights (2007); Writing History in the Global Era (2014). Readings: Moyn (2007); Bell (2007); McClure (2015).
nodes.scope_note: Connects the cultural turn to disputes within social explanation. Hunt authored the 1989 introduction and edited the collection; she did not author all its essays. Her political-culture work rests on the existing reading of the 1984 book’s chapter openings, and her later revolution argument on the 2003 address read through the AHA web text. Inventing Human Rights and Writing History in the Global Era are presented through their reviewers (Moyn, Bell, McClure); the books themselves are unread here. The atlas’s Identity histories grouping is her later classification and does not make her its founder. No human-rights entry exists; the 2007 book is drawn as a contribution to cultural history and as the object of a critique.

nodes.label: Catherine Hall
nodes.date_label: Family Fortunes 1987 · White, Male and Middle Class 1992 · Defining the Victorian Nation 2000 · Civilising Subjects 2002 · Legacies of British Slave-ownership 2009– · Macaulay and Son 2012 · Lucky Valley 2024
nodes.description: A historian of gender, class, race and empire. With Leonore Davidoff she related English middle-class formation to gender, family, religion and economic life in Family Fortunes (1987), investigating class identities and gender relations together rather than in separate accounts. Civilising Subjects (2002), whose “central argument”, she wrote, “is that being a colonizer was part of the construction of Englishness”, followed Birmingham abolitionists and Baptist missionaries to Jamaica; she credited C. L. R. James with showing what can be gained by studying “metropole and colony in one lens”. Angela Woollacott (2006) reads it as postcolonial history for its “insistence on the interconstitutive connections between colony and metropole”, and Edward Said (2003) praised it while asking for subaltern voices. From 2009 she led, with her research associates Nicholas Draper and Keith McClelland, University College London’s Legacies of British Slave-ownership project, tracing the slave-owners compensated at emancipation into Victorian Britain. In 2014 she and her coauthors identified a move toward modified versions of Williams’s thesis among economic historians, and she argued, against the British Marxist historians’ neglect of “race, slavery and the Caribbean”, that gender and race shaped the formation of capital. Lucky Valley (2024) turns to Edward Long and “racial capitalism”.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: With Leonore Davidoff, Family Fortunes: Men and Women of the English Middle Class 1780–1850 (1987); White, Male and Middle Class (1992); with Keith McClelland and Jane Rendall, Defining the Victorian Nation (2000); Civilising Subjects: Metropole and Colony in the English Imagination, 1830–1867 (2002); Macaulay and Son: Architects of Imperial Britain (2012); with Nicholas Draper, Keith McClelland, Katie Donington and Rachel Lang, Legacies of British Slave-ownership (2014); “Gendering Property, Racing Capital” (History Workshop Journal, 2014); Lucky Valley: Edward Long and the History of Racial Capitalism (2024). nodes.label: Lorraine Daston
nodes.date_label: Classical Probability 1988 · The Image of Objectivity 1992 · The Moral Economy of Science 1995 · Objectivity 2007 · Science Studies and the History of Science 2009 · Rules 2022
nodes.description: A historian of science who historicizes the categories of scientific knowing. Her books include Classical Probability in the Enlightenment (1988) and, with Katharine Park, Wonders and the Order of Nature, 1150–1750 (1998). In “The Moral Economy of Science” (1995) she argued that certain forms of empiricism, quantification and objectivity “require moral economies”, “a web of affect-saturated values”, drawing on Elias’s civilizing process and distinguishing her sense of the term from E. P. Thompson’s. With Peter Galison she studied objectivity itself: their 1992 article distinguishes mechanical objectivity from other historically formed components of the concept, and their book Objectivity (2007) treats it, in reviewers’ readings, as one epistemic virtue beside others rather than their successor. She was a director at the Max Planck Institute for the History of Science from 1995 until 2019. In 2009 she argued that the history of science had become “a discipline” while science studies remained “undisciplined”, and that “to historicize the category of the fact, objectivity, or proof is not thereby to debunk it”.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Classical Probability in the Enlightenment (1988); with Peter Galison, “The Image of Objectivity” (1992); “The Moral Economy of Science” (1995); with Katharine Park, Wonders and the Order of Nature, 1150–1750 (1998); with Peter Galison, Objectivity (2007); “Science Studies and the History of Science” (2009); Rules: A Short History of What We Live By (2022). Joint works; retain all coauthor credits. Readings: Henning (2008); Switzer (2009); Lahav (2023).
nodes.scope_note: Adds a substantive history-of-science contribution beyond gender history. Galison retains equal authorship and argument credit for the 1992 article and the 2007 book, and Park for Wonders. Their historical analysis does not assert that scientific objectivity is simply impossible: in 2009 she wrote that “‘If historical, then relative’ is a non sequitur”. The 1995 and 2009 essays are read in her own words; Objectivity and Rules remain unread: their content is mediated by reviewers (Switzer and Henning; Lahav) and Rules by its publisher’s description, and the 1988 and 1998 books are dated from her 2009 author note and the Collège de France biography and carry no argument here. “Historical epistemology” in her sense is not the French tradition of the atlas’s Historical epistemology entry, and no edge connects them.

Spanish original pp. 17–18; a programme for collaboration, not an attribution of all technical work to historians or a claim that digital history replaces older inquiry.
strands.works: La historia digital en la era del Web 2.0. Introducción al dossier Historia digital

strands.title: Writing The Historian’s Macroscope in Public
strands.focus: Graham, Milligan and Weingart propose computational exploration of large historical collections with public research notebooks, treating algorithms and datasets as perspectives open to scrutiny and revision. Their 2014 methodological and collaborative account, not an independent replication of its topic-model example or a reading of either book edition. Public collaboration is presented as part of the method.
strands.works: Writing The Historian’s Macroscope in Public

strands.title: Digital History’s Perpetual Future Tense
strands.focus: Blevins recognizes digital history’s archival, pedagogical and public achievements while calling for more explicit argument-driven academic scholarship and less rhetoric of future potential. An attributed 2016 disciplinary assessment, not a field-wide quantitative audit. His later discussion explicitly recognizes interpretation in public-history projects; the distinction concerns organizing priorities, not an absence of arguments.
strands.works: Digital History’s Perpetual Future Tense

strands.title: State of the Field: Digital History
strands.focus: Romein and colleagues distinguish successive computing practices and stress that corpus composition and changing meanings constrain quantitative text analysis. Source-specific assessment, not a definition of the whole field. Digital history, computational history and digital humanities remain separate candidate identities; their relations require historical argument.
strands.works: State of the Field: Digital History

strands.title: The Transformation of Historical Research in the Digital Age
strands.focus: Milligan treats search, digitization and online scholarly practice as changes affecting ordinary historical research, not only specialist computational projects. Source-specific assessment, not a definition of the whole field. Digital history, computational history and digital humanities remain separate candidate identities; their relations require historical argument. Milligan distinguishes the field of Digital History from wider digitized historical practice and identifies public-history and quantitative traditions among its lineages. Selected section 1.3, pp. 7–8; an attributed retrospective account of plural roots, not a single founding date or an influence arrow from every earlier tradition.
strands.works: The Transformation of Historical Research in the Digital Age

strands.title: The Transnational and the Text-Searchable: Digitized Sources and the Shadows They Cast
strands.focus: Putnam examines how digitized search changes transnational research and the contextual learning formerly required by place-based work. Abstract only. Direct page access failed; no full-article or broader reception claim. Relevance spans digital and transnational history.
strands.works: The Transnational and the Text-Searchable: Digitized Sources and the Shadows They Cast

strands.title: Making a Case for the Black Digital Humanities
strands.focus: Gallon proposes Black digital humanities as a critique of racialized knowledge and a practice of historical recovery. An attributed programme within digital humanities; not an equivalence between digital humanities and digital history.
strands.works: Making a Case for the Black Digital Humanities

strands.title: Complicating a “Great Man” Narrative of Digital History in the United States
strands.focus: Leon criticizes Thomas’s digital-history genealogy for omitting women historians. Leon’s specific critique; Thomas’s chapter has not been independently read in this batch. Leon links exclusions in digital-history narratives to academic status, institutional location and the invisibility of collaborative labour. Selected chapter paragraphs, US-focused argument; her grant tallies are not independently reproduced here or adopted as this graph’s demographic baseline.

nodes.label: Laurentian & national tradition
nodes.date_label: Staple studies 1923–40 · Creighton 1937 · Lower 1946 · Careless 1954 · Centenary Series volumes 1964–85 · Berger's analysis 1976
nodes.description: English-Canadian historical writing that took the transcontinental nation-state as its frame, from the interwar years to the centennial. Its economic core is the staple approach: Innis's studies of the fur trade (1930) and cod fisheries (1940) read Canada's development through exports to imperial centres, an approach Watkins later called Canada's most distinctive contribution to political economy. Creighton's Commercial Empire of the St. Lawrence (1937) simplified and expanded Innis's thesis, making Montreal's merchants the 'spiritual fathers' of Confederation; his Macdonald biography followed. Liberal nationalists such as Lower and Underhill and conservative nationalists such as Creighton and Stacey disagreed politically while sharing the nation-state as the frame of reference. Careless offered a metropolitan interpretation (1954), which Donald Davis (1985) found indeterminate, and Morton asked in 1946 on what critical premises the established interpretations rested. The Canadian Centenary Series, from 1964, gathered national syntheses, including translated volumes by the Quebec historians Trudel and Ouellet. Cook's and Careless's 'limited identities' (1967, 1969) and the new regional history of Acadiensis (1971) challenged the frame, and Berger's Writing of Canadian History (1976) analysed the English-Canadian tradition as a historiographical subject. French-Canadian historians such as Michel Brunet pursued a rival national vision, treated under Quebec historiography.

nodes.scope_note: A teaching umbrella, not one school. The staple approach (political economy), Creighton's Laurentian narrative, liberal and conservative nationalisms, metropolitanism and the Centenary Series are distinct projects; roster inclusion is not membership. The label avoids 'Laurentian school': no checked source uses that phrase. French-Canadian and Quebec national historiography belongs to Quebec historiography: Trudel and Ouellet are named only in the Centenary Series strand, and the Creighton–Brunet comparison is carried by the relationship note, not the roster. Stacey (official history, external policy) is placed in Canadian military history and Political, international & national history; Stanley appears as a secondary row for The Birth of Western Canada. Critics appear as critics.

nodes.label: English-Canadian intellectual & cultural history
nodes.date_label: Berger 1970, 1976 · McKillop 1979 · Owram 1980, 1986 · cultural turn: McKay 1994, Vance 1997, Nelles 1999 · selected later readings
nodes.description: English-Canadian intellectual and cultural history studies how Canadians thought about empire, nation, religion, science and the state, and later how traditions, myths and public memories were made. Carl Berger's The Sense of Power (1970) examined imperialist ideas of Canadian character and mission and argued that Canadian imperialism was one form of Canadian nationalism; his The Writing of Canadian History (1976) made English-Canadian historical writing itself a subject. A. B. McKillop, Marlene Shore and Doug Owram followed ideas into the university, social science, western expansion and the interwar 'service state'. Ramsay Cook's The Regenerators (1985) joined the field to religious history. Critics charged it with what Clarence Karr (1989) called a 'narrow, elitist, biographical methodology': group biographies of academics, journalists and clergy that said little about what most Canadians thought. Susan Mann Trofimenkoff (1979) had argued that a field anchored to nationalism left women almost invisible. From the 1990s a cultural history of invention and memory developed alongside it. Ian McKay's The Quest of the Folk (1994) showed tourism promoters and cultural producers refashioning Nova Scotians as a simple folk. Daniel Francis wrote on the 'imaginary Indian' and national myths, and Jonathan Vance on the memory of the First World War. H. V. Nelles, Keith Walden, E. A. Heaman and Ian Radforth studied pageants, exhibitions and royal tours, and Colin Coates and Cecilia Morgan the commemoration of heroines. Yvan Lamonde's social history of ideas in Quebec runs on a separate francophone track.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Berger, The Sense of Power (1970), The Writing of Canadian History (1976; 1986), Science, God, and Nature in Victorian Canada (1983); Cook, The Maple Leaf Forever (1971), The Regenerators (1985); McKillop, A Disciplined Intelligence (1979), Matters of Mind (1994); Owram, Promise of Eden (1980), The Government Generation (1986); Shore, The Science of Social Redemption (1987); Litt (1992); Vipond (1992); Francis, The Imaginary Indian (1992), National Dreams (1997); McKay, The Quest of the Folk (1994); Vance, Death So Noble (1997); Walden (1997); Heaman, The Inglorious Arts of Peace (1999); Nelles, The Art of Nation-Building (1999); Coates and Morgan, Heroines and History (2002); Radforth, Royal Spectacle (2004); Igartua (2006). Critiques: Trofimenkoff, “Nationalism, Feminism & Canadian Intellectual History” (1979); Karr, “What Happened to Canadian Intellectual History?” (1989). Comparisons: Lamonde, Histoire sociale des idées au Québec (2000); Lears, No Place of Grace (1981).
nodes.scope_note: English-Canadian by design; Quebec's histoire sociale des idées is a comparison (Lamonde). Intellectual history (ideas, intellectuals, the university) and cultural history (spectacle, myth, memory) are distinct strands with different methods. The religious strand is shared with Religion, social reform & secularization in Canada, postwar identity with Canada’s 1960s. Editorial observation, not a sourced claim: Indigenous people appear in this field mostly as settler representations (Francis, Heaman), which is a limit to flag in teaching. PhD evidence (2009–2026): engagement with the field's anchor scholars is steady (ratio 1.02; 1.14 in a fixed panel of 14 universities), while its older works are cited less; the classics are ageing, not the field. Owram's 'Intellectual History in the Land of Limited Identities' (JCS 24:3, 1989; abstract checked, not cited as a source) is a practitioner's self-assessment that also notes the field's nationalist roots and the differing methods of francophone and anglophone writers; it is not treated as a critique.

nodes.label: Religion, social reform & secularization in Canada
nodes.date_label: Allen, The Social Passion 1971 · Cook, The Regenerators 1985 · secularization debate: Gauvreau 1991, Marshall 1992 and 1993–94, Christie and Gauvreau 1996 · selected later readings
nodes.description: Historical writing on Christianity as a force in Canadian reform, culture and everyday life, and on whether and when Canada secularized. Its central argument came in 1985–96. Ramsay Cook’s The Regenerators (1985) read late Victorian social criticism as the sacred becoming secular, and David Marshall’s Secularizing the Faith (1992) followed Protestant clergy through a crisis of belief to the 1920s as “an era of drift”. Their critics attacked this as the secularization thesis. Michael Gauvreau’s The Evangelical Century (1991) argued that the evangelical creed adapted to Darwinism and higher criticism; Marshall replied in 1993–94 that attempts to dismiss secularization were premature. In A Full-Orbed Christianity (1996) Nancy Christie and Gauvreau argued that the Protestant churches reached their greatest cultural influence before 1940 and placed secularization after the Second World War. Behind the debate stands Richard Allen’s The Social Passion (1971), which made the social gospel central to the history of reform, though recent doctoral work cites it far less. Social histories of Protestant culture, Methodism, gender and leisure (Westfall, Semple, Marks) moved the question from doctrine to lay practice. Catholic history developed alongside: Hamelin and Gagnon’s synthesis of Quebec Catholicism, Perin on Rome, McGowan on Irish Toronto. Gauvreau later carried the revision into Quebec, tracing the Quiet Revolution to Catholic Action (2005). Later work studies irreligion in settler British Columbia (Marks 2017), distinguishes political from social secularization (Van Die) and treats religion as a vehicle of the liberal order (Christie). Moral reform as regulation belongs to a neighbouring field.

Comparison: Brown, The Death of Christian Britain (2001).
nodes.scope_note: A research field containing a debate. “Secularization thesis” is the name its critics gave to Cook’s and Marshall’s accounts (Laverdure’s 1998 review of Christie and Gauvreau); Marshall defended the concept in 1993–94. Both sides appear as historians. Catholic and Protestant histories have different genealogies; Irish Catholic history (McGowan, Perin) stays here. The Catholic Action revision of the Quiet Revolution (Meunier and Warren, Bienvenue, Gauvreau 2005) has its main home in Quebec historiography. Moral reform as regulation (Valverde) is placed in Moral regulation.

nodes.label: Liberal order framework
nodes.date_label: State-formation roots: Curtis 1988, Greer and Radforth 1992 · McKay’s prospectus Dec. 2000 · debate volume 2009 · selected later readings
nodes.description: A proposal to write Canadian history as the history of a liberal project of rule. Ian McKay's prospectus in the Canadian Historical Review (2000) offered a way past the impasse between socio-cultural and national-political history: map 'Canada' as the project through which liberal order (in Fecteau's paraphrase, an individualism of liberty, equality and property) became common sense in northern North America from the 1840s. Commentators identify Gramsci's hegemony and Fernande Roy's study of francophone business liberalism as its sources and link it to earlier state-formation research: Bruce Curtis on schooling and the census, and Allan Greer and Ian Radforth's Colonial Leviathan (1992). Constant and Ducharme's Liberalism and Hegemony (2009) tested it on rights, municipalities, conservation, families, women and racialized people, and First Nations. This entry reads the framework as closer to a history of capitalism than to moral regulation: its subject is how property, the individual and market relations became the terms of rule. In his 2009 reply McKay held that liberal order and capitalism cannot be conflated, yet after the 1840s could not easily be separated. Earlier social histories of seigneurial Quebec (Greer 1985) and Montreal's wage-earning families (Bradbury 1993) are read alongside it. Critics answered: Bryan Palmer argued that the framework sidesteps capitalism's changing structures. Jerry Bannister proposed a loyalist order before 1840. Ruth Sandwell found a-liberal families, and Nancy Christie faulted its neglect of religion and of women. Later histories of land, enclosure and taxation (Weaver, Greer, Heaman) carry its questions further.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Roots: Curtis, Building the Educational State (1988), True Government by Choice Men? (1992), The Politics of Population (2001); Greer and Radforth, eds., Colonial Leviathan (1992). Prospectus: McKay, “The Liberal Order Framework” (CHR, 2000), drawing on Roy, Progrès, harmonie, liberté (1988). Debate: Sandwell (2003); Constant and Ducharme, eds., Liberalism and Hegemony (2009), with Bannister, Heaman, Curtis, Sandwell, Perry, Brownlie and McKay’s reply; the Underhill Review round table (Ajzenstat, Christie, Fecteau, Pâquet) and Palmer (2009). Liberty: Ducharme (2010), McNairn (2000). Transition to capitalism (read alongside): Greer, Peasant, Lord, and Merchant (1985); Bradbury, Working Families (1993). Property and capitalism: Weaver (2003), Greer (2012, 2018), Heaman (2017). Left history: McKay (2005, 2008).
nodes.scope_note: A programme and its debate rather than a school: roster inclusion is not adoption. Curtis, Greer and Radforth wrote its roots before it was named; Christie, Palmer, Sandwell, Fecteau and Ajzenstat appear as critics; Bannister proposes a loyalist order for 1750–1840 (chapter title), its relation to McKay not characterized. Kept separate from moral regulation by the user (2026-10-12) as "a different project closer to history of capitalism"; that reading is editorial and is stated as such in the description. The overlap with histories of capitalism is noted in the description; it is not drawn as a link, because the fields have not connected (user, 2026-10-12). Greer (1985) and Bradbury (1993) are read alongside the framework, not as its roots or applications.

nodes.label: Moral regulation
nodes.date_label: International roots (Corrigan 1981; Corrigan and Sayer 1985) · Kinsman 1987 · Valverde and Weir 1988 · Valverde 1991 · critiques 1994–97 · Strange and Loo 1997 · selected publication milestones, not boundaries
nodes.description: Studies how morality, sexuality, health and conduct were made objects of governance by reformers, churches, professions, courts and the state, and how regulation shaped the selves of the regulated. The concept came into historical sociology through Philip Corrigan's work (1981) and Corrigan and Sayer's The Great Arch (1985), which treated English state formation as a cultural revolution; Ruonavaara describes their framework as fusing Durkheimian and Foucauldian analysis with Marxist theory. In Canada, Mariana Valverde and Lorna Weir offered preliminary remarks on moral regulation in Resources for Feminist Research (1988), and Valverde's The Age of Light, Soap, and Water (1991) argued that Protestant social-purity reformers were not simply repressive and that they linked sexual health to racial purity and slum clearance. Kinsman's The Regulation of Desire (1987), and later The Canadian War on Queers (2010, with Gentile), examined sexual regulation and the national-security campaign against gays and lesbians. Studies of contraception and eugenics (McLaren), women, girls and the law (Backhouse, Lévesque, Dubinsky, Strange, Sangster), welfare and single mothers (Little), and postwar normality (Adams, Gleason) widened the field. Adams tied moral regulation to state formation through venereal-disease policy, and Strange and Loo surveyed law and moral regulation from 1867 to 1939 (1997). Critics reformulated the concept: Dean (1994) recast Corrigan's account through Foucault's governmentality, and Ruonavaara (1997) rejected a monolithic, state-only project. The liberal order framework (McKay 2000) is a separate entry, closer to a history of capitalism.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: International roots: Corrigan, "On Moral Regulation" (1981); Corrigan and Sayer, The Great Arch (1985). Canadian work: McLaren and McLaren, The Bedroom and the State (1986); Kinsman, The Regulation of Desire (1987); Valverde and Weir, "The Struggles of the Immoral" (1988); Lévesque, La norme et les déviantes (1989); McLaren, Our Own Master Race (1990); Valverde, The Age of Light, Soap, and Water (1991); Backhouse, Petticoats and Prejudice (1991); Mitchinson, The Nature of Their Bodies (1991); Dubinsky, Improper Advances (1993); Adams, "In Sickness and in Health" (1994) and The Trouble with Normal (1997); Little, "Manhunts and Bingo Blabs" (1994); Valverde, ed., Studies in Moral Regulation (1994); Strange, Toronto's Girl Problem (1995); Strange and Loo, Making Good (1997); Gleason, Normalizing the Ideal (1999). Critiques and reformulations: Dean (1994); Hunt (1997, 1999); Ruonavaara (1997); Valverde, Diseases of the Will (1998). Later readings: Sangster, Regulating Girls and Women (2001); Kinsman and Gentile, The Canadian War on Queers (2010).
nodes.scope_note: A research field, international in its theory and Canadian in most of its historical work. The liberal order framework is a separate project, 'closer to history of capitalism' (user, 2026-10-12); state formation (Curtis) is shared ground, not membership. Feminist legal and sexual history overlaps Canadian women's & gender history; youth and normality overlaps Childhood, youth & family in Canada. Roster inclusion does not mean a scholar adopts the moral-regulation framework.

nodes.label: Canadian working-class history
nodes.date_label: Earlier institutional histories (Logan 1948) · Labour/Le Travailleur founded 1976 · Palmer 1979, Kealey 1980 · debate over culture 1981 · gender and family 1989–93 · selected later works
nodes.description: Canadian working-class history took shape in the 1970s as a new labour history of class, culture and community, set against an older institutional history of unions, labour politics and industrial relations (Logan 1948; Abella 1973; Bercuson 1974). The Canadian Committee on Labour History founded Labour/Le Travailleur in 1976. Palmer’s skilled workers in Hamilton (1979), Kealey’s Toronto workers (1980) and their history of the Knights of Labor (1982) were among its early monographs. In 1981 Kenneth McNaught framed the contrast as ‘E. P. Thompson vs Harold Logan’ and, by a later account, objected that social historians took a revolutionary goal as history’s purpose; Bercuson questioned working-class culture as an explanatory framework, and Kealey defended class analysis and culture. Social historians of poverty and the state widened the field: Copp’s Montreal working class (1974), Finkel on business and reform (1979), Struthers on unemployment (1983). Feminist historians remade it from within: Sangster on women on the left (1989), Parr’s gender of breadwinners (1990) and Bradbury’s working families (1993). Rouillard wrote the history of Quebec unionism in French (1989), and Heron’s Workers’ Revolt in Canada (1998) took the 1917–25 upheaval as a national subject. Palmer’s Descent into Discourse (1990) attacked the linguistic turn in social history. In 2000 Morton argued that the journal’s founding team had concealed a decade of stasis. Later work turned to deindustrialization (High 2003), the history of the left (McKay 2008) and Indigenous labour and the settler order.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Logan, Trade Unions in Canada (1948); Abella, Nationalism, Communism, and Canadian Labour (1973); Bercuson, Confrontation at Winnipeg (1974); Copp, The Anatomy of Poverty (1974); Labour/Le Travailleur (1976); Palmer, A Culture in Conflict (1979); Finkel, Business and Social Reform in the Thirties (1979); Kealey, Toronto Workers Respond to Industrial Capitalism (1980); McNaught, Bercuson and Kealey (1981); Kealey and Palmer, Dreaming of What Might Be (1982); Struthers, No Fault of Their Own (1983); Palmer, Working-Class Experience (1983; 1992); Heron, Working in Steel (1988); Rouillard, Histoire du syndicalisme au Québec (1989); Sangster, Dreams of Equality (1989); Palmer, Descent into Discourse (1990); Parr, The Gender of Breadwinners (1990); Lutz, “After the Fur Trade” (1992); Bradbury, Working Families (1993); Kealey, Workers and Canadian History (1995); Heron, The Workers’ Revolt in Canada (1998); Morton and Sangster in Labour/Le Travail 46 (2000). Later: High, Industrial Sunset (2003); McKay, Reasoning Otherwise (2008); Burrill (2019); Finkel on Palmer (2021).
nodes.scope_note: A national research field within labour history. The ‘old’ institutional history and the ‘new’ labour history are positions in a debate, not successive stages; Bercuson and McNaught are critics (their 1981 essays are now checked through Bercuson’s abstract and Finkel’s account of McNaught), and Morton’s 2000 critique comes from outside the new labour history. Marxist and Thompsonian resources are documented by McNaught’s title and Kealey’s defence of class analysis; no single theory is attributed to the field. Gender historians (Sangster, Parr, Bradbury) are treated mainly in Canadian women’s and gender history; they appear here for their working-class histories. Quebec labour history in French (Rouillard) is part of the field and of Quebec historiography. Poverty and welfare-state histories overlap with political history. Immigrant workers (Avery) are in the immigration entry; Indigenous labour is a strand, not a claim of adoption. Palmer’s Descent into Discourse (1990) is placed here as a critique of the linguistic turn, not as a critique of women’s history. McKay’s left history is a post-2000 contributor row; his main entry is Liberal order framework.

nodes.label: Canadian women's & gender history
nodes.date_label: Earlier women writers of history (recovered by Boutilier and Prentice 1997) and Cleverdon’s suffrage history 1950 · collections and studies 1976–79 · Collectif Clio 1982 · Prentice et al. 1988 · Parr 1990 · Left History exchange 1995–96 · selected publication milestones, not boundaries
nodes.description: Canadian women's history studies women as historical actors in Canada and, increasingly from the 1990s, gender as a relation shaping work, family, politics, law and the state. Earlier women wrote national, local and regional history, recovered by Boutilier and Prentice (1997); Cleverdon studied the suffrage movement (1950); collections and studies of reform and women's organizations followed in the later 1970s (Cook and Mitchinson; Strong-Boag; Kealey). Two syntheses had different starting points. The Collectif Clio's L'histoire des femmes au Québec depuis quatre siècles (1982) rejected a male-centred history presented as everyone's history; Prentice and colleagues' Canadian Women: A History (1988) offered a collaborative survey. Studies of women and war (Pierson), women on the left (Sangster), working families in Montreal (Bradbury) and housewives in the Depression (Baillargeon) joined the field to labour and family history. Parr's comparison of two Ontario towns (1990) challenged assumptions about the separateness of gender and class roles. In the 1990s historians argued over whether gender history extended or displaced women's history: Pierson weighed the turn to deconstruction and Scott's theory of gender against experience and voice (1991), and Sangster's 'Beyond Dichotomies' (1995), by her later account, protested a hierarchy that set gender history above a 'limited' women's history; replies in Left History defended gender history (1996). Later work examined masculinity and gendered political languages (Morgan), sexuality and the law, and postwar domesticity and consumption (Parr, Korinek, Fahrni). Lévesque asked how far Quebec historiography had integrated women (1997); Quebec women's history is treated mainly under Quebec historiography.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Earlier women writers of history: Machar, Skinner, Skelton, Esther Clark Wright, Neatby, Ormsby, Daveluy, as recovered in Boutilier and Prentice, eds., Creating Historical Memory (1997); Cleverdon, The Woman Suffrage Movement in Canada (1950). Cook and Mitchinson, eds., The Proper Sphere (1976); Strong-Boag, The Parliament of Women (1976); Kealey, ed., A Not Unreasonable Claim (1979). Collectif Clio, L'histoire des femmes au Québec depuis quatre siècles (1982; Quebec Women, 1987); Prentice et al., Canadian Women: A History (1988). Pierson, "They're Still Women After All" (1986); Danylewycz, Taking the Veil (1987); Strong-Boag, The New Day Recalled (1988); Sangster, Dreams of Equality (1989); Lévesque, La norme et les déviantes (1989); Parr, The Gender of Breadwinners (1990); Baillargeon, Ménagères au temps de la crise (1991); Mitchinson, The Nature of Their Bodies (1991); Bradbury, Working Families (1993); Dubinsky, Improper Advances (1993). Debate: Pierson (1991); Parr (1995); Sangster (1995, 1996); Iacovetta and Kealey (1996); Dubinsky and Marks (1996); Lévesque (1997); Sangster's retrospect (2011). Morgan, Public Men and Virtuous Women (1996); McPherson, Morgan and Forestell, eds., Gendered Pasts (1999); Parr, Domestic Goods (1999); Korinek, Roughing It in the Suburbs (2000); Christie, Engendering the State (2000). Comparison: Van Kirk, "Many Tender Ties" (1980); Perry, On the Edge of Empire (2001). Later readings: Fahrni (2005), Campbell (2009), Bienvenue on Daveluy (2018), Bienvenue and Dorais, eds., Profession historienne? (2023).
nodes.scope_note: A Canadian research field joining women's history and gender history; the entry does not decide the 1990s argument between them. Quebec women's history (Collectif Clio, Lévesque, Baillargeon) has its primary treatment in Quebec historiography; this entry keeps those authors' work on family, work and sexuality and a critique edge to Quebec historiography. Fur-trade women (Van Kirk) and gender and empire (Perry) are treated mainly in Indigenous–newcomer relations & fur-trade history and Settler colonialism and appear here as comparison rows; sexuality, law and regulation overlap with Moral regulation; childhood and family with Childhood, youth & family in Canada. Palmer's Descent into Discourse is treated in Canadian working-class history, as a critique of the linguistic turn, not of women's history.

strands.title: Earlier women writers of history
strands.focus: Women wrote Canadian history long before women’s history was a field: popular, local and regional historians (Machar, Skinner, Esther Clark Wright), the independent scholar Isabel Skelton, and a few university historians, among them Hilda Neatby and Margaret Ormsby, the CHA’s first and second women presidents (1962–63; 1965–66). In French Canada, Marie-Claire Daveluy wrote on New France. Most wrote national, local, fur-trade or political history; only Skelton (who “sought to write women back into Canadian history”, per Coulter’s reading of Crowley) and Daveluy (Bienvenue 2018) are documented as writing women in. They are earlier women writers of history, not founders of women’s history. Boutilier and Prentice’s Creating Historical Memory (1997) recovered this work and asked how professionalization masculinized history; the editors note that their subjects come mainly from “the white, Anglo-Celtic segment of society”. Cleverdon’s suffrage history (1950) is the earlier study of women that PhDs still cite. Bienvenue and Dorais (2023) extend the recovery to French Canada (after 2000).

The four Left History papers (1995–96) were read for revision 1.136 (Joy Parr's person entry): Iacovetta and Kealey call Parr 'a major figure in the field', and Sangster answers both replies.

strands.focus: Van Kirk’s women in fur-trade society (1980) and Perry’s gender and race in colonial British Columbia (1995, 2001) are treated mainly in Indigenous–newcomer relations & fur-trade history and Settler colonialism. nodes.label: Childhood, youth & family in Canada
nodes.date_label: Sutherland 1976 · Parr, ed., 1982 · Rooke and Schnell 1983 · 1990s expansion (Comacchio 1993 to Gleason 1999; Marshall 1998) · selected publication milestones, not boundaries
nodes.description: Studies children, adolescents and families in Canadian history, and the reformers, experts, courts, schools and welfare programmes that sought to shape them. Neil Sutherland's Children in English-Canadian Society (1976) traced the reformers who pursued social improvement through children. Parr's study of British child immigrants (1980) and her collection Childhood and Family in Canadian History (1982), Rooke and Schnell's history of child rescue and the welfare state (1983) and Bradbury's family economies of industrial Montreal (1993) tied the field to family and labour history. The 1990s brought studies of maternal and infant welfare (Comacchio 1993), the baby boom (Owram 1996), youth and the making of heterosexuality (Adams 1997) and psychology and the 'normal' family (Gleason 1999). Francophone work examined family allowances and compulsory schooling (Marshall 1998), juvenile reform schools (Ménard 2003) and the medicalization of motherhood (Baillargeon 2004). Comacchio treats adolescence as a sociohistorical construction (2006); Myers studies girls, the courts and the policing of children in Montreal and beyond (2006, 2019). John Bullen's review essay on recent approaches to child-welfare history (1985) is the one early critique found. Historians also ask how young people's own experience can be recovered: Sutherland on adult memories of childhood (1992), and Gleason's critique of 'agency traps' (2016). The field overlaps with women's and gender history and with moral regulation; residential schooling of Indigenous children is treated primarily in the Native–newcomer entry.

Later readings: Sangster, Girl Trouble (2002); Ménard, Des enfants sous surveillance (2003); Baillargeon, Un Québec en mal d'enfants (2004); Comacchio, The Dominion of Youth (2006); Myers, Caught (2006) and Youth Squad (2019); Gleason et al., eds., Lost Kids (2010); Gleason, Small Matters (2013) and "Avoiding the Agency Trap" (2016).

nodes.label: Immigration, ethnicity & race in Canada
nodes.date_label: Ward 1978 · Avery 1979 · Abella and Troper 1982 · Perin 1983 · Anderson 1991 · Walker on race and the law 1997 · Backhouse 1999 · selected publication milestones, not boundaries
nodes.description: Studies immigration, ethnic communities, racism and the state in Canada: immigrant workers and their reception, ethnic identity, and the legal and spatial making of racial categories. The field expanded from the late 1970s. Ward's White Canada Forever (1978) traced west-coast prejudice against Asian residents and the discriminatory policies it produced; Avery's 'Dangerous Foreigners' (1979) examined European immigrant workers and labour radicalism; Abella and Troper studied Canada and the Jews of Europe, 1933–48 (1982). Perin's 'Clio as an Ethnic' (1983) asked whether ethnic groups had been 'discovered' just when the state faced challenges such as Quebec nationalism. Studies of Toronto neighbourhoods (Harney, who co-founded the Multicultural History Society of Ontario in 1976), Italian migrants in Montreal (Ramirez), Chinese Montrealers (Helly), Quebec's immigration policy (Pâquet 1997), British Columbia politicians (Roy), Italian immigrants in postwar Toronto (Iacovetta) and Ukrainian-Canadian women (Swyripa) followed. Anderson (1987, 1991) treated 'Chinese' and 'Chinatown' as racial categories made through government practice and place, which a reviewer saw as moving beyond earlier studies of white prejudice; Walker's Supreme Court case studies (1997) and Backhouse's Colour-Coded (1999) traced racism through law. Black Canadian history, including Black migration and immigration control, is a separate entry. Post-2000 work turned to Cold War reception and citizenship (Iacovetta 2006; Bohaker and Iacovetta 2009).

Black migration (cross-reference to Black Canadian history): Calliste, "Race, Gender and Canadian Immigration Policy" (1993–94); Shepard, Deemed Unsuitable (1997). Later readings: Epp, Iacovetta and Swyripa, eds., Sisters or Strangers? (2004); Pâquet, Tracer les marges de la Cité (2005); Iacovetta, Gatekeepers (2006); Bohaker and Iacovetta (2009).

Roster inclusion is not adoption of one framework: Ward's 'attitudes and public policy' and Anderson's 'racial category' approaches differ. A reviewer saw Anderson moving beyond earlier studies of white attitudes and prejudice (Stanley 1993); no checked text has Anderson distancing herself from White Canada Forever by name, so she is not listed as Ward's critic.

nodes.label: Black Canadian history
nodes.date_label: Earlier work: Trudel on slavery in French Canada 1960 · Winks's survey 1971 · Walker's Black Loyalists 1976 · Calliste on sleeping car porters 1987 · Brand's oral history of Black working women 1991 · We're Rooted Here, African Canadian women's history 1994 · Walker's five orientations 1997 · Cahill–Walker Black Loyalist exchange 1999 · selected publication milestones, not boundaries · selected later works
nodes.description: Historical writing on people of African descent in Canada: slavery in New France and British North America, Black Loyalists and refugees, fugitive slaves and the settlements of Canada West, Black communities and churches, migration from the United States and the Caribbean, and racism in work, law and the state. Marcel Trudel documented slavery in French Canada (1960; dictionary 1990). After earlier work by Landon, Riddell and Trudel, Robin Winks's survey The Blacks in Canada (1971), which Walker reviewed critically, and James Walker's The Black Loyalists (1976) gave the field book-length studies; Walker's put Black community at the centre, and Winks credited it with ending the 'victims' school. From the late 1980s Agnes Calliste studied sleeping car porters and Caribbean migrants, Dorothy Williams Black Montreal, and Dionne Brand and the authors of We're Rooted Here (1994) Black women's history. In 1997 Walker sorted the historiography into five orientations by the role it gives Black people, from 'clients' of white philanthropy (Landon, Riddell) through 'victims' and 'achievers' to 'community' and 1990s 'survivors', and argued that community is the key. Barry Cahill called the Black Loyalists a scholars' myth that sidelined the enslaved (1999); Walker replied, placing his book in the civil-rights era. After 2000 the field grew around slavery (Cooper, Whitfield, Mackey), migration and labour (Mathieu), law (Barrington Walker) and Black Montreal (Austin, Mills), countering the image of Canada as a haven at the end of the Underground Railroad.

Contemporary: Forsythe, ed., Let the Niggers Burn! (1971). Later readings: Gay, Les Noirs du Québec (2004); Cooper, The Hanging of Angélique (2006); Whitfield, Blacks on the Border (2006) and North to Bondage (2016); Austin, "All Roads Led to Montreal" (2007) and Fear of a Black Nation (2013); Nelson, Razing Africville (2008); Mackey, Done with Slavery (2010); Mathieu, North of the Color Line (2010); B. Walker, Race on Trial (2010); Flynn, Moving Beyond Borders (2011); Mills, A Place in the Sun (2016); Morton and Wright, "Black History in Atlantic Canada: A Bibliography" (2021).
nodes.scope_note: A research field on people of African descent in Canada, defined by its subject, from slavery in New France to Black migration, community and racism. Created on the user's decision of 2026-10-12: it was a strand of Immigration, ethnicity & race in Canada, and Walker's 1997 essay treats it as its own historiography. Its relation to immigration history is a comparison, not a hierarchy; works on Black migration and immigration control (Calliste 1993–94, Shepard 1997) are cross-referenced in that entry. Several roster people are treated mainly elsewhere (Trudel: Quebec historiography; Mills: Canada’s 1960s; Austin is also in Canada’s 1960s). Community and non-academic historians (Hill, Brand, Ruck, Mackey) are included because Walker's reading list and PhD bibliographies use them; Ruck and Forsythe are cited as community and participants' accounts. Indigenous slavery in New France (panis) is not covered; Rushforth's Bonds of Alliance (2012; 20 PhDs), whose title pairs Indigenous and Atlantic slaveries, is excluded from the counts because its Black-history content was not checked.

nodes.label: Indigenous–newcomer relations & fur-trade history
nodes.date_label: Earlier resources: Innis 1930, Stanley 1936 · Ray 1974 · Van Kirk and Brown 1980 · Trigger’s Natives and Newcomers 1985 · Miller 1989 · Milloy 1999 · selected later works
nodes.description: A Canadian historiography of relations between Indigenous peoples and European newcomers, centred first on the fur trade and then on policy, schools, missions, health and labour. Innis’s Fur Trade in Canada (1930) was subtitled ‘an introduction to Canadian economic history’. From the 1970s historians, geographers and archaeologists recast it with Indigenous people as actors: trappers, hunters and middlemen (Ray 1974), wives and kin in fur-trade society (Van Kirk; Brown, both 1980), and Wendat history across contact (Trigger 1976, 1985; Delâge 1985), while Dickason studied European representations of them (1984). The field long called itself ‘native–newcomer’ history, after Trigger’s Natives and Newcomers (1985); current usage prefers ‘Indigenous’. Miller (1989) offered a national synthesis of ‘Indian–white relations’. Later work studied reserve farming and policy (Carter 1990), residential schools (Miller 1996; Milloy 1999), health (Kelm 1998) and wage labour (Lutz 1992). Brownlie and Kelm (1994) asked whether agency-centred work on Indian policy and the potlatch law (Cole and Chaikin; Miller; Loo) had made Native agency a colonialist alibi. Indigenous scholars questioned the framing: Sioui (1989) found conventional history without a method for Indigenous self-interpretation; Winona Stevenson (Wheeler) (1998) argued that historians of ‘Indian–White relations’, relying on one side’s records, kept even agency-centred work within a colonialist framework and set oral history aside; LaRocque (1999) found that the cross-cultural ethnohistory of Trigger, Brown and Van Kirk still ‘othered’ its subjects. After 2000, settler-colonial analysis read this history as continuing dispossession; Greer replied that the fur trade’s commercial penetration was a different form of invasion.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Innis, The Fur Trade in Canada (1930); Stanley, The Birth of Western Canada (1936); Ray, Indians in the Fur Trade (1974); Fisher, Contact and Conflict (1977); Van Kirk, “Many Tender Ties” (1980); Brown, Strangers in Blood (1980); Trigger, The Children of Aataentsic (1976), Natives and Newcomers (1985), “The Historians’ Indian” (1986); Delâge, Le pays renversé (1985); Dickason, The Myth of the Savage (1984), Canada’s First Nations (1992); Smith, Sacred Feathers (1987); Miller, Skyscrapers Hide the Heavens (1989), Shingwauk’s Vision (1996); Carter, Lost Harvests (1990); Coates, Best Left as Indians (1991); Lutz, “After the Fur Trade” (1992); Brownlie and Kelm, “Desperately Seeking Absolution” (1994); Kelm, Colonizing Bodies (1998); Milloy, “A National Crime” (1999). Later: Rutherdale (2002), Brownlie (2003), Raibmon (2005), Podruchny (2006), Lutz, Makúk (2008). Critics and alternatives: Sioui (1989), Paul, We Were Not the Savages (1993; 2000 edition), Stevenson [Wheeler], “The Othering of Indigenous History” (1998), LaRocque (1999); in the US, Fixico (2009) and S. A. Miller (2009).
nodes.scope_note: A research field in mostly academic, mostly non-Indigenous Canadian historiography, built on company, church and state archives together with archaeology and anthropology. It is not the atlas’s Indigenous history entry, which centres Indigenous historical traditions, community knowledge and authority. Several people sit in both (Dickason, Miller, Lutz, Trigger); their existing contexts are kept, and Indigenous historical practice is not subsumed here. It is not Settler colonialism, which reads dispossession as a continuing structure: most works here predate that framework, and whether any adopts it was not checked; and Greer’s critique points the other way. Indigenous critiques of the ‘relations’ framing (Sioui, LaRocque; Fixico and S. Miller in the US) appear as critics, not members, and the roster records no identity classification. Francophone work is thin in this selection (Delâge, Sioui); New France encounter history overlaps with Quebec historiography. The label keeps the field’s word ‘newcomer’ but uses ‘Indigenous’; ‘native–newcomer’, Trigger’s 1985 term, is explained in the description as the field’s historical name. ‘Indigenous–settler’ is avoided so as not to collide with Settler colonialism.

strands.title: The fur trade in national history
strands.focus: Innis makes the fur trade an introduction to Canadian economic history (1930); Stanley’s history of the West and the Riel resistances (1936) is reprinted and cited for decades. Both are resources the field later reworks, not its founders.
strands.works: Innis, The Fur Trade in Canada (1930); Stanley, The Birth of Western Canada (1936)

strands.title: Indigenous people as actors in the trade
strands.focus: Ray reconstructs Indigenous people’s roles as trappers, hunters and middlemen (1974); Fisher writes British Columbia contact as Indian–European relations (1977).
strands.works: Ray, Indians in the Fur Trade (1974); Fisher, Contact and Conflict (1977)

strands.title: Fur-trade families, Métis peoples and voyageurs
strands.focus: Women and kinship (Van Kirk) and company families (Brown) recast fur-trade society in 1980; Peterson and Brown’s collection treats Métis peoples in their own right (1985). Podruchny (2006) and Macdougall (2010) carry the strand past 2000.
strands.works: Van Kirk (1980); Brown (1980); Peterson and Brown, eds. (1985); Podruchny (2006); Macdougall (2010)

strands.title: Contact, the Wendat and European representations
strands.focus: Trigger joins archaeology and documents to Wendat/Huron history before and after contact (1976) and reconsiders the ‘heroic age’ of New France (1985). Delâge writes the same encounter in French (1985); Dickason studies European representations (1984). Shared with the Ethnohistory entry.
strands.works: Trigger, The Children of Aataentsic (1976), Natives and Newcomers (1985); Delâge, Le pays renversé (1985); Dickason, The Myth of the Savage (1984)

strands.title: How historians wrote about Indigenous peoples
strands.focus: Walker (1971) and Trigger (1986) survey Canadian historical writing about Indigenous peoples. Trigger dates such studies from 1971 and describes ethnohistorical work across disciplines moving into national history.
strands.works: Walker, “The Indian in Canadian Historical Writing” (1971); Trigger, “The Historians’ Indian” (1986)

strands.title: Syntheses of relations and policy
strands.focus: Miller’s national synthesis of ‘Indian–white relations’ (1989), Dickason’s history of First Nations (1992), and regional or biographical studies (Smith 1987; Coates 1991). Miller’s and Dickason’s books differ in authorship and standpoint; they are grouped here as syntheses, not as one interpretation.
strands.works: Smith, Sacred Feathers (1987); Miller, Skyscrapers Hide the Heavens (1989); Coates, Best Left as Indians (1991); Dickason, Canada’s First Nations (1992)

strands.title: Reserves, residential schools and Indian agents
strands.focus: Reserve agriculture and policy (Carter 1990), residential schools (Miller 1996; Milloy 1999) and Indian agents (Brownlie 2003). Most predate the settler-colonial framework; whether any adopts it was not checked.
strands.works: Carter, Lost Harvests (1990); Miller, Shingwauk’s Vision (1996); Milloy, “A National Crime” (1999); Brownlie, A Fatherly Eye (2003)

strands.title: Health, missions and authenticity
strands.focus: Kelm reads health and healing through the body and colonial power (1998); Rutherdale studies gender and race in the mission field (2002); Raibmon treats authenticity as made by unequal collaborators (2005).
strands.works: Kelm, Colonizing Bodies (1998); Rutherdale, Women and the White Man’s God (2002); Raibmon, Authentic Indians (2005)

strands.title: Indigenous labour after the fur trade
strands.focus: Lutz treats Aboriginal people in British Columbia as a labouring class (1992) and later rewrites Aboriginal–white relations (2008). This is the strand that meets Canadian working-class history.
strands.works: Lutz, “After the Fur Trade” (1992); Makúk (2008)

strands.title: Agency as alibi? An internal critique
strands.focus: Brownlie and Kelm (1994) criticised agency-centred work on Indian policy and the potlatch law (Cole and Chaikin 1990; Miller; Loo 1992): stressing Native agency exaggerated how far it became effective self-defence, trivialising the harm of colonial policy and serving as an ‘alibi’ for it. A critique within policy history, not of the fur-trade literature; targets known from a secondary source, essay unread.
strands.works: Robin Brownlie and Mary-Ellen Kelm, “Desperately Seeking Absolution: Native Agency as Colonialist Alibi?” CHR 75:4 (December 1994): 543–56

strands.title: Indigenous critiques of the relations frame
strands.focus: Sioui (1989), Stevenson/Wheeler (1998) and LaRocque (1999) criticise the relations framing from Indigenous standpoints: its reliance on colonial documents, its disregard of oral history and its ethnological distance. Fixico and S. Miller (2009, US) question ‘Indian–white relations’ as the premise of Indian history. Paul’s We Were Not the Savages (1993; the 2000 Fernwood edition is the one PhDs cite), subtitled ‘a Mi’kmaq perspective’, rejects the ‘savage’ category (title and subtitle only). Adams’s Prison of Grass (1975) is an earlier counter-history of official history, not a critique of this field, and Dickason is a member of the field. Trigger (1986) and Brownlie and Kelm (1994) are non-Indigenous critiques from inside. These are critics and alternatives, not members.
strands.works: Sioui (1989); Paul (1993; 2000 ed.); Stevenson [Wheeler] (Fall 1998); LaRocque (1999); Fixico (2009); S. A. Miller (2009)

strands.title: After 2000: the settler-colonial reading and its critics
strands.focus: Settler-colonial analysis reads reserves, schools and dispossession as a continuing structure. Greer replies that the settler mode dominates some periods and regions and fades in others, and that commercial penetration (the fur trade’s mode) and extractivism are other forms of invasion. Konishi records Indigenous scholars’ critiques of settler colonial studies. Later readings only.
strands.works: Greer, “Settler Colonialism and Beyond” (JCHA 2019); Konishi (2019)
