nodes.label: Quebec historiography
nodes.date_label: Earlier national history (Groulx) · Institut d’histoire de l’Amérique française founded 1946, its Revue from 1947 · Montreal and Laval schools 1950s–60s · Histoire du Québec contemporain 1979 · Rudin’s critique 1992 · selected later readings (Catholic Action revision 2002–05)
nodes.description: Historical writing on Quebec and French Canada, mostly in French, long organized around the nation, the Conquest of 1760 and the meaning of modernity. Lionel Groulx’s national history of French Canada closes what a francophone anthology calls the time of the ‘ancients’; Groulx founded the Institut d’histoire de l’Amérique française (1946) and its Revue (1947). In the 1950s historians at Montréal (Séguin, Frégault, Brunet) made the Conquest and its consequences their central problem. At Laval, Trudel wrote the history of New France, and Hamelin and Ouellet economic and social history, Ouellet in a conjunctural idiom indebted to Labrousse. Their agricultural-crisis thesis (1962) was contested by Paquet and Wallot (1972–73); Dechêne, trained in the Annales milieu in France, wrote the social history of seventeenth-century Montreal (1974). After 1970 a modernist generation turned to contemporary, urban and industrial Quebec and to its whole population (Linteau, Durocher and Robert, 1979). Women’s history followed, from the Collectif Clio (1982) to Baillargeon (1991); Lévesque (1997) asked how far colleagues had integrated it. Behiels (1985) found the Quiet Revolution’s prelude in 1945–60; Rouillard (1997) recorded a shift from reading it as rupture to turn. Ronald Rudin (1992, 1997) argued that the modernists’ search for a ‘normal’ society muted religion, rurality and ethnicity; Linteau and Fecteau replied (1995). Bouchard and Lamonde (2000) close the period; after 2000, Meunier and Warren, Bienvenue and Gauvreau traced the Quiet Revolution to Catholic Action.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Groulx, Histoire du Canada français depuis la découverte (1950); IHAF (1946) and RHAF (1947); Séguin, La “nation canadienne” et l’agriculture (thesis 1947; 1970); Frégault, La guerre de la Conquête (1955); Brunet, La présence anglaise et les Canadiens (1958); Trudel, L’esclavage au Canada français (1960) and Histoire de la Nouvelle-France (1963–); Hamelin, Économie et société en Nouvelle-France (1960); Ouellet and Hamelin, “La crise agricole dans le Bas-Canada” (1962); Ouellet, Histoire économique et sociale du Québec, 1760–1850 (1966); Paquet and Wallot (1972–73); Wallot, Un Québec qui bougeait (1973); Dechêne, Habitants et marchands (1974); Savard (1974); Gagnon, Le Québec et ses historiens (1978); Linteau, Durocher and Robert, Histoire du Québec contemporain (1979; 1986); Collectif Clio (1982); Linteau, “La nouvelle histoire du Québec vue de l’intérieur” (1983); Behiels, Prelude to Quebec’s Quiet Revolution (1985); Lévesque, La norme et les déviantes (1989) and “Réflexions sur l’histoire des femmes dans l’histoire du Québec” (1997); Baillargeon, Ménagères au temps de la Crise (1991); Rudin, “Revisionism and the Search for a Normal Society” (1992; French 1995) and Making History in Twentieth-Century Quebec (1997); Linteau and Fecteau (1995); Dumont, Genèse de la société québécoise (1993); Dickinson and Young, A Short History of Quebec (1993 ed.); Bouchard (1996, 2000); Martel (1997); Rouillard, “La Révolution tranquille: rupture ou tournant?” (1997); Lamonde (2000). Later: Meunier and Warren, Sortir de la « grande noirceur » (2002); Bienvenue, Quand la jeunesse entre en scène (2003); Gauvreau, The Catholic Origins of Quebec’s Quiet Revolution (2005); Bédard and Goyette, eds., Parole d’historiens (2006); Baillargeon, Brève histoire des femmes au Québec (2012).
nodes.scope_note: A research field defined by its object (Quebec and French Canada) and largely by its language. The Montreal school, Laval, the modernists and their critics are distinct and overlapping positions, not one school; Savard warns against treating ‘École de Québec’ as a unit. The post-1970 generation is called ‘modernist’ after Bédard and Goyette’s part title; Linteau calls it a ‘nouvelle histoire’; Rudin’s polemical name for it is used only in the normal-society debate strand. Annales influence is indirect and contested: Ouellet’s Labroussian economic history, Mandrou’s preface and Dechêne’s training in the Annales milieu are documented, while Linteau says his generation owed more to sociology and American historians. Groulx’s nationalism and clerical politics are historical subjects here, not the atlas’s categories. Quebec women’s history (Clio, Lévesque, Baillargeon) and the Catholic Action revision of the Quiet Revolution have their primary homes here. English-language historians of Quebec (Behiels, Dickinson, Young, Rudin, Greer) belong to the field. Acadian and francophone-minority historiography outside Quebec is only touched by Martel. New France encounter history with Indigenous peoples is in Indigenous–newcomer relations & fur-trade history.

strands.title: Groulx and French-Canadian national history
strands.focus: Groulx’s national history and his conception of history. Groulx founded the Institut d’histoire de l’Amérique française in 1946 and its Revue in 1947, and wrote in its first issue. The anthology places him at the end of ‘le temps des Anciens’.
strands.works: Histoire du Canada français depuis la découverte (1950); IHAF (1946); RHAF 1:1 (1947)

strands.title: The Montreal school and the Conquest
strands.focus: Séguin, Frégault and Brunet make the Conquest and its economic and national consequences their central problem; Savard groups them by shared ideological outlook. Ouellet (1985) calls Séguin the ‘théoricien de l’École néo-nationaliste’, for whom the Conquest decapitated the national bourgeoisie, a thesis Brunet took up in the 1950s; Tousignant (1980) calls Séguin the school’s ‘maître à penser’ and describes the gulf between it and Ouellet.
strands.works: Séguin (thesis 1947; 1970); Frégault, La guerre de la Conquête (1955); Brunet, La présence anglaise et les Canadiens (1958)

strands.title: Laval: economic and social history
strands.focus: Trudel’s history of New France and of slavery in French Canada; Hamelin and Ouellet’s economic and social history of New France and Lower Canada. Savard notes Ouellet’s debt to Labrousse and Chaunu, and Mandrou prefaces his 1966 book. Savard treats Trudel and Ouellet as distinct despite the label ‘École de Québec’.
strands.works: Trudel, L’esclavage au Canada français (1960), Histoire de la Nouvelle-France (1963–); Hamelin, Économie et société en Nouvelle-France (1960); Ouellet, Histoire économique et sociale du Québec (1966)

strands.title: The Lower Canadian agricultural crisis debate
strands.focus: Ouellet and Hamelin’s 1962 thesis that a fall in wheat production from 1802, with population pressure and peasant routine, lay behind French-Canadian nationalism and, ‘en grande partie’, the rebellion of 1837–38; Paquet and Wallot’s 1972 rejection of it as ‘irrecevable’ and their market-rational habitant, with Wallot’s Quebec ‘qui bougeait’; Ouellet’s reply (1976), defending the production-based explanation and disputing his critics’ reading of his argument; Le Goff’s review of the controversy (1974, unread); Tousignant’s critique of Le Bas-Canada (1980); and Greer’s rejection of the ‘atavistic mentality’ explanation (1981). Ouellet (1985) names later entrants (Isbester, McCallum, McInnis, Courville). The 1962, 1972, 1976 and 1980 texts and Greer (1981) were read for the Ouellet person entry. The exchange is not presented as resolving the crisis’s chronology, causes or explanatory reach; Paquet and Wallot themselves doubted the debate was settled.
strands.works: Ouellet and Hamelin (1962); Ouellet (1966, 1976); Paquet and Wallot (1972, 1973); Wallot (1973); Le Goff (1974); Tousignant (1980); Greer (1981)

strands.title: New France as social history
strands.focus: Dechêne’s habitants and merchants of seventeenth-century Montreal, from a Paris doctorate (1973) after training in the Annales milieu of Mandrou and Goubert; Hamelin’s economy and society of New France.
strands.works: Dechêne (1974); Hamelin (1960)

strands.title: The modernist synthesis
strands.focus: Linteau describes his generation’s turn to c. 1850–present, to urban and industrial Quebec, and to the history of Quebec’s whole population rather than French Canadians alone; social history and serial sources, with Annales influence filtered through sociology and American history. Histoire du Québec contemporain and Dickinson and Young’s Short History are its syntheses.
strands.works: Linteau, Durocher and Robert (1979; 1986); Linteau (1983); Dickinson and Young (1993 ed.)

strands.title: Quebec women’s history
strands.focus: Collectif Clio’s four-century history (1982), Lévesque’s norms and “deviant” women (1989), Baillargeon’s Depression housewives (1991) and her short synthesis (2012). Lévesque (1997) judged that women’s history had redefined traditional Quebec history while some colleagues were slow to integrate women. The anthology places Clio and Micheline Dumont in its modernist part. Primary here: 31 of 34 PhDs citing this literature engage Quebec historiography; Canadian women's & gender history keeps its critique edge (edge_841). The Collectif Clio (1982) was Micheline Dumont, Michèle Jean, Marie Lavigne and Jennifer Stoddart; shared methods or positions are not inferred.
strands.works: Collectif Clio (1982); Lévesque (1989, 1997); Baillargeon (1991, 2012)

strands.title: Origins of the Quiet Revolution: rupture or turn?
strands.focus: Behiels finds the Quiet Revolution’s prelude in 1945–60 liberal and neo-nationalist debate (1985); Rouillard records historians’ shift from ‘rupture’ to ‘tournant’ (1997). The Catholic Action strand extends the argument after 2000.
strands.works: Behiels (1985); Rouillard, “La Révolution tranquille: rupture ou tournant?” (1997)

strands.title: Catholic Action and the Quiet Revolution
strands.focus: Against the Quiet Revolution’s own story of a clerical “grande noirceur”, Catholic Action, personalism and lay movements from the 1930s are read as preparing the 1960s. Two versions (Baum): social democracy (Meunier and Warren) and the family and gender (Gauvreau). Gauvreau judged that Quebec religious history had repeated the Quiet Revolution’s own ideology until these studies. After 2000; moved from Religion, social reform & secularization in Canada: 75 of 85 PhDs citing this literature engage Quebec historiography (lift 5.6), 36 of them at francophone universities.
strands.works: Meunier and Warren (2002); Bienvenue (2003); Gauvreau (2005)

strands.title: The ‘normal society’ debate
strands.focus: Rudin argues that the revisionists’ normal, Western Quebec muted religion, rurality and ethnicity (1992; 1995; 1997). Linteau and Fecteau reply in the Bulletin d’histoire politique (1995), and Fecteau reviews Rudin’s book on nationhood and the “revisionist school” (CHR 1999). A named controversy with dated published contributions.
strands.works: Rudin (CHR 1992; BHP 1995; 1997); Linteau (BHP 1995); Fecteau (BHP 1995); Fecteau (CHR 1999)

strands.title: Quebec historians on their historiography
strands.focus: Savard’s quarter-century survey (1974), Serge Gagnon on Quebec historians from Garneau to Groulx (1978), Rudin (1997), and Bédard and Goyette’s anthology (2006), whose four parts give a francophone periodization.
strands.works: Savard (1974); Gagnon (1978); Rudin (1997); Bédard and Goyette, eds. (2006)

strands.title: Society, ideas and comparison at the turn of the century
strands.focus: Dumont’s genesis of Quebec society (1993), Bouchard’s Saguenay and comparative New World nations (1996, 2000), Lamonde’s social history of ideas (2000) and Martel on the end of a pan-Canadian French Canada (1997).
strands.works: Dumont (1993); Bouchard (1996, 2000); Martel (1997); Lamonde (2000)

strands.title: Interpreting the rebellions of 1837–38
strands.focus: Ouellet’s reading of the rebellion as, in large part, ‘une réponse détournée’ to agricultural crisis and demographic pressure (1962), with a peasantry led by the liberal professions; the national and social readings Ouellet himself describes as polarised (1985: Bernard, Bernier, Bourque, Dubuc, Ouellet, Ryerson); Bernard’s collection on the Patriotes in memory and historiography (1983, unread); and Greer’s rural history of 1837 (1993, unread; through reviews), which reviewers say breaks with Ouellet’s manipulated peasantry.
strands.works: Ouellet and Hamelin (1962); Ouellet, 'Le mythe de « l'habitant sensible au marché »' (1976); Bernard, ed. (1983); Greer (1993)

nodes.label: Canadian military history
nodes.date_label: Duguid’s only official volume 1938 · Stacey’s official histories 1955–70 · Nicholson’s replacement CEF history 1962 · Broken Promises 1977 · war-and-society studies 1986–93 · Walker on race and recruitment 1989 · Valour and the Horror broadcast and hearings 1992 · Vance 1997 · selected later works
nodes.description: Canadian military history has three overlapping modes: official and operational history, war and society, and memory and public history. Early work was largely official history, published by authority of the Minister of National Defence. Duguid’s official history of the Great War produced only one volume (1938); Nicholson’s Canadian Expeditionary Force (1962) replaced it. Stacey wrote volumes I (1955) and III (1960) of the Official History of the Canadian Army in the Second World War, and his Arms, Men and Governments (1970) made war policy a subject; Stanley’s Canada’s Soldiers (1954) called Canadians ‘an unmilitary people’. Conscription and French-Canadian participation recur, from Armstrong’s Crisis of Quebec (1937) to Granatstein and Hitsman’s Broken Promises (1977) and francophone histories of the 22nd Battalion (Gagnon 1986) and of bilingualism in the forces (Pariseau and Bernier 1987). From the 1980s war-and-society history turned to soldiers, veterans, psychiatry and women: Morton’s military and political histories (1981, 1985), veterans’ return (Morton and Wright 1987), battle exhaustion (Copp and McAndrew 1990) and Pierson on wartime womanhood (1986). Walker (1989) studied the enlistment of visible minorities, and Dempsey Prairie First Nations soldiers (1999). Popular history (Berton’s Vimy, 1986) and the CBC series The Valour and the Horror (1992), which led to Senate hearings and an ombudsman’s report, made military history a major public controversy. Vance’s Death So Noble (1997) treated the Great War as a cultural force in interwar memory. Cook (2002, 2006) showed that the records and narratives of Stacey’s officers were neither neutral nor unbiased.

I (1938, the only volume published); Stanley, Canada’s Soldiers (1954); Stacey, Official History of the Canadian Army in the Second World War, vol. I, Six Years of War (1955), and vol. III, The Victory Campaign (1960), Arms, Men and Governments (1970); Nicholson, Canadian Expeditionary Force (1962); Granatstein and Hitsman, Broken Promises (1977); Morton, Canada and War (1981), A Military History of Canada (1985), When Your Number’s Up (1993); Gagnon, Le 22e bataillon (1986); Pierson, “They’re Still Women After All” (1986); Berton, Vimy (1986); Morton and Wright, Winning the Second Battle (1987); Pariseau and Bernier, Les Canadiens français et le bilinguisme dans les Forces armées canadiennes, tome 1 (1987); Walker, “Race and Recruitment in World War I” (1989); Copp and McAndrew, Battle Exhaustion (1990); Bercuson and Wise, eds., The Valour and the Horror Revisited (1994); Dick, “‘The Valour and the Horror’ Continued” (1993); Gagnon (1995); Keshen, Propaganda and Censorship (1996); Vance, Death So Noble (1997); Dempsey, Warriors of the King (1999). Community and veteran histories: Ito, We Went to War (1984); Ruck, The Black Battalion (1987). Later: Cook, “Clio’s Soldiers” (2002) and Clio’s Warriors (2006); Keshen (2004); Rutherdale (2004); McKay and Swift, Warrior Nation (2012).
nodes.scope_note: A research field with three overlapping modes: official and operational history, war and society, and memory and public history. They are not successive stages; official historians also wrote policy history, and war-and-society historians also wrote operations. Popular history (Berton) and public controversy are included as part of the field’s public life, not as academic scholarship. Francophone work on conscription and French-Canadian participation is part of the field and meets Quebec historiography. Several roster people are treated mainly elsewhere (Stanley, Granatstein, Copp, Bercuson, Pierson, Vance); they appear for specific works. Imperial, naval and air histories and the Royal Military College tradition are thin in this selection. Critics of militarized memory (McKay and Swift) are after 2000. Black and Japanese-Canadian soldiers appear through Walker (1989, scholarly) and two community and veteran histories (Ruck 1987, Ito 1984). The Valour and the Horror controversy is a strand here, called a major public-history controversy on a contemporary witness (Dick 1993); Carr’s later treatment (CHR 2005) is unread, so it is not called a defining historiographical controversy.

nodes.label: Political, international & national history
nodes.date_label: Granatstein 1975, 1977, 1982 · Whitaker 1977 · Stacey 1977–81 · Bothwell, Drummond and English 1981 · Owram 1986 · Buckner 1993 · Whitaker and Marcuse 1994 · British World 2006 · CHA political history prizes first listed 2011 · Heaman's 'new political history' 2017 · selected later works
nodes.description: Research on the Canadian state, its parties, officials, wars and foreign relations, and the national syntheses built from them. Granatstein's histories of the King government at war (1975), of conscription (with Hitsman, 1977) and of the Ottawa mandarins (1982), Whitaker's study of the Liberal party and the state (1977) and Owram's history of the intellectuals who argued for planning and reform (1986) examined how federal power was organized, staffed and justified. Stacey's history of external policies (1977, 1981), Hillmer and Granatstein's Empire to Umpire (1994) and Bothwell's Alliance and Illusion (2007) treated Canada's place in the world. Bothwell, Drummond and English's Canada since 1945 (1981) and Thompson and Seager's Centenary Series volume (1985) offered national syntheses; political biography (Brown on Borden, Bélanger on Laurier, English on Pearson) and Bliss's business history kept leaders and enterprise in view. Whitaker and Marcuse's Cold War Canada (1994) turned to the security state. Buckner's 1993 address, asking historians to restore the settlement colonies to imperial history, led to the British World volume (2006). Chapnick (2000, 2005) questioned the middle-power 'golden age'. Granatstein and Bliss also led the national side of the 'Who Killed Canadian History?' debate. Since 2011 the CHA's political history prizes have rewarded a 'new political history' of state, tax and governance: Heaman on taxation (2017), Loo on forced relocation (2019), Bohaker on Anishinaabe governance (2020), and francophone studies of Hydro-Québec (Savard) and cultural policy (Harvey) that are recognized but not yet widely cited.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Granatstein, Canada's War (1975), Broken Promises (with Hitsman, 1977), The Ottawa Men (1982); Whitaker, The Government Party (1977); English, The Decline of Politics (1977), Shadow of Heaven (1989); Stacey, Canada and the Age of Conflict (1977, 1981); Bothwell, Drummond and English, Canada since 1945 (1981); Thompson and Seager, Canada 1922–1939 (1985); Brown, Robert Laird Borden (1975, 1980); Bélanger, Wilfrid Laurier (1986); Owram, The Government Generation (1986); Bliss, A Living Profit (1974), Northern Enterprise (1987), Right Honourable Men (1994); Drummond, Progress without Planning (1987); Bercuson, True Patriot (1993); Hillmer and Granatstein, Empire to Umpire (1994); Whitaker and Marcuse, Cold War Canada (1994); Buckner, "Whatever Happened to the British Empire?" (1993); Buckner and Francis, eds., Canada and the British World (2006); Bothwell, Alliance and Illusion (2007). Critique: Chapnick (2000, 2005). New political history (prize-recognized, after 2000): Heaman, Tax, Order, and Good Government (2017); Loo, Moved by the State (2019); Bohaker, Doodem and Council Fire (2020). Francophone (recognized, little cited): Savard (2010, 2013); Harvey, Histoire des politiques culturelles au Québec (2022).
nodes.scope_note: A research field for the political, diplomatic and national history of the Canadian state, widened to include the 'new political history' of state, tax and governance (Heaman's subtitle) that the CHA's political history prizes have recognized since they were first listed in 2011; business history and the British World are distinct strands. The debate over national history is a separate entry (The 'Who Killed Canadian History?' debate, user decision 2026-10-12): Granatstein's and Bliss's polemics are placed there, their scholarship here; Bliss's main entry is here, with a debate roster row there (user decision 2026-10-12). Military history is a separate entry (Canadian military history); Stacey and Granatstein are shared, not merged. Francophone political history (Bélanger; Savard and Harvey, recognized by CHA prizes but not yet widely cited) is thin in the PhD corpus; Quebec political history belongs mostly to Quebec historiography. Post-2000 works are selected later readings.

nodes.label: The 'Who Killed Canadian History?' debate
nodes.date_label: Roots: Cook 1967, Careless 1969 · Bliss's 'Privatizing the Mind' and the JCS replies 1991–92 · Strong-Boag's CHA address 1994 · Granatstein's book 1998 · CHR replies (McKillop, Palmer) and francophone reviews 1998–99 · CHR forum, Buckner, McKay and Osborne 2000 · Dummitt and Dawson 2009
nodes.description: A quarrel among English-Canadian historians in the 1990s over whether national history had been lost, taught here as a moment in the profession's view of itself, not as current practice: few recent theses cite its texts. It had two phases. In 1991–92 Bliss's 'Privatizing the Mind' argued that intense specialization had replaced older historians' concern with explaining the country, and asked historians to remember that their subject was Canada. A 'Point-Counterpoint' in the same journal answered him: Gregory Kealey's class history was 'neither privatizing, nor sundering' (1992), and Linda Kealey, Pierson, Sangster and Strong-Boag asked whose 'national' history was being lamented. Strong-Boag's 1994 presidential address answered 'neo-conservative laments' by indicting an old history of white male elites. In 1998 Granatstein's Who Killed Canadian History? took the charge to a public audience. In the Canadian Historical Review McKillop (1999) argued that Granatstein's narrow national history was itself political legitimation, and Palmer offered a dissident view. Francophone reviewers answered too: Dubuc read a lament for political history; Dumont, an indictment of social historians built on wrong facts about Quebec schooling. It grew from the 'limited identities' of region, culture and class that Cook named (1967) and Careless popularized (1969). In 2000 Létourneau proposed a narrative of Canada beyond unitarist and fragmenting versions, Cook called identities contingent and multiple, Buckner revisited limited identities, and McKay offered the liberal order framework as a way past the impasse. Dummitt and Dawson (2009) sought to move beyond political-versus-social history.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Roots: Cook, "Canadian Centennial Cerebrations" (1967); Careless, "'Limited Identities' in Canada" (1969); Reid (1987); Buckner (1988). Phase one: Bliss, "Privatizing the Mind" (1991–92), answered in the JCS Point-Counterpoint by G. Kealey (1992) and L. Kealey, Pierson, Sangster and Strong-Boag (1992); Strong-Boag, "Contested Space" (1994). Phase two: Granatstein, Who Killed Canadian History? (1998), answered in the CHR by McKillop, "A View from the Trenches" (1999) and Palmer, "Of Silences and Trenches" (1999); Strong-Boag's review (1999); francophone reviews by Dionne (RHAF 1998), Bouvier, Fahmy-Eid, Jedwab and Slogar, and Dubuc (BHP 1999) and Dumont (CHA Bulletin 1999). Reassessments: Létourneau and the CHR forum (2000); Cook, "Identities Are Not Like Hats" (2000); Buckner, "'Limited Identities' Revisited" (2000); McKay, "The Liberal Order Framework" (2000); Osborne (2000). Later: Dummitt and Dawson, eds., Contesting Clio's Craft (2009); Hamilton (2012).
nodes.scope_note: A debate entry measured through its texts, not its people, and written as a teaching entry about the profession's self-understanding rather than current practice: any core debate text is cited by 34 of 1,303 strict 2009–2026 History PhDs (2.6%), falling to 2.0% in 2020–26. It has two phases: Bliss and the Journal of Canadian Studies replies (1991–92), and Granatstein and the Canadian Historical Review replies (1998–99); the 1992 JCS pieces answer Bliss, not Who Killed Canadian History?. Most participants' citations in the PhD corpus come from their other work. Bliss and Granatstein's scholarship is in Political, international & national history; Bliss's main entry is Political, international & national history; this entry keeps his debate row (user decision 2026-10-12). The replying fields are Canadian working-class history, Canadian women's & gender history and Canadian regional history. Several replies are characterized by title only (Gregory Kealey 1992; Kealey, Pierson, Sangster and Strong-Boag 1992; Palmer 1999). The exchange among the main protagonists was English-Canadian, but francophone historians answered Granatstein in RHAF, the Bulletin d'histoire politique and the CHA Bulletin (1998–99); no francophone reply to Bliss was found. Létourneau's 2000 CHR essay is the francophone voice in the 2000 reassessments. Quebec's own debate over national and political history (the BHP from 1992, Bélanger 1997, later the 2006–07 school programme) ran separately; its checked texts do not cite Bliss or Granatstein, and it is related here only by comparison. Osborne's school-history essay links to history education, which the atlas does not treat as an entry.

strands.title: Roots: limited identities
strands.focus: Cook's phrase (1967) and Careless's programme (1969) made region, culture and class the frame; Buckner (1988) judged it premature to abandon; Reid (1987) records the first worries about fragmentation. The debate grows out of this, not out of the 1990s alone.
strands.works: Ramsay Cook, "Canadian Centennial Cerebrations," International Journal 22, no. 4 (1967): 659–663.; J. M. S. Careless, "'Limited Identities' in Canada," Canadian Historical Review 50, no. 1 (1969): 1–10.; Phillip A. Buckner, "'Limited Identities' and Canadian Historical Scholarship: An Atlantic Provinces Perspective," Journal of Canadian Studies 23, no. 1–2 (1988): 177–198.; John G. Reid, "Towards the Elusive Synthesis: The Atlantic Provinces in Recent General Treatments of Canadian History," Acadiensis 16, no. 2 (1987): 107ff.

strands.title: Phase one, 1991–92: Bliss and the Journal of Canadian Studies replies
strands.focus: Bliss's 'Privatizing the Mind' (JCS 26:4, 1991–92): specialization had displaced older historians' concern with explaining the country (abstract). A 'Point-Counterpoint' in JCS 27:2 (1992) answered him with 'counter-positions … on the centralist views of Canadian history as articulated by Michael Bliss' (MUSE framing): Gregory Kealey defended class analysis as 'neither privatizing, nor sundering'; Linda Kealey, Pierson, Sangster and Strong-Boag asked whose 'national' history was being lamented (both title level). Strong-Boag's 1994 CHA address answered 'neo-conservative laments' (abstract). These pieces predate Who Killed Canadian History? and are not replies to it.

Kealey, "Class in English-Canadian Historical Writing: Neither Privatizing, Nor Sundering," Journal of Canadian Studies 27, no. 2 (1992): 123–129.; Linda Kealey, Ruth Pierson, Joan Sangster and Veronica Strong-Boag, "Teaching Canadian History in the 1990s: Whose 'National' History Are We Lamenting?" Journal of Canadian Studies 27, no. 2 (1992): 129–131.; Veronica Strong-Boag, "Presidential Address: Contested Space: The Politics of Canadian Memory," Journal of the Canadian Historical Association 5, no. 1 (1994): 3–17.

strands.title: Phase two, 1998–99: Granatstein and the Canadian Historical Review replies
strands.focus: Granatstein's Who Killed Canadian History? (1998), which named the debate, took the charge to a public audience (as McKillop summarizes it: academic historians had abandoned a national past for 'overspecialized and ideologically driven forms of history'). In the CHR McKillop (80:2, June 1999) argued that Granatstein miscasts the scholar as citizen and that his national history is itself political legitimation; Palmer (80:4, December 1999) offered 'a dissident view' (title level). Strong-Boag reviewed the book in Historical Studies in Education (1999; unread). Francophone historians answered the book too, as reviewers: Dionne in RHAF (1998); Bouvier, Fahmy-Eid, Jedwab and Slogar, and Dubuc in the BHP (1999), Dubuc reading it as a lament for political history as a discipline (first page); and Dumont in the CHA Bulletin (1999, read in full), who corrected its claims about Quebec schooling and called it a fierce indictment of social historians. No francophone reply to Bliss was found.

A View from the Trenches," Canadian Historical Review 80, no. 2 (1999): 269–300.; Bryan D. Palmer, "Of Silences and Trenches: A Dissident View of Granatstein's Meaning," Canadian Historical Review 80, no. 4 (1999): 676–686.; Veronica Strong-Boag, review of Who Killed Canadian History?, Historical Studies in Education 11, no. 2 (1999): 283–285.; Bernard Dionne, review, RHAF 52, no. 2 (1998).; Félix Bouvier, review, BHP 7, no. 2 (1999).; Nadia Fahmy-Eid, review, BHP 7, no. 3 (1999).; Jack Jedwab and Grégory Slogar, review, BHP 7, no. 3 (1999).; Alfred Dubuc, "À propos de : Qui a tué l'histoire du Canada ?", BHP 8, no. 1 (1999).; Micheline Dumont, review, CHA Bulletin 25, no. 1 (1999).

strands.title: Reassessments of 2000
strands.focus: The CHR forum on Létourneau's call for a narrative of Canada beyond unitarist and fragmenting versions (respondents include Cook, Valverde, Miller, Owram, Tillotson, Palmer, Iacovetta, Mitchinson); Cook on contingent, multiple identities; Buckner revisiting limited identities; McKay's liberal order as an exit from the impasse; Osborne on school history.

R. Miller, Doug Owram, Shirley Tillotson, Bryan D. Palmer, Franca Iacovetta and Wendy Mitchinson (pp. 230–301).; Ramsay Cook, "'Identities Are Not Like Hats'," Canadian Historical Review 81, no. 2 (2000), CHR forum.; P. A. Buckner, "'Limited Identities' Revisited: Regionalism and Nationalism in Canadian History," Acadiensis 30, no. 1 (Autumn 2000): 4–15.; Ian McKay, "The Liberal Order Framework: A Prospectus for a Reconnaissance of Canadian History," Canadian Historical Review 81, no. 4 (2000): 616ff.; Ken Osborne, "'Our History Syllabus Has Us Gasping': History in Canadian Schools — Past, Present, and Future," Canadian Historical Review 81, no. 3 (2000): 403ff.

strands.title: Beyond the impasse
strands.focus: Contesting Clio's Craft (2009) seeks to move past political-versus-social history through transnational and comparative approaches; Palmer's review finds old debates "at times … misrepresented"; Hamilton (2012) finds most Journal of Canadian Studies contributors of 1999–2009 adopted limited identities.

nodes.label: Canadian regional history
nodes.date_label: Morton's Manitoba 1957 · Ormsby's British Columbia 1958 · Craig's Upper Canada 1963 · 'limited identities' 1967–69 · Acadiensis 1971 · Acheson 1972 · Forbes 1979 · Friesen 1984 · Barman 1991 · reassessments 2000
nodes.description: Histories of Canada's regions as places with their own economies, societies and identities rather than as peripheries of a central-Canadian story. Provincial syntheses such as Morton's Manitoba (1957) and Ormsby's British Columbia (1958) preceded the 'limited identities' argument: Cook (1967) suggested that Canadianism might be found in regional, ethnic and class identities, and Careless (1969) made the phrase a programme. Acadiensis was revived in 1971 (Windsor's initiative; Buckner editor), its first editorial faulting historians 'obsessed with the great "national" themes'. Acheson (1972) traced Maritime industrial growth under the National Policy and its subordination to Montreal capital, and Forbes studied the Maritime Rights movement (1979). Friesen (1984), Barman (1991), Conrad and Hiller (2001) and Waiser (2005) wrote regional syntheses, while Owram, Carter and Harris tied western and Pacific history to expansionist ideas, reserve policy and colonial geography. Ontario had provincial histories of its own (Craig 1963; Nelles 1974; McCalla 1993). Acadia became a growing Atlantic literature: Griffiths on Acadian history and identity (1992, 2005), Plank and Faragher on conquest and expulsion (2001, 2005), and Reid, Basque and colleagues on 1710 (2004). Francophone regional history worked at other scales: Painchaud on the Church and French Prairie settlement (a 1970s study, published posthumously in 1987), Landry and Lang's Histoire de l'Acadie (2001), and Quebec's intraprovincial regional histories, which Harvey contrasts with interprovincial regionalism. By 2000 McKay asked whether 'region' could hold the new histories of gender, ethnicity and community, and Buckner revisited limited identities.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Morton, Manitoba (1957); Ormsby, British Columbia (1958); Cook, "Canadian Centennial Cerebrations" (1967); Careless, "'Limited Identities' in Canada" (1969) and Frontier and Metropolis (1989); Buckner, "Acadiensis II" (1971), (1988) and (2000); Acheson, "The National Policy and the Industrialization of the Maritimes" (1972); Forbes, The Maritime Rights Movement (1979); Owram, Promise of Eden (1980); Craig, Upper Canada (1963); Nelles, The Politics of Development (1974); Drummond, Progress without Planning (1987); McCalla, Planting the Province (1993); Friesen, The Canadian Prairies (1984); Painchaud, Un rêve français dans le peuplement de la Prairie (1987, posthumous); Griffiths, The Contexts of Acadian History (1992) and From Migrant to Acadian (2005); Plank, An Unsettled Conquest (2001); Landry and Lang, Histoire de l'Acadie (2001); Faragher, A Great and Noble Scheme (2005); Carter, Lost Harvests (1990); Barman, The West Beyond the West (1991); Harris, The Resettlement of British Columbia (1997); Stonechild and Waiser, Loyal till Death (1997); Conrad and Hiller, Atlantic Canada (2001); Reid, Basque et al., The "Conquest" of Acadia (2004); Waiser, Saskatchewan (2005); Baskerville, Sites of Power (2005); Reimer, Writing British Columbia History (2009); Sandwell, Contesting Rural Space (2005); Harvey (2006). Critique: McKay, "A Note on 'Region'" (2000).
nodes.scope_note: A research field for Canada's regions (the Prairie West, British Columbia, the Atlantic provinces including Acadia, and Ontario) and the limited-identities argument. Provincial syntheses, regional economic history, rural history and regional identity are distinct strands. Indigenous and settler-colonial histories of the West and British Columbia overlap strongly (Carter, Harris) and are primarily placed in Indigenous–newcomer relations & fur-trade history, Settler colonialism and environment. Ontario has a strand of provincial syntheses and economic histories chosen by PhD citation counts; Acadia has its own Atlantic strand. The North and Newfoundland are small in the PhD corpus (about 18 and 9 titles) and get only this note. Quebec's regional history appears only as a contrast of scale. Roster inclusion does not imply that historians accepted "limited identities".

strands.title: Acadia (Atlantic)
strands.focus: Acadia before and after the expulsion of 1755. In the PhD corpus this is a substantial and rising literature: 101 of 1,303 PhDs (2009–2026) cite Acadian history works, 5.1% in 2009–14 and 8.9% in 2020–26, 23 of them at francophone universities. Griffiths, an authority on pre-1755 Acadia, wrote on its contexts to 1784 (1992) and the emergence of Acadian identity (2005); Plank (2001) and Faragher (2005) studied the British campaign against the peoples of Acadia and the expulsion; Reid, Basque and colleagues read the 1710 conquest from imperial, Acadian and Mi'kmaw perspectives (2004). Landry and Lang's Histoire de l'Acadie (2001) is a francophone university synthesis of Maritime Acadia over four centuries that sets out to recount the experience of the whole Acadian people, not only its elite. Most of these works are later readings, after 2000. Readers of this literature also engage Quebec historiography (lift 3.2): see the comparison with Quebec historiography.
strands.works: N. E. S. nodes.label: Canada’s 1960s
nodes.date_label: Early accounts: Kostash 1980, Levitt 1984 · Behiels 1985 · Owram 1996 · Igartua 2006 · Palmer, Warren 2008–09 · Mills 2010 · Debating Dissent 2012 · selected later readings
nodes.description: Historical writing that treats Canada's long 1960s as a subject in its own right: the baby boom and youth revolt, the New Left and labour militancy, Quebec's Quiet Revolution and its radicalisms, rights movements, decolonization and Red Power, and the remaking of national identity. Early book-length accounts include Kostash's interview-based history of her own generation (1980) and Levitt (1984). Doug Owram's Born at the Right Time (1996) followed the baby-boom generation from suburb and school to counterculture and youth radicalism. José Igartua's The Other Quiet Revolution (2006) traced English Canada's British self-definition giving way to a civic, rights-based identity, and Dominique Clément studied its rights associations. Bryan Palmer's Canada's 1960s (2009) read the decade through the ironies of national identity, with chapters on wildcat strikes, the New Left, Quebec and the 'discovery' of the 'Indian'. Sean Mills's The Empire Within (2010) traced postcolonial thought in Montreal activism, and David Austin race, sex and security there. Campbell, Clément and Kealey's Debating Dissent (2012) and Ian Milligan's Rebel Youth (2014), on young workers and New Leftists, widened the field. Francophone historians debate continuity and rupture. Michael Behiels, E.-Martin Meunier and Jean-Philippe Warren, and Louise Bienvenue found the Quiet Revolution's roots in postwar liberalism and in Catholic Action, against its own story of a 'grande noirceur'. Warren's Une douce anarchie (2008) historicized the student revolt of 1968. It is a recent synthesis literature resting on a few reference works (Owram, Palmer, Mills, Igartua), not a school like the atlas's New Left entry.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Kostash, Long Way from Home (1980); Levitt, Children of Privilege (1984); Behiels, Prelude to Quebec’s Quiet Revolution (1985); Couture, Le mythe de la modernisation du Québec (1991); Owram, Born at the Right Time (1996); Gélinas (1996, 2007); Martel, Le deuil d’un pays imaginé (1997); Meunier and Warren (2002); Bienvenue (2003); Gauvreau (2005); Igartua, The Other Quiet Revolution (2006); Clément, Canada’s Rights Revolution (2008); Warren, Une douce anarchie (2008); Palmer, Canada’s 1960s (2009); Mills, The Empire Within (2010); Kinsman and Gentile (2010); Henderson, Making the Scene (2011); Campbell, Clément and Kealey, eds., Debating Dissent (2012); Austin, Fear of a Black Nation (2013) (with Forsythe, ed., Let the Niggers Burn!, 1971, as a contemporary participants' collection); Milligan, Rebel Youth (2014); Rutherford, Canada’s Other Red Scare (2020). Comparison: Marwick, The Sixties (1998).
nodes.scope_note: A research field defined by its subject, the long 1960s (roughly late 1950s to early 1970s), not by a method or school. It replaces the "postwar Canada" data cluster (user, 2026-10-12: "1960s is its own thing"). Distinguish the atlas's New Left entry (radical historians as a school) from histories of the New Left as a movement. The Quebec strand overlaps Quebec historiography and the Catholic Action revision in religion history; those works remain treated mainly there. Register: a recent synthesis literature resting on a few reference works (Owram 71 and Palmer 67 citing PhDs; Mills; Igartua), with engagement modestly falling (ratio 0.78; fixed panel 0.81), not a school. Black Canadian sixties history: Austin (2013) is a later reading; before 2000 the only verified work is a contemporary participants' collection (Forsythe, ed., 1971), so pre-2000 scholarly coverage is a gap.

nodes.label: Settler colonialism
nodes.date_label: Earlier settler-society studies 1983–95 · Wolfe 1999 · selected later readings: Wolfe 2006, Veracini 2010, journal 2011, critiques 2013–20; field chronology unresolved
nodes.description: Historical inquiry into colonial formations in which newcomers came to stay, acquired land and claimed sovereignty over Indigenous territories. Patrick Wolfe's account of settler colonialism as a structure rather than an event treats invasion as a continuing relation rather than a completed frontier past. Lorenzo Veracini's work and the journal Settler Colonial Studies (2011) distinguished settler colonial from colonial phenomena. Comparative studies of settler capitalism and settler societies, and decolonization-era uses of the term, came earlier. In Canadian historical writing the framework meets an older historiography of dispossession, reserves, gender and the state in the West and British Columbia. It also meets Indigenous political theory of recognition, sovereignty and resurgence. Its uses extend to labour, science, memory and settler identity. The field is contested from several directions. Indigenous scholars ask whether it recentres settlers and displaces Indigenous studies and Indigenous-authored histories. Historians question its structural inevitability and its fit across regions and periods, proposing other modes such as commercial penetration and extractivism. Black studies scholars question how it places slavery. Settler colonialism overlaps with Indigenous history, postcolonial critique and historical geography without being equivalent to any of them.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Earlier: Denoon, Settler Capitalism (1983); Stasiulis and Yuval-Davis, eds., Unsettling Settler Societies (1995). Wolfe, Settler Colonialism and the Transformation of Anthropology (1999) and “Settler Colonialism and the Elimination of the Native” (2006); Elkins and Pedersen, eds. (2005); Veracini, Settler Colonialism (2010) and Settler Colonial Studies (2011). Read with Coulthard (2014), A. Simpson (2014), L. B. Simpson (2011, 2017), Byrd (2011) and Tuck and Yang (2012). Canadian historiography: Carter (1990, 2008), Harris (2002, 2004, 2020), Perry (2001), Regan (2010), Daschuk (2013), Battell Lowman and Barker (2015), Burrill (2019). Critiques: Macoun and Strakosch (2013), Rowse (2014), Kauanui (2016), Greer (2019), Shoemaker (2019), Konishi (2019), Garba and Sorentino (2020).
nodes.scope_note: A selective research field whose theoretical consolidation came mostly after 2000; the entry covers its roots through 2000 and cites selected later works as readings. Settler-colonial theory, Indigenous political thought, Canadian histories of dispossession and comparative imperial history have different genealogies. Roster inclusion is not adoption of the paradigm: Carter, Perry, Harris and Daschuk wrote earlier or beside it. No single founder, origin or Canadian consensus is asserted. Critics appear as critics. Francophone uptake in the PhD corpus is near zero.

nodes.label: Patrick Wolfe
nodes.date_label: Settler Colonialism and the Transformation of Anthropology 1999 · later essays 2001, 2006
nodes.description: Reads the history of anthropology through settler colonialism. Settler Colonialism and the Transformation of Anthropology (1999) studies virgin birth in anthropology and in Australian settler discourse, and Victorian anthropology on mother-right, totemism and E. B. Tylor. Later essays address land, labour and race (2001) and the elimination of the native (2006).

nodes.scope_note: This entry presents the 1999 book. Its introduction (pp. 1–2, read) distinguishes settler from franchise colonies, holds that settler colonies 'were (are) premised on the elimination of native societies' and states that 'invasion is a structure not an event'; the rest of the book is checked at contents and catalogue level. The 2001 and 2006 essays are later readings. He did not originate the term, which has earlier usage (Veracini 2013), and he is not presented as the field's founder.

nodes.label: Ian McKay
nodes.date_label: Tartanism Triumphant 1992 · The Quest of the Folk 1994 · 'A Note on Region' and the liberal order prospectus 2000 · later readings 2005, 2008, 2009
nodes.description: Reads twentieth-century Nova Scotia's 'folk' as a cultural selection by folklorists, handicraft planners, writers and the tourist state, and as a local version of an international antimodernist wave (1992, 1994). In 2000 he proposed treating Canada as a project of liberal rule, to be studied through the implantation of liberalism across a heterogeneous terrain, and asked how 'region' fits that project. Later work turns to the Canadian left as a counter-project (2005, 2008) and answers the framework's critics (2009).
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Ian McKay (b. 1953); “Tartanism Triumphant: The Construction of Scottishness in Nova Scotia, 1933–1954” (1992); The Quest of the Folk: Antimodernism and Cultural Selection in Twentieth-Century Nova Scotia (1994); “A Note on ‘Region’ in Writing the History of Atlantic Canada” (2000); “The Liberal Order Framework: A Prospectus for a Reconnaissance of Canadian History” (2000). Later readings: Rebels, Reds, Radicals (2005); Reasoning Otherwise (2008); “Canada as a Long Liberal Revolution” (2009).
nodes.scope_note: This entry presents the 1992 article and the 1994 book on antimodernism and the folk, and the two essays of 2000 on region and liberal order. The 1992 article is read at pp. 5–9 and 13–14; the 1994 book is checked at summary and contents level, with its closing argument (p. 306) quoted by Muise (1998); the region essay is read in full; the prospectus is checked at abstract level, with pp. 620–21 quoted by Fecteau (2009). The framework takes its name from his prospectus, but state-formation studies (Curtis 1988; Greer and Radforth 1992) precede it and commentators name Gramsci and Fernande Roy (1988) as its sources; he is not presented as the founder of a field. The 2005, 2008 and 2009 works are later readings.

nodes.label: Harold A. Innis
nodes.date_label: The Fur Trade in Canada 1930 · The Cod Fisheries 1940 · Empire and Communications 1950 · The Bias of Communication 1951
nodes.description: A Toronto political economist whose staple studies read Canada's development through the export of raw materials to industrial centres in Britain and the United States. The Fur Trade in Canada (1930) concludes that 'the economic history of Canada has been dominated by the discrepancy between the center and the margin of western civilization', that the history of the fur trade is 'the history of contact between two civilizations', and that 'the present Dominion emerged not in spite of geography but because of it'. The Cod Fisheries (1940) follows a second staple as the history of an international economy. After 1940 he turned to the media of communication and empire (Empire and Communications, 1950; The Bias of Communication, 1951).
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Harold A. Innis (1894–1952); The Fur Trade in Canada: An Introduction to Canadian Economic History (1930); The Cod Fisheries: The History of an International Economy (1940); Empire and Communications (1950); The Bias of Communication (1951; 1964 reissue with an introduction by Marshall McLuhan). Readings: Brady's memoir (1953); Watkins, “A Staple Theory of Economic Growth” (1963); Salmon (1997).
nodes.scope_note: This entry presents the staple studies. The Fur Trade in Canada is checked at its contents and its conclusion (pp. 386–397, read in a scan of the 1930 edition); The Cod Fisheries and the two communication books are checked at catalogue level, and the turn to communication rests on Brady's 1953 memoir. He is not presented as the originator of the staple approach. Watkins (1963) calls him its 'leading innovator' but adds that 'others tilled the same vineyard'. Salmon (1997) notes that 'Innis never claimed to have originated the staples theory', Brady names Adam Shortt 'the pioneer in these economic studies', and Mackintosh's 1923 article precedes the fur-trade book. The 1930 conclusion's statements about Indigenous peoples (their 'limited cultural background'; that Canada 'has had no serious problems with her native peoples') are recorded as claims of 1930, not adopted. The atlas has no communication-studies entry; the McLuhan introduction is noted from the catalogue only.

nodes.label: Kenneth Pomeranz
nodes.date_label: The Making of a Hinterland 1993 · The Great Divergence 2000 · exchange with Huang 2002–2003 · Journal of Global History 2006 · “Histories for a Less National Age” 2014
nodes.description: A historian of China whose reciprocal comparisons of Eurasian core regions recast the divergence of European and Chinese economies. The Great Divergence (2000) takes 'Why wasn’t England the Yangzi Delta?' as seriously as the reverse question and argues that 'Europe, too, could have wound up on an “east Asian,” labor-intensive path'. Coal, and land-intensive goods from New World colonies worked by enslaved people, relieved Europe's constraints of land and energy. The earlier Making of a Hinterland (1993), in its publisher’s description and Bianco’s review, traces the economic and ecological costs for inland North China when the late Qing and Republican state abandoned many hinterland areas. The Great Divergence became central to the debate over the “California School”. Philip Huang answered that England and the Yangzi delta stood “at opposite poles” of development and involution (2002–2003); Brenner and Isett located England’s divergence in early modern social-property relations (2002); Broadberry and Gupta found the advanced parts of Asia closer to Europe’s stagnating periphery in wages and prices (2006); Allen and colleagues disputed urban real-wage parity between the Yangzi delta and England (2011); and Broadberry, Guan and Li placed the divergence between leading regions around 1700 (2021). He was a co-founding editor of the Journal of Global History (2006), and his AHA presidential address (2014) asked how history might be reframed “for a less national age”.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Kenneth Pomeranz (b. 1958); The Making of a Hinterland: State, Society, and Economy in Inland North China, 1853–1937 (1993); The Great Divergence: China, Europe, and the Making of the Modern World Economy (2000); “Beyond the East-West Binary” (2002) and “Facts are Stubborn Things” (2003), replies to Philip Huang; co-founding editor of the Journal of Global History (2006); “The Great Himalayan Watershed” (2009); “Histories for a Less National Age” (AHA presidential address, 2014). Readings: Bianco’s review (1996); Cooper’s review (2000); Huang (2002, 2003); Brenner and Isett (2002); Broadberry and Gupta (2006); Allen and colleagues (2011); Broadberry, Guan and Li (2021).
nodes.scope_note: This entry presents the argument of The Great Divergence as its introduction states it (pp. 3–27 read, with the contents, in a preview of the later Princeton edition; page numbers are that edition's). The Making of a Hinterland is checked at contents level and through Bianco's 1996 review, read in full; its text is unread. He is not presented as the originator of reciprocal comparison: he writes that the approach was 'anticipated in important ways by my colleague R. Bin Wong', takes the 'encompassing comparison' from Charles Tilly, and notes parallels with Sugihara Kaoru. Arguments from colonial extraction (Williams, Frank, Amin) precede his. His estimates are contested: Cooper (2000) notes 'plausible guesstimates', and Bianco (1996) judges that the 1993 book 'postule plus qu'il ne prouve' a deliberate strategy of selective development. Later critiques (Huang 2002–2003; Brenner and Isett 2002; Broadberry and Gupta 2006; Allen and colleagues 2011; Broadberry, Guan and Li 2021) appear as critique arrows and do not change what the 2000 introduction is read as arguing. The ‘California School’ is a label for Pomeranz, Wong and colleagues (AHA biography), not an atlas entry. The 2014 address is read through the AHA web text without pagination; the 2009 essay is dated from its opening only.

nodes.label: William Cronon
nodes.date_label: Changes in the Land 1983 · Nature’s Metropolis 1991 · “The Trouble with Wilderness” 1995
nodes.description: A historian of North American environments who treats ecological change as a two-way relation between people and the rest of nature, worked out through property, markets and ideas of nature. Changes in the Land (1983) assumes that 'the interactions of the two are dialectical' and finds in colonial New England not a choice between landscapes with and without people but 'two human ways of living, two ways of belonging to an ecosystem'. Nature’s Metropolis (1991) follows grain, lumber and meat between Chicago and its hinterland on the premise that 'city and country have a common history, so their stories are best told together'. 'A Place for Stories' (1992) asks environmental historians for 'stories about stories about nature', and 'The Trouble with Wilderness' (1995) calls wilderness 'quite profoundly a human creation'. Reviewers found the Chicago book distant from farmers and townspeople, or moralising; he replied that he saw 'no pure heroes or pure villains'.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: William Cronon (b. 1954); Changes in the Land: Indians, Colonists, and the Ecology of New England (1983); “Modes of Prophecy and Production: Placing Nature in History” (JAH 1990); Nature’s Metropolis: Chicago and the Great West (1991); “Kennecott Journey: The Paths out of Town” (1992); “A Place for Stories: Nature, History, and Narrative” (JAH 1992); “The Uses of Environmental History” (1993); “The Trouble with Wilderness” (1995). Readings: the Annals of Iowa forum on Nature’s Metropolis, with his response (1992); Sessions’s reply on wilderness (1996); his own afterword to Changes in the Land (2003).
nodes.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-13: chapter 1 of Changes in the Land in an unpaginated web transcription; 'A Place for Stories' (JAH 1992; pp. 1347–1351 and 1369–1376 read) and 'The Uses of Environmental History' (1993; OCR of the author’s scan, journal pagination); 'Kennecott Journey' (1992); passages of 'The Trouble with Wilderness' in the author’s reflow; and the 1992 Annals of Iowa forum on Nature’s Metropolis, with his response read in full. Nature’s Metropolis itself is unread: its words appear here only as forum contributors quote them with page numbers. 'Modes of Prophecy and Production', his 1990 response to Worster in the JAH round table, is paywalled and unread. He is not presented as a founder. He places environmental history among the 'new' histories 'born or reenergized in the wake of the 1960s' (1993, p. 2), names Nash, Hays, Worster, Merchant, Tarr and Pyne as practitioners (pp. 2–3), footnotes lessons to Crosby, Richard White, McEvoy and others (pp. 8–10), and echoes Leopold (n. 11). On Mahoney’s reading (1992, p. 492), Nature’s Metropolis demonstrates 'this fundamental urban historical premise' rather than inventing it. His approaches were contested in period: Danbom (1992, p. 503) finds 'environmental moralism'; Mahoney (p. 491) that urban and economic history 'seem only to serve the interests of environmental history'; Sessions (1996) that the wilderness essay underweights wild habitat. His 2003 afterword, McNeill (2003) and Canadian uses after 2000 are later readings.

nodes.label: Donald Worster
nodes.date_label: Nature's Economy 1977 · Dust Bowl 1979 · Rivers of Empire 1985 · 'Transformations of the Earth' 1990
nodes.description: A historian of the American Great Plains and arid West who set out a three-level model of environmental history. In 'Doing Environmental History' (1988) he wrote that 'there are three levels on which the new history proceeds': 'understanding nature itself', 'the socioeconomic realm as it interacts with the environment', and 'the purely mental or intellectual', which together 'constitute a single dynamic inquiry'. His 1990 Journal of American History essay turned to 'that middle level, the analysis of modes of production as ecological phenomena', chiefly the capitalist transformation of agriculture, which Dust Bowl (1979) had called 'the decisive factor in this nation's use of nature'; Rivers of Empire (1985) described the West as 'a modern hydraulic society'. Merchant's 1990 response called the levels 'a significant framework for research and writing in this emerging field' but found that the essay 'lacks a gender analysis'. Cronon (1992) read Dust Bowl as a story whose 'chief agent' is capitalism and whose plot 'proclaims an apocalyptic prophecy'.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Donald Worster (b. 1941); Nature's Economy: The Roots of Ecology (1977); Dust Bowl: The Southern Plains in the 1930s (1979); Rivers of Empire: Water, Aridity, and the Growth of the American West (1985); 'Appendix: Doing Environmental History', in The Ends of the Earth (1988); 'Transformations of the Earth: Toward an Agroecological Perspective in History', Journal of American History (1990), reprinted in The Wealth of Nature (1993). Readings: Merchant's round-table response (1990); Cronon, 'A Place for Stories' (1992); Hennessey's review of Rivers of Empire (1987); McDean (1986).
nodes.scope_note: This entry presents the three-level model in Worster's 1988 wording, checked in an abridged reprint and by full-text search of the 1988 edition, and the 1990 essay in his own 1993 reprint; the Journal of American History pages of 1990 were not reachable and are given only where another writer cites them (Isenberg 2013). Dust Bowl and Rivers of Empire are quoted at the pages given by Cronon (1992) and Hennessey (1987), with the wording confirmed by search of the original editions. He is not presented as the founder of the field or the sole author of the scheme: he grounds the idea in Aldo Leopold's call for 'an ecological interpretation of history', and Arthur McEvoy's ecology, production and cognition triad appeared in the same 1988 volume. The scheme was contested at once: Merchant (1990) added gender and 'a fourth analytical level, that of reproduction', Cronon (1992) treated Dust Bowl as a declensionist narrative, and McDean (1986) criticised its generalisation across the Plains. The 1990 objections of White and Cronon in the round table are known here only through Isenberg (2013), a later reading.

nodes.label: Alfred W. Crosby
nodes.date_label: The Columbian Exchange 1972 · Virgin Soil Epidemics 1976 · Ecological Imperialism 1986
nodes.description: A historian of the biological consequences of European expansion. The Columbian Exchange (1972) followed pathogens, plants and animals between the Americas and the Old World after 1492, and 'Virgin Soil Epidemics' (1976) defined epidemics among peoples who, as Jones (2003, pp. 703–704) quotes the definition, 'have had no previous contact with the diseases that strike them' (the 1976 article itself is unread). Ecological Imperialism (1986) starts from the fact that 'European emigrants and their descendants are all over the place, which requires explanation', asks why 'the sun never sets on the empire of the dandelion', and suggests that 'the success of European imperialism has a biological, an ecological, component': crops, livestock, weeds and diseases helped Europeans make temperate 'Neo-Europes'. Later critics charge the model with ecological determinism and argue that the virgin-soil idea was flattened into a claim that Indigenous Americans had 'no immunity'.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Alfred W. Crosby (1931–2018); The Columbian Exchange: Biological and Cultural Consequences of 1492 (1972); 'Virgin Soil Epidemics as a Factor in the Aboriginal Depopulation in America' (William and Mary Quarterly, 1976); Ecological Imperialism: The Biological Expansion of Europe, 900–1900 (1986); 'The Past and Present of Environmental History' (American Historical Review, 1995). Readings: Miller's review (1987); Cook (1990); Cronon (1993); Subrahmanyam (1997); later, Jones (2003), McNeill (2003) and Isenberg (2013).
nodes.scope_note: This entry presents Ecological Imperialism as its prologue states the argument (pp. 1–7 read, with the contents and acknowledgments, in the publisher's sample of the 2004 second edition; page numbers are that edition's). The Columbian Exchange (1972), 'Virgin Soil Epidemics' (1976) and the 1995 AHR essay are unread: the 1972 book is characterised from Cook (1990) and McNeill (2003), and the 1976 wording is quoted as Jones (2003) quotes it. His 1978 American Heritage essay on New England, read in full, states the disease argument in his own words: 'Innocent of immunity or experience, the Indians were helpless.' He is not presented as the founder of environmental history: the ASEH's own history lists him among several 'founding members' with Worster, Flader and Opie, and in 1982 among 'the already widely known historians'; he thanks William McNeill, who 'read the whole thing in first draft'. Contested readings: in period, Subrahmanyam (1997) calls the books 'oft-cited (and oft-criticized)', while Miller (1987) finds Crosby 'careful not to overestimate the significance of any single component'. Later, McNeill (2003) records that 'Some readers felt that Crosby had relocated historical agency (and responsibility for genocide and colonialism) from humans to wheat and whooping cough'; Isenberg (2013) judges that his analysis 'devolved into little more than ecological determinism'; Jones (2003) argues that the virgin-soil model 'has been misunderstood and misrepresented', that the 1976 article itself stressed malnutrition and 'the social chaos generated by European colonization', and that Crosby's other writings stressed lack of immunity. These are later readings, not evidence for the edges. The 2004 preface, in which he calls Pomeranz's Great Divergence 'The clearest exposition of the new scenario', is a later self-reading and is not used.

nodes.label: Carolyn Merchant
nodes.date_label: The Death of Nature 1980 · Ecological Revolutions 1989 · Radical Ecology 1992
nodes.description: A historian of science and environmental historian who argued in The Death of Nature (1980) that a science 'reconceptualizing reality as a machine rather than a living organism, sanctioned the domination of both nature and women'. In Ecological Revolutions (1989), a study of New England from 1600 to 1860, she treated major changes in human relations with nature as arising from tensions 'between a society’s mode of production and its ecology, and between its modes of production and reproduction', which in turn reshape consciousness. Answering Worster's three levels of ecology, production and cognition in 1990, she wrote that environmental history 'needs a fourth analytical level, that of reproduction' and a gender analysis of each level. Her reading of Bacon's metaphors was disputed in the 1990s (Soble 1995; Pesic 1999, whom she answered in 2006), and a 1991 reviewer, praising her integration of gender, found 'painfully few people making history' in the New England book.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Carolyn Merchant (b. 1936); The Death of Nature: Women, Ecology, and the Scientific Revolution (1980); “The Theoretical Structure of Ecological Revolutions” (1987); Ecological Revolutions: Nature, Gender, and Science in New England (1989); “Gender and Environmental History” (JAH round table, 1990); Radical Ecology: The Search for a Livable World (1992). Readings: Cronon (1993); Steinberg's review (1991); Soble (1995); Leach and Green (1997); Pesic (1999); Merchant's own retrospectives (1998, 2006).
nodes.scope_note: This entry presents Merchant's framework as her own in-period texts state it: the 1987 Environmental Review article and the 1990 JAH response (both read in full, original pagination); The Death of Nature (1980) and Ecological Revolutions (1989) through author-hosted reprinted excerpts (pages are the reprints'); and the 1992 conclusion to Radical Ecology (facsimile, original pages). She is not presented as the founder of environmental history or of ecofeminism. She builds on Kuhn and on Marx and Engels, on Meillassoux, Peterson and Bridenthal for reproduction, and on Worster's levels; in 1998 she credits Hessen, Zilsel, Leiss and Kubrin ('It was Kubrin’s idea that the key concept of early modern science was that matter was dead'). She separates her socialist ecofeminism from a radical feminism that 'runs the risk of perpetuating the very value hierarchies it seeks to overthrow' (1989). The Bacon reading is contested (Soble 1995 and Pesic 1999, abstracts only), Leach and Green (1997) place The Death of Nature among the ecofeminist histories they criticise, and Steinberg (1991) faults the New England book's narrative. McNeill (2003) and Merchant's 2006 Isis response are later readings, not evidence for the 1980–1992 framework.

nodes.label: Richard White
nodes.date_label: Land Use, Environment, and Social Change 1980 · The Roots of Dependency 1983 · field survey 1985 · The Middle Ground 1991 · The Organic Machine 1995
nodes.description: A historian of the American West, of Native American history and of environmental history. The Middle Ground (1991; quoted from Cambridge Core first-page excerpts of the introduction and chapters) rejects accounts of Indian–white contact with 'but two outcomes', conquest or persistence, because contact 'creates as well as destroys': in the Great Lakes pays d'en haut, French and Algonquian allies 'had to arrive at some common conception of suitable ways of acting', a middle ground which White describes as a process of creative and often expedient misunderstanding, sustained because whites could not simply command Indians or disregard them, until in the nineteenth century its compromises 'yielded to stark choices between assimilation and otherness'. His environmental books trace Salish and settler land use and environmental change in Island County, Washington (1980), subsistence, environment and dependency among the Choctaws, Pawnees and Navajos (1983), and the Columbia River as an organic machine, an energy system remade by human labour that keeps natural qualities, in which human work is energy as much as the river's flow (1995). His 1985 Pacific Historical Review essay surveyed environmental history as a new field, and he responded to Worster's agroecological essay in the 1990 Journal of American History round table.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Richard White (b. 1947); Land Use, Environment, and Social Change: The Shaping of Island County, Washington (1980; 1992 paperback with Cronon's foreword and a new preface); The Roots of Dependency: Subsistence, Environment, and Social Change among the Choctaws, Pawnees, and Navajos (1983); “American Environmental History: The Development of a New Historical Field” (1985); “Environmental History, Ecology, and Meaning” (1990); The Middle Ground: Indians, Empires, and Republics in the Great Lakes Region, 1650–1815 (1991); The Organic Machine: The Remaking of the Columbia River (1995); “‘Are You an Environmentalist or Do You Work for a Living?’” (1995). Readings: Savard (1992), Edmunds (1993) and D. R. Miller (1994) on The Middle Ground; Cronon's foreword (1992) to Land Use.
nodes.scope_note: Not Hayden White (node white). Witnesses for The Middle Ground: Cambridge Core first-page excerpts (full pages, folios observed) of the introduction (1991 p. ix) and of the chapters opening at pp. 50, 94 and 518; the next page of the introduction (1991 p. x = 2011 p. xxvi) and pp. 52–53 and 93 only in Google Books search-within snippets of the 2011 twentieth-anniversary edition, whose body pagination matches 1991 at the pages checked (the equation 1991 p. x = 2011 p. xxvi is inferred from the introduction's opening at 1991 p. ix and 2011 p. xxv). The rest of the book is unread, and wording witnessed only by snippets is paraphrased in node text. Land Use (1980; 1992 paperback) and The Organic Machine (1995) are known from Google Books search-within snippets of their framing pages, not from page images; The Organic Machine's preface folios were not visible, so its framing is paraphrased. The Roots of Dependency (1983), the 1985 survey, the 1990 round-table response and the 1995 Uncommon Ground essay are unread (paywalled or not previewed) and are known through Cronon (1993, 1994), Worster (1990, Portuguese translation), Cook (1990), Isenberg (2013) and the publisher's records. He is not presented as a founder of environmental history: Land Use credits James Malin's neglected Great Plains studies as a trail to follow (snippet, p. 7), and Isenberg (2013) names him in a group of synthesisers. The middle ground was contested in period: Savard (1992) doubts its premise of Iroquois devastation, Edmunds (1993) finds the post-1770 chapters 'less convincing', and D. R. Miller (1994) notes the neglect of peoples neither Iroquoian nor Algonquian; Merrell's in-period critique (Into the American Woods, 1999) is known here only through White's later 2011 response. Havard (2003) and Deloria (2006) are later critiques, also known here only through that 2011 preface, a later reading. Canadian environmental historians cite him chiefly for the 1985 survey; Canadian use of The Middle Ground before 2000 is checked only in reviews and one legal article.

nodes.label: Aldo Leopold
nodes.date_label: Land ethic and ecological interpretation of history · A Sand County Almanac 1949
nodes.description: A forester, wildlife ecologist and conservationist, not a historian, whose posthumous A Sand County Almanac (1949) set out a 'land ethic' that 'changes the role of Homo sapiens from conqueror of the land-community to plain member and citizen of it'. In the same essay he wrote that an 'ecological interpretation of history' shows that 'many historical events, hitherto explained solely in terms of human enterprise, were actually biotic interactions between people and land', and took as his example the Kentucky canelands that became bluegrass under 'the cow, plow, fire, and axe of the pioneer'. He asked: 'Is history taught in this spirit? It will be, once the concept of land as a community really penetrates our intellectual life.' Environmental historians later cited the call: Worster (1988) wrote that Leopold 'projected such an alliance' between history and ecology, and Cronon (1993) described the field's subject as 'the history recorded in Aldo Leopold’s tree rings'.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Aldo Leopold (1887–1948); A Sand County Almanac, and Sketches Here and There (1949), especially 'Good Oak' and 'The Land Ethic'. Readings: Nash, Wilderness and the American Mind (1967), chapter 'Aldo Leopold: Prophet'; Worster, 'Doing Environmental History' (1988) and 'Transformations of the Earth' (1990); Cronon, 'The Uses of Environmental History' (1993) and History 901 syllabus (1994). Later readings: Wynn (2001); MacEachern (2002); Cronon's afterword to Changes in the Land (2003).
nodes.scope_note: This entry presents Leopold as a precursor whose writing environmental historians cited, not as a historian and not as the founder of environmental history. 'The Land Ethic' and 'Good Oak' are read in two unpaginated transcriptions (the 1966 enlarged Oxford text and an excerpt of the 1949 essay); the 1949 page of the history passage (p. 205) is the one Worster (1990, n. 1) and Wynn (2001, n. 55) both cite. Worster's 1988 essay dates 'the idea of environmental history' to the 1970s, the global-predicament conferences and the environmental movement, not to Leopold. His 1990 essay, read only in Portuguese translation, cautions that the Kentucky case is more complicated than Leopold's example and needs more than a simple environmental determinism, and adds that bluegrass was a European import, which Leopold had said was not known. Cronon's 1993 uses are echoes of a moral and literary voice, not a borrowed method. Canadian writing differs: MacEachern (2002, p. 219) faults a history of Ontario conservation for assuming, without evidence, that Leopold 'was being read by Canadians, let alone influencing them' (a remark about naturalists of the 1950s, not about historians), and Wynn (2001, p. 145), a historical geographer, urges geographers to 'respond to Leopold’s call' and observes: 'Few have done so'.

nodes.label: Rachel Carson
nodes.date_label: Silent Spring 1962
nodes.description: A marine biologist and science writer whose Silent Spring (1962) was a catalyst for environmental concern and became a shared text for US environmental historians; it is not a work of history. The book argued that 'the central problem of our age has therefore become the contamination of man’s total environment' by persistent chemicals, followed pesticides through 'the web of life — or death — that scientists know as ecology', and called the 'control of nature' 'a phrase conceived in arrogance'. It did not reject all control: 'control must be geared to realities, not to mythical situations'. Historians who shaped the field took the book up as a starting point: John Opie's 1971 reader opens 'The Contemporary Controversy Begins' with her, and Donald Worster's history of ecological ideas (1977) places Silent Spring near the opening of 'The Age of Ecology'.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Rachel Carson (1907–1964); Silent Spring (1962). Readings: Opie's reader, with Graham's account of the outcry (1971); Worster, Nature's Economy (1977); Dunlap, DDT (1981); Hays, in collaboration with Barbara D. Hays, Beauty, Health, and Permanence (1987); Nash, The Rights of Nature (1989); Cronon's graduate seminar (1994). Later readings: Lear's introduction (2002); Carruthers (2004).
nodes.scope_note: A precursor entry for a catalyst of environmental concern, not a historian. Silent Spring is quoted from the 2002 Mariner edition (a partial scan was read: pp. 1–9, 172–198, 278–279 and 296–297, with Lear's introduction); Worster's 1977 notes cite pp. 8 and 297 for the same sentences, so the pagination matches the 1962 edition at those points. She is not presented as a founder or as the catalyst of environmental history as a discipline. Worster (1977; Internet Archive full-text search, page located by the index) credits her with launching the recent ecology movement, which is the movement, not the field. The disciplinary claim is a later, geographically qualified reading: Carruthers (2004) reports that Grove conceded Silent Spring's importance to the discipline only for the United States. The Canadian self-accounts read for this batch name her as 1960s context, not as a model. The book was contested from the start. Velsicol's general counsel attributed attacks on the chemical industry to sinister influences (his letter as quoted by Graham, 1970, in Opie's reader, p. 93 from a running head). Dunlap (1981, pp. 3–4 and 7 from running heads) records that defenders of DDT condemned her as a crank, and judges that she had done no original research. Nash (1989, p. 80 from a running head) finds much traditional anthropocentrism in her ethics. These three are known only through Internet Archive full-text search of borrow-only scans (page images not seen), so they are paraphrased. Lear (2002), a later reading, writes that the cancer evidence still fuels an 'acrimonious' debate. The 1962 reviews in Science (Baldwin) and Time were not read.
