nodes.label: Dipesh Chakrabarty
nodes.date_label: Rethinking Working-Class History 1989 · “Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History” 1992 · Provincializing Europe 2000 · “The Climate of History” 2009 · The Calling of History 2015 · The Climate of History in a Planetary Age 2021
nodes.description: A historian of modern South Asia in the Subaltern Studies collective. He argues that, within university-based historical discourse, an imagined 'Europe' remains its dominant theoretical reference: 'the sovereign, theoretical subject of all histories, including the ones we call “Indian,” “Chinese,” “Kenyan”', where 'Europe' and 'India' are 'hyperreal terms', figures of the imaginary 'subject to contestation' (1992). Rethinking Working-Class History (1989) reads Bengal’s jute-mill workers against an assumption of 'a hegemonic bourgeois culture' in Marx’s category of capital. 'Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History' (1992) calls Europe 'a silent referent in historical knowledge', and Provincializing Europe (2000) criticises the historicist 'first in Europe, then elsewhere' that placed colonized peoples in 'an imaginary waiting room of history', while holding European thought 'both indispensable and inadequate'; a 2000 essay separates History 1, the past 'posited by capital', from History 2, pasts that are 'not pasts separate from capital' but 'inhere in capital and yet interrupt and punctuate' its logic. In period, Sumit Sarkar called the trajectory he described 'debilitating', and the labour historian Rajnarayan Chandavarkar found a 'static, timeless, indeed Orientalist' culture in his Bengal book. Later readers of Provincializing Europe disputed it: Carola Dietze (2008, abstract only) regarded him as 'a thinker of radical historicism rather than as a critic of the discipline of history', and a 2014 symposium on Vivek Chibber’s critique divided: William Sewell found its 'Europe' a construct 'fused with' Marxism and preferred Chibber’s account, while Bruce Cumings called Chibber’s portrayal of Chakrabarty 'a preposterous caricature'; at its twentieth anniversary Christopher Hill found 'ambiguities and contradictions' in it that were also 'the source of its wide impact' (2020). After 2000 he turned to climate. 'The Climate of History' (2009) argued that climate change spells 'the collapse of the age-old humanist distinction between natural history and human history', a distinction he later traced 'from Hegel and Marx to Croce and Collingwood'. His Tanner Lectures (2015) questioned Big History's hope that large-scale history yields 'global citizenship', and The Climate of History in a Planetary Age (2021) sets the planet beside the globe: 'The global is anthropocentric while the planet de-centers and provincializes the human' (2022). He also took up a long exchange with Bruno Latour (2013–20). Critics answered from several sides: Malm and Hornborg (2014), whose abstract (the article is unread) questions the 'species' category, holding inequalities within humanity 'part and parcel of the current ecological crisis' (that they address him is his own report); the environmental historian Timothy LeCain (2016) and the historian of science Richard Staley (2024) on the novelty of the divide; the political theorist Brooke Ackerly (2022) on his use of Indigenous histories, which she called 'dismissive and extractive'. Answering her, he grants that 'there is room for a deeper engagement with Indigenous traditions' while defending the meaning he gives Earth System Science, whose 'earth system' is 'my category “planet”', as no dismissal of 'other traditions and forms of planetary thought'; on capitalism he answers that capital and empire are 'a necessary but insufficient framework' (2022). The Calling of History (2015) studies the colonial historian Jadunath Sarkar and what a reviewer, Girija Joshi, calls the question of when a society values the 'objectivity' of historical research.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Dipesh Chakrabarty (b. 1948); 'Communal Riots and Labour' (Past & Present, 1981); Rethinking Working-Class History: Bengal 1890–1940 (1989); “Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History: Who Speaks for ‘Indian’ Pasts?” (Representations, 1992); “Minority Histories, Subaltern Pasts” (Perspectives, 1997); Provincializing Europe: Postcolonial Thought and Historical Difference (2000; new preface 2007); “Universalism and Belonging in the Logic of Capital” (Public Culture, 2000). After 2000: Habitations of Modernity (2002); “The Climate of History: Four Theses” (Critical Inquiry, 2009); Tanner Lectures, “The Human Condition in the Anthropocene” (2015); The Calling of History: Sir Jadunath Sarkar and His Empire of Truth (2015); “Anthropocene Time” (History and Theory, 2018); The Climate of History in a Planetary Age (2021); One Planet, Many Worlds (2023). Readings: Nair’s review (1990); Dirlik (1994); Chandavarkar (1997); Sarkar (1997); Dietze (2008); Sewell (2014); Whose Anthropocene? (2016); Práticas da História anniversary issue (2020); The Review of Politics symposium (2022); Arffman (2022); Staley (2024).
nodes.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-14: the 1989 preface (pp. xi–xv) and introduction (pp. 3–6) in the publisher preview; 'Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History' (Representations 37, 1992, pp. 1–26) in full; the 1997 AHA essay in full (web text, no page numbers); the Provincializing Europe introduction (pp. 3–23, in the publisher’s excerpt); 'Universalism and Belonging in the Logic of Capital' (Public Culture, 2000), which he describes as a slightly different version of the book’s chapter 2; and 'The Climate of History' (2009) in full. The rest of the 1989 and 2000 books is unread, including chapter 2 itself. He is not presented as a founder. He calls Ranajit Guha 'the founder of the group' (1997) and writes that his 'argument for provincializing Europe follows directly from my involvement in this project' (2000, p. 15). The book’s critique of historicism builds on Guha’s rejection of Hobsbawm’s 'prepolitical' and cites Fabian’s 'denial of coevalness' (pp. 8, 11–15). Contested in period: by Sarkar (1997), by Chandavarkar (1997) and, in a critique aimed mainly at Prakash, by Dirlik (1994). O'Hanlon and Washbrook (1992) criticised the wider post-Orientalist programme, principally Prakash's, without naming him; only their opening page and notes were read. Work after 2000 rests on readings made on 2026-10-19: the 2015 Tanner Lectures, read in part (unpaginated); his introduction and response in The Review of Politics symposium (2022, read in full), with Pitts and Ackerly read in full and Getachew in part; the 2020 anniversary interview, editorial and Hill essay, read in full, and Stråth in part; reviews read in full by Arffman (2022), Staley (2024) and, for The Calling of History, Joshi (2016); Sewell's symposium contribution (2014) in full and Cumings's in part; and the 2013–20 texts with Latour recorded on the Latour entry. The books after 2000 are unread and are known through publisher pages, contents and these readers. The 2008 exchange with Dietze, the 2012, 2017 and 2018 articles, Malm and Hornborg (2014) and Seth (2017) are known from abstracts only; that Malm and Hornborg criticise him by name is his own report. The 2009 essay and its later reception are not evidence for any claim about his work before 2000.

nodes.label: Bryan D. Palmer
nodes.date_label: ‘Most Uncommon Common Men’ 1976 · A Culture in Conflict 1979 · ‘Response to Joan Scott’ 1987 · Descent into Discourse 1990 · E. P. Thompson: Objections and Oppositions 1994 · ‘Radical Reasoning’ 2009
nodes.description: A Canadian historian of labour and the left who took up E. P. Thompson's account of class and culture and later defended historical materialism against the linguistic turn. His first essay in Labour/Le Travailleur (1976) traced artisan culture and restated what he called 'a standard axiom of an emerging social history': 'As a class for itself, the working class was born, not in the factory, but in the workshop'; the critic David Bercuson read his study of Hamilton's skilled workers (1979) as 'echoing E.P. Thompson' (1981). In the International Labor and Working-Class History forum of 1987 he answered Joan Scott's case for reconceiving labour history through language and gender, which on his reading reduced class and its material relations to discourse, while granting, as Ted McCoy (2021) quotes him, that 'to say that language matters is not to say it is all that matters'; and Descent into Discourse (1990) held, as the Marxist reviewer Alex Callinicos quoted it, that 'historical materialism remains the foundation upon which studies of the past must be erected', while granting that discourse theory 'contains insights and guides'. Scott replied that 'class struggle is produced in discourse', a discourse she took to include 'ways of organizing lives, institutions, societies', not words alone, and that there is no choice, 'as Bryan Palmer insists there is, between a focus on class or gender'; Callinicos, broadly sympathetic, suggested that his treatment of class might underestimate 'the objective determinants of subjective action' and noted that he took Thompson and Raymond Williams 'to task for abandoning the metaphor of base and superstructure'. In 2009 he criticised Ian McKay's liberal order as, in his reading, 'a seemingly trans-historical analytic framework' that 'sidesteps the need to confront and elucidate capitalism's changing historical structures'.

nodes.label: The Science Wars
nodes.date_label: Higher Superstition 1994 · Social Text "Science Wars" issue and Sokal's hoax 1996 · The Golem in Physics Today 1996–97 · Impostures intellectuelles 1997 (English 1998) · A House Built on Sand 1998 · Pandora's Hope and Shapin's reply 1999 · Later reading: Latour 2004
nodes.description: A dispute of the mid-1990s in which scientists and philosophers charged science studies with relativism and hostility to science, and sociologists and historians of science answered them. It is taught here as a moment in the reception of science studies: most of the attackers were scientists or philosophers, not historians. Gross and Levitt's Higher Superstition (1994) went after what an SHPS editorial called the "exponents of science studies -- that is, historians, philosophers and sociologists of science", the Edinburgh strong programme among them. Social Text planned a "Science Wars" issue in response; Sokal's parody appeared in it (1996), and his confession attacked "epistemic relativism" in cultural studies. In Physics Today Mermin judged that The Golem showed "what can go wrong if you focus too strongly on the social perspective", and Collins and Pinch replied that many scientists were "scientific fundamentalists". Sokal and Bricmont (1997; English 1998) called the strong programme "either a valid and mildly interesting corrective ... or else a gross and blatant error" and charged Latour with sliding from "Nature's representation" to "Nature". Historians of science answered: Shapin (1999) called the charge of hostility to science "malevolently misinformed", and Latour wrote that science studies had "added reality to science, not withdrawn any from it" (1999).
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Attack: Gross and Levitt, Higher Superstition (1994); Sokal, "Transgressing the Boundaries" and "A Physicist Experiments with Cultural Studies" (1996); Weinberg, "Sokal's Hoax" (1996) and "The Revolution That Didn't Happen" (1998); Mermin's Physics Today columns (1996–97); Sokal and Bricmont, Impostures intellectuelles (1997; Intellectual Impostures, 1998); Koertge, ed., A House Built on Sand (1998). Answers: Social Text 46/47, "Science Wars", ed. Ross (1996); Robbins and Ross (1996); Fish (1996); Collins and Pinch (1996); Wise in Isis (1996); Edge, "The Umpire Strikes Back" (1997); Jardine and Frasca-Spada in SHPS (1997); Schweber (1997); Krige (1998); Beller (1998); Latour, Pandora's Hope (1999); Shapin, "Rarely Pure and Never Simple" (1999). Clarification: Hacking, The Social Construction of What? (1999). Later reading: Latour, "Why Has Critique Run out of Steam?" (2004).
nodes.scope_note: A debate entry about the reception of science studies, measured through its texts. The texts read are listed in the source notes; several central ones were not. Higher Superstition was not read: its words are given only as its in-period readers (Edge, Jardine and Frasca-Spada, Sokal and Bricmont) quote them. Wise's Isis review, the Social Text essays, Latour's Le Monde article of 18 January 1997, most of A House Built on Sand (read only in publisher abstracts), Kitcher's and Hacking's books and The Golem itself were not read. The Jardine and Frasca-Spada editorial is the only source for Latour's Le Monde wording; the same journal later printed an "Apology" by the two editors (1997, unread), so that wording should be checked before it is relied on. Pandora's Hope was read in a retyped copy without book pages. Sokal's 1996 confession named no sociologist of science; his criticism of SSK and Latour dates from 1997. Mermin was a qualified critic who later defended Latour. Jardine and Frasca-Spada criticised both sides and are not drawn as one-way critics. Hacking and Kitcher present themselves as mediators and are not drawn as critics. Haraway and Latour are treated as broadly aligned (editorial decision, 2026-10-14); Haraway is not drawn as a critic of Latour. The 2000 end of the label is a convenience: Latour's 2004 retrospective is cited as a dated later reading, and later collections (The One Culture?, 2001; After the Science Wars, 2001) are named but unread.

representative_people.context: Co-author of Higher Superstition, which opened the dispute. As quoted by its in-period readers, it named the Edinburgh strong programme and Bloor among the targets of "social constructivism" (pp. 25, 52, via Edge). Book unread here.

nodes.label: Carl Berger
nodes.date_label: The Sense of Power 1970 · The Writing of Canadian History 1976; 2nd ed. 1986
nodes.description: A University of Toronto historian of English-Canadian ideas. The Sense of Power (1970) is 'a study in Canadian nationalist thought': against the 'so-called liberal nationalist school', for which imperialism and nationalism added up to 'a struggle between the past and the future', he argued that 'Imperialism was one form of Canadian nationalism', a 'type of awareness of nationality which rested upon a certain understanding of history, the national character, and the national mission'. The Writing of Canadian History (1976; second edition 1986) examines 'aspects of English-Canadian historical thought and literature since the turn of the century' through the 'central teachings' of Wrong, Shortt, Martin, Innis, Lower, Underhill, Creighton and Morton, and treats written history as 'a self-conscious effort to establish the meaning of experience for the present'; he left French-Canadian writing aside because the two language traditions had been 'preoccupied with the backgrounds of two rather different “nations”'. In period, Jacques Monet thought the imperialism thesis 'très difficile, sinon impossible, à réfuter' (1972), while Douglas Cole and Graham Carr held that it over-Canadianized a Britannic movement, Susan Mann Trofimenkoff called his imperialists' nationalism 'decidedly masculine' (1979), Allen Mills found that his account of all Canadian historians as nationalists put 'much too much weight on that over-used term' (1977), and Ronald Rudin rejected his assumption that historians were 'united by their search for the truth' (1997).
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Carl Berger (b. 1939); ed., Imperialism and Nationalism, 1884–1914: A Conflict in Canadian Thought (1969); The Sense of Power: Studies in the Ideas of Canadian Imperialism, 1867–1914 (1970; 2nd ed. 2013, with an introduction by Doug Owram); The Writing of Canadian History: Aspects of English-Canadian Historical Writing, 1900–1970 (1976; 2nd ed., … since 1900, 1986, with a new chapter, 'Tradition and the “New” History'); Science, God, and Nature in Victorian Canada (1983). Readings: Monet (1972); Mills (1977); Terry Cook (1977–78); Trofimenkoff (1979); Carr (1982); Karr (1989); Rudin (1997). Later reading: Owram (2013).
nodes.scope_note: This entry presents the two framework books. Neither could be read continuously: both are borrow-only on the Internet Archive. Berger's own words are quoted from Google Books snippet views (The Sense of Power, 2013 printing with the 1970 pagination: introduction pp. 3, 9–10, conclusion p. 259; The Writing of Canadian History, 1986 edition: both prefaces and pp. 181, 261–262, 289, 298, 312), and are corroborated by in-period reviews read in full: Monet (1972), Mills (1977) and Terry Cook (1977–78). Science, God, and Nature in Victorian Canada (1983) is checked at metadata level only. He is not presented as the originator of the imperialism thesis: Monet notes that Norman Penlington's Canada and Imperialism (1965) had already suggested it. Contested in period: Page, Cole and Nelles (1970, as Monet reports them), Cole (1971), Carr (1982, journal abstract), Karr (1989) on the elite group-biography method, Trofimenkoff (1979) on women, and Rudin (1997) on French-Canadian writing and on the assumption of a common search for truth. No in-period text found here faults The Writing of Canadian History for treating only male historians; Trofimenkoff's critique is of the field. Owram's 2013 introduction is a later reading.

nodes.label: Ramsay Cook
nodes.date_label: “Canadian Centennial Cerebrations” 1967 · The Maple Leaf Forever 1971 · “Regionalism Unmasked” 1983 · The Regenerators 1985 · “Cabbages Not Kings” 1990 · “Identities Are Not Like Hats” 2000
nodes.description: An English-Canadian historian of nationalism, Quebec and Victorian thought. Attacking a nationalist manifesto in the centennial year, he suggested that 'instead of constantly deploring our lack of identity, we should attempt to understand and explain the regional, ethnic and class identities that we do have. It might just be that it is in these limited identities that “Canadianism” is found' (1967, as quoted by Buckner); Careless made 'limited identities' a programme in 1969. Cook did not make region his unit of analysis: reviewing regional syntheses, he doubted 'the existence of the phenomena we have for so long called regions' and judged that 'as a tool of analysis, “regionalism” is a concept whose time has gone' (1983). The Regenerators (1985) read late Victorian social critics as replacing 'man's salvation' with 'a concern for social salvation', so that Christianity became 'less rather than more relevant' (as quoted by Gauvreau); Michael Gauvreau answered in 1991 that the book rests on 'military metaphors' that recent studies had abandoned, and a 1998 review named Cook, with David Marshall, the strongest advocate of the 'secularization thesis'. His lecture 'Cabbages Not Kings' (1990) proposed an ecological reading of contact in which 'Cabbages, at least as much as kings, led to the transformation of the new world'. In the quarrel over national history he called the debate between 'nationalists' and 'limited identitarians' 'arid' (1993), and in 2000 he argued that identities are 'contingent' and 'multiple rather than single'.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Ramsay Cook (1931–2016); Canada and the French-Canadian Question (1966); “Canadian Centennial Cerebrations” (International Journal, 1967); The Maple Leaf Forever: Essays on Nationalism and Politics in Canada (1971); Canada 1896–1921: A Nation Transformed (1974, with Robert Craig Brown); “The Burden of Regionalism” (Acadiensis, 1977); “Regionalism Unmasked” (Acadiensis, 1983); The Regenerators: Social Criticism in Late Victorian English Canada (1985); “Cabbages Not Kings: Towards an Ecological Interpretation of Early Canadian History” (Journal of Canadian Studies, 1990–91); “The New History of Atlantic Canada” (Acadiensis, 1993); “‘Identities Are Not Like Hats’” (Canadian Historical Review, 2000). Readings: Careless (1969); Gaffield (1986); Karr (1989); Gauvreau (1991); Marshall (1993–94); Buckner (2000).
nodes.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-14: three of Cook's Acadiensis review essays in full (1977, 1983, 1993), the opening of the 1967 article (OpenAlex text) and the abstract of his 2000 forum piece. The limited-identities sentence (1967) and the 1970 essay reprinted in The Maple Leaf Forever are known through Buckner's (2000) and Karr's (1989) quotations. The Regenerators is unread: its words appear here as quoted by Gauvreau (1991) and Karr, with Gaffield's 1986 review and the book's contents. 'Cabbages Not Kings' was read for the environment drafts on 2026-10-13 and is not re-read here. Canada and the French-Canadian Question is unread. He is not presented as a founder: Buckner says Cook coined 'limited identities' and Careless popularized it, and Cook wrote in 1995 that the phrase was 'usually attributed to Maurice Careless and I have decided that he is welcome to it!' (quoted by Buckner). Contested in period: Gauvreau (1991) on The Regenerators and on limited identities as a frame that marginalized religion; Karr (1989) on his 'anti-national crusade'; Buckner (2000) on the additive idea of identity he attributes to Cook and Careless. Bliss's 'Privatizing the Mind' (1991–92) is read only in its abstract, which does not name Cook.

nodes.label: J. M. S. Careless
nodes.date_label: “Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History” 1954 · Brown of the Globe 1959–63 · “‘Limited Identities’ in Canada” 1969 · “Limited Identities — Ten Years Later” 1981 · Frontier and Metropolis 1989
nodes.description: A University of Toronto historian of nineteenth-century Canada and biographer of George Brown (Brown of the Globe, 1959–63). 'Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History' (1954) criticised the Canadian historians who had adapted Turner's frontier thesis and proposed instead the study of the metropolis, a city that organizes a wide area 'through control of communications, trade, and finance'; in that view the frontier 'is in the largest sense a dependent', though 'if we reject a frontier determinism we should hardly replace it with a metropolitan determinism'. In 1969 he took up Ramsay Cook's phrase and argued that the Canadian experience must be understood through the 'limited identities of region, culture and class' (as quoted by Buckner, 2000); a decade later he added that 'Metropolitanism is not the antithesis of regionalism' and that limited identities 'should not limit his own perception' (1981). Frontier and Metropolis (1989), based on his 1987 Creighton Lectures, restated both themes. In period, Donald Davis (1985) judged his metropolitan approach 'of only limited usefulness in guiding research', and Phillip Buckner (2000) rejected the view, which he attributed to Careless and Granatstein, of regionalism as 'a construct designed to justify the dismantling of the Canadian state'.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: J. M. S. Careless (1919–2009); “Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History” (Canadian Historical Review, 1954); Brown of the Globe, vol. 1, The Voice of Upper Canada, 1818–1859 (1959) and vol. 2, Statesman of Confederation, 1860–1880 (1963); “‘Limited Identities’ in Canada” (Canadian Historical Review, 1969); “Limited Identities — Ten Years Later” (Manitoba History, 1981); Frontier and Metropolis: Regions, Cities, and Identities in Canada before 1914 (1989). Readings: Davis (1985); Szostak (1990); Irwin (1997); Buckner (2000).
nodes.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-14: the 1954 article in full (Canadian Historical Review 35:1, pp. 1–21, in an Internet Archive scan of the issue); the 1979 Jackson lecture 'Limited Identities — Ten Years Later' in full (Manitoba History no. 1, 1981, web text without page numbers); Davis (Urban History Review, 1985, pp. 95–113) in full; Szostak's review of Frontier and Metropolis (Journal of Economic History, 1990, pp. 499–501) in full; and Buckner (Acadiensis, 2000), pp. 4–10. The 1969 article is unread here: its wording is taken from Buckner's quotations and from Careless's own quotation of its last page in 1981. Frontier and Metropolis and Brown of the Globe are unread (catalogue records; the book's content through Szostak's review). He is not presented as the originator of either idea. In 1954 he credits metropolitanism to Lower, to Masters's Rise of Toronto (1947) and its source in N. S. B. Gras, and to the Laurentian school of Innis and Creighton (pp. 16–17); Davis (1985, p. 97) notes that Lower discussed metropolitanism 'some eight years before'. He wrote in 1981 that he 'did not invent the term “limited identity”' but acquired it from Ramsay Cook, so that his 1969 article 'was thus essentially a commentary on his initial idea'; Cook's coinage belongs to Cook's entry. Contested in period: by W. L. Morton and S. D. Clark (both as quoted by Davis), by Davis (1985), by Szostak (1990), by Irwin (1997, abstract) and by Buckner (2000). Michael Bliss (1991–92) is not recorded as a critic of Careless: Buckner (2000, p. 9) pairs Bliss's fragmentation charge with Careless's own later worry.

nodes.label: Donald Creighton
nodes.date_label: The Commercial Empire of the St. Lawrence 1937 · Dominion of the North 1944 · John A. Macdonald 1952, 1955 · CHA presidential address 1957 · “The Decline and Fall of the Empire of the St. Lawrence” 1969 · Canada’s First Century 1970
nodes.description: A Toronto historian whose The Commercial Empire of the St. Lawrence (1937) built Canadian history around the one river system 'that leads from the Atlantic Seaboard to the heart of the continent', which inspired Canadians 'to build a great territorial empire, both commercial and political, in the western interior' (his own restatement of 1969); Dominion of the North (1944) calls the river 'the natural basis of a great commercial empire' and beaver fur 'the first staple of the St. Lawrence commercial system'. His two-volume John A. Macdonald (1952, 1955) completed what he called 'a trilogy on one theme'; in 1969 he accepted 'the parentage of an idea' others called 'the Laurentian interpretation of Canadian history', but rejected the story that his first book was 'the fruit of my friendship with Harold Innis'. As president of the Canadian Historical Association (1957) he attacked the Liberal 'Authorized Version' of Canadian history and the imported 'Marxian doctrine of the class struggle' and 'Frontier thesis', and in 1969 he traced the 'decline and fall' of the Empire of the St. Lawrence and of the Canada built on it, calling official bilingualism and a special position for Quebec 'a repudiation of the intentions of the Fathers of Confederation'. Contested in period: Michel Brunet (1953) found the Macdonald biography full of 'nombreux préjugés', Guy Frégault (1955) asked 'où sont les Canadiens français dans tout cela ?', and W. L. Morton, as Davis (1985) reports him, held that the metropolitan view he associated with Creighton seemed 'necessarily to minimize the importance of the hinterland'. From the late 1960s the national frame the Laurentian narrative supported gave way to regional history and 'limited identities' (Buckner, 2000).
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Donald Creighton (1902–1979); The Commercial Empire of the St. Lawrence, 1760–1850 (1937; reissued as The Empire of the St. Lawrence, 1956); Dominion of the North: A History of Canada (1944); John A. Macdonald: The Young Politician (1952) and The Old Chieftain (1955); Presidential Address, Canadian Historical Association (1957); Harold Adams Innis: Portrait of a Scholar (1957); “The Decline and Fall of the Empire of the St. Lawrence” (1969); Canada’s First Century, 1867–1967 (1970). Readings: Heaton (1938); Brunet (1953); Frégault (1955); Woodcock (1979); Ouellet (1984); Davis (1985); Salmon (1997); Buckner (2000).
nodes.scope_note: This entry presents the Laurentian narrative and Creighton's later nationalism. Read on 2026-10-14: his 1957 presidential address (pp. 1–12) and his 1969 lecture 'The Decline and Fall of the Empire of the St. Lawrence' (pp. 14–25), both in full from page images; Dominion of the North (1944) at its contents and selected pages (pp. 21, 24–25, 166, 270, 272, 298, 419, 505–507) in an open Internet Archive copy. The Commercial Empire of the St. Lawrence (1937) itself is unread: the Internet Archive copies are borrow-only, and its argument is checked through the 1944 book, his own 1969 retrospect (labelled as such) and the first page of Herbert Heaton's 1938 review. He is not presented as the founder of a school: in 1969 he reported that others regarded the 1937 phrase as 'the inspiration, at least in part, of a new school' and the 'genesis' of 'the Laurentian interpretation', and said only that he had 'no wish to disavow the parentage of an idea'. The Innis lineage is recorded as contested: readers from Woodcock (1979) and Ouellet (1984) to Salmon (1997) tie the book to Innis's staple studies, while Creighton said the subject was suggested by W. P. M. Kennedy, 'not by Harold Innis, whom I barely knew at the time'. The 1957 and 1969 texts are polemics; their judgements of Mackenzie King, Quebec and bilingualism are recorded as his claims, not adopted. Morton's 'Clio in Canada' (1946) and his later hinterland critique are known here only through Davis (1985); Careless's 'Frontierism, Metropolitanism' (1954), Berger's chapter on Creighton (1976), Canada's First Century (1970) and the Innis biography (1957) are unread (catalogue or review level only).

nodes.label: Joy Parr
nodes.date_label: Labouring Children 1980 · 'Nature and Hierarchy' 1985 · The Gender of Breadwinners 1990 · 'Gender History and Historical Practice' 1995 · Domestic Goods 1999 · Sensing Changes 2010
nodes.description: A Canadian historian of work, gender, childhood, consumption and the environment. In 1985 she wrote that what set women and children apart as historical subjects was not nature but 'proximity to power', and asked historians to 'allow as a possibility that gender/sex hierarchies and class hierarchies function simultaneously, each according to its own logic, often in conflict'. The Gender of Breadwinners (1990) tested this in two Ontario towns, Paris, a knitting-mill town where most wage earners were women, and Hanover, a furniture town where most were men; reviewers quote it rejecting 'an ahistorical hierarchy of oppressions' and treating 'class/gender, male/female, market/nonmarket, public/private' as pairs whose meanings 'are multiple and mutable'. In the Left History exchange of 1995–96 Iacovetta and Kealey called her 'a major figure in the field' of gender history, while Sangster criticised the tie her 1995 essay drew between gender history and 'the post-structuralist premise that identities were made in relationships'; the labour historian Craig Heron praised the book but found that it had 'suppressed the impact of class' in a 1949 strike. Labouring Children (1980) grew from her Yale thesis on British child immigrants; later books turned to postwar household goods (Domestic Goods, 1999) and to sensory histories of megaprojects and environmental change (Sensing Changes, 2010).
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Joy Parr (1949–2024); PhD Yale 1977 ('The Home Children: British Juvenile Immigrants to Canada, 1868–1924'); Labouring Children: British Immigrant Apprentices to Canada, 1869–1924 (1980); Childhood and Family in Canadian History (ed., 1982); “Nature and Hierarchy: Reflections on Writing the History of Women and Children” (Atlantis, 1985); “Disaggregating the Sexual Division of Labour” (CSSH, 1988); The Gender of Breadwinners: Women, Men, and Change in Two Industrial Towns, 1880–1950 (1990); “Gender History and Historical Practice” (CHR, 1995; reprinted in Gender and History in Canada, ed. with Mark Rosenfeld, 1996); “Household Choices as Politics and Pleasure in 1950s Canada” (ILWCH, 1999); Domestic Goods: The Material, the Moral, and the Economic in the Postwar Years (1999). After 2000: “Smells Like?” (Environmental History, 2006); Sensing Changes: Technologies, Environments, and the Everyday, 1953–2003 (2010). Readings: Drystek (1980); Heron, Guildford, Scheinberg and Dennis (1991); Bertaux (1992); Benson (1993); the Left History exchange (Sangster 1995, 1996; Dubinsky and Marks 1996; Iacovetta and Kealey 1996); Brush (2000); Owram (2001); Jackson and Rumiel (2011).
nodes.scope_note: Her own words are read in 'Nature and Hierarchy' (Atlantis, 1985, pp. 39–44, in full), the first-page extract of the 1988 CSSH article and the abstract of the 1999 ILWCH article. Her books are not read here: The Gender of Breadwinners, Domestic Goods and Sensing Changes are quoted only as their reviewers quote them, with the reviewers' page references, and the 1995 CHR essay only as Iacovetta and Kealey (1996) and Sangster (1996) quote it. In-period reviews read in full: Drystek (1980), Heron (CHR, 1991), Guildford (Atlantis, 1991), Scheinberg (Archivaria, 1991), Dennis (EcHR, 1991), Bertaux (JEH, 1992), Benson (JAH, 1993), Brush (EH.NET, 2000); later reception: Owram (BC Studies, 2001); the four Left History papers of 1995–96 are read in full. She is not presented as a founder: her 1985 essay places itself among 'a good many others' asking for the change, and the Canadian gender-history debate also turned on Pierson (1991) and Scott. The 1995 CHR essay appeared in an issue of historiographical essays, not in a CHR exchange; the exchange that took it up was in Left History. The environmental work dates from 2006–10 and is used only for the environment edge; a 2026 CHR forum on The Gender of Breadwinners is a later reading.

nodes.label: Mariana Valverde
nodes.date_label: “The Struggles of the Immoral” (with Weir) 1988 · The Age of Light, Soap, and Water 1991 · “Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State” 1992 · Diseases of the Will 1998 · Law’s Dream of a Common Knowledge 2003
nodes.description: A sociologist and criminologist, not a historian by training (PhD in social and political thought, York, 1982; University of Toronto Centre of Criminology from 1993); historians read her study of social purity in English Canada as a statement of moral regulation. The Age of Light, Soap, and Water (1991) follows reformers who sought 'to reshape the ethical subjectivity of both immigrants and native-born Canadians' and argues that their movements 'helped to shape the bourgeoisie, which led the movements, as well as the working class'; her notes trace the term to Corrigan and Sayer's The Great Arch but 'restrict the term to mean the formation of ethical subjectivity', and she held, as 'Foucault and his followers have pointed out', that 'the state has no monopoly on moral regulation'. In 1992 she endorsed Mitchell Dean's argument that classical liberalism was 'a particular system of economic, social, and moral regulation' and faulted Jean-Marie Fecteau's account of relief institutions as means of class control as 'a rather functionalist formulation'. Historians used and contested the frame: Tina Loo asked that it 'address Christianity and certainly Protestantism more fully, even if only to dismiss its importance' (1992), Donald Wright found that the reformers' silent audiences gave 'the impression of top-down social control, precisely what Valverde sought to avoid' (1995), and Nancy Christie and Michael Gauvreau wrote that she and Doug Owram 'have adhered to a caricature of the antiquated and esoteric Victorian theologue to excise the churches from “progressive” currents of modern thought and social action' (1996). Later books turn to alcohol and the will (Diseases of the Will, 1998) and to law (Law's Dream of a Common Knowledge, 2003).
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Mariana Valverde (b. 1955); “The Struggles of the Immoral: Preliminary Remarks on Moral Regulation” (with Lorna Weir, Resources for Feminist Research, 1988); “Poststructuralist Gender Historians: Are We Those Names?” (Labour/Le Travail, 1990); The Age of Light, Soap, and Water: Moral Reform in English Canada, 1885–1925 (1991; reissued 2008 with a new introduction); “Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State” (Labour/Le Travail, 1992); Gender Conflicts (ed. with Franca Iacovetta, 1992); Studies in Moral Regulation (ed., 1994); “Deconstructive Marxism” (Labour/Le Travail, 1995); Diseases of the Will: Alcohol and the Dilemmas of Freedom (1998). After 2000: Law’s Dream of a Common Knowledge (2003); “Introduction to the 2008 Edition” of The Age of Light, Soap, and Water. In-period readings: Loo, Dehli and McCormick (reviews, 1992); Wright (1995); Christie and Gauvreau (1996); Strange and Loo, Making Good (1997); Hunt (1997, 1999).
nodes.scope_note: Read on 2026-10-14: her review essays 'Poststructuralist Gender Historians' (1990) and 'Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State' (1992) in full, and 'Deconstructive Marxism' (1995) at pp. 329–332; four in-period reviews or review essays of The Age of Light, Soap, and Water in full (Loo 1992, Dehli 1992, McCormick 1992) or in their Valverde section (Wright 1995, pp. 122–126). The book itself is known here only through those reviewers' quotations and through search-within snippets of the 2008 reissue, which keeps the 1991 pagination for the original text (checked: pp. 15, 17, 165 and 166 match the 1992 reviewers' page references; the 1991 preface's p. 9 appears as p. ix). Christie and Gauvreau (1996), Strange and Loo (1997), Hunt (1999) and Diseases of the Will (1998) are known only through such snippets. 'The Struggles of the Immoral' (1988, with Lorna Weir) is unread. She is not presented as the originator of moral regulation: Corrigan (1981) and Corrigan and Sayer (1985) precede her, and she credits their theorization as 'influential here' while finding that it obscures 'the agencies of regulation internal to civil society'. She called herself a sociologist working between disciplines; Loo (1992) and Wright (1995) read her that way, and the 2008 introduction, a later reading, says that 'no history department in Canada would ever hire me'. The 2003 book is cited at title level only; the 2008 introduction is a later reading and carries no claim about the 1990s.

nodes.label: Edward Said
nodes.date_label: Orientalism 1978 · The Question of Palestine 1979 · Covering Islam 1981 · “Orientalism Reconsidered” 1985 · Culture and Imperialism 1993
nodes.description: A Palestinian-American literary critic whose Orientalism (1978) reads European writing on 'the Orient' as 'a Western style for dominating, restructuring, and having authority over the Orient': a discourse in Foucault's sense, durable through what Gramsci called hegemony, though he held, 'unlike Michel Foucault', to 'the determining imprint of individual writers' and denied that the Orient was 'a creation with no corresponding reality'. The Question of Palestine (1979) examined 'Zionism from the Standpoint of Its Victims', Covering Islam (1981) took up American reporting on Islam, and 'Orientalism Reconsidered' (1985) traced Orientalism to historicism, including the 'science of world history'. Culture and Imperialism (1993) added what Orientalism had 'left out', resistance to empire, and proposed reading the metropolitan canon 'contrapuntally, with a simultaneous awareness both of the metropolitan history that is narrated and of those other histories against which (and together with which) the dominating discourse acts'. In period, Bernard Lewis charged him with 'very arbitrary decisions' of scope, and Said replied in their 1982 exchange that it was 'idiotic to say that Orientalism is a conspiracy'; Sadik al-'Azm called his account of Marx 'a travesty' (1981); and a 1996 review summarised feminist critics as holding that critics of Orientalism 'continue to write out gender'.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Edward W. Said (1935–2003); Orientalism (1978); The Question of Palestine (1979); Covering Islam (1981); “Orientalism Reconsidered” (Cultural Critique, 1985); foreword to Selected Subaltern Studies (1988); Culture and Imperialism (1993). Readings: Sadik Jalal al-'Azm, “Orientalism and Orientalism in Reverse” (1981); Bernard Lewis, “The Question of Orientalism” and the Said–Lewis exchange (New York Review of Books, 1982); Cheryl McEwan on Reina Lewis, Gendering Orientalism (1996). Later: Robert Irwin, Dangerous Knowledge (2006).
nodes.scope_note: A literary critic, not a historian; the entry is for a framework historians meet across fields. It rests on texts read on 2026-10-14: Orientalism in the 1978 Pantheon first edition (introduction pp. 1–28 in full; pp. 94, 153–156, 204 and 321 for passages used); The Question of Palestine (1980 Vintage reprint of the 1979 book; pp. 56–59 and 74–76); the Covering Islam introduction (p. ix); 'Orientalism Reconsidered' (1985) in full; the foreword to Selected Subaltern Studies (1988, pp. v–x) in full; and Culture and Imperialism (1993 Knopf first edition; introduction pp. xii–xiv and xxv, and pp. 41–42, 51, 66, 240–245, 251 and 278). Not read: 'Traveling Theory' (The World, the Text, and the Critic, 1983) and 'Foucault and the Imagination of Power' (1986), both lending-only or closed here; his critique of Foucault is taken from Culture and Imperialism, which cites the 1986 essay as 'my critique'. He is not presented as a founder: a 1992 critique calls his blend of themes 'virtually a paradigm for a new generation of historians and anthropologists' (O'Hanlon and Washbrook, first page only) and a 1996 review calls Orientalism 'undoubtedly' the inspiration behind critical interest in 'empire, knowledge and power' (McEwan); these are readers' judgements. Contested in period by Lewis (1982) and al-'Azm (1981), both read; James Clifford's review (History and Theory, 1980), Lata Mani and Ruth Frankenberg (Economy and Society, 1985), Dennis Porter (1983) and Aijaz Ahmad (1991–92) are recorded but were not read: Porter is known here from Said's 1985 reply, Ahmad from Robert Irwin's later account (2006), Reina Lewis (1996) from McEwan's review. No post-2000 work by Said is used; Irwin (2006) is a labelled later reading.

nodes.label: Ranajit Guha
nodes.date_label: A Rule of Property for Bengal 1963 · “On Some Aspects of the Historiography of Colonial India” 1982 · Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency 1983 · “The Prose of Counter-Insurgency” 1983 · “Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography” 1989 (book 1997) · History at the Limit of World-History 2002
nodes.description: A historian of colonial India, who taught at Sussex and the Australian National University and edited Subaltern Studies from its first volume (1982) until he left the editorial team in 1988. The opening statement holds that the historiography of Indian nationalism 'has for a long time been dominated by elitism—colonialist elitism and bourgeois-nationalist elitism', and that it leaves out 'the politics of the people', 'an autonomous domain' that 'neither originated from elite politics nor did its existence depend on the latter', while allowing 'a great deal of overlap' between the two (1982). Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency (1983) attributes 'a consciousness' to the rebel peasant, holds that Hobsbawm's 'pre-political' 'helps little in understanding the experience of colonial India', and reads that consciousness through the records of counter-insurgency; 'The Prose of Counter-Insurgency' (1983) finds colonial, nationalist and radical histories alike making the rebel 'only a contingent element in another history with another subject'. 'Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography' (1989; book 1997) defines hegemony, against 'the Gramscian juxtaposition of domination and hegemony', as dominance in which 'Persuasion (P) outweighs Coercion (C)', and argues that colonial dominance had 'quite erroneously been endowed with hegemony'. In period, Spivak (1985) read the recovery of subaltern consciousness as 'a strategic use of positivist essentialism', O'Hanlon (1988) found 'the classic figure of Western humanism' readmitted 'in the figure of the subaltern himself', Bayly (1988) found that the approach sometimes seemed to postulate an 'unchanging peasantry', and Sarkar (1997) an 'unnoticed drift' towards nationalist positions 'even in Guha's initial formulation of the project'. His first book, A Rule of Property for Bengal (1963), traced the Permanent Settlement to the mercantilist, physiocratic and classical political economy of East India Company officials, in Gurminder Bhambra’s reading (2024), which faults it for leaving the colonial context aside. Reviewing Dominance without Hegemony, Amalendu Chakraborty (2000) found the subalterns’ own voices missing from what he called “a mere armchair ideological ‘discourse’”. After 2000, History at the Limit of World-History (2002), lectures given at Columbia’s Italian Academy, takes Hegel’s World-history to task as a statist frame and asks historians to learn from literature the “historicality” of everyday life, in its reviewers’ accounts; Guha’s claim, as Bernardo Michael quotes it, is that World-History reached India “as an instrument of the East India Company’s colonial project”. Michael welcomed the turn to everyday life but warned that “losing sight of the state ... might mean the loss of it as an object of critique”; he also found the argument “mostly confined to the conceptual level”, without showing how Hegel’s ideas became colonial practice (2004). Dipesh Chakrabarty later called the book “his farewell to the discipline of history”, after which Guha wrote in Bengali (2024). Vivek Chibber’s Postcolonial Theory and the Specter of Capital (2013) made Dominance without Hegemony a central target, arguing that its contrast between Indian and European bourgeoisies rests on “a highly mythologized story about the great Bourgeois revolutions”; William Sewell agreed that Guha’s portrayal of the English and French revolutions was “standard-issue orthodox Marxism”, while Partha Chatterjee, as Chibber reports him, denied that Guha made claims about those revolutions at all (2013–14).
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Ranajit Guha (1923–2023); A Rule of Property for Bengal: An Essay on the Idea of Permanent Settlement (Paris: Mouton, 1963); Preface and “On Some Aspects of the Historiography of Colonial India”, Subaltern Studies I (1982); Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency in Colonial India (Delhi, 1983); “The Prose of Counter-Insurgency”, Subaltern Studies II (1983); “Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography”, Subaltern Studies VI (1989), and Dominance without Hegemony: History and Power in Colonial India (1997); Selected Subaltern Studies, edited with Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak (1988). After 2000: History at the Limit of World-History (Columbia University Press, 2002). Readings: Spivak (1985); O'Hanlon (1988); Bayly (1988); Sarkar (1997); Chakraborty (2000); Chakrabarty (2000); Michael (2004); Chibber (2013–14) and the Journal of World-Systems Research symposium, with Sewell, Steinmetz and Cumings (2014); Holmwood, Bhambra and Seth (2024); Chakrabarty (2024).
nodes.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-14: the Subaltern Studies I preface and opening statement in the Selected Subaltern Studies reprint (1988, pp. 35–44); the introduction of Elementary Aspects (pp. 1–17), its bibliography and pp. 89–90; 'The Prose of Counter-Insurgency' (Subaltern Studies II, 1983, pp. 1–42) in full; and 'Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography' (Subaltern Studies VI, 1989), pp. 210–215, 227–233, 276–277, 291–292 and 299–303. The 1963 and 1997 books are unread; they are known here from metadata, later quotation and the reviews added in revision 1.151. The rest of Elementary Aspects and of the 1989 essay is unread. He is not presented as the founder of a field. In period, Chakrabarty called him 'the founder of the group' (1997) and James C. Scott wrote that Elementary Aspects 'became, in effect, the founding document' of 'the Subaltern Studies School', while finding 'school' too rigid a term (1999); his own 1982 statement claims 'no more than to try and indicate an orientation'. Contested in period by Spivak (1985, a reading from within the project), O'Hanlon (1988), Bayly (1988) and Sarkar (1997); Javeed Alam's Marxist critique (Social Scientist, 1983) is known only through O'Hanlon and is unread. Vinay Bahl (1997) is unread. Chakrabarty's 2000 account of the project is a member's later reading and carries no edge alone. Not Ramachandra Guha, the environmental historian, who has a separate people record. Revision 1.151 adds readings made on 2026-10-19: Michael's review of History at the Limit of World-History (2004, in full) and the publisher's description; Chakraborty's review of Dominance without Hegemony (2000, in full); Chibber's 2014 response to Chatterjee (in part) and the 2014 Journal of World-Systems Research symposium (Hung and Sewell in full; Steinmetz, Cumings and Chibber's reply in part); the 2024 Discover Society remembrance (Holmwood, Bhambra and Seth, in full); and Chakrabarty's obituary for the Australian Academy of the Humanities (2024, in full). History at the Limit of World-History, A Rule of Property and Chibber's book are unread; their arguments are given as these readers state them. Chatterjee's 2013 reply to Chibber is known only through Chibber. Guha's Bengali writings after 2000 are not identified here; Chakrabarty mentions a literary prize without naming it. His death (28 April 2023) is recorded in the obituary sources, not as a timeline event.

nodes.label: Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak
nodes.date_label: Of Grammatology (translation) 1976 · “Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography” 1985 · “Three Women’s Texts” 1985 · “Can the Subaltern Speak?” 1988 · A Critique of Postcolonial Reason 1999 · Death of a Discipline 2003 · “Righting Wrongs” 2004 · An Aesthetic Education 2012
nodes.description: A literary theorist and the translator of Derrida’s Of Grammatology (1976), whose essays on colonial India became reference points for historians. In ‘Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography’ (1985) she read the collective ‘from within but against the grain’, proposing that its recovery of subaltern consciousness be read ‘as a strategic use of positivist essentialism in a scrupulously visible political interest’, and argued that it overlooked ‘how important the concept-metaphor woman is’ to its own discourse. ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ (1988) separates representation as ‘speaking for’ from ‘re-presentation’, argues that in Foucault and Deleuze’s conversation intellectuals, ‘representing them, ... represent themselves as transparent’, and reads the British abolition of sati through the sentence ‘White men are saving brown women from brown men’, set against the nativist ‘The women actually wanted to die’: between them ‘One never encounters the testimony of the women’s voice-consciousness.’ She later called the essay’s closing ‘the subaltern cannot speak!’ ‘an inadvisable remark’ (1999). In period, Gyan Prakash (1992) held that she ‘very correctly marks the silencing of the subaltern woman’ as a limit of historical understanding, Rosalind O’Hanlon (1988) urged hesitation ‘before accepting’ her proposal to re-inscribe the series’ strategy ‘as a strategy for our times’, and Terry Eagleton (1999), crediting the book with addressing ‘the economic realities which too many post-colonial critics culturalise away’, found her Critique ‘too well-mannered, as well as too episodic’ and ‘too deeply invested in feminism and post-colonialism to launch a full-scale socialist critique of these currents’. After 2000 her major books addressed comparative literature and the teaching of the humanities. Her Wellek Library Lectures (2000) were published as Death of a Discipline (2003), which in Ferial Ghazoul’s reading proposes to “yoke Comparative Literature with Area Studies” and sets planetarity against globalization, defined, as Ghazoul quotes it, as “the imposition of the same system of exchange everywhere” (2003). Alfred López granted her “cogent and necessary arguments for comparative literature as a corrective supplement to ‘the apparitions of Cultural and Ethnic Studies’” but found that her planetarity “comes off as a rather traditional sounding humanism” (2004). A 2002 Interventions forum on A Critique of Postcolonial Reason included Ritu Birla’s essay, whose abstract (the essay is unread) reads the book’s chapter on history for the limits of history writing, “the selective production of the archive” and “the supplementary relationship of literature and history”. In “Righting Wrongs” (2004) she defined the subaltern as “those removed from lines of social mobility” and asked that human-rights work be supplemented by an education of the humanities. Shahidha Bari reads An Aesthetic Education in the Era of Globalization (2012), twenty-five essays spanning twenty-three years, as centred on teaching (“teacher” is the label Spivak “most readily reaches for in this book”) and on renewed attention to “how to hear the subaltern speak”; Rosalie Siemon Lochner, in the part of her review read, reports that its introduction argues for a “productive undoing” of Enlightenment aesthetics that trains the imagination for “learning to live with contradictory instructions” (2013). Two historians read here were critical: Richard Eaton named her 1985 reading of Subaltern Studies as one hinge of a turn to literary criticism whose costs, he argued, outweighed its gains (2000), and Arik Moran, rereading the Sirmur records behind her 1985 History and Theory essay, found “profound discrepancies” between her reading and the rani’s position (2014). She reviewed Vivek Chibber’s critique of postcolonial theory (2014); as his publisher reports, she wrote that she had “no foothold in this book except as an object of mockery”. She received the Kyoto Prize (2012), whose citation credits her with “an influence on historical studies”, and the Holberg Prize (2025).
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak (b. 1942); translator’s preface to Jacques Derrida, Of Grammatology (1976); “Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography” (Subaltern Studies IV, 1985; introduction to Selected Subaltern Studies, 1988); “Three Women’s Texts and a Critique of Imperialism” (Critical Inquiry, 1985); “Can the Subaltern Speak?” (in Nelson and Grossberg, eds., Marxism and the Interpretation of Culture, 1988; revised in A Critique of Postcolonial Reason, 1999); “The New Subaltern: A Silent Interview” (2000). “The Rani of Sirmur: An Essay in Reading the Archives” (History and Theory, 1985); Selected Subaltern Studies, edited with Ranajit Guha (1988). After 2000: Death of a Discipline (Wellek Library Lectures 2000; 2003); “Righting Wrongs” (2004); Other Asias (2008); An Aesthetic Education in the Era of Globalization (2012); review of Chibber (2014). Readings: O’Hanlon (1988); Chakrabarty (1992); Prakash (1992); Sarkar (1994); Pandey (1995); Eagleton (1999); Eaton (2000); Ghazoul (2003); López (2004); Chatterjee (2010); Bari (2012); Lochner (2013); Moran (2014).
nodes.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-14: ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ in the 1988 text as reprinted in Williams and Chrisman, Colonial Discourse and Post-Colonial Theory (1993; pp. 66–111, opening abridged), with page numbers of that reprint; two 1988 page anchors (p. 277 and p. 308) come from Chakrabarty (1992, n. 48) and Sunder Rajan (2010). The 1999 revision was read in Morris’s 2010 reprint, which has no page numbers. ‘Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography’ was read in Subaltern Studies IV (1985), pp. 330–363, in full; ‘Three Women’s Texts’ pp. 243–245; the translator’s preface to Of Grammatology at p. lxxvii of the 1997 corrected edition. She is a literary critic, not a historian, and is not presented as a founder of postcolonial studies; she joined the Subaltern Studies editorial collective in the 1990s (Chaturvedi gives Subaltern Studies IX, 1996; Chatterjee recalls 1993) and in 2000 called herself ‘a sometime member’. Benita Parry’s in-period critique (Oxford Literary Review, 1987), Aijaz Ahmad’s In Theory (1992) and Lata Mani’s work on sati (1987, 1998) were not read; Ahmad appears only through Eagleton’s report of her contrast with him. Chatterjee (2010) is a later reading by a member of the collective and carries no in-period claim. Later work, added in revision 1.151 from readings made on 2026-10-19: “Righting Wrongs” (2004) was read in part and her Holberg acceptance speech (2025) in full; Eaton (2000, pp. 57–61, 77–78), Moran (2014, in part), Ghazoul (2003), López (2004) and Bari (2012) were read, and Lochner's review (2013) only in the publisher's excerpt of its first pages. The 2002 Interventions forum is known from abstracts only. Death of a Discipline, Other Asias and An Aesthetic Education are unread and appear only through named reviewers and publisher pages. “The Rani of Sirmur” (1985) is known through Moran and metadata. Her 2014 review of Chibber and his reply are known only from their opening lines and from Verso’s quotations. Historians’ reception after 2000 in what was read is critical (Eaton, Moran) or bounded (Roosa); the prize citations are the prize bodies’ judgements.

nodes.label: Fernand Ouellet
nodes.date_label: “La crise agricole dans le Bas-Canada” (with Jean Hamelin) 1962 · Histoire économique et sociale du Québec, 1760–1850 1966 · Éléments d’histoire sociale du Bas-Canada 1972 · Le Bas-Canada, 1791–1840 1976 (English adaptation 1980) · “Le mythe de « l’habitant sensible au marché »” 1976 · “La modernisation de l’historiographie” 1985
nodes.description: A Laval historian whose economic and social history of Quebec, in a conjunctural idiom whose debt to Labrousse and Chaunu he acknowledged (as Savard reports), made an agricultural crisis the hinge of Lower Canadian history: with Jean Hamelin he argued in 1962 that after 1802 'la tendance majeure se renverse' and that 'la révolution de 1837-38 apparaît-elle, en grande partie, comme une réponse détournée aux problèmes posés par l'action conjointe des tensions démographiques et de la crise agricole', while adding that the crisis was not 'le seul moteur' of those years. The explanation joined prices and population to mentalities: the crisis revealed 'deux entités culturelles' with 'une grande disparité dans leur degré d'évolution' (1962), and in 1976 he held that the habitant who had adapted to the export market before 1802 then 'se durcit et résiste aux pressions en faveur de la rénovation du système agricole'. Contested in period: Gilles Paquet and Jean-Pierre Wallot (1972) found that, 'comme la plupart de ses prédécesseurs', he painted the habitants as 'désespérément embourbés dans des traditions routinières', and judged the thesis 'irrecevable'; Pierre Tousignant (1980) wrote that the Ouellet of the 1966 book 'faisait écho aux vieux préjugés de l'historiographie canadienne-anglaise', and that in the 1976 synthesis, where the 'retard des mentalités' no longer stood 'au premier plan', there was 'une notable amélioration'; Allan Greer (1981) answered that blaming the habitants for their predicament 'would be adding ideological insult to economic injury'. In 1985 he surveyed the turn of Quebec historiography to social history, reading the Montreal school's Conquest thesis, Séguin's 'décapitation' of the national élite, and its later softening as nationalist schemes.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Fernand Ouellet (1926–2021); with Jean Hamelin, “La crise agricole dans le Bas-Canada, 1802–1837” (1962); Histoire économique et sociale du Québec, 1760–1850: structures et conjoncture (1966, preface by Robert Mandrou); Éléments d’histoire sociale du Bas-Canada (1972); Le Bas-Canada, 1791–1840: changements structuraux et crise (1976; English adaptation Lower Canada, 1791–1840: Social Change and Nationalism, 1980); “Le mythe de « l’habitant sensible au marché »” (1976); “La modernisation de l’historiographie et l’émergence de l’histoire sociale” (1985). Critics and readers: Paquet and Wallot (1972); Le Goff (1974); Tousignant (1980); Greer (1981, 1993); Dessureault (1998); Cardinal (1999); Savard (1974); Bouchard (1990); Rudin (1995).
nodes.scope_note: This entry presents the agricultural-crisis and mentalities explanation of Lower Canada and Ouellet's later account of Quebec historiography. Read on 2026-10-14: the 1962 article with Hamelin (pp. 17–33), his 1976 reply to his critics (pp. 115–132) and his 1985 survey (pp. 11–29, 38, 47, 51–52, 64–68), all in full or in the parts named, from Érudit page images. His books (1966, 1972, 1976) are unread; their words appear only as Paquet and Wallot (1972) and Tousignant (1980) quote them, labelled so. He is not presented as the founder of social history in Quebec: Bouchard (1990, ¶13) says Ouellet and Hamelin 'avec quelques autres, ont introduit ici l'histoire sociale'. Le Goff's review of the controversy (1974) and Paquet and Wallot's CHR reply (1975) are unread; Ouellet reports that Le Goff concluded for a crisis 'dès le début du XIXe siècle'. Greer's Patriots and the People (1993) is unread; its relation to Ouellet is given in reviewers' words (Dessureault 1998, Cardinal 1999), not as Greer's. Ouellet's 1995 review essay on Greer (Histoire sociale) could not be reached. Judgements on French Canadians, the Patriotes and nationalism quoted here are his claims, not adopted.

nodes.label: Gregory S. Kealey
nodes.date_label: ‘The Honest Workingman’ 1976 · ‘The Working Class in Recent Canadian Historical Writing’ 1978 · Toronto Workers Respond to Industrial Capitalism 1980 · ‘Prospects in the 1980s’ 1981 · Dreaming of What Might Be (with Palmer) 1982 · ‘1919: The Canadian Labour Revolt’ 1984 · Class, Gender, and Region 1988 · RCMP Security Bulletins (with Whitaker) 1989–97 · Spying on Canadians 2017
nodes.description: A Canadian historian of the working class, and later of political policing, who argued for putting class at the centre of Canadian history. Of Toronto's craftsmen he wrote that 'Skilled workers in the nineteenth century exercised far more power than we have previously realized', amounting to 'a high degree of workers' control of production' (1976); in 1981 he held that 'it is now necessary to locate class conflict and class struggle at the centre of modern Canadian history', and he criticised the regional turn, under which 'Canadian historians have come to believe everything was different everywhere', as he had criticised the 'so-called "limited identities"' in 1978. David Brody, reviewing Toronto Workers Respond to Industrial Capitalism (1980), found it marked by 'what might be termed the Gutman school' and a useful foundation, but judged that Kealey had 'overreached himself' in its interpretation; Bettina Bradbury (1987) faulted him and Bryan Palmer for partially dismissing a Knights of Labor editor's picture of the ideal working-class wife as 'crude moralizing', and Joan Sangster (2000) found in both men's early books 'a proclivity to centre on skilled male workers and their actions in the public sphere'. From the late 1980s he edited the RCMP's security bulletins with Reg Whitaker and studied state surveillance of labour and the left, concluding that 'For the RCMP the Cold War began in 1919, not in 1946' (1992).
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Gregory S. Kealey (b. 1948); with Russell Hann, Linda Kealey and Peter Warrian, Primary Sources in Canadian Working Class History, 1860–1930 (1973); “‘The Honest Workingman’ and Workers’ Control: The Experience of Toronto Skilled Workers, 1860–1892” (Labour/Le Travailleur, 1976); with Peter Warrian, eds., Essays in Canadian Working Class History (1976); “The Working Class in Recent Canadian Historical Writing” (Acadiensis, 1978); Toronto Workers Respond to Industrial Capitalism, 1867–1892 (1980); “Labour and Working-Class History in Canada: Prospects in the 1980s” (Labour/Le Travailleur, 1981); with Bryan D. Palmer, Dreaming of What Might Be: The Knights of Labor in Ontario, 1880–1900 (1982); “1919: The Canadian Labour Revolt” (Labour/Le Travail, 1984); “The Structure of Canadian Working-Class History” (1985); ed., Class, Gender, and Region: Essays in Canadian Historical Sociology (1988); with Reg Whitaker, eds., R.C.M.P. Security Bulletins (1989–97); “State Repression of Labour and the Left in Canada, 1914–20” (CHR, 1992); “The RCMP, the Special Branch, and the Early Days of the Communist Party of Canada” (Labour/Le Travail, 1992); Workers and Canadian History (1995). After 2000: with Lara Campbell and Dominique Clément, eds., Debating Dissent (2012); with Reg Whitaker and Andrew Parnaby, Secret Service (2012); Spying on Canadians (2017). Readings: Bercuson (1981); Brody (1981–82); McKay (1981–82); Bradbury (1987); Morton (2000); Sangster (2000).
nodes.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-14, all in the journals' own PDFs unless stated: his 1976 Labour/Le Travailleur essay (pp. 32–34 and 58–62 read closely, the rest skimmed); his 1978 Acadiensis review essay (pp. 116–117 and 134–135, UNB Libraries PDF); his 1981 'Prospects in the 1980s' in full; '1919: The Canadian Labour Revolt' (1984), pp. 11–17 and 34 and the conclusion; his introduction to Class, Gender, and Region (1988), pp. 1–7, in the CCLH reprint on AU Press's site; and the opening of his 1992 RCMP documentary article (pp. 169–171). Reception read: Bercuson (1981), pp. 95–96; David Brody's review of Toronto Workers (Labour/Le Travailleur 8/9, 1981–82, pp. 361–364) in full; Ian McKay (1981–82), pp. 185–186, 214 and 219–224; Bettina Bradbury (1987), pp. 23–25 and 34–36; Desmond Morton (2000), pp. 11 and 22–27; Joan Sangster (2000), pp. 130 and 133; Careless's 1979 Jackson lecture (web text). Unread: the monographs Toronto Workers (1980) and Dreaming of What Might Be (1982), quoted only as Brody, Bradbury and Morton quote them; 'The Structure of Canadian Working-Class History' (1985), known through Bradbury's quotation; 'The writing of social history in English Canada, 1970–1984' (Social History, 1985); his 1992 Journal of Canadian Studies reply to Bliss (Project MUSE served a verification wall); the 1992 CHR and Intelligence and National Security articles, the Security Bulletins, Secret Service (2012) and Spying on Canadians (2017), cited at title and catalogue level; McNaught (1981) and Ramsay Cook's 'The Making of Canadian Working-Class History' (1983). He is not presented as a founder: Freeman (2002) names him with Palmer and Sangster in the founding generation of Labour/Le Travail; Morton (2000) calls him the group's 'undoubted inspirational leader'; in 1981 he stressed 'the collective nature of the work' and noted that the group's first collective statement was 'drafted by Russell Hann'. The 1981 essay is not a reply to Bercuson's essay in the same issue: both were first given at the McGill 'Class and Culture' conference in March 1980 (p. 68 n.), and Kealey answers Bercuson's 1979 charge of 'obeisance to E.P. Thompson'. Contested in period by Bercuson (1981), Brody (1981–82), McKay (1981–82, on the concept of culture), Bradbury (1987) and Sangster (2000) on gender, and Morton (2000). Post-2000 works are dated in labels and text.

nodes.label: Sylvia Van Kirk
nodes.date_label: “Many Tender Ties” 1980 · “The Reputation of a Lady” 1986 · “Tracing the Fortunes of Five Founding Families of Victoria” 1997–98 · “From ‘Marrying-In’ to ‘Marrying-Out’” 2002
nodes.description: A Canadian historian of women in fur-trade society and of families of mixed descent in colonial Red River and Victoria. 'Many Tender Ties' (1980) treated traders' marriages with Indigenous and later mixed-descent women, à la façon du pays, as the core of a fur-trade society; as a 1981 reviewer quoted it, the book set out to show that the trade 'constituted a social and cultural complex as well as an economic activity' and claimed support for 'the claims of theorists in women's history that sex roles should constitute a category of historical investigation'. Her later articles turn on race and gender: the missionaries' 'racist attitudes, particularly with regard to women' and the rivalry among women 'compounded by the issue of race' in Red River (1986), and an acculturation in early Victoria that was 'gendered' (1997–98). Reviewers paired the book with Jennifer Brown's Strangers in Blood from 1981. One found its picture of fur-trade unions 'may be too complimentary', and Emma LaRocque (1999) placed her with Brown, Trigger and others in a 'neo cross-cultural approach' which, 'Compared to earlier racist material', was 'a much improved approach to Native history', but whose ethnological description 'results in Othering the very people the researcher is trying to make understandable'.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Sylvia Van Kirk; PhD, University of London, 1975, on women in fur-trade society, supervised by Glyndwr Williams (per Brown 2012; thesis unread); “Many Tender Ties”: Women in Fur-Trade Society in Western Canada, 1670–1870 (Winnipeg: Watson & Dwyer, 1980; Norman: University of Oklahoma Press, 1983); “What if Mama Is an Indian?: The Cultural Ambivalence of the Alexander Ross Family” (in Peterson and Brown, eds., The New Peoples, 1985; title only); “The Reputation of a Lady: Sarah Ballenden and the Foss-Pelly Scandal” (Manitoba History, 1986); two papers on the trader George Nelson (1984, 1988; titles only, per Brown 2012); “Tracing the Fortunes of Five Founding Families of Victoria” (BC Studies, 1997–98). After 2000: “From ‘Marrying-In’ to ‘Marrying-Out’: Changing Patterns of Aboriginal/Non-Aboriginal Marriage in Colonial Canada” (Frontiers, 2002); Brownlie and Korinek, eds., Finding a Way to the Heart (2012), essays in her honour. Readings: Bowsfield (1981); Gagan and Turner (1982); Brown (1983); Pierson (1992, reference list only); LaRocque (1999); McPherson (2000); Fiske (2000). Later readings: Perry (2008); Brown (2012).
nodes.scope_note: Her own words are read in 'The Reputation of a Lady' (Manitoba History 11, 1986; the society's web edition, read in full, without page numbers) and in 'Tracing the Fortunes of Five Founding Families of Victoria' (BC Studies 115/116, 1997–98, pp. 149–51 only: the journal PDF is damaged after its seventh page). 'Many Tender Ties' is not read: Internet Archive copies are borrow-only and search-inside returned 'Item not available', and the Google Books quota was exhausted. The book is quoted only as Bowsfield (1981) quotes it, without page references, and as LaRocque (1999) cites pp. 101–103. Her 1977 CHA paper 'Women in Between' sits on Érudit and was not fetched. In-period readings read in full: Bowsfield (Archivaria 12, 1981), Gagan and Turner (Archivaria 14, 1982), Brown (CJNS, 1983), LaRocque (dissertation, 1999, PDF pp. 54 and 249), McPherson and Fiske (Atlantis 25:1, 2000). Later readings, labelled as such: Perry (Left History, 2008) and Brown (2012, read in its 2017 reprint). She is not presented as a founder: Bowsfield reviews her book within a fur-trade literature already being recast by Ray, Trigger and others, and Perry (2008, n. 4) notes that she and Brown 'were not entirely alone in this', naming Dickason, Peterson, Foster and Spry. The early-1990s critiques that Perry names (Pierson 1992; Emberley 1990–91) are not read; Project MUSE returned a verification page. No identity classification is recorded for any critic named here.

nodes.label: Jennifer S. H. Brown
nodes.date_label: Strangers in Blood 1980 · “Woman as Centre and Symbol in the Emergence of Metis Communities” 1983 · The New Peoples (ed. with Peterson) 1985 · The Orders of the Dreamed (with Brightman) 1988 · “Ethnohistorians: Strange Bedfellows, Kindred Spirits” 1991 · Reading Beyond Words (ed. with Vibert) 1996 · An Ethnohistorian in Rupert’s Land 2017
nodes.description: An anthropologist and historian of fur-trade families, the Métis, and Cree and Ojibwe history in the old Hudson's Bay Company territory. Strangers in Blood (1980) compared Hudson's Bay Company officers and North West Company partners as husbands and fathers; as a 1981 reviewer quoted it, the title took the British legal term for any relationship 'that the law refused to admit as legitimate' as 'one way of characterizing the meetings of Whites and Indians' in the fur trade. In 1983 she asked how women shaped Métis emergence, finding among North West Company fathers who had children baptized in Montreal that daughters were twice as likely as sons to stay in the Indian country, and in 1985 she co-edited with Jacqueline Peterson The New Peoples: Being and Becoming Métis in North America. As president of the American Society for Ethnohistory she spoke of 'our field, methodology, approach, or whatever it is we do when we do ethnohistory' (1991). A 1981 reviewer found the book weighed down by 'bits of anthropological theory'; Emma LaRocque (1999) placed her with Van Kirk in a 'neo cross-cultural approach', 'a much improved approach' on earlier work that still othered its subjects; and later scholarship rejects defining Métis by mixed descent, the biological starting point ('the meeting and mingling of Indian and white racial groups') that her 1983 essay set against a complex social history.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Jennifer S. H. Brown (b. 1940); doctoral study in anthropology at the University of Chicago, the dissertation revised as Strangers in Blood (per Brown 2012, 2017; dissertation unread); “A Demographic Transition in the Fur Trade Country” and “Changing Views of Fur Trade Marriage and Domesticity” (Western Canadian Journal of Anthropology, 1976); “Linguistic Solitudes and Changing Social Categories” (in Judd and Ray, eds., Old Trails and New Directions, 1980); Strangers in Blood: Fur Trade Company Families in Indian Country (Vancouver: UBC Press, 1980); “Children of the Early Fur Trades” (in Parr, ed., Childhood and Family in Canadian History, 1982); “Woman as Centre and Symbol in the Emergence of Metis Communities” (Canadian Journal of Native Studies, 1983); The New Peoples (ed. with Jacqueline Peterson, 1985), including her “Diverging Identities: The Presbyterian Métis of St. Gabriel Street, Montreal”; The Orders of the Dreamed: George Nelson on Cree and Northern Ojibwa Religion and Myth, 1823 (with Robert Brightman, 1988); “The Blind Men and the Elephant: Fur Trade History Revisited” (1990); “Ethnohistorians: Strange Bedfellows, Kindred Spirits” (Ethnohistory, 1991); Reading Beyond Words: Contexts for Native History (ed. with Elizabeth Vibert, 1996). After 2000: “Partial Truths: A Closer Look at Fur Trade Marriage” (2001); “‘All These Stories About Women’: ‘Many Tender Ties’ and a New Fur Trade History” (2012); An Ethnohistorian in Rupert’s Land: Unfinished Conversations (2017). Readings: Gresko (1981); Bowsfield (1981); Gagan and Turner (1982); LaRocque (1999); Fiske (2000); McPherson (2000). Later readings: Perry (2008); Gaudry (2013).
nodes.scope_note: Her own in-period words are read in 'Woman as Centre and Symbol in the Emergence of Metis Communities' (Canadian Journal of Native Studies 3:1, 1983, pp. 39–46, in full) and in an indexed excerpt only of her 1991 presidential address (Ethnohistory 38:2; OpenAlex's abstract field; p. 113 is the recorded first page, and the page itself was not inspected). Strangers in Blood and The New Peoples are not read: the Internet Archive copy of the 1980 book is borrow-only, and the 1985 collection is title-level. The book is quoted only as Gresko (1981) quotes it. An Ethnohistorian in Rupert's Land (2017, open access) was read in part: its acknowledgements, part introductions, chapter 3 and the opening of chapter 9 (reprints of 1990 and 1985 essays), and chapter 11 (her 2012 essay on Van Kirk). The 2017 reprints are labelled as later texts. The press notes that some chapter titles were modified, and chapter 3 cites a 2014 book, so the reprints do not witness the 1985 or 1990 wording. In-period readings read in full: Gresko (Canadian Woman Studies, 1981), Bowsfield (Archivaria, 1981), Gagan and Turner (Archivaria, 1982), LaRocque (1999, PDF p. 249), Fiske and McPherson (Atlantis, 2000). Later readings: Perry (2008), Gaudry (2013). She is not presented as a founder of Métis or fur-trade social history: her 1983 essay sets her questions beside Peterson's and Van Kirk's, and The New Peoples came from a 1981 Newberry Library conference that she helped organise.
