nodes.label: Sherry Olson
nodes.date_label: 'Baltimore Imitates the Spider' 1979 · Baltimore: The Building of an American City 1980 · 'Occupations and Residential Spaces' 1989 · 'Le peuplement de Montréal' 1997 · MAP, Montréal, l'avenir du passé, from 2000 · Peopling the North American City (with Patricia Thornton) 2011 · 'Rebuilding a Neighbourhood of Montreal' (with Dufaux) 2014
nodes.description: A historical geographer, at Johns Hopkins and then McGill, whose Baltimore: The Building of an American City (1980) is 'about city building', read as 'a boom-and-bust sequence of "long swings," with eighteen years or so separating the neighboring peaks'. In Montreal she and her collaborators, among them the demographer Patricia Thornton, followed sampled families through parish registers, censuses and municipal taxrolls and mapped them; her 1997 chapter for the Atlas historique du Québec, mapped with GIS at McGill, sets out to 'saisir … les processus par lesquels la cité se construit'. With Robert Sweeny, Jason Gilliland and others she built MAP (Montréal, l'avenir du passé, begun in 2000), a collective historical GIS in which, as she and François Dufaux wrote in 2014, 'the spatial links place the household on the cadastral lot'. The editors of Historical GIS Research in Canada (2014) name MAP, 'led by' Olson and Sweeny, among the few Canadian HGIS projects since the 1990s, and a Victoria team that includes Gilliland calls her Montreal work 'a model of spatial history'; Sweeny, MAP's co-director, warned in 2009 that 'the ontology of geographic information systems is antithetical to historical understanding'. With Thornton she wrote Peopling the North American City: Montreal, 1840–1900 (2011), which, by its publisher's description, follows families of twelve surnames.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Sherry H. Olson; The Depletion Myth: A History of Railroad Use of Timber (1971); “Baltimore Imitates the Spider” (Annals of the AAG, 1979); Baltimore: The Building of an American City (1980; bicentennial edition 1997); with Patricia Thornton and Quoc Thuy Thach, “Dimensions sociales de la mortalité infantile à Montréal au milieu du XIXe siècle” (Annales de démographie historique, 1989); “Occupations and Residential Spaces in Nineteenth-Century Montreal” (Historical Methods, 1989); with David Hanna, “The Social Landscape of Montréal, 1901” (Historical Atlas of Canada, vol. 3, plate 30, 1990); “Le peuplement de Montréal” (Atlas historique du Québec: Population et territoire, 1997); with Jason Gilliland, “Claims on Housing Space in Nineteenth-Century Montreal” (Urban History Review, 1998). After 2000: MAP, Montréal, l'avenir du passé (from 2000, with Robert Sweeny and others); “Ethnic Partition of the Work Force in 1840s Montréal” (Labour/Le Travail, 2004); with Gilliland, “Residential Segregation in the Industrializing City” (Urban Geography, 2010); with Gilliland and Danielle Gauvreau, “Did Segregation Increase as the City Expanded?” (Social Science History, 2011); with Patricia Thornton, Peopling the North American City: Montreal, 1840–1900 (2011); with François Dufaux, “Rebuilding a Neighbourhood of Montreal” (2014). Readings: Sweeny (2009); Sager (2012); Horner (2013); Bonnell and Fortin (2014); Lutz, Dunae, Gilliland, Lafreniere and Harvey (2014).
nodes.scope_note: A method entry for historical GIS, not a Quebec-historiography entry: the Quebec self-accounts read for the atlas (Ouellet 1985, Bédard, Bouchard, Rudin, Savard, Linteau) do not name her. Her own words are read in the introduction and acknowledgments of Baltimore (1980), in full in 'Le peuplement de Montréal' (1997), in part in the 2004 Labour/Le Travail research note, and in part in her 2014 chapter with Dufaux; the 1979, 1998, 2010 and 2011 articles are known from their abstracts, and the 1989 Historical Methods article and the 1990 atlas plate at title level only. Peopling the North American City is unread; it is known from publisher copy and the opening paragraphs of Sager's (2012) and Horner's (2013) reviews. In-period reviews of Baltimore exist (AHR, JAH, Technology and Culture, JEH 1981; JIH, Journal of Historical Geography 1982) but were not readable here. The GIS work begins in the 1990s; MAP dates from 2000 and is collective, co-led with Robert Sweeny, whose team built the electronic framework from the Cane map of 1846. She is not presented as the founder of HGIS in Canada: 'pioneering' is the Victoria team's word, and the editors of the 2014 volume list national repositories in the United States and Britain as 'some of the most important work in the field'. The 2014 volume's chapter 2 (Beard, Macfarlane and Clifford) is not used.

nodes.label: Bruce Curtis
nodes.date_label: With Corrigan, “Education, Inspection and State Formation” 1985 · Building the Educational State 1988 · True Government by Choice Men? 1992 · The Politics of Population 2001 · “After ‘Canada’” 2009 · Ruling by Schooling Quebec 2012
nodes.description: A historical sociologist (Carleton University) whose studies of schooling, school inspection and the census in the Canadas read administration as a means of rule. In Building the Educational State (1988), as a reviewer quotes it, education 'was not a means to government; education was government: government of the self' (p. 110), and the educational state was built 'only through the destruction of a prior educational organization' (p. 15); in True Government by Choice Men? (1992) 'Educational inspection was about state formation: the creation, stabilization and normalisation of relations of power, authority, domination and exploitation' (p. 32). His census history (2001) holds that 'Census making ... is not in any simple sense the taking of things as they are; in an important sense it is the making of things to be taken' (p. 305, as Belshaw quotes it), and in a 1996 review he wrote that 'The census simply cannot tell us much about the value of distributed property, about the gendered distribution of property, certainly nothing about inheritance patterns'. Reviewers credited his joining of Foucault's analysis of power to a Marxist theory of state formation but found gender relations missing (Davey 1989; Miller 1993), and Bryan Palmer judged the inspection study, taken as a model, 'overstated to the point of distorting actual historical relations in the evolution of state and civil society' (1993). In the debate over Ian McKay's liberal order framework, Nancy Christie cites 'Bruce Curtis's important point that what McKay is really describing is governmentality' (2009).
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Bruce Curtis (b. 1950); with Philip Corrigan, “Education, Inspection and State Formation: A Preliminary Statement” (CHA Historical Papers, 1985); Building the Educational State: Canada West, 1836–1871 (1988); True Government by Choice Men? Inspection, Education, and State Formation in Canada West (1992); The Politics of Population: State Formation, Statistics, and the Census of Canada, 1840–1875 (2001); “After ‘Canada’: Liberalisms, Social Theory, and Historical Analysis” (2009); Ruling by Schooling Quebec: Conquest to Liberal Governmentality – A Historical Sociology (2012).
nodes.scope_note: This entry presents Curtis's state-formation studies of schooling, inspection and the census (1985–2001) and their place in the liberal order debate. Read on 2026-10-14: his review of Darroch and Soltow (1996, pp. 107–110) in full, and four in-period or near-period reviews of his books in full: Davey (1989) on Building the Educational State, Miller (1993) and Palmer (1993) on True Government by Choice Men?, and Belshaw (2002) on The Politics of Population; Christie (2009) was re-read for its Curtis passage. His books are unread: his words from them are reviewers' quotations, with the reviewers' page references. The 1985 article with Corrigan, the 2009 chapter and Ruling by Schooling Quebec (2012) are title- or summary-level only. He is a sociologist, not a historian by department; the atlas's moral regulation entry treats his state-formation work as shared ground with the liberal order framework, not membership.

nodes.label: Allan Greer
nodes.date_label: “Fur-Trade Labour” 1981 · “A Critique of Pentland” and Peasant, Lord, and Merchant 1985 · Colonial Leviathan (ed. with Radforth) 1992 · The Patriots and the People 1993 · Property and Dispossession 2018 · “Settler Colonialism and Beyond” 2019
nodes.description: A historian of Lower Canada and colonial North America whose rural social history described a feudal, household-centred habitant society: in 1985 he held that Lower Canadian 'agriculture was organized primarily around the satisfaction of family subsistence needs through family production', with part of the surplus 'diverted to priests and seigneurs through feudal exactions', a view he set against both Ouellet's routine-bound peasant (1981) and the commercial farmer of Paquet and Wallot, while allowing that 'Feudal peasants or market-conscious farmers? No doubt the debates will continue' (1985). The same essay, a critique of Clare Pentland's Labour and Capital in Canada, faulted the staples tradition of Innis and Creighton for confining attention to 'relations of exchange'. With Ian Radforth he edited Colonial Leviathan (1992), on mid-nineteenth-century state formation, which Bryan Palmer found to lack coherence (1993) and which Greer later said 'neglected everything to do with Indigenous peoples and processes of elimination' (2019); his history of the 1837 rebellion (1993) is known here through reviewers, who read it as breaking with Ouellet's manipulated peasantry. His later work on 'property formation' (2018) and his 2019 lecture treat settler colonialism as one mode of colonial invasion among several, 'a dominant force in some periods and regions' that 'fades to insignificance in others', while insisting 'I am not here to trash or dismiss settler-colonial theory'.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Allan Greer (b. 1950); “Fur-Trade Labour and Lower Canadian Agrarian Structures” (1981); “Wage Labour and the Transition to Capitalism: A Critique of Pentland” (Labour/Le Travail, 1985); Peasant, Lord, and Merchant: Rural Society in Three Quebec Parishes, 1740–1840 (1985); ed. with Ian Radforth, Colonial Leviathan: State Formation in Mid-Nineteenth-Century Canada (1992); The Patriots and the People: The Rebellion of 1837 in Rural Lower Canada (1993; French translation Habitants et Patriotes, 1997); “Commons and Enclosure in the Colonization of North America” (2012); Property and Dispossession: Natives, Empires and Land in Early Modern North America (2018); “Settler Colonialism and Beyond” (2019).
nodes.scope_note: This entry presents Greer's account of rural Lower Canada and the transition to capitalism (1981–85), the state-formation collection (1992) and his later historicising of settler colonialism (2018–19). Read on 2026-10-14: 'Wage Labour and the Transition to Capitalism' (1985, pp. 7–22) and 'Settler Colonialism and Beyond' (2019, pp. 61–86) in full; the introduction to Property and Dispossession (2018, pp. 1–24) on Cambridge Core, which shows no page markers; Palmer's 1993 review of Colonial Leviathan in full. 'Fur-Trade Labour' (1981) was read in full for the Ouellet entry and its critique of Ouellet is carried by edge_989, not repeated here. Peasant, Lord, and Merchant (1985) and The Patriots and the People (1993) are unread (lending-only copies); the 1985 book is known from its publisher's description and the 1993 book from reviews. Ouellet's review essay on the 1993 book (Histoire sociale / Social History, 1995) is unread, so no reply by Ouellet is quoted. His New France and Jesuit work (The People of New France, 1997; Mohawk Saint, 2005) is not covered.

nodes.label: Cole Harris
nodes.date_label: The Seigneurial System in Early Canada 1966 · Historical Atlas of Canada, vol. 1 (editor) 1987 · The Resettlement of British Columbia 1997 · ‘Social Power and Cultural Change in Pre-Colonial British Columbia’ 1997–98 · Making Native Space 2002 · ‘Revisiting the Native Land Question’ 2003 · ‘How Did Colonialism Dispossess?’ 2004 · A Bounded Land 2020
nodes.description: A Canadian historical geographer of early Canada and of colonialism in British Columbia. He edited the first volume of the Historical Atlas of Canada (1987), whose preface says it sought 'to emphasize the economic and social circumstances of ordinary life rather than the more usual fare of historical atlases' (as quoted by MacDonald, 1990). From the 1990s he wrote British Columbia's colonization as geographical change. Against the 'cultural enrichment hypothesis' of contact-era history he set 'epidemics, increased violence, depopulation, and, for many, a drastic loss of cultural and historical memory' (1997–98). He explained the reserve system as dispossession: its capacity 'rested on raw firepower', its momentum 'came from capital seeking profits and from settlers seeking livelihoods', and its legitimation 'lay with a cultural discourse that located civilization and savagery' (2003); in 2004 he argued that the emphasis on culture in studies of colonialism 'tends to obscure other forms of colonial power'. Reviewers found few Native voices in the work: Tina Loo (1998) saw Native peoples 'emerge as victims' in The Resettlement of British Columbia, and Val Napoleon (2004) wrote that Making Native Space 'recreates, from a settler perspective, BC history' and that Harris 'should have incorporated contemporary Aboriginal voices' where history gave way to proposals for the future.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Cole Harris (R. Cole Harris, 1936–2022); The Seigneurial System in Early Canada (1966); 'Theory and Synthesis in Historical Geography' (Canadian Geographer, 1971); 'The Simplification of Europe Overseas' (Annals of the AAG, 1977); 'The Historical Mind and the Practice of Geography' (1978); ed., with Geoffrey J. Comments from an Edge of Empire' (Annals of the AAG, 2004); A Bounded Land: Reflections on Settler Colonialism in Canada (2020). Readings: MacDonald (1990); Loo (1998); Clayton (2003); Fiske (2003); Napoleon (2004); Perry (2016, later reading).

His own words, read: 'Social Power and Cultural Change in Pre-Colonial British Columbia' (BC Studies 115/116, 1997/98, pp. 45–82; pp. 45–47, 56–60, 68–70 and 80–82 read closely, the rest skimmed); 'Revisiting the Native Land Question' with Fiske's and Gibson's commentaries and his reply (BC Studies 138/139, 2003, pp. 137–163, read in full); the abstract of 'How Did Colonialism Dispossess?' (2004), read in the publisher's abstract as recorded by OpenAlex (the article body is closed and unread); the preface of the Historical Atlas of Canada, vol. 1 (1987), known only through MacDonald's quotations. Reception read in full: Graham A. MacDonald on the Atlas (Manitoba History 20, 1990, web text); Tina Loo on The Resettlement of British Columbia (BC Studies 117, 1998, pp. 64–67); Daniel Clayton's guest editorial on Making Native Space (BC Studies 138/139, 2003, pp. 5–11); Val Napoleon on Making Native Space (BC Studies 141, 2004, pp. 114–118). Later reading: Perry's 2016 reply in the BC Studies forum on her Colonial Relations (p. 112). Unread: the books themselves (The Seigneurial System, the Atlas, The Resettlement of British Columbia, Making Native Space, A Bounded Land), the 1977 and 1991 Annals essays (known through Clayton's note), the 1994 Ethnohistory article on smallpox, the Canadian Geographer review symposium on Making Native Space (2003; known through Napoleon's summary), and the Native Studies Review forum 'Appraising Cole Harris' Making Native Space' (16:2, 2005; the copy on the University of Saskatchewan site returned 404). He is not presented as a founder of historical geography or of settler-colonial history: the Atlas was a collective work with a cartographer and many contributors, and the texts read do not cite Wolfe. Contested in period by Loo (1998) and Napoleon (2004) on Native voices and agency, by Fiske (2003) on the symbolic, and by the Canadian Geographer symposium (2003, as Napoleon summarises it). Post-2000 works are dated in labels and text.

nodes.label: Adele Perry
nodes.date_label: ‘Oh I’m Just Sick of the Faces of Men’ 1995 · On the Edge of Empire 2001 · ‘Presence, Absence, and the Writing of BC History’ 2001 · ‘Women, Racialized People, and the Making of the Liberal Order’ 2009 · Colonial Relations 2015
nodes.description: A Canadian historian of gender, race and colonialism in British Columbia and the British Empire. In 1995 she argued that Canadian historians had explained the shortage of white women in the West with a 'scarcity model' and a 'volcano theory' of male sexuality that were 'based on essentialist understandings of both sexuality and race' and belonged to 'colonial discourse itself'. On the Edge of Empire (2001), which she said was 'initially inspired not by local experience but by a rich international literature on gender and colonialism', studied white miners' homosocial culture, mixed-race relationships and the schemes to bring white women to the colony, and found, in her words as reviewers quote them, 'a sharp disjuncture between colonial discourse and colonial practice on this edge of empire'. Reviewers placed it in whiteness studies and asked for more on Indigenous people: Sarah Carter (2002) wanted the 'social centrality and political agency' of Aboriginal peoples further developed, and Paul Orlowski (2002) found First Nations resistance 'lacking' and a 'binary racial divide' that set aside Chinese workers. In 2016 she described the 2001 book as arguing that British Columbia's history 'is best understood within a comparative framework of settler colonialism'.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Adele Perry; “‘Oh I’m Just Sick of the Faces of Men’: Gender Imbalance, Race, Sexuality, and Sociability in Nineteenth-Century British Columbia” (BC Studies, 1995); “‘Fair Ones of a Purer Caste’: White Women and Colonialism in Nineteenth-Century British Columbia” (1997); “The Historian and the Theorist Revisited” (Histoire sociale/Social History, 2000); On the Edge of Empire: Gender, Race, and the Making of British Columbia, 1849–1871 (2001); “Presence, Absence, and the Writing of BC History” (BC Studies, 2001/02); “The Autocracy of Love and the Legitimacy of Empire: Intimacy, Power and Scandal in Nineteenth-Century Metlakahtlah” (2004); “Women, Racialized People, and the Making of the Liberal Order in Northern North America” (in Liberalism and Hegemony, 2009); Colonial Relations: The Douglas-Connolly Family and the Nineteenth-Century Imperial World (2015). nodes.label: Philip C. C. Huang
nodes.date_label: Modern China founded 1975 · The Peasant Economy and Social Change in North China 1985 · The Peasant Family and Rural Development in the Yangzi Delta 1990 · “The Paradigmatic Crisis in Chinese Studies” 1991 · Civil Justice in China 1996 · Code, Custom, and Legal Practice 2001 · exchange with Pomeranz 2002–2003
nodes.description: A historian of rural China and Chinese law and the founding editor of Modern China (1975). Huang argued that Ming–Qing commercialization proceeded without capitalist development through involution: output per unit of land rose while the marginal returns to additional labour on family farms diminished, “growth without development”, a claim about marginal rather than average productivity that his critics contested. He took the term from Clifford Geertz’s “agricultural involution” and the mechanism partly from Chayanov, as he acknowledged in 1985 and again in 1991. The Peasant Economy and Social Change in North China (1985) and The Peasant Family and Rural Development in the Yangzi Delta (1990) developed the argument, and “The Paradigmatic Crisis in Chinese Studies” (1991) held that Western and Chinese models, Marxist “incipient capitalism” among them, shared assumptions that Chinese evidence made “paradoxical”. His legal histories include Civil Justice in China (1996) and Code, Custom, and Legal Practice in China (2001). He took “practice” from Bourdieu while preferring “the study of practice as historical process” (2005), and rejected culturalist claims, which he attributed to Said, that facts are “no more than representations” (1998). After 2000 he was a prominent critic of Kenneth Pomeranz, arguing that eighteenth-century England and the Yangzi delta stood “at opposite poles in a continuum from development to involution” (2002); Pomeranz answered that involution was “internally inconsistent” (2003).
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Philip C. C. Huang; The Peasant Economy and Social Change in North China (1985); The Peasant Family and Rural Development in the Yangzi Delta, 1350–1988 (1990); “The Paradigmatic Crisis in Chinese Studies: Paradoxes in Social and Economic History” (Modern China, 1991); Civil Justice in China (1996); Code, Custom, and Legal Practice in China (2001); “Development or Involution in Eighteenth-Century Britain and China?” (Journal of Asian Studies, 2002) and “Further Thoughts on Eighteenth-Century Britain and China” (2003); “Theory and the Study of Modern Chinese History: Four Traps and a Question” (1998); “Divorce Law Practices and the Origins, Myths, and Realities of Judicial ‘Mediation’ in China” (2005); “Our Sense of Problem” (2016). Founding editor of Modern China (1975). Readings: Mann’s and Duara’s reviews (1986); Pomeranz’s replies (2002, 2003).
nodes.scope_note: Involution is presented as Huang defined it in the 1985 book (pp. 7–11 read) and restated it in 1991 (pp. 299–302 and 314–317 read), 2002 (whole article OCRed; selected passages read closely, remaining text searched; map images not inspected) and 2003 (pp. 157–158 and 164–165 read). The 1990 book is unread; it is known through those restatements, Pomeranz’s citation of its pp. 11–17 and Day’s review. Geertz and Chayanov are his acknowledged resources (1985, p. 8; 1991, p. 317) and Boserup a third (1991, n. 9); he redefined Geertz’s term. The exchange with Pomeranz appears once, as two critique arrows. Huang conceded a misplaced decimal in the 1990 book (2003, p. 157) and, as he reports it, Pomeranz’s reply granted declining average returns as cotton displaced grain. Brenner and Isett (2002) and the real-wage study of Allen and colleagues (2011) side partly with him on living standards and divergence, not on the mechanism. His legal histories of 1996 and 2001 are dated only and their arguments are unread here; his use of Bourdieu’s “practice” is taken from a 2005 note and a 1995 article read in part by a second research pass, and his wider later work on practice falls outside this reading. His 1998 critique of Said is read at pp. 193–195. Life dates are not established from texts read.

nodes.label: Capitalism, divergence and industrialisation
nodes.date_label: Capitalism and Slavery 1944 · Dobb–Sweezy 1950 · Brenner debate 1976–85 · Wrigley 1988 · de Vries 1994 · The Great Divergence 2000 · Allen and The Enlightened Economy 2009 · Empire of Cotton 2014 · Hilt 2017 · Burnard and Riello 2020
nodes.description: A set of linked arguments about why capitalism, industrialisation and Western wealth arose where and when they did. Marxist historians disputed whether trade or class relations ended feudalism: Dobb answered Sweezy that trade worked 'to the extent that it accentuated the internal conflicts' (1950). Brenner's property-relations thesis (1976) opened a second round, in which Bois called his approach 'political Marxism' and Wood made it a programme. Economic historians slowed the British Industrial Revolution while reasserting 'an important discontinuity' (Crafts and Harley, 1992), and Berg and Hudson answered that growth accounting had 'mis-specified' it; explanations multiplied in Wrigley's escape from an 'organic economy', de Vries's 'industrious revolution', Mokyr's 'Industrial Enlightenment' and Allen's high wages and cheap energy. Wong challenged Europe's status as the comparative norm; Pomeranz acknowledged that method while giving greater weight to global conjunctures, ecological constraints, coal and New World resources; critics answered from property relations, knowledge, wages and the state. Williams's Capitalism and Slavery (1944) returned through Inikori, the Legacies of British Slave-ownership project and an American 'history of capitalism' whose economic-historian critics charged 'specious arguments' (Hilt, 2017). Readers join these debates themselves: Burnard and Riello set the new history of capitalism beside the Brenner debate and Pomeranz (2020).

nodes.scope_note: A Debate entry with five components, each with its own strands: the transition debate; the Brenner debate and political Marxism; explaining industrialisation; the Great Divergence; slavery and capitalism. It gathers exchanges; the related field strands remain in place, while person entries hold the relationships stated below. The field strands, not moved, are: marx/transition, economic/marxist, economic/household_demand, economic/wrigley_growth, economic/regional_divergence, economic/divergence_household_dispute and economic/coal_constraints_dispute (the Huang–Pomeranz exchange), economic/slavery_productivity_exchange, economic/empire, global/comparison, global/reciprocal_comparison_resources, global/protoindustry_trade_limits, consumption/household_labor, technology/invention_adoption, demography/aggregate_population, dependency/worldsystems, atlantic/earlier and quant/slavery_debate. Existing person entries (Dobb, Hilton, Williams, Pomeranz, Huang, Hall) keep their own relations; Brenner and Wood gained person entries in 1.145; Mokyr, Wrigley, de Vries and Wong follow in 1.146. Readings are recorded per source, many through publisher excerpts, abstracts, Cambridge Core chapter openings or reviewers; unread books are given only as named readers report them. Quotations from The Brenner Debate (1985) beyond its Cambridge Core chapter openings were withdrawn before drafting. The 'California School' is a readers' label, attributed by Frank (2001) and Vries (2009) to Goldstone. Toynbee (1884) is a dated precursor, not a start. Mokyr, Wrigley, de Vries and Wong hold their contributions to the debate on their own entries (the arrows drawn for them in 1.145 from demography, consumption and technology now start from those entries); Allen and Beckert remain roster rows here.

strands.title: The transition debate: Dobb, Sweezy and their readers, 1946–1976
strands.focus: Dobb's Studies (1946) defined feudalism by the coercive relation between producer and lord; Sweezy (1950) answered that feudalism was 'a system of production for use' dissolved by 'causes external to the system', above all trade, while granting that 'no theory which fails to take into account the factors which Dobb stresses … can be regarded as correct'. Dobb replied that trade 'exercised its influence to the extent that it accentuated the internal conflicts', and carried the argument to the absolutist state and the English Revolution. Takahashi (1952) developed an analysis of production relations and the social form of labour, and pressed for fuller French and German comparison. Hilton collected the exchange with later essays in 1976. Positions within one Marxist debate, not a school. The field strands marx/transition and economic/marxist keep each author's own contribution.
strands.works: Dobb, Studies in the Development of Capitalism (1946); Sweezy and Dobb, Science & Society 14:2 (1950): 134–167; Takahashi (1952); Merrington, 'Town and Country in the Transition to Capitalism' (NLR, 1975); Hilton (ed.), The Transition from Feudalism to Capitalism (1976); see marx/transition and economic/marxist

strands.title: Against 'neo-Smithian Marxism': Brenner on Sweezy, Frank and Wallerstein, 1977
strands.focus: Brenner traced Wallerstein's world-system and Frank's development of underdevelopment back to Sweezy's side of the 1950 debate and, through it, to 'the model put forward by Adam Smith'. He acknowledged a 'great debt' to Dobb, and credited Frank with breaking 'the suffocating orthodoxies' of stage theory. Callinicos (1990) called the critique 'a valuable corrective'. See dependency/worldsystems for Wallerstein's own account.
strands.works: Brenner, NLR I/104 (1977); Wallerstein, The Modern World-System I (1974); Frank (1966–)

strands.title: The Brenner debate in Past and Present, 1976–1985
strands.focus: Brenner argued that class structure decides how demographic and commercial change affects growth. Postan and Hatcher called his charges against them 'groundless'; Le Roy Ladurie defended a 'neo-Malthusian' model; Croot and Parker, Wunder and Klíma tested his English, French, German and Bohemian comparisons; Bois agreed against 'the Malthusian model' but not with Brenner's method. Brenner's reply (1982) spoke of 'social-property systems'. Hilton introduced the collection (1985) as 'a continuation' of the transition debate. The respondents are read only in their Cambridge Core openings; their later pages are unread, and Bois's specified later passages (pp. 115–116) are known only as quoted by Wikipedia and Callinicos (1990); see annales/serial for Le Roy Ladurie's Languedoc.
strands.works: Past and Present 70 (1976) to 97 (1982); Aston and Philpin (eds), The Brenner Debate (1985)

strands.title: Political Marxism: from Bois's charge to a school, 1978–2016
strands.focus: Bois called Brenner's approach 'political Marxism', 'a voluntarist vision of history' (1978, as quoted by Wikipedia and Callinicos, 1990). By the accounts of Callinicos (1990) and Brenner (2016), Wood accepted the label while rejecting the charge of voluntarism. She argued that 'the economic' and 'the political' are differently joined in pre-capitalist and capitalist societies (1981), against G. A. Cohen's technological determinism. Critics answered that it was 'little more than a sociology of domination' (Callinicos) and that Brenner, taking up Dobb, narrowed class struggle to the countryside (Harman).
strands.works: Bois (1978); Wood, 'The Separation of the Economic and the Political in Capitalism' (NLR, 1981), Democracy Against Capitalism (1995); Harman (1989); Callinicos, 'The Limits of "Political Marxism"' (NLR, 1990); Harman and Brenner (2004, printed 2006); Brenner (2016) and Hirschkop (2016) on Wood

strands.title: The origin of capitalism and its critics, 1991–2004
strands.focus: Wood argued that England was 'the world's first capitalist society' (1991), siding with Thompson against the Nairn–Anderson theses. In 'Eurocentric Anti-Eurocentrism' (2001) she set the transition debate and Brenner's 'market dependence' against the 'commercialization model'; The Origin of Capitalism (1999; 2002), unread here, is known through its jacket and McAuley's quotations. McAuley (2001), drawing on Blaut, criticised 'the Brenner-Wood thesis' for treating colonialism as marginal; Wood replied that slave plantations mattered 'quite a while after the emergence of capitalism in the English countryside'. This exchange joins the strand to the slavery and divergence components.
strands.works: Wood, The Pristine Culture of Capitalism (1991), The Origin of Capitalism (1999; 2002), 'Eurocentric Anti-Eurocentrism' (2001), replies (2002); McAuley (2001)

strands.title: Revolution or gradual growth? The Industrial Revolution revised, 1884–1994
strands.focus: Toynbee's posthumous lectures (1884) defined the Industrial Revolution as 'the substitution of competition for the medieval regulations'. Crafts and Harley's output estimates slowed its pace while reasserting 'the industrial revolution as an important discontinuity' (1992); Berg and Hudson answered that growth accounting had 'mis-specified' the subject and left out women's and children's labour, regional specialisation and innovation (1990 working paper; 1992). De Vries (1994) read the revisionists as 'cleansing the temple of the "false god of the take off"', not pulling down the pillars.
strands.works: Toynbee, Lectures on the Industrial Revolution in England (1884); Crafts and Harley (1992); Berg and Hudson (1990 working paper; EHR 1992); de Vries (JEH 1994), pp. 249–251; see historicalecon/british_teaching

strands.title: Rural industry and industrious households, 1972–2016
strands.focus: Mendels (1972) treated market-oriented rural industry as 'a first phase which preceded and prepared modern industrialization proper', and later called it 'a plausible and interesting set of hypotheses' (1984); the Göttingen group (Kriedte, Medick, Schlumbohm, 1977) placed rural industry in 'the genesis of capitalism'. Coleman (1983) titled his critique 'a concept too many'. De Vries's 'industrious revolution' (1994; 2008), a term he and van Nederveen Meerkerk trace to Akira Hayami, made household labour and demand precede the Industrial Revolution; reviewers asked whether consumption had become 'a new deus ex machina' (2009). Rosenband (2016), from French and English papermaking, challenged the model: paperworkers 'already labored exhausting hours at the outset of de Vries's period of newfound industriousness', and women and adolescents worked for wages long before it (abstract). See economic/household_demand, consumption/household_labor and global/protoindustry_trade_limits for the field contributions.
strands.works: Mendels (JEH 1972) and NYRB letter (1984); Kriedte, Medick and Schlumbohm (1977; English 1981); Medick (1976); Coleman (1983); de Vries (1994; 2008); van Nederveen Meerkerk (2009); Rosenband (2016)

strands.title: Why Britain? Energy, knowledge and wages, 1988–2023
strands.focus: Wrigley (1988) questioned the Industrial Revolution as 'a cumulative, progressive, unitary phenomenon' and contrasted an 'organic economy' bounded by land with a mineral-based energy regime. Mokyr's 'Industrial Enlightenment' was 'the key to sustained and accelerating invention' (2002 draft); reviewing The Enlightened Economy (2009), Harley questioned whether the Industrial Enlightenment explained economic change or largely redescribed it (2010). Allen (2009) argued that 'Wages were remarkably high, and energy was remarkably cheap', so 'it paid to invent it there'; Humphries charged the high-wage account with a 'patriarchal perspective' (2013), and Allen replied with evidence 'that women and children participated in the high wage economy' (2015, abstract). Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda found that, across English counties, industrialisation occurred where wages began low and mechanical skills high (2023); the result concerns differences within England, not Britain's international wage advantage. The article sets it 'directly counter' to Allen's argument (pp. 60–61), as their 2014 essay had argued from British workers' human capital against his high wages. Clark and Jacks's coal-rent estimates imply a negligible income contribution from England's possession of coal reserves (2007). See economic/wrigley_growth and technology/invention_adoption.
strands.works: Wrigley, Continuity, Chance and Change (1988), The Path to Sustained Growth (2016); Mokyr (2002 paper), The Enlightened Economy (2009); Harley (2010); Allen (2009; 2015); Humphries (2013); Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda (2014; 2023); Clark and Jacks (2007)

strands.title: The Great Divergence and the so-called California School, 1997–2021
strands.focus: Wong (1997) challenged Europe's status as the comparative norm. Pomeranz (2000) followed 'a procedure outlined in Wong's recent China Transformed' while giving 'greater stress than Wong does on global conjunctures', and greater weight to ecological constraints, coal and New World resources; he dated divergence late. Readers attribute the label 'California School' to Goldstone (Frank 2001; Vries 2009), whose 'efflorescences' (2002) put pre-modern growth outside Europe too while locating the modern breakthrough in British engines, science and craft culture. Frank's ReOrient (1998) and a debate with Landes scheduled for December 1998, announced in a notice written from Frank's side, marked the polemical poles. Parthasarathi carried the argument to India (2011). Rosenthal and Wong explained divergence by political fragmentation and war (2011, as Ma's review reports and Wong restated in 2016); Ma found the hypothesis 'supported by fairly meager evidence'. Critics answered from property relations (Brenner and Isett 2002), knowledge (Mokyr 2002, 2012), wages and national accounts (Broadberry and Gupta 2006; Allen et al. 2011; Broadberry, Guan and Li 2021) and the state (Vries 2009, 2013). The Huang–Pomeranz exchange stays in economic/divergence_household_dispute and economic/coal_constraints_dispute.
strands.works: Wong, China Transformed (1997); Frank, ReOrient (1998); Landes, The Wealth and Poverty of Nations (1998); Pomeranz, The Great Divergence (2000); Frank's review (2001); Goldstone (2002); Brenner and Isett (2002); Mokyr (2002; 2012); Broadberry and Gupta (2006); Vries (2009; 2013); Parthasarathi (2011); Rosenthal and Wong (2011); Allen et al. (2011); Broadberry, Guan and Li (2021); see global/comparison and global/reciprocal_comparison_resources

strands.title: Capitalism and Slavery and its critics: the Williams thesis, 1944–2020
strands.focus: Williams (1944) advanced distinct propositions, which readers keep apart: that slave-trade and plantation wealth financed and stimulated British industry; that slave-derived wealth mattered in eighteenth-century Britain; and that the West Indies' economic decline, with changing economic interests, explains abolition. Drescher's Econocide (1977), in its publisher's description, challenged decline-based explanations of the 1807 abolition and stressed public mobilisation; Solow and Engerman's volume (1987) sifted the 'legacy'. Solow judged that slavery 'did not cause the Industrial Revolution but played an active role in its pattern and timing' (as quoted by Burnard and Riello), while Eltis and Engerman (2000), as Hilt and Burnard and Riello report them, judged its growth linkages to British industry small. Inikori (2002), as O'Rourke reports, reasserted the thesis through Atlantic trade and African producers and consumers. Hall (2014) and Burnard and Riello (2020) identify modified Williams arguments in Pomeranz and Inikori. The Legacies of British Slave-ownership team investigates slave-ownership's British legacies; its compensation evidence supports some Williams propositions, on slave-derived wealth, and qualifies the decline thesis, while leaving the industrialisation controversy unresolved ('Our material cannot resolve these controversies'). See economic/empire and atlantic/earlier.
strands.works: Williams, Capitalism and Slavery (1944); Drescher, Econocide (1977) and 'Capitalism and Slavery after Fifty Years' (1997); Solow and Engerman (eds), British Capitalism and Caribbean Slavery (1987); Eltis and Engerman (JEH 2000); Inikori, Africans and the Industrial Revolution in England (2002); Hall et al., Legacies of British Slave-ownership (2014)

strands.title: Slavery's capitalism and its economic-historian critics, 2013–2020
strands.focus: This strand selects the slavery controversy within the broader history of capitalism, a field whose early definition by Beckert, Hilt notes, is so broad that it 'includes most of the fields of labor, political, social, and business history', and whose work, Regele notes, began before the 2007–2009 financial crisis. Mainly Americanist historians, publicised as historians of capitalism in 2013, put slavery at the centre of American and global capitalism: Johnson's River of Dark Dreams (2013; Johnson does not count himself a historian of capitalism, Hilt notes), Baptist's argument, in Hilt's account, that torture drove cotton productivity (2014), Beckert's 'war capitalism' (2014) and Beckert and Rockman's Slavery's Capitalism (2016). Olmstead and Rhode answered that the books 'make fundamental errors in economic reasoning' (2017); Hilt, that 'specious arguments and failures of analytical reasoning sometimes undermine' them as social criticism, while granting that economic research supports some of their arguments and calling for 'dialogue, if not collaboration' (2017); Burnard and Riello, that US cotton came 'too late to cause an Industrial Revolution' (2020). Readers trace the movement to Polanyi, the 2008 crisis and a turn from labour history (Hilt; Regele) and to Williams and Pomeranz (Burnard and Riello). Fogel and Engerman's earlier slavery debate stays in quant/slavery_debate.
strands.works: Johnson, River of Dark Dreams (2013); Baptist, The Half Has Never Been Told (2014); Beckert, Empire of Cotton (2014); Beckert and Rockman (eds), Slavery’s Capitalism (2016); Olmstead and Rhode (AHA 2017; EEH 2018); Hilt (JEH 2017); Burnard and Riello (JGH 2020); Regele (2023)

coverage.basis: Surveyed through 2000 in the research of 2026-10-18 (data/extension-2026/capitalism-debate-2026-10-18/evidence-industrialisation.md, evidence-great-divergence.md, evidence-slavery-capitalism.md; data/extension-2026/brenner-2026-10-18/evidence-brenner.md, evidence-transition-political-marxism.md). Selected later interventions are dated individually through 2023 (Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda; Regele). Later work, including substantial later political Marxism and Great Divergence literature, is not yet surveyed for this entry.

nodes.label: Robert Brenner
nodes.date_label: “The Civil War Politics of London’s Merchant Community” 1973 · “Agrarian Class Structure and Economic Development in Pre-Industrial Europe” 1976 · “The Origins of Capitalist Development” 1977 · “The Agrarian Roots of European Capitalism” 1982 · The Brenner Debate (Aston and Philpin, eds) 1985 · Merchants and Revolution 1993 · The Economics of Global Turbulence 1998 (book 2006) · with Christopher Isett, “England’s Divergence from China’s Yangzi Delta” 2002
nodes.description: An American historian of early modern Europe whose 'Agrarian Class Structure and Economic Development in Pre-Industrial Europe' (Past and Present, 1976) opened the Brenner debate. Against the 'demographic model' of Postan and Le Roy Ladurie, and the 'commercialization model' it had displaced, he argued that 'it is the structure of class relations, of class power, which will determine the manner and degree to which particular demographic and commercial changes will affect long-run trends in the distribution of income and economic growth — and not vice versa'. Similar population trends accompanied serfdom's decline in the West and its rise in the East. English landlords who consolidated holdings and let them to capitalist tenants made agrarian capitalism; in France secure peasant property and the absolutist state blocked it, so that 'the most complete freedom and property rights for the rural population meant poverty'. A companion essay in New Left Review (1977) charged Sweezy, Frank and Wallerstein with a 'neo-Smithian' Marxism that made trade, not class relations, the motor of development, and acknowledged his 'great debt' to Dobb's critique of Sweezy. Postan and Hatcher (1978) replied that he misrepresented historians who had never given population 'an all-determining role'; Le Roy Ladurie found him 'extremely insular'; Croot and Parker doubted his England–France contrast; the Marxist Guy Bois welcomed the attack on 'the Malthusian model' but called the approach 'political Marxism', 'a voluntarist vision of history' (as quoted by Wikipedia and Callinicos, 1990). Brenner's reply (1982) restated the argument as one about 'social-property systems'. Introducing the collected debate (1985), Hilton read it as a continuation of the Dobb–Sweezy transition debate. Merchants and Revolution (1993) gave the English Revolution what Gentles called 'a new social interpretation', centred on London's colonial merchants; later work turned to the postwar world economy (1998) and, with Christopher Isett (2002), answered Pomeranz on England and the Yangzi delta.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Robert Brenner (b. 1943); 'The Civil War Politics of London's Merchant Community' (Past and Present 58, 1973); 'Agrarian Class Structure and Economic Development in Pre-Industrial Europe' (Past and Present 70, 1976); 'The Origins of Capitalist Development: A Critique of Neo-Smithian Marxism' (New Left Review I/104, 1977); 'The Agrarian Roots of European Capitalism' (Past and Present 97, 1982); T. H. Aston and C. H. E. Philpin (eds), The Brenner Debate (1985), with R. H. Hilton's introduction; Merchants and Revolution: Commercial Change, Political Conflict, and London's Overseas Traders, 1550–1653 (1993); The Economics of Global Turbulence (New Left Review I/229, 1998; book 2006); with Christopher Isett, 'England's Divergence from China's Yangzi Delta' (Journal of Asian Studies, 2002). Respondents and readers: M. M. Postan and John Hatcher (1978); Patricia Croot and David Parker (1978); Heide Wunder (1978); Emmanuel Le Roy Ladurie (1978); Guy Bois (1978); J. P. Cooper (1978); Arnošt Klíma (1979); Chris Harman (1989; debate with Brenner, 2004); Ian Gentles and Alex Callinicos (1994); Ellen Meiksins Wood (1996); Kenneth Pomeranz (2000); Prasannan Parthasarathi (2011); Thomas Leng (2024).
nodes.scope_note: Read on 2026-10-18: 'Agrarian Class Structure' (1976): the whole article (pp. 30–75, page numbers from the running heads) OCRed; pp. 30–34, 42–43, 47, 53, 56, 61–62 and 71–75 read closely, the remaining pages searched by keyword and skimmed; wording cross-checked against a transcription; 'The Origins of Capitalist Development' (1977) in full, in a transcription without New Left Review pages, cited by section; the 1985 volume's responses and Brenner's 1982 reply only in Cambridge Core's open chapter openings, with Bois's coinage of 'political Marxism' as quoted by Wikipedia and Callinicos (1990). The journal texts of 1978–82 are unread. Readers: Harman (1989, in part); the Harman–Brenner exchange of November 2004 (in full; Brenner's contributions were reworked for print); the openings of Gentles's and Callinicos's 1994 reviews; Wood's 1996 abstract; Leng (2024); Parthasarathi (2011, pp. 3–5) and Allen (2009, p. 4) in their publishers' excerpts. Merchants and Revolution, The Economics of Global Turbulence and the 1973 article are unread; their content is given only through named readers. The 2002 article with Isett was read in its opening and, for revision 1.144, in a truncated repost. He is not presented as the first to give class structure priority: he wrote that the view 'obviously derives from Marx's arguments', acknowledged Dobb, and used Tawney's and Hilton's evidence; Postan and Hatcher wrote that his 'essentials … have been put forward many times before'. The label 'political Marxism' was Bois's criticism in 1978 before it named a school. The debate as a whole is held by the group entry capitalismdebates; the respondents' critiques are drawn from it to this entry. The Pomeranz exchange (2000–2002) is later and smaller. Not to be confused with namesakes on Wikidata (an Austrian physicist, a German mining engineer).

nodes.label: Ellen Meiksins Wood
nodes.date_label: “The Separation of the Economic and the Political in Capitalism” 1981 · The Retreat from Class 1986 · The Pristine Culture of Capitalism 1991 · Democracy Against Capitalism 1995 · The Origin of Capitalism 1999 (expanded 2002) · “Eurocentric Anti-Eurocentrism” 2001 · Empire of Capital 2003 · Citizens to Lords 2008 · Liberty and Property 2012
nodes.description: A political theorist and historian, at York University in Toronto from 1967, who became the principal exponent of what Guy Bois, criticising Robert Brenner, had called 'political Marxism'. By the accounts of Alex Callinicos (1990) and Brenner (2016), she accepted the label while rejecting Bois's charge of voluntarism. 'The Separation of the Economic and the Political in Capitalism' (1981; revised for Democracy Against Capitalism, 1995) argued against G. A. Cohen's technological determinism that Marxism must not perpetuate 'the rigid conceptual separation of the "economic" and the "political"', since capitalism alone draws that line. The Pristine Culture of Capitalism (1991) turned the Nairn–Anderson theses of a backward Britain around: 'Britain - or rather England - was the world's first capitalist society', and the Continental 'modern' state signalled 'the continuing strength of pre-capitalist social property relations'. She sided there with E. P. Thompson's 'persuasive charge' against an idealised model of bourgeois revolution. In 'Eurocentric Anti-Eurocentrism' (2001) she traced a line from Marx's 'so-called primitive accumulation' through the transition debate, in which Dobb and Hilton 'challenged the commercialization model', to Brenner, who explained 'the emergence of what he calls "market dependence"'. The Origin of Capitalism (1999; expanded 2002) is unread here: its jacket says it challenges accounts that make capitalism's emergence 'seem natural and inevitable', and McAuley (2001) quotes it on 'the naturalization of capitalism, which denies its specificity' (pp. 7–8). Against anti-Eurocentric histories she held that the confusion of commerce with capitalism was itself Eurocentric. Critics called her position 'little more than a sociology of domination' (Callinicos), faulted 'the Brenner-Wood thesis' for making colonialism marginal (McAuley, after Blaut), and took it to be a caricature of Brenner's (Harman). She answered that slave plantations mattered 'quite a while after the emergence of capitalism in the English countryside'. She also wrote that Christopher Hill's work 'inspired' Brenner's social interpretation of the English Revolution.

Readers and critics: Alex Callinicos (1990); Christopher McAuley (2001); Chris Harman (2004); Robert Brenner (2016); Ken Hirschkop (2016).
nodes.scope_note: Read on 2026-10-18: 'The Separation of the Economic and the Political in Capitalism' (1981), opening sections and notes, in Verso's authorised repost, and the Cambridge Core openings of Democracy Against Capitalism (1995); the publisher's extract from The Pristine Culture of Capitalism (1991), without page numbers; 'Eurocentric Anti-Eurocentrism' (2001), her two replies (2002) and her essay on Christopher Hill (2003), in full on the Marxists Internet Archive; the abstract of her 1996 essay on the Brenner debate. The Origin of Capitalism is unread; its argument is given through its jacket, her own later summaries and quotations by McAuley (2001). Her acceptance of the label 'political Marxism' is reported by Callinicos (1990), Brenner (2016) and Hirschkop (2016); the passage where she accepted it was not read. She is not presented as the originator of the agrarian thesis, which she credited to Marx and Brenner, nor of the label, which was Bois's. Most of her readers and critics named here are Marxist political theorists rather than historians; her relation to historians runs through Brenner, Thompson and Hill. Her work on ancient and early modern political thought (1978–2012) is listed but not surveyed. The debate she joined is held by the group entry capitalismdebates.

nodes.label: Joel Mokyr
nodes.date_label: “Demand vs. Supply in the Industrial Revolution” 1977 · The Lever of Riches 1990 · editor’s introduction, The British Industrial Revolution 1999 · The Gifts of Athena 2002 · Max Weber Lecture on the European Enlightenment 2007 · The Enlightened Economy 2009 · with Kelly and Ó Gráda, “Precocious Albion” 2014 · A Culture of Growth 2016 · “The Mechanics of the Industrial Revolution” 2023 · with Tabellini, “Why China and Europe Diverged” 2023 · economics prize 2025
nodes.description: An economic historian of technology at Northwestern University who explained sustained growth by the growth of “useful knowledge”. In 1977 he judged demand factors “of a secondary order of importance” in the Industrial Revolution. His 1999 introduction defended the term against the charge that it was “a concept too many” and defined the Industrial Revolution as “a clustering of macroinventions leading to an acceleration in microinventions”. Two drafts of 2002, which say they adapt The Gifts of Athena (2002; unread here, though its reviewer Zorina Khan reports the same scheme), divided useful knowledge into “propositional” knowledge of natural regularities and “prescriptive” instructions (February), and called the Enlightenment’s contribution “the Industrial Enlightenment”, “the key to sustained and accelerating invention”, finding Pomeranz’s coal and New World land “not incorrect but by itself” unable to explain the gap (October). In a 2007 lecture the Enlightenment kept the early Industrial Revolution from “fizzling out”. Reviewing The Enlightened Economy (2009), C. Knick Harley wondered whether “causation from Enlightenment … to economic change actually existed”, while finding that the book made “a strong case” that “the history of ideas and their place in society needs to be at the core of the story” (2010). In Claude Diebolt’s account of A Culture of Growth (2016), culture works “as the invisible hand”, in a phenomenon “related to an elite” of philosophers, scientists, engineers, instrument makers and industrialists; Diebolt regretted “the lack of in-depth consideration of the German language literature” (2017). With Morgan Kelly and Cormac Ó Gráda he answered Robert Allen’s high-wage explanation with British workers’ human capital (2014), and found that across England’s 41 counties industrialisation occurred where wages began low and mechanical skills high (2023). With Guido Tabellini he traced China’s and Europe’s political divergence to clans and corporations (2023). In 2025 he was awarded a share of the economics prize in memory of Alfred Nobel, cited “for having identified the prerequisites for sustained growth through technological progress”.

nodes.label: E. A. Wrigley
nodes.date_label: Cambridge Group founded (with Laslett) 1964 · with Schofield, The Population History of England 1981 · Ellen McArthur lectures 1987 · Continuity, Chance and Change 1988 · with Davies, Oeppen and Schofield, English Population History from Family Reconstitution 1997 · Poverty, Progress, and Population 2004 · Energy and the English Industrial Revolution 2010 · The Path to Sustained Growth 2016
nodes.description: A historical demographer and economic historian at Cambridge, who founded the Cambridge Group for the History of Population and Social Structure with Peter Laslett in 1964. With Roger Schofield he reconstructed England’s population from the registers of 404 parishes by “back projection”, making it “possible for the first time” to follow “a secular cycle of population development” and its relation to economic change (1981); a family-reconstitution study, a technique perfected by Louis Henry, was its complement (1997). He called the industrial revolution his “first main research interest”, to which he “returned increasingly” after years of population history. In Continuity, Chance and Change (1988), from his 1987 Ellen McArthur lectures, he questioned it as “a cumulative, progressive, unitary phenomenon”: growth came from two sets of forces with “only an accidental relationship to one another in the early stages of their overlap in time”, as an “organic economy” bounded by the productivity of the land met a new one using mineral energy. Energy and the English Industrial Revolution (2010) asked “not how the period of more rapid growth began, but why it did not come to an end”, without offering energy as the only explanation: there could be “no single, ‘true’ account”, and to downplay institutional and scientific explanations would be “presumptuous and mildly ridiculous”. Mining coal “provided the solution” (2016). He judged Rostow’s “take-off” “now almost impossible to maintain” (2004). Berg and Hudson questioned causal inference from Wrigley and Schofield’s aggregate studies (1990). Readers set his energy argument beside Pomeranz’s coal (Mokyr in a draft of 2002, Huang in 2002, Clark and Jacks in 2007), and Wong said that China Transformed had followed his arguments on coal (2016).

Schofield, English Population History from Family Reconstitution, 1580–1837 (1997); Poverty, Progress, and Population (2004); Energy and the English Industrial Revolution (2010); “Energy and the English Industrial Revolution” (Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A, 2013); The Path to Sustained Growth (2016). Co-founder, with Peter Laslett, of the Cambridge Group for the History of Population and Social Structure (1964). Readers and critics: Maxine Berg and Pat Hudson (1990); Joel Mokyr and Philip Huang (2002); Gregory Clark and David Jacks (2007); R. Bin Wong (2016).

People, Cities and Wealth (1987) is unread. The comparisons with Pomeranz are readers’: no passage in which Pomeranz acknowledges Wrigley’s energy argument was read. Wong’s statement that China Transformed followed Wrigley is his 2016 retrospective. The wider argument about why industrialisation happened in Britain is held by the debate entry capitalismdebates; his population work stays on demography/aggregate_population.

nodes.label: Jan de Vries
nodes.date_label: The Economy of Europe in an Age of Crisis, 1600–1750 1976 · “The Industrial Revolution and the Industrious Revolution” 1994 · with van der Woude, The First Modern Economy 1997 · The Industrious Revolution 2008
nodes.description: An economic historian of the Netherlands and early modern Europe at Berkeley. The Economy of Europe in an Age of Crisis (1976) studied “the last great epoch before the onset of industrialization”; Pomeranz later called it “a good general critique of the overseas extraction thesis”. His “industrious revolution”, proposed in his Economic History Association presidential address published in 1994, was meant “to place the Industrial Revolution in a broader historical setting”: “a household-level change with important demand-side features that preceded the Industrial Revolution, a supply-side phenomenon”. In The Industrious Revolution (2008) he dated it to “roughly 1650–1850”, when households in north-western Europe and British North America reallocated “the time of their members” to earn money and to buy goods. He took the term from Akira Hayami, who had contrasted Japan’s labour-intensive path with Western industrialisation. He built the argument on the revisionist macroeconomics that cut British growth estimates “by more than half”, on the Cambridge Group’s finding that the western European nuclear family long predated industrialisation, and on Becker’s household economics; against a supply-side orthodoxy he illustrated with Mokyr, he sought to “restore demand as one of the cutting blades of Marshall’s supply and demand scissors” (2008). With Ad van der Woude he presented the Dutch Republic as “the first modern economy” (1997), against historians who saw its achievement as “backward looking”; van Zanden doubted that Dutch growth was much faster than England’s (2002). Pomeranz used the industrious revolution for Chinese households (2000). Reviewers found The Industrious Revolution “on all the main points, convincing” (Voth, 2009), or thought it made consumption a new “deus ex machina” and played down power between the sexes (van Nederveen Meerkerk, 2009). From the history of papermaking, Leonard Rosenband challenged its chronology and mechanism: paperworkers already laboured long hours at the outset of the period, and women and adolescents worked for wages in paper mills long before it (2016).

Readers and critics: Kenneth Pomeranz (2000); Philip Huang (2002); Jan Luiten van Zanden (2002); Hans-Joachim Voth and Elise van Nederveen Meerkerk (2009); Leonard Rosenband (2016).

nodes.label: R. Bin Wong
nodes.date_label: with Will, Nourish the People 1991 · China Transformed 1997 · with Rosenthal, Before and Beyond Divergence 2011 · “Divergence Displaced” 2016
nodes.description: A historian of China at UCLA whose China Transformed (1997) compared Chinese and European economic change, state formation and popular protest without treating Europe as the norm. As Joel Mokyr read it, Wong held that before 1800 Europe and China shared “Smithian expansion, rural industry, population expansion, a growth in consumer demand”, and that the “supply-driven Industrial Revolution that followed the demand-led Industrious Revolution in Europe did not happen in China” (1997, p. 31, as Mokyr quotes it). Kenneth Pomeranz wrote that he was “following a procedure outlined in Wong’s recent China Transformed”, while giving “greater stress than Wong does on global conjunctures” (2000). Wong later said that the book had located Europe’s difference in science and technology, “following arguments of E. A. Wrigley” on coal (2016). With Jean-Laurent Rosenthal, in Before and Beyond Divergence (2011), he turned to “political fragmentation in Europe and the presence of an unitary state for the Chinese empire”: war drew European craft production into cities, so that the question became “why was industrialization more likely to occur in Western Europe than in China” (his 2016 account); as Debin Ma reported the mechanism, higher urban wages there biased innovation towards saving labour. Ma judged the book “a good contribution in the Great Divergence debate” but found this “stimulating and striking hypothesis” “supported by fairly meager evidence in the chapter” (2012). In “Divergence Displaced” (2016) he judged Brenner’s agrarian social relations, Pomeranz’s coal and colonies and his own earlier book alike open to “non-falsifiability”. Mokyr had objected that “Bin Wong does not cite any book by Needham” (2002 draft).

nodes.scope_note: Read in his own words on 2026-10-18: “Divergence Displaced” (Comparativ, 2016, open access), pp. 71–80 closely, with pp. 81–100, a critique of Peer Vries, skimmed; China Transformed only in chapter openings read in an earlier revision. China Transformed’s argument is otherwise given through Mokyr’s quotations (2002), Pomeranz (2000), Huang (2002) and Parthasarathi (2011); Before and Beyond Divergence (2011, with Rosenthal) through Wong’s own 2016 summary and Ma’s review (2012); Nourish the People (1991, with Will) is dated from metadata only. Co-authored arguments are his co-authors’ as well. His statement that China Transformed followed Wrigley is a 2016 retrospective. The “California School” is a readers’ label, attributed by Frank and Vries to Goldstone, and is not used here as Wong’s own. The Great Divergence debate is held by capitalismdebates; global/comparison, global/eurasian_states and global/reciprocal_comparison_resources keep his comparative method.

nodes.label: The languages of class debate
nodes.date_label: The Making 1963 · Languages of Class 1983 · ILWCH forum 1987 · Descent into Discourse 1990 · Visions of the People 1991 · Vernon 1994 · “The End of Social History?” 1995 · Speaking for the People 1998 · ILWCH 57 2000 · The Future of Class in History 2007
nodes.description: Linked disputes over how experience, language, gender and social relations shape class formation and historical explanation. Thompson's preface (1963) made class a relationship, not a thing; Stedman Jones's Languages of Class (1983) set 'the linguistic cat among the social history pigeons' (Eley and Nield's words), while holding that 'how the two relate' — social and linguistic — 'must be rethought' (as quoted by Epstein). Foster, Gray, Epstein and Kirk answered (1985–87); Joan Scott asked that language and gender be taken seriously; Bryan Palmer replied (1987–90). Patrick Joyce set a 'family of populisms' against class (1991) and asked 'The End of Social History?' (1995); James Vernon asked who was afraid of the linguistic turn (1994); Jon Lawrence combined 'realist' and 'constructivist' approaches (1998). Related and intersecting controversies developed across several regions: Rancière and Sewell in France, Wilentz and Katznelson in the US, Canning in Germany, Chakrabarty and Chandavarkar in India, James in Latin America, Cooper in Africa, Parr and Sangster in Canada. Eley and Nield asked for 'a truce in the Left's culture wars' (Cooper, 2000) and wrote its retrospective (2007).
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Baseline: Thompson, The Making of the English Working Class (1963), preface; Johnson, 'Edward Thompson, Eugene Genovese, and Socialist-Humanist History' (1978); the Ruskin History Workshop debate (December 1979); Anderson, Arguments within English Marxism (1980). First round: Stedman Jones, 'The Language of Chartism' (1982), Languages of Class (1983); Foster (1985); Gray, Epstein, Cronin (1986); Kirk (1987); Scott, 'On Language, Gender, and Working-Class History', with Palmer, Stansell and Rabinbach, and 'A Reply to Criticism' (1987); Scott, Gender and the Politics of History (1988); Palmer, Descent into Discourse (1990). Second round: Joyce, Visions of the People (1991), Democratic Subjects (1994); Cannadine (1992–93); Mayfield and Thorne (1992; 1993); Lawrence and Taylor, 'The Poverty of Protest' (1993); Vernon, Politics and the People (1993), 'Who's Afraid of the "Linguistic Turn"?' (1994); Kirk (1994); Tilly, 'Softcore Solipsism' (1994); Joyce, 'The End of Social History?' (1995), ed., Class (1995); Eley and Nield, 'Starting Over' (1995); Joyce's reply and Steinberg (1996); Wahrman (1995); Vernon, ed., Re-reading the Constitution (1996); Lawrence and Taylor, eds, Party, State and Society (1997); Lawrence, Speaking for the People (1998); Cannadine, Class in Britain (1998); Vernon's review (1999) and Lawrence's response (2010). Spread: Sewell, Work and Revolution in France (1980); Rancière, 'The Myth of the Artisan' (1983) and reply (1984); Wilentz, 'Against Exceptionalism', with Salvatore and Hanagan (1984); Katznelson and Zolberg, eds, Working-Class Formation (1986); Reddy (1984; 1987); Steedman (1986); James, Resistance and Integration (1988); Chakrabarty, Rethinking Working-Class History (1989); Viotti da Costa, with Weinstein (1989); Bergquist (1990); Parr (1990; 1995); Valverde (1990; 1995); Roediger (1991); Canning (1992; 1996); Rose (1992); Hall (1992); Berlanstein, ed. (1993); Lüdtke (1993); Chandavarkar (1994; 1997; 1998); Clark (1995); Cooper (1995; 2000); French and James, eds (1997); Sangster (2000). Retrospective: Eley and Nield, 'Farewell to the Working Class?', with Cooper, Scott and the reply (2000), The Future of Class in History (2007); Joyce, 'What Is the Social in Social History?' (2010); Gunn and Vernon, eds, The Peculiarities of Liberal Modernity in Imperial Britain (2011).
nodes.scope_note: A Debate entry gathering exchanges; each author's own contribution stays on the field and person entries (gareth_stedman_jones, patrick_joyce, james_vernon, jon_lawrence, ep_thompson, joan_wallach_scott, bryan_d_palmer, joy_parr, dipesh_chakrabarty). Twelve strands: the British rounds (from Thompson's preface to Languages of Class; the first critics and the 1987 ILWCH forum; Visions of the People; the new political history; 'the end of social history?'; gender, race and class; the retrospectives of 2000–16) and the spread (United States, Canada, France, Germany; South Asia, Africa and Latin America). Research of 2026-10-22 (data/extension-2026/languages-of-class-2026-10-22/evidence-stedman-jones.md, -part2.md, evidence-joyce-vernon-lawrence.md, evidence-spread.md). Read in full: Foster 1985; Epstein 1986; the ILWCH editors' remarks of 1983, 1984 and 1987; Rancière's reply (1984); Salvatore (1984); Stedman Jones's 1975 review; Tilly 1994; the Joyce–Cannadine letters (1993); Vernon's review of Lawrence and Lawrence's response (1999/2010); Oddy and Vernon (2008/09); Lawrence 2011; Gunn and Vernon's introduction and Joyce's foreword (2011); Joyce 2014; Koditschek 2014; Eley and Nield 2000 (with the reply in part), Cooper 2000, Scott 2000; Sangster 2000; Bergquist 1990 (both pieces); the 2007 preface. Read in part: Kirk 1987 (pp. 2–5, 44–47 and earlier reads); Visions of the People, Democratic Subjects and Speaking for the People (chapter openings); Joyce 1996 and 2010 (openings); abstracts or publisher pages for Mayfield–Thorne 1992, Sewell 1980, Reddy 1987, Katznelson–Zolberg 1986, Canning 1996 (contents), Chandavarkar 1994 and 1998, James 1997–2001, Rose, Steedman, Roediger, Wahrman, Palmer 1990 (Temple page). Unread, known by title, metadata or named readers: Languages of Class itself (pages cited as quoted by Foster, Epstein and Kirk); Gray 1986; Cronin 1986; Scott's 1987 essay beyond p. 1 and her 1988 chapters; the whole Social History exchange of 1992–96 (Mayfield–Thorne, Lawrence–Taylor, Joyce's note and 1995 article, Vernon 1994, Kirk 1994, Eley–Nield 1995, Steinberg 1996); Johnson 1978; Anderson 1980; Sewell 1990; Wilentz and Hanagan 1984; Berlanstein 1993; Canning 1992; Eley 1989; Lüdtke; Kocka; Cooper 1995; Viotti da Costa 1989; Parr 1990 and 1995; Hall 1992; Cannadine 1992 and 1998; Dorothy Thompson 1984; Palmer 1990; The Future of Class in History beyond its preface. Chandavarkar 1997 is carried in the atlas's existing reading, whose route awaits re-verification on the publisher's site. Hostile characterisations (Eley and Nield's 'most viciously' of Palmer; Scott's 'Assent to Discourse'; Tilly's 'softcore solipsism') are recorded as the readers' words, not adopted. Rows for Stansell, Rabinbach, Wilentz, Reddy, Viotti da Costa, Steedman, Rose, Roediger and Hall rest on first pages, reference lists, publisher descriptions or metadata, as each row states.

representative_people.context: The Making's preface (1963; its wording on edge_924) is the text every round argued over, from Johnson's 'culturalism' (1978) to Cooper's 'people struggling not to be a working class' (2000) and Eley and Nield's 'Thompsonian rhetorics of experience' (2000).

representative_people.context: Found in The Making 'a disconcerting lack of objective coordinates as the narrative of class formation unfolds' (p. 33, as quoted by Bergquist 1990); the publisher's page says the book takes up 'human agency' through The Making. Body unread.
representative_people.works: Arguments within English Marxism (1980)

representative_people.context: Opens the debate: political language studied in its own right, Chartism as a political movement, 'experience' no longer the link between social being and consciousness (1982–83); restated the approach against 'the determinist fix' (1996; title) and in Lüdtke's Göttingen volume (1997; unread).
representative_people.works: 'The Language of Chartism' (1982); Languages of Class (1983); 'The Determinist Fix' (HWJ 42, 1996)

representative_people.context: Her Chartist Experience (1982, with Epstein) printed the first version of the essay; The Chartists (1984) is the 'social' account the revisionists oppose (Kirk 1987, n. 2), though Stedman Jones does not address her work directly (Kirk, n. 8); her interview records objections to inflated claims for a new attention to language.
representative_people.works: The Chartist Experience (ed. with Epstein, 1982); The Chartists (1984)

representative_people.context: The subject of Stedman Jones's 1975 review answered the book: its Saussurean assumptions 'are not argued'; the political/economic distinction fails on the 1842 strike; the result is 'an intellectual declassing of our understanding of language' (1985, read in full).
representative_people.works: Class Struggle and the Industrial Revolution (1974); 'The Declassing of Language' (NLR 150, 1985)

representative_people.context: Review essay in Social History: post-structuralist work on language is a field of debate rather than a firmly constituted method (p. 367, as quoted by Kirk 1987); Eley and Nield quote him on language as 'multilayered, complex, fractured' (2000, p. 7). Article unread.
representative_people.works: 'The Deconstructing of the English Working Class' (Social History 11:3, 1986)

representative_people.context: Co-editor of the volume that first printed the essay; accepted its descriptive analysis of Chartist ideology and its account of the state, rejected the restriction to public political language and the 'relatively autonomous force of language': the contest over 'the people' was 'a form of class struggle' (1986). Later, for Vernon, 'one of the first, and one of the best, practitioners of the new cultural history of British politics' (2004).
representative_people.works: The Chartist Experience (ed. with Dorothy Thompson, 1982); 'Rethinking the Categories of Working-Class History' (Labour/Le Travail 18, 1986); Radical Expression (1994); In Practice (2003)

representative_people.context: The most sustained reply of the first round: 'full support' for the opposition to reductionism, but the 'non-referential' approach is formalist, the state thesis thinly evidenced, and Chartism's class character 'falsely denied' — 'an unconvincing idealism' (1987, pp. 2–5, 44–47 read); 'a materialist view' of post-modernism followed (1994; title).
representative_people.works: 'In Defence of Class' (IRSH 32:1, 1987); 'History, Language, Ideas and Post-Modernism: A Materialist View' (Social History, 1994)

representative_people.context: Opened the North American round (ILWCH 1987): labour historians 'reduce this important concept [language] to the study of "words"' (p. 1); Stedman Jones had used language theory 'in an essentially conservative manner' (editors' summary); 'class struggle is produced in discourse' (reply, p. 40). In 2000 she answered Eley and Nield: 'Assent to Discourse'; her questions 'don't exclude class, but they don't require it either' (pp. 69, 72).

representative_people.context: Answered Scott from the Halifax strikes of 1842, 'Conscious of "the need to avoid economic determinism"' (1987, p. 14); Descent into Discourse (1990): 'Critical theory is no substitute for historical materialism; language is not life' (publisher's description; the book is unread, its pages known as quoted by Callinicos 1992). representative_people.context: Held that in Stedman Jones language 'is as instrumentalized in the notion of politics as economic interest is in the notion of class' (1987, p. 30, first page read); his notes run from de Man and Derrida to Rancière's La nuit des prolétaires.
