edges.evidence_note: Time essay pp. 58–59 uses Evans-Pritchard and Bourdieu; Moral Economy p. 135 invokes Mintz on markets. These are distinct resources, not a uniform anthropological model or proof that his cultural comparisons generalize universally.

edges.relationship: Rudé’s crowd history supplies an explicit resource for the moral-economy essay
edges.evidence_note: Primary 1971 pp. 76–78 credits Rudé and Rose when questioning reductive riot explanations. This group arrow is a particular crowd-history exchange; it does not imply all political history was prior to Thompson.
edges.map_label: Rudé and the study of crowds

edges.relationship: Thompson challenges explanations that treat workers chiefly as inputs or disturbances in industrial growth
edges.evidence_note: Making preface names Smelser; Moral Economy p. 77 criticizes Rostow’s tension chart; Time’s conclusion questions Moore/Kerr/Siegel. These specific objections do not refute every modernization account, and Thompson retains developmental assumptions of his own. Smelser’s checked publisher description identifies the cotton/family differentiation project; Rostow’s own chapter 2 includes political choices and timing qualifications. These narrower readings preserve Thompson’s specific objections without using his polemic as a complete account of either work.

edges.relationship: The moral-economy essay links market protest with customary expectations and legitimacy
edges.evidence_note: Selected primary opening and conclusion place material pressures within social obligations and organized action. This is an English historical inquiry; full case evidence and later revisions are not yet checked.

edges.relationship: The time-discipline essay embeds clocks in employment relations and cultural change
edges.evidence_note: Selected primary opening and conclusion examine task rhythms, wages, education and coercion. Technical innovation is part of an uneven social process, not a sufficient cause of one universal industrial sequence.

edges.relationship: Whigs and Hunters investigates property, common rights and the ambivalent operation of law
edges.evidence_note: Selected Peluso review identifies the 1975 book’s problem of domination and legal constraint. Original argument and case evidence remain unread; later political-ecology reception is not projected into the mapped period.

edges.relationship: Dobb explicitly uses Marx’s rent and production categories to frame feudal relations
edges.evidence_note: Reply pp. 157–159 and 164 cites Capital III; he interprets different compulsory surplus forms. This is named conceptual use, not proof of every historical generalization.

edges.relationship: Dobb credits Tawney’s account of rising small and middle producers
edges.evidence_note: Primary reply p. 164 names Tawney in his argument about capitalist formation. The precise Tawney passage is not independently identified here; the link is narrower than agreement on religion, politics or all transitions.

edges.relationship: Kosminsky and Unwin supply named historical resources in Dobb’s reply
edges.evidence_note: Primary pp. 164–165 cites Kosminsky’s peasant interpretation and tentatively recalls Unwin on guild development. Unwin attribution retains its uncertainty; Hilton’s later 1956 Kosminsky citation is not projected backward.

edges.relationship: Sweezy and Takahashi challenge different aspects of Dobb’s definition and geographical coverage
edges.evidence_note: Sweezy pp. 134–137 questions breadth and regional transfer; Takahashi pp. 313–315 calls for fuller French/German engagement while developing production-relation analysis. Two distinct interventions, not a united school or complete reading of both critiques. Revision 1.145: Sweezy's critique, now read in full (pp. 134–157), was offered as a correction from within: 'no theory which fails to take into account the factors which Dobb stresses … can be regarded as correct' (p. 142); his own model made feudalism 'a system of production for use' (p. 136) and the growth of trade 'the root cause' of its decline (p. 142).

edges.relationship: The transition debate makes coercion, trade interaction and accumulation hypotheses explicit
edges.evidence_note: Dobb’s reply pp. 159–167 rejects a simple internal/external either-or and admits inadequate evidence for a realization-phase hypothesis. Colonial-finance suggestions remain proposed research, not verified causal facts.

edges.relationship: Hilton explicitly adopts Bloch’s question of recurring peasant–lord conflict
edges.evidence_note: Bond Men introduction pp. 11–14 names Bloch while recognizing changes across periods. The resource is a research question, not endorsement of every Bloch conclusion or a timeless peasant model.
edges.map_label: Recurring conflict as a research question

edges.relationship: Duby supplies economic and cultural resources for Hilton’s medieval inquiry
edges.evidence_note: Bond Men names Duby among resources; the 1974 review opening positively evaluates exchange across Marxist/non-Marxist positions and distinguishes mentalities from class consciousness. Duby-specific reception, not membership or wholesale Annales adoption.

edges.relationship: Hilton questions Duby’s emphasis on late-medieval crisis when discussing peasant revolt
edges.evidence_note: Bond Men introduction pp. 12–14 recognizes Duby’s acknowledgment of earlier resistance but challenges its relative treatment. Applies to this particular Duby argument, not all Annales; the unread conclusion of the 1974 review is not the evidence.

edges.relationship: Genet questions period differentiation and the changing state in Hilton’s account
edges.evidence_note: Genet’s 1980 review p. 1069 praises the inquiry while criticizing early-medieval flattening and treatment of later state/fiscal intervention. One named reviewer, not a journal-wide consensus or independently adjudicated historical verdict.
edges.map_label: Genet: period differences and fiscal power

edges.relationship: Hilton questions Power’s relative absence of central-medieval peasant disturbances
edges.evidence_note: Bond Men introduction p. 12 cites Power’s Cambridge Medieval History discussion while advancing a longer conflict inquiry. Her original chapter is not independently read here; his conjecture about her twentieth-century context is not adopted as an established influence.

edges.relationship: Hilton names Maitland, Postan and Kosminsky among resources for peasant reconstruction
edges.evidence_note: Primary introduction pp. 10–11 specifies historians and the evidence they help reconstruct: holdings, crops, rents and status. Group arrow names particular scholarship, not economic history as one unitary source.

edges.relationship: Hilton acknowledges Hill’s corrections and advice on Bond Men Made Free
edges.evidence_note: Primary acknowledgments also credit Birrell, Dyer, Razi and students. Draft reading is a specific contribution, not coauthorship or blanket intellectual influence.

edges.relationship: Hilton relates peasant movements to organization, beliefs and differentiated outcomes
edges.evidence_note: Selected Bond Men introduction and concluding discussion distinguish structural antagonism from constant open fighting and caution against universal transfer. A preindustrial contribution to this broader social-history conversation, not the foundation of every later movement study.

edges.relationship: Torr translates, annotates and selects Marxist texts for English readers
edges.evidence_note: Renton identifies Selected Correspondence, Capital notes and Marx on China. These are editorial/pedagogical contributions with political contexts; original editions and every translation choice are not independently checked.

edges.relationship: Hill helps prepare chapters of Torr’s Mann biography
edges.evidence_note: Archive guide CP/IND/TORR/01/02–03 describes Hill/Morton contributions and Hill chapter drafts. Catalogue-level evidence supports collaboration; the manuscripts and exact published divisions are not independently collated.

edges.relationship: Torr supports publication and discussion of Hill’s English Revolution argument
edges.evidence_note: Renton describes her publishing role and quotes her 1948 letter crediting Hill’s work. This is specific support mediated through scholarly research; neither the original letter nor full pamphlet is newly read. The 1955 preface/opening is now read independently; the full pamphlet and original Torr letter remain outside the reading scope.

edges.relationship: Edward edits later fragments of Torr’s unfinished Mann project
edges.evidence_note: Hobsbawm’s memoir note identifies Our History 26–27 (1962); the archive guide records an earlier drafted chapter that did not appear in vol. 1. Editorial continuation is not a completed second volume or proof that the draft and published fragments were identical.

edges.relationship: The Mann project places a labour activist’s life within radical political history
edges.evidence_note: Renton and Murphy establish the project and competing interpretations; archival descriptions make collective preparation visible. Original monograph and fragment text remain unread, so no claim to have audited its case evidence.
edges.map_label: A labour life and its political framing

edges.relationship: Murphy questions Torr’s Marxian framing of Mann’s ethical and religious development
edges.evidence_note: The contemporary 1956 review combines praise with disagreement and personal acquaintance. This group arrow identifies Murphy specifically, not all biographers or an unqualified rejection of Torr.
edges.map_label: Murphy: moral vision and explanatory framing

edges.relationship: Hill’s “Norman Yoke” supplies Hobsbawm with an example of cultural inquiry within social explanation
edges.evidence_note: The 1980 reply cites the 1954 essay, reprinted in Puritanism and Revolution (1958). This specific use does not establish agreement on every aspect of Hill’s work.
edges.map_label: The Norman Yoke and cultural explanation

edges.relationship: Hobsbawm uses Braudel to question a simple division between narrative and structural history
edges.evidence_note: The narrative reply cites Braudel’s historical practice and 1980 Manceron review. Cited works are not independently read here.

edges.relationship: Hobsbawm uses Geertz’s cockfight essay in discussing small-scale interpretation
edges.evidence_note: The narrative reply identifies Deep Play as an example relevant to broader analytical questions; this is specific reception rather than adoption of all interpretive anthropology.

edges.relationship: Hobsbawm challenges Stone’s diagnosis of a retreat from analytical history
edges.evidence_note: The complete 1980 reply separates topics, explanation and presentation; his interpretation of other historians is situated, not a settled account of a universal turn.
edges.map_label: Changing subjects need not end explanation

edges.relationship: Blok challenges the social-bandit model through power and patronage
edges.evidence_note: Hobsbawm’s revised Postscript acknowledges the objection. Blok’s original article remains unread; the link records the named criticism as received by Hobsbawm.

edges.relationship: Sánchez and Meertens supply Colombian political-bandit research
edges.evidence_note: Bandits chapter 10 note 19 explicitly follows their ideas and identifies the 1987 chapter. Original chapter unread; the link identifies incoming research rather than assuming one-way European transmission.

edges.relationship: Hobsbawm’s bandit research prompts revision of protest models and cultural evidence
edges.evidence_note: The revised edition separates mediated heroic stories from conduct and addresses power and local differences. It does not abandon every social-protest claim.

edges.relationship: Hobsbawm explicitly uses Gellner’s definition and Hroch’s comparative distinctions
edges.evidence_note: Introduction pp. 9–12 identifies these resources; their original books are not newly read.

edges.relationship: Hobsbawm questions Gellner’s emphasis on modernization from above
edges.evidence_note: Introduction pp. 10–11 argues for investigating ordinary people’s differing identifications. This is Gellner-specific.

edges.relationship: Hobsbawm distinguishes official nationalism from changing popular identification
edges.evidence_note: Introduction pp. 11–12 states a research problem, not a completed empirical demonstration for every society.

edges.relationship: Hill identifies Dobb’s Studies as a resource for revising his revolution argument
edges.evidence_note: Explicit in the 1955 preface, not the original 1940 pamphlet. Hill acknowledges oversimplification; no full monograph reading is claimed.

edges.relationship: Hill credits Hilton with correcting errors and improving readability
edges.evidence_note: The World Turned Upside Down preface ix–x names this draft contribution. Reciprocal advice differs from coauthorship or uniform theoretical agreement.

edges.relationship: Hill names Yates’s work as a resource for reconstructing earlier intellectual settings
edges.evidence_note: Introduction pp. 1–6 relates magic, religion and rationality historically. This acknowledged resource does not establish that Hill accepted every Yates thesis.

edges.relationship: Hill identifies Rattansi and Webster among resources on earlier knowledge
edges.evidence_note: The primary introduction names particular scholarship in reconstructing intellectual settings; the group arrow does not imply a single history-of-science method or founding relationship.

edges.relationship: Barg’s differentiated Soviet comparisons inform Hill’s revolutionary historiography
edges.evidence_note: The accessible 1986 review opening values Barg and explicitly recognizes disagreement within Soviet scholarship. Original Russian works and the rest of the review remain unread.

edges.relationship: Davis challenges the Ranter account associated with Hill and Morton
edges.evidence_note: The 1987 exchange documents the dispute; organized sect, milieu and hostile labeling must be distinguished. Davis’s full monograph and Hill’s later reply are unread. Other correspondents do not share one verdict.

edges.relationship: Thompson defends Hill’s radical inquiry while distinguishing a milieu from a uniform sect
edges.evidence_note: The 1987 review and reply provide an intervention in the Ranter debate, not a definitive resolution of the historical evidence.

edges.relationship: Davis, Scott and Smith contest different parts of Thompson’s Ranter defense
edges.evidence_note: The letters address representation, anachronism, evidence and theology. Smith also criticizes Davis; the group arrow does not turn these scholars into one school.

edges.relationship: Hill makes radical religious alternatives part of English revolutionary history
edges.evidence_note: The primary introduction distinguishes porous movements and possibilities from later established sects; the subsequent disagreement does not erase the research question.

edges.relationship: Maitland, Gay and Savine supply named resources for Tawney’s agrarian inquiry
edges.evidence_note: The 1912 introduction evaluates previous reconstruction and evidence. This records particular scholarship, not an undifferentiated economic-history influence; original cited works remain unread.

edges.relationship: Tawney questions Weber’s causal weighting and treatment of religious differences
edges.evidence_note: Religion chapter IV note 32, pp. 316–317, values the problem while questioning nonreligious omissions and Calvinist/Puritan flattening. It also rejects purely economic reduction; acknowledgment and criticism coexist.

edges.relationship: Power shares unpublished earlier-period research with Clark
edges.evidence_note: Clark’s preface explicitly identifies this help in addressing the lack of medieval comparison material. It does not certify every comparison or establish coauthorship.

edges.relationship: Lilian Knowles directs Clark’s historical research
edges.evidence_note: Clark’s original preface names sustained guidance. The economic-history arrow identifies Knowles specifically and does not imply one uniform institutional doctrine.

edges.relationship: Schreiner supplies Clark’s question about women’s past economic conditions
edges.evidence_note: The primary preface explicitly credits Woman and Labour and separately names Gerlach’s encouragement. No wholesale theoretical identity or independent reading of Schreiner’s full book is claimed.

edges.relationship: Knowles guides Pinchbeck’s early research and use of materials
edges.evidence_note: Original preface vi distinguishes Knowles’s early contribution from Power’s later direction and manuscript criticism. It does not establish agreement on every finding.

edges.relationship: Dorothy George’s London inquiry supplies evidence used by Pinchbeck
edges.evidence_note: Introduction pp. 2–3 cites London Life for work, insecurity and poverty. Original George passages are not independently read; its 1925 date has separate catalogue support.

edges.relationship: Hamilton Thompson, Coulton and Postan contribute different documentary and editorial work
edges.evidence_note: Power’s 1922 preface names transcripts, translations and critical reading; Postan’s 1963 preface identifies later reconstruction. These are distinct mechanisms and dates, not one theoretical inheritance.
edges.map_label: Documentary help and later editorial reconstruction

edges.relationship: Power invokes Carlyle’s call to recover how people lived
edges.evidence_note: The Bodo opening quotes Carlyle as a resource for social inquiry. Her broad narrative of disciplinary innovation is not independently adopted, nor is the original Carlyle passage newly collated.
edges.map_label: Carlyle: ordinary lives as a historical question

edges.relationship: Erickson questions Clark’s chronology and assumptions about household equality
edges.evidence_note: The 1992 introduction combines criticism with appreciation; main case-by-case discussion remains unread.

edges.relationship: Power makes personal reconstruction a method of teaching social relations
edges.evidence_note: Her 1924 preface pairs people with documentary genres. This is a contribution to writing lives, not proof that narrative or social history began with her.
edges.map_label: Individual lives and explicit source genres

edges.relationship: Clark’s treatment of unpaid production remains a resource in Erickson’s reassessment
edges.evidence_note: Erickson explicitly values this dimension while disputing other claims. The link concerns a named reception, not every later gender historian.
edges.map_label: Unpaid production as a historical resource

edges.relationship: Maitland and Stubbs supply scholarly resources; Vinogradoff and documentary teachers support Cam’s work
edges.evidence_note: Cam’s primary Stubbs opening and Cheney’s account distinguish reading, publication sponsorship and Hall/Jenkinson training. The group arrow names different mechanisms rather than a uniform doctrine.

edges.relationship: Cheney questions some legal deductions and broad narratives of legal progress
edges.evidence_note: Memoir pp. 303–305 combines these reservations with substantial appreciation. It does not reject the value of Cam’s local inquiry or independently settle each legal case.
edges.map_label: Cheney: juristic inference and broad conclusions

edges.relationship: Cam interprets Maitland’s scholarship in a prefatory memoir
edges.evidence_note: Cheney p. 304 identifies the 1957 memoir for Selected Historical Essays. Its full text is not newly read; this is a documented contribution to historians’ life writing.

edges.relationship: Bing, Gombrich, Walker and R. W. Yates contribute to Yates’s reconstruction
edges.evidence_note: Primary preface names draft criticism, discussions, translation checking and drawings. Warburg’s questions reach Yates through Bing, not personal contact. The proposed Globe reconstruction is an argument, not a verified building plan.

edges.relationship: Rossi’s memory research supplies a resource Yates uses with qualifications
edges.evidence_note: Preface xiii and chapter XVII explicitly use Clavis universalis (1960); pp. 372–373 qualify agreement over Bacon. Rossi’s full book is not independently read.
edges.map_label: Rossi: a resource with different emphases

edges.relationship: Gombrich recalls evidential hesitation and internal criticism alongside admiration
edges.evidence_note: The complete 1983 memorial describes Bing/Saxl criticism and Yates’s defense of larger interpretations. It declines full evaluation; no case-by-case disproof or unanimous Warburg position is claimed.

edges.relationship: Wedgwood participates in Tawney’s economic-history seminar
edges.evidence_note: Woolrych p. 529 documents attendance after graduation. This is a teaching encounter, not proof that her mature narrative adopted Tawney’s causal conclusions.

edges.relationship: Neale advises on structure; Cooper, Kearney and Aylmer contribute to revaluation
edges.evidence_note: Woolrych pp. 523–524 differentiates early advice from later scholarship and newly available documents. Original correspondence and the cited scholars’ cases remain unread.
edges.map_label: Advice and research behind Strafford’s revaluation

edges.relationship: Parker challenges the framing and negative conclusion of The Thirty Years War
edges.evidence_note: Woolrych p. 525 n. 5 attributes criticism to Parker’s 1984 book, pp. xv and 216–217. These original pages are not independently collated; criticism coexists with recognition of the book’s achievement.

edges.relationship: Woolrych questions occasional eulogy and limits of biographical scale
edges.evidence_note: Memoir pp. 523–525 assesses early Strafford and William the Silent while valuing the later revaluation. It is not a claim that all her biographies share one uncorrected flaw.

edges.relationship: Wedgwood connects poetry and visual culture with political imagination
edges.evidence_note: Woolrych p. 532 discusses Poetry and Politics under the Stuarts (1960), including court masques and popular verse. Original cases remain unread; the placement does not imply Burckhardt/Huizinga descent.

edges.relationship: Schwimmer and Grierson help shape archival projects through proposal, disagreement and sustained institutional work
edges.evidence_note: Voss-Hubbard pp. 19–30 differentiates Schwimmer’s pacifist project from the broader WCWA and Grierson’s collecting/access work at Smith. Collective practice is not doctrinal agreement or sole authorship.

edges.relationship: Black women’s archival participation exposes unequal authority and support within WCWA
edges.evidence_note: Voss-Hubbard pp. 20–21 reports Thurman/Bethune/NCNW involvement and dissatisfaction, with no Black directors and limited support for fieldwork. This criticism of organizational practice is mediated through the 1995 study, not a claim that all Black women shared one response or a direct refutation of the 1946 book.
edges.map_label: WCWA: racial inclusion, authority and resources

edges.relationship: Mary Beard coauthors broad histories of American civilization with Charles Beard
edges.evidence_note: The Rise of American Civilization (1927) and America in Midpassage (1939) are documented collaborative works. Precise division of authorship and identical interpretations are not established; her separate women’s-history work remains distinct.

edges.relationship: Charles Beard participates in the documented partnership of historical writing
edges.evidence_note: The reciprocal contribution names a particular coauthor rather than a uniform school acting on Mary Beard. No surviving correspondence between the couple is claimed, nor a precise allocation of chapters.

edges.relationship: Anne Firor Scott reintroduces Spruill through later editions and recovery of earlier scholarship
edges.evidence_note: Richter documents the 1972 introduction and revised 1998 introduction; Smithsonian records Spruill’s inclusion in Scott’s Unheard Voices (1993). This is editorial reception, not an influence on the original 1938 research.

edges.relationship: Julie Richter identifies questions not asked about Black and Native women
edges.evidence_note: The 1999 review explicitly acknowledges their presence in the book while questioning the scope of inquiry; it also values regional/status distinctions and documents practical use. No total absence or dismissal of the book is asserted.
edges.map_label: Richter: racial scope of the inquiry

edges.relationship: Spruill examines household material life and separates prescribed ideals from recorded conduct
edges.evidence_note: Richter describes dwellings, utensils, clothing and books, quoting p. 208 on reading prescriptions. This is a documented earlier research resource, not proof of direct transmission to a later consumption school.
edges.map_label: Household objects, reading and prescribed ideals

edges.relationship: Wright and the Massachusetts bureau help design and tabulate the domestic-service inquiry
edges.evidence_note: The original preface identifies schedules, advance census data, bureau collation and Wadlin/Pidgin assistance. Named methodological work is distinct from ownership of Salmon’s conclusions or modern probability sampling.

edges.relationship: Salmon treats household employment as a labor question connected to industrial change
edges.evidence_note: Chapters I–II challenge the reduction of domestic service to personal relations and describe changing production/division of labor. Her general historical explanation and normative judgments are attributed; proposed remedies are not independently evaluated.

edges.relationship: Salmon combines employer and worker questionnaires with statistical comparisons and discussion of nonresponse
edges.evidence_note: Original preface explains network distribution, respondent hesitations and comparative tabulation. This is earlier quantitative practice; no general influence on later cliometrics or independent validation of the tables is claimed.

edges.relationship: Vassar women distribute schedules and Underhill supports manuscript production
edges.evidence_note: The original preface acknowledges students/alumnae, respondents and A. Underhill’s manuscript, proof and index work. Collection description identifies Adelaide Underhill’s partnership; unnamed respondents remain visible rather than being absorbed into a solitary-author narrative.
edges.map_label: Survey networks and Underhill’s editorial work

edges.relationship: Tyler’s teaching supplies Salmon with a principle for evaluating a work by its purpose
edges.evidence_note: The 1906 Apologia vi explicitly recalls this instruction. The broad critical-scholarship endpoint identifies Tyler’s contextual place, not a demonstrated Ranke-to-Salmon line or proof that all her methods derive from one teacher.
edges.map_label: Tyler: evaluating the purpose of a work

edges.relationship: Black historical collections and Terrell’s papers supply documentary resources for Flexner’s wider coverage
edges.evidence_note: Rupp p. 163 identifies Schomburg, Howard and Terrell collections in Flexner’s bibliography. This is mediated evidence of documentary use, not direct personal advice, consultation of those archives here or a claim that Black women’s activity was fully covered.
edges.map_label: Schomburg, Howard and Terrell documentary resources

edges.relationship: Rupp questions the limits of movement categories and the absence of private relationships in Flexner’s account
edges.evidence_note: Available 1992 passages value the inclusion of Black and white working women while questioning other exclusions and distinguishing historical self-identification from broader collective activity. Missing preview pages are not inferred; this is later reception.

edges.relationship: Ostrander questions suffragist self-definition and the causal integration of other reforms
edges.evidence_note: The complete review recognizes extensive research and Flexner’s narrower stated aim while examining abolition, temperance and evangelical support. His criticism is a specific intervention, not the position of all political historians.

edges.relationship: Frances James asks for a structural explanation through private property and a program beyond reform
edges.evidence_note: The 1960 review also welcomes labor and Black women’s coverage. This particular Marxist criticism does not make the book devoid of explanation, identify James with Janet Wilson James or establish a uniform Marxist response.

edges.relationship: Tuchman explicitly invokes Ranke’s historical truth while acknowledging limits to reconstruction
edges.evidence_note: The publisher excerpt of “In Search of History” names Ranke and insists on staying within evidence. This is documented reception of a principle, not proof that all Tuchman’s methods descend from Ranke or that every claim is accurate.
edges.map_label: Ranke: truth, evidence and incomplete recovery

edges.relationship: Named teachers, researchers, medieval specialists and an editor support Tuchman’s historical practice
edges.evidence_note: Her excerpt recalls McIlwain’s teaching; A Distant Mirror acknowledges Brown and Henneman’s advice, Alma’s substantial research and critical reading, and Gottlieb’s editing, among other assistance. The broad endpoint groups specific contributions, not a school’s unified doctrine or adviser endorsement.
edges.map_label: Teaching, specialist advice, research and editing

edges.relationship: Stone questions whether Tuchman’s narrative selection explains institutions and historical change
edges.evidence_note: The 1978 review praises scholarship and public communication while criticizing modern analogy and event selection. Placement connects a specific narrative-method debate to the later revival neighborhood; it does not backdate the 1979 diagnosis or make Stone opposed to all narrative.

edges.relationship: Fox-Genovese defends narrative interpretation and challenges Stone’s assumptions about crisis and progress
edges.evidence_note: Her December 1978 letter explicitly states that Tuchman does not subscribe to Marxism. This is a supportive critical intervention in reception, not an influence on the completed book or endorsement of every conclusion; Stone’s reply remains visible in the same source.

edges.relationship: Tuchman uses Coucy’s life as a narrative vehicle through a wider historical period
edges.evidence_note: The foreword explains the selection and documentary gaps; Stone questions the protagonist’s biographical visibility and the relation to institutional explanation. The method is a resource for discussing biography’s scale and limits, not proof of representative sampling.
edges.map_label: Coucy: a life organizing a wider narrative

edges.relationship: Delbrück explicitly locates his military source criticism in Ranke’s spirit
edges.evidence_note: The 1900 preface names this commitment while integrating practical checks. A documented self-positioning, not a claim that Ranke founded all military scholarship or that Delbrück merely repeats him.

edges.relationship: Beloch’s ancient population estimates supply Delbrück with a resource for assessing military numbers
edges.evidence_note: Delbrück explicitly credits the 1886 work while correcting estimates. The later teaching umbrella includes this earlier population inquiry; no influence from the 1964 Cambridge Group is backdated. Revision 1.142: Delbrück’s 1913 lectures (pp. 5–23, read) make ‘the number of the warriors’ the first question of military history and weigh Thucydides’ figures for Athenian citizen soldiers as ‘subjectively beyond every doubt’ while their meaning ‘is not absolutely to be determined’ (pp. 16–17); Beloch is not named in the pages read.
edges.map_label: Beloch: population constraints and military figures

edges.relationship: Completing Pertz’s Gneisenau biography becomes a route into Delbrück’s wider military scholarship
edges.evidence_note: Delbrück’s first preface recalls Brühl’s mediation of the 1877 commission, Clausewitz reading and officer conversations. This is a specific self-reported research trajectory, not generic subject overlap; correspondence has not been independently examined.
edges.map_label: Pertz, Brühl and the Gneisenau project

edges.relationship: Howard and Paret reinterpret Clausewitz through their collaborative 1976 translation
edges.evidence_note: Strachan documents the proposal and changing publication plan and later criticizes modernized political vocabulary. This is an attributed account of translation and reception, not an independent German/English collation or a claim that every change is an error.
edges.map_label: Howard and Paret: translation as interpretation

edges.relationship: Keegan challenges Clausewitz through an account that places culture against political explanation
edges.evidence_note: The 1993 argument is mediated by Bassford’s critical 1994 reception; Keegan’s original book passages remain unread here. Keep this distinct from The Face of Battle and from a unified military-history rejection of strategic theory.
edges.map_label: Keegan: culture and the Clausewitz debate

edges.relationship: Bassford disputes Keegan’s separation of culture from politics and his reading of Clausewitz
edges.evidence_note: The complete 1994 polemic values Keegan’s earlier battle study and acknowledges limits to Clausewitz. Personal motive claims are not adopted; later web corrections about ideal/absolute war and translation are separately dated.
edges.map_label: Bassford: culture, politics and textual interpretation

edges.relationship: The military-revolution debate tests the explanatory role of technical change
edges.evidence_note: Rogers’s introduction presents Parker’s fortification argument and competing causal accounts. This makes technical causation a historical question; it does not certify a uniform technological determinism.
edges.map_label: Military change and competing causal explanations

edges.relationship: Military finance research qualifies automatic links between war and state centralization
edges.evidence_note: Rogers summarizes I. A. A. Thompson’s political-bargaining argument. This is a specific contribution to comparative state-formation questions, with the original essay still unread.

edges.relationship: Bourdieu questions retrospective coherence in biographical accounts
edges.evidence_note: The 1986 essay examines institutional naming, interviews and trajectories across changing fields. It criticizes a manner of constructing lives, not every biography or all agency; the practice umbrella is not a unified position.
edges.map_label: Bourdieu: the constructed unity of a life

edges.relationship: Davis explicitly uses Certeau’s account of stories in interpreting Glikl’s life writing
edges.evidence_note: The selected Glikl opening and acknowledgments document a named resource and intellectual debt. This differs from Bourdieu’s criticism; sharing a teaching umbrella does not collapse their arguments.
edges.map_label: Certeau: stories as a resource for Davis

edges.relationship: Davis draws on dispersed relations of power when assessing the position of her three subjects
edges.evidence_note: Her conclusion cites History of Sexuality I, pp. 92–93, while showing that European women’s marginality can coexist with colonial domination. This is a specific use in 1995, not a claim that Foucault founded comparative biography.
edges.map_label: Davis: marginality and relations of power

edges.relationship: Levi develops a method for examining choices, norms and group formation through lives
edges.evidence_note: The complete 1989 essay accepts Bourdieu’s warning but emphasizes bounded room to act within contradictory norms. This methodological contribution coexists with the undirected comparison of biography and microhistory; it does not make all life writing microstoria.

edges.relationship: Levi questions assumed group cohesion in Chartier’s account of representations and practices
edges.evidence_note: Printed pp. 1334–1335 and notes 18/20 target the essay in La rappresentazione del sociale (1989). Levi values the intervention but argues that individuals and groups need distinct procedures and that group formation itself needs explanation. Do not conflate this citation with another 1989 French article or generalize to all Chartier.
edges.map_label: Levi: how are coherent groups produced?

edges.relationship: Robbe-Grillet’s challenge to coherent life narration supplies Bourdieu with an explicit literary resource
edges.evidence_note: Bourdieu cites Le Miroir qui revient (1984), p. 208, while declining to adopt all the associated philosophy. The original literary work remains mediated; this is a specific resource for the 1986 essay, not the origin of all practice theory.

edges.relationship: Levi uses discontinuous and dialogic literary narration to question the uniformly coherent historical actor
edges.evidence_note: Sterne and Diderot are named examples in the 1989 essay. This is a documented later methodological use, not a claim that novels founded Italian microhistory; the original novels were not read here.
edges.map_label: Levi’s literary examples and historical actors

edges.relationship: Woolf tests the limits of Strachey’s literary biography through contrasting royal lives
edges.evidence_note: Her 1939 essay praises Queen Victoria while criticizing Elizabeth and Essex for its combination of invention and limited evidence. Preserve the positive judgment and the specificity of her target; it is not a uniform condemnation of Strachey or literary form.

edges.relationship: A Freud reading circle stimulates Gay’s historical interests
edges.evidence_note: Gay recalls Neumann, his unnamed wife and Marcuse in 1950/1951. This is participant testimony about a specific resource, not the origin of all psychohistory.

edges.relationship: Schapiro questions the historical evidence of Freud’s Leonardo interpretation
edges.evidence_note: Translation, manuscript context and alternative explanations constrain inference. Schapiro separates criticism of this application from a rejection of psychoanalysis; his inclusion here is methodological.
edges.map_label: Schapiro: evidence for the Leonardo interpretation

edges.relationship: Pollock questions deMause’s selected sources and broad story of childhood improvement
edges.evidence_note: Her 1981 thesis, section 2.2.3, criticizes evidential selection and a progressive ending. This is a named childhood-history intervention within the demographic/family umbrella, not a consensus verdict.
edges.map_label: Pollock: selection and the progress narrative

edges.relationship: deMause challenges Pollock’s inferences from silence in parental diaries
edges.evidence_note: His 1988 response targets her 1983 book and says earlier childrearing modes can persist. This criticism is attributed; the book and diary witnesses were not independently collated here.
edges.map_label: deMause: what diary silence can establish

edges.relationship: deMause invokes paradigm change to explain resistance to his childhood-history program
edges.evidence_note: His 1988 conclusion and note 116 cite The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962). This records an appropriation of Kuhn, not Kuhn’s endorsement or proof that criticism signals scientific validity.

edges.relationship: Althusser credits Lacan with a reading lesson extending beyond Freud
edges.evidence_note: Reading Capital Part I note 1 explicitly acknowledges the debt. The Freud and Lacan public excerpt and editorial also document appropriation and Althusser’s later correction of his own culturalist overtones; Lacan’s endorsement is not implied.
edges.map_label: Lacan’s reading of Freud as a methodological resource

edges.relationship: Bachelard, Canguilhem and Cavaillès provide explicitly acknowledged epistemological resources
edges.evidence_note: For Marx credits Bachelard’s break; Reading Capital note 1 names the readers and note 21 cites Canguilhem’s 1955 reflex study. This establishes acknowledgment, not a newly read original Canguilhem argument or uniform philosophical agreement.

edges.relationship: Althusser names Foucault among his resources for reading learned works
edges.evidence_note: Reading Capital Part I note 1 explicitly acknowledges Foucault alongside other readers. The acknowledgment alone does not identify a particular borrowed Foucault passage or establish later agreement.
edges.map_label: An explicit acknowledgment in Reading Capital

edges.relationship: Althusser uses Gramsci to expand the problem of state power and superstructures
edges.evidence_note: The 1962 conclusion and 1970 apparatus discussion/footnote 7 name Gramsci. Althusser values the extension beyond a repressive state while judging the notes unsystematized; that judgment is his, not an independent verdict on Gramsci.
edges.map_label: Civil institutions, ideology and state power

edges.relationship: Althusser invokes Freud in explaining the familial constitution of subjects
edges.evidence_note: The interpellation section explicitly names Freud when discussing the expected child and family ideology. The NLR excerpt supplies philosophical context; universal developmental and binary assumptions are attributed, not established facts. This is distinct from Lacan’s methodological contribution.
edges.map_label: Freud and the expected familial subject

edges.relationship: Scott questions universal sexual antagonism as an explanation of historical variation
edges.evidence_note: Scott pp. 1062–1066 finds constructed subjectivity instructive but questions phallic universality and binary antagonism, including in her discussion of Alexander. This is a particular critical use, not a rejection of every psychoanalytic history or a consensus of gender historians.

edges.relationship: Derrida questions the language of Foucault’s archaeology of silence and his Descartes interpretation
edges.evidence_note: The Cogito opening asks whether the historical reading of Descartes and the attempt to let madness speak can escape the language of reason. Derrida also recognizes qualifications within Foucault’s book. Selected primary pages support this objection, not a verdict on the entire book or all later Foucault.
edges.map_label: Reason and the language of an archaeology of silence

edges.relationship: Foucault disputes Derrida’s Descartes reading and its account of discursive practice
edges.evidence_note: The reply differentiates meditative exercise from demonstration and alleges that Derrida textualizes discursive practices. This is Foucault’s situated criticism, not a neutral definition of deconstruction; Derrida’s 1983 letter explicitly includes social and institutional structures.
edges.map_label: Meditative practice and the limits of textual reading

edges.relationship: Scott uses deconstruction to historicize hierarchical oppositions
edges.evidence_note: Scott’s 1986 p. 1066 explicitly invokes Derrida and Culler in rejecting fixed oppositions as the basis for historical analysis. This particular productive use differs from her criticism of universal Lacanian antagonism and does not establish a consensus among gender historians.
edges.map_label: Scott’s critical use of hierarchical oppositions

edges.relationship: Combe’s study of archival access supplies an explicit historical resource to Derrida
edges.evidence_note: Archive Fever p. 4 note 1 names Combe’s Archives interdites and discusses professional and gendered archival authority. The memory entry locates this particular archival-history interlocutor; the whole field is not claimed to have shaped Derrida. Combe’s original cited pages remain uncollated.
edges.map_label: Sonia Combe on archives and historical authority

edges.relationship: Derrida contributes an account of archival authority and technical inscription
edges.evidence_note: Archive Fever opening and pp. 7–15 distinguish archives from spontaneous memory and ask about recording, preservation and destruction. This is a conceptual contribution to questions of memory and archives, not evidence of universal uptake by memory historians.
edges.map_label: Archives, inscription and the limits of recollection

edges.relationship: Derrida reworks Freud’s destruction drive and technical model of memory
edges.evidence_note: Archive Fever pp. 7–15 explicitly discusses Civilization and Its Discontents, Beyond the Pleasure Principle and the Mystic Pad, recalling an earlier Derrida essay. The selected pages establish a philosophical appropriation and criticism, not independent validation of the drive or a new reading of every cited original.
edges.map_label: Freud’s destruction drive and the Mystic Pad

edges.relationship: Foucault compares critiques of rationality across distinct French and Frankfurt inquiries
edges.evidence_note: The 1985 Canguilhem excerpt draws the comparison while preserving different domains and styles. The 1982 essay’s particular Habermas qualification does not establish a wholesale rejection or direct descent. Undirected teaching comparison, not influence or a shared doctrine.
edges.map_label: Different inquiries into rationality and its history

edges.relationship: Nietzsche quotes Burckhardt on Renaissance cultural recovery
edges.evidence_note: The 1874 essay §3 explicitly invokes Burckhardt while examining antiquarian uses of history. This is a specific textual resource located through the earlier-cultural-history entry, not an assertion that Nietzsche adopts Burckhardt’s entire approach or politics; the original quotation is not collated.

edges.relationship: Barthes explicitly invokes Nietzsche when discussing historical facts and meaning
edges.evidence_note: The Discourse of History section III quotes Nietzsche as a resource for questioning facts in themselves. The original aphorism witness remains unidentified; Nietzsche’s own Genealogy also calls for documentary inquiry, so the quotation is not treated as a complete account of his epistemology.
edges.map_label: Facts, meaning and a named Nietzsche quotation

edges.relationship: Nietzsche contributes questions about history’s uses, genealogical explanation and objectivity
edges.evidence_note: The 1874 essay and Genealogy preface, II.12–13 and III.12 support these distinct philosophical questions. This is an earlier conceptual contribution, not membership in later analytic disputes or proof of universal reception. BeckerIII directly quotes Beyond Good and Evil in questioning the self-effacing historian; its original aphorism is not newly collated.
edges.map_label: Uses of history, changing functions and perspective

edges.relationship: Hebdige adapts Barthes’s image analysis and account of naturalized meaning to subcultural style
edges.evidence_note: Subculture pp. 100–102 explicitly invokes The Rhetoric of the Image and Mythologies, making an analogy between emphatic styles and advertising. This documents a particular appropriation, not the claims of all cultural studies or Barthes’s own empirical research into the subcultures.
edges.map_label: Hebdige: style, images and naturalized meanings

edges.relationship: Bann uses Barthes to analyze the rhetorical construction of historical reference
edges.evidence_note: Bann’s selected 1983/1990 discussion explicitly adopts semiological analysis while preserving the achievement of historical research and its source-based construction. This is particular reception, not a consensus or an assertion that textual effects replace evidential scrutiny.

edges.relationship: Bann questions the suggestion that historians have moved beyond concern with reality
edges.evidence_note: The selected discussion on pp. 40–41 questions the generality of Barthes’s 1967 conclusion while retaining its analytical value. Bann’s speculation that Barthes might later revise it is not evidence that such a revision actually occurred.
edges.map_label: Bann: reality remains a historical concern

edges.relationship: Barthes explicitly connects formal myth analysis with Marxian historical criticism
edges.evidence_note: Myth Today invokes Marx on human production/use and Engels on coordinating distinct sciences. This is a specified conceptual resource for examining naturalized meanings, not an assertion that semiology is sufficient or that all Marxists share Barthes’s class and revolutionary claims.
edges.map_label: Historical production behind apparently natural meanings

edges.relationship: Vernant’s study of tragic ambiguity supplies a named resource to Barthes
edges.evidence_note: The Death of the Author invokes Vernant on words heard differently by dramatic characters and spectators. The anthropology entry locates this historical-cultural interlocutor; it does not establish the influence of an entire discipline or independently verify Vernant’s original work.
edges.map_label: Vernant on tragic language and spectators

edges.relationship: Barthes questions narrative transparency through readings of Michelet and Thierry
edges.evidence_note: The historical-discourse and reality-effect essays analyze how narration and details signify the real. This is a particular criticism of representational claims, not a dismissal of all national histories or an independent refutation of their factual content.
edges.map_label: Michelet, Thierry and narrative claims to reality

edges.relationship: Michelet explicitly draws on Vico and quotes Mill in explaining historical self-formation
edges.evidence_note: The umbrella locates two named resources in Michelet’s preface, not the influence of all philosophy on all national history. Original Vico/Mill texts remain uncollated.
edges.map_label: Vico and Mill in Michelet’s account

edges.relationship: Michelet reflects on how historical inquiry transforms its author
edges.evidence_note: The preface pp. 143–144 makes the historian’s involvement an explicit epistemic question. This is a conceptual contribution, not a claim of universal later reception or permission to invent evidence.
edges.map_label: History and historian form one another

edges.relationship: Lamprecht explicitly credits Herder’s attention to collective historical life
edges.evidence_note: What Is History? pp. 19–21 cites Herder while constructing Lamprecht’s own historical-method argument. The origin claim and developmental hierarchy are attributed, and Herder’s original text is not independently collated.

edges.relationship: Lamprecht contests the explanatory priority of individual-centered history while distinguishing Ranke from his disciples
edges.evidence_note: Lecture I pp. 16–23 discusses idealism, collective conditions and Ranke’s distinctive achievement; von Sybel’s role is separately assessed. This is Lamprecht’s polemical interpretation, not a settled characterization of all Rankean practice.
edges.map_label: Lamprecht: collective conditions and Ranke’s legacy

edges.relationship: Chatterjee extends the Subaltern critique from nationalist historiography to nationalist thought as a 'derivative discourse' (1986)
edges.evidence_note: Guha's 1982 statement (read) opened the critique of elite historiography; his own critique is the separate edge from his person entry. This edge records the distinct extension to nationalist thought. Sarkar (1997, pp. 91–92, read), a former member, traces how Partha Chatterjee's Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World (1986) carried the critique to the colonized intelligentsia's 'derivative discourses', and objects that 'A project that had started with a trenchant attack on elite nationalist historiography had now chosen as its hero the principal iconic figure of official Indian nationalism' (p. 92). Later reading, labelled: Chakrabarty (2000, p. 25) writes that Chatterjee's book 'extended Guha's criticisms of nationalist historiography into a full-blown, brilliant critique of nationalist thought itself'. The arrow does not claim a denial of all national histories.

edges.relationship: Huizinga asks how surviving images and texts produce different pictures of an age
edges.evidence_note: The chapter XIX opening distinguishes the evidence preserved by art, literature and official records and asks about lost practical settings. This is a question about historical knowing, not proof that any source class transparently preserves an entire culture.

edges.relationship: Cultural and national syntheses both connect political arrangements with wider forms of life
edges.evidence_note: Burckhardt’s political-cultural argument and Michelet’s organic national reconstruction show overlapping questions with different methods and objects. This editorial comparison asserts no transmission or shared doctrine.

edges.relationship: Dilthey reworks Kant’s critical project and Hegel’s objective spirit
edges.evidence_note: Named resources supported by Makkreel and the volume editors; the later program adapts these resources with disagreements. No uniform influence of all philosophy on all historicism, and no original Hegel corpus collation.
edges.map_label: Kant and Hegel as Dilthey’s resources

edges.relationship: Croce contests Droysen’s treatment of historical source categories while recognizing its philosophical value
edges.evidence_note: Part I chapter I discusses Droysen directly and also defends preservation as useful. The target is a specified methodological distinction within critical scholarship, not an attack by all idealists on Ranke or documents.

edges.relationship: Droysen distinguishes source criticism from the further work of historical interpretation
edges.evidence_note: Selected §§28–41 make uncertainty, conditions, will and interpretive limits explicit. Ranke’s own selections also join factual inquiry to wider relations. This identifies conceptual work, not a claim that later philosophers all read these passages.

edges.relationship: Dilthey, Croce and Collingwood formulate distinct accounts of historical knowing
edges.evidence_note: Primary selections support human sciences and practical statements, present historical questions, and evidence-dependent rethinking respectively. This contribution is distinct from the existing undirected comparison with general-law explanation; no single doctrine or blanket reception is inferred. BeckerII explicitly credits Croce’s contemporaneity; Carr chapter1 critically engages Croce, Collingwood and Oakeshott. These now supply particular reception in addition to the earlier conceptual passages.

edges.relationship: Langlois and Seignobos’s contextual language rules precede later linguistic debates
edges.evidence_note: Book II chapter VI makes historical usage, context and the separation of meaning from truth explicit. This editorial comparison challenges a claim that attention to language began only with the later turn; it establishes no direct reception by the later theorists.
edges.map_label: Historical language before the later turn

edges.relationship: Dilthey makes individual lives and their historical surroundings a methodological problem
edges.evidence_note: His Schleiermacher biography and later reflections on biography/autobiography are discussed by Makkreel. This is a specific contribution, not proof that all later life writing derives from him; no original biographical chapter has been independently read.
edges.map_label: Dilthey: life, initiative and historical context

edges.relationship: Meinecke connects historical individuality and development to national statehood
edges.evidence_note: Paddock’s selected reading of the 1907, 1924 and 1936 works supplies the specific connection and criticizes its assumptions about organic statehood and power. The scholarly interpretation is attributed; no uniform historicist politics is asserted.
edges.map_label: Meinecke’s national state and its assumptions

edges.relationship: Skinner explicitly credits the Investigations in asking about historical language use
edges.evidence_note: Interview answer 6 recalls reading and discussing the work, connecting it to purposeful discourse and public intentions. This retrospective evidence concerns Skinner’s pre-2000 practice; it does not establish one philosophy shared by Pocock or all contextual historians. The 1969 article p. 37 directly cites Investigations §§43 and 79, adding contemporary primary evidence to the retrospective interview.

edges.relationship: Ryle invokes Freud against an assumption of transparent consciousness
edges.evidence_note: The Concept of Mind, p. 14, names Freud’s account of unrecognized impulses as a challenge to an assumption in the official doctrine. This bounded resource does not make Ryle a psychoanalyst or establish agreement with Freud’s whole theory.
edges.map_label: Freud and the limits of conscious self-knowledge

edges.relationship: Both examine intelligible use and action through distinct philosophical projects
edges.evidence_note: The selected primary texts support a comparison of contextual use, competent practice and conceptual confusions. Tanney discusses parallel development and possible reciprocal learning; the current evidence does not warrant choosing one general transmission direction.
edges.map_label: Use, action and distinct philosophical methods

edges.relationship: Skinner and Dunn explicitly use Kuhn among interpretive resources
edges.evidence_note: Skinner (1969), p. 7, invokes the priority of paradigms and chapter V of Structure; Dunn’s notes also acknowledge the work. This bounded methodological use does not derive the entire Cambridge grouping from a theory of scientific revolutions.
edges.map_label: Kuhn as a specified interpretive resource

edges.relationship: Dunn uses Ryle’s reconstruction of Plato’s intellectual activity
edges.evidence_note: Dunn (1968), p. 94 and note 20 p. 103, discusses Plato’s Progress (1966) as a reconstruction from difficult evidence. This is a particular reception in historical-philosophical interpretation, distinct from Geertz’s use of Ryle or the knowing-how argument; the full Ryle book remains unread.

edges.relationship: Skinner criticizes Collingwood’s inference from identifying a problem to solving it
edges.evidence_note: Skinner (1969), pp. 50–51, argues that intelligible attempts may fail to solve their problems. This specific criticism coexists with his acknowledged question/answer resource; it does not reject all contextual interpretation or every historicist position. Collingwood’s original passage remains to be collated.

edges.relationship: Koselleck invokes Nietzsche on historically accumulated concepts resisting definition
edges.evidence_note: Futures Past, chapter 5, p. 85, explicitly quotes the difficulty of defining what has a history. This supports a particular conceptual resource, not a complete Nietzschean genealogy of conceptual history.
edges.map_label: Historical concepts and limits of definition

edges.relationship: Koselleck uses Weber’s legitimacy typology to distinguish analytical categories
edges.evidence_note: Futures Past, chapter 5, p. 92, discusses transformation of historical political vocabulary into a scientific category. This specific example does not establish Weber as a founding inspiration of the entire program; Olsen’s introduction note 9 explicitly disputes that larger genealogy.
edges.map_label: Weber’s typology as an analytical example

edges.relationship: Gumbrecht and Reichardt use Elias for the courtly setting of philosophe
edges.evidence_note: The 1985 French Handbuch article, p. 12 and note 4, cites The Civilizing Process in discussing court interaction and affect regulation. This is documented reception in one French conceptual-history case, not a claim about the origins of all German or French lexicon work.
edges.map_label: Elias in the French philosophe study

edges.relationship: Schmoller and the Verein provide an institutional setting for Weber’s agrarian inquiry
edges.evidence_note: Kim’s scholarly biographical section identifies mentorship and the agrarian commission. This is a specified research setting, not a claim that Weber simply inherits every methodological position of the German historical school.
edges.map_label: Schmoller, the Verein and agrarian research

edges.relationship: Rostow reworks production theory; Lipset uses Schumpeter’s electoral definition
edges.evidence_note: Rostow’s 1960 chapter 2 closes with a dynamic-production account critically related to classical and Keynesian models. Lipset 1959 p. 71 explicitly cites Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy for an electoral definition. These are separate resources, not a single economics-to-modernization genealogy.

edges.relationship: Lipset and Huntington pose distinct historical questions about legitimacy and institutions
edges.evidence_note: Lipset 1959 compares development and legitimacy while rejecting automatic democratization; Huntington 1968 pp. 1–7, 12–13 distinguishes institutionalization from growth and electoral form. This contribution identifies questions and comparative tools, not adoption by every political historian or endorsement of their national typologies.

edges.relationship: Eisenstadt reconstructs comparative inquiry around multiple modern programs
edges.evidence_note: The 2000 article pp. 1–4, 24–26 rejects Western convergence and examines continually reconstructed cultural and institutional programs, including destructive possibilities. Its contribution coexists with the opposite-direction Moore/Bendix criticism; it does not retrospectively attribute the later program to every 1950s theorist.

edges.relationship: Vogel reworks Marxian categories for gender and reproduction of material life
edges.evidence_note: The checked publisher description identifies this specific constructive feminist inquiry in the 1983 book. It does not verify every mechanism in the unread body or identify all gender history with Marxism; the primary-passage limitation is retained.
edges.map_label: Vogel’s feminist reworking of Marxian categories

edges.relationship: Weber defends materialist historical inquiry against a particular juristic refutation
edges.evidence_note: The available Objectivity excerpt rejects the inference that legally regulated economic life must therefore be explained only by conscious legal purposes. Legal forms can persist while their practical social significance changes. This bounded defense is neither wholesale adherence to Marxism nor a complete account of Weber’s disagreements with Marx.
edges.map_label: A qualified defense of materialist inquiry

edges.relationship: Wallerstein contests Dobb’s definition of capitalism and the transitional period
edges.evidence_note: Wallerstein 1974 pp. 393, 399 names Dobb and quotes Capitalism Yesterday and Today. He prefers a world-economy/market-production unit that includes coerced labor. This records disagreement, not a verdict against Dobb’s historical evidence.
edges.map_label: Wallerstein challenges Dobb’s unit and definition

edges.relationship: Dos Santos disputes a comparative-cost account of dependent economies
edges.evidence_note: The Structure of Dependence pp. 235–236 targets free-competition/comparative-cost assumptions and policy sufficiency. Prebisch’s earlier qualified use of trade theory differs; this is not rejection of economics as a whole.
edges.map_label: Dos Santos: comparative costs and dependence

edges.relationship: Prebisch’s structuralism and Polanyi’s exchange analysis provide distinct resources
edges.evidence_note: Dos Santos uses ECLA research while criticizing its policies; Wallerstein 1974 p. 390 explicitly cites Polanyi’s instituted-economy essay. Prebisch’s trade/industrialization argument specifies the structuralist context without making all dependentistas structuralists.
edges.map_label: Structuralist research and Polanyi’s exchange forms

edges.relationship: Alice and Staughton Lynd develop a participatory organizer-history collection
edges.evidence_note: Rank and File (1973), introduction 1–8, explains referrals, editing and participant correction. It combines interviews with written accounts and speeches; the sample is selective and the testimony mediated.
edges.map_label: The Lynds: testimony and participant correction

edges.relationship: Genovese uses Fogel and Engerman’s statistical and analytical work
edges.evidence_note: His acknowledgments explicitly credit their supplied work and Engerman’s manuscript reading. This resource does not imply acceptance of all their conclusions and does not cancel Gutman’s separate criticism of Time on the Cross.
edges.map_label: Fogel and Engerman’s research supplied to Genovese

edges.relationship: Slavery scholarship and source collections provide resources for Genovese
edges.evidence_note: The preface and acknowledgments name Rawick, Levine and Litwack; permissions also identify Du Bois and Black historical source collections. This particular use respects Black history’s independent institutions and does not derive that field from the New Left.

edges.relationship: Feminist historical analysis helps constitute new cultural inquiry
edges.evidence_note: Hunt’s 1989 introduction identifies Davis, Smith-Rosenberg and Scott as formative resources and discusses gender within Desan’s community/ritual inquiry. This particular route does not subsume racial-formation scholarship or make all cultural historians share one feminist position.

edges.relationship: Smith-Rosenberg contributes to Spiegel’s social and textual method
edges.evidence_note: Romancing the Past introduction note 7 cites The Body Politic and thanks Smith-Rosenberg for a draft; acknowledgments credit sustained exchange and her reading every chapter. This is a concrete reciprocal contribution, not gender history receiving theory only from outside.

edges.relationship: Laqueur’s humanitarian-narrative inquiry expands social-historical questions
edges.evidence_note: Hunt’s introduction explicitly presents Laqueur’s chapter as extending social history’s attention to class and power through narrative. This is Hunt’s editorial interpretation; the chapter body and downstream reception are not newly checked.

edges.relationship: McNeill makes world history an explicit problem of evidence and interpretation
edges.evidence_note: The complete1986 address distinguishes source criticism from selection and interpretation, argues that some accounts fit facts and broader experience better, and advocates ecumenical synthesis. His normative program is not a proof of eventual convergence or a claim that all stories are equivalent.
edges.map_label: McNeill: evidence, interpretation and world history

edges.relationship: Subrahmanyam contests Goldstone’s autonomous-state model and ideological partitions
edges.evidence_note: Connected Histories758–759 names Revolution and Rebellion1991, objecting to demographic/fiscal sequencing and an eschatological/cyclical partition in light of circulating ideas. Records his criticism; the complete Goldstone book and empirical dispute are not adjudicated. The regional critique was rechecked in the second pass. Goldstone’s separately read preface and France/Spain comparison emphasize institutional conjunctions and divergent outcomes. His self-description therefore differs from the critic’s sharply reductive characterization; these passages are not a reply to Subrahmanyam, and do not settle the disputed ideological categories in the unread chapter 5.

edges.relationship: Wong uses Thompson’s food-protest research in a Eurasian comparison
edges.evidence_note: China Transformed chapter9 opening209 explicitly cites Thompson1971 with Rudé and Louise/Charles Tilly before examining Chinese grain conflicts. This is a named methodological resource; the displayed opening does not establish identical Chinese and European moral economies.
edges.map_label: Thompson’s crowd research in Wong’s comparison

edges.relationship: Cultural inquiry supplies mediated self-writing and imperial-symbolism resources
edges.evidence_note: Subrahmanyam740n13 cites Kafadar’s1989 Ottoman diary essay, explicitly linked to Davis1986;739n11 cites Gruzinski on indigenous power and colonial imagination. These are particular and partly mediated resources; the original cited bodies are not newly read.
edges.map_label: Davis through Kafadar; Gruzinski’s imperial imagination

edges.relationship: Subrahmanyam rejects a national winner–loser developmental ranking
edges.evidence_note: Connected Histories745 explicitly targets the road-to-industrial-capitalism question associated there with Marx and Rostow, and develops local/supraregional alternatives. This attributed criticism is narrower than rejecting every modernization inquiry or all material explanation.
edges.map_label: Against national rankings on one developmental road

edges.relationship: Gramsci uses Weber’s account of German political personnel
edges.evidence_note: Intellectuals author noteH explicitly refers to Parliament and Government in the New Order in Germany in discussing Junker control. This is a particular resource, not agreement with Weber’s whole sociology.
edges.map_label: Weber on political personnel in Gramsci

edges.relationship: Hobsbawm critically values Gramsci’s historical and political analysis
edges.evidence_note: The1974 review connects Gramsci to rebellion and organization while questioning the continuing value of the organic/traditional distinction. This supports qualified reception, not an unverified provenance claim for every earlier Hobsbawm book. Revision 1.147: the reception continues in How to Change the World (2011), where, as Eagleton reports (LRB, 2011, read), Hobsbawm "thinks that Gramsci is the most original thinker produced by the West since 1917". Eagleton reports this judgment within a paragraph of criticisms (of the book's handling of Althusser, feminism and Trotskyism), not as his own view; the book is unread.

edges.relationship: White situates cultural criticism within an explicit Marxian commitment
edges.evidence_note: The1999 afterword315–316 and322 names his commitment, Lukács and Jameson. This particular intervention complicates treating him as simply outside Marxian inquiry.

edges.relationship: White identifies Foucault as a resource while disputing his categories
edges.evidence_note: Metahistory2–3 says White has benefited from Foucault while criticizing the tropological limits he perceives; the1999 afterword323 offers a conditional positive reference. Reception changes with the argument.
edges.map_label: An acknowledged and contested Foucault resource

edges.relationship: Mink makes narrative comprehension a distinct philosophical question
edges.evidence_note: The1970 article questions Gallie and Hardy and compares Morton White’s causal account; truth and knowledge remain separately assessed. This is an intervention in narrative inquiry, not the origin of the whole linguistic turn.

edges.relationship: Becker connects everyday research to an account of social memory
edges.evidence_note: The1931address links practical documentary checking with wider shared remembrance. A conceptual contribution, not proof of direct descent to later memory studies.
edges.map_label: Becker: everyday inquiry and social memory

edges.relationship: Mattingly’s Armada narrative supplies Mink with a counterexample
edges.evidence_note: Mink546 observes that prior knowledge of the outcome does not invalidate reading Mattingly, challenging an account of understanding based on suspense. The book itself is not newly read.

edges.relationship: Benjamin explicitly cites Nietzsche on history and life
edges.evidence_note: Thesis XII uses Nietzsche’s historical-need formulation within Benjamin’s own argument; this citation does not establish complete agreement.

edges.relationship: Benjamin challenges empathetic identification with historical victors
edges.evidence_note: Thesis VII targets a quoted prescription by Fustel de Coulanges; this is a specific polemic, not a fair summary of every historicist.

edges.relationship: Feminist historical evidence challenges public-sphere exclusion
edges.evidence_note: Fraser uses Landes and Ryan alongside Eley to revise Habermas while retaining a normative resource. The historians’ original texts are mediated through Fraser.
edges.map_label: Landes and Ryan in Fraser’s critique

edges.relationship: Spivak’s vocabulary enters Fraser’s counterpublic formulation
edges.evidence_note: Fraser note 22 credits Spivak’s subaltern and Rita Felski’s counterpublic together. This lexical route does not imply agreement with all Subaltern Studies.
edges.map_label: Spivak and Felski in Fraser’s terminology

edges.relationship: Eley’s Gramscian interpretation informs Fraser’s public-sphere critique
edges.evidence_note: Fraser 62 explicitly presents a Gramscian reading through Eley; the transmission is mediated and distinct from her term’s derivation in note 22.

edges.relationship: Tawney supports the Institute’s exile network
edges.evidence_note: Jay’s account names Tawney among those supporting the London office. Institutional assistance does not establish doctrinal agreement.

edges.relationship: Durkheimian scholars assist the Institute in exile
edges.evidence_note: Jay names Bouglé and Halbwachs in the Paris arrangements. This records their institutional help, not a Durkheim-to-critical-theory doctrinal lineage.
edges.map_label: Bouglé and Halbwachs support exile research

edges.relationship: Benveniste supplies de Certeau’s enunciation resource
edges.evidence_note: Introduction xiii and note 3 name the language model; this is a particular appropriation.

edges.relationship: Mauss and Greek practical intelligence inform de Certeau
edges.evidence_note: Notes 9 and 20 cite bodily techniques and Détienne/Vernant; no unified anthropological position is implied.

edges.relationship: De Certeau questions an emphasis on disciplinary production
edges.evidence_note: Introduction xiv–xv seeks users’ operations while drawing on Foucault. This critique also acknowledges a resource.

edges.relationship: Swidler uses Thompson’s historical cultural analysis
edges.evidence_note: Page 283 identifies The Making as a resource for understanding cultural reappropriation; her argument adds its own action framework.

edges.relationship: Sewell’s artisan history supplies Swidler with a historical example
edges.evidence_note: Swidler 283 explicitly cites Sewell’s 1974/1980 work on French artisans. This is a documented route distinct from the existing broad social/practice comparison.

edges.relationship: Elias explicitly credits Freud’s books
edges.evidence_note: Interview paragraph 60 names New Introductory Lectures and Anna Freud on defense mechanisms. Retrospective testimony supports this reading claim, not identical theories.

edges.relationship: Elias connects Suicide with his relational thinking
edges.evidence_note: Interview paragraph 46 explicitly discusses the book. His retrospective attribution does not date every borrowing.

edges.relationship: Duerr challenges civilizational accounts of shame
edges.evidence_note: Publisher description identifies the cross-cultural dispute; the book’s evidence and replies remain unchecked, so no verdict is asserted.

edges.relationship: Beard cites Cunningham on testing historical hypotheses
edges.evidence_note: Chapter 1 invokes William Cunningham’s methodological advice. This specific citation does not establish agreement on all economic interpretations.

edges.relationship: Libby’s sectional mapping supplies Beard with a resource
edges.evidence_note: Beard’s preface and chapter 1 explicitly credit Libby; the latter’s introduction explains the procedure and its proxies.

edges.relationship: Beard questions Bancroft’s providential explanation
edges.evidence_note: Chapter 1 criticizes a named national-history account while recognizing documentary scholarship. Beard’s characterization is a polemic, not an exhaustive description of Bancroft.

edges.relationship: Hartz disputes Marx’s explanation of socialist ideology
edges.evidence_note: Chapter 1 section 2 proposes an alternative relation between feudal heritage and socialist thought. This is Hartz’s claim alone; the existing Beard/materialism comparison remains distinct.

edges.relationship: Starn directs Stone to Metahistory
edges.evidence_note: Stone’s note 2 explicitly credits the recommendation and cites White alongside Gossman. This particular reading route is distinct from the existing undirected comparison.

edges.relationship: Stone uses Deep Play as a methodological example
edges.evidence_note: Page 14 names the cockfight essay while distinguishing historians’ mediated access from field observation.

edges.relationship: Stone includes Elias in his account of renewed cultural interests
edges.evidence_note: Page 16 names The Civilizing Process. This supports reception in Stone, not his sweeping claim of forty years without readers.

edges.relationship: Stone identifies contextual histories of political thought as a resource
edges.evidence_note: Page 14 names Pocock, Skinner and Bailyn in discussing changed meanings. His general assessment is not proof of one shared method.
edges.map_label: Pocock, Skinner and Bailyn in Stone

edges.relationship: White participates in and disputes the cultural reassessment
edges.evidence_note: The 1999 preface records conference participation; afterword 315–318 states his Marxian commitment and deconstructive argument. This is distinct from criticism directed at him in edge_257.

edges.relationship: Jenkins uses Foucault on classification and the operation of truth
edges.evidence_note: The 1991 discussion 36–39 cites Order of Things through Alan Sheridan and separately quotes Power/Knowledge; the mediation and Jenkins’s own interpretation remain explicit.

edges.relationship: Histories of science contribute distinct resources to debates about historical knowledge
edges.evidence_note: The 1999 editors’ introduction 14–15 describes her comparative/global research proposal; the 1994 coauthored book also situates historical truth alongside science. This is not a single position of science studies. Another specific resource is now identified: Appleby/Hunt/Jacob chapter 7 note 5 cites Daston and Galison’s 1992 article in discussing the inherited objectivity/subjectivity dichotomy. This is reception of a particular historical study, not agreement with every claim in it.
edges.map_label: Jacob, Daston and Galison: knowledge and objectivity

edges.relationship: Feierman’s healing inquiry questions historical categories
edges.evidence_note: The 1999 editors explain how embodied performance and unfamiliar temporal/person categories challenge conventional narratives and simple scale choices. This is their account of his essay, whose body remains unread.

edges.relationship: Gender and bodily history shape the reassessment
edges.evidence_note: Rose’s moral-discourse inquiry and Bynum’s historical bodies supply different questions in the editors’ introduction 20–22. These are specific resources, not one gender-theory consensus.
edges.map_label: Rose and Bynum: discourse and embodiment

edges.relationship: Defends the difference between fact and fiction against “postmodernist” fashions (“We cannot invent our facts”, 1993) and reads the coauthors’ manuscript of Telling the Truth about History (1994)
edges.evidence_note: The 1994 acknowledgments name his detailed reading while absolving all readers of responsibility for the conclusions. This records assistance, not agreement. Revision 1.147 adds his own 1993 words, read in full ("The New Threat to History", NYRB, 16 December 1993): "postmodernist" fashions "imply that all “facts” claiming objective existence are simply intellectual constructions. In short, that there is no clear difference between fact and fiction.
