But there is, and for historians, even for the most militantly antipositivist ones among us, the ability to distinguish between the two is absolutely fundamental. We cannot invent our facts." The passage is brief ("I need say little about the first of these responsibilities"); the lecture's main subject is the nationalist abuse of history (see the nationaltradition critique). A contribution on the side of facts, not a critique of the 1994 coauthors.

edges.relationship: Samuel supplies different interventions in historical self-reflection
edges.evidence_note: Jenkins introduction 3/note 7 invokes Grand Narratives (1990); Evans introduction II/note 22 cites Reading the Signs II (1992). Their uses of these texts differ and do not establish a unified Workshop position.
edges.map_label: Samuel as interlocutor for Jenkins and Evans

edges.relationship: African health histories contribute to historical study of medical knowledge
edges.evidence_note: Feierman and Janzen’s 1992 editorial project joins historical and social questions about health and healing. Publisher description and contents support this shared research programme; no particular downstream reception or uniform therapeutic system is inferred.
edges.map_label: Historical inquiry into health and healing

edges.relationship: African material-culture history contributes technical-history methods
edges.evidence_note: Hountondji’s summary presents Mêtinhoué’s combined oral, archaeological and material approach. This records an editorial account of a named project; the chapter body remains unread.

edges.relationship: Human geography contributes to Canguilhem’s examination of norms
edges.evidence_note: Canguilhem invokes Vidal’s genre de vie and discusses Sorre as confirming an argument already drafted. This is documented reception, not an original causal debt.

edges.relationship: Halbwachs’s critique of the average person supplies a conceptual resource
edges.evidence_note: Canguilhem explicitly uses Halbwachs1912 in examining Quetelet and norms. The claim concerns this work, not a transfer of collective-memory theory.

edges.relationship: Durkheim supplies an explicitly named resource for Bloor’s programme
edges.evidence_note: Bloor’s opening chapter invokes Elementary Forms and identifies Durkheim among the programme’s resources. This limited reception claim does not certify every later Durkheimian argument.

edges.relationship: Bloor’s symmetry principle contributes to Latour’s early approach
edges.evidence_note: Latour’s 1999 reply acknowledges this debt and describes French translation, teaching and publication with Callon. It also explains his subsequent departure. The documented contribution coexists with the undirected comparison, edge_138.

edges.relationship: Bray joins gender history with the history of everyday technologies
edges.evidence_note: Her1997project supplies a specific feminist historical intervention situated in China. Publisher description and contents establish its scope; this does not certify every argument or a field-wide reception.

edges.relationship: Weber questions how Knies derives economic method from its subject matter
edges.evidence_note: The opening of the1905second article selects logical problems and explicitly disclaims a full historical assessment. This particular critique coexists with Weber’s institutional debts; it does not reject all historical economics.

edges.relationship: Marx criticizes the wage dependence produced by Wakefield’s colonial land scheme
edges.evidence_note: Capital I chapter33 attacks a scheme that Mill endorses in V.11§14. Marx does not name Mill in that chapter; this connection identifies a shared policy object, not a direct quotation or comprehensive Indigenous critique.

edges.relationship: Naoroji redeploys Mill’s capital propositions against colonial investment assurances
edges.evidence_note: Naoroji’s1901discussion55–56 uses Mill to argue that drain restricts Indian accumulation. This is a specific appropriation, not an endorsement of empire or a claim that Mill founded anti-colonial history.
edges.map_label: Mill’s categories in Naoroji’s drain argument

edges.relationship: Massey contributes to the journal’s spatial-history debate
edges.evidence_note: Her 1995 article and Driver/Samuel’s coauthored editorial document a particular exchange; neither establishes that geography founded History Workshop. Editorial body unread.

edges.relationship: Hayden uses geographical arguments in urban public history
edges.evidence_note: Her 1995 book explicitly uses Harvey and cites Massey’s feminist criticism. Selected passages document this connection.

edges.relationship: Massey uses Gilroy’s changing tradition as a resource
edges.evidence_note: Places and Their Pasts 184 explicitly invokes The Black Atlantic against a closed account of tradition. This is documented reception, not a new full-book check.

edges.relationship: Said supplies a critically received resource for Driver
edges.evidence_note: Driver’s 1992 abstract explicitly names Said and resists totalizing imaginative geographies. Abstract-level support only; the full argument remains unread.

edges.relationship: Sauer praises Febvre’s environmental criticism while contesting his portrayal of geography
edges.evidence_note: Morphology reprint 347–348 directly discusses La Terre and Berr’s foreword. Sauer values their attack on environmentalist explanations but calls their knowledge of geographical thought limited and questions their elevation of Vidal. This is Sauer’s specific judgment, not a verdict shared by all geographers.

edges.relationship: Sauer uses Febvre and Berr’s geographical criticism as a resource
edges.evidence_note: Morphology reprint 347–349 quotes La Terre and its foreword while distinguishing useful criticism from disagreements. The contribution records this explicit reception beside Sauer’s separate critical response; it does not imply that Febvre founded cultural geography.
edges.map_label: La Terre as a critically received resource

edges.relationship: Compare situated Indigenous life histories with environmental histories of property, conservation and unequal burdens
edges.evidence_note: Editorial comparison of different questions and author positions: Auntie Rita’s described displacement and paired voices, Bullard’s documented organizing and inequality, and existing Cronon/Carruthers selections. No direct influence or agreement is inferred; book-body access limits remain attached.

edges.relationship: Rita and Jackie Huggins collaborate with Jacobs on a published place-history intervention
edges.evidence_note: Kooramindanjie names all three authors; the AIATSIS public finding aid independently describes the collaborative project. This records coauthored participation in geographical historical inquiry, not transmission from a single Indigenous tradition or a full reading of the article.

edges.relationship: Rita and Jackie Huggins contribute with Jacobs to the journal’s 1995 spatial-history section
edges.evidence_note: OUP verifies coauthorship and publication within the section. Contribution means a specific published intervention, not journal founding or universal editorial agreement.

edges.relationship: Guha uses Inden’s critique of Orientalist representations in his deep-ecology argument
edges.evidence_note: Guha77–78/note9 explicitly uses Inden’s 1986 discussion of romantic and pejorative images of India. A specific analytical resource, not a claim that all environmental history derives from postcolonial theory; original Inden article unread.
edges.map_label: Inden’s critique in Guha’s environmental argument

edges.relationship: Goody questions the uniqueness and scale of European marriage comparisons
edges.evidence_note: Goody1983,8–9 explicitly discusses Hajnal1965, noting geographic and social variation and counterexamples cited from Tibet and Roman Egypt. Those underlying studies are not newly audited. Hajnal’s own regional qualifications are retained, so this is a specific criticism rather than a claim that he asserted complete uniformity.

edges.relationship: Nair questions fixed cultural survivals and insufficient gender analysis in Chakrabarty’s Bengal labor history
edges.evidence_note: Nair (1990), 98–99, appreciates the book’s theoretical contribution while asking how cultural traditions are rearticulated within capitalism. Her examples and alternative possibilities remain a specific review intervention; they do not reject the whole Subaltern Studies project or independently settle the empirical disputes.

edges.relationship: Canning asks how historical actors transform the discourses shaping experience
edges.evidence_note: Canning’s 1994 response to Scott retains the critique of transparent experience while asking for a clearer account of agency and discursive change. This specific disagreement does not reject linguistic analysis.

edges.relationship: Tilly’s state-building model informs Lucassen and Zürcher’s recruitment comparison
edges.evidence_note: The authors explicitly identify Tilly’s 1990 book as their framework at 406 and note 4. This is a documented use in one study, not a claim about all military historians.

edges.relationship: Skocpol questions Sewell’s anonymous conception of culture in revolutionary explanation
edges.evidence_note: The reply’s primary opening explicitly proposes a less anonymous approach and questions anthropological cultural systems. This scoped objection coexists with her acknowledgment of an inadequate treatment of ideology; the full rejoinder and French-case reasoning remain unread. It does not represent all historical sociology opposing cultural history.
edges.map_label: Skocpol replies on culture and ideology

edges.relationship: Wehler challenges Alltagsgeschichte’s conceptual precision and claims to replace broader explanation
edges.evidence_note: Selected primary critique acknowledges valuable work on culture, experience and overlooked people, then questions autonomous concepts and the claim to an ethnological replacement paradigm. Applies to the Alltagsgeschichte component of the microhistory umbrella; not a blanket rejection of microhistory or culture. Lüdtke’s named response is separately recorded.

edges.relationship: Frevert questions class definitions built around men’s property and educational positions
edges.evidence_note: Her 1991 criticism names Kocka and Wehler’s class analyses. It challenges their handling of gender while retaining class as a problem for research; not a uniform feminist rejection of social history.

edges.relationship: Levi questions fixed cultural contexts in Geertz’s interpretive practice
edges.evidence_note: The 1985 essay criticizes textualization and explanatory circularity while praising Geertz’s skill. This is Levi’s specific intervention, not a verdict shared by every microhistorian.

edges.relationship: Levi challenges Darnton’s use of predetermined cultural frameworks
edges.evidence_note: The review targets The Great Cat Massacre’s interpretation of tales and the printers’ episode. Levi acknowledges his selective reading; neither all cultural history nor all microhistory speaks with one voice.

edges.relationship: Frisch: editing oral testimony for public audiences
edges.evidence_note: The checked methodological introduction specifies mediation and editorial choices; collaboration does not remove editorial authority.
edges.map_label: Frisch: editing oral testimony for public audiences

edges.relationship: Local participation and public historical practice
edges.evidence_note: Samuel’s local/oral work offers a British comparison to the US professional programme; no institutional descent is asserted.
edges.map_label: Local participation and public historical practice

edges.relationship: Everyday pasts and historical authority
edges.evidence_note: Rosenzweig and Thelen’s US survey connects these questions without equating memory with professional historical inquiry.

edges.relationship: Callinicos: popular history within South African struggle
edges.evidence_note: Her 1986 opening links historical education with labour and community organizing; this particular practice is not the source of all public history.
edges.map_label: Callinicos: popular history within South African struggle

edges.relationship: Hayden: interpreting urban landscapes
edges.evidence_note: The existing scoped reading connects spatial inquiry and collaborative public interpretation.

edges.relationship: Social relations within medical history
edges.evidence_note: Patient agency and public-health institutions connect these entries. Sigerist’s earlier programme prevents a claim that New social history originated every social approach to medicine.

edges.relationship: Duden: historicizing embodied experience
edges.evidence_note: The documented project studies women’s bodily experience through situated medical records; broader gender historiography is not assigned a single origin.

edges.relationship: Feierman and Janzen: histories of African healing
edges.evidence_note: Their 1992 coedited programme already belongs to African historiography in the atlas and also develops historical approaches to health.
edges.map_label: Feierman and Janzen: histories of African healing

edges.relationship: Knowledge, therapeutic practice and institutions
edges.evidence_note: The shared African healing project illustrates overlap; medical history is not reduced to scientific discoveries.

edges.relationship: Colonial medical discourse and power
edges.evidence_note: Vaughan’s project supplies a defined comparison with colonial-power questions. No influence from a particular postcolonial theorist is claimed.

edges.relationship: Thernstrom: linked records and mobility
edges.evidence_note: Poverty and Progress supplies a named quantitative urban inquiry; Newburyport is not assumed representative of every city.

edges.relationship: Environmental perspectives on city–hinterland connections, assessed in period by an urban historian as a contribution to urban history (1991–92)
edges.evidence_note: In-period evidence: the 1992 Annals of Iowa forum on Nature’s Metropolis (open PDF, text layer read). The urban historian Timothy Mahoney judges that the book 'makes significant theoretical and substantive contributions to both economic and urban history by placing urban and economic development in an environmental context', and that Cronon 'has, perhaps inadvertently, brought urbanization as a “process” forward from its current relegation as a kind of assumed stage set for monographs on local occurrences in cities' (p. 491). Of the premise that 'to really understand how and why cities developed, one must study how they organized their hinterlands', he writes: 'Cronon’s study of Chicago demonstrates the explanatory power of this fundamental urban historical premise' (p. 492). He also finds that in the book 'urban and economic history seem only to serve the interests of environmental history' (p. 491). Cronon’s response: 'One of my most important agendas in Nature’s Metropolis was to try to convince environmental historians that the city is among the most important historical loci of environmental change'; 'Surely such an argument can only strengthen the claims of urban history as a field, setting the process of urbanization in a broader context that is as important to urban historians as it is to environmental ones' (p. 520). The arrow rests on one book, one urban historian’s in-period assessment and the author’s reply; it does not claim that urban history as a field adopted environmental questions. Context only, not support for the claim: Cronon’s 1993 ASEH address names Joel Tarr’s 'many studies of pollution and waste streams' (p. 3, n. 6) and cites Melosi’s Garbage in the Cities (n. 24). cronon_urban_reception (2022) is a later reading. Cronon’s own contribution is the separate edge from his person entry (revision 1.131).

edges.relationship: King: colonial spatial development
edges.evidence_note: A specified Delhi-centred inquiry connects spatial organization to social power; no universal colonial-city model is endorsed.

edges.relationship: Racial exclusion in urban institutions
edges.evidence_note: Sugrue’s Detroit history addresses racial inequality across work and housing; a shared problem does not establish descent from every Black historiographical tradition.

edges.relationship: Hayden: urban landscapes as public history
edges.evidence_note: One named project supplies a bridge between the fields; neither field is absorbed into the other.
edges.map_label: Hayden: urban landscapes as public history

edges.relationship: Sauer: reconstructing cultural landscapes
edges.evidence_note: A specific geographical programme provides one resource; historical geography is not reduced to environmental determination.

edges.relationship: Driver and Samuel: the 1995 spatial-history forum
edges.evidence_note: Coeditorship and Massey’s accompanying intervention document a particular forum; the unread editorial body is not assigned a detailed argument.
edges.map_label: Driver and Samuel: the 1995 spatial-history forum

edges.relationship: Harley: power and cartographic knowledge
edges.evidence_note: Harley explicitly draws on Foucault, alongside a distinct Derridean resource. This names a reception, not Foucault as founder of historical geography.

edges.relationship: Harley: rhetoric and textuality of maps
edges.evidence_note: Harley acknowledges an eclectic combination of partly incompatible ideas; the edge records this particular use.
edges.map_label: Harley: rhetoric and textuality of maps

edges.relationship: Gregory and Southall: statistics across changing boundaries
edges.evidence_note: The 1998 HGIS abstract describes a spatial framework for historical statistics. It supports a methodological contribution, not validation of every quantitative result.
edges.map_label: Gregory and Southall: statistics across changing boundaries

edges.relationship: Hayden: interpreting urban places
edges.evidence_note: One documented landscape project connects spatial interpretation with urban history.

edges.relationship: Carter: colonial naming and territorial narratives
edges.evidence_note: Editorial comparison of a specific Australian spatial inquiry with postcolonial questions; no reception by a named postcolonial theorist is inferred.
edges.map_label: Carter: colonial naming and territorial narratives

edges.relationship: Skinner, Pocock and Brett: contextual inquiries
edges.evidence_note: Named approaches contribute to a wider field without defining it or subsuming every intellectual historian.
edges.map_label: Skinner, Pocock and Brett: contextual inquiries

edges.relationship: Koselleck: concepts and historical temporalities
edges.evidence_note: Selected primary passages distinguish semantic inquiry from direct reduction to social structures.

edges.relationship: LaCapra: texts and their contexts
edges.evidence_note: Publisher-supported scope of one methodological project, not a claim that intellectual history uniformly accepted poststructuralism. Toews’s detailed intervention remains unread.

edges.relationship: Darnton: material circulation of Enlightenment ideas
edges.evidence_note: Publishing and distribution connect intellectual and cultural questions in a named project; neither field is claimed to descend from the other.
edges.map_label: Darnton: material circulation of Enlightenment ideas

edges.relationship: Maruyama: thought and Japanese transformation

edges.relationship: Subaltern Studies accounts of colonial workers' culture and consciousness taken into labour history, and contested there by labour historians (1989–97)

'While, at first, the subaltern historians borrowed liberally from Thompson's ideas, rhetoric and example, they seemed to take little account of wider developments in social history' (p. 182). 'The Subaltern followers of Thompson' espoused the view that rural migrants 'imported a peasant culture into the industrial setting' (p. 184), and 'some Subaltern historians mistook the received wisdom and commonplace of colonial officials for interpretative novelty' (p. 185); his note cites Arnold's 'Industrial Violence' as well as Chakrabarty (n. 32). Janaki Nair's 1990 review in International Labor and Working-Class History questions cultural determination and the treatment of gender (graph verification note; not re-read in 1.132). edges.relationship: Cree narration and interwar writing

edges.relationship: Canadian historical synthesis
edges.evidence_note: Her historical scholarship examines European representations and places First Peoples within a broad Canadian historical synthesis. MNO recognizes her Métis contribution. She is one major historian within a wider field, not its sole origin. This teaching link presents the named approach; it does not establish intellectual descent or a contribution to every part of the umbrella field.

edges.relationship: Colonialism and Métis historical interpretation
edges.evidence_note: Métis scholar’s critique of Canadian colonialism joins historical interpretation and Marxist politics. This teaching link presents the named approach; it does not establish intellectual descent or a contribution to every part of the umbrella field.

edges.relationship: Autohistory and self-interpretation
edges.evidence_note: In his 1991 interview, explains autohistory as bringing Indigenous self-interpretation and transmitted traditions into historical discourse. His moral and philosophical proposal is situated; its account of Amerindian values does not define every nation. This teaching link presents the named approach; it does not establish intellectual descent or a contribution to every part of the umbrella field.

edges.relationship: Historical synthesis and institution-building
edges.evidence_note: Earlier historical synthesis and institution-building: the Newberry finding aid records his 1949 work and participation in creating its history centre in 1972. This teaching link presents the named approach; it does not establish intellectual descent or a contribution to every part of the umbrella field.

edges.relationship: Community–university historical practice
edges.evidence_note: Stó:lō community and university participants combine different research resources in this particular field-school programme. This comparison records overlapping practice; it does not make either field the origin of the other.

edges.relationship: Land and colonial geography
edges.evidence_note: Harris’s 1997 geographical inquiry offers a specific connection to histories of Indigenous–settler land relations. This comparison does not assert adoption of his methods by Indigenous historians.

edges.relationship: A radical historians' school and a field about the decade
edges.evidence_note: The atlas entry is a US school of radical historians; the Canadian field studies the New Left as a subject: Palmer's chapter "New Left Liberations", Milligan on New Leftists and young workers, Lexier on student movements in Debating Dissent. Comparison only; no checked source claims descent from the US school.

edges.relationship: The sixties between memory, myth and history
edges.evidence_note: Hébert: "les années 68 sont devenues mythiques", built on oral tradition and memory, and Warren brings them into scholarship; Campbell and Clément title their introduction "Time, Age, Myth: Towards a History of the Sixties". Comparison: the field historicizes memory rather than adopting memory-studies method.

edges.relationship: Decolonization thought as a subject of sixties history
edges.evidence_note: Mills's subtitle and chapters ("The International Dimension of Resistance", "The Language of Liberation") study activists' use of postcolonial thought; Rutherford places Indigenous protest in a transnational frame. PhD context: 10 of 53 PhDs citing Mills also cite Fanon (lift 5.2). Comparison: anti-colonial writing is the historians' subject, not their method.

edges.relationship: Young workers, wildcat strikes and the New Left
edges.evidence_note: Milligan treats young workers' wildcat militancy and the New Left as one youth revolt; Palmer's chapter "Wildcat Workers"; McInnis on sixties wildcat strikes in Debating Dissent.

edges.relationship: Sexual regulation and surveillance in the 1960s
edges.evidence_note: Kinsman and Gentile on national security as sexual regulation from the 1950s; Hewitt and Sethna on RCMP "sex spying" on women's liberation groups (Debating Dissent); Palmer's chapter "Scandalous Sex".

edges.relationship: Red Power and Indigenous protest in the sixties
edges.evidence_note: Rutherford on Indigenous protest as a confrontation with settler colonialism; Palmer's "Indians of All Tribes: The Birth of Red Power" and his chapter on the "discovery" of the "Indian". These are mostly settler historians' studies of Indigenous activism; the comparison records no Indigenous-authored source.

edges.relationship: Women's liberation and sexual revolution
edges.evidence_note: Mills's chapter "Québécoises deboutte!"; Hewitt and Sethna on surveillance of women's liberation groups; Owram's "Sexual Revolutions and Revolutions of the Sexes".

edges.relationship: African-Canadian historiography
edges.evidence_note: Walker's 1997 essay (full text read) identifies five orientations in African-Canadian historiography by the role assigned to Black people, ties the Community turn to Black Power, Black pride and social history, and to 'the collective nature of the black struggle in North America'. Later Canadian work is published in and framed by Black diaspora history: Mathieu (abstract) connects Black migrants and porters to 'black diaspora history during the Jim Crow era'; Austin publishes in the Journal of African American History (2007, metadata). Moved here from Immigration, ethnicity & race in Canada. The atlas entry's own scope note warns that diaspora links do not make Black histories one national tradition: this is a contribution, not a sub-field.

edges.relationship: Black migration and racialized immigration control
edges.evidence_note: Calliste (abstract read) shows immigration officials restricting Black Caribbean settlers while employers recruited their labour, 1900–32; Shepard (via Walker 1997) studies African American migration from Oklahoma to the prairies before 1914 and, by its subtitle, the racism the migrants met; Mathieu (abstract) joins immigration and Black diaspora history. Black Canadian history is not a sub-field of immigration history: of 177 PhDs citing Black Canadian history works, 45% engage Immigration, ethnicity & race in Canada (lift 3.4; 39% and lift 3.0 on a narrower definition). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence; lifts are high for most Canadian pairs.

edges.relationship: Black Montreal in the long 1960s
edges.evidence_note: Austin's Fear of a Black Nation (description read) centres the 1968 Congress of Black Writers and the Black-led protest at Sir George Williams University; Forsythe's 1971 collection is a contemporary participants' account, not scholarship; Austin 2007 is title-level. All selected scholarship is post-2000, so this comparison rests on later work; Canada’s 1960s declined a black – Canada’s 1960s edge for the same reason, and this edge is the narrower Canadian pair. PhD context: 40% of PhDs citing Black Canadian history works engage Canada’s 1960s (lift 2.8).

edges.relationship: Slavery in New France and Black Quebec
edges.evidence_note: Trudel, a Laval historian of New France on the Quebec roster, wrote the francophone history of slavery in French Canada (1960, checked against Hamelin's RHAF review heading) and its dictionary (1990, which Walker 1997 lists among works on slavery); Gay (2004) and the French edition of Mackey (2013) continue a francophone strand, and Mackey is read mostly at francophone universities (5 of 9 PhDs). Bibliographic level only; no checked text frames the two literatures against each other. PhD context: 16 of 177 PhDs citing Black Canadian history works are at francophone universities; 37% engage Quebec historiography (lift 2.3).

edges.relationship: African Canadian women's history
edges.evidence_note: Walker (1997, full text) notes that 'black women have been receiving increasing attention' and uses Brand's No Burden to Carry as his example of the Survivors orientation; We're Rooted Here (1994) is a six-author volume of African Canadian women's history; Bonner's review (read) calls Flynn's Moving Beyond Borders a contribution to 'a sparse literature relative to the lives of African Canadian women'. PhD context: 61% of PhDs citing Black Canadian history works engage Canadian women's & gender history (lift 2.4).

edges.relationship: Black workers, porters and segmented labour
edges.evidence_note: Calliste (1987, title-level) treats Black sleeping car porters as an 'ethnically submerged split labour market'; Mathieu (abstract read) follows porters and their union, white railwaymen's demands for a segregated workforce, and porters as civil-rights leaders. PhD context: 48% of PhDs citing Black Canadian history works engage Canadian working-class history (lift 2.2). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

edges.relationship: Black soldiers and race in recruitment
edges.evidence_note: Walker's 'Race and Recruitment in World War I' (CHR 1989, metadata) is the scholarly study of visible-minority enlistment in the CEF that Canadian military history also uses, and Ruck's Black Battalion (1987) is a community history of the No. 2 Construction Battalion; Walker 1997 lists both in his reading for African-Canadian history. Title-level only. PhD context: 17% of PhDs citing Black Canadian history works engage Canadian military history (lift 1.2), so this is a narrow shared subject, not a shared readership.

edges.relationship: Childhood and family as historical subjects
edges.evidence_note: The demography umbrella's strand on childhood evidence (Ariès; Pollock) and its household studies can be read alongside Canadian childhood and family history, which grew from social and family history (Parr, ed., 1982; Bradbury, ed., 1992) more than from family reconstitution. PhD context: 12 of 132 PhDs engaging this group cite Ariès (9% vs 3%; lift 2.96). Comparison; no descent from Ariès is asserted.

edges.relationship: Girls, mothers and families
edges.evidence_note: Much of the childhood and family field grew within women's history: Strong-Boag on girls and women (1988), Bradbury on family economies (1993), Comacchio on saving mothers and children (1993), Baillargeon on the medicalization of maternity (2004). Shared people are rosters, not edges. PhD context: 50 of 54 2009–2026 PhDs engaging Childhood, youth & family in Canada also engage Canadian women's & gender history (93%; lift 3.94), counted after removing shared anchors (Bradbury, Comacchio, Korinek, Strong-Boag). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence; lifts are high for most Canadian pairs.

edges.relationship: The baby boom as a generation
edges.evidence_note: Owram's history of the baby-boom generation (1996) is the most-cited work for this group's engaged PhDs and also anchors Canada’s 1960s. Title-level. PhD context: 49 of 107 2009–2026 PhDs engaging Childhood, youth & family in Canada also engage Canada’s 1960s (46%; lift 4.06), counted after removing shared anchors (Owram). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence; lifts are high for most Canadian pairs. Owram's chapters on babies, school days and "the cult of the teenager"; Gauvreau credits Bienvenue with treating youth as a constructed category rather than an anthropological constant.

edges.relationship: Indigenous children and the residential school system
edges.evidence_note: Milloy's history of the residential school system follows a government system whose underfunding affected 'the health, education, and well-being of entire generations of Aboriginal children' (publisher description). The Canadian childhood field leaves residential schooling to the Native–newcomer entry; this edge cross-references the two rather than claiming the residential-school literature for childhood history. PhD context: 34% of the 44 PhDs citing A National Crime engage childhood history (lift 3.4). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

edges.relationship: An English-Canadian instance of national narrative
edges.evidence_note: Buckner (2000, pp. 4–5): before the 1960s Canadian historians emphasized "the economic and political unity of Canada as it evolved from a colony into an independent nation-state", and "virtually every English-Canadian historian accepted the legitimacy of the Canadian nation-state as a frame of reference". Morton (1946) treats "well-defined interpretations of Canadian history" as objects of criticism. Comparison only: the atlas umbrella is broader and includes anticolonial counter-histories; no descent is claimed.

edges.relationship: The staple approach as a Canadian contribution to economic history
edges.evidence_note: Watkins (1963): the staple approach "is primarily a Canadian innovation; indeed, it is Canada's most distinctive contribution to political economy", with Innis as "the leading innovator". Salmon (1997): the staple thesis gave "an economic rationale for Canadian political development". Contribution to the field, not a claim that economic history adopted it generally. The atlas economic entry has no Canadian anchors, so no PhD overlap is computed.

edges.relationship: National consensus in Canadian and US historiography
edges.evidence_note: Buckner (2000, p. 5) calls the pre-1960s Canadian approach "similar to that of the consensus school in the United States": minimizing internal divisions and stressing what united Canadians. Davis (1985, p. 102) likewise says Careless's metropolitan interpretation "fits the mould of 'consensus' history". Comparison with the consensus half of the atlas entry only. Careless's 1954 article, read for revision 1.136, criticises the Canadian historians who adapted Turner's frontier thesis; that critique is the separate edge from his person entry (j_m_s_careless → progressive), not this comparison.

edges.relationship: English-Canadian and French-Canadian national traditions
edges.evidence_note: Miville (2016) compares Creighton and Brunet as public intellectuals: both denounced official bilingualism, Creighton to defend Macdonald's founding vision, Brunet because the country was built by two nations. The Centenary Series translated Trudel (1973) and Ouellet (1980) into the English national synthesis; Berger's subtitle restricts his analysis to English-Canadian writing. Comparison, not influence. PhD context: 68 of 173 2009–2026 PhDs engaged with Laurentian & national tradition also engage the Quebec historiography anchor set (39% vs 16% of all; lift 2.51). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence. Brunet’s ‘English presence’ and ‘two Canadas’ (1958 subtitle) and the Laurentian national tradition are parallel national historiographies with different subjects and politics. Title-level.

edges.relationship: Urban history rejects the metropolitan thesis
edges.evidence_note: Davis (1985, abstract): metropolitan theses are several rather than one; their indeterminacy about relations between classes is why urban historians "feraient mieux d'abandonner complètement l'approche métropolitaine". Targets the metropolitan strand only, not the staple approach or national synthesis.

edges.relationship: Canadian political history of party, state and officials
edges.evidence_note: A Canadian case of the atlas field: Whitaker's Government Party (contents: "The national Liberal party, 1930–58"; "Party and state in the Liberal era") and Owram's Government Generation (description: intellectuals and the planning of the welfare state, 1900–45) study institutions and the people who ran and justified them. Comparison: the atlas entry is international and methodologically plural; the Canadian field is not presented as a branch of Namier or Tilly.

edges.relationship: From national tradition to a specialized political and international history
edges.evidence_note: Buckner (2000, pp. 4–5) places Stacey with Creighton among the conservative nationalists who took the nation-state as their frame; Stacey's external-policy history (1977, 1981) is the most-cited external-policy work here. Thompson and Seager's volume (1985) belongs to the Centenary Series. Comparison only: no lineage of teachers and students is asserted. PhD context: 118 of 242 2009–2026 PhDs engaged with Political, international & national history also engage the Laurentian & national tradition anchor set (49% vs 13% of all; lift 3.67). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

edges.relationship: Canada and the British World: imperial history from the settler colonies
edges.evidence_note: Buckner (1993, abstract) argues that historians of the second British Empire neglect the colonies of settlement and Pocock's "Greater Britain", and that historians of the settler colonies share the blame; Canada and the British World (2006) surveys Canadian history "through a British lens" while eschewing nostalgia. The atlas has no separate imperial-history entry; nationaltradition (national and imperial narratives) is the nearest. Comparison, scoped to the British World strand.

edges.relationship: War policy, conscription and the state
edges.evidence_note: Stacey's official history of war policy (1970) and Granatstein's histories of the King government at war (1975) and of conscription (with Hitsman, 1977) sit between political and military history. Metadata-level only: no abstract or contents page was read for these books. PhD context: 142 of 242 2009–2026 PhDs engaged with Political, international & national history also engage the Canadian military history anchor set (59% vs 14% of all; lift 4.16). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence. Stacey’s Arms, Men and Governments: The War Policies of Canada (1970) and Morton’s Canada and War: A Military and Political History (1981) join military to political history; Granatstein anchors both entries. Title-level.

edges.relationship: Regional history against the national themes
edges.evidence_note: Buckner (1971, p. 3): historians "are still obsessed with the great 'national' themes", the CHR "has done very little to encourage local and regional history", and only the Atlantic Provinces lack a journal; footnote 1 cites Careless 1969. Buckner (2000, pp. 4–5) explains limited identities as a turn away from the nation-state frame. Targets the national frame, not every national historian. PhD context: 95 of 194 2009–2026 PhDs engaged with Canadian regional history also engage the Laurentian & national tradition anchor set (49% vs 13% of all; lift 3.69). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

edges.relationship: Regional history and social history
edges.evidence_note: McKay (2000, pp. 89–90) contrasts the 1990s agenda of gender, ethnicity and community with "1970s and early-1980s topics" of regional underdevelopment and class conflict, and calls the new pluralism "a continuation of … the social-history revolution of the 1960s and 1970s". Comparison: overlapping projects, not a hierarchy.

edges.relationship: Region, scale and historical geography
edges.evidence_note: Harris's colonial geography of British Columbia (existing source: displacement and colonial geographical change) and Harvey (2006, abstract) on how geographic scale shapes regional identity in the West, the Maritimes and Quebec. Comparison.

edges.relationship: Regional scales and Acadia
edges.evidence_note: Harvey (2006, abstract): Quebec's regional studies, by historians and sociologists, chose the intraprovincial scale rather than the interprovincial one that structures the West and the Maritimes. Histoire de la Gaspésie (1981) is an example. Comparison. PhD context: 69 of 194 2009–2026 PhDs engaged with Canadian regional history also engage the Quebec historiography anchor set (36% vs 16% of all; lift 2.27). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence. Acadia: readers of Acadian history works (101 of 1,303 PhDs, 2009–2026) engage the Quebec historiography anchors at 50.5% (lift 3.23), more than any other group (answers/data-answers.json, Q86_87_acadia). Landry and Lang's francophone synthesis (2001) was reviewed in the RHAF; Griffiths's From Migrant to Acadian (2005) was reviewed there too. Comparison, not derivation: Acadian historiography is placed in Canadian regional history (Atlantic), not in Quebec historiography.

edges.relationship: Regional histories and Indigenous–newcomer relations
edges.evidence_note: Reid, Basque et al. (2004, abstract) treat 1710 through its effects on "aboriginal inhabitants, Acadians, and New Englanders" at local, regional and imperial scales; Carter (1990) and Stonechild and Waiser (1997) are western examples (catalogue level). The PhD overlap is the strongest of this entry's Canadian links. PhD context: 153 of 194 2009–2026 PhDs engaged with Canadian regional history also engage the Indigenous–newcomer relations & fur-trade history anchor set (79% vs 19% of all; lift 4.21). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

edges.relationship: Regional economic history of the Maritimes
edges.evidence_note: Acheson (1972, pp. 3–4) revisits the National Policy from the Maritimes: a staple economy, rapid industrial growth under the tariff in the 1880s, then local entrepreneurs' acquiescence "to the industrial leadership of the Montreal business community". A specific regional contribution; no general claim about economic history.

edges.relationship: The fragmentation charge against the new social history
edges.evidence_note: Bliss (abstract): twenty-five years of "intense … specialization" replaced older historians' concern for explaining the country. Granatstein, as McKillop summarizes him, accused academic historians of abandoning the national past for "overspecialized and ideologically driven forms of history". Cook (2000, abstract) identifies the target as the social history that flowered from limited identities. The critique is from the debate's national side; the replies follow as separate critiques. Scoped to Canadian social history; if Canadian working-class history and Canadian women's & gender history are accepted they carry the specific replies.

edges.relationship: Labour historians answer the fragmentation charge
edges.evidence_note: Two phases. Gregory Kealey answered Bliss's 'Privatizing the Mind' in the 1992 Journal of Canadian Studies 'Point-Counterpoint', titled "Class in English-Canadian Historical Writing: Neither Privatizing, Nor Sundering"; Palmer's "Of Silences and Trenches: A Dissident View of Granatstein's Meaning" (CHR 80:4, 1999) answers Granatstein's 1998 book. Title and metadata only: neither text was read. PhD context: 22 of 34 2009–2026 PhDs citing a core debate text also engage the Canadian working-class history anchor set (65% vs 22% of all; lift 2.96). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

edges.relationship: Women's and gender historians answer the lament for national history
edges.evidence_note: Linda Kealey, Ruth Pierson, Joan Sangster and Veronica Strong-Boag, "Whose 'National' History Are We Lamenting?" (JCS 1992, title), part of the Point-Counterpoint answering Bliss, not Granatstein. Strong-Boag's 1994 address (abstract): "Neo-conservative laments about the state of Canadian history abound"; the old history's "preoccupation with white male elites" and neglect of women and gender, "race" and class show "a restricted vision". She also reviewed Granatstein's book (1999; unread). PhD context: 19 of 34 2009–2026 PhDs citing a core debate text also engage the Canadian women's & gender history anchor set (56% vs 25% of all; lift 2.22). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

edges.relationship: Limited identities and regional history as the debate's ground
edges.evidence_note: Buckner (2000, pp. 4–5): Cook coined and Careless popularized "limited identities" of region, culture and class. Cook (2000, abstract): the hypothesis "played a major role in the flowering of social history whose dominance is now being called into question by proponents of a renewed 'national' approach". Reid (1987) and Buckner (1988) show the fragmentation worry and the Atlantic defence of limited identities before Bliss. Contribution as background and defence; regional historians are not presented as one side. PhD context: 14 of 34 2009–2026 PhDs citing a core debate text also engage the Canadian regional history anchor set (41% vs 15% of all; lift 2.77). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

edges.relationship: National-political history as one side of the debate
edges.evidence_note: Contesting Clio's Craft (description) names "the political vs. social history debates that have dominated the field since the 1970s". McKay (2000) calls it the "socio-cultural versus national-political impasse". Bliss and Granatstein are political and business historians (see Political, international & national history). Comparison: not every political historian took Granatstein's side. PhD context: 24 of 34 2009–2026 PhDs citing a core debate text also engage the Political, international & national history anchor set (71% vs 19% of all; lift 3.8). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

edges.relationship: Lament for an older national history
edges.evidence_note: Bliss (abstract) contrasts specialization with "older Canadian historians' concern for explaining the nature of the country" while warning against "nationalist mythologizers"; Buckner (2000) describes that older consensus around the nation-state. Comparison: the debate invokes the tradition; it does not restore the staple or Laurentian theses. PhD context: 20 of 34 2009–2026 PhDs citing a core debate text also engage the Laurentian & national tradition anchor set (59% vs 13% of all; lift 4.43). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

edges.relationship: Parallel debates over national narrative in English Canada and Quebec
edges.evidence_note: Dumont's review of Who Killed Canadian History? (CHA Bulletin 1999, read in full) joins the two debates: she corrects Granatstein's claims about Quebec schooling, calls his book a fierce indictment of social historians with 'visées politiques', and cites Ferretti's chapter in Comeau and Dionne, eds., À propos de l'histoire nationale (1998), and Létourneau's student surveys. Dionne, who reviewed the book in RHAF (1998; title level), co-edited that volume. Létourneau (CHR 2000, abstract) proposes a narration of Canada that is neither unitarist nor fragmenting. Comparison: concurrent, separate debates with limited, one-way textual engagement (Dumont's 1999 review cites Ferretti and Létourneau); no checked Quebec-debate text cites Bliss or Granatstein, and only 4 strict 2009–2026 PhDs cite texts from both. PhD context: 14 of 34 2009–2026 PhDs citing a core debate text also engage the Quebec historiography anchor set (41% vs 16% of all; lift 2.63). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

edges.relationship: Two 1990s disputes over what historians owe facts and publics
edges.evidence_note: McKillop (1999, abstract) answers Granatstein that "event-driven facts are inseparable from considerations of value and therefore from the realm of the interpretive". Comparison only: the Canadian debate was about national history and specialization, not postmodernism; no checked text links it to Jenkins, Evans or Appleby, Hunt and Jacob.

edges.relationship: A national field within intellectual history
edges.evidence_note: Titles name the field's objects (Canadian thought, intellectuals and the state, historical writing); Gauvreau's Evangelical Century was presented as transforming "the way Canadian intellectual history is interpreted". Comparison: the Canadian field developed largely apart from the contextualist and conceptual programmes in the atlas entry; no checked source links them.

edges.relationship: Canadian studies of collective memory, pageantry and the public past
edges.evidence_note: Vance studies Canada's collective memory of the First World War; Nelles "the politics of memory" at the 1908 tercentenary; McKay and Bates the making of Nova Scotia's public past. A contribution of case studies, not a claim that the field originated memory studies.

edges.relationship: Ideas and representations of Canadian nationhood
edges.evidence_note: Berger's chapters on Canada First and "The Canadian Character"; Vance on war memory and Canadian nationalism; Igartua on the shift from ethnic to civic national identity. Comparison: the Canadian works rarely engage the modernist theory debates of the atlas entry in the checked pages.

edges.relationship: Spectacle, exhibition and representation
edges.evidence_note: Heaman's "Exhibition Culture" and commodification, Walden's exhibition and urban culture, and Radforth's public spectacle share the new cultural history's attention to representation and performance. Comparison only: no checked page cites the new cultural historians.

edges.relationship: Tourism, heritage and the making of public pasts
edges.evidence_note: McKay and Bates trace tourism/history and the cultural politics of whiteness in Nova Scotia; McKay's Quest of the Folk shows the tourism industry refashioning regional identity. These study public history as a subject rather than practising it.

edges.relationship: Historical writing treated as a domain of English-Canadian intellectual history and its national preoccupation examined (1971–86)
edges.evidence_note: In-period evidence. Trofimenkoff (1979, p. 9, read): 'some of the people have suggested that the leit motiv of both English and French Canadian historical writing, in itself a domain of intellectual history, has been the concern for survival, a nationalist concern'; her note 4 cites Ramsay Cook's essays 'La Survivance French Canadian Style' and 'La Survivance English Canadian Style' in The Maple Leaf Forever (1971, pp. 114–40, 141–65; not read here). Karr (1989, p. 161, read) places Berger's analysis of 'the national conceptual frameworks in which professional historians functioned and wrote' among the English-Canadian intellectual historians' studies of nationalism. Berger's 1986 chapter records that 'J.M.S. Careless joined Ramsay Cook in condemning the undue emphasis on national history and unity' (p. 261, snippet view). The arrow records intellectual historians making the national tradition's writing an object of study; Berger's own contribution is the separate edge from his person entry (the Canadian persons Tier 1 revision).

edges.relationship: Religious thought and social criticism
edges.evidence_note: Cook's Regenerators belongs to both fields; Gauvreau's Evangelical Century reassesses Cook as intellectual history. PhD context: 34 PhDs engage both entries (lift 3.5).

edges.relationship: Intellectual history answers the liberal order framework
edges.evidence_note: McNairn's chapter is titled "In Hope and Fear: Intellectual History, Liberalism, and the Liberal Order Framework"; McKay and Heaman write in both fields. PhD context: 43 PhDs engage both entries (lift 3.5). Title-level only.

edges.relationship: Postwar national identity and the generation of the 1960s
edges.evidence_note: Igartua traces English Canada's "other Quiet Revolution" in national identity, 1945–71; Owram moves from intellectuals and the state (1986) to the baby boom (1996). PhD context: 40 PhDs engage both entries (lift 2.5).

edges.relationship: An intellectual historian criticizes Granatstein's national history
edges.evidence_note: McKillop argues that Granatstein "miscasts the role of the scholar as citizen" and that his narrow national history is itself political legitimation. A critique of Granatstein's position within the debate by one intellectual historian, not the whole field's position.

edges.relationship: English-Canadian and Quebec histories of ideas and commemoration
edges.evidence_note: Lamonde's histoire sociale des idées is Quebec's counterpart; Nelles studies Quebec's tercentenary and Coates and Morgan Madeleine de Verchères. PhD context: 16 of 27 PhDs citing Lamonde (2000) are at francophone universities, against 2 of 48 for Berger (1976).

edges.relationship: War memory as cultural history
edges.evidence_note: Vance's Death So Noble "deals with cultural history more than military history" while treating the war's memory. Comparison only.

edges.relationship: Race as a historically made category
edges.evidence_note: Anderson (1987, abstract read) treats racial categories as cultural ascriptions whose construction cannot be taken for granted and shows government inscribing 'Chinese' and 'Chinatown' in practice and space; racial formation treats race as historically specific and produced through social and political relations. Parallel, not derivation: PhD context shows Omi or Winant cited by 1 of 172 PhDs engaging this group (and by 7 of 1303 overall).
edges.map_label: Racial formation and Canadian race history

edges.relationship: Ethnicity, recognition and the politics of its discovery
edges.evidence_note: Perin's opening asks whether it is coincidence that ethnic groups were 'discovered' when the US faced the civil rights movement and Canada an assertive Quebec nationalism. The identity umbrella groups historical recovery with struggles over exclusion and recognition and is itself open to criticism. Comparison; Perin's full argument was not read.

edges.relationship: Immigrant workers and labour radicalism
edges.evidence_note: Avery's 'Dangerous Foreigners' (1979; reviewed by Bruno Ramirez in International Labor and Working-Class History) and Ramirez's On the Move (1991) study immigrant workers; Iacovetta's 'Manly Militants' (1995) reviews how historians wrote about immigrants (title-level). PhD context: 97 of 142 2009–2026 PhDs engaging Immigration, ethnicity & race in Canada also engage Canadian working-class history (68%; lift 3.37), counted after removing shared anchors (Palmer). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence; lifts are high for most Canadian pairs.

edges.relationship: Immigrant, ethnic and racialized women
edges.evidence_note: Iacovetta (1992), Swyripa (1993) and Epp, Iacovetta and Swyripa, eds., Sisters or Strangers? (2004) work at the meeting of the two fields. Title-level. PhD context: 94 of 133 2009–2026 PhDs engaging Immigration, ethnicity & race in Canada also engage Canadian women's & gender history (71%; lift 2.98), counted after removing shared anchors (Iacovetta). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence; lifts are high for most Canadian pairs.

edges.relationship: Citizenship programmes for newcomers and Indigenous peoples
edges.evidence_note: Bohaker and Iacovetta (abstract read) show that from 1950 to 1966 the Indian Affairs branch sat in the Department of Citizenship and Immigration and modelled its activities on citizenship campaigns for immigrants. A post-2000 comparison across the two fields. PhD context: 74 of 172 2009–2026 PhDs engaging Immigration, ethnicity & race in Canada also engage Indigenous–newcomer relations & fur-trade history (43%; lift 2.3), counted after removing shared anchors. Bibliographies record consultation, not influence; lifts are high for most Canadian pairs.

edges.relationship: Religious thought as Canadian intellectual history
edges.evidence_note: Gauvreau's Evangelical Century treats the evangelical creed as "the intellectual expression" of Protestant culture and was presented as transforming how Canadian intellectual history is read; Marshall's summary calls secularization "a key development in Canadian religious and intellectual history". Comparison: much of the field is social rather than intellectual history.

edges.relationship: Social-history methods turn the field toward lay practice
edges.evidence_note: Marks studies church and leisure participation by class and gender in three Ontario towns; Christie and Gauvreau subtitle their 2010 synthesis "A Social History of Religion in Canada". Neither names the new social history as a source; the contribution is of method and subject, not an influence claim.

edges.relationship: Gender, family and religious life
edges.evidence_note: Marks's chapters on church ladies, freethinkers and working-class women in the Salvation Army; Gauvreau on Catholic Action, the family and women's desire (per Baum); Households of Faith on separate spheres, masculinity, fatherhood and personalist feminism. Comparison only.

edges.relationship: National and Quebec syntheses of women's history
edges.evidence_note: The atlas's women entry groups national and regional syntheses (French, German, Nigerian) in a strand with different scopes and documentary bases. The Collectif Clio's Quebec synthesis (1982), which rejects a male-centred collective history, and Prentice et al.'s survey (1988) can be read alongside them. Comparison, not descent: Canadian women's history is not presented as a branch of any one national model.

edges.relationship: Canadian debates over gender as a category
edges.evidence_note: Pierson's 1991 essay opens on feminist historians' turn to deconstruction and discourse analysis, naming Scott's theory of gender as the most acclaimed example. Parr (1995) and the 1995–96 Left History exchange (Sangster; Iacovetta and Kealey; Dubinsky and Marks) argued over gender history and women's history; their citations are checked, and Sangster's own position is taken from her 2011 retrospect; the replies are read only as defences of gender history. PhD context: 64 of 328 PhDs engaging this group cite Scott (20% vs 9% of all; lift 2.12).

edges.relationship: Women's history questions a male-centred Quebec history
edges.evidence_note: The Collectif Clio's introduction argues that a history centred on male figures had been presented as the collective history of the whole population. Lévesque's 1997 assessment says women's history redefined traditional Quebec history and hopes the slowness of some colleagues to integrate women is a matter of time and generation. A specific critique of how Quebec historiography treated women, not a rejection of that historiography. Coexists with edge_879 (comparison): a broad comparison and this specific critique can stand together, as GRAPH-FORMAT.md allows. Kept after Quebec women’s history (Clio, Lévesque, Baillargeon) was made primary in Quebec historiography.

edges.relationship: Gender as a dimension of class and family economies
edges.evidence_note: Parr's comparison of a textile town where most wage earners were women with a furniture town challenges conventional views of the distinctiveness of gender and class roles (author's book page). Bradbury's Working Families (age, gender and family survival) and Sangster's Dreams of Equality (women on the left) are title-level. Contribution of gender analysis to labour history; it does not claim the new labour history lacked it entirely. PhD context: 130 of 287 2009–2026 PhDs engaging Canadian women's & gender history also engage Canadian working-class history (45%; lift 2.81), counted after removing shared anchors (Bradbury, Parr, Sangster). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence; lifts are high for most Canadian pairs.

edges.relationship: Postwar domestic goods, magazines and households
edges.evidence_note: Parr's Domestic Goods (1999), Korinek's reading of Chatelaine (2000) and Fahrni's Household Politics (2005) place women and households at the centre of postwar consumption. Title-level only: none of these books was read, so the comparison is a teaching pointer to the consumption entry, not a claim about their arguments.

edges.relationship: The liberal order framework is Gramscian: liberal order as hegemony and the national-political 'commonsense' (2000)
edges.evidence_note: McKay's abstract (2000) maps Canada as 'a project of liberal rule in northern North America' through which 'liberal order became the national-political ‘commonsense’'. Ajzenstat (2009) describes McKay as recommending 'a Gramscian approach to Canadian history'; Pâquet (2009) names Gramsci, with Fernande Roy (1988), as one of the prospectus's two explicit influences; Palmer (2009) argues that McKay's reading of Gramscian hegemony is too seamless, conflating hegemony and domination. McKay's own Gramscian outlook is drawn separately (gramsci → ian_mckay, revision 1.149). PhD context: 9 of the 91 PhDs citing McKay 2000 also cite a Gramsci work.

edges.relationship: Liberal order and capitalism: analytically separate, historically entangled
edges.evidence_note: Fecteau quotes McKay that liberalism and capitalism must be kept "analytically separate" (2000, 629) yet after the 1840s "could not be easily separated" (2009, 385), and quotes McKay in 1994 on a "liberal capitalist order … based on possessive individualism". A teaching comparison between historical-materialist categories and the framework, not a descent.

edges.relationship: Property, land, taxation and market society
edges.evidence_note: Weaver relates property rights to the growth of democracy and the market economy; Heaman places "the propertied versus the people" at the centre of Canadian political history; Greer studies property formation. These carry the framework's questions into economic and social history. The atlas has no history-of-capitalism entry.

edges.relationship: Draws social and political history into a renewed political history
edges.evidence_note: Parnaby: McKay argued that liberalism as a "project of rule" could draw social and political history into one problematique, and interest in that question has reinvigorated histories of political ideas, institutions, census taking, border making and tax collecting. A contribution, not a claim that it founded political history in Canada.

edges.relationship: Liberal rule and moral regulation: neighbouring, distinct projects
edges.evidence_note: The user kept them apart (2026-10-12): the framework is "a different project closer to history of capitalism". Pâquet links the framework to studies of "liberal social regulation", and Valverde places moral reform at the centre of English Canada's race, class and gender organization. PhD context: 27 of 91 McKay-citing PhDs also cite Valverde (lift 3.6). Comparison only.

edges.relationship: Offers a way past the social versus national-political impasse
edges.evidence_note: McKay's abstract frames the prospectus as a way past "the present socio-cultural versus national-political impasse in Canadian history writing"; Ajzenstat sets it against Granatstein's attempt to revive national history. An intervention in the debate's terms, not a party to every exchange in it.

edges.relationship: Property formation, land and dispossession
edges.evidence_note: Greer studies property formation and the dispossession of Indigenous peoples; Weaver the appropriation of land and the emergence of property rights in settler societies; Brownlie's chapter title calls First Nations' relation to the liberal order "a persistent antagonism". Comparison only: no checked source joins the two frameworks.

edges.relationship: Francophone histories of liberalism and liberty
edges.evidence_note: Pâquet names Fernande Roy's history of francophone business liberalism as an explicit source of the prospectus; Ducharme's history of liberty in the two Canadas and Fecteau's critique carry the debate in Quebec scholarship. PhD context: Roy (1988) is cited by 16 PhDs, 8 at francophone universities.

edges.relationship: State formation as historical sociology
edges.evidence_note: Curtis presents Ruling by Schooling Quebec as "A Historical Sociology" and Pâquet ties the framework to studies of state formation. Comparison only: no checked source links the Canadian work to the comparative historical sociology the atlas entry describes. Corrigan and Sayer's Great Arch is co-cited (6 of 10 citing PhDs also cite McKay 2000) but unread.

edges.relationship: A national field within military history
edges.evidence_note: The atlas’s Military history entry has no Canadian participants. Cook’s account of Stacey and the Army Historical Section (official history as archive-making and narrative) parallels the military entry’s concern with source access and narrative framing. Comparison: the Canadian field is not presented as derived from Howard or Keegan. Revision 1.142 adds an official-history strand to the Military history entry, the international parallel to Cook’s account: Edmonds’s preface (1922, read) describes a Historical Section ‘charged with the sorting and arrangement of the records’ and a history read in proof by officers who took part; Morgan-Owen and Finch (2022, pp. 65–67, read) describe British official commissions during and after the Second World War drawing academic historians to war. Stacey and Duguid stay in the Canadian entry.
edges.map_label: Canadian military history and military history

edges.relationship: Great War memory in interwar Canada
edges.evidence_note: Vance’s Death So Noble examines Canada’s collective memory of the Great War in the 1920s and 1930s as a cultural and philosophical force (publisher description). A contribution to the memory entry’s war_mourning strand alongside Winter; no claim that Vance derives from Winter. Cook (2006) extends the question to historians’ own role. PhD context: Death So Noble is cited by 67 PhDs 2009–2026, the most of any work by this roster.
edges.map_label: Vance: memory of the Great War

edges.relationship: Conscription and French-Canadian participation
edges.evidence_note: Armstrong (1937), Granatstein and Hitsman (1977), Gagnon (1986, 1995) and Pariseau (1987) write conscription and French-Canadian participation; Gagnon’s 1995 essay assesses French-Canadian historians’ treatment of the Second World War in a Bulletin d’histoire politique dossier on ‘myths and realities’. Overlapping subject and venues, different questions. PhD context: 53 PhDs engage both rosters (expected 26.9).

edges.relationship: Women and war
edges.evidence_note: Pierson’s “They’re Still Women After All”: The Second World War and Canadian Womanhood (1986) belongs to both fields; Pierson anchors the women and gender entry. Title-level.
edges.map_label: Women and the Second World War

edges.relationship: Military history as public argument
edges.evidence_note: The CBC series The Valour and the Horror aired in January 1992; Senate subcommittee hearings began in late June 1992 and the CBC Ombudsman’s report was released on 10 November 1992. Dick (Archivaria, 1993) says the series ‘prompted unprecedented public reaction and discussion’. Official and academic historians wrote reports for the Ombudsman, collected with an appendix on the RCAF official history in Bercuson and Wise (1994; contents checked). Berton’s popular Vimy (1986) is a second witness. Comparison with the Public history entry; no direction asserted.

edges.relationship: Foucauldian analysis contributes to the concept of moral regulation and its governmentality reformulation
edges.evidence_note: Ruonavaara's abstract describes Corrigan and Sayer's framework as fusing Durkheimian and Foucauldian analysis with basic Marxist theory; Dean's abstract argues that problems in Corrigan's account are better formulated through Foucault's problematic of governmentality. Drawn as a contribution, the atlas's usual kind for Foucault's outgoing edges. Valverde's own acknowledgement (checked 2026-10-14 for revision 1.136, in Google Books search-within snippets of the 2008 reissue, 1991 pagination): 'Following but modifying Foucault's approach, I take the term "discourses" to refer not to language as separate from the real world but rather to organized sets of signifying practices' (preface, p. x) and 'as Foucault and his followers have pointed out, the state has no monopoly on moral regulation' (p. 165; also quoted by Dehli 1992, p. 317). Wright (Acadiensis, 1995, p. 123, read) reads her as modifying 'Foucault's archaeology' with 'an important commitment to social agency'. Strange and Loo (1997, p. 5, snippet): 'Theorists influenced by philosopher Michel Foucault have urged scholars to abandon the social-control model for a more flexible concept of regulation'. Not a claim about every Canadian study in the roster.

edges.relationship: State formation as cultural revolution
edges.evidence_note: Ruonavaara: Corrigan and Sayer introduced moral regulation to sociological debate in their historical sociology of English state formation, The Great Arch (1985). Adams applies it to state formation through Ontario VD policy. Corrigan and Sayer are not in the historicalsociology roster; this edge records a contribution from comparative historical sociology, not membership.
edges.map_label: Corrigan and Sayer: The Great Arch

edges.relationship: Sexual regulation and the national-security campaign against queers
edges.evidence_note: Kinsman's The Regulation of Desire (1987) and Kinsman and Gentile's history of the security campaign that spied on, interrogated and harassed gays and lesbians from the 1950s to the late 1990s (publisher page read) contribute Canadian studies of sexual regulation. Complements the queer entry's regulation strand; it does not claim Canadian priority.

edges.relationship: Protestant reformers as regulators and as religious actors
edges.evidence_note: Valverde studies the moral fervour of Protestant social reformers (publisher description); the religion-and-reform entry studies the same churches and social gospel as religious history (Christie and Gauvreau 1996, title-level). The two fields read the reformers differently. In period, Loo (Labour/Le Travail 30, 1992, p. 278, read) asked Valverde's book to 'address Christianity and certainly Protestantism more fully, even if only to dismiss its importance', and Christie and Gauvreau (1996, p. xiii, Google Books snippet) said she and Doug Owram used 'a caricature of the antiquated and esoteric Victorian theologue to excise the churches'. Those objections concern one book and are recorded on the edge from the mariana_valverde entry (revision 1.136); this field-level edge stays a comparison. Valverde places moral reform at the centre of English Canada's race, class and gender order; Cook's Regenerators covers the same reformers' religious thought. Comparison only.

edges.relationship: Women, girls, sexuality and the law
edges.evidence_note: Feminist legal and sexual histories sit in both fields: Backhouse (1991), Lévesque (1989), Dubinsky (1993), Strange (1995), Sangster (2001), and Little's study of the moral scrutiny of single mothers (1994, abstract read). Shared people are rosters, not edges. PhD context: 136 of 155 2009–2026 PhDs engaging Moral regulation also engage Canadian women's & gender history (88%; lift 3.52), counted after removing shared anchors (Mitchinson). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence; lifts are high for most Canadian pairs.

edges.relationship: Youth, normality and the psy-sciences
edges.evidence_note: Adams studies discourses on youth, delinquency, indecent literature and sex education as producers of heterosexual norms (publisher description); Gleason studies psychology and the normal family. PhD context: 74 of 142 2009–2026 PhDs engaging Moral regulation also engage Childhood, youth & family in Canada (52%; lift 5.66), counted after removing shared anchors (Adams, Gleason). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence; lifts are high for most Canadian pairs.

edges.relationship: Moral reform, racial purity and law
edges.evidence_note: Valverde's reformers linked sexual health to racial purity (publisher description); Backhouse's Colour-Coded traces racism through law (title-level). PhD context: 72 of 149 2009–2026 PhDs engaging Moral regulation also engage Immigration, ethnicity & race in Canada (48%; lift 3.99), counted after removing shared anchors (Backhouse). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence; lifts are high for most Canadian pairs.

edges.relationship: Disease, eugenics and the body as objects of regulation
edges.evidence_note: Adams reads Ontario's 1918 commission on venereal disease and feeble-mindedness as targeting bourgeois-defined immorality as much as infection (abstract). McLaren on eugenics and Mitchinson on women and their doctors are title-level. Comparison with the medical history entry, not a claim that medical history is regulatory history.

edges.relationship: Ethnohistorical method in Canadian native–newcomer history
edges.evidence_note: Trigger’s Wendat/Huron history joins archaeology, ethnography and contact records (existing atlas source), and his 1986 survey describes historians, anthropologists, archaeologists, geographers and economists combining in ethnohistorical research that was being integrated into national history. Bruce Trigger is already on the Ethnohistory roster; this edge records a contribution, not a founding claim.

edges.relationship: Indigenous history and native–newcomer historiography
edges.evidence_note: Overlapping subjects and people (Dickason, Miller, Lutz), different centres: Indigenous history centres Indigenous historical authority; this field centres relations, policy and encounter, often from colonial archives. The Indigenous entry’s existing strand native_newcomer_institutions (Miller) is the in-atlas meeting point. Comparison only: neither field is a subset of the other.

edges.relationship: Indigenous critiques of the relations frame
edges.evidence_note: Sioui proposes autohistory: Indigenous self-interpretation and transmitted traditions in historical discourse (interview, 1991). Winona Stevenson (Wheeler) (Saskatchewan History, Fall 1998; read in full) argues that historians of ‘Indian–White relations’, relying on one side’s records, keep even agency-centred work within a colonialist framework. LaRocque’s 1999 dissertation criticises the ‘neo cross-cultural approach’ of Trigger, Brown, Van Kirk and others as still othering (PDF pp. 249, 102, 109, 30 n.). Fixico (2009, US) says the premise of ‘Indian–white relations’ must be turned over for an Indian point of view. Fixico and S. Miller write about US historiography; they are cited as parallel critiques, not as statements about the Canadian books listed here. No identity classification is recorded.
edges.map_label: Indigenous critiques: autohistory, othering and colonizing practices

edges.relationship: Relations and encounter versus a structure of dispossession
edges.evidence_note: The same archives and subjects (reserves, schools, policy) are read as relations and encounter here and as a continuing settler structure in the Settler colonialism entry. Greer argues the settler mode dominates some periods and regions and fades in others; commercial penetration, the fur-trade mode, is another. Most native–newcomer works predate the settler framework and do not adopt it. PhD context: among 2009–2026 PhDs engaging this roster (two or more people cited), the share also citing Wolfe’s or Veracini’s settler-colonial works rises from 1 of 66 (2009–14) to 14 of 88 (2015–19) and 26 of 65 (2020–26), while engagement with the roster holds steady (16.1% → 16.0% of all PhDs). Bibliographies record consultation, not adoption.

edges.relationship: Innis’s fur trade and later fur-trade history compared
edges.evidence_note: Innis made the fur trade an introduction to Canadian economic history (1930). Ray’s later study of Indigenous traders treats the same subject; a later UTP reissue of Innis carries Ray’s credit (catalogue only). Comparison only: shared subject matter. How Ray engaged Innis is not checked (catalogue level). PhD context: Innis is cited by 82 PhDs, The Fur Trade in Canada by 48.

edges.relationship: Aboriginal people as a labouring class
edges.evidence_note: Lutz’s “After the Fur Trade: The Aboriginal Labouring Class of British Columbia” (1992) brings Indigenous wage and exchange labour into working-class history. One specific intervention; Canadian labour historians are not assumed to have adopted it. Distinct from the settler packet’s Burrill (2019) edge, which proposes a settler-order framework for the same field.

edges.relationship: Gender, marriage and missions in fur-trade and colonial society
edges.evidence_note: Van Kirk’s women in fur-trade society (1980) and Rutherdale’s gender and race in the mission field (2002) belong to both fields; Van Kirk also anchors the women and gender entry. Comparison, no direction asserted.

edges.relationship: Colonized bodies and Aboriginal health
edges.evidence_note: Kelm’s publisher description reads health and healing through postcolonial conceptions of the body and the power relations of colonization, as ethnohistory. A specific overlap with the Medical & health history entry; optional.

edges.relationship: Labroussian economic and social history at Laval
edges.evidence_note: Savard (1974) says Ouellet owed a debt to Labrousse and Chaunu; Robert Mandrou prefaced Ouellet’s 1966 book (review heading). Dechêne trained in France in the Annales milieu of Mandrou and Goubert before her Paris doctorate (1973), published as Habitants et marchands (1974) (Charron, Dictionnaire universel des créatrices; formal supervision not asserted). Linteau (1983) says social history began in Quebec in the 1960s under Annales influence but that his generation was shaped more by French and Quebec sociologists and American historians. Specific contributions to the Laval and New France strands, not an Annales origin for Quebec historiography.

edges.relationship: The modernist generation adopts social history
edges.evidence_note: Linteau (1983) describes his cohort adopting social history and serial sources (censuses, civil registers), becoming more quantitative, and widening the subject from French Canadians to Quebec’s whole population. Self-description of one generation.
edges.map_label: New social history and the modernists

edges.relationship: French-Canadian national history and its revision
edges.evidence_note: Groulx’s national history and the Montreal school’s Conquest belong to the national-narratives umbrella; Rudin’s opening sets the historians’ ‘normal’ Quebec against both nationalist history and politicians’ distinct society. Comparison only: the field is not reducible to national narrative, and the modernists rejected that frame.

edges.relationship: Quebec labour and working-class history
edges.evidence_note: Rudin names Rouillard among the historians he criticizes; Rouillard writes the history of Quebec unionism, and Copp and Bradbury write Montreal’s working class (Canadian working-class history sources). Overlap in people and subject; no direction asserted. PhD context: 79 PhDs engage both rosters (expected 34.6, lift 2.28).

edges.relationship: Catholicism and the Quiet Revolution
edges.evidence_note: Rouillard’s ‘turn not rupture’ and the Catholic Action revision (now a strand here) connect this field to religion and secularization. Gauvreau anchors the religion entry. Broad comparison; title and abstract level.

edges.relationship: Women’s history in French
edges.evidence_note: Quebec women’s history (Collectif Clio 1982; Lévesque 1989, 1997; Baillargeon 1991, 2012) is primary here, and its authors also appear in the women and gender entry, which keeps a specific critique edge (edge_841). Bédard and Goyette place Clio and Micheline Dumont in Quebec historiography’s ‘modernist’ part.
edges.map_label: Collectif Clio and Quebec women’s history

edges.relationship: The Quiet Revolution as a Sixties subject
edges.evidence_note: Rouillard’s abstract makes the early 1960s the contested hinge of Quebec history. Coordination edge with the Canada’s 1960s entry, which lists Quebec historiography as related.
