Sewell Jr. (JWSR, 2014, read) reports that Chibber answers the 1989 book by showing that European and American capitalists "have repeatedly relied on personal authority and particularist identities" (p. 301; Chibber's book unread here), and prefers "Chibber's version of the two histories to Chakrabarty's" (p. 302); in the same symposium Bruce Cumings (read in part) calls Chibber's account "a preposterous caricature of Chakrabarty's scholarship" (p. 292), so the symposium did not agree on Chibber's reading.

edges.relationship: Hobsbawm's category 'prepolitical', as quoted in Provincializing Europe, criticised as an instance of the historicism Western Marxism cultivated: the critique Guha began (1983), extended by Chakrabarty (2000)
edges.evidence_note: His own text. Provincializing Europe (2000), introduction pp. 11–15 read in the publisher's excerpt: 'Hobsbawm's category “prepolitical” revealed the limits of how far historicist Marxist thought could go in responding to the challenge posed to European political thought by the entry of the peasant into the modern sphere of politics' (p. 11). Hobsbawm 'readily admitted that it was the “acquisition of political consciousness” by peasants that “made our century the most revolutionary in history”', yet 'missed the implications of this observation for the historicism that already underlay his own analysis' (p. 11). Chakrabarty quotes Hobsbawm calling peasants 'pre-political people who have not yet found, or only begun to find, a specific language in which to express themselves. [Capitalism] comes to them from outside, insidiously by the operation of economic forces which they do not understand', and writes that in 'Hobsbawm's historicist language, the social movements of the peasants of the twentieth century remained “archaic”' (p. 12). Hobsbawm's words are given here only as Chakrabarty quotes them (a quoted-in witness; the bracketed '[Capitalism]' is in Chakrabarty's text). 'The analytical impulse of Hobsbawm's study belongs to a variety of historicism that Western Marxism has cultivated since its inception', including the language of 'survivals' and 'remnants' and 'variations on the theme of “uneven development”' (p. 12). The work quoted: the 1.132 adversarial review, reading a transcription of the book's notes, reports that note 36 (p. 261) cites Hobsbawm, Primitive Rebels (Manchester, 1978 edition; first published 1959), pp. 2–3, and that note 35 concerns rational-choice theory, not Hobsbawm. Neither the notes nor Hobsbawm's pages were read for this revision: the publisher's excerpt omits the notes, the transcription and the open OCR copies of Primitive Rebels were blocked or truncated, and the Internet Archive copies are borrow-only. The identification is therefore the reviewer's, and Hobsbawm's own wording is unverified here. The review also reports, from an OCR witness, that Hobsbawm's p. 2 speaks of the participants' aspirations where Chakrabarty's quotation has 'express themselves', and that Hobsbawm treats the movements of these pre-political people as consequential, not marginal; his book studies a selection of 'archaic forms of social movement' (its subtitle). The edge therefore records Chakrabarty's critique of the category as he presents it, not a verified reading of Hobsbawm's argument. He credits the critique to Guha: Subaltern Studies registered 'a deep sense of unease with the very idea of the “political”' in English-language Marxist historiography, 'Nowhere ... more visible than in Ranajit Guha's criticism of the British historian Eric Hobsbawm's category “prepolitical” in his 1983 book Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency' (p. 11). He keeps Marx: 'Marx is critical for the enterprise' (p. 18), and in 1992 Marx 'remains ... a relevant and fundamental critic of both capitalism and liberalism' ('Artifice', p. 4). The same argument appears in Public Culture (2000, p. 670): read historically, Marx's 'not yet' 'refers us back to the idea of history as a waiting room ... the period to which the Third World is often consigned'. No in-period reply by Hobsbawm was looked for or read.

edges.relationship: Climate change and the collapse of the distinction between natural and human history: humans as geological agents, species history and the history of capital (2009), developed into a distinction between globe and planet (2015–22)
edges.evidence_note: Dated 2009, after the atlas's 1920–2000 frame: drafted after the user's decision of 2026-10-14 to end the 2000 break. No claim here concerns his work before 2000. 'The Climate of History: Four Theses', Critical Inquiry 35, no. 2 (Winter 2009), pp. 197–222, read in full. The first thesis: 'Anthropogenic Explanations of Climate Change Spell the Collapse of the Age-old Humanist Distinction between Natural History and Human History' (p. 201). His readings in 'globalization, Marxist analysis of capital, subaltern studies, and postcolonial criticism ... had not really prepared me for making sense of this planetary conjuncture' (p. 199). On environmental history: 'the rise of environmental history in the late twentieth century made the breach wider', but 'environmental history, where it was not straightforwardly cultural, social, or economic history, looked upon human beings as biological agents', quoting Crosby's preface to The Columbian Exchange (p. 205); 'Scholars writing on the current climate-change crisis are indeed saying something significantly different from what environmental historians have said so far ... Humans now wield a geological force' (p. 206); the distinction between human and natural histories, 'much of which had been preserved even in environmental histories that saw the two entities in interaction—has begun to collapse' (p. 207). 'The mansion of modern freedoms stands on an ever-expanding base of fossil-fuel use' (p. 208). 'A critique that is only a critique of capital is not sufficient' (p. 212), yet 'the story of capital ... cannot be denied by recourse to the idea of species' (p. 219); the task is 'to mix together the immiscible chronologies of capital and species history' (p. 220). He ends with a 'negative universal history' (p. 222). Reception after 2009, labelled by date: Robert Emmett and Thomas Lekan, eds., Whose Anthropocene? Revisiting Dipesh Chakrabarty's 'Four Theses' (RCC Perspectives 2016/2, from a February 2015 workshop; read in part): the essay 'has become a primary text for understanding the problematic nature of the Anthropocene as a cultural category' (p. 7) and challenges 'ecological histories that situate humans as biological agents' (p. 8). The environmental historian Timothy J. LeCain (2016) writes, tentatively, that the theses 'may prove more radical than even he intended, or perhaps desires' (p. 15). Criticism: in his 2016 response Chakrabarty concedes to Carol Boggs that 'one can no longer separate the biological agency of humans from their geological agency in the way in which I appeared to do' (p. 104), and reports that 'Andreas Malm and Alf Hornborg took me to task' over 'There are no lifeboats for the rich', quoting Kathleen McAfee: 'Contra Chakrabarty, the rich may face the same storms and they do have lifeboats' (p. 108). Malm and Hornborg (2014) are known here through their abstract, which holds that "Intra-species inequalities are part and parcel of the current ecological crisis", and through his reports; the body of their article is unread. A contribution that disputes the field's prior framing of human agency, not a founding claim for climate history. Later work, added in revision 1.151: the Tanner Lectures (2015, read in part) distinguish humanity as "homo" from the scientists' "anthropos" and conclude that "we have fallen into 'deep' history"; The Climate of History in a Planetary Age (2021; publisher's page and contents; unread) is summarised in his own words: "The global is anthropocentric while the planet de-centers and provincializes the human" (Review of Politics, 2022, p. 593). In environmental history's own journal, Atte Arffman (Environment and History, 2022, read) writes that "historians can no longer dismiss material realities and non-human world" and that "not many have delved as deep as Chakrabarty does". The criticisms of the species category and of the divide's novelty are now drawn separately (environment → Chakrabarty; science → Chakrabarty).

edges.relationship: Craft culture and class conflict: skilled workers' culture as a resource in working-class formation, from 'Most Uncommon Common Men' (1976) to A Culture in Conflict (1979), carried on with Kealey in Dreaming of What Might Be (1982; known here only through later readings); contested by Bercuson (1981)
edges.evidence_note: His own in-period statement. 'Most Uncommon Common Men: Craft and Culture in Historical Perspective', Labour/Le Travailleur 1 (1976), pp. 5–31, read in full in the journal's PDF. Artisan radicalism 'was part and parcel of a larger context, a matrix of institutions, ideologies and traditions which, taken together, define the contours of a singular culture' (p. 7); 'in viewing culture as a resource and society as the arena in which that resource is utilized, we are necessarily led to a refinement of our conception of the "levels" at which culture operates' (p. 8); 'It has become a standard axiom of an emerging social history of the working class that the artisan, not the debased proletarian, fathered the labour movement. As a class for itself, the working class was born, not in the factory, but in the workshop' (p. 14), where Thompson, the Webbs, Musson and Pelling are cited as agreeing on the skilled mechanic's influence. In-period reception, from a critic: David Bercuson, 'Through the Looking Glass of Culture', Labour/Le Travailleur 7 (1981), pp. 95–112, pp. 95–97 re-read in the journal's PDF. He quotes A Culture in Conflict (his n. 10: pp. xii–xiv) for a method of 'sharp detail of limited chronology or restricted region to illustrate the human dimensions of the past', in which 'theory is meant to inform historical inquiry and, in turn, to be informed by historical research', and (n. 11: p. xiii) for 'a tradition of empirical Marxism' (p. 96); 'Palmer calls the skilled the cutting edge of the working class. They could just as easily be labelled the rearguard'; 'Palmer, echoing E.P. Thompson, regards culture and conflict as "complementary processes"' (p. 97). Bercuson's methodological objection (pp. 107–108, read in the journal's PDF): 'Historians must prove that Canadian workers, men and women, skilled and unskilled, were bound by a common culture that was primarily the product of their class experience before they can use culture to explain anything'; workers 'seem to have responded as much from consciousness of job, place, church, ethnic group, and other factors as from a culture of class'; he asks whether 'class was a more important means of self-identification than gender' (p. 107), and writes that 'Even if Thompson is right about England, his concepts do not necessarily apply anywhere else' (p. 108). Kealey's companion defence in the same issue defends class analysis and culture (wcreq_kealey_1981; not re-read in 1.134). A Culture in Conflict (1979), Dreaming of What Might Be (1982) and Working-Class Experience (1983; 1992) were not read here; they are cited at title level and through Bercuson. The edge's in-period evidence covers 1976–81; the 1982 Knights of Labor book is mentioned in the relationship text but rests only on McCoy's later quotation, so the label's dates stop at 1979. Later readings, labelled as such: Nicholas Rogers (2021) reads A Culture in Conflict as following Thompson in finding resistance among skilled artisans and in quoting Thompson's working-class culture as a 'way of struggle' rather than a 'way of life' (citing pp. xii, xiv); Ted McCoy (2021) quotes Kealey and Palmer's chapter on the Knights: 'A subordinate class must reach toward an alternative hegemony if it ever hopes to dominate the ethos of society' (Dreaming, p. 277, as quoted). A contribution, not a founding: Freeman (2002) names Palmer with Kealey and Sangster in the founding generation of Labour/Le Travail, and the 1976 essay calls its thesis an axiom of an emerging field. edge_890 (ep_thompson → cdn_working_class) and edge_886 (marx → cdn_working_class) stay: they record the Thompsonian and Marxist resources and the 1981 debate; this edge records Palmer's own contribution.

edges.relationship: Answers Scott's case for reconceiving labour history through language and gender, which he read as reducing class and its material relations to discourse (International Labor and Working-Class History forum, 1987); Scott replied that class struggle is produced in discourse, which she defined to include institutions and social practices. Descent into Discourse (1990) was his subsequent book-length intervention
edges.evidence_note: Scott's position in her own words. 'On Language, Gender, and Working-Class History', International Labor and Working-Class History 31 (Spring 1987), pp. 1–13; only p. 1 was read (publisher's preview image): gender 'has not been considered seriously for what it could provide in the way of a major reconceptualization of (labor) history'; theories of language 'offer a way of thinking about how people construct meaning, about how difference (and therefore sexual difference) operates in the construction of meaning'; labour historians' recent articles on 'language' 'reduce this important concept to the study of "words"' (p. 1). Palmer's response in the same issue, 'Response to Joan Scott', pp. 14–23; only p. 14 (preview image) and the notes listed by the publisher were read. It opens on the Halifax strikes of August 1842, with Palmer imagining himself at the scene, 'Conscious of "the need to avoid economic determinism" and aware of the extent to which "our needs are made of words"', thirsting 'for a dialogue with the participants that will both reveal all and deepen the discourse' (p. 14); n. 2 says the quoted phrases come from Stedman Jones's introduction to Languages of Class and from Ignatieff, 'texts that I take to be related to one another'. Scott's 'A Reply to Criticism', ILWCH 32 (Fall 1987), pp. 39–45, read in full, reports and quotes his response: Palmer and Christine Stansell 'share a fundamental disagreement with my emphasis on "language," arguing instead that material reality, social experiences, real or concrete events are the stuff of social history' (p. 39); she quotes his 'No discourse today! The class struggle has intervened' and answers: 'The opposition discourse versus class struggle is one I cannot accept, for class struggle is produced in discourse'; 'There is no social experience apart from people's perception of it' (p. 40). She defines the term at once: 'By discourse I do not mean utterances, or "words" ... but whole ways of thinking, of understanding how the world operates and what one's place is in it. And not only ways of thinking, but ways of organizing lives, institutions, societies, ways of implementing and justifying inequalities, but also of refusing them'; to say that 'the working class family was created within working-class discourse' 'is not to say that "words" alone brought families into being' (p. 40). The reduction-to-discourse objection is therefore Palmer's interpretation of her argument, which she rejected. She says 'Most of his critique is directed at Stedman Jones, not me, and little of it has to do with either women or gender' (p. 41), that he implies she has deviated from Marx's dialectical and historical materialism, to which she answers that 'there is more to Marx, greater complexity in his materialism, than Palmer's crude invocation of it' (p. 43), and that 'There is no choice, as Bryan Palmer insists there is, between a focus on class or gender; each is necessarily incomplete without the other' (p. 45). These are Scott's characterisations of his text. The forum had four voices, not two camps. Christine Stansell ('A Response to Joan Scott', pp. 24–29; only p. 24 read, publisher's preview image) called Scott's essay 'a welcome and important attempt to import some of the sophisticated concerns of current literary criticism into labor history' and sided 'with Joan Scott in believing that historians' willful lack of interest in poststructuralist debate is our loss—or, more properly, our missed opportunity' (p. 24). Anson Rabinbach ('Rationalism and Utopia as Languages of Nature: A Note', pp. 30–36; only p. 30 read) restated with approval her case that Stedman Jones's language 'is as instrumentalized in the notion of politics as economic interest is in the notion of class' (p. 30). Scott grouped Palmer with Stansell on 'language' and wrote that Rabinbach 'endorses and expands on my analysis' (p. 39); she answered Stansell's worry about losing 'woman, the subject' (p. 42) and Rabinbach's case for rationalism and universalism (p. 44) separately. The rest of Stansell's and Rabinbach's essays was not read. Later readings, labelled as such: Ted McCoy (2021) quotes the response: 'To say that language matters is not to say it is all that matters' (p. 16, emphasis original) and 'Class is indeed a difficult development to grasp precisely because in both its subjective and objective guises it reproduces the social order at the same time as it challenges it. Language and gender figure in this decisively' (p. 22); he reads Palmer as granting that attention to the gendered features of language is 'indisputable'. Descent into Discourse (1990; unread here) carried the dispute into its chapter on gender: Nicholas Rogers (2021) and Chad Pearson (2021) quote it on Scott's appraisal of women in The Making of the English Working Class: in Pearson's quotation it 'thus tilts too problematically toward the determining power of discourse' (p. 85), while Rogers paraphrases it as tilting 'too problematically towards' it, and as quoting Scott's 'There is no social experience apart from people's perception of it' (p. 180), the sentence read above in her 1987 reply. The arrow records Palmer's critique and Scott's rejoinder; it does not judge the dispute. Scott's own critique of Thompson's gendered account of class remains on edge_314 (gender → ep_thompson). Revision 1.152 (data/extension-2026/languages-of-class-2026-10-22/evidence-spread.md §§1.1, 1.5): the publisher's page for Descent into Discourse (Temple University Press; read 2026-10-22; the book remains unread) states its thesis — 'Critical theory is no substitute for historical materialism; language is not life'; reliance on poststructuralism 'reifies discourse and sidesteps structures of oppression and resistance'. Two later readers, labelled as such: Eley and Nield (2000, n. 46, read) call the book the reaction to Scott 'represented most viciously', a hostile characterisation recorded here, not adopted; Scott (2000, p. 69, read in full) puns on its title, 'Assent to Discourse'. The three 2021 Dissenting Traditions essays in the source list are later readings, as this note already says. Palmer's part in the debate as a whole is drawn as bryan_d_palmer → languages_of_class.

edges.relationship: Descent into Discourse: the linguistic turn in social history criticised as a 'reification of language', with class held to originate in relations of production rather than in discourse; Stedman Jones's languages of class a principal target (1987–90)
edges.evidence_note: The book (Temple University Press, 1990) remains unread; the publisher's page (read 2026-10-22 for revision 1.152) states its thesis in the press's words: 'Critical theory is no substitute for historical materialism; language is not life', and that reliance on poststructuralism 'reifies discourse and sidesteps structures of oppression and resistance'. Its page-level wording is taken from an in-period review that quotes it with page numbers: Alex Callinicos, Labour/Le Travail 29 (1992), pp. 311–313, read in full in the journal's PDF. Callinicos quotes Palmer: 'Much writing that appears under the designer label of poststructuralism/post modernism is, quite bluntly, crap' (199); Callinicos describes Palmer's standpoint, in his own words, as 'not that of a defensive empiricism but of a critical, anti-Stalinist Marxism', and quotes the book: 'historical materialism remains the foundation upon which studies of the past must be erected' (xiii); yet discourse theory 'contains insights and guides capable of opening new doors of understanding to historians committed to a materialism that recognizes the need for a rigorous reading of documents and texts/contexts' (189). The book is 'a critical survey of "the reification of language"' from the Russian Formalists through Foucault and Derrida that 'traces the vulgarization of their ideas by historians working in the fields of politics, gender, and class' (p. 312). Against 'the reduction by Gareth Stedman Jones et al. of class as a discursive construct', Palmer writes that 'class relations are, in origin, economic relations rooted in the capitalist process of accumulation, whereby one social stratum expropriates surplus from another' (138) (p. 312). Callinicos's in-period objections: Palmer is 'too willing to fall in line with the dominant way in which poststructuralism has been received in the English-speaking world' and misreads Foucault's Archaeology (p. 312); his claim that 'class as an objective economic reality is not present before the arrival of industrial capitalism' (139) sits oddly with Ste Croix; 'Perhaps, like Edward Thompson before him, Palmer has reacted to the dissolution of agency into structure by underestimating the objective determinants of subjective action' (p. 313). He calls the results 'admirable' and his disagreements 'relatively minor' (p. 312). The target was already set in 1987: Palmer's ILWCH response (p. 14 and n. 2, read) borrows phrases from Stedman Jones's Languages of Class for the first-person scene that opens it, and Scott's reply says 'Most of his critique is directed at Stedman Jones, not me' (ILWCH 32, p. 41). Later readings, labelled as such: Rogers (2021) quotes Palmer in 1993 granting that 'Poststructurally inclined historians rightly stress the need for closer attention to language and representation' ('The Poverty of Theory Revisited', Left History 1:1, 1993, p. 94, as quoted; unread here); Finkel (2021) calls the book Palmer's 'anger with the discursive turn'. Scope: a critique of the linguistic turn's treatment of class, not of attention to language as such. edge_105 (language → social) and edge_200 (historyworkshop–language) stay. Revision 1.152: Scott (2000, p. 69, read in full) puns on the title, 'Assent to Discourse', and Eley and Nield (2000, n. 46, read) call the book the reaction to Scott 'represented most viciously', a hostile characterisation recorded, not adopted. The debate entry languages_of_class now holds the exchanges (bryan_d_palmer → languages_of_class), and edge_200 has become gareth_stedman_jones → language.

edges.relationship: Liberal order criticised as an elastic, seemingly trans-historical category that sidesteps capitalism's changing historical structures, in a review of McKay's Reasoning Otherwise (2009)
edges.evidence_note: Dated 2009. 'Radical Reasoning', a feature review essay on Ian McKay, Reasoning Otherwise (2008), The Underhill Review (Carleton University), Fall 2009, read in full (web text; locators below are pages of the print PDF, https://www3.carleton.ca/underhillreview/09/fall/reviews/print/Palmer.pdf). He reads McKay's liberal order as a project 'in which liberty, equality, and private property are sanctified as the foundations of a civil society that valorizes individualism', and says past leftists 'never spoke of an enemy that they named "liberal order."' 'As an elastic category, liberal order can contain almost anything associated with what has traditionally been understood about modern developing societies'. 'The danger in deploying liberal order in this way, as a seemingly trans-historical analytic framework, is that it actually sidesteps the need to confront and elucidate capitalism's changing historical structures'; 'it may well be impossible to discern anything distinctly Canadian about the notion of liberal order'; 'The most serious problem with the liberal order perspective, then, is that it allows mainstream historians to avoid confronting just how critically important it is to name the frontline enemy: capitalism as systematic exploitation and endlessly proliferating oppression.' He adds that McKay's 'elastic understanding of Gramsci's hegemony conflates what Gramsci differentiated as a "separation of powers"'. The elasticity and capitalism argument is at pp. 3–4 and the Gramsci criticism at pp. 4–5. Qualifications kept: 'McKay is not necessarily captive of such tendencies himself' (p. 4), and the book 'stands as an undeniable achievement' (p. 31). This is Palmer's interpretation of the framework. McKay's own position, recorded under lof_mckay_2009 and known here through Fecteau's quotation, distinguishes the two analytically while treating them as historically close: 'Liberal order and capitalism cannot be conflated. Yet, after the 1840s, they also could not be easily separated' (p. 385, as quoted by Fecteau, 2009). That chapter appeared in the same year and is not a reply to Palmer; no direct rejoinder was found. Scope: the essay reviews Reasoning Otherwise and quotes Rebels, Reds, Radicals (2005, p. 84); it does not discuss the 2000 prospectus directly. McKay's reply, if any, was not checked. The critique-audit of 2026-10-14 proposed a group edge cdn_working_class → liberal_order_framework on this text; with the person entry, the person edge carries it and the group edge is not proposed. edge_845 (karl–liberal_order_framework, comparison) stays.

edges.relationship: Thompson's history of class and culture as a model for Palmer's labour history and the subject of his studies of Thompson (1976–94), with disagreements Palmer stated, including on base and superstructure
edges.evidence_note: In-period evidence. Palmer's 1976 essay (read) cites Thompson's Making for the skilled mechanic's leading role (p. 14 and notes). Bercuson (1981, p. 97, re-read): 'Palmer, echoing E.P. Thompson, regards culture and conflict as "complementary processes."' Kealey (1981, p. 82; existing note, not re-read) cites Palmer's forthcoming book as the place where Thompson's work is analysed at length. Palmer's 1987 ILWCH response (notes as listed by the publisher) leans on Thompson: n. 8 cites The Making (pp. 529–40) for how historians have interrogated the language of sources, n. 10 says 'This unity of the political and the economic is fundamental to Thompson's Making', and n. 14 cites The Poverty of Theory (pp. 235–36). 'Homage to Edward Thompson', Labour/Le Travail 32 (1993) and 33 (1994), read at Part I pp. 67–68 and Part II pp. 16–18: Palmer sets out Thompson's socialist humanism against 'the mechanical idealism of Stalinism's appropriation of the base/superstructure metaphor' (Part I, p. 68) and quotes Thompson calling The Making 'a polemic against abbreviated economistic notations of Marxism' (Part II, p. 17; Thompson's interviews, cited in n. 9, not read). Palmer's two books on Thompson, The Making of E. P. Thompson: Marxism, Humanism, and History (1981) and E. P. Thompson: Objections and Oppositions (1994), are cited at title and imprint level only (Open Library). Stated disagreement, in period: Callinicos (1992, p. 313) notes that Descent into Discourse 'takes Thompson and Raymond Williams to task for abandoning the metaphor of base and superstructure' (pp. 209–11 of the book, unread here). Later readings, labelled as such: Nicholas Rogers (2021) quotes Palmer's 1993 interview in Left History: 'it was relooking at The Making that convinced me to do labour history' (Left History 1:2, 1993, pp. 111–12, as quoted; the journal's PDF was behind a bot wall); Rogers calls The Making 'an exemplary model' for Palmer's dissertation, finds Palmer 'sympathetic and defensive of Thompson's position', but notes that 'Palmer does not necessarily agree with Thompson's reading of Marx' and 'is not a wholehearted advocate of Thompson's socialist humanism', since he holds to a revolutionary vanguard. Influence, not discipleship: the arrow records Thompson's work as Palmer's model and subject; it does not claim that Palmer adopted Thompson's positions whole.

edges.relationship: From within Marxism, rejects the 'economic automatism' of Stalinist base-and-superstructure Marxism and the treatment of class as 'a thing', holding to the 'dialectical interaction between social consciousness ... and social being' and faulting Marx's own 'clumsy static model' (1957–78)
edges.evidence_note: Thompson's own in-period statements. (1) 'Socialist Humanism: An Epistle to the Philistines', The New Reasoner 1 (Summer 1957), pp. 105–143, read in full in the Marxists Internet Archive transcription (no page numbers). Of Stalinist theory: 'How much easier if the people had no minds, if the "superstructure" was cut out and society was all "base"'; 'This economic automatism certainly is not Marxism.' 'In all their historical analysis Marx and Engels always kept in view this dialectical interaction between social consciousness (both active and passive) and social being. But in trying to explain their ideas they expressed them as a make-belief "model", the "basis" of social relations (in production) and the "superstructure" ... In fact no such basis and superstructure ever existed; it is a metaphor to help us to understand what does exist – men, who act, experience, think and act again. It turns out that it is a bad and dangerous model, since Stalin used it not as an image of men changing in society but as a mechanical model, operating semi-automatically and independently of conscious human agency.' 'An idea is not a reflex of a gasometer'; 'No "basis" ever invented a steam engine, or sat on the National Coal Board.' He does not exempt Marx: 'because Marx reduced his concept of process to a clumsy static model, Stalinism evolved this mystique'; features of Stalinism 'can be traced to ambiguities in the thought of Marx and, even more, to mechanistic fallacies in Lenin's writings'. Stalinism's three features are 'anti-intellectualism, moral nihilism, and the denial of the creative agency of human labour'. The revolt against Stalinism 'will, if successful, confirm the revolutionary confidence of the founders of the socialist movement'. (2) Preface to The Making of the English Working Class (1963), university-hosted transcription read in full (transcription pp. 1–2; printed pagination not collated): class is 'something which in fact happens (and can be shown to have happened) in human relationships'; 'There is today an ever-present temptation to suppose that class is a thing. This was not Marx's meaning, in his own historical writing, yet the error vitiates much latter-day "Marxist" writing', in which the class-consciousness that '"it" ought to have' is deduced and 'a cultural superstructure' lets recognition dawn 'in inefficient ways'; 'If we remember that class is a relationship and not a thing, we can not think in this way.' The same passage finds 'a similar error ... on the other side of the ideological divide', in the static sociology of Smelser and Dahrendorf, so the preface's target is reification in both camps. The preface's 'I am seeking to rescue the poor stockinger ...' is aimed at Fabian, economic-historian and 'Pilgrim's Progress' orthodoxies, not at Marxism, and is not used here. (3) 'The Poverty of Theory' (1978), section x, re-read in the Marxists Internet Archive transcription: 'Stalinism afforded a caricature of Marxism, which offered ... an identical reification of process, in which a "superstructure" was reduced to confirming or legitimating a base' (the identity is with Smelser's sociology), and no analogies 'derived from mechanical or organic mechanism' can 'encompass the logic of indeterminate historical process', since no analogy from another area can have 'any more than a limited, illustrative, metaphoric value (and often, as with basis and superstructure, a static and damaging one)'; in section vii he calls himself 'deeply indebted for certain concepts to Marx's own practice'. In-period readings: Palmer's 'Homage to Edward Thompson' (1993, Part I, p. 68) describes Thompson's socialist humanism as directed against 'the mechanical idealism of Stalinism's appropriation of the base/superstructure metaphor', and (1994, Part II, p. 17) quotes Thompson calling The Making 'a polemic against abbreviated economistic notations of Marxism' (from interviews, not read). The critique was itself contested inside Marxism: Callinicos (1992, p. 313) reports that Palmer's Descent into Discourse took Thompson and Raymond Williams 'to task for abandoning the metaphor of base and superstructure'. Later reading, labelled as such: Rogers (2021) sees in Thompson a 'rejection of economic determinism and the base–superstructure model of explanation favoured by many Marxists', preferring 'the co-determination of social being and social consciousness, mediated by experience'. Scope: a critique of economistic and Stalinist uses of historical materialism, and of Marx's own static model, made from within Marxism; it is not a rejection of historical materialism. The Althusser critique stays on edge_310 (ep_thompson → althusser) and edge_027 (marx → althusser); his contribution to Marxist social history stays on edge_309 (ep_thompson → marx).

edges.relationship: Scientists and philosophers charge that the strong programme and The Golem leave nature out of the explanation of scientific belief (1994–98)
edges.evidence_note: In-period texts read. Sokal, "What the Social Text Affair Does and Does Not Prove" (author's text, 1997; printed 1998; cited by note): "The extreme versions of social constructivism and relativism -- such as the Edinburgh 'strong programme' -- are, I think, largely based on the same failure to distinguish clearly between ontology, epistemology, and the sociology of knowledge"; he quotes Collins (n. 10) as saying "the natural world has a small or non-existent role in the construction of scientific knowledge", while allowing that Collins may intend a methodological injunction. Sokal and Bricmont, Intellectual Impostures (1998; Profile 1999/2003 printing): most scientists "point out the substantial missing piece in this kind of explanation: Nature itself" (p. 79); the strong programme "is ambiguous in its intent; and, depending on how one resolves the ambiguity, it becomes either a valid and mildly interesting corrective to the most naive psychological and sociological notions - reminding us that 'true beliefs have causes too' - or else a gross and blatant error" (p. 84). Mermin, Physics Today 49:3 (1996), p. 11: Collins and Pinch "infer from these studies a seriously deficient picture of the scientific enterprise"; The Golem is "an instructive demonstration of what can go wrong if you focus too strongly on the social perspective". Mermin frames this as a question of balance, not a refutation. Gross and Levitt (1994; book unread) are known here only through Edge (1997, n. 4), who reports that they name "the 'strong programme' in sociology of science associated with the Edinburgh school" (p. 25) and Bloor (p. 52) while listing no work by Barnes or Bloor in their references. The replies are the separate ssk → sciencewars edge. Two targets share this arrow: the Edinburgh strong programme (Barnes, Bloor, Henry), named by Gross and Levitt (as quoted), Sokal, and Sokal and Bricmont; and The Golem of Collins and Pinch, Mermin's target, which belongs with SSK's replication studies. No strand is set for that reason.
edges.map_label: Strong programme and The Golem attacked, 1994–98

edges.relationship: Sociologists of scientific knowledge answer that their methodological relativism was misread as hostility to science (1996–97)
edges.evidence_note: In-period replies in the sociologists' own words. Collins and Pinch, letter in Physics Today 49:7 (1996), p. 11, answering Mermin: "Many scientists, especially those who have become spokespersons, are evidently scientific fundamentalists. ... Where we sociologists think of ourselves as trying to gain social and historical insight into science, the fundamentalists see heresy"; The Golem is "about as inoffensive a social analysis of science as one could wish for"; they cite historical work on the slow reception of relativity. Mermin replied on the same page that "the rightness/wrongness axis is not a relevant dimension in their kind of sociological analysis of science". David Edge, "The Umpire Strikes Back" (EASST web text, February 1997; read in a web reproduction): "A powerful group of American scientists, apparently for political reasons, have chosen to mount a vicious attack on those scholars whom they take to be 'flying from science and reason'. One of their prime targets is 'social constructivism'"; the Edinburgh group "has always maintained that reality plays a central role in what comes to be believed about it". Edge is not on the ssk roster; he is on this debate's roster. Shapin's 1999 defence of methodological relativism is carried by the science → sciencewars edge. Bloor's own reply to the warriors was not found; his 1999 complaint that Latour joined "the recent contributors to The Flight from Science and Reason" is on the ssk → latour edge.

edges.relationship: Physicists charge Latour with sliding from representations of nature to nature and with misreading relativity (1996–98)
edges.evidence_note: In-period texts read. Sokal and Bricmont, Intellectual Impostures (1998; Profile 1999/2003 printing): Latour's works "contain a great number of propositions formulated so ambiguously that they can hardly be taken literally" (p. 85); on the Third Rule of Method, "Note how Latour slips, without comment or argument, from 'Nature's representation' in the first half of this sentence to 'Nature' tout court in the second half" (p. 85); his 1988 article on relativity "illustrates perfectly the problems encountered by a sociologist who aims to analyse the content of a scientific theory he does not understand very well" (p. 115), and "Latour's analysis is fatally flawed by his inadequate understanding of the theory Einstein is trying to explain" (p. 121). Sokal (1997/98, cited by note): "Latour has produced 40 pages of comical misunderstandings of a theory that is nowadays routinely taught to intelligent college freshmen"; Sokal in Le Monde (31 January 1997, author's translation): Latour "mixes up ontology and epistemology, and he attacks positions that no one would defend". Weinberg (New York Review of Books, 1996): "The objective nature of scientific knowledge has been denied by Andrew Ross and Bruno Latour". Dissent among physicists: Mermin (Physics Today 50:10, 1997, p. 11) wrote of the relativity essay, "I believe such attacks miss the point of Latour's essay". Steve Fuller's report of the Sokal–Latour debate at the LSE (1998) judged that "Latour won 'on points'". Latour's replies are the separate latour → sciencewars edge.

edges.relationship: Latour answers the physicists: science studies "added reality to science" and is "not at war" (1996–99)
edges.evidence_note: His own words where read. Pandora's Hope (1999), ch. 1, "Do You Believe in Reality? News from the Trenches of the Science Wars" (read in a retyped copy without book pages; to be checked against the printed book): "in this guerrilla warfare being conducted in the no-man's-land between the 'two cultures,' we were the ones being attacked by militants, activists, sociologists, philosophers, and technophobes of all hues, precisely because of our interest in the inner workings of scientific facts"; "If science studies has achieved anything, I thought, surely it has added reality to science, not withdrawn any from it"; "we are not at war"; and, of the other side, "a few disgruntled cold-war physicists". Earlier, as quoted by others: Sokal (Le Monde, 31 January 1997) reports Latour telling Libération (3 December 1996) that the hoax was "a clever joke" that thrashed people who deserved it but not researchers in science studies; Jardine and Frasca-Spada (SHPS 1997) translate a sentence of Latour's Le Monde article of 18 January 1997 about "A small number of theoretical physicists deprived of the fat budgets of the cold war". That article was not read, and the same editors later printed an "Apology" (unread), so the wording is given only as theirs. Fuller (1998) reports that at the LSE Latour "supported" constructivism but "opposed" relativism. Later reading, not evidence for the claim: in 2004 Latour asked, "Was I wrong to participate in the invention of this field known as science studies?", while refusing "to swear that I will never be a constructivist any more".

edges.relationship: Historians of science answer the charge that their field is hostile to or ignorant of science (1996–99)
edges.evidence_note: In-period replies by historians of science, read. Steven Shapin, "Rarely Pure and Never Simple" (Configurations 7, 1999), writing as "a historian and a sociologist of science": methodological relativism "implies nothing at all about epistemological evaluations or ontological judgments" (pp. 3–4); the charge of hostility to science or ignorance of it, "—when directed to the work of many distinguished historians and sociologists of science—now deserves to be called by its proper name: it is malevolently misinformed" (p. 11). He names no protagonist; his target is identified by its arguments, such as Sokal's challenge to jump from a window. John Krige (Physics World, December 1998): Intellectual Impostures "is essentially a political tract" and "lamentably indifferent to the history and philosophy of science". Mara Beller (Physics Today 51:9, 1998): "The philosophical pronouncements of Bohr, Born, Heisenberg and Pauli deserve some of the blame for the excesses of the postmodernist critique of science." M. Norton Wise reviewed Higher Superstition in Isis (1996; unread); Edge reports his charge of "a willful strategy of distortion and demonization" (p. 323). Jardine and Frasca-Spada (SHPS 1997) criticised both sides and are not counted as one-way critics. Not every historian of science sided against the warriors: Margaret Jacob wrote against Latour in A House Built on Sand (1998; see the truthdebate → latour edge). Physicists also criticised historians' method (Weinberg 1996 on Whig history; Sokal and Bricmont 1998, p. 69 n. 88); that thinner charge is not drawn as a sciencewars → science edge. The arrow targets the debate as a whole: these historians answered the attackers' arguments (Gross and Levitt, Sokal, Sokal and Bricmont, Weinberg), not the respondents' strand in which they sit.

edges.relationship: Selected constructionist and relativist positions within science studies attacked (1994–98)
edges.evidence_note: In-period texts. Jardine and Frasca-Spada (SHPS 1997, §I, read) report that Gross and Levitt went after "exponents of science studies -- that is, historians, philosophers and sociologists of science" (the book itself unread). Sokal (1997/98, read) disclaims that the hoax proves "the whole field of cultural studies, or cultural studies of science -- much less sociology of science -- is nonsense", yet attacks "the sloppy thinking and glib relativism that have become prevalent in many parts of Science Studies". The Social Text editors (Robbins and Ross, 1996, read) say science studies and cultural studies had "been subject recently to so much derision from conservatives in science". Koertge's anthology (1998; publisher abstract, not her text) addresses the view in "Science, Technology and Society Studies (STS)" that scientific results are "social constructions". An STS reply in its own words was not read: the Social Text essays (Harding, Fuller, Winner and others) are unread, and Robbins and Ross wrote as cultural-studies editors, so no sts → sciencewars edge is drawn.

edges.relationship: Physicists blame an "immoderate" Kuhn for founding relativism about science, while sparing the "moderate" Kuhn and leaving him to historians (1996–98)
edges.evidence_note: In-period texts read. Sokal and Bricmont (1998; Profile 1999/2003 printing), following Tim Maudlin, separate "a moderate Kuhn and his immoderate brother": "We have no objection of principle to the moderate Kuhn, and we leave to historians the task of investigating the extent to which these ideas are correct in concrete situations. By contrast, the immoderate Kuhn - who became, perhaps involuntarily, one of the founding fathers of contemporary relativism - thinks that changes of paradigm are due principally to non-empirical factors" (p. 70). Weinberg (1996) lists Kuhn, "as I understand them", among those who deny "The objective nature of scientific knowledge"; in 1998 he wrote that Kuhn's later conclusions "have made Kuhn a hero to the philosophers, historians, sociologists, and cultural critics who question the objective character of scientific knowledge", and that "Kuhn made the shift from one paradigm to another seem more like a religious conversion than an exercise of reason." Sokal's parody (1996, n. 2) cites Kuhn (1970) first among the "revisionist studies" it mocks. This is a critique of Kuhn and of his reception; Kuhn died in 1996 and did not reply. His own earlier rejection of irrationalism ("labels which I categorically reject", 1970) is recorded on the science → kuhn edge.

edges.relationship: Appleby, Hunt and Jacob judge the strong programme's relativism inadequate to historical and scientific truth (1994)
edges.evidence_note: The historians' own words: Telling the Truth about History (1994), read in the Norton 2011 e-book, which has no print page numbers; cited by chapter. Ch. 5 ("Discovering the Clay Feet of Science"): the social constructionists "could not explain the way in which technical problems, or new natural phenomena like viruses, set whole research agendas"; the social insight "does not, however, underwrite the more extreme claims of strong programmers who have never offered an adequate theory to address the complexity of circumstances and situations that produce reasonably true human knowledge"; "relativism fails the needs of historians just as it skirts the possible existence of truths in science" (n. 24 cites Barnes and Bloor, "Relativism, Rationalism and the Sociology of Knowledge"). Ch. 7 calls social constructionists "once called strong programmers". The book was published in 1994, before the 1996 hoax. No SSK reply to it was found; Shapin's 1999 complaint that methodological relativism is "routinely misrepresented" (n. 6) is a general answer, not a reply to this book. Print pages remain to be checked.
edges.map_label: Telling the Truth against the strong programme, 1994

edges.relationship: Telling the Truth about History assimilates Latour's laboratory studies to postmodernism (1994); Jacob carries the objection to the Science Wars anthology (1998)
edges.evidence_note: Telling the Truth about History (1994; Norton 2011 e-book, no print pages), ch. 6 ("Postmodernism and the Crisis of Modernity"), quotes the claim that "'Nothing special'" and "'nothing extraordinary'" happens in the laboratory, attributes it in n. 9 to Latour, "Give Me a Laboratory and I Will Raise the World" (1983), and comments: "Latour calls himself an 'a-modernist,' but his position seems indistinguishable from postmodernism." Margaret Jacob, one of the three authors, then wrote "Reflections on Bruno Latour's Version of the Seventeenth Century" for A House Built on Sand (1998). Only the publisher's abstract was read; it says the essay "seeks to show how wrong-headed" We Have Never Been Modern is about early modern politics. That wording is the publisher's, not Jacob's. Moderate support: one sentence of the book, plus an abstract. No reply by Latour to these historians was found.

edges.relationship: Two 1990s disputes over relativism and truth: historians defending historical knowledge, and scientists attacking science studies
edges.evidence_note: Comparison only. The disputes overlap in time and in people but neither is a critique of the other. Margaret Jacob took part in both: Telling the Truth about History (1994) already criticised the strong programme and Latour from the historians' side, and she wrote for A House Built on Sand (1998; abstract only). Richard Evans, a truthdebate historian, cited Sokal approvingly in 1999 as having done "far more effectively and knowledgeably" what he had only touched on in criticising Derrida and Lyotard. The historians' book was published in 1994, before the 1996 hoax, and Evans endorses Sokal rather than criticising him, so no critique edge is drawn in either direction. The Science Wars concerned the natural sciences and their students; the truth debate concerned historical writing.

edges.relationship: Popper, Lakatos and the historian L. Pearce Williams criticise Kuhn's normal science and theory change: indoctrination, irrationalism, "mob psychology" and too little history (1965–70), answered by Kuhn
edges.evidence_note: In-period texts read in Lakatos and Musgrave, eds., Criticism and the Growth of Knowledge (1970; the 1965 Bedford College symposium). Popper, already a critic on the science roster: the normal scientist "has been taught in a dogmatic spirit: he is a victim of indoctrination" (p. 53); "Kuhn's logic is the logic of historical relativism" (p. 55); the Myth of the Framework "is, in our time, the central bulwark of irrationalism" (p. 56); yet "'Normal' science, in Kuhn's sense, exists" (p. 52). Lakatos, a contributor on the science roster: Kuhn's message "had some authoritarian and irrationalist overtones" (p. 92 n. 3); "in Kuhn's view scientific revolution is irrational, a matter for mob psychology" (p. 178, italicised in the original); he also absorbs Kuhn, offering his research programmes as a reconstruction of Kuhn's "socio-psychological concept of 'paradigm'" (p. 179 n. 1). L. Pearce Williams, a historian of science, aims at Kuhn and Popper alike: "the history of science cannot bear such a load at this time. We simply do not know enough to permit a philosophical structure to be erected on a historical foundation"; "As a historian, then, I must view both Popper and Kuhn with a somewhat jaundiced eye" (p. 50), while continuing to use both as guides. Kuhn's replies: charges of "irrationality, relativism, and the defence of mob rule" are "labels which I categorically reject" (p. 234); such misinterpretations "are voiced only by philosophers" (p. 260); to Pearce Williams, "There is no area in which I am more deeply conscious of the need for additional historical research, though I dissent from the conclusions Pearce Williams draws from that need" (pp. 251–252); and in the 1970 Postscript, good reasons "function as values" (p. 199) and "That is not a relativist's position" (p. 206). The irrationalism charge came from philosophers on the science roster; the historian's objection was evidential. edge_332 (science → kuhn, influence) stays.

edges.relationship: Latour and Callon: the strong programme's symmetry is itself asymmetrical, explaining nature by society, so SSK must take "one more turn" (1992–99), after an acknowledged debt
edges.evidence_note: Latour's own words, read. Debt first: in 1988 he wrote that Bloor "has most clearly defined the task of any sociology of science by introducing the notion of symmetry" and that "the principle of symmetry remains the basis of most work in the area", while dropping social explanation (Pasteurization of France, p. 256 n. 21); in 1999, "I feel entirely in David's debt" (p. 114); edge_685 records that debt. Critique: "One More Turn after the Social Turn" (1992; author's typescript, §2): "Bloor's book (1976) was the high tide mark of this asymmetrical philosophy"; "Society was supposed to explain Nature!" (p. 278 as cited by Bloor); §3: the "intermediary solution —social realism alternating with natural relativism— advocated for many years by colleagues like David Bloor or Harry Collins" is "in the long run, counterproductive for the field as well as for their own program". Callon and Latour (1992): "We have never been interested in giving a social explanation of anything, but we want to explain society" (p. 348); their yardstick lets them "read most of SSK as 'reactionary,' because they start from a closed definition of the social and then use this repertoire as an explanation of nature" (p. 349); Collins "simply shifts the burden to the Edinburgh school" (p. 355), though "We learned a great deal from Collins's work" (p. 344). We Have Never Been Modern (1993, p. 94; OCR gaps): Bloor's principle of symmetry "leads rapidly to an impasse"; "Constructivist where Nature is concerned, it is realistic about [Society]". "For David Bloor… and Beyond" (1999): "The Strong Program was useful and still is against the few remaining epistemologists. It has become an obstacle for the continuation of science studies" (p. 116). Bloor's reply: Latour's "criticisms are based on a systematic misrepresentation of the position he rejects" (Anti-Latour, 1999, p. 82); see ssk → latour. Callon has no entry and sits on the sts roster.
edges.map_label: The strong programme as an obstacle, 1992–99

edges.relationship: Bloor answers that Latour misrepresents the Strong Program and that his own alternative is "obscurantism" (1999); Collins and Yearley had called the actor-network approach a "backward step" (1992)
edges.evidence_note: Bloor's own words, read in "Anti-Latour" (SHPS 30, 1999): "Bruno Latour is a vehement critic of the sociology of knowledge in general, and the Strong Program in particular" (p. 81); "I think Latour is wrong ... If anything they are a step backwards" (p. 82); "his criticisms are based on a systematic misrepresentation of the position he rejects, and ... his own approach, in so far as it is different, is unworkable" (p. 82); the charge that SSK explains nature by society "is a profound misrepresentation. The aim isn't to explain nature, but to explain shared beliefs about nature" (p. 87); Latour's vocabulary of actants "looks like a formula for imposing confusion on ourselves: it is obscurantism raised to the level of a general methodological principle" (p. 97); "Latour has endorsed, and encouraged, a wholly false stereotype of the Strong Program", joining "the recent contributors to The Flight from Science and Reason" (pp. 110–111). He partly concedes: "Latour, rightly, rejects the symmetry principle understood in this way" (p. 84). He cites other critiques he finds "devastating" (p. 95), including Collins and Yearley (1992), Schaffer (1991) and Shapin (1988), none read here. Collins and Yearley's chapter is known only through Callon and Latour's quotations (1992, p. 347): "The consequences of the semiotic method [of Latour] amount to a backward step". Latour's reply acknowledges the charge: "The result is a devastating critique" (1999, p. 113) and calls Schaffer's similar critique "exactly as ill-conceived" (n. 6). Bloor's rejoinder (SHPS 30, pp. 131–136) was not located.

edges.relationship: Kuhn calls the strong programme's claims "absurd: an example of deconstruction gone mad" (1991)
edges.evidence_note: Kuhn's own words, read: "The Trouble with the Historical Philosophy of Science" (Rothschild Lecture, Harvard, 19 November 1991; published 1992; in The Road Since Structure, 2000): "I am among those who have found the claims of the strong program absurd: an example of deconstruction gone mad. And the more qualified sociological and historical formulations that currently strive to replace it are, in my view, scarcely more satisfactory" (p. 110); the strong program "has been widely understood as claiming that power and interest are all there are" (p. 110). In the 1995 Athens interview (same volume) he says of Shapin and Schaffer's Leviathan and the Air-Pump, "The scholarship is often damn good!", while objecting that they "totally miss" the barometer's "vastly greater explanatory power" (pp. 316–317); that remark concerns the science roster's practice strand and is context only. No SSK reply to the lecture was read. The SSK reading of Kuhn ran the other way, as appropriation (Barnes, T. S. Kuhn and Social Science, 1982, unread); edge_132 (kuhn → ssk, influence) stays.

edges.relationship: A historian of consumption and material culture criticises actor-network theory's "flat view of modern history" while proposing to historicise its concerns (2009)
edges.evidence_note: Dated 2009. Frank Trentmann, "Materiality in the Future of History" (Journal of British Studies 48, 2009; read in full). He writes as a historian of consumption (author note: director of the Cultures of Consumption research programme, 2002–07) and sets material-culture studies against material politics (p. 285). "The most influential (if controversial) platform for exploring the 'agency' of things in the past couple of decades has been actor-network theory (ANT). Spearheaded by Bruno Latour, Michel Callon, John Law, and others" (p. 290); n. 33 notes "the difficulty of integrating historical formations of power and culture in an analysis primarily concerned with reconstructing a network of actors and actants at a specific moment in time" (p. 290). "It is perhaps ironic that a theory like ANT, so concerned with resisting grand narratives and abstractions (like 'society'), draws on such a flat view of modern history"; "It is hard to see a general turning away from things, as presumed by Latour and others" (p. 291); "this rather monochromatic view of modernity supposedly so divorced from things" (p. 301). The critique is qualified: "Before simply rejecting Latour as problematic history, however, we might historicize his concerns into questions for research" (p. 301), and whatever one thinks of the claim that things have agency, "things and humans are inseparably interwoven in mutually constitutive relationships" (p. 307). No reply by Latour was found. A historian's critique of Latour; not a claim that consumption history as a field rejected ANT.

edges.relationship: Canadian imperialism read as one form of Canadian nationalism, through the ideas of its leading spokesmen (1970)
edges.evidence_note: His own statement (1970; Google Books snippet view of the 2013 second edition (volume -Y-BAAAAQBAJ); its pages 3–265 reprint the 1970 text with the same pagination (Monet 1972 cites pp. 132 and 261 for passages found on those pages here). Snippets are short fragments returned by search; the continuous text was not read). The introduction opens 'This book is a study in Canadian nationalist thought' (p. 3). Of the earlier critics he writes that 'When critics belaboured imperialism because of its hostility to “Canadian nationalism” what they really meant was that they believed it incompatible with that kind of nationalism which they endorsed. There have been many varieties of Canadian nationalism'; imperialism was 'one variety of Canadian nationalism', a 'type of awareness of nationality which rested upon a certain understanding of history, the national character, and the national mission' (p. 9). His method: 'inquiring into the ideas and ideals which men in the past read into their interpretations of Canada and by exploring the relationship between these conceptions and the environment in which they circulated' (p. 10). The conclusion opens 'Imperialism was one form of Canadian nationalism' (p. 259). In-period reception. Jacques Monet (RHAF 1972, pp. 274–276, read in full): the book's 'grande originalité' is to conclude that the imperialists were not 'des agents d'une puissance étrangère' but 'de vrais Canadians nationalistes' (pp. 274–275); the thesis, 'déjà suggérée par la monographie de Norman Penlington', 'sera dorénavant très difficile, sinon impossible, à réfuter' (p. 275); the book is 'une contribution majeure — sinon un premier modèle — à l'histoire des idées (oui, il y en a) au Canada anglophone' (p. 276). Monet also reports the first criticisms (p. 275 and nn. 2–4): neglect of the economic and military sides of imperialism (Robert Page, JCS 1970), the folding into a Canadianizing ideology of witnesses 'qui seraient plutôt des représentants du pan-britannisme' (Douglas Cole, JCS 1970), and too much weight on 'une petite élite' of intellectuals (H. V. Nelles, Canadian Forum 1970); Page, Cole (1970) and Nelles are not read here. Cole's 1971 comparative article (notes read; body closed) says that Berger 'makes the strongest case for a Canadian nationalistic consciousness within these terms' (n. 33). Susan Mann Trofimenkoff (1979, read): he 'manages to suspend the reader's initial disbelief and argue persuasively that turn-of-the-century imperialists were really nationalists', but 'Their nationalism and their imperialism were, however, decidedly masculine affairs' (p. 10); intellectual history 'will have to take women into account' (p. 10). Clarence Karr (1989, re-read): Berger 'rescued the previously outcast imperialists and transformed them into significant Canadian nationalists' (p. 161); 'Carl Berger's critics accuse him of an over-Canadianization of imperialism and of ignoring a broader Anglo-Saxon perspective in what Graham Carr refers to as a “scavenger hunt for nationalism”' (pp. 162–163); since his book, group biography 'has been upheld by many historians in Canada as the best method of addressing the Canadian intellectual tradition' (p. 167), and its premise that imperialism can 'only be understood in relation to the characters who espoused it and who came to personify it' risks making thought 'whatever a single advocate chooses to believe' (p. 168). Carr's article (JCS 1982) is checked at its journal abstract only. A contribution, not an origin: Monet credits Penlington with the suggestion. Later reading, not evidence for this edge: Doug Owram's introduction to the 2013 edition (snippet view) calls it 'pretty much the standard interpretation of the way in which Canadian nationalism evolved' (p. xi).

edges.relationship: The English-Canadian national tradition analysed as historiography: its major figures, their nationalism and its limits (1976; 2nd ed. 1986)
edges.evidence_note: His own statement (1976 preface, reprinted 1986; Google Books snippet view of the 1986 second edition (volume jRN6AAAAMAAJ, University of Michigan copy; preface page not reported by Google), with the 1976 edition (bix6AAAAMAAJ) checked for the preface opening and contents. Snippets are short fragments; the continuous text was not read): 'This study is an examination of aspects of English-Canadian historical thought and literature since the turn of the century. It deals with the central teachings of the major figures - George Wrong, Adam Shortt, Chester Martin, Harold Innis, Arthur Lower, Frank Underhill, Donald Creighton and William Morton - and also, in a less detailed fashion, with a more numerous group of other professional scholars who shaped the way Canadians understood their past'; 'The main emphasis is on the creative edge of historical writing and on those authors who broke the traditional patterns of interpretation'; 'Written history represents a self-conscious effort to establish the meaning of experience for the present'. The 1976 conclusion, as Allen Mills quotes it (CJPST 1977, pp. 134–137, read in full): 'Canada's historians have all been nationalists of various hues, and sometimes their judgments about what was central to the past and what was peripheral arose as much from divergent conceptions of nationality as from disagreements about interpretations of the same evidence' (p. 259; Mills p. 136). The 1986 edition replaces that conclusion with a chapter on 'the vast exfoliation of historical literature over the last twenty years' (preface to the second edition). There 'A few historians in the sixties, moreover, subjected the tradition in which they had grown up to searching criticism. J.M.S. Careless joined Ramsay Cook in condemning the undue emphasis on national history and unity' (p. 261), and he quotes Careless (1969) that the 'nation-building approach' 'neglects and obscures even while it explains and illuminates' (p. 262); social history's 'initial impact was to magnify the diversity of Canadian history' (p. 298). In-period reception. Mills: the book 'makes a substantial contribution to the intellectual history of English Canada' and 'is really about' its eight 'superluminaries' (p. 135); 'his description of all Canadian historians as nationalists places much too much weight on that over-used term', since they 'have very different conceptions of the nation that is to survive' (p. 136); but 'Berger's claim that Canadian historians have been generally unconcerned to explore the group loyalties of class, region, culture and family is unimpeachable' (pp. 136–137). Terry Cook (Archivaria 5, 1977–78, pp. 198–203, read in full) calls it 'a remarkably subtle analysis of major trends in Canadian historiography' that 'transcends historiography to become an intellectual history of English Canada in the twentieth century' (p. 202). (Cook gives the 'nation-building' passage at p. 263 of the 1976 edition without naming Careless; the 1986 text attributes it to Careless.) Karr (1989, p. 161): 'As a sequel he analysed the national conceptual frameworks in which professional historians functioned and wrote.' The French-Canadian limit is his own choice, explained in the preface: 'two language traditions have, in historical thought as well as in other non-political spheres, occasionally touched and intersected, but in general they have been preoccupied with the backgrounds of two rather different “nations”', and a comparison 'must rest on preliminary appraisals of the individual traditions'; 'the two traditions of historical writing flowed in separate channels' (p. 181). Ronald Rudin (1997; snippet view) shares 'Berger's belief that historical writing can “reveal a good deal about the intellectual climate in which it was composed”' but does 'not accept his assumption, implicit in Writing of Canadian History, that historians across the twentieth century have been united by their search for the truth' (p. 4), and finds that 'Berger failed, however, to consider the way in which Groulx had, by the 1930s, altered his view of the Dollard affair' (p. 58). Gregory Kealey (1982, reprinted 1995; snippet view) notes that the Marxist Stanley Ryerson 'was not considered for systematic evaluation in The Writing of Canadian History' (1995, p. 84), while finding 'little to argue with' in Berger's 1986 summary of the labour-history debate (1995, p. 18).

edges.relationship: The liberal nationalist account of imperialism as a colonial past defeated by Canadian nationalism, criticised (1970)
edges.evidence_note: His own words (1970; Google Books snippet view of the 2013 second edition (volume -Y-BAAAAQBAJ); its pages 3–265 reprint the 1970 text with the same pagination (Monet 1972 cites pp. 132 and 261 for passages found on those pages here). Snippets are short fragments returned by search; the continuous text was not read). The interpretation he set out to revise: 'The conflict between imperialism and nationalism added up to a struggle between the past and the future, the desire to remain a colony and the wish to be a free nation. Once this framework was accepted, it was easy to account for the failure of imperialism: it succumbed to Canadian nationalism. The main outlines of this interpretation survived largely because of the great influence of O. D. Skelton's biography of Laurier and because of the long dominance of a particular school of Canadian historiography of which it was the finest expression. This so-called liberal nationalist school has lately come under some penetrating scrutiny, its insufficiencies have been exposed and its continued relevance questioned. Naturally, its interpretation of imperialism has also been found wanting, at least by implication' (p. 9). Against it he argued that critics who attacked imperialism for 'its hostility to “Canadian nationalism”' 'really meant that they believed it incompatible with that kind of nationalism which they endorsed' (p. 9). In-period corroboration that this was the received English-Canadian view: Jacques Monet (RHAF 1972, read in full) writes that the imperialists 'ont eu très mauvaise presse parmi les historiens du Canada' and that English-Canadian historians, 'partisans pour la plupart de l'explication de l'équipe gagnante', saw them as 'des conservateurs retardataires' (p. 274); Berger 'vient maintenant nuancer ces jugements... téméraires' (p. 274). The same judgement runs into his historiography: in The Writing of Canadian History (1976) the main criticism of English-Canadian historians, as Allen Mills reads it (1977, read), is that they wrote 'as if they were contributing to pressing matters of contemporary public concern, especially the matter of national survival' (Mills's words, pp. 135–136). A counter-critique: Graham Carr (JCS 1982; journal abstract only) argues that 'revisionists such as Carl Berger, while ostensibly challenging Whig assumptions about imperialism/nationalism, actually share many of the traditional views'. The arrow records Berger's criticism of a position, the liberal nationalist account of imperialism; it does not claim that the national-tradition historians shared one view, and Skelton, whom he names, has no atlas entry.
edges.map_label: Against the liberal nationalist reading of imperialism, 1970

edges.relationship: 'Limited identities': the regional, ethnic and class identities Canadians have, proposed as the place where 'Canadianism' might be found (1967), a phrase Careless made a programme (1969)
edges.evidence_note: Cook's own text, 'Canadian Centennial Cerebrations', International Journal 22:4 (1967), pp. 659–663: the opening, read in the OpenAlex text of the article, attacks Canadian Dimension's 'Open Letter to Canadian Nationalists', likens it to Canada First's 1874 manifesto and asks 'Who says Canadian nationalism is difficult to define? Jobs!' (p. 659). The limited-identities sentence was not read on Cook's page; Buckner quotes it (2000, p. 4): 'Perhaps instead of constantly deploring our lack of identity, we should attempt to understand and explain the regional, ethnic and class identities that we do have. It might just be that it is in these limited identities that “Canadianism” is found'. Taken up: Careless (CHR 1969; unread here, quoted by Buckner, p. 4) held that the 'Canadian experience' must be 'discerned and defined' through the 'limited identities of region, culture and class referred to by Professor Cook'. Buckner (p. 5) writes that 'Cook and Careless' embraced the concept partly in response to Quebec separatism, quoting Cook's 1970 essay as reprinted in The Maple Leaf Forever (p. 213): 'Nationalism by nature tends strongly to centralism and uniformity: Canada is by nature federal, sectional and pluralist'; 'historians in Atlantic Canada eagerly espoused the concept of “limited identities”, but their motivations were rather different' (p. 5). In period, Buckner's 1988 abstract (recorded in cdng_buckner_1988, not re-read) calls it 'the catch phrase of the Canadian historical profession in the 1960s' and judges it 'premature to abandon'. Criticism: Reid (1987, opening, recorded in cdng_reid_1987) notes that during the 1980s 'concern has increasingly been expressed that fragmentation has been the result'; Gauvreau (1991, p. 164 n. 10) writes that limited identities 'has underwritten much of the “new social history”', which, like the older national history, 'marginalizes religious history'; Buckner (2000, p. 12) writes 'I think it implied to Cook and Careless' that national identity was the sum of component identities, calls that idea 'nonsensical', and argues that 'All identities are socially constructed'. Influence rather than contribution: Cook named the identities but wrote no regional history, and later questioned region as a unit of analysis (edge 2). The roster row calls him a precursor.

edges.relationship: Region questioned as a unit of analysis: regional history's strengths and weaknesses weighed (1977), and regions recast as provinces, 'a concept whose time has gone' (1983)
edges.evidence_note: Cook's own review essays in Acadiensis, read in full. 'The Burden of Regionalism' (7:1, Autumn 1977, pp. 110–115), reviewing Bercuson's Canada and the Burden of Unity among other books, notes 'the tendency to see regionalism as a virtue of Canadian life rather than an obstacle to Canadian unity' (p. 110). Bercuson's contributors assume 'that Canadian history is best understood from a regional perspective' (p. 112), but 'neither he nor anyone else in the book attempts to define the term' (p. 114); 'the “regional” approach to Canadian history, and to its discontents, has both strengths and weaknesses. The whole may not be greater than the parts, but it is at least the sum of them' (p. 115). 'Regionalism Unmasked' (13:1, Autumn 1983, pp. 137–142), reviewing L. D. McCann's Heartland and Hinterland (1982): 'I have begun to doubt seriously the existence of the phenomena we have for so long called regions, though regionalism as a rationalization of certain interests may have some reality' (p. 140); McCann's definition of region 'applies at least as well, and perhaps better, to a province as to a region. So why not call a region what it really is — a province' (p. 140); with Cole Harris's chapter, the book 'can really lead to no other conclusion than that, as a tool of analysis, “regionalism” is a concept whose time has gone' (p. 141). He qualifies this: 'Stripped of its rhetoric there remains with the regional approach, especially as practised by historical geographers, a legitimate preoccupation with some profoundly important aspects of our history: class, sex, family, ethnicity, for example' (p. 141), and he calls Wynn's Maritimes chapter 'the finest section of the book' (p. 138). In-period response: Buckner (2000, pp. 8–10) cites both reviews, though he dates the first 1974 and renders 'whose time is gone' where the 1983 page reads 'has gone'. He calls the fragmentation charge 'patently absurd, at least when applied to the Atlantic region' (p. 8) and holds that the Atlantic Provinces 'had legitimate grievances within Confederation' (p. 10), adding that he was 'initially ... as skeptical as Cook' (p. 10). The critique targets the regional framework and heartland–hinterland synthesis, not regional research as such.

edges.relationship: The Laurentian view criticised as regional rather than national, and the national school read as superseded (1977–83)
edges.evidence_note: Cook's own words, read in full. 'The Burden of Regionalism' (Acadiensis 7:1, 1977, p. 110): 'The so-called national schools have, in reality, had a rather obviously regional focus. Those who live in the Valley of the Fraser, the Red or the Restigouche can hardly accept the Laurentian view of Canadian history as “national”, unless, of course, they are content to be considered as “colonials” — a point made long ago by W. L. Morton. And the other nationalist themes fare little better.' 'Regionalism Unmasked' (Acadiensis 13:1, 1983, p. 137): 'the so-called “national” approach to the interpretation of the Canadian past has come under a destructive barrage of criticism' (the decade before it is garbled in the text layer); Berger's The Writing of Canadian History (1976) 'might be viewed as a lengthy epitaph on the headstone of the national school's grave'; Morton's 'Clio in Canada' (1946) 'made explicit what had long been implicit in the Innis-Creighton laurentian thesis: the metropolitan-hinterland relationship was not one of equality'. In-period context: Buckner (2000, pp. 4–5) sets limited identities (edge 1) against a post-war consensus of 'liberal nationalists such as A.R.M. Lower and Frank Underhill' and 'conservative nationalists such as Donald Creighton and C.P. Stacey' for whom the nation-state was the frame of reference. Limits: Cook credits the point to Morton; he co-wrote a Centenary Series volume (1974); and by Buckner's account (p. 8) he 'warned regional historians of the danger of ignoring the “national experience”' in 1977 ('The Golden Age of Canadian Historical Writing', Historical Reflections; unread here). The critique is of the Laurentian claim to speak for the nation, not of the staple studies' economics. edge_805 (cdn_regional → cdn_national_tradition, critique) carries the regional historians' version of the argument.

edges.relationship: The Regenerators: late Victorian social criticism read as the replacement of individual by social salvation, and the sacred becoming secular (1985)
edges.evidence_note: The book is unread here: UTP and De Gruyter refused automated access, and the Internet Archive copy is borrow-only. Its contents are recorded in crr_cook_1985, including the closing chapter 'The Sacred Becomes the Secular'. Cook's words are known as quoted in in-period readings. Gauvreau (Acadiensis 1991, pp. 161–162) quotes 'the orthodox Christian preoccupation with man's salvation was gradually replaced by a concern for social salvation' and 'the substitution of theology, the science of religion, with sociology, the science of society' (Regenerators, p. 4); Christianity became 'less rather than more relevant' (p. 6); social conservatism 'went hand in hand with scientific conservatism, and both were founded on religious conservatism' (p. 12); and social regeneration became 'a substitute for the formidable labour of reformulating theological doctrine' (p. 229). Karr (Acadiensis 1989, p. 162) quotes that the book's subjects 'almost never alluded to the cultivation of a national sentiment' (p. 6). Gaffield's review (History: Reviews of New Books 14:5, 1986, p. 144; scanned page read by OCR and checked against the image) summarizes it: 'the call for social salvation emerged from a strong religious commitment but led to increasing secularization', and Cook 'treats religious thinking as an independent factor'. Contested in period. Gauvreau (1991) calls it 'important' but says it 'does not fully resist the temptation to view the 19th-century religious experience in relation to the 20th-century mind-set' (p. 161). He reads it as a '“neo-conservative” appropriation' of Allen's categories (p. 163); 'The appearance of The Regenerators in 1985 marked the beginning of the assault on Allen's position' (p. 163 n. 9). He adds that 'the emerging consensus seems to be away from “military metaphors” of the type employed by Cook' (p. 164). Van Die, he reports, 'ultimately accepts Cook's central thesis of the decline and irrelevance of Protestant religion, but does not agree with the conflict model' (p. 173). Marshall (CCHA Historical Studies 1993–94, web text without page numbers) names 'the secularization thesis outlined by McKillop, Cook, and Marshall' as Gauvreau's target and cites Regenerators pp. 228–32 (n. 6). Laverdure's 1998 review (crr_laverdure_1998, not re-read) says Christie and Gauvreau 'challenge the secularization thesis, most strongly advocated by Ramsay Cook … and David Marshall'. Karr (1989, p. 163 n. 21) finds 'an equally forceful Ontario bias' answering Allen's Western one. The name 'secularization thesis' is the critics', as the strand note says.

edges.relationship: An ecological interpretation of early Canadian history: contact as the interaction of ecologies, 'cabbages, at least as much as kings' (1990)
edges.evidence_note: Reuses the reading recorded on 2026-10-13 for the environment-family drafts (pe131_extras_cook_1990; canon-evidence-canada.md, text C1).
