It was not re-read for this entry because Project MUSE refused automated access. Cook's W. L. Morton Lecture (Trent, October 1990; JCS 25:4, 1990–91) starts from Morton's 1946 remark that history 'is concerned with ecology too' (p. 5): 'It is an insight which I would like to try to build upon' (p. 6). He marks a break with the staple historians: 'for this earlier generation of historians the exploitation of the environment was accepted as natural and necessary, even though excesses might be deplored' (pp. 6–7), while 'More recent environmental historians have a different focus. They are no longer much concerned with explaining the impact of the environment on man; it is the impact of man on nature that is at the centre of their work' (p. 7). Following Crosby, 'contact was even more significantly the interaction of different ecologies or environments' (p. 13). His conclusion: 'Cabbages, at least as much as kings, led to the transformation of the new world' (p. 15, as recorded in canon-evidence-canada.md; not in the source's verification note). In-period reading: Gauvreau (Acadiensis 1991, pp. 164–165 n. 12), arguing about Cook's religious history, called the lecture his 'recent “conversion experience” concerning the happy convergence of nature and culture'. Later reading, labelled: Wynn (2004, p. 33, recorded in pe131_extras_wynn_2004) quotes Cook's claim that Canadian historical writing 'has always been concerned with the environment' to describe Canadians who 'seemed to wonder what all the fuss was about'. A contribution, not a founding. edge_913 (harold_a_innis → environment) carries his continuity claim and Forkey's 1998 rejection of it; this edge carries his own ecological reading of contact.

edges.relationship: Between 'nationalists' and 'limited identitarians': class, ethnicity and gender as what Canadians share, and identities as contingent and multiple (1993–2000)
edges.evidence_note: Cook's own words. 'The New History of Atlantic Canada' (Acadiensis 23:1, Autumn 1993, pp. 146–152, read in full) came between Bliss's 'Privatizing the Mind' (1991–92) and Granatstein's book (1998): 'one of the sweet ironies in the arid debate between “nationalists” and “limited identitarians” on historiography is that neither side appears to recognize that class, ethnicity and gender describe what groups of Canadians have in common, while “nationalism” most often provokes divisions — “regionalism”!' (p. 146). He holds that 'for all the emphasis on differences during recent decades, Canadians from all regions and linguistic groups have, in fact, been growing more alike, at least in aspiration if not in reality' (p. 146). His 2000 CHR forum essay (pp. 260–265 per Buckner's n. 15) is read only in its abstract: the 'limited identities' hypothesis 'has played a major role in the flowering of social history whose dominance is now being called into question by proponents of a renewed “national” approach'; the debate ignores 'the easy assumption that identities, limited or national, are essential rather than contingent', and 'it is too often forgotten that identities are multiple rather than single'. Context: Bliss's abstract (1991–92) asks historians to remember 'that their subject, after all, is Canada' and does not name Cook. Buckner (2000) writes that Cook in 1995 called the phrase 'usually attributed to Maurice Careless and I have decided that he is welcome to it!' (p. 8; Canada, Quebec and the Uses of Nationalism, 2nd ed., p. 230, unread here). Buckner then groups Bliss, Granatstein and Owram with Careless's later view that the search for limited identities had 'gone too far' (p. 9). A contribution: Cook is a root of the debate (edge 1) and a respondent who in 1993 placed himself outside both camps.

edges.relationship: Nationalism as an object of criticism: English-Canadian nationalist intellectuals read from Canada First to the 1960s, against a 'strait-jacket identity' (1967–71)
edges.evidence_note: Cook's own text, 1967 (opening read in the OpenAlex text): Canadian Dimension's call for a union of nationalists 'of all parties' is set beside the 1874 call of 'William Foster and his exuberant young friends' (Canada First), and he answers 'Who says Canadian nationalism is difficult to define? Jobs!' (International Journal 22:4, p. 659). Two passages from 1970 are known only through quotation. Karr (Acadiensis 1989, p. 162) quotes Cook (Saturday Night, April 1970): 'Every generation of Canadian nationalist intellectuals ... seems to play the part of Sisyphus. Their permanent task is to push the millstone of Canadian nationalism up a steep mountain, only to find that it rolls back down again to await the labour of the next generation. This means that much of Canadian intellectual history sounds like a broken record'. Buckner (2000, p. 4) quotes the 1970 South Atlantic Quarterly essay, reprinted in The Maple Leaf Forever (1971, pp. 197–214): Canada 'stubbornly refuses to exchange its occasionally anarchic pluralism for a strait-jacket identity. Perhaps it is this heterogeneous pluralism itself that is the Canadian identity'. In-period reading: Karr (1989, p. 162) writes that 'it was Ramsay Cook who did so much to heighten English Canada's understanding of French-Canadian nationalism who led the anti-national crusade', and that 'While it may be easy for many to agree with Cook's belittling of this recurring obsession with national identity, there are problems inherent in extremes on both sides'. His n. 18 adds: 'while Cook is opposed to divisive nationalism, he is a centralist and appears to be searching for a cohesive, positive form of national consensus' (p. 162). Gaffield (1986, p. 143) calls him 'one of Canada's major anglophone “windows” on francophone Québec'. The Maple Leaf Forever and Canada and the French-Canadian Question (1966) are unread here. The Regenerators' place in this field is carried by edge_825.

edges.relationship: Metropolitanism: Canadian history read through metropolitan centres that organize frontiers and hinterlands, proposed as a wider framework than the frontier-environmentalist reading (1954)
edges.evidence_note: His own in-period statement. 'Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History', Canadian Historical Review 35:1 (1954), pp. 1–21, read in full in an Internet Archive scan of the issue. He sorts English-Canadian historiography into 'schools', 'merely for convenience' (p. 2): a Britannic school, a School of Political Nationhood, and 'the Environmentalist School, or North Americans All', which 'built particularly on the concept of the frontier in North American history derived from Turner' (p. 5); he names Munro, Underhill, Sage, Lower, Landon, A. S. Morton and A. L. Burt, adding that 'no tight determinism is intended in thus naming these authors, nor, on the whole, did they display any' (p. 6, n. 6). He finds in them 'a certain tendency to fix values', so that western farmers were 'Good' and eastern business men 'Evil' (p. 12), and 'a tendency to overvalue the influence of native North American forces and the material environment, and a tendency to undervalue forces transferred from Europe and the non-material environment' (pp. 13–14); 'while in no way underrating the very great contributions which frontierism and environmentalism have made', it 'does seem necessary to look for a wider framework' (p. 14). The Laurentian school of Innis and Creighton offered 'a metropolitan rather than a frontier viewpoint', and 'The result was virtually to establish “metropolitanism” in Canadian historiography' (p. 16). The metropolis is 'a city of outstanding size' dominating 'other cities and their countrysides, the whole area being organized by the metropolis, through control of communications, trade, and finance, into one economic and social unit' (p. 17), in 'almost a feudal chain of vassalage' (p. 17); 'the rise of metropolitanism is the other side of the coin to frontier expansion' (p. 18). His examples include the Clear Grits organized around Toronto, the Globe and George Brown (p. 19). He limits the claim: 'if we reject a frontier determinism we should hardly replace it with a metropolitan determinism' (p. 19), and concedes that a metropolitan interpretation may 'only restate old problems in somewhat different terms. It may be so: but what is particularly needed is a restatement' (p. 21). A contribution, not a founding: he credits Lower's Colony to Nation and essays, Masters's The Rise of Toronto (1947) and its source in Gras (p. 17, nn. 30–31), and the Laurentian school (p. 16). In-period reception and criticism, from Donald F. Davis, Urban History Review 14:2 (1985), pp. 95–113, read in full: the article 'heralded the arrival of “metropolitanism” as a “vitalizing approach”'; 'few other journal articles have been more widely cited or more frequently quoted' (p. 95); for most historians it became, in Carl Berger's words as Davis quotes them, 'the programmatic statement of the metropolitan approach' (pp. 95–96). Davis quotes W. L. Morton's objection that the metropolitan thesis, 'which he associated with both Creighton and Careless', 'seems necessarily to minimize the importance of the hinterland' (p. 98), and S. D. Clark's at the 1974 CHA meeting that 'it serves no useful purpose to work with such categories or concepts as metropolis and hinterland when what is metropolis can also be considered hinterland' (p. 107); both are quoted-in witnesses, not read here. Davis's own judgment: Careless, combining Gras's ecological model with the Laurentian school's elites, 'has produced a relatively sterile hybrid', 'of only limited usefulness in guiding research' (p. 102); his interpretation 'fits the mould of “consensus” history' (p. 102); 'the Gras-Careless statement of metropolitanism is weak on causality; it is more taxonomic than explanatory' (p. 103). Davis also reports that Careless disclaimed 'such a metropolitan “thesis”' in 1973 while keeping the 'approach' (p. 96, quoting Acadiensis 3, 1973). edge_800 (urbanhistory → cdn_national_tradition) stays: it records the urban historians' critique at group level.

edges.relationship: Turner's frontier thesis, and the frontierism Canadian historians took from it, criticised as environmental determinism; the frontier recast as a dependent of the metropolis (1954)
edges.evidence_note: His own words. 'Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History' (1954), read in full. He summarises Turner's thesis that 'the greatest formative influence' in American history had been 'the open frontier, the hither edge of free land' (p. 6) and judges: 'This was environmental determinism at its most forthright. The wilderness and the men it produced had made America' (p. 7). Against it he sets the metropolitan reading: the frontier's culture 'originally stems from a metropolitan community; at root, learning and ideas radiate from there—and thus is Turner answered' (p. 18); 'the frontier, far from being essentially independent and self-reliant, is in the largest sense a dependent' (p. 18); and 'the functioning of metropolitanism may do more to explain the course of Canadian history than concepts of frontierism borrowed from the United States and set forth before the significance of the modern metropolis was clear' (p. 20). 'At any rate, frontierism, along with earlier schools and approaches, has had its use and its day' (p. 21). His qualifications are kept: 'Defenders of Turner might claim that he had not proposed a frontier hypothesis as the only key to American history' (p. 7); the frontier thesis 'proper' was never 'adopted as fully or dogmatically in Canada as it was in the United States—and there, of course, it has long been the subject of qualification and criticism' (p. 1); Canadian environmentalists took over 'the general approach and mood of Turner and company ... rather than the precise frontier thesis, which received little direct application in Canada' (p. 6). He draws on American critics of Turner (Hayes, Fox, Schlesinger Jr.; pp. 7–8) and on Canadian ones (McDougall 1929, Stanley 1940; p. 10, n. 21). The critique is therefore aimed at Turner's thesis and above all at its Canadian adaptation; the Canadian historians he names sit in cdn_national_tradition and are covered by edge 1. In-period reading: Davis (1985, p. 95, read) calls the article 'Conceived in part as an obituary for the frontier thesis of Frederick Jackson Turner'. Davis (p. 109) also quotes Careless on television saying of Turner's thesis that 'like any view of history which gets oversimplified, overpopularized, it becomes untrue; it becomes a myth' (undated, a quoted-in witness). No reply by a Turnerian historian was found or read.

edges.relationship: Cook's phrase 'limited identities' made a programme for Canadian history (1969), and region read through the metropolitan systems that structure it (1979–89)
edges.evidence_note: The 1969 article (CHR 50:1, pp. 1–10) is unread here; its wording comes from two witnesses. Buckner (Acadiensis 30:1, 2000, p. 4, read): Careless 'insisted that the “Canadian experience” must be “discerned and defined” through the “limited identities of region, culture and class referred to by Professor Cook”', and concluded that 'the whole may indeed be greater than the sum of its parts, producing through its internal relationships some sort of common Canadianism'. Careless himself, in 'Limited Identities — Ten Years Later' (Manitoba History no. 1, 1981; a lecture given in 1979; read in full, web text without page numbers), summarises the article as noting that these identities 'had tended to bulk larger for Canadians in their history than any identification with overall national patterns of values and attitudes', and quotes its p. 10: 'by pursuing a line largely of sociocultural inquiry, one may hope to uncover satisfactions in the limited identities ... which have added up to some positive balance of satisfaction with Canada itself'. The phrase is Cook's: Careless wrote that he 'did not invent the term “limited identity”, but acquired it from an article by Ramsay Cook, cited in my own article — which was thus essentially a commentary on his initial idea' (1981, n. 1); Buckner (p. 4) says Cook 'coined' it and Careless 'popularized' it. This edge carries Careless's programme, not the coinage. The 1981 lecture joins it to metropolitanism: regionalist historians often present 'an over-simple dichotomy' between a metropolitan central Canada and their own region, whereas 'regions are structured into metropolitan systems both within and beyond their territories'; 'Metropolitanism is not the antithesis of regionalism. Each is inherent in the other'. Frontier and Metropolis (1989) is unread; Rick Szostak's review (Journal of Economic History 50:2, 1990, pp. 499–501, read) reports that in it 'Cities become the foci of regional identity' and that Atlantic Canada 'develops a regional identity despite having no one dominant metropolis' (p. 500). In-period reception: the 1973 bibliography by Hann, Kealey, Kealey and Warrian opened with 'For some time J. M. S. Careless has called for ... a historical appreciation of the varieties of “limited identities” that constitute Canada' (as Careless quotes it in 1981; a quoted-in witness). Criticism: Buckner (2000, p. 10) answers critics who treat regional studies as, 'as Careless and Granatstein seem to believe, a construct designed to justify the dismantling of the Canadian state'; Robert Irwin (Journal of Canadian Studies 32:3, 1997; abstract only) argues that prairie identity 'must be understood as an autonomous layer of consciousness rather than a “limited identity” within a national consciousness'; Szostak found the book 'descriptive rather than analytical' and expected readers to be 'left unconvinced' (p. 500). Buckner (p. 5) also notes the different motives: Cook and Careless embraced the concept partly in response to Quebec separatism, Atlantic historians for other reasons. edge_805 and edge_814 stay as group-level arrows.

edges.relationship: The metropolis–hinterland approach, taken up by Canadian urban historians in the 1970s and then contested by them (1954–85)
edges.evidence_note: His own statements. The 1954 article proposes the metropolis and its hinterland as a field of study, including 'social and cultural associations' as well as economic ties (pp. 17–18), and names Masters's The Rise of Toronto as the closest application (p. 17). In 1981 he writes that 'urban history' grew within regional writing because cities 'are also centres that focus and structure regions or sub-regions about them. The interplay of city and region thus demands and has received attention', and that he had 'always sought to emphasize the reciprocal and complementary nature of the relations between the great city and the territory it dominates' (Manitoba History no. 1, web text). Davis (1985) lists his urban-history articles: 'Urban Development in Canada', Urban History Review 1 (1974), and 'Metropolis and Region', Urban History Review 3 (1979) (nn. 6, 11; unread). In-period reception, from Davis, Urban History Review 14:2 (1985), read in full: 'In the 1970s metropolitanism helped preside over the birth of a new sub-discipline, urban history', and according to Artibise and Linteau (1984) the articles by Careless on metropolis and region 'marked, in some ways at least, the self-conscious beginning of urban history' in Canada (p. 96; a quoted-in witness); urban historians 'have remained the most faithful to the metropolitan concept of J.M.S. Careless, the godfather of their subdiscipline' (p. 96); Gilbert Stelter called the metropolitan thesis in 1977 'the most significant approach to Canadian urban history' (p. 96, quoted). A contribution, contested within the field: Davis argues that 'there is no single metropolitan thesis' (p. 107), that Careless's approach 'has fallen into desuetude in historical circles' (p. 103), that Artibise found the metropolis/hinterland concept 'not really a theory that explain[ed] Canadian urban development' (p. 103, quoted), and that urban historians 'might do better by abandoning the metropolitan approach altogether' (abstract, p. 95). Davis also records Careless's own reserve: he would 'disclaim and deny such a metropolitan “thesis”' (p. 96, quoting 1973). This is a Canadian contribution; it does not claim that Dyos's or US urban history drew on Careless. edge_800 (urbanhistory → cdn_national_tradition, critique) stays: it records the field's rejection of metropolitanism, this edge the field's use of it.
edges.map_label: Metropolis and hinterland in Canadian urban history, 1954–85

edges.relationship: Limited identities and his own early warning against particularism (1969, 1979–81) as the ground of the later fragmentation debate
edges.evidence_note: His own words, 'Limited Identities — Ten Years Later' (lecture of 1979, Manitoba History no. 1, 1981; read in full, web text). Ten years after 1969 he sees 'a massive outpouring' of writing on regional interests, cultural discords and class disparities in which 'national concerns are by and large passed over or discounted', and says: 'I feel a little like the farmer in the midst of a flood, when he declared “Lord, I know I prayed for rain — but this is ridiculous.”' He disclaims responsibility for the flood ('I scarcely caused the flood') and does not withdraw the concept: 'I do feel the concept has had much value, and still has'. But 'Unity in diversity' now seems rather 'diversity Unlimited', and 'limited identities remain crucial subjects for the historian's regard — but they should not limit his own perception'; 'Now the task is to cut the sight-lines through'. In-period readings: John G. Reid (Acadiensis 16:2, 1987) records that during the 1980s 'concern has increasingly been expressed that fragmentation has been the result', an argument made in Canada by Careless (graph verification note; not re-read here). Buckner (Acadiensis 30:1, 2000, read): Careless 'too had come to the conclusion that the search for limited identities had gone too far and threatened the very existence of the Canadian nation-state' (pp. 8–9, citing this lecture); 'More recently the same point has been made, somewhat crudely, by Michael Bliss and Jack Granatstein and with greater sophistication by Doug Owram' (p. 9). Buckner contests the premise, calling the 'so-called fragmentation of the historical profession' 'patently absurd, at least when applied to the Atlantic region' (p. 8). An influence as precursor, not participation: his texts predate the 1991–99 exchanges, and no debate text read here names him except Buckner's. Bliss's 1991–92 article (abstract only) does not name him; Bliss is not presented as answering him. edge_814 (cdn_regional → who_killed_debate) stays: it records regional history as the debate's ground.
edges.map_label: From limited identities to the fragmentation worry, 1969–81

edges.relationship: The Laurentian narrative: the St. Lawrence commercial system as the basis of a transcontinental Canada (1937), carried through Dominion of the North (1944) and the Macdonald biography (1952–55)
edges.evidence_note: In-period, his own text. Dominion of the North (1944; pages read in an open copy): the post at Quebec gave the French 'the one great river system which led to the Atlantic seaboard from the heart of the continent'; 'Inevitably the river came to seem the natural basis of a great commercial empire stretching far into the distant west; and the achievement of this empire became the common objective of successive generations of Canadians, though their methods altered and the staple products of their trade were sometimes changed. The first staple of the St. Lawrence commercial system was beaver fur' (p. 21); the rivalry of 'the northern and southern routes, between Montreal and New York, for the control of the Great Lakes system and the command of the western trade', a conflict that 'was to remain essentially the same' (pp. 24–25); 'Quebec had been the origin of the empire of the St. Lawrence; it was to be the genesis of the Dominion of Canada' (p. 298). In-period reception. Herbert Heaton's review (CJEPS, 1938; first page, p. 565, read) quotes the book as 'an attempt to trace the relations between the commercial system of the St. Lawrence and the political development of Canada' (the book's words as Heaton quotes them; the 1937 book is unread) and reads it as a test of the economic interpretation of history that 'has pleased neither the Marxians nor their enemies'. Michel Brunet (RHAF, 1953, p. 579) calls him 'l'un des maîtres contemporains de l'historiographie anglo-canadienne'; Guy Frégault (RHAF, 1955, p. 446) sums up the Macdonald biography as 'Nationalisme antiaméricain, impérialisme et centralisation : synthèse canadienne, — je veux dire anglo-canadienne'. His own retrospect, 1969 (read in full; a later statement by the author, not evidence of what the 1937 book says): 'This Laurentian theme has its basis in the fact that the St. Lawrence is the one great river system that leads from the Atlantic Seaboard to the heart of the continent of North America'; the river 'has inspired generations of Canadians to build a great territorial empire, both commercial and political, in the western interior of the continent' (p. 16); 'The west, it was believed, would make Canada a nation, and the east-west axis would be its backbone' (p. 17); in choosing Macdonald he had 'stumbled upon the only satisfactory method of writing the second phase', so that he had written 'a trilogy on one theme' (p. 16). The phrase, he says, came to be regarded 'as the inspiration, at least in part, of a new school of Canadian historians and as the genesis of a new historical doctrine, the Laurentian interpretation of Canadian history'; he had 'no wish to disavow the parentage of an idea' (p. 14). Later readings: Ouellet (1984, pp. 226–227) calls him 'le chef de l'Ecole laurentienne'; Salmon (1997) says he 'simplified and expanded Innis' thesis'. Contested in period: Brunet found French-Canadian newspapers unread ('Il n'a pas jugé nécessaire de dépouiller un seul journal canadien-français', p. 580) and 'nombreux préjugés' (p. 581); Frégault asked 'où sont les Canadiens français dans tout cela ? Tout simplement, ils n'y sont pas' (p. 447), while praising the work as 'fondé sur une compréhension exacte de l'histoire du Canada' (p. 444); W. L. Morton, as quoted by Davis (1985), saw in Creighton 'the preponderant role commercial monopoly and centralized business have played' (Davis, p. 97) and held that the metropolitan thesis, which he associated with Creighton and Careless, 'seems necessarily to minimize the importance of the hinterland' (Davis, p. 98); the critic George Woodcock (1979, p. 140) called his treatment of Confederation as centralist 'a major distortion'. A contribution, not a founding.

edges.relationship: Innis's staple studies as a resource for Creighton's Laurentian narrative, as Creighton's own staple vocabulary and later readers show; Creighton rejected the story that the 1937 book grew from their friendship
edges.evidence_note: His own texts. Dominion of the North (1944) frames the St. Lawrence system by its staples ('The first staple of the St. Lawrence commercial system was beaver fur', p. 21), and its reading list (pp. 505–507) names Innis's The Fur Trade in Canada (1930) and The Cod Fisheries (1940). The 1957 presidential address recalls 'the 1930's, when the influence of Harold Innis was at its height and everybody was writing and talking about staple production' (p. 3), and exempts Innis from the Marxian fashion: 'most of the professional economists — and especially Innis — refused to accept the simplified Marxian version of historical determinism' (p. 6). In 1957 he also published Harold Adams Innis: Portrait of a Scholar (unread); Benoît Brouillette's review (1957, p. 529, read) reports Creighton's account of Innis's Canada as an east–west system 'marqué par le Saint-Laurent et les Grands-Lacs', at once 'transocéanique et transcontinental'. The qualification, his own (1969, pp. 14–15): 'The Empire of the St. Lawrence, it is sometimes confidently asserted, was the fruit of my friendship with Harold Innis ... These explanations, like most simple generalizations, happen to be wrong'; the subject was suggested 'not by Harold Innis, whom I barely knew at the time, but by W. P. M. Kennedy', and he was 'reluctantly convinced by the weight of his own evidence' about the Montreal merchants (p. 16). Readers: George Woodcock (1979, p. 134): 'Creighton's master was H. A. Innis, especially the Innis of The Fur Trade in Canada, which contained the essential germ out of which — with Innis's encouragement — Creighton built the scenario of his first book'; Fernand Ouellet (1984, p. 226): Creighton started 'partant de la théorie des staples'; Deborah Harrison (1981), as quoted by Davis (1985, p. 97): 'probably the first to advance a metropolitanist interpretation, although the closely related "staples" thesis had been put forward by Innis much earlier'; Salmon (1997): he 'simplified and expanded Innis' thesis'. The edge records Innis's work as a resource the Laurentian narrative used, not a teacher–pupil derivation; Creighton's denial concerns the origin of the subject, not the use of the staple framework.
edges.map_label: Staples behind the Laurentian narrative, contested

edges.relationship: Turner's frontier thesis, as taken up by Canadian historians in the 1930s and 1940s, rejected as an imported 'continental revelation' that Canadian history would not fit (1957)
edges.evidence_note: His own text, the 1957 CHA presidential address (read in full). Canadian historians had 'accepted, for historical purposes, the two highly fashionable political theories which dominated the thought of the inter-war and war years': 'the Marxian doctrine of the class struggle' and 'the Frontier Theory' (p. 6). Of the second: 'Turner ... fixed upon the movement of settlement across the continent as the most important fact in its history'; 'the source of creative inspiration and action was found not at the centre, but at the periphery, of western culture' (p. 8). Applied to Canada, 'painful difficulties were immediately encountered': the frontier's progress 'had been evidently modified by all sorts of extraneous and unnatural things such as railways, efficient police, governmental supervision'; in 1837 'the rebels had come, not from the frontier, but from the older settled parts of the province'; yet its believers 'kept insisting that Canadian democracy was "forest-born"' (p. 9). He ends: historians bought 'a couple of suits of imported intellectual reach-me-downs' and a new generation would show 'less deference for imported theories of historical change and more respect for the manifold facts of Canadian experience' (p. 12). The critique inverts his own Laurentian premise, that change radiates from the centre. Limits: the address is a polemic and names no Canadian frontierist; Turner is not quoted beyond the phrases Creighton cites, and the atlas's own reading of Turner (progressive/multiple_hypotheses) shows him advocating multiple hypotheses rather than a single doctrine. Context: Careless's 1954 CHR article, unread here, was 'conceived in part as an obituary for the frontier thesis of Frederick Jackson Turner' (Davis 1985, p. 95). No in-period reply to the address was looked for.

edges.relationship: Gender and class as simultaneous hierarchies, and gender history as a practice in Canadian women's history (1985–96)
edges.evidence_note: In-period, her own words (Atlantis, 1985, read in full): women and children are not tied together as subjects by nature; 'What distinguishes feminine and preschooler from masculine and prime of life is not naturalness versus artificiality but proximity to power' (p. 39). She criticises the mid-1970s Canadian literature on reform for characterising 1880–1920 as 'an era of "maternal feminism"', seeing women's public actions 'definitionally as an extension of the private' (p. 41), and asks historians to 'stop shying away from the word "patriarchy"' and to 'allow as a possibility that gender/sex hierarchies and class hierarchies function simultaneously, each according to its own logic, often in conflict' (p. 44). She presents this as a change 'a good many others have already begun to suggest' (p. 39). The Gender of Breadwinners (1990), unread here, as reviewers quote it: Guildford (Atlantis, 1991, p. 140) says she rejects 'an ahistorical hierarchy of oppressions' (p. 8) and argues 'that class and gender are made and experienced simultaneously'; Bertaux (JEH, 1992, p. 241) quotes p. 9 on 'these galloping pairs—class/gender, male/female, market/nonmarket, public/private' whose meanings 'are multiple and mutable'. Reception in the Left History exchange (all read in full): Sangster calls the book 'One of the path breaking books on gender history' (1995, p. 120); Iacovetta and Kealey call her 'recognized as a leading practitioner of gender history' (1996, p. 222) and 'a major figure in the field', quoting her 1995 CHR essay (pp. 362–63) that 'gender history made masculinity and femininity commensurably problematical historically, while insisting that neither could be well understood without companion inquiries into the other hierarchies with which they were mutually intertwined' (p. 228); Dubinsky and Marks cite her for refraining 'from imposing one category - be it class or gender - on historical actors' (1996, p. 211). Criticism: Sangster (1996, p. 240 n. 2) characterises Parr's essay (its reprint in Gender and History in Canada, 1996, p. 11, unread here) as placing critics 'feminist and anti-feminist alike, in the same oppositional group' (Sangster's wording, not a quotation from Parr), notes that she had been reproached for not offering 'more criticism of historians such as Mariana Valverde and Joy Parr' (p. 240 n. 3), and, quoting Parr's line that the move to gender 'began from the post-structuralist premise that identities were made in relationships' (reprint p. 14), questions 'the prevailing assumption that gender history as the field, post-structuralism as the method, equals a superior, more broad-minded history' (pp. 244, 246). The 1995 essay itself is unread: its words here are quoted by Iacovetta and Kealey and by Sangster. Not a founding: the field's gender debate also runs through Pierson (1991) and Scott (edge_891). Later reading, labelled: a 2026 CHR 'great books' forum (abstract only) calls the book 'a path-breaking study that challenged established dichotomies in social theory'.

edges.relationship: Gender in the making of class: a women's town and a men's town, Paris and Hanover, Ontario (1985–90)
edges.evidence_note: In-period, her own words (Atlantis, 1985): 'students of men's work and men's participation in labour organisations', with women's historians and historians of childhood, 'have reified the skill-unskill boundary' (p. 42); 'Skill, too, is a socially constructed category' (pp. 42–43). Of the Marxist analysis in Women at Work, Ontario, 1850–1930 (1975) she writes, quoting feminist critics (n. 20: Phillips and Taylor; Hartmann), that it 'explains why a hierarchy of labour is necessary within the waged labour force, but tells us nothing about why women end up at the bottom of this hierarchy' (p. 43). The Gender of Breadwinners (1990; unread here) compares Paris and Hanover, Ontario. Heron, a labour historian, reviewing it (CHR, 1991, read in full): 'the most exhilarating, challenging book to appear in modern Canadian social history in many years'; it 'integrates and surpasses' women's, labour, technological and economic history, and 'Parr gives the boot to neo-classical analysis, simplistic Marxism, and radical feminism' (p. 218). He quotes its introduction that 'the parts and proportions of the social landscape covered by class and gender alter' (p. 10) but finds that in the 1949 Paris strike 'she has suppressed the impact of class where it was undeniably a crucial force' (p. 220). From her own figures he suggests that 'the portrait of the "women's town" may be slightly misleading' (p. 219). He also finds that she downplays the wars and the state and 'seldom makes any reference to the considerable Canadian literature on work, class, gender, or small-town life' (pp. 220–21). He concludes that she 'has pushed us onto new terrain where gender is neither ignored nor is it given a monocausal explanatory force' (p. 221). Scheinberg (Archivaria, 1991) sees 'a more dynamic alternative to the old and stale studies that focused more on workers' industrial and organizational activities', while doubting conclusions drawn from 'the testimony of seven women' (p. 175). Dennis (EcHR, 1991) calls it 'an important contribution to the literature of labour history and locality studies' (p. 762). A contribution from inside the field's gender strand, alongside Sangster (1989) and Bradbury (1993). It does not claim that labour history lacked gender before 1990. edge_842 and edge_889 (cdn_women_gender → cdn_working_class) already carry the entry-level contribution and critique.

edges.relationship: British child immigrants as labouring children (1977–80), and childhood as a history of power (1985)
edges.evidence_note: In-period. Her Yale PhD (1977), 'The Home Children: British Juvenile Immigrants to Canada, 1868–1924', is recorded in the AHA Directory of History Dissertations (record 45612; adviser Robin Winks). Drystek's review of Labouring Children (Archivaria 11, 1980–81, read in full) names the thesis as the source of its sample of 997 Barnardo case histories (p. 241). He quotes the book's aims: a 'study of the life and work of child immigrants in Britain and Canada' (p. 13) that would 'reveal a darker side of evangelicalism, of turn-of-the-century childhood, and of Canadian rural life than the record has so far been allowed to express' (p. 12). His reading is critical: 'because of the authors' almost uniformly negative approach, the study is of limited value', the sample's statistical basis is unexplained, and 'the argument that a British child immigrant suffered a special burden is not convincing' (pp. 241–42). The book itself is unread here. Her own words (Atlantis, 1985) turn the subject into a question about power: she finds it troubling to treat women and children 'as part of one subject', admits to being 'part of a group who wrote, reviewed, lectured and squabbled this cluster into convention', and asks 'Is it nature which ties women and children together as subjects? Clearly not' (p. 39); the family 'is experienced by members of different generations in very different ways' (p. 44). She also edited Childhood and Family in Canadian History (1982; title-level, see edge_792). A contribution among the field's early works, not its origin: Sutherland's Children in English-Canadian Society (1976) precedes it.

edges.relationship: Disaggregating the sexual division of labour: gender and class compared across workplaces, read beyond Canada (1988–93)
edges.evidence_note: In-period, her own words: the CSSH article of 1988 (first-page extract read, p. 511) observes that 'economists and feminist theorists have been interested in sexual divisions as general features of the economic or sex/gender system rather than as boundaries between tasks forged in defined contexts by particular clashes of interest', and that 'most analysts have dealt with gender division as a characteristic of the work force as a whole'. Reviews of The Gender of Breadwinners outside Canada (all read in full): Benson (JAH, 1993, p. 1630) writes that 'few historians have successfully integrated the discussion of these two fundamental relationships' and that 'Parr joins this small but growing group'. On p. 1631 Benson continues: 'Like others influenced by post-structuralist theory, she emphasizes the shifting and multivalent meanings often obscured by dualisms'; Parr 'gives gender and class coordinate roles in her analysis but downplays ethnicity'. Dennis (EcHR, 1991) finds that she 'goes far beyond previous accounts of connections between capitalism and patriarchy' (p. 761) but faults graphs that 'cavalierly use straight lines to connect a handful of isolated observations' (p. 762). Bertaux (JEH, 1992) wants 'a basic quantitative summary of work force data' (p. 240) but concludes that 'the topic of gender and work is not strictly a "women's issue"' (p. 241). The book itself is unread here. This records reception in international journals, not adoption. Optional: edge_840 (cdn_women_gender → gender) already links the Canadian field to the international entry.

edges.relationship: Postwar Canadian consumption as a politics of nation, class and gender: domestic goods, designers and householders (1999)
edges.evidence_note: In-period, her own words: the abstract of 'Household Choices as Politics and Pleasure in 1950s Canada' (ILWCH 55, 1999, a special issue on class and consumption) reads 'How much consumption matters is a cultural difference, a shared national predicament, a politics grounded in the circumstances of class, and learned as a gendered responsibility', and asks 'When producers were not paramount in the regulation of consumption, to what priorities was commerce subsidiary?' Domestic Goods (1999) is unread here; as Brush quotes it (EH.NET, 2000, read in full), it is 'an archeology of the material, moral, and economic choices and constraints which formed Canadian commodity culture in the two decades after the Second World War' (p. 17). It asks 'How much can citizens talk back to manufacturers and the state about domestic goods?' (pp. 3–4). It sets itself against accounts that 'naturalize[d] these hortatory American norms as the intrinsic qualities of "consumer society"' (p. 11), and it places studies of material culture 'into unaccustomed company' (p. 3). Brush notes that Parr 'locates the history of consumption as a history primarily of women as consumers, in contrast to the male-dominated fields of design and manufacturing'. Criticism: Owram (BC Studies 129, 2001, read in full) finds the book's 'strength is in its parts rather than in some seamless thesis' (p. 103). He reads her as arguing that 'the assumption of consumer sovereignty is facile' (p. 104), and answers that 'Canadians, both men and women, preferred Fords to Volvos, and that is what they got' (p. 105). edge_843 (cdn_women_gender ↔ consumption, comparison) is title-level; this edge adds read evidence.

edges.relationship: Embodied, sensory histories of megaprojects and environmental change in Canada, 1953–2003 (2006–10)
edges.evidence_note: Dated 2006–2011; no claim here concerns her work before 2000. Sensing Changes: Technologies, Environments, and the Everyday, 1953–2003 (UBC Press, 2010) is unread here. As Jackson quotes it (Senses and Society 6:2, 2011, read in full), Parr seeks to move beyond 'representations . . . in language . . . , to open interpretive space in which to study the robust materiality of technologies, environments, and the everyday, to encounter them as directly and as fleshly as possible' (p. 9). Jackson describes chapters on the NATO base at Gagetown, nuclear power and heavy water on Lake Huron, the St Lawrence Seaway at Iroquois, the Columbia River reservoir and Walkerton's water, each read through a sense ('Smell and Risk', 'Taste and Expertise'). She adds that Parr counts proprioception, kinesthetics and proxemics among the senses (pp. 225–27). Jackson places the book in the UBC Press Nature/History/Culture series (p. 225). Rumiel (Left History 15:1, 2011, read in full) notes 'the people whose lives and senses of self had been transformed' by megaprojects (p. 189). She suggests that 'a comparative analysis of a related case in a Canadian Aboriginal or Inuit community' was a missed opportunity (p. 189). The environmental line begins earlier with 'Smells Like?: Sources of Uncertainty in the History of the Great Lakes Environment' (Environmental History 11:2, 2006; metadata only). A contribution: it records her later field, not influence on environmental history's formation.

edges.relationship: Moral regulation as the formation of ethical subjectivity, carried out by philanthropies, churches and professions as well as the state: social purity in English Canada, 1885–1925 (1991–92; the 1988 article with Weir is listed but unread)
edges.evidence_note: Her own in-period statements. 'Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State', Labour/Le Travail 30 (1992), pp. 213–222, read in full: 'I have argued elsewhere that the discourse of moral reform needs to be analyzed seriously, not merely dismissed as a cover for class interests', though 'moral discourse does as a matter of contingent fact legitimize certain class, gender, and racial interests' (p. 216); she credits Corrigan and Sayer's The Great Arch with pioneering 'the liberal state's role in constituting subjectivities' (p. 217). The Age of Light, Soap, and Water (1991) is known here through in-period reviewers' quotations and through Google Books search-within snippets of the 2008 University of Toronto Press reissue (volume ghqEyXf5950C; partial preview, page images not viewable here because the viewing limit was reached), which keep the 1991 pagination: reformers sought 'to reshape the ethical subjectivity of both immigrants and native-born Canadians' (p. 17; quoted by Dehli 1992, p. 316); purity work 'was not simply a question of banning obscene books or suppressing prostitution but was rather a campaign to educate the next generation' (p. 17; quoted by McCormick 1992, p. 124); the reform movements 'helped to shape the bourgeoisie, which led the movements, as well as the working class' (p. 15; Dehli, p. 318); 'Moral regulation is very closely linked to state formation, as the British school of historical sociology has argued; but as Foucault and his followers have pointed out, the state has no monopoly on moral regulation' (p. 165; snippet, the last clause also quoted by Dehli, p. 317); '[m]oral regulation is an important aspect of ruling, helping to constitute class, gender, sexual, and race relations' (p. 166, as quoted by Wright 1995, p. 124). Her notes, seen only as snippets, place the concept: in The Great Arch 'the role of the state in moral regulation is highlighted, and their theorization has been influential here; but the agencies of regulation internal to civil society are obscured' (n. 34, p. 171); Corrigan and Sayer 'do not differentiate between moral and other modes of social regulation; by contrast, I restrict the term to mean the formation of ethical subjectivity' (p. 173). Note 33 (p. 171) cites the 1988 article with Lorna Weir, which is unread here. In-period reception by historians. Tina Loo (Labour/Le Travail 30, 1992, pp. 277–279, read) calls the book 'a provocative and valuable contribution to the history of social reform and, more significantly, because of its self-conscious use of theory, to the writing of Canadian history' (p. 279). Donald Wright (Acadiensis, 1995, pp. 122–126 read) calls it a 'much talked about treatise' by 'a sociologist' (p. 122) and its concept of 'slippages' among class, gender, sexuality and race her 'most original' contribution (p. 124). Carolyn Strange and Tina Loo's Making Good: Law and Moral Regulation in Canada (1997; Google Books snippets, pp. 5, 63) write that 'Theorists influenced by philosopher Michel Foucault have urged scholars to abandon the social-control model for a more flexible concept of regulation' (p. 5) and cite 'Mariana Valverde and others' on prostitution as 'the social evil' (p. 63). Mary Louise Adams's 'In Sickness and in Health: State Formation, Moral Regulation, and Early VD Initiatives in Ontario' (1994) is cited at title level only. In-period criticism. Loo finds the second argument, on philanthropy and the state, 'more asserted than proved' (p. 279). Kari Dehli (Historical Studies in Education, 1992, pp. 315–319, read) would draw 'not quite so sharply drawn' conclusions about state and civil society and finds that she moves 'quickly from analysis of discursive strategies ... to drawing conclusions about people's motives and intentions' (pp. 318–319). Wright judges her claim that audiences 'knew precisely what was meant' 'untenable' and finds 'the impoverished immigrant and the "fallen woman" ... conspicuously silent', so that 'the silence of the consumer amidst the din of the producer gives the impression of top-down social control, precisely what Valverde sought to avoid' (pp. 125–126). Chris McCormick (Atlantis, 1992, pp. 123–125, read) asks how her interpretations are made and judges that a 'thorough' reading of context is 'optimistic' (p. 123), while agreeing that 'Regulation is a better word than control' (p. 124). Sociologists reformulated the concept: Alan Hunt's 1997 abstract (read) treats moral regulation not as 'a specific moral arena' but as 'a component of all fields of social relations', a wider definition than hers; in Governing Morals (1999; snippets) he writes 'I do not take issue with Valverde's invocation of ethical subjectivity, but I emphasise the mundane features of self-governing' (p. 155). Dean (1994) and Ruonavaara (1997) are cited through their abstracts as on the moral_regulation node. A contribution, not a founding: Corrigan (1981) and Corrigan and Sayer (1985) precede her, and she credits them. Diseases of the Will (1998), on alcohol and the governance of the will, is title-level here (snippets only) and does not support this edge.
edges.map_label: Light, soap and water: moral regulation, 1991

edges.relationship: Protestant reformers read as moral regulators rather than as religious actors, and the church historians' objection that this excised the churches from progressive thought (1991–96)
edges.evidence_note: Her object overlaps the field's. The book studies Methodist and Presbyterian church organizations, the Salvation Army, the WCTU, the YWCA and the National Council of Women (Dehli 1992, p. 316, read), with familiar reformers such as Chown, Shearer and Woodsworth (Loo 1992, p. 277, read). Her reading is regulatory: purity work 'was rather a campaign to educate the next generation' (p. 17, quoted by McCormick 1992, p. 124), and the discourse of moral reform 'needs to be analyzed seriously, not merely dismissed as a cover for class interests' ('Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State', 1992, p. 216, read). In-period objections from historians of religion and reform. Loo (Labour/Le Travail 30, 1992, p. 278, read) finds that 'religion and sectarian differences' get 'rather short shrift', suggests Richard Allen's typology of radical, progressive and conservative reformers, and holds that 'any discussion of the discourse of moral reform in Canada needs to address Christianity and certainly Protestantism more fully, even if only to dismiss its importance'. Nancy Christie and Michael Gauvreau, A Full-Orbed Christianity (1996), known here only through Google Books search-within snippets: 'historians such as Doug Owram and Mariana Valverde have adhered to a caricature of the antiquated and esoteric Victorian theologue to excise the churches from "progressive" currents of modern thought and social action' (p. xiii); 'Valverde has argued that in early twentieth-century Canada issues such as social purity and immigration were controlled by a hegemonic exercise of power by the state and middle-class organizations' (p. 187), and her analysis 'wrongly posits the view that given the hegemonic influence of the state, there was only one option regarding immigration policy – that of racism and the annihilation of immigrant culture', against which they set 'three divergent strands of opinion on the immigration question' among Protestant clergy (p. 188; n. 95, p. 328, cites her pp. 15, 112, 123–8). Their p. 187 summary attributes to her a state-centred hegemony that her own p. 165 qualifies ('the state has no monopoly on moral regulation'); the disagreement is recorded, not adjudicated. A comparison, as her roster row and edge_861 (moral_regulation – cdn_religion_reform) have it: the criticism runs from the church historians to her, and she did not answer it in a text read here. The dispute is person-level, which is why it is drawn from her entry; edge_861 stays the field-level comparison.

edges.relationship: Liberalism read as a system of moral regulation and the liberal state as a constitutor of subjectivities (1991–92), beside the liberal order framework's later history of property, the individual and rule
edges.evidence_note: Her own in-period statements, before McKay's prospectus (2000). 'Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State', Labour/Le Travail 30 (1992), pp. 213–222, read in full, endorses Mitchell Dean's argument 'that classical English liberalism was not a negation of state regulation but rather a particular system of economic, social, and moral regulation', so that 'a history of pauperism is also a genealogy of liberalism' (p. 217). She reviews Jean-Marie Fecteau's Un nouvel ordre des choses (1989) as 'a landmark work' whose 'theoretical sophistication' crosses 'the traditional historiographical boundaries separating coercion from benevolence and the state as a whole from charity' (pp. 221–222), but faults its 'moyens de contrôle' as 'a rather functionalist formulation', a 'model of negative class power', and adds that 'These moral codes are not intrinsic to the logic of capital, since capitalism works quite efficiently in different cultural systems' (p. 222). Note 10 (p. 220) cites Fecteau's essay in Greer and Radforth's Colonial Leviathan (1992), and the essay thanks Allan Greer for comments on a draft (p. 222). In the 1991 book (Google Books search-within snippets of the 2008 reissue, 1991 pagination) note 35 (p. 171) cites Bruce Curtis's 'Preconditions of the Canadian State', and she writes that moral regulation 'might be an important social process, which is intertwined with but is not an effect of either the economic or the political' (p. 165) and that 'one has to be sceptical of any claims that envision a clear separation between moral and economic regulation' (p. 166). Reviewers read the book's state argument in the same terms: private philanthropy 'allowed liberal democratic states to adhere to their policy of non-interference in the private sphere' (Loo 1992, p. 278, her paraphrase). Comparison only. The user decided (2026-10-12) that the liberal order framework is 'a different project closer to history of capitalism'; Fecteau and Curtis are shared ground (state formation), not membership. No in-period text by the framework's authors discussing her was read here (McKay's 2000 prospectus is paywalled and unread). edge_848 (liberal_order_framework – moral_regulation) is the field-level comparison. This edge is an editorial comparison of her 1992 argument with the later framework (McKay, 2000); she did not distinguish herself from a framework not yet formulated.

edges.relationship: Scott's poststructuralist programme criticised by a sympathetic reader, who suggested that it may exaggerate what Foucault and Derrida can do for historians, for passing over discourse analysis's bias towards 'the sociology of domination', and (1995) for setting theory against working-class history
edges.evidence_note: Her own in-period words (1990 essay read in full; 1995 essay, pp. 329–332 read). 'Poststructuralist Gender Historians: Are We Those Names?', Labour/Le Travail 25 (1990), pp. 227–236, reviews Scott's Gender and the Politics of History with Denise Riley's 'Am I That Name?'. She grants that Scott's approach 'has much to commend it' but finds her four elements of gender 'somewhat arbitrary' and asks whether the definition 'finally succeeds in transcending the idealism/materialism dichotomy' (p. 230). Scott's case studies show limitations 'symptomatic of the general limitations of discourse analysis as it has been used by social historians (myself included!)' (p. 231): there is 'an inherent bias in discourse analysis in favour of what some call "the sociology of domination." This problem, not discussed by Scott, does not discredit or make redundant discourse analysis' (p. 232). Scott's 'rather polemical book tends to sing the praises of discourse analysis without mentioning many of its problems', with a 'grandiose claim made by Scott on Foucault's behalf' (p. 232), and 'It may be that she exaggerates the contribution Foucault and Derrida can make to historical work' (p. 233). She ends that 'Scott's work deserves to be carefully read even by those who find some of its more polemical claims hard to swallow' (p. 233). 'Deconstructive Marxism', Labour/Le Travail 36 (1995), pp. 329–340 (pp. 329–332 read), sharpens the judgment: Scott 'made an influential attempt to extend the reach of deconstruction within historical writing to the certainties of class. Her argument was limited in many ways' (pp. 331–332); 'Scott probably used her new-found theories to justify a break with Marxism that she, like so many other former leftists on both sides of the Atlantic, wanted to make anyway', and 'the book undoubtedly made an important contribution to the feminist analysis of both politics and history: but it did so, or at least gave the appearance of doing so, at the expense of working-class history' (p. 332). She criticises the other side too: 'for many labour historians, any hint of theoretical sophistication became prima faciae evidence of political backsliding' (p. 332), and her note names Bryan Palmer's Descent into Discourse as 'the by now standard Marxist critique of Scott' (p. 332, n. 5). edge_891 (joan_wallach_scott → cdn_women_gender) already cites the 1990 essay as evidence of Canadian engagement with Scott; this edge records her own criticism of Scott's position, which edge_891 does not carry. A critique within broad sympathy, not a rejection: the qualifications above are part of the claim.

edges.relationship: Orientalism as discourse and as a style of domination: Western knowledge and representation of 'the Orient' read through knowledge and power, extended to contrapuntal reading of the metropolitan canon with empire (1978–93)
edges.evidence_note: His own in-period statements. Orientalism (New York: Pantheon, 1978, first edition; page images checked): 'The Orient was almost a European invention' (p. 1); Orientalism as 'a style of thought based upon an ontological and epistemological distinction made between "the Orient" and (most of the time) "the Occident"' (p. 2) and as 'a Western style for dominating, restructuring, and having authority over the Orient' (p. 3). He qualifies it at once: 'it would be wrong to conclude that the Orient was essentially an idea, or a creation with no corresponding reality'; 'The relationship between Occident and Orient is a relationship of power, of domination, of varying degrees of a complex hegemony' (p. 5); and he leaves open 'how one can study other cultures and peoples from a libertarian, or a nonrepressive and nonmanipulative, perspective. But then one would have to rethink the whole complex problem of knowledge and power' (p. 24). Covering Islam (1981, introduction, p. ix): 'The underlying theme of Orientalism is the affiliation of knowledge with power.' 'Orientalism Reconsidered', Cultural Critique 1 (1985), read in full: the issues are 'the representation of other cultures, societies, histories; the relationship between power and knowledge' (p. 89); 'what for the most part got left out of Orientalism was precisely the very history that resisted its ideological as well as political encroachments' (p. 94); 'Orientalism is a praxis of the same sort, albeit in different territories, as male gender dominance, or patriarchy' (p. 103). Culture and Imperialism (New York: Knopf, 1993, first edition): 'What I left out of Orientalism was that response to Western dominance which culminated in the great movement of decolonization' (p. xii); 'we begin to reread it not univocally but contrapuntally, with a simultaneous awareness both of the metropolitan history that is narrated and of those other histories against which (and together with which) the dominating discourse acts' (p. 51); 'contrapuntal reading must take account of both processes, that of imperialism and that of resistance to it' (p. 66). In-period reception and criticism. Bernard Lewis, 'The Question of Orientalism', New York Review of Books, 24 June 1982 (web text, read in full, no page numbers): 'To prove this point, Mr. Said makes a number of very arbitrary decisions. His Orient is reduced to the Middle East, and his Middle East to a part of the Arab world'; 'a history of Arabic studies in Europe without the Germans makes as much sense as would a history of European music or philosophy with the same omission'; 'The most rigorous and penetrating critique of Orientalist scholarship has always been and will remain that of the Orientalists themselves.' Said's reply (NYRB, 12 August 1982): 'It is idiotic to say that Orientalism is a conspiracy or to suggest that "the West" is evil', while its 'modern discourse is correctly perceived as a discourse of power'; Lewis answered that 'It is difficult to argue with a scream of rage' and that the book 'takes a genuine problem of real importance, and reduces it to the level of political polemic and personal abuse'. Sadik Jalal al-'Azm, 'Orientalism and Orientalism in Reverse', Khamsin 8 (1981) (web text, read in full) credits 'laying bare Orientalism's persistent belief that there exists a radical ontological difference' between Orient and Occident, but holds that tracing Orientalism back to Homer 'simply lends strength to the essentialistic categories of "Orient" and "Occident"'. Rosalind O'Hanlon and David Washbrook (CSSH 1992; first-page extract only, as recorded in its source note) call Said's blend of themes 'virtually a paradigm for a new generation of historians and anthropologists' in Indian colonial history. Cheryl McEwan, Journal of Historical Geography 22 (1996), read in full: 'The inspiration behind the critical interest in empire, knowledge and power was undoubtedly Edward Said's groundbreaking and provocative Orientalism' (p. 489); feminist scholars 'argue that the critics of Orientalism and ethnocentric scholarship continue to write out gender' (p. 489); Reina Lewis's Gendering Orientalism (1996) is 'a response to Said in its efforts to destabilize the homogenizing tendencies of twentieth-century critiques of Orientalism' (p. 490). Said answered Dennis Porter's charge that he is 'ahistorical and inconsistent' as 'more weighty in assertion than it is in proof' (1985, p. 90); Porter's essay (1983) was not read. Not read: James Clifford's review essay (History and Theory 19, 1980) and Lata Mani and Ruth Frankenberg, 'The Challenge of Orientalism' (Economy and Society 14, 1985); both are recorded as metadata only. Later reading, labelled: Robert Irwin (2006, p. 299) writes that 'Early reviews of Orientalism were mostly hostile'. A contribution to postcolonial critique; the evidence does not make him its founder. edge_107 (language → post), edge_419 (post → indigenous) and edge_693 (post → geography) name him as a resource for others and stay.

edges.relationship: Foucault's notion of discourse used to identify Orientalism, with an explicit disagreement over the weight of individual authors (1978)
edges.evidence_note: Said's own in-period statements. Orientalism (Pantheon, 1978; page images checked): 'I have found it useful here to employ Michel Foucault's notion of a discourse, as described by him in The Archaeology of Knowledge and in Discipline and Punish, to identify Orientalism. My contention is that without examining Orientalism as a discourse one cannot possibly understand the enormously systematic discipline by which European culture was able to manage—and even produce—the Orient politically, sociologically, militarily, ideologically, scientifically, and imaginatively during the post-Enlightenment period' (p. 3). 'Yet unlike Michel Foucault, to whose work I am greatly indebted, I do believe in the determining imprint of individual writers upon the otherwise anonymous collective body of texts constituting a discursive formation like Orientalism'; 'Foucault believes that in general the individual text or author counts for very little; empirically, in the case of Orientalism (and perhaps nowhere else) I find this not to be so' (p. 23). Elsewhere he writes of 'what Michel Foucault calls a discourse, whose material presence or weight, not the originality of a given author, is really responsible for the texts produced out of it' (p. 94), and he groups 'Gramsci, certainly, and Foucault and Raymond Williams in their very different ways' as illustrating that hegemonic culture's constraints on writers 'were productive, not unilaterally inhibiting' (p. 14). In-period criticism of the combination: al-'Azm (1981, read) objects that for Said 'representations, images, words, metaphors ... are, if not the very stuff of reality, then certainly much more important and informative substitutes for raw reality itself'. Later reading, labelled: Irwin (2006, pp. 289–290) sets the p. 23 and p. 94 passages against each other and argues that 'Foucault and Gramsci have different and contrasting notions of discourse'; Ahmad (1991–92) is reported by Irwin (p. 300) as finding that 'Said's allegiance to Foucault ... got him into the worst muddles'; Ahmad's texts were not read. The edge records Said's stated use and revision of Foucault, not a reading of Foucault's own position; Said's later criticism is edge 4.

edges.relationship: Gramsci's hegemony and civil society used to explain the durability of Orientalism, and his 'inventory' of historical traces taken as the book's personal starting point (1978); consent for distant rule framed as 'a very Gramscian' question (1993)
edges.evidence_note: Said's own in-period statements. Orientalism (Pantheon, 1978; page images checked): 'Gramsci has made the useful analytic distinction between civil and political society'; culture works in civil society 'not through domination but by what Gramsci calls consent'; 'the form of this cultural leadership is what Gramsci has identified as hegemony, an indispensable concept for any understanding of cultural life in the industrial West. It is hegemony, or rather the result of cultural hegemony at work, that gives Orientalism the durability and the strength I have been speaking about so far' (pp. 6–7). Orientalism depends on 'this flexible positional superiority, which puts the Westerner in a whole series of possible relationships with the Orient without ever losing him the relative upper hand' (p. 7). 'In the Prison Notebooks Gramsci says: "The starting-point of critical elaboration is the consciousness of what one really is ..."'; Said notes that the English translation omits Gramsci's conclusion, 'therefore it is imperative at the outset to compile such an inventory', and calls his study 'an attempt to inventory the traces upon me, the Oriental subject' (p. 25). Culture and Imperialism (Knopf, 1993): 'The important point—a very Gramscian one—is how the national British, French, and American cultures maintained hegemony over the peripheries. How within them was consent gained and continuously consolidated for the distant rule of native peoples and territories?' (p. 51). In 1988 he described the Subaltern Studies scholars as influenced by 'many varieties of Western Marxism, Gramsci's most eminently' (foreword, Selected Subaltern Studies, p. x). Later reading, labelled: Irwin (2006, pp. 289–290) argues that 'Foucault and Gramsci had rather different ideas about the relationship between power and knowledge'. The edge records Said's stated use of Gramsci; it makes no claim about Gramsci's own Orient, which Said does not discuss in the pages read.

edges.relationship: Foucault criticised for discounting individual authors (1978) and for ignoring empire and dissolving the individual in a 'microphysics of power' that it is 'hopeless to resist' (1993)
edges.evidence_note: Said's own in-period statements. Orientalism (1978): 'Foucault believes that in general the individual text or author counts for very little; empirically, in the case of Orientalism (and perhaps nowhere else) I find this not to be so' (p. 23), while declaring himself 'greatly indebted' to Foucault (p. 23). Culture and Imperialism (Knopf, 1993): of Foucault and Raymond Williams, 'In the main I am in considerable sympathy with the genealogical discoveries of these two formidable scholars, and greatly indebted to them. Yet for both the imperial experience is quite irrelevant, a theoretical oversight that is the norm in Western cultural and scientific disciplines' (p. 41). Comparing Foucault and Fanon: 'Foucault's work moves further and further away from serious consideration of social wholes, focussing instead upon the individual as dissolved in an ineluctably advancing "microphysics of power" that it is hopeless to resist'; 'ignoring the imperial context of his own theories, Foucault seems actually to represent an irresistible colonizing movement that paradoxically fortifies the prestige of both the lonely individual scholar and the system that contains him'; Foucault 'swerves away from politics entirely' (p. 278). His note 198 refers the reader to 'my critique in "Foucault and the Imagination of Power"' (in David Hoy, ed., Foucault: A Critical Reader, 1986, pp. 149–155); that essay, and 'Traveling Theory' (1983), were not read. On p. 26 he also describes Foucault's turn to 'the local micro-physics of power that surround the individual'. Foucault's position is given only as Said presents it; no reply by Foucault was looked for. The critique is from a writer who kept using Foucault (edge 2); it is a disagreement within an acknowledged debt. edge_386 (post → foucault, Spivak and Stoler) records other postcolonial critics' engagements and stays.

edges.relationship: Marx's 1853 writings on British rule in India read as an instance in which Orientalist generalisation overrode his sympathy for Asian suffering (1978), a reading contested in period as a travesty
edges.evidence_note: Said's own in-period statements. Orientalism (Pantheon, 1978; page images checked), pp. 153–156. Marx 'identified the notion of an Asiatic economic system in his 1853 analyses of British rule in India, and then put beside that immediately the human depredation introduced into this system by English colonial interference, rapacity, and outright cruelty' (p. 153). After quoting Marx on England as 'the unconscious tool of history' and his Goethe citation: 'Marx's economic analyses are perfectly fitted thus to a standard Orientalist undertaking, even though Marx's humanity, his sympathy for the misery of people, are clearly engaged. Yet in the end it is the Romantic Orientalist vision that wins out' (p. 154); 'The idea of regenerating a fundamentally lifeless Asia is a piece of pure Romantic Orientalism' (p. 154); 'Marx is no exception. The collective Orient was easier for him to use in illustration of a theory than existential human identities' (p. 155); 'In part, of course, Marx was concerned with vindicating his own theses on socio-economic revolution' (p. 155); Marx is 'the case by which a non-Orientalist's human engagements were first dissolved, then usurped by Orientalist generalizations' (p. 156). The introduction announces it: 'The same kind of paradox is to be found in Marx, as I try to show in this book' (p. 14). In 1985 he names Marx among the historicists whose one human history 'either culminated in or was observed from the vantage point of Europe' ('Orientalism Reconsidered', p. 101). Marx's words appear here only as Said quotes them; the 1853 articles were not read. In-period counter-critique: al-'Azm (Khamsin 1981, read): 'I think that this account of Marx's views and analyses of highly complex historical processes and situations is a travesty'; 'only Said's excessive fascination with the verbal, textual and linguistic could lead him to portray Marx's mind as somehow usurped'; Marx's explanation 'testifies to his theoretical consistency in general, and to his keen realism'. Aijaz Ahmad's criticism of the same pages ('Between Orientalism and Historicism', Studies in History 1991; In Theory, 1992) is known here only from Irwin (2006, n. 32 to p. 296), who reports that Ahmad suggests 'Marx's position on rural Indians was not significantly different from his position on rural Germans'; Ahmad was not read. Later reading, labelled: Irwin (2006, pp. 295–296) calls the treatment a travesty and asks why there is no discussion of 'the Asiatic mode of production, Oriental despotism'.

edges.relationship: The named world-historical syntheses (Braudel, Wallerstein, Perry Anderson, Wolf) criticised as heir to Orientalist historicism: a homogenising scheme observed from a European vantage point that avoids its own relation to imperialism (1985); not a critique of every global or connected-history method
edges.evidence_note: Said's own in-period statements. 'Orientalism Reconsidered', Cultural Critique 1 (Autumn 1985), pp. 89–107, read in full (JSTOR copy). 'One of the legacies of Orientalism, and indeed one of its epistemological foundations, is historicism'; historicism 'meant that the one human history uniting humanity either culminated in or was observed from the vantage point of Europe, or the West'; out of the recuperation of what 'Eric Wolf has called people without history ... a still later disciplinary step was taken, the founding of the science of world history, whose major practitioners include Braudel, Wallerstein, Perry Anderson, and Wolf himself' (p. 101). He grants it 'greater capacity for dealing with ... the non-synchronous experiences of Europe's Other', but finds 'a fairly uniform avoidance of the relationship between European imperialism and these variously constituted, variously formed and articulated knowledges' (p. 101). 'The curious result is that the theories of accumulation on a world scale, or the capitalist world state, or lineages of absolutism depend (a) on the same displaced percipient and historicist observer who had been an Orientalist or colonial traveler three generations ago; (b) they depend also on a homogenizing and incorporating world historical scheme that assimilated non-synchronous developments, histories, cultures, and peoples to it'; 'the problem is once again historicism' (p. 102). He also rejects 're-cycling the old Marxist or world-historical rhetoric' (p. 103). In 1993 he contrasts revisionist works with 'the so-called world historians as well as the colonial Orientalists, who have tended to herd immense amounts of material under simple and all-encompassing rubrics' (Culture and Imperialism, pp. 41–42). The named historians' positions appear only as Said characterises them; no replies were looked for. The critique names practitioners mapped across several entries (Wolf on global; Wallerstein on dependency; Anderson on historicalsociology; Braudel's person entry); global is the target because he names 'the science of world history' as the object. edge_124 (post → global, Chakrabarty) stays.
edges.map_label: Said's critique of named world-historical syntheses, 1985

edges.relationship: Foreword introducing Subaltern Studies to an Anglo-American readership, with his own caution that subaltern and elite histories are 'different but overlapping and curiously interdependent territories' (1988)
edges.evidence_note: His own in-period text. Foreword to Ranajit Guha and Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak, eds., Selected Subaltern Studies (Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1988), pp. v–x, read in full (page images of a Digital Library of India scan, OCR checked against the images). He describes Guha's opening essay as 'fiercely theoretical and intellectually insurrectionary' (p. v) and the word subaltern as deriving 'from Gramsci's usage in the Prison Notebooks' (p. vi); 'rewriting Indian history today is an extension of the struggle between subaltern and elite' (p. vii). His addition: 'Yet even though his analysis is explicit on all the main issues, there is something that could perhaps be added to it here. And that is that no matter how one tried to extricate subaltern from elite histories, they are different but overlapping and curiously interdependent territories. This, I believe, is a crucial point. For if subaltern history is construed to be only a separatist enterprise ... then it runs the risk of just being a mirror opposite the writing whose tyranny it disputes' (p. viii). He places the group in 'the vast post-colonial cultural and critical effort' (p. ix) and calls its borrowing from Foucault 'the sharing of a paradigm, rather than slavish copying' (p. x); the volume is 'a crossing of boundaries, a smuggling of ideas across lines' (p. x). In 1985 he had already listed 'the group around Ranajit Guha (Subaltern Studies)' among anti-Orientalist projects ('Orientalism Reconsidered', pp. 104–105). A contribution of framing and reception to the series' Anglo-American appearance; it does not make him a member of the collective, a founder, or the source of its theory (the existing roster row says the same). edge_115 (subaltern → post) stays.

edges.relationship: Culture and Imperialism's account of resistance culture: anticolonial histories such as James's The Black Jacobins and Antonius's The Arab Awakening read as a 'voyage in' to metropolitan culture, alongside post-independence critiques by Guha and Alatas (1993)
edges.evidence_note: His own in-period text. Culture and Imperialism (Knopf, 1993), chapter 3, 'Resistance and Opposition'. He distinguishes liberal anti-colonialism, which did 'not dispute the fundamental superiority of Western man', from anti-imperialism, and argues 'there was no overall condemnation of imperialism until—and this is my point—after native uprisings were too far gone to be ignored or defeated' (pp. 240–241). Anti-imperialist work by writers from the peripheries in the metropolis is 'usually an extension into the metropolis of large-scale mass movements'; 'There is thus an overlap and interdependence that cannot theoretically be described as only the reactive assertion of a separate colonial or native identity'; 'The voyage in, then, constitutes an especially interesting variety of hybrid cultural work' (p. 244). He reads 'C.L.R. James's The Black Jacobins, published in 1938, and, appearing at almost the same time, George Antonius's The Arab Awakening' as works 'intended as serious works of scholarship and advocacy addressed from within a national movement for independence to a general audience', set against Ranajit Guha's A Rule of Property for Bengal (1963) and S. H. Alatas's The Myth of the Lazy Native (1977), which are 'post-colonial and specialist' (p. 245); 'history for Guha is critique, not the dutiful replication of colonialist objects, ideologies, and arguments' (p. 251). He also treats Fanon as one who 'programmatically seeks to treat colonial and metropolitan societies together' (p. 278). The introduction frames the chapter: 'What I left out of Orientalism was that response to Western dominance which culminated in the great movement of decolonization' (p. xii). Read: pp. xii, 240–245, 251, 278; the rest of the chapter (including the Fanon and Cabral sections) was not read closely. No in-period review assessing this chapter for historians was read. A contribution to how anticolonial histories are read and placed, not a claim that he wrote anticolonial history in their sense; The Question of Palestine (1979) is mentioned in the node, not used for this edge.
edges.map_label: Resistance culture and the voyage in, 1993

edges.relationship: The programme statement of Subaltern Studies: a critique of colonialist and bourgeois-nationalist elitism, an autonomous but overlapping domain of 'the politics of the people', and a method of reading rebel consciousness through counter-insurgency records (1982–83)
edges.evidence_note: His own in-period statements. Preface to Subaltern Studies I (dated Canberra, August 1981), read in the Selected Subaltern Studies reprint (Oxford, 1988), p. 35: the series is to 'rectify the elitist bias characteristic of much research and academic work' in South Asian studies; 'subaltern' is taken in the Concise Oxford sense, 'of inferior rank', as 'a name for the general attribute of subordination in South Asian society whether this is expressed in terms of class, caste, age, gender and office or in any other way'. 'On Some Aspects of the Historiography of Colonial India' (same reprint, pp. 37–44; Subaltern Studies I pagination is pp. 1–8): elitist historiography 'is of course not without its uses' (p. 38) but 'fails to acknowledge, far less interpret, the contribution made by the people on their own, that is, independently of the elite' (p. 39); 'What clearly is left out of this un-historical historiography is the politics of the people', 'an autonomous domain, for it neither originated from elite politics nor did its existence depend on the latter', 'As modern as indigenous elite politics' (p. 40); the two domains were not 'hermetically sealed off'; 'there was a great deal of overlap' (p. 42); the same class 'dominant in one area ... could be among the dominated in another' (p. 44). He claims a direction, not a doctrine: 'Let a hundred flowers blossom and we don't mind even the weeds' (p. 43); 'We claim no more than to try and indicate an orientation' (p. 43).
