Method, Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency (1983), introduction read (Duke 1999 printing, which keeps the 1983 Oxford pagination): 'To acknowledge the peasant as the maker of his own rebellion is to attribute ... a consciousness to him' (p. 4); 'How then are we to get in touch with the consciousness of insurgency when our access to it is barred thus by the discourse of counter-insurgency?'; 'It should be possible therefore to read the presence of a rebel consciousness as a necessary and pervasive element within that body of evidence' (p. 15). 'The Prose of Counter-Insurgency', Subaltern Studies II (Delhi, 1983), pp. 1–42, read in full: historiography takes the peasant rebel 'merely as an empirical person or member of a class, but not as an entity whose will and reason constituted the praxis called rebellion' (p. 2); 'Cause is made to stand in as a phantom surrogate for Reason' (p. 3); the historian should 'stop pretending that it can fully grasp a past consciousness and reconstitute it' (p. 33). In-period reception, a member's reading first: Spivak, 'Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography', Subaltern Studies IV (Delhi, 1985), pp. 330–363 (read): the group 'offers a theory of change' (p. 330); its practice is 'closer to deconstruction' (p. 332) and its presuppositions are 'not, strictly speaking, consonant with a desire to find a consciousness (here of the subaltern) in a positive and pure state' (p. 333); quoting Elementary Aspects p. 15, she reads 'the project to retrieve the subaltern consciousness' 'as a strategic use of positivist essentialism in a scrupulously visible political interest' (pp. 341–342), which 'would get the group off the dangerous hook of claiming to establish the truth-knowledge of the subaltern and his consciousness' (p. 356); 'The group is scrupulous in its consideration towards women' but overlooks 'how important the concept-metaphor woman is' (p. 356). Rosalind O'Hanlon, 'Recovering the Subject' (Modern Asian Studies 22:1, 1988, pp. 189–224; read in the Verso reprint, 2000, pp. 72–115, whose pages are cited): 'the classic figure of Western humanism—the self-originating, self-determining individual ... is readmitted through the back door in the figure of the subaltern himself' (p. 74). C. A. Bayly, 'Rallying Around the Subaltern' (Journal of Peasant Studies 16:1, 1988, pp. 110–120; Verso reprint pp. 116–126): the Subalterns 'acted mainly as a catalyst' for an existing minority interest (p. 116); Guha's approach 'seems sometimes to postulate the existence of an unchanging peasantry and unified peasant consciousness defined by struggle with colonialism' (p. 121). Sumit Sarkar, 'The Decline of the Subaltern in Subaltern Studies' (1997; pp. 82–87 and 90–94 read, pp. 84–87 against the page images): the early volumes were 'largely ignored in the West' while debated in 'Left-leaning intellectual circles in India' (p. 84); 'it was argued with considerable justice by Guha and other contributors' that anti-colonial movements had been explained 'far too often' by economic pressures and mobilization from the top (p. 85); the claims of a new 'paradigm' 'were certainly over-flamboyant' (p. 86); the theoretical turn 'had its origins in Guha's attempt to use some of the language and methods of Lévi-Straussian structuralism' (p. 87). Founder language is attributed, not adopted: Chakrabarty (1997) calls him 'the founder of the group' (subaltern source); Scott's foreword to the 1999 Duke printing writes that Elementary Aspects 'became, in effect, the founding document of what is now known as the Subaltern Studies School', adding that 'The term school conveys far too much in the way of a rigid orthodoxy' (p. ix). Later reading, labelled: Chakrabarty (Nepantla, 2000) treats 'the work of the historian Ranajit Guha in the period when he acted as the founding editor' as 'the founding texts of the project' (p. 11). edge_115 (subaltern → post) and edge_159 (gramsci → subaltern) stay.

edges.relationship: Colonialist and bourgeois-nationalist histories of India criticised as two forms of elitism that write nationalism as 'a sort of spiritual biography of the Indian elite' and leave out popular initiative (1982), extended to the shared liberal assumption that colonial dominance was hegemonic (1989)
edges.evidence_note: His own in-period statements. 'On Some Aspects of the Historiography of Colonial India' (1982; Selected Subaltern Studies reprint, 1988, pp. 37–44, read): 'The historiography of Indian nationalism has for a long time been dominated by elitism—colonialist elitism and bourgeois-nationalist elitism'; both 'share the prejudice that the making of the Indian nation and the development of the consciousness—nationalism—which informed this process were exclusively or predominantly elite achievements' (p. 37). The colonialist kind treats nationalism as 'a sort of “learning process”' driven by 'the expectation of rewards' (p. 38); the nationalist kind writes it up 'as a sort of spiritual biography of the Indian elite' (p. 38). Neither can explain 'the anti-Rowlatt upsurge of 1919 and the Quit India movement of 1942' as 'popular initiative asserting itself ... in defiance or absence of elite control' (p. 39). The qualification he keeps: 'Elitist historiography is of course not without its uses' (p. 38), and 'even the elitists have a part to play if only by way of teaching by negative examples' (p. 43). 'The Prose of Counter-Insurgency' (Subaltern Studies II, 1983, read): in bourgeois-nationalist historiography 'it is an elite consciousness which is read into all peasant movements as their motive force', producing 'such grotesqueries as the characterization of the Indigo Rebellion of 1860 as “the first non-violent mass movement”' (p. 38). 'Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography' (Subaltern Studies VI, 1989, pp. 210–309; pp. 210–215, 227–233, 291–292 and 299–303 read): 'There was one Indian battle that Britain never won. It was a battle for appropriation of the Indian past' (p. 210); 'History became thus a game for two to play as the alien colonialist project of appropriation was matched by an indigenous nationalist project of counter-appropriation' (p. 212); both rest on 'a fundamental agreement between the Indian bourgeoisie and the British' from 'the standpoint of liberalism' (p. 212); 'dominance under colonial conditions has quite erroneously been endowed with hegemony' (p. 228). On the Cambridge historians: 'The subject of this neo-colonialist historiography is the Empire' (p. 292); Anil Seal's 'general explanation' is 'a kind of academic confidence trick' (p. 300). In-period criticism of the stance: Sarkar (1997, p. 92, read) sees 'an unnoticed drift implicit even in Guha's initial formulation of the project in Subaltern Studies I': 'The “historiography of colonial India” somehow slides quickly into that of Indian nationalism', and the central problematic 'ultimately becomes “the historic failure of the nation to come into its own”' (quoting Subaltern Studies I, pp. 2–3, 7). Later reading, labelled: Chakrabarty (2000, p. 14) describes the series as starting 'as a critique of two contending schools of history: the Cambridge school and that of the nationalist historians'. This edge carries the story now told by edge_604 (subaltern → nationaltradition), whose relabel is proposed; edge_114 (subaltern → anticolonial) is discussed under edge_revisions.
edges.map_label: Against elitist histories of Indian nationalism, 1982–89

edges.relationship: Peasant insurgency in colonial India read as deliberate political action against a composite dominance of landlord, moneylender and state, whose limits define 'the quality of that politics' rather than denying it (1983)
edges.evidence_note: His own in-period statements. Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency in Colonial India (1983), introduction pp. 1–17 read (Duke 1999 printing; 1983 Oxford pagination, checked against the Delhi edition's text): 'Insurgency was thus the necessary antithesis of colonialism' (p. 2); the first histories of revolt were 'a discourse of power' (p. 3). Spontaneity is rejected as 'an idea that is elitist as well as erroneous' (p. 4). For colonial India, 'there was nothing in the militant movements of its rural masses that was not political' (p. 6), because 'the hitherto discrete powers of the landlord, the moneylender and the official came to form, under colonial rule, a composite apparatus of dominance over the peasant', a subjection 'primarily political in character' (p. 8). 'There was nothing spontaneous about all this in the sense of being unthinking and wanting in deliberation'; 'insurgency affirmed its political character precisely by its negative and inversive procedure' (p. 9). He keeps the limits: rebel aims that failed 'to rise above localism, sectarianism and ethnicity' do 'not take away from the essentially political character of their activity but defines the quality of that politics by specifying its limitations' (p. 10); 'It would be wrong of course to overestimate the maturity of this politics' (p. 10); it was 'a somewhat inchoate and naive state of consciousness' (p. 11). In-period criticism: O'Hanlon (1988; Verso reprint, 2000) sets his book apart from cruder 'literal' readings of autonomy ('I want to distinguish Ranajit Guha's work in the book Elementary Aspects', p. 85), yet, following Dipankar Gupta, finds the 'culturological' style 'carried to an extreme' there, so that 'the failure of peasant movements to spread' is explained by a 'habit of thinking and acting on a small and local scale' rather than by structural features (pp. 86–87); she sees 'his forceful insistence upon humanism's unitary subject-agent in its most extreme form' (p. 89). Sarkar (1997) writes that Guha's analyses of rumour, crime and insurgency 'were appreciated by many who could not accept the overall framework of Elementary Aspects' (p. 86). Later reading, labelled: Chakrabarty (2000) calls the redefinition of 'the political' 'the critical theoretical break' (p. 15). The related critique of Hobsbawm's 'pre-political' is edge 4. edge_357 (subaltern → political) tells the same story under Guha's name; its relabel is proposed.

edges.relationship: Hobsbawm's category 'pre-political', credited as pioneering, judged to help 'little in understanding the experience of colonial India', where peasant militancy was political (1983)
edges.evidence_note: His own text. Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency in Colonial India (1983), introduction pp. 5–6 read (Duke 1999 printing; 1983 Oxford pagination): those who identify consciousness with organization and politics can call mass activity 'unconscious, hence pre-political' (p. 5). 'The image of the pre-political peasant rebel in societies still to be fully industrialized owes a great deal to E. J. Hobsbawm's pioneering work published over two decades ago'; Hobsbawm 'uses this term again and again to describe a state of supposedly absolute or near absence of political consciousness or organization' (p. 5). Hobsbawm's words as Guha quotes them: 'the social brigand appears ... only before the poor have reached political consciousness or acquired more effective methods of social agitation'; 'The bandit is a pre-political phenomenon and his strength is in inverse proportion to that of organized revolutionism and Socialism or Communism'; 'traditional forms of peasant discontent' were 'virtually devoid of any explicit ideology, organization or programme'; 'pre-political people' are those 'who have not yet found, or only begun to find, a specific language in which to express their aspirations about the world' (pp. 5–6). His note cites 'Hobsbawm: 2, 5, 13, 23, 96, 118' and Hobsbawm and Rudé's Captain Swing (pp. 19, 205); his bibliography lists Primitive Rebels (Manchester, 1959) and Captain Swing (London, 1969). He grants the European case and notes an inconsistency: 'Hobsbawm's material is of course derived almost entirely from the European experience and his generalizations are perhaps in accord with it, although one detects a certain contradiction' between banditry having 'next to no organization or ideology' and being 'a rather primitive form of organized social protest' (p. 6). Then: 'Whatever its validity for other countries the notion of pre-political peasant insurgency helps little in understanding the experience of colonial India. For there was nothing in the militant movements of its rural masses that was not political' (p. 6). Elsewhere the book credits 'E. J. Hobsbawm's pioneering formulation of the concept of “social banditry”' (p. 90, read in the 1983 Delhi edition's text). Hobsbawm's words are given only as Guha quotes them; Primitive Rebels was not read. Guha's quotation has 'express their aspirations about the world', the wording the 1.132 review reported from an OCR witness of Primitive Rebels p. 2, where Chakrabarty (2000, Provincializing Europe p. 12) has 'express themselves'; Chakrabarty's Nepantla essay (2000, p. 16) also quotes 'aspirations', citing Hobsbawm (1978, 2). This gives a second, earlier quoted-in witness for the edge_917 wording question, not a reading of Hobsbawm. Reception: Chakrabarty credits the critique to Guha in Provincializing Europe (2000, p. 11; post source) and writes that rejecting the category 'fundamentally pluralizes the history of power in global modernity' (Nepantla, 2000, p. 19). No reply by Hobsbawm was looked for or read. This edge is the origin edge_917 (dipesh_chakrabarty → eric_hobsbawm) names ('the critique Guha began (1983)').

edges.relationship: Thompson's account of the rule of law as 'a cultural achievement of universal significance' (Whigs and Hunters, 1975) rejected from colonial India, where bourgeois culture 'hits its historical limit', after drawing on the same book for comparisons with peasant crime (1983–89)
edges.evidence_note: His own text. 'Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography', Subaltern Studies VI (Delhi, 1989), pp. 276–277 read (Digital Library of India scan of the volume): asking 'What rule of law' existed under the Raj (p. 276), he finds the answer in 'the pervasive power of the ideology of law in English political thought', which assumed 'the status of “a cultural achievement of universal significance” in the eyes not only of English liberals and colonialists like Dodwell, but also, alas, of English radicals like E. P. Thompson from whom those words are taken' (p. 277). 'Neither the special pleading by Dodwell ... nor the ingenuity of Thompson when he tries unsuccessfully to disentangle himself from the metaphysical implications of his statement by allowing for the class manipulation of the rule of law, can take away from the fact that bourgeois culture hits its historical limit in colonialism' (p. 277). His notes cite Whigs and Hunters (London, 1975), p. 265, and pp. 258–69, especially 265–7. Whigs and Hunters was not read for this draft; the phrase is taken as Guha quotes it. The critique follows earlier use: Elementary Aspects (1983) draws on Thompson's account of the Blacks, the authorities' 'one common blur' of 'outrages by the Blacks' (p. 89) and the Blacks as an intermediate type between 'social bandits' and 'agrarian rebels' (p. 90), read in the 1983 Delhi edition's text. In-period context: Sarkar (1997, p. 83, read) writes that among historiographical influences on Subaltern Studies 'that of British Marxian social history was probably the most significant', that 'Ranajit Guha seems to have often used “subaltern” somewhat in the way Thompson deployed the term “plebeian”', and (n. 3) that Elementary Aspects 'frequently cited Thompson with approval', to Whigs and Hunters and Albion's Fatal Tree. The edge therefore records a dispute over one claim, not a rejection of Thompson. No reply by Thompson was looked for. edge_083 (marx → subaltern, Thompson's reception) stays.

edges.relationship: Gramsci's notes on subaltern groups, spontaneity and the 'first elements' of politics frame the founding preface and Elementary Aspects (1982–83); hegemony is later redefined against 'the Gramscian juxtaposition of domination and hegemony' (1989)
edges.evidence_note: His own in-period statements. Preface to Subaltern Studies I (1982; Selected Subaltern Studies reprint, p. 35, read): the series cannot 'even remotely match the six-point project envisaged by Antonio Gramsci in his “Notes on Italian History”'; subordination is 'one of the constitutive terms in a binary relationship of which the other is dominance, for “subaltern groups are always subject to the activity of ruling groups, even when they rebel and rise up”'. The quoted words are Gramsci's (Selections from the Prison Notebooks, 1971, p. 55, checked in the gramsci source; the preface does not name the source). Elementary Aspects (1983), introduction read: the critique of 'pure spontaneity' follows 'Antonio Gramsci whose words are quoted above' ('there is no room for pure spontaneity in history', p. 5), with the quoted passage on a 'scholastic and academic historico-political outlook' (p. 4) taken from 'Spontaneity and Conscious Leadership' (n., Gramsci: 196–200); leadership is described 'in Gramsci's words, as “multiple elements of 'conscious leadership' but no one of them ... predominant”' (p. 10); and the book's title concept comes from the 'first elements' which Gramsci called 'the pillars of politics and of any collective action whatsoever' (p. 12, citing Gramsci: 144; the passage, 'Elements of Politics', checked at Selections p. 144). 'Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography' (1989, pp. 231–232, read): 'As used in this essay, hegemony stands for a condition of Dominance (D), such that, in the organic composition of the latter, Persuasion (P) outweighs Coercion (C)'; this 'avoids the Gramscian juxtaposition of domination and hegemony (a term sometimes used in the Prison Notebooks synonymously with leadership) as antinomies, which has, alas, provided too often a theoretical pretext for the fabrication of a liberal absurdity—the absurdity of the idea of an uncoercive state—in spite of the basic drive of Gramsci's own work to the contrary'. The same definition is quoted from the 1997 book, p. 23, in Spivak's 'The New Subaltern' (Verso, 2000, n. 3), a later quoted-in witness. In-period readings: Sarkar (1997, p. 82) notes 'evocations of Gramsci' in Guha's 1982 preface and essay; O'Hanlon (1988; Verso reprint p. 102) finds 'no concerted attempt to construct a theory of domination as hegemony, as the invocation of Gramsci might have led us to expect', and agrees with Suneet Chopra and Javeed Alam 'that the series has not turned out to be a Gramscian project at all' (Alam and Chopra unread). Wikidata Q475026 states 'influenced by' Antonio Gramsci (P737); this is recorded as a Wikidata statement, not evidence. edge_159 (gramsci → subaltern) stays for the collective adaptation (for example David Arnold's 'Gramsci and Peasant Subalternity in India', reprinted in Mapping Subaltern Studies, 2000, ch. 3; not read); edge_159's evidence note names Guha, and a reviewer may trim that clause.

edges.relationship: Guha's critique of the 'pre-political' and his founding statements for Subaltern Studies, which Chakrabarty names as the starting point of his own argument for provincializing Europe (1997–2000)
edges.evidence_note: In Chakrabarty's own in-period words. 'Minority Histories, Subaltern Pasts' (Perspectives, AHA, November 1997; subaltern source, read for 1.132) calls Guha 'the founder of the group'. Provincializing Europe (2000), introduction (post source, read for 1.132): Subaltern Studies registered 'a deep sense of unease with the very idea of the “political”', 'Nowhere ... more visible than in Ranajit Guha's criticism of the British historian Eric Hobsbawm's category “prepolitical” in his 1983 book Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency' (p. 11); Guha's critique 'fundamentally pluralizes the history of power in global modernity' (p. 14); 'My argument for provincializing Europe follows directly from my involvement in this project' (p. 15). 'Subaltern Studies and Postcolonial Historiography', Nepantla 1:1 (2000), pp. 9–32, read in the Project MUSE PDF: he reads 'the work of the historian Ranajit Guha in the period when he acted as the founding editor', 'the founding texts of the project' (p. 11), to show 'a radical departure from English Marxist historiographical traditions' (p. 11); 'In rejecting the category “pre-political”, however, Guha insists on the specific differences in the histories of power in colonial India and in Europe. This gesture is radical in that it fundamentally pluralizes the history of power in global modernity and separates it from any universal history of capital' (p. 19). He also reads a 'tension between a familiar narrative of capital and a more radical understanding of it' within Elementary Aspects, which 'sometimes does speak within' a Marxist transition narrative of 'lingering feudalism' (p. 18). Earlier, documented working ties: Guha's 1982 statement thanks 'Dipesh Chakrabarty' among those who commented on an earlier version (Selected Subaltern Studies reprint, p. 37, n. 1), and the Elementary Aspects preface names him among the colleagues of the collective who read the final draft. Criticism of the trajectory: Sarkar (1997, pp. 84–85) calls the path Chakrabarty outlined 'debilitating in both academic and political terms' (recorded on edge_915). This is an influence edge, not a claim that Chakrabarty's argument is Guha's; the Nepantla essay is Chakrabarty's own account of the project.
edges.map_label: From Guha's critique of the 'pre-political' to provincializing Europe, 1983–2000

edges.relationship: ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’: the two senses of representation, the epistemic violence of colonial law and knowledge, and the subaltern woman silenced between colonial and indigenous patriarchal discourse on sati (1985–99)
edges.evidence_note: Her own in-period statements. ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ (1988), read in the Williams and Chrisman reprint (pages of that reprint; its opening is abridged): ‘Some of the most radical criticism coming out of the West today is the result of an interested desire to conserve the subject of the West, or the West as Subject’ (p. 66). ‘Two senses of representation are being run together: representation as “speaking for”, as in politics, and representation as “re-presentation”, as in art or philosophy’; ‘representing them, the intellectuals represent themselves as transparent’ (p. 70); running vertreten and darstellen together ‘leads to an essentialist, utopian politics’ (p. 71). The codification of Hindu law is her ‘example of epistemic violence’ (pp. 76–77), and she asks whether, ‘inside and outside the circuit of the epistemic violence of imperialist law and education’, ‘can the subaltern speak?’ (p. 78). On sati she sets the sentence ‘White men are saving brown women from brown men’, which she says she ‘put together’ (p. 92), against ‘the Indian nativist argument’, ‘“The women actually wanted to die”’: ‘The two sentences go a long way to legitimize each other. One never encounters the testimony of the women’s voice-consciousness’ (p. 93). She qualifies: ‘Given that the abolition of sati was in itself admirable’ (p. 94); ‘Obviously I am not advocating the killing of widows’ (p. 97). ‘Between patriarchy and imperialism, subject-constitution and object-formation, the figure of the woman disappears ... into a violent shuttling’ (p. 102). She welcomes ‘all the information retrieval in these silenced areas’ in history and other disciplines, while warning that the assumed ‘consciousness or subject’ will ‘cohere with the work of imperialist subject-constitution’ (p. 90). The close: ‘The subaltern cannot speak. There is no virtue in global laundry lists with “woman” as a pious item. Representation has not withered away’ (reprint p. 104, wording restored from the unpaginated 1988 text in Morris, 2010; 1988 p. 308 per Sunder Rajan in the same volume). She credits Lata Mani’s 1983 thesis on sati as ‘a brilliant account’ and ‘profited from discussion with Ms Mani’ (n. 65, p. 109). The 1999 revision (A Critique of Postcolonial Reason, ch. 3; read in Morris’s unpaginated reprint; CPR p. 308 per Sunder Rajan) says: ‘in the first version of this text, I wrote, in the accents of passionate lament: the subaltern cannot speak! It was an inadvisable remark’, and that Bhubaneswari Bhaduri ‘was not a “true” subaltern’. ‘Three Women’s Texts’ (Critical Inquiry, 1985, read pp. 243–245) opens: ‘It should not be possible to read nineteenth-century British literature without remembering that imperialism, understood as England’s social mission, was a crucial part of the cultural representation of England to the English’, and finds it ‘particularly unfortunate when the emergent perspective of feminist criticism reproduces the axioms of imperialism’ (p. 243). In-period readings by historians: Gyan Prakash, ‘Can the “Subaltern” Ride?’ (CSSH 1992; Verso reprint 2000, pp. 226–227, read): ‘as Spivak states starkly, the debate left no room for the woman’s enunciatory position’; ‘Spivak very correctly marks the silencing of the subaltern woman as the point at which the interpreter must acknowledge the limits of historical understanding’. Sumit Sarkar, ‘Orientalism Revisited’ (Oxford Literary Review, 1994; reprint p. 254, n. 14, read), criticising Mani’s Saidian assumptions, contrasts ‘the much more substantive discussion of pre-colonial and colonial discourses on sati in Spivak’. Contested in period: Terry Eagleton (LRB, 13 May 1999; web text, no page numbers, read) on A Critique of Postcolonial Reason: ‘too well-mannered, as well as too episodic’ to be the critique its title promises, ‘too deeply invested in feminism and post-colonialism to launch a full-scale socialist critique of these currents’, yet ‘this study boldly addresses the economic realities which too many post-colonial critics culturalise away’; he reports that she contrasts her own critique with Aijaz Ahmad’s ‘scorching assault’ in In Theory (1992; unread here). Benita Parry, ‘Problems in Current Theories of Colonial Discourse’, Oxford Literary Review 9 (1987), pp. 27–58, is the best-known in-period critique; it is closed access and unread, and no claim is made about its argument. A contribution, not a founding: the post entry already lists Said (1978) before her, and edge_107 (language → post) and edge_115 (subaltern → post) stay. Later reception, added in revision 1.151: Interventions 4:2 (2002) devoted a special issue to A Critique of Postcolonial Reason, from a panel at the IAPL conference in 2000, with her response (metadata and abstracts only); Mark Sanders's abstract holds that placing "Can the subaltern speak?" in the book's "History" chapter "emphasizes its deconstruction of Marxist politics". Ritu Birla's abstract (the essay is unread) explores "the challenges of radical history writing" through the book's chapter on history, under the themes of "limits, the open secret, and value/transvaluation"; it sets Spivak beside Joan Scott's critique of "experience", opening "a discussion of the supplementary relationship of literature and history", and connects the limit of history to "the selective production of the archive".

edges.relationship: A critique from within: the collective's recovery of subaltern consciousness read as 'a strategic use of positivist essentialism', and woman shown to be 'the neglected syntagm' of its accounts of insurgency (1985–88); the subaltern later reformulated as those 'removed from lines of social mobility' (2004)
edges.evidence_note: Her own in-period statements. ‘Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography’, Subaltern Studies IV (Delhi, 1985), pp. 330–363, read in full: the group ‘offers a theory of change’, plotting change ‘as confrontations rather than transition’ (p. 330); its practice is ‘closer to deconstruction’ than its self-description (p. 332); ‘This is why I hope to align them with deconstruction’ (p. 336). ‘Reading the work of Subaltern Studies from within but against the grain’ (p. 341), she reads the project to retrieve subaltern consciousness ‘as a strategic use of positivist essentialism in a scrupulously visible political interest’ (p. 342), which ‘would get the group off the dangerous hook of claiming to establish the truth-knowledge of the subaltern and his consciousness’ (p. 356). On gender: ‘The group is scrupulous in its consideration towards women’, but ‘I think they overlook how important the concept-metaphor woman is to the functioning of their discourse’ (p. 356); ‘Analogous research into the figure of the “worker” is performed by Chakrabarty. No such luck for the “female”’ (p. 357); ‘Male subaltern and historian are here united in the common assumption that the procreative sex is a species apart’ (p. 358); ‘woman is the neglected syntagm of the semiosis of subalternity of insurgency’ (p. 359); ‘if the question of female subaltern consciousness ... is a red herring, the question of subaltern consciousness as such must be judged a red herring as well’ (p. 360). She qualifies: ‘The making-visible of the figure of woman is perhaps not a task that the group should fairly be asked to perform’, but ‘a feminist historian of the subaltern must raise the question of woman as a structural rather than marginal issue’ (p. 361). ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ (1988; Williams and Chrisman reprint): of Guha’s ‘autonomous domain’, ‘I cannot entirely endorse this insistence on determinate vigor and full autonomy’ (p. 79; this disagreement with Guha is drawn as its own person-to-person critique, Spivak → Guha, in this revision, and is no longer named in this edge's relationship); ‘the colonized subaltern subject is irretrievably heterogeneous’ (p. 79); ‘If, in the context of colonial production, the subaltern has no history and cannot speak, the subaltern as female is even more deeply in shadow’ (pp. 82–83). In-period readings from historians of the field: Rosalind O’Hanlon, ‘Recovering the Subject’ (Modern Asian Studies, 1988; Verso reprint, read), takes up her phrase (p. 80, citing SS IV p. 342) but warns ‘we should certainly hesitate before accepting Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak’s suggestion that the strategy of the Subaltern series “in claiming a positive subject-position for the subaltern might be re-inscribed as a strategy for our times”’ (p. 105, citing SS IV p. 345). Gyanendra Pandey, a member, reads the 1988 close as Gramsci’s point: ‘“The subaltern cannot speak,” writes Gayatri Spivak, making, I suggest, much the same point’ (Ethnos, 1995; reprint p. 285, read). Vinayak Chaturvedi (2000, p. xviii, n. 46, read) writes that the 1988 essay ‘brought issues of gender to the forefront of Subaltern Studies’ and ‘may have provided a major impetus’ for the gender and voice themes of Subaltern Studies IX (1996). Her own later account (‘The New Subaltern’, 2000, read): ‘Except in the work of Susie Tharu ... Subaltern Studies is not informed by feminist theory as such’ (p. 325), and of 1985, ‘Subaltern Studies had no need of such apologetics. But the theoretically inclined metropolitan identitarians did’ (p. 332). Later reading, labelled: Partha Chatterjee (2010; Morris volume, unpaginated) recalls first reading both essays in 1985 with ‘bewilderment’ and calls her intervention ‘the poststructuralist moment in Subaltern Studies’, adding that a changed political context also drove the shift. A critique from within, not a rejection: she joined the editorial collective in the 1990s. edge_389 (gender → subaltern) carries the same story under the gender entry; see the proposed relabel. Guha’s person edge (pe137_guha_rel_01, guha draft) cites the same 1985 essay as reception; this edge is hers. Later reformulation and reading, added in revision 1.151 and dated after 2000: in "Righting Wrongs" (South Atlantic Quarterly, 2004; read in part, from a February 2001 lecture) she writes, "By subaltern I mean those removed from lines of social mobility" (p. 531), and warns that leaders from the domestic "below" ignore "the historically established discontinuity between themselves and the subaltern" (p. 535). Richard M. Eaton (Journal of World History, 2000, read p. 60) summarises the 1985 essay as criticism of "subalternist historians" for "positivist methodologies" (see the truthdebate critique).
edges.map_label: Strategic essentialism and the gendered subaltern, 1985–2004

edges.relationship: Foucault's account of power criticised as blind to imperialism and the international division of labour, and for an intellectual who lets the oppressed 'speak for themselves' while remaining transparent; his analyses of disciplinary institutions kept as useful (1988)
edges.evidence_note: Her own in-period text: ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ (1988; Williams and Chrisman reprint, read in full). She takes as her object ‘Intellectuals and power: a conversation between Michel Foucault and Gilles Deleuze’ (p. 66), whose participants ‘systematically ignore the question of ideology and their own implication in intellectual and economic history’ (p. 66). In her summary of the conversation, ‘the oppressed can know and speak for themselves’ (p. 74); she adds ‘to Said’s analysis the notion of the surreptitious subject of power and desire marked by the transparency of the intellectual’ (p. 75). ‘Foucault is a brilliant thinker of power-in-spacing, but the awareness of the topographical reinscription of imperialism does not inform his presuppositions’ (p. 85); ‘The clinic, the asylum, the prison, the university - all seem to be screen-allegories that foreclose a reading of the broader narratives of imperialism’ (p. 86). She keeps part of his work: ‘what remains useful in Foucault is the mechanics of disciplinarization and institutionalization, the constitution, as it were, of the colonizer’ (p. 90), and calls his model of localized resistance ‘an admirable program’ that, universalized, ‘accommodates unacknowledged privileging of the subject’ (p. 85). Foucault’s position is given only as she presents it, from the translated conversation and Power/Knowledge; no reply was looked for (he died in 1984). Reception: Eagleton (1999, read) groups Derrida and Foucault as thinkers who ‘veer between a cult of theoretical “madness” ... and a more restrained, reformist sort of politics’, a criticism of her allies, not a defence of Foucault. edge_386 (post → foucault, Spivak and Stoler) carries her name with Stoler’s; see the optional relabel. Said’s separate critique of Foucault is pe137_said_rel_04 (said draft); she cites Said’s criticism and extends it (p. 75).

edges.relationship: Derrida's deconstruction, which she translated and introduced (1976), used and tested as a method for reading colonial texts and subaltern historiography, without being celebrated 'as feminism as such' (1976–88)
edges.evidence_note: Her own in-period texts. Translator’s preface to Of Grammatology (1976; read at p. lxxvii of the 1997 corrected edition): ‘To locate the promising marginal text, to disclose the undecidable moment, to pry it loose with the positive lever of the signifier; to reverse the resident hierarchy, only to displace it; to dismantle in order to reconstitute what is always already inscribed. Deconstruction in a nutshell. But take away the assurance of the text’s authority, the critic’s control, and the primacy of meaning, and the possession of this formula does not guarantee much.’ Subaltern Studies IV (1985): ‘This is the greatest gift of deconstruction: to question the authority of the investigating subject without paralysing him, persistently transforming conditions of impossibility into possibility’ (p. 336). ‘Three Women’s Texts’ (1985) sets ‘the lessons of deconstruction’ aside for the essay, choosing to ‘strategically take shelter in an essentialism’ (p. 244). ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ (1988; Williams and Chrisman reprint): ‘Derrida is hard to read; his real object of investigation is classical philosophy. Yet he is less dangerous when understood than the first-world intellectual masquerading as the absent nonrepresenter who lets the oppressed speak for themselves’ (p. 87); reading ‘Of grammatology as a positive science’, she reads him as placing the ethnocentric constitution of the Other as ‘Not a general problem, but a European problem’, and ‘As a postcolonial intellectual, I am not troubled that he does not lead me ... to the specific path that such a critique makes necessary’ (p. 89); ‘I have attempted to use and go beyond Derridean deconstruction, which I do not celebrate as feminism as such’ (p. 104); ‘In a certain way, then, the critique of imperialism is deconstruction as such’ (n. 47, p. 108). In-period reception: Eagleton (1999, read) calls Derrida ‘a consecrated figure for this book, about whom hardly a breath of criticism seems permissible’. Prakash (1992; reprint pp. 224–225, read) quotes her definition of deconstruction as an ‘impossible “no” to a structure, which one critiques, yet inhabits intimately’. Later reading, labelled: Chatterjee (2010) recalls that in 1982 the subalternists ‘did not imagine that Jacques Derrida ... could have anything remotely to do with Indian peasants’. Wikidata’s ‘influenced by’ (P737) lists Paul de Man, not Derrida; that is a Wikidata statement, not evidence here. Her translation’s publication dates (first American edition 1976, corrected 1997) are already checked on derrida_grammatology_corrected. edge_025 (derrida → post) tells her story under the group entry; see the proposed relabel.

edges.relationship: Chakrabarty uses 'Spivak's subaltern' as an analogy for the subject whom university history's transition narrative can only represent, the 'Indian' history that 'cannot speak itself as “theory”' (1992)
edges.evidence_note: Chakrabarty’s in-period text. ‘Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History’, Representations 37 (1992), read (JSTOR copy; spacing restored): the antihistorical subject ‘cannot speak itself as “theory” within the knowledge procedures of the university even when these knowledge procedures acknowledge and “document” its existence. Much like Spivak’s “subaltern” (or the anthropologist’s peasant who can only have a quoted existence in a larger statement that belongs to the anthropologist alone), this subject can only be spoken for and spoken of by the transition narrative’ (p. 19, n. 52, citing ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ and her 1990 Socialist Review interview). He also borrows, ‘in Gayatri Spivak’s words’, ‘the feeling of community that belongs to national links and political organizations’ (p. 18, n. 48, citing the 1988 essay at p. 277; Williams and Chrisman reprint p. 72); she is among those thanked in the unnumbered first note (p. 23), and n. 43 (p. 25) credits her with an expression (‘personal communication’). Her side, in period: Subaltern Studies IV (1985) discusses his labour essays (pp. 331, 344) and sets them against the collective’s neglect of gender: ‘Analogous research into the figure of the “worker” is performed by Chakrabarty. No such luck for the “female”’ (p. 357). The influence is bounded: Chakrabarty’s provincializing argument ‘follows directly’ from his work in Subaltern Studies (2000, p. 15; on edge_914), and the guha draft proposes Guha → Chakrabarty for the critique of the ‘pre-political’. This edge records one acknowledged borrowing in the 1992 programmatic essay, not a genealogy.
edges.map_label: ‘Spivak’s subaltern’ in the artifice of history, 1992

edges.relationship: An agricultural crisis from 1802, joined to population pressure and a peasantry slow to change its methods, as the ground of French-Canadian nationalism and, in large part, of the 1837–38 rebellion (1962–76)
edges.evidence_note: In-period, his own texts. With Jean Hamelin (1962, read in full): 'la détérioration rapide de l'agriculture bas-canadienne après 1802 prouve le caractère superficiel des conquêtes antérieures. Dès le début du 19e siècle, la tendance majeure se renverse' (p. 20); 'la routine paysanne, la pauvreté des moyens de transport, les habitudes de consommation de l'habitant canadien-français et l'incompréhension des politiciens expliquent la lenteur des départs et des progrès'; 'Aussi la révolution de 1837-38 apparaît-elle, en grande partie, comme une réponse détournée aux problèmes posés par l'action conjointe des tensions démographiques et de la crise agricole' (p. 31); the crisis reveals 'deux entités culturelles sans aucun doute distinctes mais offrant une grande disparité dans leur degré d'évolution', so that 'c'est moins la diversité des valeurs que la différence des niveaux d'évolution qui fut la source fondamentale des conflits raciaux'; qualification: 'Ce n'est pas que cette crise soit le seul moteur des événements de cette époque troublée' (p. 32). His 1976 restatement (read in full): the habitant, 'un paysan traditionnel', adapted positively to the export market from 1760 to 1802 (p. 115); thereafter 'le paysan, au lieu de transformer ses façons de faire, se durcit et résiste aux pressions en faveur de la rénovation du système agricole'; nationalism was born 'parmi les professions libérales' and spread 'dans les milieux paysans sous l'effet de l'apparition du problème agricole et des pressions démographiques' (p. 116). His books as quoted by critics (unread here): Paquet and Wallot (1972, pp. 193–194) quote the 1966 Histoire (p. 184) that 'l'explication ultime dans la diminution des exportations de céréales réside ... dans une défaillance de la production locale', and his 1964 CHR article (p. 291) that 'la crise agricole, par ses nombreuses implications, serait donc la toile de fond de l'aventure nationaliste'. In-period readers: Paquet and Wallot (1972, p. 187): 'pour un tenant de la position Labrousse comme F. Ouellet, la "crise agricole" est le pivot de toute l'interprétation socio-économique de l'histoire du Bas-Canada au tournant du XIXe siècle'; Savard (1974, ¶8): 'Ouellet a dit sa dette envers les travaux exemplaires de Labrousse et de Chaunu'; Bouchard (1990, ¶13): 'Dans la foulée de Fernand Ouellet et de Jean Hamelin qui, avec quelques autres, ont introduit ici l'histoire sociale, toute une génération d'historiens entreprit alors une nouvelle lecture du passé québécois'. A contribution to the Laval strand and the crisis debate, not a founding; the critics are on edge 2.

edges.relationship: The agricultural-crisis thesis and its portrait of a routine-bound peasantry rejected by Paquet and Wallot (1972), criticised from Montreal by Tousignant (1980) and answered by Greer (1981; and in his 1993 book, as characterised by Dessureault, 1998, and Cardinal, 1999)
edges.evidence_note: This arrow represents Paquet and Wallot's, Tousignant's and Greer's specified interventions in the agricultural-crisis debate (quebec_historiography/agricultural_crisis_debate), not a verdict of the field, which includes Ouellet and his supporters. Paquet and Wallot (RHAF 1972, read in full): of the 1962 article, 'Cet article contient bien plus une intuition qu'une démonstration' (p. 193); Ouellet's postulates include 'le conservatisme invétéré des habitants, nous dirions même leur irrationalité' (p. 195); 'Comme la plupart de ses prédécesseurs, Ouellet peint les habitants comme des paysans essentiellement conservateurs, peu enclins à innover et désespérément embourbés dans des traditions routinières. Il s'agit là, nous semble-t-il, d'une simplification trop fréquente dans l'historiographie et qui appelle des réserves sérieuses' (pp. 201–202); 'Il n'existe pas de rationalité illimitée' (p. 202); 'les habitants ont adopté un régime agraire rationnel' (p. 221); their alternative, the Canadiens as 'd'astucieux politiques' in an 'équilibre conflictuel' with the British party (pp. 235–236), sought 'au-delà d'un économisme grossier' (p. 236); verdict, 'renvoyer comme irrecevable la thèse Ouellet' (p. 237), with the qualification that 'Quant à savoir si le débat est résolu pour autant, nous ne saurions le dire' (p. 237). Pierre Tousignant (RHAF 1980, read in full), on Le Bas-Canada (1976): the 1966 book 'faisait écho aux vieux préjugés de l'historiographie canadienne-anglaise tout imprégnée de l'idéologie de supériorité de la race anglo-saxonne', but the approach 'qui justifiait la notion désormais dépassée du «retard des mentalités» n'apparaît plus au premier plan dans Le Bas-Canada. C'est une notable amélioration' (p. 416); the periodisation of the export series 'n'est évidemment pas innocent' (p. 417); 'Il ne saurait plus être question de porter au seul compte d'une différence de mentalités l'appauvrissement progressif de la majeure partie de la paysannerie' (p. 419); 'Le professeur Ouellet nourrit de telles préventions contre le parti patriote qu'il a développé des réflexes défensifs à l'égard du parti bureaucrate' (p. 430); yet the book gives 'une intelligibilité vivante' to the period (p. 436, after Nicole Gagnon). Allan Greer (CHA Historical Papers 1981, read in full; n. 41 cites Ouellet's Lower Canada, 1980): 'The dominant explanation of Lower Canada's rural crisis emphasizes two factors, one demographic, the other cultural ... the atavistic mentality of the French-Canadian habitants led to their irrational refusal to accept technical improvements' (p. 213); 'The case of Sorel seems to challenge both elements of this interpretation'; 'To echo the commercial bourgeoisie of Lower Canada in blaming the habitants for their own agrarian predicament would be adding ideological insult to economic injury' (p. 214). On the rebellion, Greer's 1993 book is unread; reviewers say (their words): it 'brise nettement avec les travaux antérieurs de William H. Parker et de Fernand Ouellet pour qui la paysannerie était essentiellement victime de la crise économique et manipulée par des élites ultranationalistes' (Dessureault 1998, p. 206); 'à plusieurs reprises, A. Greer s'en prend aux arguments de cet historien, selon lesquels les habitants canadiens-français avaient une mentalité arriérée' (Cardinal 1999, p. 185). Ouellet's reply (1976, read): his critics 'ont réduit notre analyse à un simple rapport entre nationalisme et malaise agricole' and made the debate 'presque stérile' (p. 116); 'Le débat ne mérite plus d'être poursuivi; c'est la recherche qui exige de l'être' (p. 132). Le Goff's review of the controversy (CHR 1974) is unread; Ouellet reports that it concluded for a crisis from the early nineteenth century (1985, p. 25), so Le Goff is not counted among these critics.

edges.relationship: Ouellet's critiques of two interpretations: the Montreal school's Conquest thesis (Séguin's 'décapitation' of a national bourgeoisie, taken up by Brunet), with the habitant's trauma placed in the failing agrarian system rather than the Conquest (1962–85); and parts of the post-1960 generation's economic history, organised in his reading, in 'une grande partie' of it, around French-Canadian inferiority and the independence movement, whose revisions of Séguin's thesis Linteau, Robert and Normand Séguin followed (1985)
edges.evidence_note: The Montreal school. His own texts. 1962 (with Hamelin, read): French-Canadian historiography reflects 'les réactions émotives des classes dirigeantes canadiennes-françaises', and its simplifications result 'à la fois du mépris de l'économique et de l'idéalisation du fait politique' (p. 32; no historian is named). 1976 (read): 'Si notre « habitant » a subi un traumatisme, ce n'est pas au moment de la conquête mais au moment où le système agricole traditionnel ne peut plus fonctionner comme autrefois' (p. 116). 1985 (read): 'pour Maurice Séguin, théoricien de l'École néo-nationaliste', the leadership of New France belonged to the bourgeoisie, 'de sorte que la décapitation s'était exercée sur l'élite nationale elle-même' (p. 18); 'Cette thèse avait été épousée par Michel Brunet dès les années 1950'; in the 1970s 'la thèse de la dégradation de la bourgeoisie avait besoin d'être dédramatisée', and 'Ces retouches au modèle de Maurice Séguin furent faites par Gilles Paquet et Jean-Pierre Wallot, en particulier' (p. 19); at the core of the crisis controversy stood 'la thèse néo-nationaliste enrichie de l'idée de modernité' (p. 25). In 1984 (recorded by the 1.136 Creighton packet, not re-read here) he asked whether the scheme of Séguin, Frégault and Brunet was 'bien différent' from Creighton's post-Conquest 'société semi-féodale décadente' (p. 227). In-period Montreal reader: Tousignant (1980) on 'la profondeur du fossé qui séparait Fernand Ouellet de l'école néo-nationaliste de l'Université de Montréal et de son maître à penser, le professeur Maurice Séguin' (p. 419), and, as Tousignant reports, Ouellet had 'raillé le schéma d'interprétation freudien de l'école néo-nationaliste de Montréal à propos du «choc» de la Conquête' (p. 423); the text Tousignant refers to was not identified or read. Séguin has no entry, so the edge targets the montreal_school strand. The modernists. His own text, 1985 (read for pp. 11–29 and the pages named): the dominant preoccupation of most of those who built the new economic history 'était par trop centrée sur la situation précaire des Canadiens français en Amérique du Nord', a feeling 'pas étranger à la montée du mouvement indépendantiste québécois'; the themes of dependence, of Quebec's lag behind Ontario and of francophone inferiority 'imprègnent d'une façon ou d'une autre une grande partie de cette historiographie', and 'ces préoccupations ont entraîné les historiens à négliger des secteurs entiers de l'histoire économique et, par conséquent, à se fermer nombre de voies d'accès à une explication du social' (p. 18); after Paquet and Wallot's 'retouches au modèle de Maurice Séguin' (p. 19), 'On peut en dire presque autant des études de Jean-Claude Robert, de Paul-André Linteau et même de Normand Séguin sur le caractère dynamique de la bourgeoisie foncière rurale et urbaine' (pp. 19–20). The same 1985 survey also credits the period with the emergence of a more scientific social history; the passages above are its critical ones, and their limits ('une grande partie', 'presque autant') are kept. In-period reader: Rudin's characterisation, not Ouellet's: Rudin (1995, ¶9–10) describes Ouellet's 1985 and 1988 texts as 'une condamnation virulente de l'historiographie québécoise récente' that associates the revisionists with the 'mouvement indépendantiste des années 1970'; Rudin himself (1995b, p. 66) places Ouellet's emphasis on 'mentalités' beside his own. Limits: the 1988 English version and the 1991 essays Rudin also cites are unread; Ouellet's survey is a long review of the field, and the critical passages read are those quoted. One arrow carries both because they share endpoints and type; the strands are montreal_school and modernist_synthesis.
edges.map_label: Ouellet's critiques of the Conquest thesis and parts of post-1960 economic history, 1962–85

edges.relationship: Creighton's characterisation of post-Conquest French Canada as a decadent feudal society, cited approvingly by Ouellet and Hamelin in the 1962 crisis article
edges.evidence_note: Ouellet and Hamelin (1962, p. 32, read): the crisis reveals two cultural entities of unequal evolution, 'C'est pourquoi le professeur Creighton a pu parler, en se référant à la société canadienne-française, de société féodale décadente.' Ouellet's own 1984 survey (recorded by the 1.136 Creighton packet, pp. 226–227; not re-read here) summarises Creighton's post-Conquest French Canada as 'une société semi-féodale décadente devenue hostile aux impératifs économiques'. In-period critics pair them: Paquet and Wallot (1972, p. 186 n. 5) cite 'D. G. Creighton, The Empire of the St. Lawrence (2e éd., Toronto, 1956) et F. Ouellet, Histoire économique et sociale du Québec' as the 'historiographie traditionnelle' that saw restructurings but not modernisation; Tousignant (1980, p. 416) says the 1966 book 'faisait écho aux vieux préjugés de l'historiographie canadienne-anglaise' (no historian named). The influence rests on the 1962 citation alone; the critics' pairing and Ouellet's 1984 comparison are context and do not independently establish transmission. The edge records a borrowed characterisation, not a teacher–pupil lineage; Ouellet's Labroussian method has other sources (edge_874; edge 6).

edges.relationship: Labrousse's price and conjuncture history as a model for Ouellet's economic and social history of Quebec, as Ouellet acknowledged (per Savard) and his critics named it
edges.evidence_note: In-period readers; Ouellet's own acknowledgement is reported, not read. Savard (1974, ¶8, read): 'Ouellet a dit sa dette envers les travaux exemplaires de Labrousse et de Chaunu'. Paquet and Wallot (1972, read) call him 'un tenant de la position Labrousse' (p. 187) and contrast the 'position Labrousse', for which agriculture is the leading sector, with their own 'position Mauro-North' (pp. 187, 235). Tousignant (1980, p. 416) describes his method as quantitative series combined with a Weberian typology of mentalities, without naming Labrousse. The 1966 book's subtitle, 'structures et conjoncture', and Mandrou's preface are recorded on qcreq_ouellet_1966; the book is unread. Ouellet's 1985 survey (p. 47) describes 'L'histoire sociale à la façon de Labrousse' as one Annales tendency but does not there speak of his own debt.

edges.relationship: Workers' control and class at the centre: Toronto skilled workers' power on the job (1976) and their responses to industrial capitalism (1980), with a periodization by stages of capitalism and a case for class analysis and the materiality of culture (1978–81); contested by Bercuson and Brody (1981) and by feminist critics (1987–2000)
edges.evidence_note: His own in-period statements. '“The Honest Workingman” and Workers’ Control', Labour/Le Travailleur 1 (1976), pp. 32–68, read at pp. 32–34 and 58–62: 'Skilled workers in the nineteenth century exercised far more power than we have previously realized. … In Toronto work places, craftsmen employed their monopoly on skill and experience to dictate terms to their employers … which, in modern parlance, gave to these late nineteenth century craftsmen a high degree of workers' control of production' (p. 32); he draws on David Montgomery's 'veterans of industrial life' and on Raymond Williams's 'residual' and 'emergent' (p. 33); 'The custom of workers' control, widely regarded as a right, had become deeply embedded in working class culture' and its defence 'became the major locus of class struggle in the opening decades of the twentieth century' (p. 62). 'The Working Class in Recent Canadian Historical Writing', Acadiensis 7:2 (1978), pp. 116–135, read at pp. 116–117 and 134–135: historians still treat the new study of class 'as little more than interesting additional facts', but 'the new history is well on its way to transforming our understanding of the entire course and structure of Canadian development' (p. 116). 'Labour and Working-Class History in Canada: Prospects in the 1980s', Labour/Le Travailleur 7 (1981), pp. 67–94, read in full: the project 'never excluded the study of unions and labour politics', nor called for history 'simply "written from the bottom up," since it always placed the relationship between classes at the centre of the story' (p. 69); a periodization of 'pre-industrial capitalism to 1850; industrial capitalism, 1850 to the mid-1890s; monopoly capitalism, 1890s to 1929; and crisis and reconstruction, 1930 to the present', offered as 'at best tentative' (p. 74); 'I will certainly stand with scholars such as Thompson and Williams who have argued persuasively for the materiality of culture itself' (p. 85); class 'does have an "objective" side', but '"Class-for-itself," or the failure of the working class to develop such, is almost by definition what working-class history concerns itself with' (pp. 85–86); work on the 1880s found 'a class surprisingly united', in which divisions 'of ethnicity, skill, religion, and even sex were recognized, debated, and for a few years in the 1880s, at least, were overcome', and 'it is now necessary to locate class conflict and class struggle at the centre of modern Canadian history' (p. 89). He places himself among scholars who were 'active in the new left and influenced by the rebirth of Marxist scholarship' (p. 93). Toronto Workers (1980) is unread; Brody quotes its introduction: 'The work will have succeeded to the extent that it provides convincing evidence that the working class was not just "made" but rather was the result of a dialectical interplay of class forces in which it was one of the actors' (p. xviii, as quoted). In-period critics. David Bercuson, in the same issue (pp. 95–96, read), quotes the 1976 Essays definition of the new labour history and notes that 'Kealey's study of Toronto workers contains at least five chapters devoted to working-class and trade-union politics'; his wider objections are recorded under wcreq_bercuson_1981 and edge_919. David Brody, review, Labour/Le Travailleur 8/9 (1981–82), pp. 361–364, read in full: 'Kealey thus lays the foundation, hitherto largely lacking, for a history of the Toronto labour movement' (p. 362), but 'It is in the interpretation of this information that the book founders'; 'Every strike signifies "class conflict," every labour involvement in public life "class politics"' (p. 363); 'Having overreached himself, he has produced only a useable one' (p. 364). Ian McKay, 'Historians, Anthropology, and the Concept of Culture', Labour/Le Travailleur 8/9 (1981–82), cites Kealey's 1981 'defence of the term' (p. 214 n. 88) and argues that working-class culture has 'weak explanatory value' and that Williams's residual and emergent categories 'merely have allowed social historians to indulge in retrospective cheerleading for progressive ideas' (p. 223 and n. 122); Kealey in 1981 called McKay's unpublished paper 'one of the most substantive critiques of Thompson and culturalism' (p. 91 n.). Bettina Bradbury (1987, pp. 35–36, read) and Joan Sangster (2000, p. 133, read): see edge pe138_kealey_rel_05 and the node; Sangster: 'One of the first major collections of the new labour history contained not one article on women' (p. 133, of Kealey and Warrian's Essays, 1976). Desmond Morton (2000, pp. 23–24, read): 'some of the Kealey-Palmer claims for their "new" history were challenged'; 'If, as Kealey insisted, Toronto's working class achieved unity across ethnic and sectarian barriers, it must have been for the briefest of moments in the city contemporaries sometimes called "the Belfast of North America"'. A contribution, not a founding: Freeman (2002) names him in the founding generation of Labour/Le Travail; he presents the work as 'conceived collectively' (1981, p. 68 n. 8). Scope: this edge is Kealey's own contribution; edge_919 carries Palmer's craft culture, edge_886 and edge_890 the Marxist and Thompsonian resources. The Knights of Labor book (1982) is unread and appears in pe138_kealey_rel_05.

edges.relationship: Limited identities and regional explanation criticised from a class standpoint: 'limited identities' as 'neither "limited" nor analytically separable' (1978), region as 'the crucial variable' 'increasingly misplaced' and western exceptionalism overstated (1981), and the 1919 revolt as 'national in character' (1984)
edges.evidence_note: His own words, in period. Acadiensis 7:2 (1978), read at pp. 116–117 and 134–135: Cook and Careless 'called for a turn away from nation and politics' toward 'region, ethnicity and class' (p. 116, citing Cook 1967 and Careless 1969); 'The call for attention to "limited identities" was the death-knell of Laurentianism' (p. 117); 'The long-overdue insertion of a class analysis into Canadian historical writing already promises overviews which transcend the refreshing and liberating pluralism of the 1960s calls for attention to region, ethnicity and class. It should be increasingly clear, however, that these so-called "limited identities" are neither "limited" nor analytically separable. No historical notion of class (and there can be no other useful notion) can fail to incorporate ethnicity and place' (p. 135). Labour/Le Travailleur 7 (1981), read in full: 'NONE CAN DENY the importance of regional differences … Yet the increasing emphasis placed on "region" as the crucial variable which explains sundry problems of Canadian development seems increasingly misplaced', citing Westfall on the regional interpretation standing 'the old nationalist history on its head' (p. 74); before the 1890s 'there was not one Canadian working class but many' (p. 75); accounts of western workers are shaped by 'a strong sense of western exceptionalism', and 'the rather easy assumptions of a unique western working-class militancy have been overstated', with n. 25: 'David Bercuson has been most guilty of this' (p. 76); 'Canadian historians have come to believe everything was different everywhere … This celebration of region has fit very well with the general direction of Canadian political life in the last decade. Surely the time has come to begin to reflect on region in a critical way' (p. 76); his remedy is not 'A return to an old national history? No, of course not, but rather the consideration on a national scale of the particular class experiences of Canadian workers in local and regional contexts which adds up to something more than local and regional exceptionalism' (p. 77). '1919: The Canadian Labour Revolt', Labour/Le Travail 13 (1984), pp. 11–44, read at pp. 11–17: 'These examples are intended simply to demonstrate that the revolt was national in character and that its seeds were not rooted in any unique regional fermentation. The "radical" west and the conservative east have become sorry shibboleths of Canadian historiography'; 'the similarities of struggle begin to outweigh the initial impression of regional particularism' (p. 15). Qualifications kept: he grants 'the importance of regional differences' (1981, p. 74) and calls Maritime underdevelopment real (pp. 75–76); the 1978 sentence welcomes the 1960s pluralism as 'refreshing and liberating' before arguing that class analysis transcends it. In-period reading: Morton (2000, p. 25, read) credits Kealey, Palmer, Heron, Hann and others with bringing labour history 'back from superstructure, politics, and the exceptionalism of Western Canada to regions that had been largely neglected by their predecessors: Ontario and the Maritimes'. No reply by Bercuson to the 1981 or 1984 regional argument was checked. Distinct from Cook's 1977–83 critique of regionalism (edge from ramsay_cook to cdn_regional), which doubts region as a unit; Kealey's subordinates it to class and national-scale capitalism.

edges.relationship: Herbert Gutman's cultural history of American workers and David Montgomery's workers' control as models for Kealey's Toronto studies (1976–81), as Kealey and his reviewers said, with the criticisms of Gutman he reported and Brody's verdict that he did not follow Gutman's method
edges.evidence_note: His own statements. 1976 (Labour/Le Travailleur 1, read at pp. 32–34, 58): 'David Montgomery has suggested that we must look beyond pre-industrial cultural forms if we are to understand the behaviour of skilled workers', who were 'veterans of industrial life' (p. 33); on the meaning of shop-floor power, 'David Montgomery has argued that the major impact of this early workers' control was the skilled workers' growing awareness that the key institution for the transformation of society was the trade union' (p. 58). 1978 (Acadiensis, p. 117): the works of Thompson and Hobsbawm, 'and later of Americans such as Herbert Gutman and David Montgomery, had their effects in Canada on a new generation of graduate students'. 1981 (Labour/Le Travailleur 7, read in full): 'A cultural approach in American work on labour history also generated a significant breakthrough. Most notably associated with Herbert Gutman' (p. 81); n. 33: 'Gutman's influence can be seen in numerous recent studies. In Canada see Palmer, A Culture in Conflict and Kealey, Toronto Workers' (p. 82). He reports Dubofsky's and Montgomery's worry about 'the failure to consider the political and economic context' and Brody's charge that Gutman 'shifted the Thompsonian focus on class and culture into a focus solely on culture' (pp. 81–82). In-period readers. David Brody (Labour/Le Travailleur 8/9, 1981–82, read): 'During his tenure at Rochester a decade or so ago, Herbert G. Gutman built up a remarkable graduate program in American working-class history … Gregory Kealey's book bears the marks of what might be termed the Gutman school' (p. 361); but 'In one crucial way, unfortunately, it does not': Gutman 'invariably has drawn his ideas out from the evidence', and 'Had he adhered to the prudent craft of his mentor, Kealey might have written a powerful book' (p. 364). Morton (2000, pp. 22–23, read): the 'second generation' 'travelled abroad, to Warwick, Rochester, and Binghamton, to meet their American and British mentors', and the Knights of Labor records 'Kealey had been able to study at Rochester'. Later engagement, title level only: 'Herbert G. Gutman, 1928–1985, and the Writing of Working-Class History' (Monthly Review, 1986) and 'Gutman and Montgomery' (ILWCH, 1990; wcreq_kealey_1990). Gutman and Montgomery are historians on the newleft roster (work_cultures strand). Influence, not discipleship: the 1981 essay also gives Thompson and Williams as touchstones, and edge_890 carries Thompson's place in the field. edge_888 (newleft ↔ cdn_working_class) stays as the group-level comparison.

edges.relationship: State surveillance of labour and the left from the First World War: a 1992 documentary article on the RCMP and the Special Branch, arguing that 'For the RCMP the Cold War began in 1919, not in 1946', and the RCMP Security Bulletins he co-edited with Whitaker (1989–97); the work was announced as under way in 1988, and the later syntheses Secret Service (2012, with Whitaker and Parnaby) and Spying on Canadians (2017) are cited at catalogue level only
edges.evidence_note: The checked intervention, 1992. 'The RCMP, the Special Branch, and the Early Days of the Communist Party of Canada: A Documentary Article', Labour/Le Travail 30 (1992), pp. 169–204, introduction read (pp. 169–171; the documents themselves not read): a 1991 visit to the Public Record Office in London, 'when combined with a number of Access to Information requests to the Canadian Security Intelligence Service (CSIS), provides considerable insight into the early co-operation between the fledgling Royal Canadian Mounted Police security and intelligence apparatus of the early 1920s and its more experienced partners in England' (p. 169); the weekly RCMP security bulletin was 'circulated to Cabinet', and the bulletins were 'routinely sent to the Special Branch at the Colonial Office' (p. 170); 'Such documentation also makes clear how early Canadian intelligence efforts focused on labour radicalism and socialism. For the RCMP the Cold War began in 1919, not in 1946' (p. 171). His n. 4 (p. 170) describes 'the multi-volume Gregory S. Kealey and Reg Whitaker, eds., The RCMP Security Bulletins (St. John's 1989 and forthcoming)', drawn 'primarily' from Access requests to CSIS; the edition itself is known only through that note and review records. Earlier notice, not a checked argument: the 1988 author note in Class, Gender, and Region (p. iv, read) says only that he 'is currently working on Canadian state repression of labour and the left'; the 1919 essay (1984, p. 43, read) draws on an RCMP draft memorandum of September 1919. Later works, catalogue level only and not assessed here: 'State Repression of Labour and the Left in Canada, 1914–20' (CHR 73:3, 1992, pp. 281–314) and 'The Surveillance State' (Intelligence and National Security 7:3, 1992, pp. 179–210), both reprinted as chapters of Spying on Canadians (2017; UTP chapter records); Secret Service: Political Policing in Canada from the Fenians to Fortress America (2012), by Reg Whitaker, Gregory S. Kealey and Andrew Parnaby (publisher's description: 'the many tensions that arise when undercover police and their covert methods are deployed too freely in a liberal democratic society'). The edge therefore claims the 1992 argument and the edition, not the content of the later syntheses. Relation to the strand: security_state currently holds Whitaker and Marcuse's Cold War Canada (1945–57). Kealey's argument dates the security state's anti-communist focus to 1919; this is an extension in time by Whitaker's co-editor, not a critique of their book. No in-period reviews of the Bulletins were read (Dansereau, RHAF 1995, located only).
edges.map_label: Political policing: the Cold War from 1919, 1992

edges.relationship: Co-authors of Dreaming of What Might Be (1982) and allies in the new labour history, read together by critics as 'the Kealey-Palmer claims', though 'differently positioned politically' (Sangster) and with different emphases: workers' control and class analysis for Kealey, craft culture for Palmer
edges.evidence_note: Collaboration, in their own texts. Kealey's 1976 essay thanks Palmer, with David Frank and Craig Heron, for comments (p. 32 n.); the 1981 essay thanks him among others (p. 94), refers readers to Palmer's forthcoming Making of E.P. Thompson (p. 82), and says that 'Kealey and Palmer, "Dreaming of What Might Be"' 'argues this position at length' on the value of the romantic and utopian traditions, which gave workers 'the ability to dream of an alternative future' (p. 84 and n. 39). Read together by critics, in period. Bercuson (1981, p. 96): 'the Palmer and Kealey books' as 'restricted but intensive studies'. Bradbury (Labour/Le Travail 19, 1987, pp. 35–36, read) quotes Dreaming (p. 318) and writes that to dismiss partially a Knights of Labor editor's picture of a wife who 'can darn a stocking' 'as "offensive" and as "crude moralizing," as Kealey and Palmer do, seems to me both to deny the realities of the division of labour within the working-class family economy at that time, and to close off the possibility of examining this very important element of a skilled worker's pride'; she adds that 'Kealey and Palmer quite rightly point out' that a Montreal workman's statement stopped short of a critique of 'women's proper sphere'. Sangster (Labour/Le Travail 46, 2000, p. 133, read): 'Two seminal studies followed by Gregory Kealey and Bryan Palmer. Though differently positioned politically, they examined workers' responses to 19th century industrialization, with a proclivity to centre on skilled male workers and their actions in the public sphere.' Morton (2000, pp. 23–24, read): 'some of the Kealey-Palmer claims for their "new" history were challenged'; Stanley Ryerson (1981, as Morton reports it) argued that the Knights were 'devoutly committed to labour-employer harmony and industrial peace'. Later reading, labelled: McCoy (2021) quotes their chapter: 'A subordinate class must reach toward an alternative hegemony if it ever hopes to dominate the ethos of society' (Dreaming, p. 277, as quoted). The book itself is unread. A comparison, not an influence: the edge records co-authorship and joint reception. Their different emphases are recorded in edge_919 (Palmer's craft culture) and pe138_kealey_rel_01 (Kealey's workers' control and class analysis).

edges.relationship: Careless's second thoughts about the 'flood' of regional, cultural and class writing (1979 lecture) read as a reaction reasserting 'a "positive" unifying national history' (1988); a decade earlier the working-class bibliography Kealey co-compiled had invoked Careless's limited identities (1973)
edges.evidence_note: Kealey's words, in period. Introduction to Class, Gender, and Region: Essays in Canadian Historical Sociology (St. John's: CCLH, 1988; reprint of a Canadian Journal of Sociology special issue), pp. 1–7, read in the AU Press PDF: 'The degree to which reaction has re-emerged to reassert the need for a "positive" unifying national history can be seen by contrasting the views of J.M.S. Careless in 1969 and in 1980. In 1969, Careless enthusiastically embraced Ramsay Cook's earlier call for the study of region, class, and ethnicity … By 1980, however, he had serious doubts' (p. 2); he quotes Careless's farmer 'in the midst of the flood' and answers: 'As I hope this volume suggests, such plaintiff [sic] Toronto cries to date have not been able to dam the flood of critical scholarship on class, gender, and region' (p. 3). 'The impatience mentioned by Berger and articulated by Careless addresses itself as much to this regional revolt as it does to writings concerned with class and gender' (p. 5). Careless's text, re-read (Manitoba History no. 1, web text, unpaginated; the 1979 Jackson lecture, cited by Kealey as 1980): 'there has been a massive outpouring … on class disparities and stresses and such things as national concerns are by and large passed over or discounted. In this situation, I feel a little like the farmer in the midst of a flood'. Qualifications kept: Careless continues, 'there are reasons why I do not really feel as bad as the foregoing might suggest', calls working-class history 'one of the most active and productive areas' of the study of limited identities, and asks that class identities 'be treated in their national scope', a point close to Kealey's own (1981, p. 77). Kealey's 'reaction' is his reading of the lecture. Earlier connection: Careless (1979) quotes the introduction to Primary Sources in Canadian Working-Class History (1973, p. 11), compiled by Hann, Gregory and Linda Kealey and Warrian: 'For some time J. M. S. Careless has called for … a historical appreciation of the varieties of "limited identities" that constitute Canada'. Kealey (1981, p. 68) says that statement was 'drafted by Russell Hann'. No reply by Careless was checked. Related: edge_954 (Careless → who_killed_debate) records the fragmentation worry this passage voices; pe138_kealey_rel_02 records Kealey's separate critique of limited identities from a class standpoint (1978).

edges.relationship: Ethnic history criticised for treating ethnicity apart from class and for 'official ethnic interpreters' whose celebratory histories leave out working-class militancy, while ethnicity is kept as a subject of cultural analysis (1981)
edges.evidence_note: His own words, in period: 'Labour and Working-Class History in Canada: Prospects in the 1980s', Labour/Le Travailleur 7 (1981), section III, 'Ethnicity', pp. 77–80, read in full. 'The literature on ethnicity and immigration, even in "multicultural" Canada, too often ignores ethnicity as an ongoing factor in historical analysis. … Instead one might question the official ethnic interpreters of their history where middle class bias and, all too often, cold war assumptions have come to dominate the quasi-official version of the past. This past, which celebrates the achievements of each ethnic community, has little room in its pages for the embarrassments of working-class militancy and radical politics' (p. 78); 'Ethnicity considered independent of class often obscures important issues', with the Italian padrone 'King' Cordasco as an instance of 'important class divisions within the ethnic communities themselves'; 'Here again class will prove more crucial than some ethnic historians have previously suggested' (p. 79). He also notes that labour historians who studied militancy (Bercuson, McCormack, Abella) 'have moved towards ethnicity as a crucial variable for further study' (p. 88). Qualifications kept: 'Concern for the ethnic divisions within the working class then is important and valid' (p. 73); 'This qualification is not meant to diminish the significance of ethnicity and of the potentially divisive nature of ethnic heterogeneity to the Canadian working class' (p. 78); ethnicity 'is one of the major areas which demands a cultural analysis' (p. 77), and 'cultural analysis will be central to this project' (p. 80). He cites Avery's 'Dangerous Foreigners' (1979) and Harney on padronism in his notes (p. 79). Scope: a critique of ethnic history that sets ethnicity apart from class and of community-sponsored celebratory history, not of the immigrant-workers literature (Avery) the entry's workers_radicalism strand holds. Perin's 'Clio as an Ethnic' (1983) in the ethnic_history_debate strand is a separate, later critique; no exchange between them was checked.

edges.relationship: Women and marriage à la façon du pays at the centre of fur-trade society, and missionary racism against Native wives in Red River (1980–86)
edges.evidence_note: In-period. 'Many Tender Ties' (1980) is unread here and is quoted only as Bowsfield quotes it (Archivaria 12, 1981, review article, read in full; he gives no page references to the book). He reports her purpose as showing that the fur trade 'constituted a social and cultural complex as well as an economic activity'. He quotes her claims that 'If a man formed a liaison with a woman she was considered to be his wife, entitled to the recognition and support that a marital relationship implied' and that Indian women's work 'constituted an important contribution to the functioning of the trade'. He paraphrases her account of a marriage rite à la façon du pays and of the later turn from Indian to mixed-descent and then white wives, as younger officers became 'imbued with the Victorian middle-class desire for respectability and success' (p. 124). Gagan and Turner (Archivaria 14, 1982, read in full) summarise her argument that these marriages, 'generations of scandalized references notwithstanding, were crucial to the establishment of early western society' (p. 43). Her own words, 1986 (Manitoba History 11, web edition, read in full; no page numbers): 'Fur trade society in Rupert's Land had resulted from decades of inter-marriage among incoming white fur traders with Indian and later mixed-blood women'; 'Racist attitudes, particularly with regard to women, can be seen in the attempts of the missionaries to enforce their concepts of morality upon a society that had developed its own indigenous customs.' Brown (Canadian Journal of Native Studies 3:1, 1983, read in full) takes 'the work of Sylvia Van Kirk (1980) on the socioeconomic role of women in the fur trade' as one starting point for Métis history (p. 40). Criticism: Bowsfield notes her view that such unions were not 'casual' or 'promiscuous' and comments, 'This may be too complimentary a picture of both native women and European men' (p. 124). LaRocque's criticism (1999) is recorded on pe139_vankirk_rel_04, and edge_868 carries the Indigenous critiques at entry level. Not a founding: Bowsfield reviews the book within a fur-trade literature already recast by Ray, Trigger and others (pp. 121–24). Later reading, labelled: Perry (Left History 13:2, 2008, read in full) writes that 'In the early 1990s Van Kirk's work particularly garnered some sharp post-colonial, anti-racist, and post-structuralist critiques, ones that made clear how wedded "Many Tender Ties" was to a Eurocentric, celebratory sort of liberal feminism', and then that Van Kirk's and Brown's 'symbiotic arguments about the centrality of women and family to the Canadian fur-trade' have 'never been cast into serious doubt' (p. 163). The critiques she cites (n. 7: Pierson 1992; Emberley 1990–91) are unread here.

edges.relationship: Indigenous and mixed-descent women written into Canadian women's history, with race as a division among women (1980–98)
edges.evidence_note: In-period.
