Holberg committee (2010): it ‘demonstrated to a broader public how an individual event in early modern France could illuminate overall mentalities’. The book is unread; the French edition (1982) appeared with the film.

edges.relationship: Finlay charges an ‘excess of invention’ against ‘the sovereignty of the sources’ in her Bertrande de Rols; Davis answers that where reconstruction stops and invention begins was ‘precisely the question’ the book posed (1988)
edges.evidence_note: This arrow represents Robert Finlay’s intervention in the debate over evidence in microhistory (micro/reconstruction_invention), not a verdict of the field. Finlay, AHR 93:3 (1988), 553–571, read in full: ‘Davis fails to show that her view of women in peasant society is relevant to the case she is examining’ (p. 557); ‘self-fashioning’ ‘is merely imposed on the historical record as an ingenious assertion’ (p. 564); ‘If historical records can be bypassed so thoroughly in the service of an inventive blend of intuition and assertion, it is difficult to see what distinguishes the writing of history from that of fiction’ (p. 569); ‘speculation, whether founded on intuition or on concepts drawn from anthropology and literary criticism, is supposed to give way before the sovereignty of the sources … Davis has permitted an excess of invention’ (p. 571). He praises ‘its eloquent portrait of peasant life … its emphasis on the central role of women’ (p. 569). Davis, ‘On the Lame’, AHR 93:3 (1988), 572–603, read in part: the question ‘is precisely the question I hoped readers would ask and reflect on’; she would have preferred a critique ‘more subject to “the sovereignty of sources” to which it claims loyalty’ (p. 572); ‘he plays Savonarola to my Montaigne. Fortunately, historical practice can profit from each stance’ (p. 574); ‘proto-feminist’ is ‘a careless reporting of my text’ (p. 584). The group endpoint locates Finlay’s critique within the debate over microhistorical reconstruction; it does not assign him membership in a school. Ginzburg’s 1984 postface to the Italian edition, cited by Finlay (p. 569 n. 71), is unread.

edges.relationship: A narrative of four charivaris cited by Stone among works turning to narrative, after she criticised his draft (1979); later, pardon tales read as crafted stories without discrediting the archives (1987)
edges.evidence_note: Stone, Past & Present 85 (1979), read: p. 3, starred note, thanks ‘Natalie Davis’ among colleagues ‘for valuable criticism of an early draft of this paper’; p. 18: ‘Natalie Davis has presented a narrative of four charivaris or ritual public shame procedures in seventeenth-century Lyon and Geneva, in order to illustrate community efforts to enforce public standards of honour and propriety’ (n. 29, the essay forthcoming in Le Goff and Schmitt, Le charivari). Her own account (1997, p. 21, read): she called her 1987 book Fiction in the Archives ‘somewhat to the consternation of Lawrence Stone to whom it was dedicated’; ‘“fiction” referred not to falsification, but to the crafting element in everything we do and say. Rather than being on an extreme anti-foundationalist mission to discredit the archives, I was presenting them as a source of new evidence’. As the revival scope requires, being named by Stone does not imply that she accepted his diagnosis. Fiction in the Archives is unread.
edges.map_label: Charivari narrative; Fiction in the Archives, 1979–87

edges.relationship: Bloch’s Strange Defeat and Feudal Society as formative reading in her turn from the history of ideas to social history; Bloch and Power as the twentieth-century historians of her AHA address (1940s–1987)
edges.evidence_note: Her own retrospect (1997, read in full): ‘Before I graduated, I also read Marc Bloch’s Strange Defeat and learned that an historian can be a hero’ (p. 5); ‘I had been reading Marc Bloch’s Feudal Society, and was all ready when W. K. Jordan urged me take Ket’s Rebellion’ as her graduate work shifted ‘from the history of ideas to social history’ (p. 7); arriving in Lyon in 1952, ‘I rushed around Lyon … to find a monument to Marc Bloch’ (p. 8). Her AHA presidential address (1987; read in part through tool excerpts) considers ‘history’s two bodies’ through five historians, Bloch and Eileen Power among them, and per the tool’s summary ends on Bloch’s 1942 letter. An acknowledged formative reading recorded in retrospect; it does not make her an Annales historian: she wrote that its histoire totale ‘could not serve as a model for what I wanted to do’ (p. 13).

edges.relationship: Decentred comparison: European women’s lives set beside colonial domination and non-European respondents (1995), a Muslim traveller between worlds (2006), and a programme of ‘decentering history’ (2010)
edges.evidence_note: Her own retrospect (1997, read): Women on the Margins was to ‘expand the single microhistory into a decentered comparison of three European lives’ (p. 21); she asked about ‘the uninvited French intrusion into the American woodlands’ and Merian’s ‘African and Indian slaves’ (p. 22), introduced ‘non-European women … not just as silent objects … but as active respondents’ (p. 22), and felt ‘permanently relocated as an historian of Europe’, with a new project on ‘cultural mixture’ along ‘the caravan routes of North Africa’ (p. 23). The conclusion of Women on the Margins (davis_margins_primary, earlier reading) shows marginality coexisting with colonial domination. Holberg committee (2010, read): ‘connecting early modern Europe with new areas of comparative history, exploring cultural, geographical and religious interchange’; Women on the Margins and Trickster Travels explore ‘the translation and transmission of cultures’. ‘Decentering History’ (Holberg Symposium, 2010; abstract only) moves ‘beyond a focus on Europe or the West’. Hesse (2024): ‘there were no dark parts of the globe’. Trickster Travels (2006) and the 2011 article are unread. Subrahmanyam’s mediated link from Kafadar to Davis (1997) stays on edge_641.

edges.relationship: Geertz’s “agricultural involution” (Java, 1963), with Chayanov’s account of family-labour intensification, taken as the model for involution in North China (1985) and the Yangzi delta, as Huang acknowledged (1985, 1991)
edges.evidence_note: His own words, in period. The Peasant Economy and Social Change in North China (1985, pp. 7–11 read): "Chayanov pointed out the existence of this phenomenon in the agriculture of prerevolutionary Russia … Clifford Geertz has given the same phenomenon, in rice farming in Java, the catchy term 'agricultural involution' (1963)" (p. 8); "The peasant economy, in other words, involuted along the lines suggested by Geertz's analytical model" (p. 11). "The Paradigmatic Crisis in Chinese Studies" (1991, p. 317): "my notion of involution has drawn much from the theories of A. V. Chayanov and Clifford Geertz, both based on micro-social studies of non-Western societies." Readers in 1986 confirm it: Mann, "a model of agricultural involution derived partly from Geertz and partly from Chayanov" (JAS, p. 572); Duara, "Huang uses Clifford Geertz's notion of involution" (HJAS, p. 285). Qualifications: Chayanov (no entry) is an equal resource and Boserup a third (1991, n. 9); Huang redefines the term as diminishing marginal returns to labour on family farms (1985, p. 8 n.) and does not adopt Geertz's ecological argument about Java. This is Geertz's Agricultural Involution, not the interpretive anthropology of thick description recorded on the geertz entry.
edges.map_label: Agricultural involution, Java to North China, 1985

edges.relationship: Involution and involutionary commercialization: output growth at diminishing returns per workday on family farms, “growth without development” (1985, 1990, 1991)
edges.evidence_note: His own statements, read. 1985 (pp. 8–9): involution occurs when "the marginal output of labor diminishes", and is rational as "both enterprise behavior and consumer choice"; peasant behaviour needs "the integrated use of the formalist, Marxist, and substantivist traditions". 1991 (pp. 314–315): "Shrinking farm sizes drove peasants to accept involution, or intensification of labor input per unit area at the cost of diminishing marginal returns per workday"; "Involution, in other words, explains the paradox of growth without development"; involutionary commercialization "needs to be distinguished from the transformative commercialization that ends in modern development". 2002 (p. 503) restates the 1990 book's distinction between development, involution and intensification ("(1990, 11)"). The 1990 book is unread: Day's review quotes it ("simply wrong", p. 5; "the rationality of survival, not of profit maximization", p. 105). Readers: Mann (1986, p. 574), "a new way of thinking about Chinese society". A contested contribution: Pomeranz rejects it (2000, p. 17; 2003), and the dispute is drawn separately.

edges.relationship: England and the Yangzi delta “at opposite poles” of development and involution by 1800: Pomeranz’s comparison criticised for resting on secondary evidence, omitting the English agricultural revolution and reversing coal supply and demand (2002; rejoinder 2003)
edges.evidence_note: Huang's review essay, JAS 61:2 (May 2002), 501–538 (Whole article OCRed; selected passages read closely, remaining text searched; map images not inspected): the book "is not built on original research, but rather relies on past secondary scholarship" (p. 502); "Pomeranz says nothing at all" about the English agricultural revolution (p. 502); on coal, "it is the lack of industrial demand that explains the non-development of China’s coal industry. Pomeranz’s argument, in short, places the cart before the horse" (p. 533); England and the delta "were in fact virtually at opposite poles in a continuum from development to involution", and the eighteenth-century delta held "the roots of a massive nineteenth-century social crisis" (p. 534). Rejoinder, JAS 62:1 (Feb. 2003), 157–167 (read in part): he concedes "a misplaced decimal" in his 1990 book (p. 157), says his case rests on "conditions of production", and reports that Pomeranz now grants declining average returns as cotton replaced grain (p. 158, quoting Pomeranz 2002, p. 547). Qualifications: Huang credits "a useful contribution" and the wish "to de-center Europe" (2002, p. 533). Pomeranz's answers are drawn on the reverse arrow. Restated in 2016 (Modern China 42:2, read in part by the second research pass): "Pomeranz's work makes this kind of basic factual error because it lacks any original research" (p. 136).

edges.relationship: Involution rejected: Chinese household labour read as an industrious-revolution pattern comparable to Europe’s (2000); in reply, involution called internally inconsistent and his evidence faulted for confusing marginal with average returns and for a misplaced decimal (2002–2003)
edges.evidence_note: Pomeranz's own words. The Great Divergence (2000, p. 17, re-read): Chinese families supposedly kept women and children working below a subsistence wage, "thus producing an 'involuted economy'; I will show that there is little reason to believe this" (n. 27: "P. Huang 1990: 11–17"); labour deployment instead resembles "Europe’s 'industrious revolution'". Reply, JAS 61:2 (2002), 539–590 (publisher extract only): "He also ignores plentiful new research on both Asia and Europe". Response, JAS 62:1 (Feb. 2003), 167–181 (read in part): Huang's "concept of 'involution' was internally inconsistent"; he "had repeatedly confused marginal and average returns", compared male, female and child labour indiscriminately, and made "a basic arithmetic mistake (a misplaced decimal)" (pp. 167–168); "a gathering consensus, pace Huang, about the timing of that divergence … invalidates various old explanations of it, including his" (p. 179). Qualification: per Huang (2003, p. 158), Pomeranz's 2002 reply grants that "A decline in average returns to labor as more people move from grain to cotton farming is still evident" (p. 547); the body of the reply is unread here.

edges.relationship: Unilinear modernization and “England-derived assumptions” questioned: commercialization need not end in capitalist development, and Chinese “paradoxes” expose assumptions shared by Western and Chinese models (1991, 2003)
edges.evidence_note: His own words, read. 1991 (p. 299): a "crisis of confidence in underlying, yet unspoken, assumptions that are shared by opposing constructs"; Chinese "feudalism" and "incipient capitalism" models and Western formalist ones share them (pp. 300–302); "We customarily assume that rural commercialization is powered by the profit-maximizing activities of enterprising farmers. That was the experience of Smith’s and Marx’s England" (p. 314); his aim was to show "how its dynamic and logic were different, producing results that appear paradoxical from our England-derived assumptions" (pp. 315–316). Rejoinder (2003, p. 164): "it was precisely the objection to unilineal modernizationism that originally drove my work and that of other social historians"; p. 165: "no single path or single causal factor to modern economic development". The critique is aimed at Smithian and Marxist assumptions alike; this arrow records its target in modernization theory, not a rejection of all comparison.

edges.relationship: Village-level social history of the North China peasantry from Japanese rural surveys, archives and interviews, an alternative to the gentry-society paradigm (1985)
edges.evidence_note: Readers' explicit claims, read. Mann (JAS, 1986): "This rich and ambitious work marks a new begining [sic] for social history in the China field" (p. 572); he combined Mantetsu survey data with Qing archives and interviews in "two of the same villages studied in the 1930s" (p. 572); his model is "an alternative to the gentry society paradigm that has dominated the field for decades" (p. 574). Duara (HJAS, 1986, p. 283): "a very adroit methodology which combines the use of intensive case studies with extensive quantitative data". Huang and Bernhardt (2024, p. 3) place Modern China's early symposia in "the rising wave of the 'new social history'". Qualifications: Duara doubts the evidence for excess labour (p. 286) and the solidary/atomized village typology (pp. 287–288).
edges.map_label: Village social history of North China, 1985

edges.relationship: Bourdieu’s “practice” and “logic of practice” taken into Chinese legal and rural history, recast as practice over historical time (1995–2005)
edges.evidence_note: His acknowledgement, read by the second research pass. 2005 (Modern China 31:2, n. 3): "Readers familiar with the writings of Pierre Bourdieu will recognize the source of the terms 'practice' and 'logic of practice' as they are used here"; Bourdieu "did not consider practice as process over time. My own preference, no doubt partly due to my bias as a historian, is for the study of practice as historical process." 1995 (Modern China 21:1, pp. 109–110): Bourdieu extended "Marxist structural analysis from the objective into the representational (or 'symbolic') realm" but "has not 'problematized' possible disjunctions between representational and objective realities". Civil Justice in China: Representation and Practice in the Qing (1996) carries the terms in its title; the book is unread. A modified borrowing, not adoption of Bourdieu’s whole theory.

edges.relationship: Against the “incipient capitalism” model: commercialization and wage labour in Ming–Qing China without capitalist development (1985–1998)
edges.evidence_note: His own texts. 1985 (p. 11, read by both passes): the Chinese "incipient capitalism" model, "First set forth by Mao (1939)", held that capitalism had "sprouted" before imperialism. 1991 (read in part by both passes): Chinese scholars "maintained that if Western imperialism had not intruded into China, the capitalist sprouts of the Ming and Qing would have led to transformative capitalist development" (p. 313, as the second pass reads it); "given China’s non-capitalist nineteenth century, what sense does it make to speak of the earlier period as incipient capitalist?" (p. 302). 1998 (p. 188, read by the second pass): "contrary to the predictions of Marxist theory, I simply could not find in 'managerial farming' substantial advances in productivity, despite its use of the 'capitalist production relations' of wage labor". A critique of a specific Marxist model, not of Marxian analysis as such: he credits Marxist and substantivist resources (Tilly, Paige; 1998, p. 186).

edges.relationship: Against “culturalism” in China studies: representations do not dissolve facts, and Orientalism’s later parts are “much less convincing” (1998)
edges.evidence_note: His own text, read by the second research pass ("Four Traps and a Question", Modern China 24:2, 1998, pp. 193–195): "While culturalist theories are surely correct to emphasize that facts come with constructed representations, I believe they are wrong to jump from there to the conclusion that facts are no more than representations … But that is the conclusion that is drawn by Said, on the theoretical inspiration of Michel Foucault" (he then quotes Orientalism, pp. 272–273); "Said's (1978) book, to be sure, makes effective and telling points, especially in the first part … But the discussions in the second and third parts are much less convincing. The connections drawn become more and more tenuous" (p. 195). A China historian's critique of Said, distinct from Said's own critique of Foucault (edge_971).

edges.relationship: Broadberry and Gupta place the advanced parts of Asia with Europe's stagnating periphery on wages and prices (2006); Vries finds differences, not 'surprising resemblances' (2009); Allen and colleagues dispute Chinese–English urban real-wage parity (2011); Broadberry, Guan and Li place divergence between leading regions around 1700 (2021)
edges.evidence_note: This arrow represents named interventions within the debate entry, not a verdict of it; the entry includes Pomeranz and his allies, and each intervention establishes something different. Broadberry and Gupta (EHR 59:1, 2006; summary and pp. 2–3 read), on wages and prices: "Contrary to the claims of Pomeranz, Parthasarathi, and other 'world historians', the prosperous parts of Asia between 1500 and 1800 look similar to the stagnating southern, central, and eastern parts of Europe … The 'great divergence' … was already well underway before 1800" (p. 2). Vries ('A World of Surprising Resemblances?', 2009, pp. 35–38, 47–48 read), on agriculture and the state: 'I would not call that a "surprising resemblance"' (p. 38); 'Coal and colonies definitely were fundamental in the Rise of the West. But reference to them cannot suffice to explain it' (p. 48). Allen, Bassino, Ma, Moll-Murata and van Zanden (EHR 2011, read pp. 8–9, 29–31), on urban real wages: 'our findings also dispute the revisionists’ claim that the advanced parts of China, such as the Yangzi Delta, were on a par with England'; 'Adam Smith’s pessimism looks closer to the truth than the revisionists’ optimism' (p. 31); they also find Chinese urban wages on a par with central and southern Europe, against the 'rise of the west' literature (pp. 30–31). Broadberry, Guan and Li (JEH 2021, read pp. 958–959), on regional GDP per capita: 'The Great Divergence thus began around 1700, earlier than originally suggested by the California School, but later than implied by earlier writers' (p. 958); the qualified chronology is theirs alone. None endorses Huang's involution, whose dispute with Pomeranz is drawn on its own arrows. Revision 1.145 moved this arrow from economic to the debate entry capitalismdebates, and moved Brenner and Isett's 2002 critique to its own arrow (robert_brenner → kenneth_pomeranz), as this note had foreseen. Revision 1.146 likewise moved Mokyr's 2002 critique to its own arrow (joel_mokyr → kenneth_pomeranz), since Mokyr became a person entry; the four interventions above remain.
edges.map_label: Wages, the state and regional GDP, 2006–2021

edges.relationship: Historical scales and teaching after the nation: world history as comparison that tests “the universality or regional specificity of particular processes”, against curricula still organised by nation (AHA presidential address, 2014)
edges.evidence_note: His AHA presidential address, delivered 3 January 2014 and published in AHR 119:1 (2014), 1–22, read via WebFetch extraction of the AHA text (no pagination; the last fifth not covered). World history "makes comparisons that interrogate claims about the universality or regional specificity of particular processes"; he asks "how our discipline is responding and might respond to the changing geography of our own era"; in a survey of "218 AHA member departments", "46 percent of all classes" at the introductory level "were on national histories"; he warns that "most global history narratives thus far have been strongly materialistic, and focused on general processes"; and closes on "reframing for a less national age". A later programme statement, distinct from the 2000 method on edge_898.

edges.relationship: Consumer demand compared across Eurasian cores: sugar, cloth and “consumerist” attitudes in China, Japan and western Europe, with differences “small and of uncertain direction” (2000)
edges.evidence_note: His own summary of chapters 3–4 in the introduction (2000, pp. 17–18; read by both research passes): Part 2 "begins by moving away from survival-oriented activities to examine new kinds of consumer demand"; differences "in both quantities of goods available and 'consumerist' attitudes among these societies seem small and of uncertain direction. (For instance, mid-eighteenth-century Chinese almost certainly consumed more sugar than Europeans, and people in the Lower Yangzi core may have produced as much cloth per capita in 1750 as Britons did in 1800.)" The chapters themselves are unread. Contested by Huang (2002, p. 521, as the second pass reads it) and answered by Pomeranz (2003, p. 168: "probably the bottom 75 percent of the Jiangnan population lived at least as well as their English counterparts").

edges.relationship: Wallerstein’s world-system grouped with the “Europe-centered stories” whose motor is western Europe’s prior advantages; Pomeranz borrows from them but argues for a late, contingent divergence (2000)
edges.evidence_note: His own introduction (2000, pp. 14–16; read by both research passes). Braudel, Wallerstein and Chaudhuri appear with North in "a second group of arguments" that "emphasize the emergence of institutions in early modern Europe" (p. 14); "the motor of Wallerstein’s story is western Europe’s unique combination of relatively free labor, large and productive urban populations, and merchants and governments" (p. 15, as the second pass quotes it); "This work borrows from these arguments—mostly those of the various 'institutionalists'—but ultimately argues for different propositions" (p. 16). A bounded critique of a Eurocentric premise, not a rejection of unequal exchange: he cites Williams, Frank and Amin as earlier arguments from colonial extraction (p. 3 n. 2). The chapter discussions are unread.

edges.relationship: Revolutionary political culture: rhetoric, symbols and the social identity of a new political class (1984); the Revolution’s contradictory futures of terror, democracy and human rights (AHA address, 2003)
edges.evidence_note: Existing reading of Politics, Culture, and Class in the French Revolution (hunt_political_culture: primary chapter openings at pp. 87, 123, 149 and 213; the contents keep both a "poetics of power" and a sociology of politics with quantitative appendices). Her AHA presidential address (AHR 108:1, 2003; read via WebFetch extraction, no pagination) asks "how could the French Revolution produce such contradictory consequences?", holds that it "also gave birth to human rights and democracy", and defines cultural revolution as "the politicization of everyday life" (n. 42, as the second research pass locates it). Her contribution to political history; edge_355 records the same 1984 book's contribution to cultural history.

edges.relationship: Practical realism with Joyce Appleby and Margaret Jacob (1994) and a reassessment of the cultural turn with Victoria Bonnell (1999)
edges.evidence_note: Existing readings. Telling the Truth about History (appleby_hunt_jacob): all three authors share every chapter; the chapter 7 "Practical Realism" section and notes name Putnam and Peirce as resources; chapter 8: "It is time to come out of the trenches." Beyond the Cultural Turn (bonnell_hunt_primary): the editors' introduction (pp. 1, 12–25 read) presents competing reassessments and explicitly acknowledges White's disagreement in his afterword. A particular response within the debate, not its resolution; co-author credits retained.
edges.map_label: Practical realism and beyond the cultural turn, 1994–99

edges.relationship: Globalization as the paradigm succeeding Marxism, modernization, Annales and identity politics, questioned for privileging economics and for threatening the gains of cultural history, as her reviewer summarises Writing History in the Global Era (2014)
edges.evidence_note: Reviewer evidence only; the book is unread here. Julia McClure (Reviews in History 1732, 2015; read via WebFetch extraction, and in full by the second research pass) summarises the argument: globalization has become a dominant "paradigm" replacing Marxism, modernization, the Annales school and identity politics; it privileges economics and macro trends and risks overshadowing "society" and "self"; and it "potentially threatens to wash away the gains of the last decades of cultural history" (Hunt, p. 59, as McClure quotes her). McClure criticises Hunt for not naming proponents of the paradigm and for treating world or global history as the history of globalization. This atlas was first developed around the book; its own words should replace this reviewer summary when read. Further pages as McClure quotes them: globalization "asserts the inescapability of the process, the primacy of economics in driving it" (p. 55); "historians need to contest the terrain it now claims, using the tools held out by cultural theories" (p. 43). McClure: her criticism "is not a criticism of historical genre, but of ideology".
edges.map_label: Writing History in the Global Era, 2014 (per McClure)

edges.relationship: Human rights made “self-evident” through imagined empathy, epistolary novels and the rejection of torture, 1760s–1790s, as reviewers summarise Inventing Human Rights (2007)
edges.evidence_note: Reviewer evidence only; the book is unread here. David A. Bell (LRB, 15 November 2007; read via WebFetch extraction) summarises it: epistolary novels such as Pamela, Clarissa and Julie taught readers to identify with others; torture was condemned by the 1780s; a "logic of rights" followed the 1789 Declaration; he calls the method "the new cultural history", which Hunt had popularised, and finds the 2007 book keeping the thesis of The Family Romance of the French Revolution (1992). Samuel Moyn (The Nation, 16 April 2007) reports her dating of the cause to "the Enlightenment and the age of democratic revolutions" and "the cascading logic of human rights". Their criticisms are drawn on the critique arrow from intellectual history. A second contribution to cultural history, distinct from the 1989 introduction (edge_756).

edges.relationship: Inventing Human Rights criticised for reading late-twentieth-century human rights back into the eighteenth century and for making “rights themselves” its protagonists (Moyn, 2007), and for a cultural-history method that flattens texts and actions (Bell, 2007)
edges.evidence_note: This arrow represents Samuel Moyn's and David A. Bell's specified criticisms, not a verdict of intellectual history. Moyn (The Nation, 16 April 2007; complete text read via WebFetch extraction): the new human-rights history "distorts the past to suit the present"; "rights talk" had "historical lineages completely different from humanitarianism"; "The protagonists of her book are not people thinking and acting on their convictions but rights themselves"; there is "little reason to locate the 'invention' of human rights as we now know them in the late eighteenth century", since they are "an invention of recent date". Bell (LRB 29:22, 15 November 2007; complete text read via WebFetch extraction): the account after 1789 through the present is compressed into 38 pages, concentrating on 1948, novels crowd out theatre and painting, ordinary people who read no novels also embraced rights, and the new cultural history tends to flatten the difference between texts and actions; he still calls the book "a rich, elegant and persuasive essay". Moyn's later book-length argument (The Last Utopia, 2010) is unread here.
edges.map_label: Moyn and Bell on Inventing Human Rights, 2007

edges.relationship: Moral economies of science: certain forms of empiricism, quantification and objectivity “require” a web of affect-saturated values (1995)
edges.evidence_note: Her own words, read (Osiris 10, 1995, pp. 3–4). "certain forms of empiricism, quantification, and objectivity itself are not simply compatible with moral economies; they require moral economies" (p. 3); a moral economy is "a web of affect-saturated values that stand and function in well-defined relationship to one another" (p. 4). n. 2 gathers studies by Hannaway, Porter, Schaffer and Shapin under the rubric. A distinct contribution from the 1992 image article (edge_761); the later book Objectivity (2007, with Galison) is dated in the chronology and read only through a reviewer.

edges.relationship: Science studies and the history of science diverged during the 1990s: the history of science “became ever more historical and science studies ever less”; science studies stayed “undisciplined”, and historicizing objectivity is not debunking it (2009)
edges.evidence_note: Her own words, read in full (Critical Inquiry 35, 2009). The fields "came to diverge … as the history of science became ever more historical and science studies ever less" (p. 800); science studies read Kuhn "as a manifesto of relativism", historians took from him that "teleology must be repudiated" (p. 802); the history of science "has … become a discipline", while science studies "has remained interdisciplinary—and, even on the testimony of some insiders, undisciplined" (p. 811); its assumptions are "Manichean" (p. 812). In the terms of the Science Wars she answers the relativism charge: "to historicize the category of the fact, objectivity, or proof is not thereby to debunk it" (p. 812); "'If historical, then relative' is a non sequitur" (p. 813), citing Latour's "Why Has Critique Run out of Steam?" (2004). Qualifications: she credits "intensive and fruitful exchanges" in the 1970s and 1980s (p. 800), doubts that disciplinarity is an unmixed good (p. 811 n. 30) and calls for "a new form of interdisciplinarity" (p. 813).
edges.map_label: Daston: history of science versus science studies, 2009

edges.relationship: Foucault’s historicism and the history of objectivity: Daston credits it with opening “proof, experience, and objectivity” to history (2009), and reviewers compare Objectivity with Foucauldian genealogy while noting its distance from his “epistemes”
edges.evidence_note: A comparison, not a documented personal borrowing. Her field-level acknowledgement, read (Critical Inquiry, 2009): the counterweight to miniaturizing history of science "has been supplied not by science studies but by a still more thoroughgoing form of historicism, namely, the philosophical history of Michel Foucault" (p. 809); "Topics like proof, experience, and objectivity … suddenly seemed fair game" (p. 810). Readers: Switzer (Foucault Studies 6, 2009, p. 99, read): "though it is unacknowledged, it is by a kind of Foucauldian genealogy that Daston and Galison conduct their study"; Henning (New Formations 64, 2008, read in full by the second research pass): virtues are aimed at through "'techniques of the self' in Foucault's sense, though this is not a straightforwardly Foucaultian argument" (p. 154), and the authors "distance themselves from Foucault's theory of historical rupture" (p. 157). Objectivity itself contrasts its history with "the static tableaux of paradigms and epistemes" (p. 19, as Switzer quotes it); the book is unread here and Galison holds equal credit. Personal transmission can be reconsidered after stronger evidence is read.

edges.relationship: Two explicitly distinguished uses of “moral economy”: the crowd’s “legitimizing notion” (1971) and the affect-laden values of science (1995)
edges.evidence_note: Daston's own note, read (Osiris 10, 1995, p. 3 n. 1): "my use of the term moral economy diverges significantly from E. P. Thompson's in 'The Moral Economy of the English Crowd in the Eighteenth Century' … My appeal here to 'economies' of affects and values has little to do with Thompson's accounts of corn markets and the tradition of 'setting the price' by persuasion or riot, although it does appeal to a broader sense of 'legitimizing notion.'" A teaching comparison of one term in two fields, not an influence: she says the usage diverges. Thompson's essay is recorded on edge_472.

edges.relationship: Elias’s civilizing process as a model for the collective self-discipline of scientific observers (1995)
edges.evidence_note: Her acknowledgement, read by the second research pass ("The Moral Economy of Science", Osiris 10, 1995, pp. 3–5 and 21–24, in the IAS-hosted scan). n. 7: "I have in mind a gradual shaping of a collective personality akin (and, as will be seen below, sometimes identical) to Norbert Elias's 'civilizing process'"; p. 22: "Norbert Elias argued that all complex coordinations of human activity partake of the 'civilizing process,' that is, the 'permanent self-control' demanded by 'the lengthening of the chains of social action and interdependence,' and science is no exception here." She applies it to the self-effacement of "aperspectival objectivity" (pp. 21–22). Compare elias → roger_chartier (edge_453).

edges.relationship: Williams’s Capitalism and Slavery tested on the compensation records: supported on slave-wealth in British society, qualified on decline, and set against a British Marxist pantheon that left James and Williams out (2009–2014)
edges.evidence_note: Her own words, read (History Workshop Journal 78, 2014). "C. L. R James and Eric Williams did not appear in their pantheon. James and Williams, in their struggle against racism and colonialism insisted on the linkage between metropole and colony … the intimate connections … between capitalism and slavery" (p. 23). "Williams never argued that slavery 'caused' the Industrial Revolution … as Nicholas Draper, Keith McClelland and I suggest in the co-authored book which documents the results of the first phase of our project on the Legacies of British Slave-Ownership (LBS), there is a move to a modified version of Williams’s thesis amongst economic historians" (p. 24); "Williams’s insight into the importance of slave-derived wealth to eighteenth-century society and culture has been greatly expanded" (p. 24). Qualifications: the modified thesis is attributed jointly to the LBS authors and set among economic historians (Pomeranz, Inikori); it is not a claim that slavery caused industrialization. The jointly written introduction to Legacies of British Slave-ownership (2014; read in part by the second research pass, without print pages) tests Williams directly: "Eric Williams' Capitalism and Slavery included four connected arguments that are critical for us"; "our findings are entirely supportive of Williams in the context of this second thesis" (slave-wealth in British society); on industrialisation "Our material cannot resolve these controversies"; and the work "complicates Williams by qualifying his 'decline' thesis". Katie Donington, a co-author, recalls that "The project foregrounded Williams's work" (Black Perspectives, 2020). Hall was the project's principal investigator (REF 2014 case study).

edges.relationship: Class as the key dynamic questioned: Hobsbawm and his fellow Marxist historians, aware of plantation economies, left “race, slavery and the Caribbean” outside their concern; gender and race proposed as analytics of capital formation (2014)
edges.evidence_note: Her own words, read (History Workshop Journal 78, 2014, a lecture at the conference "History after Hobsbawm"). He "was critical of the cultural turn"; "Feminist history, in his view, was at best interested in 'winning collective recognition'"; postcolonial approaches "were not on his radar beyond the work of Subaltern Studies" (p. 22). "Hobsbawm was well aware of the significance of plantation economies to the development of industrial capitalism" (p. 23), but "his concern, and that of his fellow Marxist historians, was not with race, slavery and the Caribbean" (p. 23); "While class was the key historical dynamic in his analytic work, gender and race have become key analytics for our 'interesting times'" (p. 24). Qualifications: a critique within a shared agenda, "connecting these insights with older Marxist traditions" (p. 22); she credits Industry and Empire on colonial markets (p. 23). Distinct from the critiques by Chakrabarty (edge_917) and Guha (edge_979).
edges.map_label: Hall: after Hobsbawm, gender and race, 2014

edges.relationship: Metropole and colony made together: Birmingham abolitionists, Baptist missionaries and Jamaica, and the shift from paternalist hopes to racial thinking, 1830–1867 (2002)
edges.evidence_note: Her own statement of the book's argument, read by the second research pass ("A Response to the Commentators", JBS 42:4, 2003): "The central argument of Civilising Subjects is that being a colonizer was part of the construction of Englishness in the nineteenth century" (p. 530); splitting the narrative between Jamaica and Birmingham meant "reasserting the gap between metropole and colony as fundamental to the maintenance of metropolitan power" (p. 534). A reader's explicit claim and her own description, read; the book is unread here. Woollacott (Connected Worlds, 2006, chapter 4, read in part): "The great strengths, in postcolonial terms, of Hall’s magnum opus include … her compelling insistence on the interconstitutive connections between colony and metropole; her interest in the historical construction of race and its connections to gender and class; and perhaps above all, her political engagement with the operation of imperialism and colonialism and their legacies." Hall (History Workshop Journal, 2014, p. 22): "As a protagonist of feminist and postcolonial work". The University of Chicago Press description: "the idea of empire was at the heart of mid-nineteenth-century British self-imagining"; by the 1860s "a harsher racial vocabulary". Woollacott notes its limit: no connections "between Jamaica and other colonies beyond Edward John Eyre’s career".

edges.relationship: Civilising Subjects praised for showing that “empire is always on top of what it rules”, but faulted for not drawing on Subaltern Studies for unrecorded colonised voices and for treating culture as propaganda rather than analysing how it disguised colonial violence (2003)
edges.evidence_note: Said's review, "Always on Top" (LRB 25:6, 20 March 2003; complete text read via WebFetch extraction, no pagination). Praise: "Hall’s excellent book"; a "dialectical" history linking ideas, institutions and daily life; it shows that "empire is always on top of what it rules". Criticisms: sermons, polemics, letters and philosophy are treated alike as "evidence"; she does not draw on Ranajit Guha and the Subaltern Studies group (Woollacott 2006 quotes him: Hall "mystifyingly doesn’t draw" on them); her treatment of culture as propaganda follows John MacKenzie and neglects how culture, in Arnold, Carlyle and Dickens, insulated and disguised colonial violence. A mixed review whose criticisms are specific and methodological; he frames the book with Culture and Imperialism's "intertwined histories".

edges.relationship: Legacies of British Slave-ownership: slave-owners compensated at emancipation traced into British commerce, politics and culture, with gender and race as forces in capital formation (project from 2009; book and essay 2014; with Draper, McClelland and colleagues)
edges.evidence_note: Her own words, read (History Workshop Journal 78, 2014): "Since 2009 a team of historians at University College London, of whom I am one, have been investigating slave-owners" (p. 24); from "Nick Draper’s study of the compensation records" they "documented all the claimants to compensation at the time of emancipation – when twenty million pounds was paid to the slave-owners" (p. 26); slave-ownership is "a way of bringing slavery home and problematizing whiteness" (p. 25); the essay "argues that gender and race are both critical to capital formation … Classical Marxist accounts of the development of industrial capitalism need to be rethought" (abstract). The 2014 book, co-authored with Draper, McClelland, Donington and Lang, is read through its publisher abstract: "one powerful way in which Empire came home to Victorian Britain". Burnard (JWH, opening) calls it "this outstanding collection of essays". Collective work; all credits retained.

edges.relationship: The Black Jacobins as a model for analysing “metropole and colony in one lens” (2003)
edges.evidence_note: Her own acknowledgement, read by the second research pass (JBS 42:4, 2003, p. 533): "Colonizers were made both in the metropole and on colonial sites. And, as C. L. R. James's The Black Jacobins (1938) taught us, much can be gained through the analysis of metropole and colony in one lens." A retrospective acknowledgement made in defending the book's method; it names a resource, not the origin of her project. Her 2014 essay also sets James and Williams against the British Marxist pantheon (History Workshop Journal 78, p. 23, read).
edges.map_label: Metropole and colony in one lens, 2003

edges.relationship: Fanon’s claim that colonialism shaped the colonizers as much as the colonized frames the question of how empire was lived “at home” (2002–2003)
edges.evidence_note: Her own statement, read by the second research pass (JBS 42:4, 2003, p. 530): "Yet if, as Frantz Fanon argued, colonialism shaped the colonizers as much as the colonized then how was this expressed in everyday culture? How was it lived 'at home' as well as in the empire?" One explicit sentence framing the project; the Fanon text is not specified. Not to be confused with edge_418 (fanon → identity), which concerns Stuart Hall.

edges.relationship: Slave-ownership reinscribed into modern British history: the Legacies of British Slave-ownership project and its database of about 46,000 compensation claims (2009–2014; with Draper, McClelland and colleagues)
edges.evidence_note: Read by the second research pass. REF 2014 case study (WebFetch excerpts): the ESRC project ran 1 June 2009 to 31 May 2012, led by "Professor Hall and her research associates, Dr Nicholas Draper and Dr Keith McClelland", and from "the records of the £20m paid in compensation to slave-owners in 1833" documented "the c.46,000 individual claims and awards". 2014 introduction (excerpts, no print pages): "our project is to reinscribe slave-ownership onto modern British history"; "The database digitises all the awards in the slave-compensation records of the 1830s". Hall (History Workshop Journal, 2014, p. 25, read): "a way of bringing slavery home". Lucky Valley (2024; publisher abstract) extends the work to Edward Long and "racial capitalism". Collective work; all credits retained. Distinct from the economic-history arrow, which records her argument about capital formation.

edges.relationship: A public Encyclopaedia of British Slave-ownership, accompanied by workshops with local and family historians and correspondence with descendants of slave-owners and the enslaved (2010–2013).
edges.evidence_note: Read by the second research pass. REF 2014 case study (WebFetch excerpts): workshops drew "mostly local and family historians from outside academia"; correspondents were "the great majority from descendants of slave-owners and the enslaved"; the online Encyclopaedia of British Slave-ownership launched on 28 February 2013 and had 137,998 visits from 108,022 unique visitors to 31 July 2013. The 2014 introduction names responsibilities "to the descendants of the enslaved people, to the descendants of the slave-owners and to other academic and non-academic constituencies" and says the project "has no position on reparations and restitution". An institutional impact statement and the team's own account; collective work. The atlas owner's separate Early Atlantic World project uses LBS-derived data; nothing from it is evidence here.

edges.relationship: Englishness as a formation of class, gender and race: imperial men, masculinities and “raced” white subjects (2002–2003)
edges.evidence_note: Her own retrospective statement, read by the second research pass (JBS 42:4, 2003): her task was "to analyze the 'racing,' to use Toni Morrison's term, of white subjects, the ways in which Englishness needs to be understood not only as a formation of class and of gender, but also of race and ethnicity" (p. 531); the book "is about men, masculinities, and the making of 'raced' subjects" (p. 536); she concedes to Holt and Levine that "There is undoubtedly more that I could have done with the women" (pp. 536–537). Civilising Subjects itself is unread. Distinct from the 1987 Family Fortunes contribution, which reaches gender history through edge_757's social-history claim and the existing roster row.

edges.relationship: The national “island story” rethought through empire: the history taught in schools and universities “needed to be rethought through the frame of empire” (2003)
edges.evidence_note: Her own words, read by the second research pass (JBS 42:4, 2003): race politics in postcolonial Britain "posed a challenge to the national story, the 'island story' of the homogeneity of the English-British nation" (p. 530); "One of my self-appointed tasks was to demonstrate the ways in which the well-established narrative of British history, the national history, the one taught in schools and universities, needed to be rethought through the frame of empire. Civilising Subjects is not only cultural and social history, it is also political history" (p. 537). Macaulay and Son (2012) extends the critique to Macaulay's History of England, as Tao Wei (Essays in History, 2014, read in full by the second pass) reads it: Hall calls him "one of the most influential proponents of liberal imperial discourse" (p. xiii); that book is unread and the edge rests on the 2003 statement.

edges.relationship: The Dobb–Sweezy transition debate (1950–76) as the first component of the debate on capitalism’s origins
edges.evidence_note: Science & Society 14:2 (1950), read in full: Sweezy's 'root cause … was the growth of trade' (p. 142) against Dobb's 'interaction of the two; although with primary emphasis … upon the internal contradictions' (p. 160). Readers who place it at the head of the line: Hilton (1978, p. 119; 1985, p. 1; Cambridge Core openings); Wood (2001, read): 'the famous Transition Debate which began in 1950 in Science and Society'; Harman (2004 transcript, read): 'The first stage took place in the 1940s and 1950s'. The field strand marx/transition keeps the positions; this arrow records the debate's place in the group entry.

edges.relationship: Feudalism defined by coercive production relations, with trade acting through internal conflicts: the debate’s founding text and reply (1946–50)
edges.evidence_note: Dobb's reply, pp. 158, 160–161, 163, 165 (read): a definition 'advisedly in terms of the relations of production'; trade 'accentuated the internal conflicts'; labour services lasted longest 'in the more advanced south-east'; the seventeenth-century 'ruling class was still feudal'. Sweezy (p. 142): 'no theory which fails to take into account the factors which Dobb stresses … can be regarded as correct'. Wood (2001) and Harman (1989) treat Dobb as the start of the line Brenner continued. Distinct from edge_319 (Dobb → marx) and edge_479 (Dobb → economic).

edges.relationship: Class structure and property relations as the key to divergent European paths: the Brenner debate (1976–85) and the critique of neo-Smithian Marxism (1977)
edges.evidence_note: Brenner 1976 (whole article OCRed; p. 31 read closely): 'it is the structure of class relations, of class power, which will determine the manner and degree to which particular demographic and commercial changes will affect long-run trends … and not vice versa' (p. 31). NLR 1977 (read in transcription): Sweezy, Frank and Wallerstein share 'the model put forward by Adam Smith' (§II). The editors' preface (1985, p. vii, Cambridge Core): 'one of the most important historical debates of recent years'. Wood (2001): 'Robert Brenner built on the foundation created by these Marxist historians'.

edges.relationship: Neo-Malthusian, Marxist and regional critics answer Brenner: the demographic historians misrepresented, 'political Marxism', doubtful England–France and east–west contrasts, class struggle narrowed to the countryside (1978–2004)
edges.evidence_note: This arrow represents the specified interventions of Postan and Hatcher, Le Roy Ladurie, Bois, Croot and Parker and Wunder in Past and Present (1978), and of Harman (1989; 2004) and Callinicos (1990); it is not a verdict of the group entry, which includes Brenner and his supporters. Postan and Hatcher: 'Both imputations are groundless' (p. 64). Le Roy Ladurie: 'somewhat superficial but also extremely insular'; 'simplistic assimilation between power (political) and surplus value (economic)' (pp. 101–102). Croot and Parker: 'Both halves of this argument are suspect' (p. 79). Wunder: 'fallen victim to the Prussian myth' (p. 91). Bois: 'radically disagreeing with his methodological orientation' (p. 107); 'a voluntarist vision of history' (pp. 115–116, as quoted by Wikipedia and Callinicos 1990). Seccombe (1983): a 'tendency to deny the explanatory power of demographic phenomena'. Harman (1989): 'a very narrow view of class struggle'. Concessions kept: Croot and Parker, 'welcome and effective'; Bois, 'courageously attacks the Malthusian model'; Cooper, 'I sympathize with him'; Callinicos, 'a valuable corrective' (p. 111). The 1978 openings are read on Cambridge Core (1985 reprint pages); later pages are not quoted directly; the specified Bois passages (pp. 115–116) are mediated, as quoted by Wikipedia and Callinicos (1990).

edges.relationship: Collects the transition debate (1976) and introduces the Brenner debate as its continuation (1985)
edges.evidence_note: Introduction to The Brenner Debate, p. 1 (Cambridge Core): 'In some respects it might be regarded as a continuation of that other well-known debate … which had been sparked off by the criticism by the American economist Paul Sweezy of the analysis given by Maurice Dobb'. 'A Crisis of Feudalism' (1978, p. 119, opening) traces the Marxist view from Dobb through Science and Society to Bois. The 1976 collection is known from its bibliographic record; its introduction is unread.

edges.relationship: Political Marxism and the agrarian origin of capitalism: the transition debate and Brenner's 'market dependence' set against the commercialization model (1981–2002)
edges.evidence_note: Wood, 'Eurocentric Anti-Eurocentrism' (2001, read in full): the Transition Debate 'challenged the commercialization model' but 'still shared significant assumptions' with it; Brenner explained 'the emergence of what he calls "market dependence"'. Pristine Culture (1991, publisher extract): 'Britain - or rather England - was the world's first capitalist society'. Readers: Callinicos (1990), 'Wood's employment of his work to construct "political Marxism"' (p. 112); Hirschkop (2016). The Origin of Capitalism itself is unread.

edges.relationship: Marxist and anti-Eurocentric critics: 'little more than a sociology of domination', colonialism made marginal, and England made the only site of capitalism (1990–2004)
edges.evidence_note: This arrow represents Callinicos (1990), McAuley (2001, with Blaut as he reports him) and Harman (2004). Callinicos (1990, pp. 112–114, read): 'Wood's "political Marxism" is little more than a sociology of domination'. McAuley (2001, read): 'the Brenner-Wood thesis' treats colonialism, in Blaut's words as he reports them, as 'a marginal process'. Harman (2004 transcript, read): her position takes Brenner's 'to a point of caricature … It is not Bob's'. Wood's replies (2002, read) are kept: 'I don't even remotely recognize my argument, or Brenner's'.

edges.relationship: Toynbee's Lectures (1884) define the Industrial Revolution as 'the substitution of competition for the medieval regulations', the concept the later debate revises
edges.evidence_note: Toynbee, Lectures on the Industrial Revolution in England (posthumous, 1884), Saylor transcription without print pages, read by lecture: Lecture I describes 'England on the eve of the Industrial Revolution'; Lecture VIII: 'The essence of the industrial Revolution is the substitution of competition for the medieval regulations which had previously controlled the production and distribution of wealth'; 'The effects of the industrial Revolution prove that free competition may produce wealth without producing well-being.' A reader's warrant: de Vries (1994, p. 249) calls the Industrial Revolution 'By far the most important such monument in economic history'. No claim that Toynbee coined the term or founded the debate; the chain to the 1980s passes through Clapham and Cannadine, unread here.

edges.relationship: Economic historians' measurement and its critics: Crafts and Harley's slower British growth with 'an important discontinuity' reasserted (1992), against Berg and Hudson's case that growth accounting 'mis-specified' the Industrial Revolution (1990/1992)
edges.evidence_note: Crafts and Harley (1992, abstract, read): 'insofar as any adjustment is required the effect is slightly to lower the estimated growth rate … The idea of the industrial revolution as an important discontinuity is reasserted.' Berg and Hudson, working paper (May 1990, read in part): 'the gradualist perspective has appeared to triumph … because of a growing preoccupation with growth accounting' (p. 1); 'N. F. R. Crafts and others may not be able to find the industrial revolution because, in addition to using problematic data, they have mis-specified their subject' (pp. 4–5); 'It is time to move on from the macro accounting framework' (pp. 38–39); 1992 abstract: 'Gradualist perspectives now dominate'. De Vries (1994, pp. 250–251, read) on Lindert and Williamson, Harley and Crafts: 'cleansing the temple of the "false god of the take off," not … pulling down the pillars'. 'Gradualist' is the critics' label; Crafts and Harley reassert a discontinuity.

edges.relationship: The Industrial Revolution as escape from an “organic economy” bounded by land: growth from two sets of forces with “only an accidental relationship to one another in the early stages of their overlap in time” (1988), the question “why it did not come to an end”, without dismissing institutional or scientific explanations (2010), and coal as “the solution” (2016); Berg and Hudson questioned causal inference from Wrigley and Schofield’s aggregate studies (1990)
edges.evidence_note: His own words, in Cambridge University Press excerpts. Continuity, Chance and Change (1988, pp. 1–8 read in revision 1.145): “After many years spent in work principally concerned with the population history of England, I had returned increasingly to my first main research interest, the better understanding of the industrial revolution” (p. 1); “My main aim in the lectures was to question the appropriateness of the view that the industrial revolution was a cumulative, progressive, unitary phenomenon” (p. 3); growth was “the product of two different sets of forces having only an accidental relationship to one another in the early stages of their overlap in time” (p. 4); the classical economists remain authoritative for “an economy bounded by the productivity of the land, what I shall term an organic economy” (p. 5). Energy and the English Industrial Revolution (2010, pp. 1–6, 9–11 read): “the most important single issue on which to focus in trying to gain a clearer understanding of the industrial revolution is not how the period of more rapid growth began, but why it did not come to an end” (p. 4); “the production horizon for all organic economies was set by the annual cycle of plant growth” (p. 9); “There can be no single, ‘true’ account of the industrial revolution” (p. 4); institutional and scientific explanations get “only glancing references”, but “it would be both presumptuous and mildly ridiculous to downplay their importance”, and the explanations are “essentially incommensurable” (pp. 4–5). The Path to Sustained Growth (2016, p. 3): “Mining coal provided the solution to this problem.” Poverty, Progress, and Population (2004, pp. 1–3): Rostow’s “take-off” is “now almost impossible to maintain” (p. 2), and Berg and Hudson put the counter-view “vigorously and effectively” (p. 3 n. 6). The 2013 article is read in abstract only. Critique: Berg and Hudson (1990 working paper, read): “The work of Wrigley and Schofield dominates the population history of this period and illustrates some of the more general problems of causal analysis based on aggregative studies.” Their objection concerns causal inference from the aggregate series, not the reconstruction as such. Revision 1.145 drew this arrow from demography because Wrigley had no entry; revision 1.146 re-sources it to e_a_wrigley and keeps its id. His population reconstruction is drawn on e_a_wrigley → demography.

edges.relationship: The “industrious revolution”: a household-level, demand-side change that preceded the supply-side Industrial Revolution (1994), built on the revision that cut British growth estimates “by more than half” and dated to roughly 1650–1850 (2008); reviewers asked whether consumption had become a new “deus ex machina” (2009), and papermaking evidence challenged its chronology and mechanism (2016)
edges.evidence_note: His own words, read. JEH 1994, abstract (Cambridge Core): “The Industrial Revolution as a historical concept has many shortcomings. A new concept—the ‘industrious revolution’—is proposed to place the Industrial Revolution in a broader historical setting … The industrious revolution was a household-level change with important demand-side features that preceded the Industrial Revolution, a supply-side phenomenon.” The Industrious Revolution (2008, publisher excerpt, pp. 6–10): “the accumulating evidence for an earlier increase of per capita income in northwestern Europe paired with a major refinement of material life casts serious doubt on the orthodoxy that the Industrial Revolution was the actual starting point for long-term economic growth” (pp. 6–7); among the literatures that “guided my thinking” is “The Revisionist Macroeconomics of the British Industrial Revolution”, which “reduces the earlier growth estimates by more than half” (pp. 7–8, citing Crafts and Harley 1992); the approach would “question the claims of the twin revolutions – the British Industrial and the French political – to function as gatekeepers to modern history” (p. 9); households “acted to reallocate their productive resources (which are chiefly the time of their members)” during “a long eighteenth century, roughly 1650–1850” (p. 10). Reviewers, read: Voth (EH.Net, 2009) finds the book “on all the main points, convincing”, with “the almost complete disconnect with behavioral economics” as its weakness; van Nederveen Meerkerk (TSEG, 2009) finds that consumption becomes “een nieuwe ‘deus ex machina’” (p. 176). Rosenband (2016, abstract): papermaking raises “fundamental challenges to this model”; “paperworkers already labored exhausting hours at the outset of de Vries's period of newfound industriousness”, and “women and adolescent workers toiled for wages in paper mills long before the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries”. The 1994 article’s pages read in earlier revisions are not quoted here. Revision 1.145 drew this arrow from consumption because de Vries had no entry; revision 1.146 re-sources it to jan_de_vries and keeps its id. Pomeranz’s use of the concept is now on jan_de_vries → kenneth_pomeranz; the household mechanism stays on consumption/household_labor.

edges.relationship: Useful knowledge as the cause of sustained growth: the “Industrial Enlightenment”, “the key to sustained and accelerating invention” (2002 draft), which kept the early Industrial Revolution from “fizzling out” (2007 lecture); with Kelly and Ó Gráda, British workers’ human capital against Allen’s high-wage explanation (2014), and low initial wages and mechanical skills across England’s 41 counties (2023)
edges.evidence_note: His own words, read. October 2002 draft (“The Enduring Riddle of the European Miracle”, p. 10): Enlightenment thinkers “created the attitudes, the institutions, and the mechanisms by which new knowledge was created, spread and put to good use. It is this specific aspect of the period that I have called the Industrial Enlightenment … the movement was not the key to invention; it was the key to sustained and accelerating invention.” Max Weber Lecture (EUI, 2007, pp. 2–5): countries of the 1914 “convergence club” “were countries that in the eighteenth century were subject to the European Enlightenment. This strong correlation is not in and of itself proof of causality” (p. 2); the tightening of propositional and prescriptive knowledge “prevented the early Industrial Revolution from fizzling out and enabled it to become the taproot of modern growth” (p. 5). With Morgan Kelly and Cormac Ó Gráda, “Precocious Albion” (2014, author-posted proof, pp. 16.2–16.4): “the main reason for its precocity was its higher level of human capital”; against Allen’s induced innovation, “the driver of technological progress was something deeper and stronger than cheap coal and high wages”. “The Mechanics of the Industrial Revolution” (JPE 2023, pp. 60–61): their prediction “runs directly counter to the influential argument of Allen (2009a)”; the finding concerns the 41 counties of England, not Britain’s international position. The Enlightened Economy (2009) is unread; reviewing it, Harley (EH.Net, 2010, read) wondered “if causation from Enlightenment, as an intellectual stance, to economic change actually existed” and found that it “seems almost to describe the nature of successful change at least as much as its cause.” Each quotation is tied to the text it comes from; the 2002 wording is not claimed for the 2009 book. Revision 1.145 drew this arrow from technology because Mokyr had no entry; revision 1.146 re-sources it to joel_mokyr and keeps its id. His theory of useful knowledge as such is drawn on joel_mokyr → technology.

edges.relationship: Pomeranz's reassessment of divergence timing, 2011, as reported by Vries: he 'probably overstated the lateness and suddenness of the Great Divergence', and parity had probably gone by 1750 'if not in 1700'
edges.evidence_note: Vries, Escaping Poverty (2013, p. 17, read), on Pomeranz's 'Ten Years After' (2011, unread): 'the most important Californian, Kenneth Pomeranz, very recently admitted that he probably overstated the lateness and suddenness of the Great Divergence and that economic parity between the two extremes of Eurasia probably had already disappeared in 1750 if not in 1700' (n. 23 cites de Vries's 'after ten years' and Pomeranz's 'Ten years after'). A contribution to the debate's chronology by its principal author, known through one reader's report; a concession, not a critique. Moderate. Pomeranz's 2002–2003 replies concern Huang and stay on edges 1043–1044.

edges.relationship: Reciprocal comparison as the California School's method: Wong (1997), Pomeranz (2000) and Parthasarathi's 'parallels in Eurasia' (2011), read by Vries as 'a new kind of comparative reciprocal history that suits global historians' (2013)
edges.evidence_note: Pomeranz (2000, pp. 7–8, read): a regional approach 'anticipated in important ways by my colleague R. Bin Wong'; 'Here, too, I am following a procedure outlined in Wong's recent China Transformed … viewing both sides of the comparison as "deviations" when seen through the expectations of the other'. Parthasarathi (2011, publisher excerpt): earlier explanations 'all identify something that made Europe different … This book takes a different approach … it rejects claims for European difference' (p. 1); 'Kenneth Pomeranz builds upon this work' (p. 5). Vries (2013, pp. 14–15, read): 'The Californians, moreover, experiment with a new kind of comparative reciprocal history that suits global historians who not only want to juxtapose but also connect.' The method strands stay on global/comparison and global/reciprocal_comparison_resources.

edges.relationship: Frank's ReOrient (1998) as the polemical wing of the divergence debate: Asia central until 1800, a debate with Landes announced for December 1998 and an endorsement of Pomeranz (2001)
edges.evidence_note: Notice announcing the Landes–Frank debate (Northeastern University, scheduled for 2 December 1998; read; written from Frank's side; whether the debate took place as announced is not independently confirmed): 'FRANK retorts that … Received social theory … is vitiated by the ingrained EUROCENTRISM of historiography'; Asia 'remained predominant in the world until at 1800'; 'LANDES retorts that Frank and his echoes are a magnet for fallacies and fantasies'. Frank's review of Pomeranz (JAS 2001; author's manuscript read): 'bar none, the biggest and most important contribution'; Pomeranz is 'the most important … member of what Jack Goldstone has called the new "California School"'. Mokyr (EH.Net 2012, read): 'The California School, most notably embodied in Kenneth Pomeranz's Great Divergence and Andre Gunder Frank's Re-Orient'. Vries (2013, pp. 15–16) quotes ReOrient (pp. 75, 259) and calls one passage 'a quite silly statement'. Burnard and Riello (2020, p. 228 n.): Beckert 'is heavily influenced by [world-systems theory's] axioms'. ReOrient itself is unread. Distinct from edge_1053 (Pomeranz → dependency).

edges.relationship: Goldstone's 'efflorescences' of pre-modern growth (2002), and the 'California School' label that readers attribute to him
edges.evidence_note: Goldstone (JWH 2002, abstract): 'many premodern and non-Western economies show spurts or efflorescences of economic growth … Medieval Europe, Golden Age Holland, and Qing China'; the distinctive Western combination 'developed from the seventeenth to nineteenth centuries only in Britain'. The label: Frank (2001, read), 'what Jack Goldstone has called the new "California School"'; Vries (2009, p. 35 n. 1, read), 'The term was introduced by Jack Goldstone.' Goldstone's own first use was not found. Vries (2009, p. 48) adds that Californians should 'broaden their approach, as some, e.g. Jack Goldstone, have already done'. Goldstone's earlier comparative work stays on historicalsociology/demographic_crises.

edges.relationship: Capitalism and Slavery (1944) as the starting point of the slavery-and-capitalism component: four arguments taken up and modified by economic historians and by the new history of capitalism
edges.evidence_note: Readers, read: Burnard and Riello (JGH 2020, p. 227): 'Four of his arguments are critical to the NHC project: that slavery was central to the Industrial Revolution; that slave wealth was important to the history of eighteenth-century Britain; that the West Indian slave economy went into decline from 1783; and that West Indian slave-owners moved from being a progressive force within mercantilism to being a reactionary force within industrial capitalism'; 'His contemporary defenders, however, use Williams for historical perspectives he never considered' (p. 227); 'a movement among economic historians that accepts a modified version of the Williams thesis' (p. 233). Hilt (JEH 2017, p. 516): 'Like Eric Williams in Capitalism and Slavery (1944), Beckert argues …'; n. 6: Inikori (2002) is 'the strongest recent defense of the Williams hypothesis'. Regele (2023, p. 7): the new work draws on 'a long history of scholarship … most notably Eric Williams's Capitalism and Slavery'. Pomeranz (2000, p. 3 n. 2): 'the generally negative current mainstream verdicts on the arguments of Eric Williams (1944)'. Distinct from edge_155 (Williams → economic) and edge_406 (Williams → atlantic).

edges.relationship: Atlantic trade and African producers and consumers in the making of the Industrial Revolution: Inikori's reassertion of Williams (2002), with the 1987 conference volume on Williams's legacy as its precedent
edges.evidence_note: O'Rourke, EH.Net review of Inikori (2003; read in part): 'His argument is that international trade was crucial to the success of that revolution, in particular trade with the Atlantic Basin (Africa, the West Indies, and the Americas); and that Africans on both sides of the Atlantic were central to this process, both as consumers and producers'; 'a lot of cliometricians will probably conclude that Inikori's argument is not as yet proven'. Burnard and Riello (2020, p. 227): Inikori is 'Williams' best modern-day defender', concerned that 'the Industrial Revolution owed much more to Africa and Africans than previously thought'. Solow and Engerman (eds, 1987): contents only, with chapters by Solow, Inikori, Richardson and Drescher. Inikori's book itself is unread. Distinct from edge_406 (Williams → atlantic).

edges.relationship: Economic historians answer the new history of capitalism: 'fundamental errors in economic reasoning' (Olmstead and Rhode, 2017) and 'specious arguments and failures of analytical reasoning' that 'sometimes undermine' the books (Hilt, 2017); Olmstead and Rhode attribute the observed productivity increase primarily to biological innovation, as Hilt reports
edges.evidence_note: Olmstead and Rhode, AHA paper (programme abstract read; scheduled for 8 January 2017): 'The "New History of Capitalism" grounds the rise of industrial capitalism on the production of raw cotton by American slaves … We show that all make fundamental errors in economic reasoning that affect their major interpretations'; Baptist's torture argument 'is at variance with the ex-slave narratives that he cites and with evidence drawn from plantation records'. Hilt (JEH 2017, read pp. 511–520): 'specious arguments and failures of analytical reasoning sometimes undermine these books' effectiveness as social criticism' (p. 511); 'None of the books makes any attempt to falsify major elements of their arguments' (p. 515); on Baptist, Olmstead and Rhode 'show that the increase in productivity they observe was due primarily to biological innovations' (p. 518). Qualification: economic-historical research 'casts doubt on some of these arguments and lends support to others' (p. 516), and Hilt calls for 'dialogue, if not collaboration' (p. 511). Hilt reports a measured productivity increase explained primarily by biological innovation; this is not a claim that coercion was absent. The 2018 article is known from metadata only. The earlier Fogel–Engerman debate stays on quant/slavery_debate.

edges.relationship: Class structure, not population or trade, decides how demographic and commercial change affects growth: serfdom in east and west, agrarian capitalism in England against peasant property in France (1976–82)
edges.evidence_note: Brenner 1976 (whole article OCRed; the quoted pages 31, 47 and 75 read closely): 'it is the structure of class relations, of class power, which will determine the manner and degree to which particular demographic and commercial changes will affect long-run trends … and not vice versa' (p. 31); the two problems are east–west serfdom and 'the rise of agrarian capitalism and the growth of agricultural productivity in England in relation to their failure in France' (p. 47); 'the most complete freedom and property rights for the rural population meant poverty' (p. 75). Restated in 1982 as 'social-property systems' (Brenner Debate p. 213, Cambridge Core). A contribution within a contested line, not a founding: he writes that the view 'obviously derives from Marx's arguments' (p. 47 n. 40); Postan and Hatcher: 'The essentials of Robert Brenner's argument have been put forward many times before' (1985, p. 64); Cooper: he 'joins a long line of expositors beginning with the Physiocrats' (p. 138).

edges.relationship: Against the 'demographic model' of Postan and its claim to orthodoxy: population substituted for trade as an 'objective variable' that leaves out class structure (1976)
edges.evidence_note: Brenner 1976 (read): Postan's 'demographic approach' as 'the standard interpretation of long-term socio-economic change in the medieval period' (p. 33); 'what might be termed secular malthusianism has attained something of the level of orthodoxy' (p. 33); 'both Postan and Le Roy Ladurie have chosen to construct new models largely by substituting a different objective variable, population, for the old, discredited one, commerce' (p. 47); 'Postan never really specified the fatal flaw of the trade-centred approach' (p. 43). North and Thomas's contractual view of serfdom is a secondary target (pp. 35–36, 43 n. 32). Hilton (1978, p. 119, Cambridge Core) calls the demographic view 'the prevailing orthodoxy, of which Robert Brenner is simply the latest critic', and Bois (p. 107) also deplores that 'the Malthusian model should have become the orthodox one'. Postan and Hatcher's reply that the charge is 'groundless' is carried by the capitalismdebates → robert_brenner critique.

edges.relationship: Le Roy Ladurie's Languedoc cycle read as a Malthusian model that cannot explain why England escaped and France did not (1976)
edges.evidence_note: Brenner 1976 (read): Le Roy Ladurie's Paysans de Languedoc applied the demographic approach 'rigorously' (p. 33); he quotes 'Malthus came too late' and 'the immense respiration of a social structure' (p. 34); 'Le Roy Ladurie never really poses the question (not only for rural Languedoc but for all of Western Europe) of why the victory of one trend rather than another occurred' (p. 46); 'To explain the failure of agrarian capitalism in France, Le Roy Ladurie falls back, in the last analysis, upon the prevalence of backward mentalities', quoting his 'cultural blockages' (p. 46 n. 37). Le Roy Ladurie's reply (1978) is carried by the capitalismdebates → robert_brenner critique.

edges.relationship: Frank and Wallerstein, with Sweezy before them, charged with a 'neo-Smithian' Marxism that makes trade and the division of labour, not class relations, the source of development and underdevelopment (1977)
edges.evidence_note: Brenner, NLR I/104 (1977), read in full in transcription (no journal pages; by section): 'the basic theoretical underpinnings for the positions set out by all three of these writers is the model put forward by Adam Smith' (§II); with Wallerstein's method 'the rise of trade determines the emergence of capitalists and capitalism; "transition" becomes the result not the source of capitalism' (§VI); Frank's later work has not 'fully broken from the neo-Smithian presuppositions' (§VII); politically, 'the notion of the "development of underdevelopment" opens the way to third-worldist ideology' (Conclusions). Qualified: 'Frank rightly stressed that the expansion of capitalism through trade and investment did not automatically bring with it the capitalist economic development that the Marx of the Manifesto had predicted' (Conclusions). The 1976 essay already cites Wallerstein (1974) as 'a recent version' of the trade explanation of eastern serfdom (p. 53 n. 55). Hilton (1985, p. 1) and Harman (2004 transcript) both name this critique. Brenner thanks Skocpol for her review essay on Wallerstein. A disagreement over method, not a verdict on world-systems research.

edges.relationship: Dobb's critique of Sweezy and his Studies acknowledged as 'of fundamental importance' and a 'great debt' (1977); readers place Brenner in Dobb's line
edges.evidence_note: Brenner's acknowledgement, NLR 1977 n. 11 (read): 'The critique of Sweezy in this exchange by Maurice Dobb, as well as (implicitly) in Dobb's Studies in the Development of Capitalism … is, of course, of fundamental importance—as is Ernesto Laclau's critique of Frank … I hope my great debt to both these writers will be apparent throughout this essay'; Dobb, Studies, pp. 38–42 cited (n. 20). Readers: Hilton (1985, p. 1) calls the debate 'a continuation' of the Dobb–Sweezy debate, and 'A Crisis of Feudalism' (1978, p. 119) traces the Marxist view of the crisis from Dobb's Studies; Harman (1989, read): 'What Brenner does, essentially, is to take up Dobb's argument, but simplify it'. Harman's own criticism shows the line is not uncritical.

edges.relationship: Reopens the transition from feudalism to capitalism around property relations and class conflict, in the line of the Dobb–Sweezy debate (1976–82)
edges.evidence_note: Hilton (1985, p. 1, Cambridge Core): the debate 'might be regarded as a continuation of that other well-known debate concerning the transition from feudalism to capitalism … sparked off by the criticism by the American economist Paul Sweezy of the analysis given by Maurice Dobb'; that debate 'was largely conducted between Marxists'. Harman (2004 transcript, read) gives 'three distinct stages' of the Marxist debate: Sweezy, Dobb and Hobsbawm; Brenner against Wallerstein and Frank; Pomeranz and Brenner. Brenner's own text locates the problem 'more generally' in 'the transition from feudalism to capitalism' (1976, p. 31). Brenner, at UCLA, is not presented as a member of the British Historians' Group.

edges.relationship: Hilton's studies of serfdom and peasant revolt supply evidence for the 1976 argument; his 1985 introduction frames the debate as a continuation of Dobb–Sweezy
edges.evidence_note: Brenner 1976 (read) cites Hilton's Decline of Serfdom (pp. 40, 44, 51 notes), 'Rent and Capital Formation' (p. 48 n. 42) and Bond Men Made Free, pp. 114–15, 125–73 (p. 56 n. 64) for commutation, seigneurial reaction and peasant revolt. Hilton framed the collected debate (introduction, p. 1, Cambridge Core). In 'A Crisis of Feudalism' (1978; 1985 p. 119, Cambridge Core opening) he called Brenner 'simply the latest critic' of the demographic orthodoxy, and traced the Marxist view from Dobb's Studies through the transition debate to Bois's Crise du féodalisme. Evidence and editorial framing, not an influence on Brenner's theory.

edges.relationship: Tawney's Agrarian Problem supplies the evidence on entry fines for the English case (1976)
edges.evidence_note: Brenner 1976 (read): Tawney's Agrarian Problem among the works 'On English agrarian change' (p. 42 n. 30); on fines at will as the landlords' lever, 'Tawney, Agrarian Problem, pp. 287–310', pp. 296–300, 307 (p. 62 nn. 76, 78). Evidence, not an acknowledged framework. Ormrod's 'Agrarian Capitalism and Merchant Capitalism: Tawney, Dobb, Brenner and Beyond' (2013) is located but unread; read it before any upgrade to influence.
