edges.relationship: With Isett, the divergence of England and the Yangzi delta traced to different social-property relations already in place, not to coal and colonies (2002)
edges.evidence_note: Brenner and Isett, JAS 61:2 (2002): 609–662. Opening read (Cambridge extract): 'Kenneth Pomeranz (2000) proposes a radical revision … by as late as 1800, there was little to choose between them'. Opening sections read for revision 1.144 in the International Socialism repost (no JAS pages): 'the institutional framework or system of social-property relations that structured the English economy was radically different … from that of the Yangzi delta'; 'It was this already existing decisive divergence, not England's capacity to gain access to the American colonies … that explains why the two economies distanced themselves'; the delta followed 'a Malthusian pattern', England 'a Smithian pattern'; 'Contra Pomeranz'. Moved here from edge_1050 in revision 1.145, as that edge's note foresaw. Same JAS issue as Huang's critique and Pomeranz's reply. A later and smaller dispute than the 1976–85 debate.
edges.map_label: Property relations against The Great Divergence, 2002

edges.relationship: Marx's account of 'so-called primitive accumulation' named as the source of the view (1976)
edges.evidence_note: Brenner 1976, p. 47 n. 40 (read): 'This view obviously derives from Marx's arguments on the barriers to and the class structural bases for the development of capitalism, especially as presented in "The So-called Primitive Accumulation of Capital", Capital, i, pt. VIII, and Pre-Capitalist Economic Formations'. In 2004 he argued against Marx's Preface model of the productive forces (transcript, read), so the debt is selective.

edges.relationship: Hill's revisions of the 'bourgeois revolution' read as the inspiration for Brenner's 'another social interpretation' of the English Revolution (1993)
edges.evidence_note: Wood, 'Christopher Hill and the Recovery of History' (Against the Current, 2003, read in full): 'Other Marxists, notably Robert Brenner, have developed another social interpretation … (See especially the Conclusion to Brenner's Merchants and Revolution …) It hardly needs saying that Hill's pioneering work has inspired these fruitful developments in Marxist historiography.' Gentles (NLR, 1994, opening): Brenner wrote 'in spite of his great admiration for the work of Christopher Hill and Lawrence Stone'. Two readers' explicit claims; Brenner's own acknowledgement is unread because the book is unread. Moderate.

edges.relationship: Brenner's account of agrarian social-property relations and 'market dependence' as the foundation of her origin of capitalism (1981–2002)
edges.evidence_note: Her acknowledgements and uses: 1981 n. * thanks Brenner, and n. 14 cites his NLR essay (Verso repost, read). In 2001 (read): 'Robert Brenner built on the foundation created by these Marxist historians … what he calls "market dependence"'. In 2002 (read): capitalism has '"rules for reproduction" (to use Brenner's term)'. Readers: McAuley (2001), 'she admittedly draws on Robert Brenner's findings and conclusions'; Callinicos (1990), 'Wood's employment of his work to construct "political Marxism"' (p. 112); Brenner (2016) on their friendship from 1978. An exchange between them on the Low Countries (Journal of Agrarian Change, 2001–02) is listed bibliographically and unexamined here.

edges.relationship: Against Cohen's technological determinism: the 'material base' is social and historical, and the separation of the economic from the political is specific to capitalism (1981)
edges.evidence_note: Verso repost of NLR I/127 (read in part): Cohen's book is used 'to support an argument against a social interpretation of materialism'; 'what Cohen's technological determinism does is to repeat the error of the political economists: he generalizes the particular historical experience of capitalism'. Callinicos (1990, read): this 'is by no means the first time that Wood has used Brenner's work to distinguish her alternative reading of historical materialism from Cohen's' (p. 111). Brenner (2016): 'Here Ellen's main target was … Gerald Cohen'.

edges.relationship: Thompson's critique of the Nairn–Anderson theses, adopted in her account of English capitalism (1991)
edges.evidence_note: Pristine Culture (1991, publisher extract, read): her preferred thesis 'is more compatible with arguments put forward by E.P. Thompson in the original debate, and less subject to his persuasive charge that Nairn-Anderson operated with an abstractly idealized model of a "Bourgeois Revolution"'. Democracy Against Capitalism ch. 2 (1995, Cambridge Core opening): anyone '(like E.P. Thompson) working somewhere in the fissures … is likely to be badly misunderstood'. 2001 (read): 'Like other Marxist historians such as E.P. Thompson, Brenner understands industrialization …'. Hirschkop (2016): 'The prominence of historians within this group (Edward Thompson and John Saville among others) was probably decisive'. Thompson's 'Peculiarities of the English' is not in the graph and unread here.

edges.relationship: Anti-Eurocentric histories (Frank's Asian-centred world economy, Blaut's 'protocapitalism') said to share the Eurocentric confusion of commerce with capitalism (2001)
edges.evidence_note: 'Eurocentric Anti-Eurocentrism' (2001, read): the critiques 'deny the "superiority" of Europe and emphasize … the dominance, of non-European economies and trading networks' (for example 'Andre Gunder Frank's argument about the Asian-dominated world'). Since Blaut 'does not conceive of capitalism as a specific social form, he can have no clear conception of non- or precapitalist modes of production'. McAuley's reply (2001) and her rejoinders (2002) are recorded on the capitalismdebates → ellen_meiksins_wood critique. Frank's later Asia-centred work is outside the dependency strands, so this is a critique of the tradition's later turn, not of the 1966 hypotheses.

edges.relationship: Useful knowledge and the epistemic base of technique: propositional and prescriptive knowledge, macro- and microinventions, and stasis where techniques rest on “narrow epistemic bases” (1999, 2002)
edges.evidence_note: His own words, read. Editor’s introduction (1999, author-posted manuscript): “a successful macroinvention meets three criteria: novelty, workability, and potential for further improvement” (p. 14); “A technological definition of the Industrial Revolution is a clustering of macroinventions leading to an acceleration in microinventions” (p. 16). “Useful Knowledge as an Evolving System” (draft revised February 2002, pp. 2–7): “in the past centuries useful knowledge has become a dominant factor in History” (p. 2); useful knowledge is partitioned into “propositional” knowledge, which “describes and catalogues natural phenomena and the relationships between them”, and “prescriptive” knowledge, “instructions that can be executed” (p. 5); “Inventions based on narrow epistemic bases have low adaptability and tend to lead to technological stasis fairly soon after their emergence” (p. 7). The draft says it adapts The Gifts of Athena (2002), which is unread; Khan’s review of that book (EH.Net, 2003, read in full) reports the same two categories and quotes it (p. 16): “so many scholars believe that if incentives and demand are right, somehow technology will follow automatically”. The Royal Swedish Academy’s 2025 press release (read) summarises the claim: “we not only need to know that something works, but we also need to have scientific explanations for why.” The 1999 distinction of invention from adoption is the existing strand technology/invention_adoption; this arrow adds the 2002 theory of knowledge. Its use to explain Britain’s Industrial Revolution is drawn on the debate arrow (edge_1086).

edges.relationship: Coal and New World land “not incorrect but by itself cannot do the job”: the gap needed “a better explanation than historical luck … or geographical accident”, and Pomeranz did not confront the Needham questions (2002)
edges.evidence_note: “The Enduring Riddle of the European Miracle”, author’s draft of October 2002 for the Riverside conference of November 2002 (pp. 2–4 read; draft pagination). Of coal: “Without denigrating the importance of coal or steam, the argument can be and has been overdone” (p. 2); “China’s coal reserves are immense” (p. 3). Of ghost acreage: “this argument is not incorrect but by itself cannot do the job” (p. 3). Pomeranz “does not confront the ‘Needham Questions’ squarely” (p. 4); “the sheer enormity of the gap requires a better explanation than historical luck (European discoveries) or geographical accident (coal, proximity to America)” (p. 4). The alternative he offers is the Industrial Enlightenment (p. 10), drawn on joel_mokyr → capitalismdebates (edge_1086). A draft (“little more than notes”, its title page says); no published version was read. Revision 1.146 moves this critique from edge_1050 (capitalismdebates → kenneth_pomeranz), where revision 1.145 listed Mokyr among five named critics, to its own arrow; edge_1050 no longer names him.

edges.relationship: Reconstructing England’s population from parish registers: with Schofield, 404 parishes and “back projection” to trace “a secular cycle of population development” and its relation to economic change (1981), complemented by family reconstitution (1997), in the Cambridge Group he co-founded (1964)
edges.evidence_note: Wrigley and Schofield, The Population History of England (1981; introduction pp. 1–5 read in the publisher excerpt of the 1989 Cambridge paperback, OCRed): “since pre-industrial societies normally experienced great difficulty in achieving a rapid expansion in their capacity to produce goods and services, population was the more dynamic element in the striking of a balance with production” (p. 1); the registers make it “possible for the first time to establish with some precision what changes took place in a pre-industrial population over a period of time long enough to encompass a secular cycle of population development, and to investigate the relationship between demographic and economic change during its course” (p. 2); monthly totals “taken from the registers of a total of 404 parishes” (p. 3); “the technique of back projection, which was developed to make the best use of the aggregative data assembled” (p. 4); the aggregative tabulations began as “a subsidiary element” of the Cambridge Group’s family-reconstitution work of “the middle 1960s” (p. 5). Wrigley, Davies, Oeppen and Schofield (1997, pp. 3–4, read): “This book is intended as a complement to the Population history of England”; family reconstitution “had then recently been perfected by Louis Henry”. The Cambridge Group’s institutional history (read) dates its founding by Laslett and Wrigley to 1964. A collaborative project: Schofield, Oeppen and Davies share these results, and the reconstruction’s estimates are not adjudicated here. Berg and Hudson’s critique of its “aggregative” use for causal analysis is on e_a_wrigley → capitalismdebates (edge_1084).

edges.relationship: Technologies to exploit coal as Europe’s difference: China Transformed (1997) followed “arguments of E. A. Wrigley”, as Wong recalled in 2016
edges.evidence_note: Wong, “Divergence Displaced” (Comparativ 26:3, 2016, p. 76, read): “The cluster of differences stressed in that work concerned European science and technologies, and in particular, following arguments of E. A. Wrigley, the importance of technologies to exploit coal as a source of energy to power new kinds of machines”; his note cites Continuity, Chance and Change (1988). Qualification: this is Wong’s retrospective account. China Transformed is read only in chapter openings, and the passage that cites Wrigley there was not read. Wrigley’s own organic-economy argument is on e_a_wrigley → capitalismdebates (edge_1084).

edges.relationship: Coal in explanations of British industrialisation, as readers compare them: Mokyr places Pomeranz in a tradition “established by … E.A. Wrigley” (2002); Huang says Pomeranz simplified “Wrigley’s sophisticated argument” (2002); Clark and Jacks find that both “have made coal central to the story” (2007)
edges.evidence_note: Readers’ comparisons, read. Mokyr (October 2002 draft, p. 2): Pomeranz’s coal argument “joins a venerable tradition established by Carlo Cipolla, E.A. Wrigley and others that looks at the Industrial Revolution as primarily a revolution of fossil fuel usage”. Huang (JAS 2002, pp. 532–533, read in revision 1.144): Wrigley (1988) is “a very different thing from arguing that chance, or coal, alone mattered”; Pomeranz has turned “Wrigley’s sophisticated argument that chance figured in England’s industrialization into a simple argument that coal and colonies alone mattered.” Clark and Jacks (European Review of Economic History 2007, abstract): “both E. A. Wrigley and Kenneth Pomeranz have made coal central to the story”; their coal-rent estimates imply a negligible income contribution from England’s possession of coal reserves. A comparison, not an influence: no passage in which Pomeranz acknowledges Wrigley’s energy argument was read (the read pages of The Great Divergence cite Wrigley only on England’s early divergence from the continent, p. 6 n. 8). Wrigley’s argument stresses chance and the end of the organic economy; Pomeranz pairs coal with colonies.

edges.relationship: The “industrious revolution” applied to Chinese household labour (2000), and de Vries’s 1976 book cited as “a good general critique of the overseas extraction thesis”
edges.evidence_note: Pomeranz’s own words, The Great Divergence (2000; later-edition preview, read): labour deployment in Chinese families “seems to closely resemble the reorientation of labor, leisure, and consumption toward the market that Jan DeVries has called Europe’s ‘industrious revolution’” (p. 17; n. 28 cites DeVries 1994b); the contents list a section “Family Labor in China and Europe: ‘Involution’ and the ‘Industrious Revolution’”; “A good general critique of the overseas extraction thesis is DeVries 1976” (p. 3 n. 2). Huang (JAS 2002, pp. 520–521, read in revision 1.144) reads the borrowing critically: “it is surprising that Pomeranz would have tried to equate the Yangzi delta with de Vries’ industrious revolution”, “along the same lines as R. Bin Wong’s brief discussion earlier (1997, 30–31)”; “he tries to take the revolution out of de Vries’ industrious revolution.” The use is Pomeranz’s; de Vries’s own later judgement of The Great Divergence (Historically Speaking, 2011) is unread and not drawn. The Huang–Pomeranz dispute over involution is on edges 1043–1044.

edges.relationship: With van der Woude, the Dutch Republic as “the first modern economy”, 1500–1815, against readings of its achievement as “backward looking”, joining Annales structural history to the New Economic History (1997); van Zanden doubted that Dutch growth was much faster than England’s (2002)
edges.evidence_note: De Vries and van der Woude, The First Modern Economy (1997, chapter 1, pp. 1–5 read in the publisher excerpt, OCRed): historians including Hobsbawm, Braudel and Wallerstein “felt certain that the Dutch achievement was essentially backward looking, the culmination of something with no future” (p. 1); they quote North and Thomas, for whom the Netherlands was “the first country to achieve sustained economic growth” (p. 2); “With this work we accept the challenge of the modern historical schools; indeed, we even seek to integrate them”: the Annales school, which “advocated a break with ‘event-centered history’”, and cliometrics, which “shifted the focus of the literature from politics and institutions to markets and rational decision makers” (p. 4); “This book, in short, presents the history of the first modern economy” (p. 4). Van Zanden (EHR 2002, abstract, read): “economic growth in the Netherlands was probably not much faster than in England, as is clear from the development of real wages”, and its modernity “appears to be a product of economic and institutional changes in the middle ages.” The book’s sectoral and analytical chapters are unread; the claim is the co-authors’ framing. De Vries’s criticism of the “backward looking” reading is recorded here, not as arrows to Braudel or Hobsbawm, because one paragraph groups them with Barbour and Wallerstein.

edges.relationship: The Cambridge Group’s finding that the western European nuclear family long predated industrialisation, with Hajnal’s marriage pattern, as one of the literatures that “guided my thinking” (2008)
edges.evidence_note: The Industrious Revolution (2008, p. 8, publisher excerpt, read): among four “modern developments in history and economics” that “have guided my thinking”, “3. The Western European Marriage Pattern. The pioneering work of ‘The Cambridge Group for the History of Population and Social Structure’ established the view that the nuclear family structures of modern western European countries and their offshoots are not a product of industrialization but have much earlier origins”, with “the seminal articles of John Hajnal”; “its distinctive economic behavior remains an open question.” The 1994 article’s reference list (Cambridge Core, metadata) cites Wrigley and Schofield (1981), Laslett (1965, 1977) and Hajnal (1965). The influence is credited to the Cambridge Group and Hajnal, not to Wrigley alone; demography/john_hajnal already records Hajnal as a resource for de Vries.

edges.relationship: Demand restored against the supply-side orthodoxy, which de Vries illustrates with Mokyr’s view that the Industrial Revolution’s “when,” “where” and “how fast” are “to be sought first and foremost in supply” (1977; 2008)
edges.evidence_note: The Industrious Revolution (2008, pp. 6–7, publisher excerpt, read): “Studies of modern economic growth are inevitably founded on a decisive ‘supply-side’ advance”; Adam Smith left no doubt that “The consumer responds to the developing productive forces, not the other way around”, with n. 17 quoting Mokyr’s “Demand vs. Supply in the Industrial Revolution” (JEH 1977, p. 1005): “The determination of ‘when,’ ‘where,’ and ‘how fast’ are to be sought first and foremost in supply, not demand-related processes”; “What began as an effort to restore demand as one of the cutting blades of Marshall’s supply and demand scissors” (p. 7). Mokyr’s 1977 abstract (Cambridge Core, read): demand factors “were definitely of a secondary order of importance”. The 1994 article’s reference list cites the 1977 article. Qualification: de Vries cites Mokyr as an exemplar of a general orthodoxy; this is not a reply to a Mokyr text on the industrious revolution, and no reply by Mokyr was read.
edges.map_label: De Vries restores demand, citing Mokyr (2008)

edges.relationship: Reciprocal comparison of China’s and Europe’s advanced regions: Pomeranz followed “a procedure outlined in Wong’s recent China Transformed”, with “greater stress than Wong does on global conjunctures” (2000)
edges.evidence_note: Pomeranz’s own words, The Great Divergence (2000, pp. 7–8, later-edition preview, read): a regional approach “anticipated in important ways by my colleague R. Bin Wong” (p. 7); “Here, too, I am following a procedure outlined in Wong’s recent China Transformed … viewing both sides of the comparison as ‘deviations’ when seen through the expectations of the other, rather than leaving one as always the norm” (p. 8); “my concrete application of this reciprocal comparative method has some significant differences from Wong’s”, with “greater stress than Wong does on global conjunctures and reciprocal influences” (p. 8 and n. 13). Readers: Parthasarathi (2011, p. 5): “Kenneth Pomeranz builds upon this work”; Huang (2002, p. 520) traces Pomeranz’s use of the industrious revolution to “R. Bin Wong’s brief discussion earlier (1997, 30–31)”. Wong (Comparativ 2016, read): Pomeranz rejected “numerous putative differences … including my China Transformed” (p. 73); China Transformed “followed the same method” (p. 76); both books “shared … the basic problem of non-falsifiability” (p. 77). The same debt is recorded as the strand global/reciprocal_comparison_resources (carried by edge_898); this arrow makes it a relationship between the two entries.

edges.relationship: From the limits of European experience to political scale: with Rosenthal, Wong argued that European fragmentation and warfare concentrated manufacturing in cities, where higher wage costs favoured labour-saving techniques (2011, as Wong summarised in 2016 and Ma reported in 2012); in 2016 he recast divergence from “why Britain” to a more general transformation
edges.evidence_note: His own words, “Divergence Displaced” (Comparativ 26:3, 2016, pp. 77–78, read): “Rosenthal and I ended up focusing on an important political difference between China and Europe – political fragmentation in Europe and the presence of an unitary state for the Chinese empire”; war gave “craft producers an incentive to locate in cities”; “We turned the issue of divergence from a question of why was Britain the first industrializer to why was industrialization more likely to occur in Western Europe than in China” (p. 77); “By making the question of the great divergence a more general one we recognize that even a profoundly transformative process like modern economic growth could take place in several ways and begin at several locations” (p. 78). Before and Beyond Divergence (2011) is unread; Ma’s review (EH.Net 2012, read in full in revision 1.145) reports the same dichotomy of “a unified and centralized imperial China versus a politically fragmented Europe” and the mechanism: warfare brought “a greater degree of concentration of trade and manufacturing in urban locations”, and, “With higher urban wages”, innovation in Europe “would be more biased towards saving labor than in China”. Ma finds this “stimulating and striking hypothesis” “supported by fairly meager evidence in the chapter”, and the evidence on public goods “even shakier”. He also reports the authors’ challenge to “the accepted thesis of China being a high interest rate and capital scarce country”, and judges the book “a good contribution in the Great Divergence debate” for addressing “some of the key issues beyond what has been done recently by Pomeranz, Allen and others”, though “far less so when it comes to providing credible support for its own thesis”. The wage mechanism is Ma’s report; Wong’s 2016 summary gives the move of craft production to cities. Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda (2014, p. 16.2) say Rosenthal and Wong “adopted” Allen’s induced-innovation argument “wholesale”. China Transformed (1997), as Mokyr quotes it, held that the “supply-driven Industrial Revolution that followed the demand-led Industrious Revolution in Europe did not happen in China” (p. 31); Mokyr objected that “Bin Wong does not cite any book by Needham” (2002 draft, pp. 3–4). The co-authored argument is Rosenthal’s as well as Wong’s.

edges.relationship: Brenner’s agrarian social relations, like Pomeranz’s coal and colonies, are traits particular to Britain, so that their necessity “cannot be falsified” (2016)
edges.evidence_note: Wong, “Divergence Displaced” (Comparativ 2016, pp. 74–75, read): “when my colleague and Marxist historian Robert Brenner famously argues that it is the absence of the agrarian social relations found in Britain that prevented the emergence of capitalism elsewhere, the importance of the system through which he sees the modern world economy emerging cannot be falsified because the enclosures and the social relations that attended them were particular to Britain. Like Pomeranz’s coal and colonies, Brenner cites traits that are British and not present elsewhere” (p. 74); “Neither the scientific revolution nor agrarian social relations lend themselves very easily to counterfactual exercises because they are themselves so large and encompassing” (p. 75). He allows that such traits “could in fact be factors helping to explain the industrial revolution” (p. 75). A methodological critique in one passage, citing the Aston and Philpin collection; it does not dispute Brenner’s evidence. Brenner’s other respondents are on capitalismdebates → robert_brenner (edge_1078), which does not name Wong.
edges.map_label: Wong questions the falsifiability of Brenner’s explanation, 2016

edges.relationship: Scott recalls first hearing “gender” used in a paper by Davis at the Berkshire Conferences of the 1970s (2008); her 1986 essay had quoted Davis’s call to study the significance of the sexes
edges.evidence_note: Scott's own acknowledgement, read in full in the authorised Spanish translation of "Unanswered Questions" (AHR 113:5, 2008; Debate Feminista 40, 2009, p. 101): "Ahí escuché por primera vez que se mencionaba el género; fue en una ponencia de Natalie Zemon Davis" (citing Davis 1976: 90). English renderings are atlas translations from Spanish. Scott sets her own limit on the same page: "yo no fui el origen del concepto de género, ni siquiera entre las historiadoras", and names a second, literary source in her Brown colleagues of the early 1980s. The 1986 quotation of Davis (p. 1054, n. 4) is the existing reading behind edge_1029, which records Davis's contribution to gender history as a field; this edge records Scott's acknowledged personal debt, with the 2008 recollection as new evidence. Not a claim that Davis shared Scott's later theoretical position.
edges.map_label: Davis and Scott’s first hearing of gender, 1970s–2008

edges.relationship: Scott draws on psychoanalytic theory, especially the concept of fantasy, to keep gender a critical question: gender as the relation between the normative and the psychic (2008), fantasy as a concept for feminist history (2011), and the productive incommensurability of psychoanalysis and history (2012)
edges.evidence_note: Her own words, read in the authorised Spanish translation of "Unanswered Questions" (2008; Debate Feminista 40, 2009, pp. 108–109): psychoanalytic theory has been useful to her, "no a sus articulaciones conservadoras"; gender is "el estudio de la relación (en torno a la sexualidad) entre lo normativo y lo psíquico, el intento de colectivizar la fantasía". Her 2012 History and Theory abstract (abstract only): psychoanalysis "can force historians to question their certainty about facts, narrative, and cause". Duke's description of The Fantasy of Feminist History (2011; publisher description): she "advocates fantasy as a useful, even necessary, concept for feminist historical analysis". In a 2018 interview she speaks of "a whole psychoanalytic dimension" in Sex and Secularism. Psychoanalysis as a body of theory is the resource; no particular Freud text is claimed. The 2008 reply explains a use of psychoanalysis that "has been useful" to her ("me ha sido útil"); it does not mark a beginning, since the 1986 essay already engaged psychoanalytic theory critically (edge_583, a separate claim about universal sexual antagonism). She still rejects "conservative" psychoanalysis.

edges.relationship: Scott argues that 1970s psychohistory, shaped by American ego-psychology, assumed a compatibility between psychoanalysis and history that undercut their critical interaction, and proposes a productive incommensurability after de Certeau (2012, in her abstract)
edges.evidence_note: Author's abstract only (History and Theory 51:1, 2012, 63–83); the article body is unread. "This was not the case with the movement for psychohistory that began in the 1970s. Then the influence of American ego-psychology on history-writing promoted the idea of compatibility between the two disciplines in ways that undercut the critical possibilities of their interaction." De Certeau supplies "theoretical insight into the uses of incommensurability"; Lyndal Roper's work shows "both its limits and its value". No strand is targeted: the abstract names American ego-psychology, not a particular psychohistorian. Moderate.

edges.relationship: French feminists caught between the abstract individual and sexual difference (Only Paradoxes to Offer, 1996), and the parity movement’s attempt to “desymbolize” sex in political representation (Parité!, 2005), as Landes and Dean read them
edges.evidence_note: Mediated: both books are unread. Landes (APSR 1997, p. 443 read) quotes Scott (p. 173): "competing feminist visions have taken one side or another of the opposition between the abstract individual (which counts women the same as men) and the individual self-defined through sexual difference (which insists on their radical unlikeness)". Dean (H-France Review 2006, read in full): the book "focuses on the challenge parité poses to French universalism" (p. 149); Scott quoted on the strategy of "desymbolization" (p. 54) and on "the human individual as plural, as a type of two" (p. 61) (Dean, p. 150); Dean's query about Muslim women and lesbians (p. 152). Scott herself links French universalism, feminist movements and the politics of the veil as objects of one question about how sexual difference is conceived (Unanswered Questions, Spanish translation, p. 108).

edges.relationship: The French headscarf ban read as a symptom of republican, colonial and sexual anxieties (The Politics of the Veil, 2007), and a genealogy of secularism contesting the claim that secular societies guarantee gender equality (Sex and Secularism, 2017), in her reviewers’ accounts and her own interview
edges.evidence_note: Mediated for the books, which are unread. Laborde (Books & Ideas, 2008, read in full): "Particularly acute are Scott’s analyses of the re-importation of the civilizing mission in post-colonial France"; the ban "acted as a (literally) hysterical diversion" from problems of "class, race and gender". Whitney (Literary Review of Canada, 2018, read in full): the book's "polemical aim" is "to counter the notion that gender equality is somehow inherent in secular societies", working through oppositions such as "west versus Orient, Christianity versus Islam". Scott in a 2018 interview (read in full): post-colonial studies were "critical of the notion that modernity was the end point of the civilizing process"; she sought "a critique or a genealogy that could expose these contradictions". Criticism carried here, not drawn as a separate arrow: Laborde finds the "normative premises and broader political implications" unclear, "a standard limitation of discourse analysis"; O'Grady (Times Higher Education, 2018), a philosopher, objects that the later book holds nineteenth-century Europeans to present moral standards: Scott is "anachronistic, ahistorical and oddly absolutist in demanding from 19th-century Europeans moral attitudes that tally with her own". Laborde's objection concerns normative premises and political implications; O'Grady's concerns anachronism. In the 2018 interview Scott names her own difficulty: "how do I write a critique of secularism without rejecting it". A contribution to postcolonial critique of the civilizing narrative, not membership of a school.
edges.map_label: Veil, secularism and the civilizing claim, 2007–2017

edges.relationship: Laura Lee Downs charges that Scott’s poststructuralist gender severs experience and subjectivity from the agency of the oppressed and treats discourse as “text-writ-large”; Scott replies that Downs misreads theory, which “analyzes how knowledge is produced” (1993)
edges.evidence_note: A named critic without a node, drawn from women's history, whose experience-and-agency tradition Downs defends. Downs (CSSH 35:2, 1993; p. 414 and the notes shown by the publisher read): Scott's book "has had an especially powerful impact upon historians, for it is through her eyes that many of us have become acquainted with post-structuralist thought"; "There is much to admire"; but it contains "a radical attack on the naïve suppositions of all previous feminist scholarship: a rejection of that ingenuous chain of reasoning which links subjectivity and experience to the hope that oppressed persons, too, might find some agency in history"; notes: "Scott treats discourse as text-writ-large". Scott's reply in the same issue (p. 438 read): "profound misapprehension"; "theory analyzes how knowledge is produced; theory does not produce either real life or practical politics." Distinct from Palmer (edge_920), Valverde (edge_967) and Canning (edge_702).

edges.relationship: Scott answers Eley and Nield that they want class 'as an effect of discourse but also as "a structural attribute of societies" as if those two were contradictory', and that insisting on class forecloses other political categories: her questions 'don't exclude class, but they don't require it either' (2000)
edges.evidence_note: Body read in full for revision 1.152 (ILWCH 57, 2000, pp. 69–75; Cambridge PDF; data/extension-2026/languages-of-class-2026-10-22/evidence-spread.md §6.3); the abstract read for 1.147 is confirmed verbatim. Eley and Nield's essay 'will surely become an indispensable assignment in introductory graduate courses because it is synthetic in many senses' (p. 69); they 'are willing to accommodate all manner of deviations from the materialist analyses … especially what some have dubbed "the linguistic turn"', so that one 'might have punned wildly and titled the Eley/Nield essay, "Assent to Discourse"' (p. 69); 'Patrick Joyce has been expelled from the fold and Kathleen Canning is now at its center' (p. 69); 'there's a tension between Eley and Nield's desires to update the old social history by detaching it from its materialist assumptions, on the one hand, and to keep writing narratives of worker political agency, on the other' (pp. 69–70); they talk of gender 'but no mention of sex, homo- or heterosexuality, and sexual difference' (p. 70); Rancière's 1983 essay is 'an important corrective to Eley and Nield' (pp. 70–71); 'They want to define class as an effect of discourse but also as "a structural attribute of societies" as if those two were contradictory. To posit them as contradictory is to misunderstand Foucault's ideas about discourse'; 'Structures come into being through discourse: Class is one way of naming, understanding, and organizing certain forms of social inequality' (p. 71); her questions 'don't exclude class, but they don't require it either' (p. 72). Eley and Nield's reply (pp. 81–86 read): 'we have some problems with Scott's ungenerous critique … It is either discourse (here signified by Jacques Rancière and Michel Foucault) or materialist social history' (p. 83), while they 'wholeheartedly applaud Scott's citation of Rancière' (p. 84). Distinct from edge_105 (the linguistic turn's critique of social history, citing her 1991 essay) and from languages_of_class → social, which carries the debate's bearing on the field. Earlier note (1.147): Publisher abstract only (ILWCH 57, 2000, 69–75); the article body is unread. Eley and Nield's essay is marked by a tension between detaching social history from "its materialist assumptions" and continuing "narratives of working-class political agency"; "By insisting that class is still the best way of analyzing inequality and mobilizing resistance to it, the authors foreclose other possibilities for thinking about contemporary politics and for writing critical history"; her questions "don't exclude class but they don't require it either". Moderate. Distinct from edge_105 (the linguistic turn's critique of social history, citing her 1991 essay).

edges.relationship: With Ethan Kleinberg and Gary Wilder, a call for “critical history” as “theorized history”, against a discipline founded on empiricism, “fetishism of archives” and a gendered dismissal of theory (Theses on Theory and History, 2018)
edges.evidence_note: The collective's own words, read in full (English booklet on the History and Theory site, 2018; cited by thesis). Prologue: theory "displaced by empires of empiricism, fetishism of archives, dictates of discipline, enforcement of orthodoxy, and impotent story-telling"; I.1: "Academic history has never managed to transcend its eighteenth century origins as an empiricist enterprise"; II.1: "An invidious distinction between a feminized philosophy and a masculinized history"; III.1: "Critical history is theorized history"; III.7: "Critical history is a history of the present". Co-authored: credit belongs to all three, and no thesis is assigned to Scott alone. A late intervention in disputes about disciplinary scrutiny, not a resolution of them.

edges.relationship: Four questions put to White (1993): whether a determinist theory of language fits the freedom White grants historians, whether his tropology should itself be historicised, what becomes of research's “heavy and demanding operations”, and how his relativism answers the Shoah and its deniers, as White restates them in his rejoinder
edges.evidence_note: Chartier's article ("Quatre questions à Hayden White", Storia della Storiografia 24, 1993, 133–142) is unread. The four questions are known through White's 1995 rejoinder, read in full in its authorised Portuguese translation (Revista de Teoria da História 28, 2025, published 14 April 2026): (1) whether it is "contraditório" to invoke a post-Saussurean, "determinista" theory of language while granting historians a poet's freedom (p. 4); (2) whether he treated one tropology as inherent to Western consciousness instead of contextualising the historians' discourses (p. 5); (3) how to regard "opérations très lourdes et exigeantes que sont la constitution d'un corpus documentaire, le contrôle des données et des hypothèses, la construction d'interprétation" (Chartier's French, quoted by White, p. 6); (4) how White's "relativismo" meets the demand for truth raised by the "crimes commis par les tyrannies ou, plus encore, la Shoah" and by revisionist denial (pp. 7–8). Metadata of both articles from Domańska's bibliography. White calls the exchange friendly (p. 4); a critique of Metahistory's assumptions, not a rejection of White's work as a whole.
edges.map_label: Chartier’s four questions to White, 1993, as White restates them

edges.relationship: White’s rejoinder (1995): no contradiction between linguistic codes that limit what can be said and freely chosen codes; his tropology was dominant in Western discourse from the late Renaissance; much of erudition’s apparatus is a ritual “theatre” of good faith; Holocaust denial raises no methodological question
edges.evidence_note: White's own words, read in full in the authorised Portuguese translation (Revista de Teoria da História 28, 2025, e83664, published 14 April 2026; English renderings are atlas translations from Portuguese; the 1995 English original, Storia della Storiografia 27, 63–70, not seen). "Eu estava falando de discursos, não do cosmos" (p. 4); the fourfold tropology was "culturalmente dominante no Ocidente desde o final do Renascimento até o Modernismo", and "O modelo talvez tenha sido menos útil do que eu imaginava; não foi muito bem recebido. Mas era melhor, penso eu, do que não ter modelo nenhum" (p. 5); "A tradução das coisas da realidade em coisas do discurso é uma ficcionalização" and much of the operations Chartier names "pertence ao “teatro” da erudição acadêmica; tem uma função ritual" (pp. 6–7); the deniers "simplesmente (e de forma bastante perversa) negam a ocorrência de certos eventos", and "Não há qualquer questão metodológica em jogo" (pp. 7–8). A reply within a courteous exchange (p. 4), including a concession about his model's reception.

edges.relationship: Practices are not reducible to discourse: the logic of discourses differs from the logic of conduct, social positions are conditions of possibility of discourse, and cultural historians have moved away from “the illusions of the linguistic turn” (2003)
edges.evidence_note: His own words, read in full (Cahiers du CRH 31, 2003, OpenEdition; paragraphs cited). The linguistic turn holds "que la « réalité » n'est pas une référence objective, extérieure au discours"; against it, accessing past practices through texts does not mean "affirmer l'identité de deux logiques" (¶25). Social positions "ne sont pas seulement un effet des discours ; elles en désignent également les conditions de possibilité" (¶26). Cultural historians "se sont éloignés tant des illusions du tournant linguistique que des héritages contraignants qui postulaient le primat du politique ou la toute-puissance du social" (¶31). Foucault's own distinction between discursive formations and non-discursive systems is one of his resources (¶25 n. 25), so this is a critique of a position, not of every author grouped under this entry; Hayden White is not named in the article.

edges.relationship: Doubts the coherence Hunt claimed for the new cultural history in 1989: by 2003 it is held together by shared questions and debate rather than by a unified approach
edges.evidence_note: His own words, read in full (Cahiers du CRH 31, 2003). He starts from Hunt's 1989 volume and its three defining traits (¶1–3) and endorses her emphasis on sexual identities as "l'un des traits originaux de la new cultural history" (¶30). Then: "La cohérence la new cultural history est-elle aussi forte que le proclamait Lynn Hunt ? La diversité des objets de recherche, des perspectives méthodologiques et des références théoriques … permet d'en douter"; the field "n'est pas, ou n'est plus, définie par l'unité de son approche, mais par l'espace d'échanges et de débats" (¶31). A bounded disagreement about one claim, within an account that adopts her categories; not a rejection of her work.
edges.map_label: Doubting a unified new cultural history, 2003

edges.relationship: Bourdieu’s distinction between practical sense and scholastic reason (cited 2003) and his account of social difference (2007 dialogue); Certeau restored the space of readers’ appropriation, though Chartier rejects reading his “poaching” as absolute freedom
edges.evidence_note: His own words. 2003 article, read in full: to think "cette irréductibilité de l'expérience au discours", historians could rely on Foucault's distinction and on "celle établie par Bourdieu entre « sens pratique » et « raison scolastique »" (¶25, n. 26: Méditations pascaliennes, 1997). 2007 dialogue with Darnton, read in part in Portuguese translation (MATRIZes 5:2, 2012): social difference "não decorre apenas dessa tradição da história social da Annales, decorre também … ao trabalho de Pierre Bourdieu" (p. 164); no contradiction between Bourdieu's sociology of cultural production and McKenzie's sociology of texts (p. 166); "De Certeau, entre outros, restituiu este espaço" between constraints and readers' appropriation, but "seria um erro acreditar que esta liberdade é absoluta" (p. 167). In 1988 he recorded five radio dialogues with Bourdieu, published as a book in 2010 (presentation, p. 162; Prismas bibliography). Named resources with qualifications, not adherence to a school.

edges.relationship: Later studies of the mobility of texts across attributions, printed versions, forms of publication, genres and translations: the lost Cardenio between Cervantes and Shakespeare (2011) and Éditer et traduire (2021), in their reviewers’ accounts
edges.evidence_note: Mediated: the books are unread. Boucheron's review of Cardenio (Books & Ideas, 2014; consulted through WebFetch extraction; selected quoted passages recorded; full text not collated): its problem is "the discrepancy between the mobility of texts and the stability of authorial names"; Boucheron expects the claim that the author function took its final form in the eighteenth century to "provoke debate, particularly among Medievalists": an anticipated objection, not a later controversy investigated here. Jouhaud (Prismas 26, 2022, pp. 236–237, read) quotes Éditer et traduire on "las cinco modalidades que suministran a las obras su movilidad" (attribution, printed variants, forms of publication, genres, translation). Chartier's own 2020–2021 Collège de France report (read via WebFetch extraction) describes research "vouées à comprendre les raisons de la mobilité des textes". Prismas's bibliography dates the books (2011; 2021). A contribution to the history of publishing and circulation within intellectual history; Darnton's separate strand membership is unchanged.
edges.map_label: The mobility of texts, 2011–2021, per reviewers

edges.relationship: History as “the raw material for nationalist or ethnic or fundamentalist ideologies”: national myths, anachronism and schoolbook pasts that historians must resist “as they are being formed” (1993 lecture)
edges.evidence_note: His own words, read in full ("The New Threat to History", lecture opening the academic year at the Central European University, published in the NYRB, 16 December 1993; no pagination). "For history is the raw material for nationalist or ethnic or fundamentalist ideologies, as poppies are the raw material for heroin addiction … If there is no suitable past, it can always be invented"; "The most usual ideological abuse of history is based on anachronism rather than lies" (examples: Macedonia, Croatian schoolbooks, Ayodhya, Kosovo 1389); "History is not ancestral memory or collective tradition. It is what people learned from priests, schoolmasters, the writers of history books"; "We must resist the formation of national, ethnic, and other myths, as they are being formed." He also credits criticism of national myths "from within" (Israel, Ireland). The link to The Invention of Tradition (1983) rests only on the lecture's own "it can always be invented" and the existing publisher record; the 1983 introduction is unread.

edges.relationship: The Age of… volumes (1962–1994) as a synthesis of “the capitalist world from 1789 to 1991”, praised by reviewers for range and analytical grasp and called “unashamedly Eurocentric” by Judt
edges.evidence_note: Mediated: the four volumes are unread. Guardian obituarists (2012, read in full): the series "distilled the history of the capitalist world from 1789 to 1991" and "were not conceived as a tetralogy". Judt (NYRB 1995, read in full): the trilogy's scheme "eventually became the “conventional” interpretation, now exposed to steady criticism and revision"; "though unashamedly Eurocentric, Eric Hobsbawm has a unique range" (his endnote 2 defends the European focus). Black (Historein 2003–4, p. 215): "authoritative and commanding overviews of international history from the 18th century to present". Anderson (LRB 2002) quotes Hobsbawm on Interesting Times as "world history shaping that experience". At the 2014 conference (Times Higher Education report) Mazower spoke of a "golden age of historical synthesis". Counterweights: Judt's Eurocentrism remark and the existing critiques by Guha and Chakrabarty (edges 979, 917).
edges.map_label: The Age of… synthesis, 1962–94, per reviewers

edges.relationship: Tony Judt: The Age of Extremes keeps the categories of the 1930s, gives Bolshevism “no critical analytical attention except on its own restricted terms”, devotes “just six pages” to “real socialism” in the lands between Germany and Russia and neglects nationalism (1995)
edges.evidence_note: A named reader without a node, drawn from political history because his charge concerns the book's political history. Judt (NYRB, 25 May 1995, read in full): the book's "defect, for there is really only one" is that "the categories right/left, fascist/Communist, progressive and reactionary seem to be very firmly set, and pretty much as they first presented themselves to Hobsbawm in the Thirties"; Bolshevism gets "no critical analytical attention except on its own restricted terms"; "“real socialism” in the lands between Germany and Russia merits just six pages"; the claim that Sovietisation followed American intervention "is simply wrong"; nationalism "is a rather neglected subject"; Hobsbawm "mostly avoids military or political narrative". Qualifications kept: Judt calls the book "a challenging, often brilliant, and always cool and intelligent account", praises its economic analysis and calls The Age of Capital "Hobsbawm’s single greatest work". The Age of Extremes itself is unread.
edges.map_label: Judt on The Age of Extremes, 1995

edges.relationship: Industrial Britain and its workers: the standard-of-living debate of the 1950s and Industry and Empire (1968), which his readers credit with recasting the economic history of Britain
edges.evidence_note: Mediated: no economic-history text by Hobsbawm was read (his 1957 Economic History Review article is metadata only). Judt (NYRB 1995): Labouring Men, Industry and Empire and Captain Swing "substantially recast the economic history of Britain and the story of the British labor movement"; Hobsbawm is "by training and inclination an economic historian, and an analytical one at that". Guardian obituarists (2012): the "once celebrated 'standard of living' debate", in which he and R. M. Hartwell "traded arguments in successive numbers of the Economic History Review", and Industry and Empire (1968) as "a compelling summation of much of his work on Britain and the industrial revolution". Black (Historein, p. 215): "a key protagonist in the standard of living in the industrial revolution debates … something of a Cold War battleground". A pre-2000 gap repair; not a claim about the transition debate.
edges.map_label: Standard of living and Industry and Empire, per readers

edges.relationship: In Herman Paul’s 2019 assessment, White’s work became philosophy of history’s shared reference point, built on by Harlan, Kleinberg and Kuukkanen and contested by others; White himself assigned philosophy of history to the “practical past” (2010)
edges.evidence_note: Paul's author manuscript, read in full (Journal of the Philosophy of History 13, 2019; manuscript pages): "no other author occupies a position in the field that is remotely as central as White’s" (ms 1); his only measure is his own JSTOR count of History and Theory articles mentioning White (ms 10 n. 22), with Harlan, Kleinberg and Kuukkanen positioning themselves towards him (ms 10–11). White's own words, read in full (Historein 10, 2010, p. 18): "philosophy of history belongs to the class of disciplines meant to bring order and reason to a 'practical past'". Counterweight: Timmins (Reviews in History, 2011) remains "to be convinced that White's impact on historical writing is as great as the current narratives claim" — a claim about historians' practice, not philosophy of history. Reciprocal to edge_166 (the earlier philosophers White engaged), not parallel to it.
edges.map_label: Paul: White as the field’s reference point, 2019

edges.relationship: Philosophers of history contest White’s narrativism, as Herman Paul reports: Ricoeur on the constraints set by sources, David Carr on narrative in lived experience, Lorenz’s internal realism, Ankersmit on untheorised tropes and Runia on presence (1985–2013)
edges.evidence_note: Mediated: the critics' texts are unread and known through Paul's manuscript, read in full (2019, ms 17–19): Ankersmit finds the tropology "not nearly philosophical enough"; for Ricoeur sources "set constraints" and White "runs a risk of erasing genre boundaries between history and fiction" (Temps et récit 3, 1985); David Carr (1986); "'internal realists' such as Chris Lorenz argue that White downplays the importance of rational debate among historians"; Runia's "presence" against "Whitean representationalism" (2006). Paul's caveat: criticism is sometimes "a response elicited by the perceived dominance of his work" (ms 19). A second witness for David Carr: Cronon (1992, pp. 1368–1369, read) prefers Carr's position to White's and Mink's. Distinct from edge_257, where historians (Ginzburg, Evans) answer postmodernism.
edges.map_label: Ricoeur, David Carr, Lorenz, Ankersmit, Runia, per Paul

edges.relationship: A historian of European thought before Metahistory, who coauthored two textbooks on liberal humanism in Western Europe (1966, 1970) and wrote essays on the tasks of intellectual history, as Paul and Sanz Loroño report; Martin Jay ranks his reflections on the craft with Skinner’s (2013)
edges.evidence_note: Mediated: the 1960s books and essays are unread. Paul (2019, ms 13 n. 32, read in full): The Emergence of Liberal Humanism: An Intellectual History of Western Europe (1966, with Coates and Schapiro) and The Ordeal of Liberal Humanism (1970, with Coates). Sanz Loroño (Historiografías, 2011, p. 143, read in full): The Fiction of Narrative reprints "The tasks of intellectual history" and "Romanticism, historicism, and realism", the latter readable "como un Metahistory anterior al impacto del (pos) estructuralismo francés". Stovall's AHA memorial (2018, WebFetch) presents him as an intellectual historian and theorist. Jay (History and Theory, 2013, abstract only): "No contemporary intellectual historian has produced more influential reflections on the historian's craft than Hayden White and Quentin Skinner". No strand is targeted.
edges.map_label: Intellectual historian of Europe, per readers

edges.relationship: White asks what limits govern the stories that can responsibly be told about the Holocaust (Probing the Limits of Representation, 1992; reprinted in Figural Realism); the quoted excerpt makes a conditional argument about facts determining plots. His 2014 contents also list “Truth and Circumstance …”; that chapter is unread
edges.evidence_note: An excerpt witness: the passages of the essay quoted by Claus and Marriott, whose framing is theirs (white_emplotment_excerpt, existing reading, re-read for revision 1.147): "Are there any limits on the kind of story that can responsibly be told about these phenomena?"; facts set limits on stories "only if we believe that the events themselves possess a 'story' kind of form and a 'plot' kind of meaning" — a conditional argument about facts determining plots, not a claim that all emplotments are equally valid, and not the full argument of the chapter. The essay's pages (37–53 in Friedländer's volume) and its discussion by Ginzburg and Funkenstein come from Domańska's bibliography; MUSE contents show it reprinted as Figural Realism ch. 2 (pp. 27–42) and the 2014 chapter "Truth and Circumstance: What (if Anything) Can Properly Be Said about the Holocaust?" (pp. 25–40), both unread. Paul (2019, ms 15) records his later "forays into 'modernist events,' … witness literature, trauma". Holocaust representation was previously carried only at group level (edges 223, 224) and in Friedländer's roster row.

edges.relationship: Cronon builds on White’s distinction between chronicle and narrative, then sides with David Carr against the White–Mink view that historians impose plots on reality (1992)
edges.evidence_note: Cronon's own text, read in part for this edge ("A Place for Stories", JAH 78:4, 1992, author-hosted copy in journal pagination): p. 1351 n. 7, "This distinction between chronicle and narrative is more fully analyzed in White, Metahistory, 5-7; White, Tropics of Discourse, 109-11"; p. 1368, White and Mink "argue that narrative is so basic to our cultural beliefs that we automatically impose it on a reality that bears little or no relation to the plots we use" (Cronon's summary of their position); n. 39 calls White's 1984 survey "useful, if biased"; pp. 1368–1369, Carr's position "gives us a way of absorbing the lessons of narrative theory without feeling we have abandoned all ties to an external reality". One essay makes both moves, so one arrow records an acknowledged and contested resource (the pattern of edge_646). edge_903 (Cronon → truthdebate) uses other pages of the same essay for his own position.
edges.map_label: Chronicle and narrative: used and contested, 1992

edges.relationship: McKay's historical work is Gramscian by his own account: cultural hegemony in The Quest of the Folk (1994), and 'the Gramscian assumptions that have shaped my outlook' (2000)
edges.evidence_note: McKay's own words, read in full ("A Note on 'Region' in Writing the History of Atlantic Canada", Acadiensis 29:2, 2000, p. 89): 'the Gramscian assumptions that have shaped my outlook'. Muise (Acadiensis 27:2, 1998, read pp. 124, 128–132) reports that in The Quest of the Folk McKay places himself 'within a neo-marxist framework associated with the work of Antonio Gramsci' and quotes the book (p. 306): 'the concept of the Folk was and remains a powerful obstacle to the formation of a counter-hegemonic cultural politics'. Wright (Acadiensis 24:2, 1995, p. 132 n. 29): 'For a very skilled handling of Antonio Gramsci's theory of cultural hegemony by an historian see Ian McKay, The Quest of the Folk'. Critic: Palmer (2009) argues that McKay's Gramsci conflates hegemony and domination. The Quest of the Folk is given through these readers. Distinct from edge_844 (Gramsci → the liberal order framework, 2000): this arrow carries the influence on McKay's work from 1994, before the prospectus.

edges.relationship: The global held to be a human-centred frame, “insufficient (but not unnecessary)” once human history meets geological time, and Big History’s hope that large-scale history yields “global citizenship” questioned (2015–22)
edges.evidence_note: His own words. Tanner Lectures (Yale, 18–19 February 2015; official text read in part, unpaginated), lecture II: "this assumption that thinking on large scales leads to a sense of human solidarity or 'global citizenship' has found a resurgent expression in a branch of historical scholarship that calls itself Big (or sometime Deep) History"; in David Christian's hands "the history of the human species merges seamlessly with the history of 'humanity'"; Christian "directly cites the world-history pioneer William McNeill's 1986 presidential address" (McNeill's words are given only as Christian quotes them). A note on Smail ("I agree, and I do not") announces "Some Friendly Amendments": an amendment, not a rejection. The Review of Politics (2022), his introduction, read in full: the convergence of human and natural histories "has rendered insufficient (but not unnecessary)" the framework of empire, race and global capitalism; labels "such as 'modern' or 'global' now have to be thought together with the much larger-scale units of geological time"; "The global is anthropocentric while the planet de-centers and provincializes the human" (p. 593); his response calls capital and empire "a necessary but insufficient framework" (p. 610). Context: the 2014 Toynbee Prize "for his contributions to global history" (university biography), presented with his lecture "From Globalization to Global Warming" on 3 January 2015 (lecture unread). Reception: Getachew (2022, p. 601) calls the planetary turn "a significant departure from and challenge to" his own anticolonial and postcolonial traditions. edge_124 (post → global, critique) records the group's 2000 critique of Eurocentric global narratives; this is a different, later claim about scale.
edges.map_label: Globe and planet: amending world and Big History, 2015–22

edges.relationship: The distinction between human and natural history, defended “from Hegel and Marx to Croce and Collingwood”, held to collapse under anthropogenic climate change: the starting point of his climate work (2009–22)
edges.evidence_note: His own words. The Review of Politics (2022), introduction, read in full: "This collapse of the distinction, defended over the last two centuries by philosophers ranging from Hegel and Marx to Croce and Collingwood, between humanist histories of humans and their natural histories provides the starting point for my book" (p. 593). The 2009 essay's first thesis (existing reading, p. 201): anthropogenic climate change spells "the Collapse of the Age-old Humanist Distinction between Natural History and Human History"; the essay was read in full in an earlier pass (2026-10-14; see its source note), but the passages then recorded (pp. 199, 201, 205–208, 212, 219–222) do not include its discussion of Croce and Collingwood, which was not rechecked in this wave and is not quoted. The edge rests on the 2022 paragraph. Richard Staley (2024, read) summarises the later book's view that postcolonial scholars "inherited a strong human/non-human nature distinction from philosophers of history who argued that history is limited to human affairs" (p. 658), while calling the first thesis "one of the most problematic arguments" of the 2009 essay (see the science critique). This concerns only the human/natural distinction of idealist philosophy of history; it is not the developmental "historicism" ("first in Europe, then elsewhere") that Provincializing Europe criticised (edge_914), a different sense of the word.
edges.map_label: Against the human/natural divide of Croce and Collingwood, 2009–22

edges.relationship: Critics of the four theses question the “species” category, holding inequalities within humanity integral to the ecological crisis (Malm and Hornborg, 2014; abstract only; that they address him is his report), and whether a divide between human and natural history ever existed (the environmental historian LeCain, 2016); Chakrabarty answers that capital is “a necessary but insufficient framework” (2015–22)
edges.evidence_note: Named critics drawn from environmental history, where the 2009 essay was taken up (edge_918). Andreas Malm and Alf Hornborg, "The Geology of Mankind?" (Anthropocene Review, 2014): abstract only; it "questions the use of the species category in the Anthropocene narrative and argues that it is analytically flawed, as well as inimical to action", and holds that "Intra-species inequalities are part and parcel of the current ecological crisis". The abstract does not name Chakrabarty; that they "took me to task" is his own report (2016 response, p. 108, existing reading; Tanner lecture I, read, whose note cites them for the "capitalocene" objection). They write as human ecologists, not environmental historians. Timothy LeCain, an environmental historian (Whose Anthropocene?, 2016, existing reading): "it becomes reasonable to ask whether there was ever a divide in the first place" (p. 17). His answers: geological names do not "assign moral responsibility" (Tanner lecture I); "My book does not deny the role of capitalism", capital being "a necessary but insufficient framework" (Review of Politics, 2022, p. 610). Pitts (2022, read) finds his reasons for holding the Capitalocene "at arm's length" in "fascinating and productive" tension (p. 607). Balance from the field: Atte Arffman, reviewing the 2021 book in Environment and History (2022, read), writes that "not many have delved as deep as Chakrabarty does". The endpoint locates named interventions; it does not make them environmental history's verdict.
edges.map_label: Species or capital? Critics of the four theses, 2014–16 (Malm and Hornborg abstract only)

edges.relationship: A historian of science finds the 2009 thesis of a collapsing human/nature divide “one of the most problematic arguments”, since histories of climate such as Golinski’s had stressed the link between human and nature, and the later politics too abstract (Staley, 2024)
edges.evidence_note: One named reader, read in full: Richard Staley, review of One Planet, Many Worlds (British Journal for the History of Science 57:4, 2024): "One of the most problematic arguments of The Climate of History was its assertion that 'Anthropogenic Explanations of Climate Change Spell the Collapse of the Age-old Humanist Distinction between Natural History and Human History'. This impression of the novelty of the Anthropocene might have been dispelled by attention to the considerable work stressing the common link between human and nature in concepts of climate, such as Jan Golinski's British Weather and the Climate of Enlightenment (2007)" (p. 658); "without engaging in significant emerging literatures on the history and politics of climate science and governance policies, we are left with the somewhat abstract entreaty" (p. 659). Kept in his appraisal: Chakrabarty "has responded to critics and sharpened his account" (p. 657), and the 2023 book is "more appropriately concerned with the recent origins of a separation between humans and nature" (p. 658). Golinski is named only by Staley. The 2023 book is unread. One reviewer, not the field's verdict.
edges.map_label: Staley on the novelty of the divide, 2024

edges.relationship: The Calling of History (2015) reads Jadunath Sarkar’s “imperial liberalism” and his public quarrels with nationalist historians over objectivity and sources, asking when a society values the “cloistered life” of history, as Joshi and the publisher report
edges.evidence_note: The book is unread; its argument is given as its readers state it. Publisher's description: through "more than twelve hundred letters", historians in colonial India "formulated the basic concepts and practices of the field via vigorous—and at times bitter and hurtful—debates in the public sphere". Girija Joshi's review (Práticas da História 3, 2016, read in full): Sarkar appeared "to be a spokesperson for what Chakrabarty calls 'imperial liberalism' (p. 49)", while his rivals of the Bharat Itihas Samshodhak Mandal valued "an ability to understand 'the spirit' of the source" (p. 152); the book asks under what circumstances "a society values the 'objectivity' ... of historical research", and when the public life of history defers to its "cloistered life" (book p. 6; review p. 153). Suman Seth (History and Theory, 2017; abstract only) reads it as "a defense of rationalist history in the face of contemporary threats posed by the rise of a politics of identity in India". A contribution to the history of colonial and national historiography in India; no strand is assigned.
edges.map_label: Jadunath Sarkar and the public life of history, 2015 (as reviewed)

edges.relationship: Historians answer the deconstructive turn she helped bring into Indian history: Eaton names her 1985 reading of Subaltern Studies as a hinge of a turn to “literary criticism” whose costs he finds greater than its gains (2000); Moran rereads the Sirmur records behind her 1985 archive essay and finds the rani “an astute ruler” (2014)
edges.evidence_note: Two named historians without nodes, drawn from the entry for historians' responses to postmodernism (the pattern of edge_257 and edge_933). Richard M. Eaton, "(Re)imag(in)ing Other²ness: A Postmortem for the Postmodern in India" (Journal of World History 11:1, 2000), read pp. 57–61 and 77–78: the collective moved "from a positivist and empiricist orientation to one grounded more squarely in a literary criticism"; in Subaltern Studies IV (1985) "Gayatri Spivak criticized subalternist historians for having adopted positivist methodologies" and, "herself a literary critic, urged historians to continue their efforts to recover subaltern consciousness even while knowing this was impossible" (p. 60); the turn's "modest reminder" is "vastly outweighed" by "an ahistorical and structuralist methodology incapable of explaining historical particularity" (p. 78). His target is the postmodern turn in Indian history as a whole, with Spivak and Cohn as named hinges. Arik Moran, "'The Rani of Sirmur' Revisited" (Modern Asian Studies 49:2, 2015; online 17 September 2014), read in part: "a close reading of the records reveals profound discrepancies between Spivak's interpretation and conditions that existed in and around the kingdom at the time"; the rani "was actually an astute ruler"; her "misreading of evidence goes beyond the boundaries of the discipline as such", although "her fresh approach to source material does point to the cardinal importance of interdisciplinary research". Moran cites Eaton (n. 3). Her 1985 History and Theory essay is unread; its claims are given only as Moran presents them. These are two historians' objections, not the discipline's verdict; in period Prakash and Sarkar read her more favourably (edge_983).
edges.map_label: Eaton and Moran: historians against the reading, 2000–14

edges.relationship: The co-editor of Selected Subaltern Studies (1988) questions Guha’s programme from within: his recovery of subaltern consciousness read as “a strategic use of positivist essentialism” (1985), and his insistence on the “full autonomy” of the subaltern domain not endorsed (1988)
edges.evidence_note: A repair to the pre-2000 core, from existing readings of her own texts. "Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography" (Subaltern Studies IV, 1985; read in full for revision 1.137): quoting Elementary Aspects while "Reading the work of Subaltern Studies from within but against the grain" (p. 341), she reads the project of retrieving subaltern consciousness "as a strategic use of positivist essentialism in a scrupulously visible political interest" (p. 342). "Can the Subaltern Speak?" (1988; existing reading of the Williams and Chrisman reprint): of Guha's autonomous domain, "I cannot entirely endorse this insistence on determinate vigor and full autonomy" (p. 79). Collaboration in the same years: Selected Subaltern Studies (Oxford University Press, 1988), edited by Guha and Spivak (title as recorded on said_subaltern_foreword_1988; Roosa, 2006, n. 4, read). A later historian's summary: Eaton (2000, p. 60) reads the 1985 essay as criticism of "subalternist historians". edge_984 (Spivak → subaltern, critique) carries her critique of the collective's recovery of consciousness and its neglect of gender, and from this revision no longer names the autonomy claim in its relationship; this edge carries the person-to-person disagreement with Guha's autonomy claim, which Guha's own entry already names among the in-period critiques. A critique from a collaborator, not a rejection.

edges.relationship: Hegel’s World-history criticised as a statist, Eurocentric frame, which in Guha’s words as Michael quotes them reached India “as an instrument of the East India Company’s colonial project”, and historians asked to learn from literature the “historicality” of everyday life (2002), as his reviewers and Chakrabarty read the book; Michael finds the argument “mostly confined to the conceptual level”
edges.evidence_note: History at the Limit of World-History (Columbia University Press, 2002) is unread; its argument is given as its readers state it. Bernardo A. Michael (Journal of World History 15:4, 2004, pp. 530–532, read in full): lectures given at the Italian Academy at Columbia; Guha "takes the German philosopher Georg Hegel and his conception of 'World-History' (Weltgeschichte) to task" (p. 530); he quotes Guha that "World-History made its way to the subcontinent as an instrument of the East India Company's colonial project and helped it set up the Raj" (book p. 51) and that history should be "a call for historicality to be rescued from its containment in World-History" (book p. 6). Michael places the book among "recent postcolonial efforts to rethink the practices of disciplinary history and thereby provincialize its European lineages" (p. 532), and objects that "losing sight of the state at the level of the everyday might mean the loss of it as an object of critique", that "Guha's arguments are mostly confined to the conceptual level", and that Guha "seems to attribute to Hegel's World-History an agency that is hard to locate in the historicality of the colonial world" (p. 532). The Company connection is therefore Guha's claim as Michael reports it, and Michael doubts that the book demonstrates how Hegel's ideas became colonial practice. The publisher's description: World-history "reduces the course of human history to the amoral record of states and empires"; historians "should learn from literature"; Tagore's critique of historiography. Chakrabarty (Australian Academy of the Humanities obituary, 2024, read in full) calls it "a grand statement about literature being a far better communicator of senses of the past in the Indian subcontinent than the European discipline of history that had come to India as a practice of the colonial state" and "his farewell to the discipline of history". The theme is older: Chakraborty (2000, read in full) reports that Dominance without Hegemony (1997) already charged colonial historiography with the Hegelian view "that precolonial India had no state, therefore no history" (p. 376). A contribution to the postcolonial critique of historicism alongside Chakrabarty's provincializing argument (edge_914), not a claim that Guha belongs to a school; edge_115 (subaltern → post) records the group.
edges.map_label: Against Hegel’s World-history, 2002 (as reviewers read it)

edges.relationship: Vivek Chibber: Dominance without Hegemony rests on “a highly mythologized story” of the English and French bourgeois revolutions, so its contrast between India’s bourgeoisie and Europe’s fails (2013–14); Sewell and Steinmetz accept the critique of Guha’s Europe, while Chatterjee, as Chibber reports him, denies that Guha made claims about those revolutions
edges.evidence_note: A named critic without a node, drawn from comparative historical sociology because his case is a comparison of the European bourgeois revolutions with Indian independence, and because his readers here include historical sociologists (Sewell is already a critic on this roster). Chibber's own words, read in part: Guha's work is "foundational for the entire Subalternist project" and "fundamentally flawed", because its "contrastive claims about the Indian bourgeoisie and Indian capitalism ... rest on a comparison with the European achievement", and "Guha quite dramatically misunderstands the European story" (response to Chatterjee, Verso, 25 February 2014); Guha's break between the bourgeoisies of West and East "flows from a highly mythologized story about the great Bourgeois revolutions, one that was rejected decades ago by historians" (JWSR 20:2, 2014, p. 313). Guha's words appear only as Chibber quotes them (Dominance without Hegemony, p. 19: the bourgeoisie's "historic triumphs in England in 1648 and France in 1789"; p. 5). Readers in the JWSR symposium: William H. Sewell Jr. (pp. 300–303, read in full) calls Guha's portrayal of the two revolutions "standard-issue orthodox Marxism—and ... well past its 'sell-by' date" (p. 301) while finding Chibber's own history "a bit shaky"; George Steinmetz (p. 284) writes that "Guha was relying on a version of Marxist political theory and German history that was demolished by the critics of the Sonderweg thesis"; Bruce Cumings finds the critique "persuasive, at least at the level of how one defines hegemony" (p. 290) but says "I don't know Guha's work" (p. 292), so Chibber's claim that all the critics accepted his reading of Guha (p. 313) is not adopted here. The defence: at the Historical Materialism conference (New York, April 2013) and in a written reply, Partha Chatterjee argued, as Chibber reports him, that Guha made no claims about the classic bourgeois revolutions and criticised only the historiography of colonial India; Chatterjee's text is unread. Chibber's book (Postcolonial Theory and the Specter of Capital, Verso, 2013) is unread; its focus on Guha and Chakrabarty is from Hung's introduction (p. 281). The endpoint locates the intervention; it does not make the critique the field's verdict.
edges.map_label: Chibber’s critique of Dominance without Hegemony, 2013–14

edges.relationship: A Rule of Property for Bengal (1963) traces the Permanent Settlement to the mercantilist, physiocratic and classical political economy of East India Company officials, as Bhambra reads it; she faults its neglect of the colonial context (2024)
edges.evidence_note: A repair to the pre-2000 core. The book (Paris: Mouton, 1963) is unread; it is known through its readers. Gurminder K. Bhambra (Discover Society, 2024, read in full): the book addresses the late-eighteenth-century debates among East India Company administrators over a "permanent settlement", and Guha "set out their different economic premises – deriving from mercantilist, physiocratic, and classical political economy – and demonstrated that, despite their differences, they nonetheless shared a common political focus, establishing the permanence of orderly dominion"; she quotes his p. 9 on entrusting revenue to "a class of native entrepreneurs who had solid interests in the land and were politically reliable". Her criticism: "his failure to locate the discussions of the East India Company administrators within their colonial context". She reports, without these being read here, Sarvepalli Gopal's 1966 view of the book as "primarily ... an exercise in British intellectual history" and Guha's answer in the 1981 preface to the second edition. Holmwood's editorial (2024) calls it "a major contribution to the history of political economy"; Chakrabarty (2024) writes that it "showed an early awareness of the importance of ideas in economic history". A contribution to the history of economic ideas in colonial policy; no claim is made about the book's reception by economists.
edges.map_label: A Rule of Property for Bengal, 1963 (as Bhambra reads it)

edges.relationship: Durkheim’s sociology criticised for taking society as the cause instead of a provisional consequence, against Tarde’s “all things are society”; actor-network theory replaces “the social” with “association” (2002), a programme restated in Reassembling the Social (2005)
edges.evidence_note: His own words. "Gabriel Tarde and the End of the Social", in Patrick Joyce, ed., The Social in Question: New Bearings in History and the Social Sciences (Routledge, 2002), pp. 117–132, read in part in the author's typescript (typescript pp. 1–2, 5, 7, 10): actor-network theory is "a deliberate attempt at terminating the use of the word 'social' in social theory to replace it with the word 'association'", and "ANT actually has a forefather, namely Gabriel Tarde" (p. 1); "Instead of saying, like Durkheim, that we 'should treat social facts as a thing', Tarde says that 'all things are society'" (p. 5); "Durkheim has taken society as the cause instead of seeing that it is never more than a highly provisional consequence" (p. 10). He concedes that he had once "never enquired further than the dismissive footnotes of the Durkheimians" (p. 2). Durkheim's position is given only as Latour presents it. Reassembling the Social (2005) is unread; the author's description presents sociology as "the science of associations and not only as the science of the social". The essay appeared in a volume addressed to historians and social scientists, edited by the historian Patrick Joyce (citation only; Joyce's introduction unread). A critique of Durkheimian sociology, not of the historians who adapted it (durkheim/historical_method).
edges.map_label: Tarde against Durkheim: the end of the social, 2002–05

edges.relationship: An “anthropology of the Moderns”: fieldwork at the heart of modern institutions (science, economy, politics, law) that refuses to believe what the West says about itself, and distinguishes modes of existence that networks alone do not qualify (2012–13)
edges.evidence_note: His own words.
