sources.title: Carl Berger, The Sense of Power: Studies in the Ideas of Canadian Imperialism, 1867–1914 (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1970; 2nd ed. 2013).
sources.citation: Carl Berger, The Sense of Power: Studies in the Ideas of Canadian Imperialism, 1867–1914 (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1970; 2nd ed. 2013).

verification.note: Contents read (2nd ed.): "Men", "Canada First", "The Loyalist Tradition", "Progress and Liberty", "The Canadian Character", "Critique of the Republic", "Social Criticism and Reform", "Mission", "Militarism". The book's thesis is not read; the first-edition year (1970 vs 1971) should be confirmed. Thesis (added 2026-10-12, partly verified): Berger's formulation that Canadian imperialism was one variety (Stamp) or version (Cook) of Canadian nationalism is known from two later scholars' quotations and the UTP publisher copy ('significantly influenced by its leading advocates' belief in nationalism'); the exact word and page in the 1970 introduction are unchecked, so the draft paraphrases and does not quote. Checked against: Open Library work OL2446797W (UTP; earliest edition record dated 1971); Crossref record of a review, International Journal 26:1 (1970–71), doi:10.2307/40201036; Crossref DOI and chapter DOIs of the 2013 second edition (contents); for the thesis: 49th Shelf UTP publisher copy (https://49thshelf.com/content/view/full/5186340), Ramsay Cook, Literary Review of Canada, April 2013 (https://reviewcanada.ca/magazine/2013/04/beverley-baxter-in-empireland/), Robert M. Stamp, Project MUSE article 675533 (search snippet only). Addendum 2026-10-14: Thesis checked in Google Books snippet view of the 2013 second edition (volume -Y-BAAAAQBAJ); its pages 3–265 reprint the 1970 text with the same pagination (Monet 1972 cites pp. 132 and 261 for passages found on those pages here). Snippets are short fragments returned by search; the continuous text was not read. Introduction opens 'This book is a study in Canadian nationalist thought' (p. 3); 'one variety of Canadian nationalism', a 'type of awareness of nationality which rested upon a certain understanding of history, the national character, and the national mission', and the critique of the 'so-called liberal nationalist school' and of Skelton's Laurier (p. 9); method (p. 10). Conclusion opens 'Imperialism was one form of Canadian nationalism' (p. 259). So both words occur: 'variety' (p. 9) and 'form' (p. 259). First edition: Monet's and Mills's reviews give University of Toronto Press, 1970 (277 pp.); Karr cites 1971.

sources.scope_note: The ideas of Canadian imperialists: character, mission, loyalism, militarism; imperialism as one form of Canadian nationalism (paraphrase, word and page unchecked).

verification.note: Full text read (answers/research/q11-intellectual-history-critique.json). Analyses the field's 'preoccupation with delineating the national mind', its 'propensity to place everything in an atmosphere of crisis' and 'its narrow, elitist, biographical methodology' (p. 160); group biography after Berger's Sense of Power focuses on 'an elite group composed primarily of academics, journalists and clergymen' (p. 169), leaving little known of what the population thought. Names Berger, McKillop, Cook, Shortt, Levitt, Allen and Francis; calls the books 'excellent studies within their self-imposed context'. Checked against: Acadiensis article page and full text (https://journals.lib.unb.ca/index.php/Acadiensis/article/view/12284; https://journals.lib.unb.ca/index.php/Acadiensis/article/download/12284/13128); Érudit record (https://www.erudit.org/en/journals/acadiensis/1989-v18-n2-acadiensis_18_2/acad18_2re04/). Addendum 2026-10-14: Re-read 2026-10-14 for the Berger person entry (Acadiensis PDF, pp. 158–174, page numbers from running heads). p. 160: 'Ever since Carl Berger used this basic approach in his impressive study of imperialism in the early 1970s, many have adopted his methodology'; p. 161: Berger 'rescued the previously outcast imperialists and transformed them into significant Canadian nationalists' and 'As a sequel he analysed the national conceptual frameworks in which professional historians functioned and wrote'; pp. 162–163: 'over-Canadianization of imperialism' and Carr's 'scavenger hunt for nationalism' (n. 20: Carr 1982; Cole 1970, 1971; Page 1970); p. 167: group biography 'upheld by many historians in Canada as the best method'; p. 168: Berger's premise (Sense of Power, p. 12, per n. 36) and 'whatever a single advocate chooses to believe'. sources.citation: Allan Greer, "Settler Colonialism and Beyond," Journal of the Canadian Historical Association / Revue de la Société historique du Canada 30, no. 1 (2019): 61–86.

verification.note: Abstract read: the settler approach has much to offer, but across 500 years of invading Indigenous North America the settler variety dominates some periods and regions and fades in others. 'Imperial/Commercial Penetration' and 'Extractivism' are other modes; extractivism has become predominant in recent decades. Addendum 2026-10-14: Read in full for the 1.139 Allan Greer person entry (Érudit PDF served to an ordinary request; text layer; folios 61–79, notes 80–86). Based on a keynote address to the CHA annual meeting (first-page note). Passages used: settler colonial theory 'does indeed have much to offer historians' but 'the settler variety stands out as a dominant force in some periods and regions, but it fades to insignificance in others' (p. 62); 'The late Patrick Wolfe, still the most important theorist of settler colonialism' (p. 62); the hazard of 'temporal flattening' 'when settler colonialism is casually invoked in ways that suggest a transhistorical, always-already quality, as though the settler-colonial condition had no discernible beginning and as if it could never end' (p. 63); 'Let me assure you that I am not here to trash or dismiss settler-colonial theory. I personally think it has a great deal to offer anyone trying to understand the present and the past of a country such as Canada' (p. 63); historians 'need to take on board the critique of settler-national historiography sketched out by Wolfe and developed more fully by others such as Lorenzo Veracini' (p. 63); 'However, that doesn't mean we need to find settler colonialism everywhere and all the time' (p. 63); 'My objective is to try to historicize settler colonialism' (p. 63); 'Imperial/Commercial Penetration' and 'Extractivism' as 'coexisting and overlapping versions of colonialism' (p. 64); early settlements 'hardly functioned as instruments of elimination and replacement except in quite limited, localized ways' (p. 64); settler colonization 'emerged as an important independent force' only from the last quarter of the eighteenth century (p. 70); 'The time may be right, then, for a renewed history of the Confederation era, one that unites the history of state formation with that of settler colonialism' (p. 73), with n. 41: 'A prime example of this problem would be Colonial Leviathan; devoted to questions of state formation, it neglected everything to do with Indigenous peoples and processes of elimination' (p. 84); 'To those who insist that Canada is, was, and always has been a settler-colonial phenomenon, I offer qualified support' (p. 73); 'settlers as such are no longer the main threat, for the invasion has adopted a different guise' (p. 74); 'Settler colonialism stands out also as a fundamental force behind the creation of a territorial nation-state' and 'An order based on territorial dispossession is not, and never has been, normal, natural, and inevitable' (p. 79). The source's page range 61–86 includes the notes.

verification.note: Abstract read: an analysis of “the concept of working-class culture as applied by some practitioners of the new labour history in Canada”; questions “the validity of using such a general framework” — the evidence at times supports working-class culture as an important determinant and at other times does not; argues that to insist history be studied “from the bottom up” is “as predeterministic as the notion that it should be studied ‘from the top down.’” Published in the issue’s Critiques section; Kealey replies in the same issue (wcreq_kealey_1981). Checked against: Labour/Le Travail article page with abstract, https://lltjournal.ca/index.php/llt/article/view/2658 (read 2026-10-12); Crossref DOI record (JSTOR); answers/verification.json Q29. Addendum 2026-10-13: Full text read (Érudit PDF, id.erudit.org/iderudit/llt7cri02, pp. 95–112). p. 97: Canadian practitioners of the new labour history “follow the thinking of E.P. Thompson in Britain, Herbert Gutman in the United States, and others in applying the culturalist approach to Canadian experience”; “Palmer, echoing E.P. Thompson, regards culture and conflict as ‘complementary processes’” (citing A Culture in Conflict, p. xii, which was not itself checked). p. 98: in Canada new labour historians “stand in the middle but so far tend to lean to the British experience. They study working-class culture for the explanation and definition they believe it offers in the Thompson sense”. p. 108: “Even if Thompson is right about England, his concepts do not necessarily apply anywhere else.” A critic’s characterization, not a self-description. Addendum 2026-10-14: Pp. 95–97 and 107–108 re-read for the 1.134 person entry in the PDF on the journal's site (https://lltjournal.ca/index.php/llt/article/view/2658). p. 96: the new labour history's method 'as Palmer describes it' ('sharp detail of limited chronology or restricted region to illustrate the human dimensions of the past'; 'theory is meant to inform historical inquiry and, in turn, to be informed by historical research'; n. 10: A Culture in Conflict, xii–xiv) and 'what Palmer labels "a tradition of empirical Marxism"' (n. 11: xiii). p. 97: 'Palmer calls the skilled the cutting edge of the working class. They could just as easily be labelled the rearguard'; 'Palmer, echoing E.P. Thompson, regards culture and conflict as "complementary processes"' (n. 13: xii). pp. 107–108: 'Historians must prove that Canadian workers, men and women, skilled and unskilled, were bound by a common culture that was primarily the product of their class experience before they can use culture to explain anything'; workers 'seem to have responded as much from consciousness of job, place, church, ethnic group, and other factors as from a culture of class'; whether 'class was a more important means of self-identification than gender' (p. 107); 'Even if Thompson is right about England, his concepts do not necessarily apply anywhere else' (p. 108). Addendum 2026-10-14: Pp. 95–96 read for the 1.138 Kealey draft (lltjournal.ca article 2658): Bercuson opens on Kealey and Warrian's 1976 definition of the new labour history and their insistence that workers be studied 'in a totality' (p. 95); 'Kealey's study of Toronto workers contains at least five chapters devoted to working-class and trade-union politics'; 'the Palmer and Kealey books' as 'restricted but intensive studies' (p. 96).

verification.note: Abstract read: a contribution to the debate on the direction of social and working-class history, commenting on periodization, regionalism, ethnicity and culture; class analysis and the utility of culture for the study of Canadian workers are strongly defended. End page inferred from Bercuson’s start page; confirm. Checked against: Crossref DOI record; OpenAlex abstract (English and French). Addendum 2026-10-13: Pages 67–68 and 82–87 read closely with their footnotes; the rest skimmed by keyword (Érudit PDF, id.erudit.org/iderudit/llt7cri01; Critiques section, pp. 67–94, which also confirms the end page the existing record inferred). p. 67: the moment for evaluating the labour history of the 1960s–70s has arrived, signalled in Britain by the confrontation of “Althusserian structuralism and Thompsonian ‘culturalist’ or ‘socialist-humanist’ history”. p. 68: names McNaught’s forthcoming “E.P. Thompson vs. Harold Logan” as making “only too clear the eminently political nature of the emerging debate”. pp. 82–83: The Making of the English Working Class “has probably been the most influential piece of historical writing in the English language published since 1960”; “For our purposes, Thompson’s influence is our concern”; in North America “the critics are most often anti-Marxists attacking works which have associated themselves with Thompson’s method”. p. 87: quotes Bercuson (1979) accusing working-class historians of paying “due obeisance to E.P. Thompson, the guru” and “shoehorning their subjects into a Thompsonian mould”, and concedes that those “who utilize the insights of British … social history” must “demonstrate convincingly that they apply to the Canadian context”. The footnotes to these pages were read; the rest of the essay was skimmed by keyword only. Addendum 2026-10-14: Read in full for the 1.138 Kealey draft in the journal's PDF (https://lltjournal.ca/index.php/llt/article/view/2657; OJS metadata confirms pp. 67–94 and gives Memorial University). Not a reply to Bercuson's essay: p. 68 calls it 'This essay and the following contribution by David Bercuson', and its starred note says 'Both essays were delivered at the McGill Conference, "Class and Culture: Dimensions of Canada's Labour Past," 7-8 March 1980', revised 'extensively'. It answers Bercuson's 1979 charge of 'obeisance to E.P. Thompson, the guru' (p. 87). Further passages: the project 'always placed the relationship between classes at the centre of the story' (p. 69); the four-stage periodization (p. 74); region 'increasingly misplaced' as 'the crucial variable', 'western exceptionalism', n. 25 'David Bercuson has been most guilty of this', 'everything was different everywhere' (pp. 74–77); ethnicity and 'the official ethnic interpreters' (pp. 77–80); Gutman's influence on Palmer's and Kealey's books (p. 82 n. 33); 'the materiality of culture itself' (p. 85); 'Class-for-itself' (p. 86); 'it is now necessary to locate class conflict and class struggle at the centre of modern Canadian history' (p. 89); McKay's unpublished paper 'one of the most substantive critiques of Thompson and culturalism' (p. 91 n.); the 1970s cohort 'active in the new left and influenced by the rebirth of Marxist scholarship' (p. 93).

verification.note: PDF citation line on p. 5: Acadiensis XXI, 2 (Spring 1992), pp. 5–47; author line Ian McKay. Pages 5–9 read closely, with notes 1–13. Nova Scotia 'became Scottish' in the second quarter of the twentieth century; 'hazy generalizations and ethnic stereotypes' became 'a natural and obvious "commonsense"'. Broad answer: 'it was part of an international anti-modernist wave, a local version of a general middle-class search for something outside and better than the crisis-ridden modern world it inhabited' (pp. 8–9). Narrow answer: Premier Angus L. Macdonald 'used the state's cultural power' to fuse a romantic, essentialist Scottishness with tourism (p. 9). Note 12 (p. 9) quotes Lears's definition of American antimodernism (No Place of Grace, p. xv) and adds 'and, I would also add, in the "simple life" and in "nature"'. Pages 13–14 and note 32 also read: the concept of 'invented tradition' is useful 'provided it is acknowledged that all traditions are historically constructed', and Trevor-Roper is said to rely on 'a naive historical realism'. Note 1: a revised version of a paper given to the CHA in 1990. The rest of the article was searched by keyword only, not read. Checked against: UNB Libraries Acadiensis article page and PDF (article/view/11913; PDF download 11913/12757).

sources.scope_note: McKay's own in-period statement of antimodernism as the frame for Nova Scotia's invented identity; his checked use of Lears.

verification.note: Érudit PDFs (llt32ob01, llt33art01) opened; Érudit citation gives pp. 10–72 and 13–68; Crossref record for Part II (doi:10.2307/25143788). Read: Part I opening, p. 10: Thompson's histories “occupy a special and influential place”, alongside “a nagging denigration of his accomplishments”; a footnote lists Greg Kealey's obituary in the St. John's Evening Telegram (5 September 1993). Keyword search of both parts found biography and political history, not an account of Thompson's reception in Canadian labour history (except Queen's University seminars in 1988 and a Kingston theatre visit). Shows that the Canadian Committee on Labour History's journal gave Thompson a two-part obituary of some 120 pages; it is not evidence of his influence on Canadian research. Addendum 2026-10-14: Both parts downloaded from the journal's site (https://lltjournal.ca/index.php/llt/article/view/4897 and /4917) for the 1.134 drafts, searched in full and read at Part I pp. 67–68 and Part II pp. 16–18. Part I, p. 68: Thompson's socialist humanism against Stalinism, 'governed as it was by anti-intellectualism, moral nihilism, and the denial of the creative agency of human labour'; 'In the mechanical idealism of Stalinism's appropriation of the base/superstructure metaphor, all of humanity's being could be reduced to a mere reflection of the economic substance of society'; n. 64 cites 'Socialist Humanism' and 'Agency and Choice' and Palmer's own Making of E.P. Thompson, 48–51. Part II, p. 17: The Making as 'a polemic against abbreviated economistic notations of Marxism' in which 'the creation of the working class was that of a determined process: steam power plus the factory system equals the working class', quoting Thompson from interviews (n. 9 lists Hogben 1988, Scott 1980 and the Visions of History interview; not read). sources.title: Lucien Bianco, review of Kenneth Pomeranz, The Making of a Hinterland: State, Society and Economy in Inland North China, 1853–1937 (1993), Études chinoises 15 (1996): 242–245.
sources.citation: Lucien Bianco, review of Pomeranz, The Making of a Hinterland (1993), Études chinoises 15 (1996): 242–245.

verification.note: Review read in full in the Persée text layer, pp. 242–245 (Persée record etchi_0755-5857_1996_num_15_1; OpenAlex W2981359141: vol. 15, issue 1, pp. 242–245). The book is 'ambitieux, intelligent, informé, bien argumenté' but 'ne convainc pas tout à fait'; Huang-Yun, where the Yellow River and Grand Canal cross, covers roughly western Shandong (p. 242). Pomeranz 'ne sépare jamais l'enquête régionale du débat théorique', setting Huang's involution model beside the 'breakthrough' theses of Myers, Rawski and Brandt (the OCR reads 'Ramski'); central thesis: the state gave up its priority on reproducing the population and its regional redistribution, concentrating resources on competitive regions and sectors; the 'coût économique, social et écologique' for a region become peripheral 'au sens skinnérien' was extremely heavy; 'La dégradation de l'environnement se taille la part du lion dans la démonstration de K. Pomeranz, qui consacre trois chapitres sur cinq au déboisement du Shandong occidental et au déclin catastrophique des travaux d'entretien du fleuve Jaune et du Grand Canal' (p. 243). Tables and appendices estimate damage from deficient water control to agriculture, transport and trade; a population 'privée de bois' burns straw, grass, roots and animal dung needed as fertiliser; 'Il postule plus qu'il ne prouve une stratégie délibérée de développement sélectif'; praise for 'la remarquable monographie sur le contrôle des eaux du Grand Canal et du fleuve Jaune' (p. 244); chapter 2 on cotton and local social structure (pp. 244–245). A reviewer's characterisation of the book's contents, not Pomeranz's text.

sources.scope_note: In-period review: the 1993 book's ecological chapters, its regional-development thesis and a critique of its proof.

verification.note: Capsule review read in full on the Foreign Affairs page (dated 2000-05-01); Crossref 10.2307/20049750: Foreign Affairs 79:3 (2000), p. 162. 'Pomeranz takes a neo-Malthusian, ecological approach that focuses on access to food and raw materials.' The core areas of China, Japan and India 'shared similar levels of technological and institutional development with Europe by 1750'; 'Europe had more institutional slack, easier access to coal (which was crucial, in the author's view), and cheap imports of sugar and cotton harvested by slaves in its New World colonies.' A later reading by Carson's biographer. 'In one of the most controversial parts of her book, Carson presented evidence that some human cancers were linked to pesticide exposure. That evidence and its subsequent elaboration by many other researchers continue to fuel one of the most challenging and acrimonious debates within the scientific and environmental communities' (p. xvi). 'It was clear to the industry that Rachel Carson was a hysterical woman whose alarming view of the future could be ignored or, if necessary, suppressed'; 'the industry spent a quarter of a million dollars to discredit her research and malign her character. verification.note: Later reading. JSTOR copy read as posted in an MITx course on edX (courses.edx.org asset 'VirginSoilWMQ'), pp. 703–711 and 718–720 closely, the rest searched for 'Crosby'. Crossref 10.2307/3491697: WMQ 60(4), October 2003, from p. 703. Jones quotes Crosby's 1976 definition (pp. 703–704). 'Even as Crosby's model of virgin soil epidemics remains a central theme of the historiography of the Americas, it has been misunderstood and misrepresented. Crosby actually downplayed the "genetic weakness hypothesis" and instead emphasized the many environmental factors that might have contributed to American Indian susceptibility to Old World diseases, including lack of childhood exposure, malnutrition, and the social chaos generated by European colonization' (p. 704). Historians 'have often reduced the complexity of Crosby's model to vague claims that American Indians had "no immunity"' (p. 704). Writers who 'attribute depopulation to irresistible genetic and microbial forces ... risk being interpreted as supporting racial theories of historical development' (p. 705). Crosby 'later described how thousands of years of disease exposure in Eurasia had created an Old World "superman"' (p. 707; the paragraph's n. 12 cites Ecological Imperialism, p. 34). 'McNeill, Crosby, and other historians utilized virgin soil theory' to restore causation (p. 711). Crosby's opening assertion of immunological defencelessness 'and the Darwinian tone of his other work jarred with the article's concluding emphasis on environmental causes of Indian susceptibility'; 'Crosby's work has been cited as both proof of immunological weakness and as evidence against it' (p. 719).

verification.note: Read in full from the journal's own PDF (galley 1543; scanned, local English OCR; folios 107–110; signed 'Bruce Curtis, Carleton University'). Passages used: 'Anyone who has worked with manuscript census data must be impressed with the meticulous and painstaking analysis undertaken here' (p. 109); 'But I cannot say I enjoyed reading this book. sources.citation: Ian Davey, review of Bruce Curtis, Building the Educational State: Canada West, 1836–1871 (Lewes and London, ON: Falmer Press and Althouse Press, 1988), Historical Studies in Education / Revue d'histoire de l'éducation 1, no. 1 (1989): 161–165.

verification.note: Read in full from the journal's own PDF (galley 1498; scanned, local English OCR; folios 162–165 from the running heads, the first page being 161 per the OJS record). Passages used: Corrigan's preface, Curtis 'makes us see differently' (p. 9 of the book, as Davey quotes it; the OCR reads 'dif3ferently'); 'one of the great strengths of Curtis' approach is his grounding of Foucault's analysis of power and subjectivity within a marxist theory of state formation and cultural forms' (p. 161); Curtis's argument that 'the construction of the Educational State was accomplished only through the destruction of a prior educational organization and the marginalization of the structure of educational possibilities' (book p. 15, quoted pp. 161–162); 'there is no reference to Gramsci or the theory of hegemony in the bibliography or the index' (p. 162); state schooling as 'the anchoring of the conditions of political governance in the selves of the governed' (no page given by Davey; p. 162); education 'was not a means to government; education was government: government of the self' (book p. 110, quoted p. 163); 'public education was administered into dominance only through a myriad of local struggles' (book p. 132, quoted p. 163); 'My major criticism of Curtis is that he fails to provide an adequate account of patriarchal relations in the period', his framework 'privileges class conflicts' (p. 165).

sources.scope_note: In-period review of Building the Educational State; the main witness to the book's wording.

sources.title: Bryan D. Palmer, review of Bruce Curtis, True Government by Choice Men? (1992), and Allan Greer and Ian Radforth, eds., Colonial Leviathan (1992), Labour/Le Travail 31 (1993): 365–367.
sources.citation: Bryan D. Palmer, joint review of Bruce Curtis, True Government by Choice Men? Inspection, Education, and State Formation in Canada West (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1992) and Allan Greer and Ian Radforth, eds., Colonial Leviathan: State Formation in Mid-Nineteenth Century Canada (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1992), Labour/Le Travail 31 (1993): 365–367 (in the issue's 'Reviews / Comptes Rendus' section, pp. 365–433).

verification.note: Read in full (pp. 365–367) in the journal's own PDF of the reviews section (lltjournal.ca article 4891, galley 5764; scanned pages with a text layer; folios 365, 366 and 367 printed in the running heads). Passages used: 'THESE BOOKS are searching for the state in pre-Confederation Canada'; 'In their purpose they can only be applauded; but their search is at times disturbingly narrow' (p. 365); Curtis 'telescopes the process of state formation in Canada West in the 1840s into the emergence of educational inspectors' and 'this study is too minutely focused' (p. 365); the promotional claim that Curtis 'presents a systematic application of the insights of ... Marx, Weber, Durkheim, Gramsci, and Foucault' (p. 365); as a 'model' Curtis's account 'is overstated to the point of distorting actual historical relations in the evolution of state and civil society' (p. 366); 'the collection lacks coherence' (p. 366); 'The single most important contribution of the articles in this collection, also developed by Curtis, is the notion that the coming of ‘responsible government’ actually entailed the subversion of the reform strategy of the 1830s' (p. 366); the gender essays read as 'complementary to the revisionist assessment of ‘responsible government’ as an expression of a slight [sic] of hand that promised popular sovereignty at the same time as it delivered institutionalized subordination and regulation' (pp. 366–367); 'Books like these make the job easier' (p. 367). Palmer names Greer's chapter on the birth of the police (the text layer prints the name as 'Allan Green's', p. 366).

sources.scope_note: In-period critique of Curtis's inspection study and of Colonial Leviathan, by the atlas's Bryan Palmer. Used in the Curtis and Greer entries.

sources.title: Allan Greer, “Wage Labour and the Transition to Capitalism: A Critique of Pentland,” Labour/Le Travail 15 (Spring 1985): 7–22.
sources.citation: Allan Greer, “Wage Labour and the Transition to Capitalism: A Critique of Pentland,” Labour/Le Travail 15 (Spring 1985): 7–22.

verification.note: Read in full (pp. 7–22) in the journal's own PDF (lltjournal.ca article 2454, galley 2857; scanned with a text layer, also OCR'd locally; folios from the running heads). Passages used: Pentland's work is 'a fundamentally incoherent book' and 'neglects the broader context needed to grasp this general transformation' (p. 9); Pentland 'follows the lead of his Toronto mentors in conflating the Canadian economy and its overseas trade' and 'While Innis, Creighton, and their contemporary disciples confine their attention to relations of exchange, however, Pentland at least focuses on the ‘social relations of production’', so 'it seems fair to regard him as the labour historian of the staples school' (p. 9); subdivision of holdings resulted from 'the introduction of domestic industry or of seasonal waged work in the fur or timber trades' (p. 16); Pentland's ethnic argument belongs to 'an ambivalent but, in the end, predominantly liberal, view of the advent of capitalism' (p. 18); 'my own view is that agriculture was organized primarily around the satisfaction of family subsistence needs through family production. There were surpluses and a portion of these were sold, but a significant proportion was diverted to priests and seigneurs through feudal exactions' (pp. 18–19); 'Feudal peasants or market-conscious farmers? No doubt the debates will continue' and 'none of these social formations were dominated by the capitalist mode of production' (p. 19; n. 16 cites Paquet and Wallot 1972 for the commercial view); 'capitalist enterprise had to adapt itself to the prevailing non-capitalist environment' (p. 20); Pentland's neglect of the household economy 'inevitably leads him to write women out of his history' (p. 20); 'If they did, I have no doubt that the aggregate agricultural output would embody vastly more labour than all the furs and squared timbers and other ‘staple products’' (p. 20); subsistence producers 'were therefore scarcely of interest to bourgeois theorists from Adam Smith to Harold Innis and Clare Pentland' (p. 21). Note 2 (p. 8) discusses Kealey's and Palmer's readings of Pentland, calling Palmer's Working-Class Experience an 'otherwise excellent synthesis'. Note 14 announces Peasant, Lord and Merchant as forthcoming.

sources.scope_note: Greer in his own words on the pre-capitalist household economy of early Canada, the transition to capitalism and the staples tradition.

verification.note: Front matter read in the Maryland State Archives electronic edition (megafile/ecp/26/037, file olson00.html: copyright page, contents, acknowledgments p. vii, introduction pp. ix–x; the HTML gives no page break inside the introduction, so introduction quotations are cited as pp. ix–x). Chapter text not read. Quoted: 'There is a tempo and a pattern to urban growth'; 'City growth is a boom-and-bust sequence of "long swings," with eighteen years or so separating the neighboring peaks. This applies equally to North America and Europe over at least two centuries, and to much of the world in the last hundred years'; 'This book is about city building, an internal dynamic of the city-state, and how Baltimoreans see themselves and their situation. In that sense, Baltimore is America, in its rhythm of building up and tearing down, swarming and dispersing'; the gaps she names: 'The most serious gap is our ignorance of the lives of slaves and servants in Baltimore', the Polish Catholic community, and 'the strategies of landowners and real estate investors in each round'; 'the city's social record is built into its dwellings' (pp. ix–x). verification.note: Read in full for pp. 5–23 for revision 1.142 (evidence-ancient-roots.md §2a), archive.org numbersinhistory00delb. Quoted: ‘We must have historians not only of the Greeks, the Romans, or the Middle Ages, but also specialists for Constitutional History, or Economic History … On this basis, for forty years, I have studied the History of the Art of War’ (pp. 5–6); from the Swiss–Burgundian battles ‘an historian might draw conclusions regarding the course of the battles of Marathon and Plataeae’ (pp. 6–10); Herodotus wrote ‘forty or fifty years after the events’, so that what people tell ‘a generation after will very often be not history, but only legend’ (pp. 8–10); ‘the first point to which in any history of war we have to direct our attention is the number of the warriors’ (p. 11); Thucydides’ figures for Athenian citizen soldiers are ‘subjectively beyond every doubt’, though ‘the interpretation of what the numbers really meant … is not absolutely to be determined’ (pp. 16–17); he questions Caesar’s numbers for the Gauls and Hannibal’s Lacinian inscription reported by Polybius (p. 16); ‘All numbers control each other mutually’, with Moltke’s 1870 deployment as ‘a common standard of measure’ (pp. 17–19); Xerxes’ host (pp. 22–23). Beloch is not named in the pages read. One shared source id for the 1913 lectures (the 1900–1960 research also cites Delbrück).

sources.scope_note: A second Delbrück text beside the 1900 preface: numbers compared across eras and analogy between periods.

verification.note: Read in part for revision 1.142 (evidence-ancient-roots.md §2b), archive.org antikeschlachtfe01krom: Vorwort pp. V–VII; Einleitung pp. 1–7; Mantinea, Beilage I, pp. 90–97 in part; Sellasia, Beilage I, pp. 252–265, and Beilage II, pp. 266–267, in part. Quoted: the book is ‘die Frucht einer Expedition “zur Erforschung antiker Schlachtfelder in Griechenland”’ of spring 1900 with Oberst Janke and ‘Goppel, Hauptmann im Großen Generalstabe’, supported by the Strasbourg faculty, the Berlin Academy and Schlieffen ‘durch Beurlaubung und Ausstattung eines Generalstabsoffiziers’ (Vorwort, signed October 1902); mottoes from Moltke (‘Die Örtlichkeit ist das von einer längst vergangenen Begebenheit übriggebliebene Stück Wirklichkeit’) and Clausewitz; the subject ‘fast allein von Männern genährt …, die von philologisch-historischen Forschungen aus an die Sache herangetreten sind’ (p. 2), with Frederick the Great and Clausewitz quoted for military neglect of antiquity; Grundy’s surveys named as an English precedent (p. 3); the Hellenistic era ‘uns kongenial’ (pp. 5–7, his own presentist framing); Polybius on Ephorus quoted and partly qualified, ‘Polybios’ Urteil setzt bestimmte, aber falsch wiedergegebene Tatsachen in den Berichten des Ephoros voraus’ (pp. 93–96); on Sellasia, Delbrück’s change of view is ‘die Folge meines Vortrages, speziell des Nachweises, daß die Oinusebene weit schmaler ist, als Delbrück, auf ungenaue Reiseberichte gestützt, angenommen hatte’ (p. 252); at stake is ‘die Beurteilung des Polybios und seine Zuverlässigkeit als Kriegschriftsteller und Historiker überhaupt’ (p. 264); Plutarch weighed against Polybius as ‘der … weit- und militärfremde Philosoph von Chäronea’ (p. 266). Delbrück’s side of the dispute (Kriegskunst II and his replies) and Kromayer’s 1900–01 lecture texts are unread; the account of Delbrück’s change of view is Kromayer’s.

sources.scope_note: Battlefield survey with General Staff collaboration (1900) and a published dispute with Delbrück.

verification.note: Read in part for revision 1.142 (evidence-ancient-roots.md §2c) through single-page OCR of a Digital Library of India scan (archive.org 30081001012420): Vorwort pp. V–VI; contents pp. VII–IX; Einleitung pp. 1–3; Kromayer’s ‘Quellen und Literatur’ pp. 14–17. Greek and Roman warfare treated together; Orient, Carthage, Gauls and Germans excluded (‘Wir wollten lieber “multum” als “multa” geben’); strategy and tactics added against ‘der vorwiegend antiquarischen Betrachtungsweise’ (Vorwort). The introduction quotes Veith, who cites Delbrück approvingly on discipline (‘Alle Verschiedenheiten des griechischen und römischen Kriegswesens gehen zurück auf die Verschiedenheit der Disziplin’) and calls the Greek ‘im innersten Wesen unsoldatisch’ (pp. 1–2), national-character generalisations of their time. Arrian ‘sachverständig’, with Ptolemy an equally expert source, and ‘Arrian allein ist militärisch gebildet’ (p. 14); Polybius’ ‘Polemik gegen die Schlachtbeschreibungen älterer Schriftsteller ist jedoch nicht immer gerechtfertigt’ (p. 14); military commentators ‘seit Folard’ projected ‘gewisse militärische Lieblingsideen, Theorien’ onto the ancients (pp. 15–16); ‘Sowohl die historisch-philologische als auch die militärische Fachbildung sind also jede für sich unzureichend’ (p. 16); Hans Droysen (1888–89) on the antiquarian side, Delbrück on ‘der Kunst der Kriegführung’ (p. 17; not Johann Gustav Droysen). sources.title: Polybius, Histories 12.25e–28a, trans. W. R. Paton, Loeb Classical Library, vol. IV (1925), LacusCurtius transcription.
sources.citation: Polybius, Histories 12.25e–28a, trans. W. R. Paton, Loeb Classical Library, vol. IV (1925), LacusCurtius transcription.

verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.142 (evidence-ancient-roots.md §1b): the Timaeus polemic on method, 12.25e–28a, with the Loeb page numbers shown on LacusCurtius. Quoted: the three parts of systematic history, ‘the first being the industrious study of memoirs and other documents and a comparison of their contents, the second the survey of cities, places, rivers, lakes, and in general all the peculiar features of land and sea and the distances of one place from another, and the third being the review of political events’ (12.25e.1, pp. 375–377); Ephorus ‘seems to me in dealing with war to have a certain notion of naval warfare, but he is entirely in the dark about battles on land’, and his Mantinea (362) is ‘quite imaginary … This becomes evident if we get a correct idea of the ground and then number the movements he describes as being carried out on it’ (12.25f, pp. 379–381); ‘It is neither possible for a man with no experience of warlike operations to write well about what happens in war, nor for one unversed in the practice and circumstances of politics to write well on that subject’ (12.25g.1, p. 381); such writers resemble ‘painters who make their sketches from stuffed bags’ (12.25h, pp. 381–383); ‘it will be well with history either when men of action undertake to write history …’ (12.28.1–5, pp. 403–405); the inquirer without experience, ‘even if present he is in a sense not present’ (12.28a, pp. 407–409). Book 12 is fragmentary and polemical, and the attack on Timaeus is also self-promotion; it is recorded as an ancient claim about who is competent to write war history, not as a neutral standard. Greek not collated. URL supplied at release (release/fixes-1.141.md, finding 12), checked by the coordinating session.

Quoted: the narrative ‘rests partly on what I saw myself, partly on what others saw for me, the accuracy of the report being always tried by the most severe and detailed tests possible’ (1.22.2); ‘want of coincidence between accounts of the same occurrences by different eye-witnesses, arising sometimes from imperfect memory, sometimes from undue partiality for one side or the other’ (1.22.3); ‘a possession for all time’ (1.22.4); of Mantinea (418), he could not put down the numbers ‘with any accuracy. verification.note: Read in part for revision 1.142 (evidence-ancient-roots.md §1f): the prologue and 1.8, in Latin only; no published English translation was collated, and English renderings in the atlas are the research compiler’s own. Quoted: what is scattered ‘apud diversos historicos vel armorum disciplinam docentes’ is to be brought together, a task needing ‘labor diligens ac fidelis’ (prologue); ‘De historiis ergo vel libris nobis antiqua consuetudo repetenda est. Sed illi res gestas et euentas tantum scripsere bellorum, ista, quae nunc quaerimus, tamquam nota linquentes’ (1.8: the historians wrote only the deeds and outcomes of wars, leaving out what is now sought, as though it were well known); he compiles what Cato the Censor, Cornelius Celsus, Frontinus, Paternus and imperial constitutions set down, ‘velut in ordinem epitomata’ (1.8). The work’s date was not verified (a publisher’s summary of Hanson’s Cambridge chapter gives about AD 400). sources.title: David A. Bell, “Un dret egal,” London Review of Books 29, no. 22 (15 November 2007) (review of Lynn Hunt, Inventing Human Rights).
sources.citation: David A. Bell, “Un dret egal,” London Review of Books 29, no. 22 (15 November 2007) (review of Lynn Hunt, Inventing Human Rights).

verification.note: Complete text read via WebFetch extraction for revision 1.144 (no pagination). Bell's summary: epistolary novels (Pamela, Clarissa, Julie) taught identification with others; torture condemned by the 1780s; a "logic of rights" after 1789. Criticisms: the account after 1789 through the present is compressed into 38 pages, concentrating on 1948 (the second research pass quotes "the period after 1789 'in a breezy 38 pages'"); he reports Moyn's criticism and calls it "partly misplaced"; novels at the expense of theatre, painting and emulation; causation hinted at; ordinary people who did not read novels also embraced rights; the "new cultural history" tends to flatten texts and actions. He calls her French Revolution studies "luminous", reads The Family Romance (1992) as tracing family imagery from paternal monarchy to fraternal republic, a thesis the 2007 book keeps, and credits her with popularising "the new cultural history". Verdict: "a rich, elegant and persuasive essay" that "raises more questions than it can answer".

verification.note: Read in part for revision 1.144 (data/extension-2026/post2000-wave1-2026-10-17/evidence-pomeranz.md §1c) in the International Socialism online reprint (posted 3 November 2004, "From The Journal of Asian Studies 61, no. 2, May 2002"); no print pagination, and the reprint breaks off mid-sentence. Read: the opening, "Pomeranz’s Argument", their thesis and the first sections on social-property relations. In Brenner and Isett's summary, Pomeranz attributes the divergence to "access to the land, raw materials, and above all slave labor, of its American colonies"; "The burden of our critique is that, from the dawn of the early modern period, the institutional framework or system of social-property relations that structured the English economy was radically different … from that of the Yangzi delta"; "It was this already existing decisive divergence, not England’s capacity to gain access to the American colonies … that explains why the two economies distanced themselves"; the delta followed "a Malthusian pattern", England "a Smithian pattern"; "Contra Pomeranz"; landlord extraction is "a major rentier element … that Pomeranz ignores". Their delta evidence draws heavily on Huang (1985, 1990, 1996). Pages to be cited from the JAS print before release. Addendum 2026-10-18: Revision 1.145: the opening paragraph was also read on Cambridge Core by the Brenner research (data/extension-2026/brenner-2026-10-18/evidence-brenner.md §7c); the critique is now drawn as robert_brenner → kenneth_pomeranz.

sources.citation: Edward Said, “Always on Top,” London Review of Books 25, no. 6 (20 March 2003) (review of Catherine Hall, Civilising Subjects).

verification.note: Complete text read via WebFetch extraction for revision 1.144 (no pagination). Summary: Birmingham and Jamaica, Baptist missionaries, the 1831 and Morant Bay rebellions, Eyre; empire continually made through "imperial personalities"; biological racism displacing paternalist rhetoric by the late 1860s. Praise: "Hall’s excellent book"; a "dialectical" history; "empire is always on top of what it rules". Criticisms: sermons, polemics, letters and philosophy treated alike as "evidence"; she does not draw on Ranajit Guha and the Subaltern Studies group for unrecorded voices; culture treated as propaganda (after John MacKenzie) rather than analysed as disguising colonial violence (Arnold, Carlyle, Dickens); objections to "map" and a "gratuitous" différance. Frames it with Culture and Imperialism's "overlapping territories" and "intertwined histories".

verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.147 in the OpenEdition HTML (paragraphs 1–31 and notes; no print pagination, so paragraphs are cited). ¶1: the category entered historians' common vocabulary when Lynn Hunt published her 1989 volume. ¶11: the critique of mentalités "était peut-être injuste"; shared demands: individual uses over statistical distributions, "les modalités spécifiques de leur appropriation", representations of the social world as constitutive of differences and struggles. ¶12: the risk of "une définition impérialiste de la catégorie". ¶19: forms "participent, elles aussi, à la construction de leur signification". ¶24: "C'est dans cet écart que s'insinuent reformulations et détournements, appropriations et résistances." ¶25: the linguistic turn holds "que la « réalité » n'est pas une référence objective, extérieure au discours"; against it, the logic of discourses and the logic of conduct are not identical; historians can rely on Foucault's distinction between "« formations discursives » et « systèmes non discursifs »" (n. 25) and Bourdieu's between "« sens pratique » et « raison scolastique »" (n. 26, Méditations pascaliennes, 1997); n. 24 cites Keith Baker for the linguistic-turn position. ¶26: social positions "ne sont pas seulement un effet des discours ; elles en désignent également les conditions de possibilité." ¶28: representation "en est presque venu à désigner en lui-même la nouvelle histoire culturelle". ¶31: "La cohérence la new cultural history est-elle aussi forte que le proclamait Lynn Hunt ? La diversité … permet d'en douter"; the field is defined "par l'espace d'échanges et de débats" among historians who refuse to reduce phenomena to one dimension and "se sont éloignés tant des illusions du tournant linguistique que des héritages contraignants qui postulaient le primat du politique ou la toute-puissance du social." verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.147 in the journal's PDF (13 pp.): translator's presentation pp. 1–3 and the rejoinder pp. 4–13, in Portuguese; the 1995 English original was not seen, so English renderings here are translations from the Portuguese. The translation is published with the permission of the Brose-White Trust and the Hayden White Literary Estate (p. 1 n. 1). Chartier's 1993 article ("Quatre questions à Hayden White", Storia della Storiografia 24, 1993, 133–142) is unread; its questions are known only as White restates them and through the French phrases he quotes. The debate ran in Storia della Storiografia "entre 1993 e 1995" (translator, p. 2). Q1 (p. 4): whether it is "contraditório" to invoke a determinist theory of language and grant historians a poet's freedom; White: "Eu estava falando de discursos, não do cosmos." Q2 (p. 5): whether tropology should be historicised; White: the fourfold model was culturally dominant from the late Renaissance to Modernism, and "O modelo talvez tenha sido menos útil do que eu imaginava; não foi muito bem recebido." Q3 (pp. 6–7): what becomes of the "opérations très lourdes et exigeantes que sont la constitution d'un corpus documentaire, le contrôle des données et des hypothèses, la construction d'interprétation" (Chartier's French as White quotes it); White: they belong largely to the "teatro" of scholarship and have "uma função ritual". Q4 (pp. 7–8): how his relativism answers the crimes of tyrannies and "plus encore, la Shoah" and revisionist denial; White: the deniers "negam a ocorrência de certos eventos" and "Não há qualquer questão metodológica em jogo". White thanks Chartier for discussing "amigavelmente" (p. 4). Dates: the journal page assigns the translation to volume 28 (2025) and gives its publication date as 14 April 2026 (rechecked 2026-10-19); 2025 is the volume year, not an established posting date. The original rejoinder is 1995.

verification.note: Complete text read for revision 1.147 (LRB page; no pagination). The memoir is offered as the "flip side" of Age of Extremes, "not world history illustrated by the experiences of an individual, but world history shaping that experience" (Hobsbawm as quoted); "a kind of fifth volume, in more personal register, of a continuous project". On remaining in the Party after 1956 (Hobsbawm quoted): "I still belong to the tail-end of the first generation of Communists"; Anderson: "Most people would see in it evidence of an exceptional integrity and strength of character". Criticism: "His treatment of the traditions of others is much less impressive. Here a lack of generosity disfigures too many judgments" (Samuel, Thompson, the New Lefts); no "real intellectual engagement with the issues that haunted the trajectory of European Communism"; Marxism Today's role in "preparing the cult of Thatcher". On history: Hobsbawm gives "a good account of the rise of the analytic social history associated with the Annales and Past & Present … regretting its later retreat with the cultural turn of the 1980s" (Anderson's report); his thinking about the past is more original than Braudel's, to be seen in On History (Anderson's judgment). The memoir is unread.

verification.note: Complete text and endnotes read for revision 1.147 (NYRB page; no pagination). A "Hobsbawm generation" of historians who began between about 1959 and 1975; Primitive Rebels "first appeared in 1959"; Labouring Men, Industry and Empire and Captain Swing "substantially recast the economic history of Britain and the story of the British labor movement"; the trilogy's scheme "eventually became the “conventional” interpretation"; The Age of Revolution 1962, The Age of Capital 1975 ("Hobsbawm’s single greatest work"), The Age of Empire twelve years later. Hobsbawm is "by training and inclination an economic historian, and an analytical one" who "mostly avoids military or political narrative"; "though unashamedly Eurocentric, Eric Hobsbawm has a unique range" (endnote 2 defends the European focus). The "one" defect: "the categories right/left, fascist/Communist, progressive and reactionary seem to be very firmly set, and pretty much as they first presented themselves to Hobsbawm in the Thirties"; Bolshevism gets "no critical analytical attention except on its own restricted terms"; "“real socialism” in the lands between Germany and Russia merits just six pages"; nationalism "is a rather neglected subject". Verdict: "a challenging, often brilliant, and always cool and intelligent account". The Age of Extremes itself is unread.

verification.note: Complete text read for revision 1.147 (NYRB page; no pagination). Headnote: the lecture "was given at the beginning of the academic year at the Central European University"; he opens: "It is an honor to be asked to open this academic year" (delivered autumn 1993, exact day not given). "For history is the raw material for nationalist or ethnic or fundamentalist ideologies, as poppies are the raw material for heroin addiction … If there is no suitable past, it can always be invented." "I used to think that the profession of history, unlike that of, say, nuclear physics, could at least do no harm. Now I know it can." "We cannot invent our facts. verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.147 (published interview; Scott's spoken words). "I got interested in this question when I was doing my book on the [veil]"; post-colonial studies were "critical of the notion that modernity was the end point of the civilizing process"; "I decided that I would go back to all these sources and try and figure out how to develop a critique or a genealogy that could expose these contradictions"; "there was a whole psychoanalytic dimension that I could explore there"; "how do I write a critique of secularism without rejecting it".

verification.note: Publisher abstract read for revision 1.147 (via OpenAlex); the article body is unread. Abstract: Eley and Nield's essay is marked by a tension between updating social history by detaching it from materialist assumptions and continuing "narratives of working-class political agency"; "By insisting that class is still the best way of analyzing inequality and mobilizing resistance to it, the authors foreclose other possibilities for thinking about contemporary politics and for writing critical history"; her questions "don't exclude class but they don't require it either". Addendum 2026-10-22: Body read in full for revision 1.152 (Cambridge PDF with text layer, accessible this session though not labelled open access; data/extension-2026/languages-of-class-2026-10-22/evidence-spread.md §6.3): pp. 69–75; the abstract confirmed verbatim; 'Assent to Discourse' (p. 69); 'Patrick Joyce has been expelled from the fold and Kathleen Canning is now at its center' (p. 69); the use of Rancière (pp. 70–71); 'Structures come into being through discourse' (p. 71); the two questions (p. 72).

verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.147 (publisher PDF, print pages). p. 149: "an elegantly argued and ambitious effort to analyze and historicize the theoretical premises and political practices that shaped the most recent struggle for gender equality in France"; the law passed on 6 June 2000; the book "focuses on the challenge parité poses to French universalism"; Only Paradoxes to Offer (Harvard, 1996) is called "much misunderstood" and described as analysing "feminism’s constitutive contradictions". p. 150: Scott's "often (but not exclusively) symptomatic reading"; the parity strategy of "desymbolization" (Scott p. 54) and "the redefinition of the human individual as plural, as a type of two" (Scott p. 61, as Dean quotes it). p. 151: Agacinski sought to "sex" the political body (Scott p. 115). p. 152: "How, more precisely, might the concept of parité be thought in reference to other multiply 'different' groups such as Muslim women and lesbians?"; "an important contribution not only to the history of French feminism and French republicanism, but to the theory of history." sources.title: Joan Wallach Scott, “The Incommensurability of Psychoanalysis and History,” History and Theory 51, no. 1 (February 2012): 63–83.
sources.citation: Joan Wallach Scott, “The Incommensurability of Psychoanalysis and History,” History and Theory 51, no. 1 (February 2012): 63–83.

verification.note: Author's abstract read for revision 1.147 (via OpenAlex); the article body is unread. "Psychoanalysis can force historians to question their certainty about facts, narrative, and cause; it introduces disturbing notions about unconscious motivation and the effects of fantasy on the making of history. This was not the case with the movement for psychohistory that began in the 1970s. Then the influence of American ego-psychology on history-writing promoted the idea of compatibility between the two disciplines in ways that undercut the critical possibilities of their interaction." De Certeau supplies "theoretical insight into the uses of incommensurability"; Lyndal Roper's work shows "both its limits and its value".

sources.citation: Cécile Laborde, “The Politics of the Veil,” Books & Ideas (La Vie des idées), 30 January 2008; review of Joan Wallach Scott, The Politics of the Veil (Princeton University Press, 2007).

verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.147 (HTML, no pagination; date from page metadata). "one of the best Anglo-American critical commentaries" on the headscarf affair and the 2004 law; Scott "takes the discourse of French republicanism … seriously"; the ban "acted as a (literally) hysterical diversion from the profound problems faced by a French society fractured around class, race and gender"; "Particularly acute are Scott’s analyses of the re-importation of the civilizing mission in post-colonial France"; an ideal of "uncovered sexuality" underlay the republican critique of Islam's "covered sexuality"; Scott draws on Baubérot, Balibar, Gaspard, Khosrokhavar and Nordmann. Criticism: "their normative premises and broader political implications remain unclear – a standard limitation of discourse analysis in general"; the counter-discourse of toleration "may turn out to be as problematic" as the republican discourse Scott criticises. Laborde's phrase calling Only Paradoxes Scott's "first major book" is inaccurate and is not reused. The book is unread.

verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.147 (HTML). A philosopher's hostile review: "a useful attempt to redress Western self-congratulation, but it subjects the West to uniquely purist standards"; "Scott claims to espouse Michel Foucault’s “genealogical” approach, yet she is anachronistic, ahistorical and oddly absolutist in demanding from 19th-century Europeans moral attitudes that tally with her own"; O'Grady quotes Scott that modern Western societies were "founded on gender inequality". sources.citation: Joan Wallach Scott, “Unanswered Questions,” American Historical Review 113, no. 5 (December 2008): 1422–1430; authorised Spanish translation by Julia Constantino, “Preguntas no respondidas,” Debate Feminista 40 (2009): 100–110.

verification.note: Read for revision 1.147. English original: first two paragraphs only (WebFetch extraction; AHR paywall), including "I want to insist that the term gender is useful only as a question." The Spanish translation, published with the author's permission (Debate Feminista 40, 2009, https://doi.org/10.22201/cieg.2594066xe.2009.40.1441), was read in full; pages below are Debate Feminista pages, and English renderings are the atlas's translations, not Scott's English. p. 101: at the Berkshire Conferences of the 1970s, "Ahí escuché por primera vez que se mencionaba el género; fue en una ponencia de Natalie Zemon Davis" (citing Davis 1976: 90); her colleagues at Brown in the early 1980s taught her "que las diferencias sexuales no las establecía la naturaleza, sino que esto se realizaba a través del lenguaje"; "yo no fui el origen del concepto de género, ni siquiera entre las historiadoras". p. 102: gender "trata del planteamiento de preguntas históricas; no es un tratado programático ni metodológico"; she quotes Heidi Tinsman: "lo que conforma una categoría útil para el análisis feminista es un asunto de geopolítica más que una actualización epistemológica" (Tinsman as Scott quotes her; Tinsman's article is unread). p. 108: Meyerowitz wrote that in questioning gender's continued vitality in the 1999 edition Scott moved "en direcciones nuevas"; Scott: "Eso no es totalmente correcto", and she asserts a continuing concern with "cómo se conciben las diferencias entre los sexos", whether the object is French universalism, feminist movements or the politics of the veil (Meyerowitz's article is unread). Also p. 108: in 1999 she worried that gender had "perdido su agudeza crítica"; "me ha sido útil acudir a la teoría psicoanalítica; no a sus articulaciones conservadoras". p. 109: "el género es el estudio de la relación (en torno a la sexualidad) entre lo normativo y lo psíquico, el intento de colectivizar la fantasía"; "es el género el que produce significados para el sexo y la diferencia sexual". pp. 109–110: the question marks removed from the 1986 title perhaps should have stayed.

verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.147 (HTML; dated 1 December 2019). Scott treats academic freedom "as an ethical practice in Michel de Certeau’s sense" (Whitaker's words), quoting her: it "defines a distance between what is and what ought to be"; "disciplinary practice is no power-free zone"; Scott ends diagnosing academic freedom "under grave threat from many different directions". Whitaker mentions Scott's service on the AAUP committee on academic freedom (dates not given; not checked). The book is unread.

sources.title: Susan Whitney, “Is Secularism Really Better for Women?,” Literary Review of Canada, January–February 2018; review of Joan Wallach Scott, Sex and Secularism (Princeton University Press, 2017).
sources.citation: Susan Whitney, “Is Secularism Really Better for Women?,” Literary Review of Canada, January–February 2018; review of Joan Wallach Scott, Sex and Secularism (Princeton University Press, 2017).

verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.147 (HTML, no pagination). Scott's introduction as Whitney quotes it: "this is not a conventional intellectual or social history of the word secularism" but "a set of arguments bound loosely by a periodization related to the emergence of modern western nation-states (from the 18th century on)"; her aim to "open—not to definitively close—a conversation". Whitney: for Scott the book exemplifies Foucault's "history of the present"; its "polemical aim" is "to counter the notion that gender equality is somehow inherent in secular societies"; terms gain meaning through opposites (secularism/religion, man/woman, public/private, west/Orient, Christianity/Islam). Whitney reports Joanne Meyerowitz calling the 1986 article a "foundational text". Verdict: "a challenging, timely, and important book". The book is unread.

sources.title: Herman Paul, “A Loosely Knit Network: Philosophy of History After Hayden White,” Journal of the Philosophy of History 13 (2019): 3–20.
sources.citation: Herman Paul, “A Loosely Knit Network: Philosophy of History After Hayden White,” Journal of the Philosophy of History 13 (2019): 3–20.

verification.note: Author's manuscript in the Leiden University repository (https://hdl.handle.net/1887/69888) read in full for revision 1.147 (21 manuscript pages with notes); pages cited are manuscript pages, not journal pages. ms 1: White's death in March 2018; "no other author occupies a position in the field that is remotely as central as White’s … philosophers of history relate to White’s work, either by building upon it or by dissociating themselves from it." ms 10–11 and n. 22: a JSTOR search of History and Theory 1960–2013 "yields 428 hits for 'Hayden White' and 142 hits for 'Hayden V. White'" (Paul's count of articles mentioning him); Harlan, Kleinberg and Kuukkanen position themselves towards White. ms 13 n. 32: the textbooks The Emergence of Liberal Humanism (1966, with Coates and Schapiro) and The Ordeal of Liberal Humanism (1970, with Coates). ms 14: "Metahistory did not intend to replace 'explanation' by 'narrative.' Instead, the book argued that historians explain, among other things, through narrative means." ms 15–16: The Content of the Form; later forays into "'modernist events,' 'intransitive writing,' witness literature, trauma, the sublime, and the 'practical past'". ms 17–19: criticism "from all sides": Ankersmit (tropology "not nearly philosophical enough"), Ricoeur (sources "set constraints"; White "runs a risk of erasing genre boundaries between history and fiction"), David Carr (1986), "'internal realists' such as Chris Lorenz" who argue that "White downplays the importance of rational debate among historians", Runia's "presence" against "Whitean representationalism"; criticism is sometimes "a response elicited by the perceived dominance of his work" (ms 19). The centrality claim is Paul's.

sources.title: Hayden White, “The Practical Past,” Historein 10 (2010): 10–19.
sources.citation: Hayden White, “The Practical Past,” Historein 10 (2010): 10–19.

verification.note: Open access (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0); read in full for revision 1.147, printed pp. 10–19 (the cover sheet's "2011" and "© 2012" are posting dates; volume 10 is dated 2010). p. 14: Kant's practical question "what should I (we) do?" leads to "the practical past". p. 16: "The practical past is made up of all those memories, illusions, bits of vagrant information, attitudes and values which the individual or the group summons up as best they can to justify, dignify, excuse, alibi or make a case for actions to be taken in the prosecution of a life project"; after Oakeshott (n. 3) and Koselleck's "space of experience" (n. 2); "the historical past was a past constructed by historians. It existed in books and scholarly essays only." p. 17: professional historiography was set up in the universities "to serve the interests of the nation-state". p. 18: "philosophy of history belongs to the class of disciplines meant to bring order and reason to a 'practical past' rather than to that 'historical past' constructed by professional historians".

verification.note: Open-access journal PDF read in full for revision 1.147, pp. 127–135. White used "the concept of the practical past, borrowed from Michael Oakeshott, as a means to argue for individual choices --ethical, moral and existential-- in contemporary life, and hence as a way to escape the burden of history" (abstract, p. 127); "if one considers 'The Burden of History' and 'The Practical Past' as the framing articles of White’s career, then Metahistory … can be seen as the instrument chosen by White to liberate humankind from the tyranny of the (positivist) past" (pp. 129–130). Mediated quotations: The Practical Past (2014), preface xiii and pp. 8–9, 12–15; White's 2005 reply to Moses, p. 336: history "has sold out any claim to relevance to present existential concerns of the societies in which it is practiced in order to purchase a much more dubious claim to 'objectivity' in the study of the past" (Spiegel, p. 132). An admirer's reception statement.

verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.151. On A Rule of Property for Bengal (Paris: Mouton, 1963): the debates among East India Company administrators over a "permanent settlement", entrusting revenue to "a class of native entrepreneurs who had solid interests in the land and were politically reliable" (Guha, p. 9, as she quotes); Guha "set out their different economic premises – deriving from mercantilist, physiocratic, and classical political economy – and demonstrated that, despite their differences, they nonetheless shared a common political focus, establishing the permanence of orderly dominion." verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.151. Reviews the Harvard University Press paperback, which he dates 1998. "A compilation of three interrelated essays", "an ideological critique of the South Asian colonial and nationalist state and its historiography from the perspective of Antonio Gramsci's philosophical reflections on 'hegemony' and 'domination'" (pp. 373–374). Reports Guha's argument that colonial historiography perpetuated "the prejudicial view, derived from the Hegelian view of history, that precolonial India had no state, therefore no history" (p. 376). Criticism: the absence of "the voices of the 'subalterns' themselves" reduces the project "to a mere armchair ideological 'discourse' on behalf of the subalterns" (p. 375); Guha "conveniently skips the portrayal of the Hindu social order in the Muslim historiography of India" (p. 377); "Guha's intellectual indebtedness to the Marxist-Leninist-Gramscian ideology of western European history does not allow him to examine Indian nationalist history from the perspective of Indian reality" (p. 379). He also calls Guha "a formidable Marxist historian" (p. 375). The reviewer is identified only by place (Minneapolis).

verification.note: Read in part for revision 1.151: the introduction and the sections "Guha and the Bourgeois Revolutions" and "Does Guha refer to the bourgeois revolutions?". Petitjean: "In April 2013, at the annual Historical Materialism conference held in New York, Vivek Chibber appeared alongside Partha Chatterjee in a much-anticipated critical debate." Chibber: "I argue in PTSC that Guha's work is both foundational for the entire Subalternist project ... and that it is fundamentally flawed. Its flaw is that it generates a set of contrastive claims about the Indian bourgeoisie and Indian capitalism that rest on a comparison with the European achievement. But the comparison fails because Guha quite dramatically misunderstands the European story"; "the European bourgeoisie was no more committed to an integrated political culture than was its Indian counterpart". Chatterjee's three replies, as Chibber reports them (Chatterjee's text is unread): Guha makes no claims about the classic bourgeois revolutions, only about the historiography of colonial India; "Indian bourgeoisie" means the Congress's middle-class leadership; any European referent is the mid-twentieth-century British state. Chibber quotes Dominance without Hegemony p. 19 (the bourgeoisie's "historic triumphs in England in 1648 and France in 1789") and p. 5 (its "failure to measure up to the heroism of the European bourgeoisie in its period of ascendancy").

verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.151. The book "grew out of a series of lectures delivered by Ranajit Guha ... at the Italian Academy for Advanced Studies in America at Columbia University" (p. 530); Guha "takes the German philosopher Georg Hegel and his conception of 'World-History' (Weltgeschichte) to task" (p. 530). Guha quoted: history outside World-History is "a creative engagement with the past as a story of man's being in the everyday world. It is in short, a call for historicality to be rescued from its containment in World-History" (book p. 6); "World-History made its way to the subcontinent as an instrument of the East India Company's colonial project and helped it set up the Raj" (book p. 51). Praise: the book joins "a growing chorus of scholars" on everyday life (Lefebvre, Certeau, Goffman, Le Roy Ladurie) and is "definitely worth a read for those interested in ... recent postcolonial efforts to rethink the practices of disciplinary history and thereby provincialize its European lineages" (pp. 531–532). Criticism: "losing sight of the state at the level of the everyday might mean the loss of it as an object of critique"; "Guha's arguments are mostly confined to the conceptual level"; he "seems to attribute to Hegel's World-History an agency that is hard to locate in the historicality of the colonial world" (p. 532). The book itself is unread.

verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.151. Citation: "Bruno Latour has undertaken an ambitious analysis and reinterpretation of modernity, challenging the most fundamental categories such as the distinction between modern and pre-modern, nature and society, human and non-human. He has completely re-imagined Science Studies, pioneering new ethnographic methods ... His influence has been felt internationally and well beyond the social study of science, in history, art history, philosophy, anthropology, geography, theology, literature and legal studies." Les Microbes (1984) and Science in Action (1987) "represents some of the most important work in the field of science studies and in the social history of knowledge"; "In We Have Never Been Modern (1991) Latour offered his major polemical statement"; "His work in the 1980s established Actor Network Theory (ANT) as a widely used methodology"; Politics of Nature (1999) is said to propose "a parliament of things"; Inquiry into Modes of Existence (2012). The page lists the 2013 Holberg Symposium "From Economics to Ecology" (4 June 2013) in his honour and records his death on 9 October 2022. A prize committee's judgement, attributed as such.

verification.note: Profile and the opening of the citation read on 2026-10-19 for revision 1.151: Latour "revolutionized the conventional view of science by treating nature, humans, laboratory equipment, and other entities as equal actors, and describing technoscience as the hybrid network of these actors. His philosophy re-examines 'modernity' based on the dualism of nature and society. He has a large influence across disciplines, with his multifaceted activities that include proposals regarding global environmental issues." With Woolgar he "opened up a new field called 'anthropology of science'"; actor-network theory was developed "in collaboration with Michel Callon, John Law, and other researchers"; "Recently, Latour has advocated the necessity of a serious understanding of the Anthropocene". verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.151 in the author's typescript (18 pp.; typescript pages cited; author's page https://www.bruno-latour.fr/node/501.html). Prepared for the Holberg Prize Symposium 2013, "From Economics to Ecology", Bergen, 4 June 2013 (note, p. 18); the author's page, rechecked on 2026-10-19, says it was "Originally written as lecture given at the occasion of the Holberg Memorial Prize Symposium 2013" in Bergen on 4 June, with the title "Which Language Should we Talk with Gaia?", which establishes delivery. "Indeed, as Dipesh Chakrabarty has proposed, it has become once again an agent of history, or rather, an agent of what I have proposed to call our common geostory" (p. 3; n. 6 cites "The Climate of History: Four Theses"). "While the older problem of science studies was to understand the active role of scientists in the construction of facts, a new problem arises: how to understand the active role of human agency not only in the construction of facts, but also in the very existence of the phenomena those facts are trying to document?" (p. 2). "It is human history that has become frozen and natural history that is taking on a frenetic pace" (p. 13). "The prefix 'geo' in geostory does not stand for the return to nature, but for the return of object and subject back to the ground" (p. 17).

sources.citation: Andrew Pickering, review of Bruno Latour, We Have Never Been Modern, trans. Catherine Porter (Harvard University Press, 1993), Modernism/modernity 1:3 (September 1994): 257–258.

verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.151. "Bruno Latour's Science in Action (1987) was the most important book on science, technology and their intertwining with society published in the 1980s"; its actor-network analysis "flew in the face of technological and social determinist perspectives" (p. 257). The argument as Pickering states it: the "modern constitution" bequeathed by Boyle and Hobbes, a "program for purifying the discourses of nature and society"; "'We have never been modern,' as Latour puts it, but we found a way of thinking that we were" (p. 257). Criticism: "Latour is explaining too much with his conception of modernity"; "There is a note of complacency here at the end of Latour's book"; "I would not want to ratify what we have always done without first getting clear on the specifics of history—the history of the factory and labor, say, of gender relations, of militarism, colonialism, empire, and so on. There is no place in Latour's story for such specifics" (p. 258). He quotes the book's "Parliament of Things" (p. 144).

verification.note: Read in part for revision 1.151 in the authors' pre-publication typescript (typescript pages cited): the joint opening and Latour's pp. 1–4, and Chakrabarty's response pp. 19–22. Published online 19 November 2020 (Crossref). Joint opening: Latour responds to Chakrabarty's "The Planet: An Emergent Humanist Category" (Critical Inquiry, 2019); the piece arose from "an actual and ongoing conversation in which we have been engaged for a while" (p. 1). Latour: "Chakrabarty's introduction of the Planetary triggered a seism in philosophy of history" (p. 3); "Geohistory breaks down any claim to have a human-oriented history" (p. 4); the aim is "to give a spatial and geopolitical ground to counteract the notion of the arrow of time implied so far by traditional philosophies of history" (p. 4). Chakrabarty: "Much of the ground my own thoughts move on is shared with Latour", and he will "suggest some friendly amendments to what Latour proposes" (p. 21).

verification.note: Read in part for revision 1.151 in the author's typescript (21 pp.; typescript pages cited): pp. 1–2, 5, 7, 10. The author's page dates the essay 2001 and lists a German translation in Soziale Welt (2001). ANT is "a deliberate attempt at terminating the use of the word 'social' in social theory to replace it with the word 'association'"; "ANT actually has a forefather, namely Gabriel Tarde" (p. 1). "I must confess that I myself never enquired further than the dismissive footnotes of the Durkheimians" (p. 2). "Instead of saying, like Durkheim, that we 'should treat social facts as a thing', Tarde says that 'all things are society', and any phenomenon is a social fact" (p. 5). "Tarde can be said to have invented microhistory many decades before its discoverers" (p. 7). "It is not only the case that Durkheim has taken society as the cause instead of seeing that it is never more than a highly provisional consequence" (p. 10); the Durkheimians "have simply taken the explanandum for the explanans" (p. 10). Durkheim's position is given only as Latour presents it; Joyce's introduction is unread.

verification.note: Read pp. 57–61 and 77–78 with notes 1–10; pp. 62–76 skimmed. Members of the collective shifted "from a positivist and empiricist orientation to one grounded more squarely in a literary criticism" (p. 60); "in the same volume [Subaltern Studies IV, 1985] Gayatri Spivak criticized subalternist historians for having adopted positivist methodologies"; "herself a literary critic, [she] urged historians to continue their efforts to recover subaltern consciousness even while knowing this was impossible" (p. 60, citing SS IV pp. 342, 345). "a collection of twenty-five essays", including revisions of "Echo", "Terror: A Speech after 9/11" and "Scattered Speculations on the Subaltern and the Popular"; "The introduction to An Aesthetic Education argues for the ab-use or 'productive undoing' of Enlightenment aesthetics in order to highlight the double binds that bind the era of globalization (1)"; ab-use is the use of "something, in this case the Enlightenment, without remaining faithful to it, turning it into a model for training the imagination for 'learning to live with contradictory instructions' (3)" (pp. 207–208; the numbers in parentheses are Lochner's citations of the book). verification.note: Read in full. The book is "the most recent in a venerable sub-genre in comparative literature of faux-prophetic visions" (p. 160); "Spivak's 'planetarity' thus comes off as a rather traditional sounding humanism—odd words indeed for a renowned deconstructivist to find herself mouthing" (p. 161); "Thus does Spivak's 'planetarity' deconstruct itself" (p. 162); but he grants "Spivak's cogent and necessary arguments for comparative literature as a corrective supplement to 'the apparitions of Cultural and Ethnic Studies'" (p. 162).

sources.title: Arik Moran, "'The Rani of Sirmur' Revisited: Sati and Sovereignty in Theory and Practice," Modern Asian Studies 49:2 (2015): 302–335; published online 17 September 2014.
sources.citation: Arik Moran, "'The Rani of Sirmur' Revisited: Sati and Sovereignty in Theory and Practice," Modern Asian Studies 49:2 (2015): 302–335; published online 17 September 2014.

verification.note: Read in part (abstract, introduction, the section on post-colonial discourse theory and Pahari sati, conclusion, notes 1–5; cited by section). Abstract: "a close reading of the records reveals profound discrepancies between Spivak's interpretation and conditions that existed in and around the kingdom at the time"; "the rani was actually an astute ruler, similar to her peers in the West Himalayan elite". Critique: "while Spivak concedes that her analysis is 'not historical work' insofar as 'historical knowledge cannot be established on single cases', her misreading of evidence goes beyond the boundaries of the discipline as such"; yet "her fresh approach to source material does point to the cardinal importance of interdisciplinary research". He cites Eaton (2000) in n. 3. His paraphrase of her 1988 answer as an unequivocal "no" is his reduction and is not reused.
